scope: All 2,164 previously non-verified records reviewed using the unchanged complete note, with explicitly labeled authoritative supplements where needed. The 1,321 previously module-verified records remain unchanged. Reference-link coverage does not establish answer certainty.

reviews.answer_text: Aggregate-only access does not uniquely identify inference control.
reviews.hint: Distinguish access restrictions from prevention of indirect disclosure in ADB24.
reviews.explanation: ADB24 defines inference control as preventing disclosure of protected individual facts indirectly through allowed aggregates. Merely hiding details while exposing aggregates can also be implemented by access-controlled views. The stem does not mention inference attacks, differencing queries or indirect disclosure. Therefore A is plausible in a statistical-database context, but B also fits the literal access description.

evidence.quote: If a question merely says aggregates visible and details hidden, access-restricted views also fit; explicitly mention prevention of indirect disclosure to identify inference control uniquely.

choices.label: A
choices.explanation: Inference control protects individuals against indirect disclosure through aggregates, but that threat is not explicitly stated.

choices.label: B
choices.explanation: An access-controlled aggregate view can expose summaries while restricting visibility of underlying details.

choices.label: C
choices.explanation: Integrity control restricts valid data rather than deciding which detail users may see.

choices.label: D
choices.explanation: Encryption protects encoded content and does not itself specify aggregate-only query access.

choices.label: E
choices.explanation: At least inference control and access control plausibly fit, so none is not supported.

reviews.answer_text: The rows-and-tables claim is false for the object-oriented model.
reviews.hint: Read persistent objects, associations and inheritance in ADB01–ADB03.
reviews.explanation: ADB01 distinguishes an OODBMS from relational rows and tables: its primary model is persistent objects with identity, state and behavior. ADB02 supports communication through methods and object references, and ADB03 supports reuse through inheritance. Relational presentation as tables is the contrasting model. Therefore A is the false statement; the source image is not needed to establish that conceptual distinction.

evidence.quote: It does not primarily present objects as rows and tables.

choices.label: A
choices.explanation: This is false: an OODBMS primarily models persistent objects rather than relational rows and tables.

choices.label: B
choices.explanation: Presenting relations as tables describes the relational contrast correctly.

choices.label: C
choices.explanation: Object identity and method-based collaboration are supported object-model concepts.

choices.label: D
choices.explanation: Inheritance and reusable object behavior support reuse, so this is not the false statement.

choices.label: E
choices.explanation: A is false, so none of the above cannot answer this negative question.

reviews.answer_text: Relation is not the defining concept of an OODBMS.
reviews.hint: Read persistent objects and stable identifiers in ADB01.
reviews.explanation: The defining unit of an object database is an object with identity, state and behavior. ADB01 explains both persistence beyond program execution and identifier stability throughout an object lifetime. Relation is instead the characteristic abstraction of the relational model. Thus C is the one statement that fails to describe an OODBMS.

evidence.quote: An object combines identity, state and behavior.

choices.label: A
choices.explanation: Objects are the defining units of the object-oriented database model.

choices.label: B
choices.explanation: An OODBMS provides persistence so objects survive the program execution that created them.

choices.label: C
choices.explanation: This is false for OODBMS: relation is the central abstraction of the relational model.

choices.label: D
choices.explanation: The object identifier remains stable throughout the lifetime of its object.

reviews.answer_text: Array is not an atom constructor.
reviews.hint: Read atomic and collection constructors in ADB04.
reviews.explanation: ADB04 lists integer, real, Boolean and string as examples of basic atomic values. An array instead supplies indexed positions and is a collection constructor, even when a programming variable holds it as one value. Consequently integers, reals and strings fit the atom category while an array is the requested exception.

evidence.quote: An atom is one basic value, such as an integer, real, Boolean or string.

choices.label: A
choices.explanation: An integer is explicitly listed as a basic atomic value.

choices.label: B
choices.explanation: A real number is explicitly included among atomic values.

choices.label: C
choices.explanation: A string is a basic atomic value under the object-model convention used here.

choices.label: D
choices.explanation: An array contains indexed positions and is a collection constructor rather than an atomic one.

reviews.answer_text: At transaction end, on commit or abort.
reviews.hint: Compare basic, strict and rigorous two-phase locking in ADB12.
reviews.explanation: Rigorous 2PL retains both shared and exclusive locks until commit or abort, unlike basic 2PL, which permits release in its shrinking phase. FDB-style early release would allow interference before completion and would not meet rigorous locking. The locks are eventually released at the transaction boundary, so never is also false.

evidence.quote: Rigorous 2PL retains both shared and exclusive locks until that point.

choices.label: A
choices.explanation: Releasing locks at the beginning would not protect the transaction's later accesses.

choices.label: B
choices.explanation: Rigorous 2PL does not permit early release during ongoing transaction execution.

choices.label: C
choices.explanation: Both shared and exclusive locks remain held until commit or abort ends the transaction.

choices.label: D
choices.explanation: Locks are released at completion; the protocol does not hold them forever.

reviews.answer_text: Two-phase commit.
reviews.hint: Read Oracle commit-point selection in ADB39.
reviews.explanation: ADB39 explicitly links Oracle COMMIT_POINT_STRENGTH to choosing the commit point site in distributed transactions. This is a role in two-phase commit, which coordinates an atomic outcome among participants. It is not a setting for acquiring or releasing locks, nor for checkpoints that bound recovery work. Higher eligible strength is preferred for the commit point.

evidence.quote: Oracle's COMMIT_POINT_STRENGTH helps choose the commit point site in its distributed transaction mechanism, with higher eligible strength preferred.

choices.label: A
choices.explanation: Commit-point strength selects an Oracle distributed-commit role within the two-phase commit mechanism.

choices.label: B
choices.explanation: Transaction locking controls concurrent access rather than choosing the distributed commit point site.

choices.label: C
choices.explanation: Two-phase locking governs lock acquisition and release, not the distributed commit decision.

choices.label: D
choices.explanation: Checkpoints record recovery state and do not choose an Oracle commit point site.

reviews.answer_text: The type-constructor, tuple and atom claims are false as printed.
reviews.hint: Read value-shape constructors versus object creation in ADB04.
reviews.explanation: ADB04 distinguishes a type constructor, which defines value shape, from an executable object constructor. A tuple groups named component values into one structured record rather than a collection of records. An atom is one basic value, not multivalued. ADB01 supports identifier immutability over an object lifetime. Therefore B, C and D are all false, making this a defective single-choice question.

evidence.quote: A type constructor defines the shape of a value; it is not the same as an executable constructor operation that creates a new object.

choices.label: A
choices.explanation: OID stability over the object lifetime is true, so it does not answer the negative stem.

choices.label: B
choices.explanation: This is false under the note's convention: a type constructor specifies shape rather than executing object creation.

choices.label: C
choices.explanation: A tuple is one structured record of components, not a collection of records.

choices.label: D
choices.explanation: An atom represents one basic atomic value rather than a multivalued collection.

reviews.answer_text: Relationship.
reviews.hint: Read inverse declarations between opposite association directions in ADB05.
reviews.explanation: An inverse declaration connects two navigation directions of the same association, such as Department.employees and Employee.department. ADB05 explains that it maintains their relationship consistency. It does not declare a class, establish inheritance or name an ordinary scalar attribute. Thus Relationship is the applicable category, and the inclusive option is false.

evidence.quote: An inverse declaration pairs opposite directions of the same relationship.

choices.label: A
choices.explanation: Inverse pairs the two directions of one relationship and expresses their consistency.

choices.label: B
choices.explanation: The other categories are not all valid uses of the inverse declaration.

choices.label: C
choices.explanation: Inverse is not the keyword that declares a class or establishes a class hierarchy.

choices.label: D
choices.explanation: The declaration links relationship directions rather than declaring an ordinary scalar attribute.

reviews.answer_text: ODL is a schema-definition language and develops logical schemas; the choices overlap.
reviews.hint: Read ODL schema definition versus storage implementation in ADB05.
reviews.explanation: ADB05 explicitly makes C and D true: ODL defines object-database schemas and is a data definition language. A is unclear because implement a logical schema may loosely mean express its definition, or may suggest actual implementation, which the note distinguishes. That uncertainty also affects All choices. The printed options cannot support a unique answer without clarifying implementation and removing the overlap.

evidence.quote: An MCQ calling ODL both a DDL and a language for developing logical schemas offers overlapping true descriptions, so its exact wording matters.

choices.label: A
choices.explanation: It fits if implement means express a schema definition, but not if it means implementing storage.

choices.label: B
choices.explanation: All depends on the unstated meaning of implement in A; it cannot remove the overlap safely.

choices.label: C
choices.explanation: ODL describes the logical object schema, including classes, attributes and relationships.

choices.label: D
choices.explanation: ODL is explicitly the schema-definition language for object databases.

reviews.answer_text: No-wait.
reviews.hint: Read timestamp-free lock conflict handling in ADB13.
reviews.explanation: ADB13 states that no-wait aborts a transaction immediately when its lock request is incompatible and requires no age timestamp. Wait-die and wound-wait instead compare requester and holder ages. Wait-wait is not a defined prevention rule in the supplied note; merely allowing waiting does not establish a deadlock-prevention algorithm.

evidence.quote: A no-wait policy aborts immediately on an incompatible lock request and needs no age timestamp.

choices.label: A
choices.explanation: Wait-wait is not a specified deadlock-prevention mechanism here; unrestricted waiting does not prevent cycles.

choices.label: B
choices.explanation: No-wait aborts on an incompatible request immediately, without comparing transaction ages.

choices.label: C
choices.explanation: Wound-wait compares requester and holder timestamps to decide whether to abort a holder or wait.

choices.label: D
choices.explanation: Wait-die uses age timestamps to distinguish an older waiting requester from a younger aborted requester.

reviews.answer_text: Column-wise.
reviews.hint: Read physical row-oriented and columnar layouts in ADB41.
reviews.explanation: ADB41 defines columnar storage as grouping values by column, which avoids reading irrelevant columns and can improve compression for scans. Row-oriented storage instead groups each record's fields. Hierarchical and network models are logical representation alternatives rather than the physical column-oriented layout requested by the stem. Columnar layout alone does not determine the logical data model.

evidence.quote: Columnar storage groups values by column, reducing unnecessary column reads and aiding compression in scans

choices.label: A
choices.explanation: Row-wise grouping is row-oriented storage, the contrasting physical layout.

choices.label: B
choices.explanation: A hierarchy describes parent-child organization, not the columnar physical storage arrangement.

choices.label: C
choices.explanation: Columnar storage groups the values of each column together.

choices.label: D
choices.explanation: A network model concerns linked records rather than this column-oriented physical layout.

reviews.answer_text: The gaming scenario lacks the workload and consistency requirements needed to choose.
reviews.hint: Read distributed placement trade-offs and the need for a workload in ADB40/ADB45.
reviews.explanation: A real-time gaming label does not determine one database design. Distribution can place data near players; replication can improve read locality or availability; partitioning can divide player state; and NoSQL is a family of models rather than a latency guarantee. ADB40 requires ownership, placement, failure and conflict rules. The stem supplies none, so no single offered concept is established.

evidence.quote: Questions using best, important, common or faster need a workload and comparison criterion.

choices.label: A
choices.explanation: Replication can improve locality or availability, but update propagation and consistency requirements are missing.

choices.label: B
choices.explanation: A suitable NoSQL model might fit player state, but the label alone guarantees neither latency nor correctness.

choices.label: C
choices.explanation: Distribution can locate data near players, but communication and coordination costs must be specified.

choices.label: D
choices.explanation: Partitioning can divide player data, but interaction patterns and cross-partition requirements are unspecified.

reviews.answer_text: Recovery Manager is closest only in a generic model; the exact MySQL component responsibility is unspecified.
reviews.hint: Read separate backups versus buffers and vendor-specific architecture in ADB26/ADB45.
reviews.explanation: ADB26 already explains separate stored backups, recovery after loss and why buffers are not durable backup. It also warns that generic recovery-manager terminology does not establish an exact MySQL component contract. D is the closest generic DBMS role, but the literal vendor-specific stem supplies no architecture model or engine/version. This is ambiguity of attribution, not missing backup/recovery knowledge.

evidence.quote: Buffer management is not durable backup. Generic recovery-manager terminology should not be mistaken for an exact MySQL component specification.
State the minimum missing information: exact DBMS/version for vendor behavior;

choices.label: A
choices.explanation: A buffer manager caches working pages; the note explicitly distinguishes this from durable backup.

choices.label: B
choices.explanation: Transaction management coordinates transaction behavior rather than specifically identifying the asserted MySQL backup component.

choices.label: C
choices.explanation: A query engine processes queries rather than defining the missing durable-copy architecture contract.

choices.label: D
choices.explanation: Closest in a generic DBMS model only; the exact MySQL component responsibility is not established.

reviews.answer_text: Search collections and RDBMS contents can both include unstructured data.
reviews.hint: Read source content versus storage-product classification in ADB43.
reviews.explanation: ADB43 includes free text, images and audio as unstructured data and says web/search collections may contain them. It also explicitly allows text and BLOBs in a DBMS, so RDBMS systems can be possible sources too. Employee and registrar database names suggest structured records but do not prove actual contents; selecting only a search engine would incorrectly assume relational storage excludes unstructured content.

evidence.quote: A DBMS can also store text or BLOBs, so a storage product does not prove all its contents are structured.

choices.label: A
choices.explanation: Search collections can contain free text, images and other unstructured material.

choices.label: B
choices.explanation: Relational DBMSs can store text or BLOBs, so they can be sources of unstructured content.

choices.label: C
choices.explanation: An employee database may contain attachments, but its actual content is not specified by the name.

choices.label: D
choices.explanation: Registrar tables are a structured example, but unspecified attachments could add unstructured data.

reviews.answer_text: Association-rule mining: shoes ⇒ socks has confidence 0.75.
reviews.hint: Read co-occurrence, support and confidence in ADB43.
reviews.explanation: The observation is a conditional co-purchase pattern: among shoe purchases, socks also appear with probability 0.75. ADB43 defines this as the confidence of an association rule and explicitly distinguishes co-occurrence mining from clustering, classification and numeric regression. The store-layout decision uses that rule; it does not change the underlying technique or prove causation.

evidence.quote: If 75 of 100 shoe purchases include socks, confidence(shoes⇒socks)=0.75.

choices.label: A
choices.explanation: The rule captures shoe/sock co-occurrence with conditional confidence 0.75.

choices.label: B
choices.explanation: Clustering groups similar cases without target labels rather than directly discovering this co-purchase rule.

choices.label: C
choices.explanation: The stated evidence is an association rule, not a separately specified predictive modeling task.

choices.label: D
choices.explanation: Regression predicts numeric outcomes rather than identifying this purchasing co-occurrence rule.

reviews.answer_text: The order depends on what testing and evaluation mean in the chosen workflow.
reviews.hint: Read modeling, validation, final testing and deployment in ADB44.
reviews.explanation: ADB44 requires training on training data, validation for tuning, and held-out testing before deployment. It also says testing and evaluation can overlap. C fits a convention in which testing precedes a distinct business evaluation; A fits evaluation during model selection before final testing. The stem gives no convention, so those labels do not establish one universally correct sequence.

evidence.quote: Testing and evaluation are sometimes overlapping labels rather than universally distinct sequential phases.

choices.label: A
choices.explanation: Evaluation can mean validation/model selection before final held-out testing and subsequent deployment.

choices.label: B
choices.explanation: Deferring the only stated evaluation until after deployment omits evaluation before release.

choices.label: C
choices.explanation: This fits a workflow that treats testing as input to a distinct predeployment evaluation phase.

choices.label: D
choices.explanation: An initial evaluation of the same model cannot precede its training without an unstated preexisting model.

reviews.answer_text: Business understanding.
reviews.hint: Read the opening CRISP-DM activity in ADB44.
reviews.explanation: ADB44 starts the data-mining workflow by defining the business decision and its success criteria. This establishes why data will be collected and modeled. Integration, cleaning and feature selection prepare data after the problem has been understood; they do not replace the initial business-understanding stage. Thus A precedes the other listed activities.

evidence.quote: CRISP-DM starts with business understanding: define the decision and success criteria.

choices.label: A
choices.explanation: Business understanding first defines the decision to support and the criteria for success.

choices.label: B
choices.explanation: Data integration prepares sources after the business problem has been identified.

choices.label: C
choices.explanation: Cleaning improves data quality during preparation rather than defining the initial business objective.

choices.label: D
choices.explanation: Selecting relevant data depends on an already understood business problem and modeling objective.

reviews.answer_text: An instance of a class.
reviews.hint: Read class definitions versus individual objects in ADB01.
reviews.explanation: ADB01 explicitly distinguishes a class specification from each object instantiated from it. A class defines available attributes and operations, while an object is one individual instance with identity, state and behavior. A collection of attributes omits identity and behavior; a key or an intertable relationship belongs to a different relational description.

evidence.quote: A class specifies the attributes and operations of its instances; an object is one instance.

choices.label: A
choices.explanation: An object is an individual instance of a class with its own identity and state.

choices.label: B
choices.explanation: Attributes describe state but omit the identity and behavior that also characterize an object.

choices.label: C
choices.explanation: A database primary key is an identifier constraint, not the definition of an object instance.

choices.label: D
choices.explanation: A relationship between tables is a relational association rather than an object instance.

reviews.answer_text: Hiding and controlling access to internal object details.
reviews.hint: Read encapsulation and information hiding in ADB02.
reviews.explanation: ADB02 describes encapsulation as grouping state with operations and controlling access to implementation details. A withdrawal method can enforce rules while hiding storage. B states the relevant information-hiding aspect. Combining classes, associating objects and defining subtype hierarchies are distinct activities; none describes the encapsulation boundary around an object's state and operations.

evidence.quote: Encapsulation groups state with operations and controls access to implementation details.

choices.label: A
choices.explanation: Encapsulation groups an object's state and operations, not multiple classes into one entity.

choices.label: B
choices.explanation: Encapsulation controls access to the internal representation behind the object's operations.

choices.label: C
choices.explanation: Links between objects are associations rather than encapsulation itself.

choices.label: D
choices.explanation: Superclass/subclass structure concerns inheritance rather than information-hiding boundaries.

reviews.answer_text: Inherit applicable attributes and behavior from a superclass.
reviews.hint: Read is-a subtype relationships in ADB03.
reviews.explanation: ADB03 defines inheritance as deriving a subtype from a superclass and reusing its applicable attributes and behavior. B captures that idea. It does not inherently require multiple parents, dynamically create objects, or merely link unrelated objects. Those alternatives concern particular inheritance forms, instantiation or association rather than the general meaning of inheritance.

evidence.quote: Inheritance derives a subtype from a superclass, reusing applicable attributes and behavior.

choices.label: A
choices.explanation: Multiple parents are not a general requirement or guarantee of inheritance.

choices.label: B
choices.explanation: A subtype inherits applicable superclass attributes and behavior.

choices.label: C
choices.explanation: Dynamic object creation is instantiation, not the capability defined by inheritance.

choices.label: D
choices.explanation: Relationships between separate objects are associations rather than the is-a subtype relationship.

reviews.answer_text: Polymorphism.
reviews.hint: Read common interfaces with differing method implementations in ADB03.
reviews.explanation: ADB03 illustrates Shape.area dispatching to Circle.area or Rectangle.area according to the actual object. The common operation name has different compatible implementations, which is polymorphism. Inheritance can provide the subtype structure used by that mechanism, but is not itself the runtime dispatch behavior. Abstraction and encapsulation concern contracts and implementation access instead.

evidence.quote: The same operation can dispatch to different implementations: Shape.area() calls Circle.area() or Rectangle.area() according to the actual object.

choices.label: A
choices.explanation: Polymorphism lets the same interface operation invoke different implementations for compatible object types.

choices.label: B
choices.explanation: Abstraction exposes a relevant contract rather than selecting among differing method implementations.

choices.label: C
choices.explanation: Encapsulation controls internal access rather than providing type-dependent method dispatch.

choices.label: D
choices.explanation: Inheritance supplies a structural subtype relation; polymorphism describes the differing implementations through a common interface.

reviews.answer_text: Encapsulation.
reviews.hint: Read the combination of state and operations in ADB02.
reviews.explanation: The question specifically asks about placing data and methods inside one entity. ADB02 identifies that grouping as encapsulation, along with controlled access to implementation details. Abstraction concerns what the contract exposes; inheritance derives compatible subtypes; polymorphism invokes different implementations through a common interface. None of those replaces the state-and-method grouping named in the stem.

evidence.quote: combining state and methods specifically describes encapsulation.

choices.label: A
choices.explanation: Inheritance derives a subtype and reuses superclass features rather than naming state/method grouping.

choices.label: B
choices.explanation: Polymorphism varies implementations behind a compatible common interface rather than grouping data and methods.

choices.label: C
choices.explanation: Abstraction presents a relevant contract; the specific grouping asked for is encapsulation.

choices.label: D
choices.explanation: Encapsulation packages state and operations together within the object boundary.

reviews.answer_text: Links and interactions between objects.
reviews.hint: Read associations versus inheritance in ADB02.
reviews.explanation: ADB02 defines association as links between objects, commonly implemented with references, and describes methods invoking operations on other objects. C is the closest description of that collaboration. An association is not an is-a inheritance hierarchy, shared attribute definitions or duplication. For example, Student belonging to Department links objects without making either a subtype of the other.

evidence.quote: An association links objects, often through references; Department.employees can reference Employee objects.

choices.label: A
choices.explanation: Inheritance is an is-a relationship between types, distinct from association links between objects.

choices.label: B
choices.explanation: Having similar attributes does not itself define an association between particular objects.

choices.label: C
choices.explanation: Associations link objects and support their interactions or collaboration through references.

choices.label: D
choices.explanation: Association represents relationships rather than duplicated copies of the same database facts.

reviews.answer_text: Polymorphism describes the common-interface use; inheritance supplies its subtype relationship.
reviews.hint: Distinguish structural inheritance from runtime substitutability in ADB03.
reviews.explanation: Treating subclass objects through a common superclass reference is subtype polymorphism, while inheritance establishes why those objects are compatible superclass instances. ADB03 explicitly warns that a question contrasting these two needs to say whether it asks for the structural prerequisite or runtime use. The wording ensures does not resolve that distinction, so A and B remain plausible.

evidence.quote: If a question asks whether treating subclasses as a superclass is inheritance or polymorphism, clarify whether it asks about the structural prerequisite or the runtime use.

choices.label: A
choices.explanation: Polymorphism describes using different compatible subclass objects through the same superclass interface.

choices.label: B
choices.explanation: Inheritance establishes the superclass/subclass relationship that makes the shared treatment valid.

choices.label: C
choices.explanation: Abstraction exposes a contract but does not alone establish the subtype compatibility in the question.

choices.label: D
choices.explanation: Encapsulation controls representation access rather than determining superclass substitutability.

reviews.answer_text: Hide implementation details while exposing a relevant contract.
reviews.hint: Read abstraction as what rather than how in ADB02.
reviews.explanation: ADB02 explains abstraction through an operation's relevant contract: what withdrawal does is exposed without showing how storage implements it. B captures hiding those irrelevant internal details. This overlaps encapsulation, but abstraction emphasizes the view or contract. Combining classes, creating associations or listing class members is not its defining purpose.

evidence.quote: Abstraction presents the relevant contract—what withdrawal does—without exposing how it is implemented.

choices.label: A
choices.explanation: Abstraction does not mean merging several classes into one entity.

choices.label: B
choices.explanation: Abstraction exposes relevant behavior while hiding implementation details from the client view.

choices.label: C
choices.explanation: Establishing links between objects is association rather than abstraction's defining purpose.

choices.label: D
choices.explanation: A class specifies attributes and behavior; abstraction chooses the relevant contract exposed to users.

reviews.answer_text: Use an object through a compatible superclass or interface type.
reviews.hint: Read compatible subtype polymorphism and its limits in ADB03.
reviews.explanation: ADB03 allows a superclass or interface reference to denote compatible subclass objects. D is correct in that sense: the same object can be treated through its actual type and a compatible supertype. This does not permit arbitrary conversion to unrelated classes. Multiple inheritance, runtime class mutation and access to another object's private methods are different concepts and are not granted by polymorphism.

evidence.quote: Subtype polymorphism lets a superclass/interface reference denote objects of different compatible subclasses.

choices.label: A
choices.explanation: Inheriting from multiple classes is multiple inheritance, not the operation described by polymorphism.

choices.label: B
choices.explanation: Polymorphism does not change the actual class of an object dynamically.

choices.label: C
choices.explanation: Polymorphism does not bypass private-access restrictions on other objects.

choices.label: D
choices.explanation: An object can be used through compatible superclass/interface types; this does not mean arbitrary unrelated classes.

reviews.answer_text: Class.
reviews.hint: Read the class/instance distinction in ADB01.
reviews.explanation: A class is the specification that defines attributes and operations for its instances, as ADB01 states. An object is an instance conforming to that specification. An attribute accounts for part of state and a method for one operation, but neither individually defines the whole structure and behavior of the object type.

evidence.quote: A class specifies the attributes and operations of its instances; an object is one instance.

choices.label: A
choices.explanation: A class specifies the structure and available operations for its object instances.

choices.label: B
choices.explanation: An object is one instance of the specification rather than the specification itself.

choices.label: C
choices.explanation: An attribute represents part of an object's state rather than its whole structure and behavior.

choices.label: D
choices.explanation: A method implements an operation but does not alone define the complete object type.

reviews.answer_text: All four are replication approaches or dimensions; the stem supplies no discriminator.
reviews.hint: Compare replication timing with snapshot versus incremental transfer in ADB37.
reviews.explanation: ADB37 describes eager and lazy replication as propagation-timing policies, and snapshot and incremental replication as ways to transfer copies or changes. These dimensions can coexist rather than being exclusive alternatives. The question asks only for a commonly used approach, with no timing or transfer requirement, so every listed approach qualifies and a unique answer is unsupported.

evidence.quote: Snapshot replication transfers a copy at intervals; incremental replication transfers changes.

choices.label: A
choices.explanation: Eager replication coordinates propagation before the specified acknowledgment or commit point.

choices.label: B
choices.explanation: Lazy replication propagates changes later and can expose stale reads or require conflict handling.

choices.label: C
choices.explanation: Snapshot replication distributes a copy at intervals rather than necessarily sending each individual update.

choices.label: D
choices.explanation: Incremental replication transfers changes and can coexist with a propagation-timing policy.

reviews.answer_text: Each listed index/storage approach can accelerate suitable queries.
reviews.hint: Read index workload trade-offs in ADB23.
reviews.explanation: ADB23 gives ordered/range access for B/B+ trees, equality access for hashing and analytic uses for bitmaps. It also notes that clustered storage keeps related rows close. Each can speed a matching workload, but none is universally faster and maintenance costs remain. Since the question says only commonly used and supplies no predicate or workload, it cannot select a unique type.

evidence.quote: B/B+ tree indexes support ordered and range predicates; hash indexes target equality; bitmap indexes can help some analytic selections.

choices.label: A
choices.explanation: B-tree indexes support selective ordered and range access for suitable queries.

choices.label: B
choices.explanation: Hash indexes can accelerate equality lookups on the indexed key.

choices.label: C
choices.explanation: Bitmap indexes can accelerate suitable analytic selection workloads.

choices.label: D
choices.explanation: Clustered storage keeps related rows close and can reduce reads for appropriate access patterns.

reviews.answer_text: Reconsider the plan using updated cost information or statistics.
reviews.hint: Read choosing a plan again in ADB23.
reviews.explanation: ADB23 defines re-optimization as choosing a plan again when statistics, parameters or observed cardinalities suggest that the existing plan is unsuitable. B is the listed description of this cost reconsideration. Merely executing again with other values does not necessarily re-optimize, and changing the query language or redesigning the schema is not the definition.

evidence.quote: Re-optimization chooses a plan again when statistics, parameters or observed cardinalities suggest the old plan is unsuitable.

choices.label: A
choices.explanation: Re-execution with new parameters can reuse the same plan and is not inherently re-optimization.

choices.label: B
choices.explanation: Updated statistics can change cost estimates and lead to choosing a new execution plan.

choices.label: C
choices.explanation: Changing query language is not required to reconsider an execution strategy.

choices.label: D
choices.explanation: Schema reorganization is a design change rather than the definition of query re-optimization.

reviews.answer_text: Query caching may mean cached results or cached execution plans.
reviews.hint: Read result, plan and buffer caches in ADB22.
reviews.explanation: ADB22 separates result caching, which reuses returned rows, from plan caching, which reuses an execution strategy. The unqualified term query caching does not specify which is intended, so A and D both fit recognized meanings. Intermediate-result storage is materialization; metadata supports optimization but is not the same as either cached query answers or plans.

evidence.quote: A vague query caching question must specify which of these it means.

choices.label: A
choices.explanation: Result caching stores answers for reuse and requires invalidation when underlying data changes.

choices.label: B
choices.explanation: Retaining intermediate rows during a query is materialization rather than the specified result/plan cache distinction.

choices.label: C
choices.explanation: Catalog metadata supports optimization but is not itself cached query results or execution plans.

choices.label: D
choices.explanation: Plan caching stores an execution strategy for reuse without storing the returned rows.

reviews.answer_text: Repeated-crash behavior needs the algorithm and durable recovery progress.
reviews.hint: Read restartable undo and compensation records in ADB31.
reviews.explanation: No checkpoints does not imply identical work lists. ADB31 explains that durable compensation records preserve undo progress and pageLSNs can skip installed redo after another crash. Other recovery algorithms may reconstruct different lists. The stem supplies neither algorithm nor durable log/page state, so none of its universal recovery outcomes follows.

evidence.quote: Absence of checkpoints alone does not imply identical undo/redo lists.

choices.label: A
choices.explanation: The lists may coincide in a simple model, but absence of checkpoints does not force this.

choices.label: B
choices.explanation: Restartable recovery can preserve consistency despite repeated crashes; inconsistency is not inevitable.

choices.label: C
choices.explanation: Durable progress metadata can avoid some repeated work, but no such algorithm is specified.

choices.label: D
choices.explanation: A further crash does not inherently prevent a supported recovery algorithm from resuming.

reviews.answer_text: Abort all deadlocked transactions or select victims until all cycles disappear.
reviews.hint: Read victim selection and remaining cycles in ADB13.
reviews.explanation: ADB13 supports aborting all deadlocked transactions or choosing victims and repeating until no cycles remain. An arbitrary half need not hit every cycle. One victim breaks the cycle containing it, but other independent cycles can remain. Thus A and D are guaranteed general remedies; C additionally needs a single-cycle assumption.

evidence.quote: Abort a suitable victim, undo its effects and release its locks; repeat if other cycles remain.

choices.label: A
choices.explanation: Aborting all involved transactions removes the deadlocked waits, though it wastes more work.

choices.label: B
choices.explanation: An arbitrary half can leave a cycle among surviving transactions.

choices.label: C
choices.explanation: One victim breaks its own cycle, but the stem does not exclude other independent cycles.

choices.label: D
choices.explanation: Suitable victims are aborted repeatedly until all remaining deadlock cycles have been eliminated.

reviews.answer_text: ARIES and deferred modification can both be log-based.
reviews.hint: Read WAL/ARIES and deferred update in ADB29/ADB31.
reviews.explanation: ARIES uses WAL, sequence numbers and logged recovery metadata. Deferred modification conventionally logs changes for redo after commit without undo. ADB45 explicitly recognizes both as log-based. Shadow paging instead preserves old pages through a page map, while recovery in multidatabase systems names an environment rather than one recovery technique.

evidence.quote: ARIES uses WAL, page log sequence numbers (pageLSN), a transaction table and a dirty-page table.

choices.label: A
choices.explanation: Multidatabase recovery names an environment rather than identifying a particular log-based technique.

choices.label: B
choices.explanation: ARIES explicitly relies on WAL and logged recovery metadata.

choices.label: C
choices.explanation: Shadow paging preserves page maps as an alternative to conventional log-based recovery.

choices.label: D
choices.explanation: Deferred modification can use a log to redo committed changes without undo.

reviews.answer_text: ARIES uses undo/redo; immediate-update requirements also depend on page policy.
reviews.hint: Read steal/force and ARIES phases in ADB28/ADB31.
reviews.explanation: ADB31 explicitly gives ARIES redo followed by loser undo. Immediate update allows persistent changes before commit, but whether both undo and redo are needed depends on steal/force policy. The stem does not supply it. Deferred update normally uses redo only. The alternatives mix a specific algorithm with an underspecified update policy, preventing a unique exclusive answer.

evidence.quote: Undo reverses loser transactions.

choices.label: A
choices.explanation: Immediate update needs undo/redo under steal/no-force, but the relevant policy is unstated.

choices.label: B
choices.explanation: Usual deferred update is NO-UNDO/REDO rather than requiring both actions.

choices.label: C
choices.explanation: ARIES repeats history in redo and then undoes loser transactions.

choices.label: D
choices.explanation: ARIES is a listed algorithm explicitly using both redo and undo.

reviews.answer_text: Transaction management broadly and recovery management specifically.
reviews.hint: Read atomicity responsibilities in ADB06.
reviews.explanation: ADB06 assigns atomicity and durability support to recovery, within the broader transaction-management subsystem. Both A and D therefore fit at different responsibility levels. Concurrency control primarily provides isolation. Application logic must use transactions correctly, but it cannot independently recover incomplete persistent effects after a crash or guarantee the DBMS atomic outcome.

evidence.quote: Concurrency control primarily enforces isolation; recovery supports atomicity and durability.

choices.label: A
choices.explanation: Transaction management is the broader subsystem coordinating transaction guarantees, including atomicity.

choices.label: B
choices.explanation: Application logic alone cannot guarantee DBMS crash rollback of partial persistent effects.

choices.label: C
choices.explanation: Concurrency control primarily handles isolation rather than undoing incomplete work after failure.

choices.label: D
choices.explanation: Recovery specifically supports all-or-none effects by undoing incomplete transaction changes.

reviews.answer_text: Processing returns results and optimization selects efficient execution strategies.
reviews.hint: Read processing and optimization scope in ADB17.
reviews.explanation: ADB17 describes parsing, translation, optimization and evaluation that returns query results. A and D describe their participation in answering database requests, while C gives the efficiency reason for choosing an execution strategy. These descriptions overlap rather than exclude one another. Based on time is too vague unless a particular response-time objective is stated.

evidence.quote: Query processing is the whole activity; selecting a suitable efficient strategy is optimization.

choices.label: A
choices.explanation: Optimization participates in the SQL-processing pipeline that produces query answers.

choices.label: B
choices.explanation: Time may be a cost objective, but based on time does not clearly define retrieval.

choices.label: C
choices.explanation: Efficient strategy selection can reduce query execution costs within the processing pipeline.

choices.label: D
choices.explanation: Both activities participate in executing queries to access database information.

reviews.answer_text: No option matches parsing/analysis, translation, optimization and evaluation.
reviews.hint: Read the query-processing sequence in ADB17.
reviews.explanation: ADB17 gives grammar/semantic checks, logical representation, optimization and evaluation. DDL is not a mandatory step before a SELECT, and the offered authentication/DDL/DML permutations are not that pipeline. Each printed sequence introduces unsupported stages or ordering. The inclusive choice therefore fails too, leaving no literal valid answer to select.

evidence.quote: DDL is not a mandatory stage before each SELECT, so authentication→DDL→DML permutations do not describe the processing sequence.

choices.label: A
choices.explanation: It wrongly inserts obligatory DDL before each query instead of the stated processing phases.

choices.label: B
choices.explanation: DDL/DML are not these processing stages, and authentication is misplaced after optimization.

choices.label: C
choices.explanation: It places authentication and DDL after optimization rather than describing parsing through evaluation.

choices.label: D
choices.explanation: All three preceding sequences fail to match the complete note's query-processing pipeline.

reviews.answer_text: Temporary read and dirty read describe the uncommitted-value dependency.
reviews.hint: Read dirty-read failure propagation in ADB08.
reviews.explanation: The second transaction accesses a value written by another transaction before that writer commits and before its failed update is undone. ADB08 defines this as a dirty read. Temporary read describes the same temporary uncommitted value. There is no stale overwrite or mixed aggregate here, so lost update and incorrect summary do not fit.

evidence.quote: Dirty read: T2 reads a value written by uncommitted T1; if T1 aborts, dependent work must be reconsidered.

choices.label: A
choices.explanation: Temporary read refers to reading another transaction's temporary uncommitted update.

choices.label: B
choices.explanation: Dirty read is the explicit name for consuming another transaction's uncommitted value.

choices.label: C
choices.explanation: An incorrect summary combines inconsistent values in an aggregate, which is not described.

choices.label: D
choices.explanation: Lost update overwrites another change using stale data rather than merely reading uncommitted data.

reviews.answer_text: A transaction groups database work into one logical unit; that option is missing.
reviews.hint: Read transaction semantics versus concurrency control in ADB06.
reviews.explanation: ADB06 defines a transaction as a logical unit of database work, including read-only work. C is related because the DBMS controls interference between transactions, but it does not state that defining purpose. Authorization, optimization and schema definition concern other mechanisms. A corrected logical-unit/all-or-none option is required rather than selecting the nearest associated subsystem.

evidence.quote: A transaction is a logical unit of database work, including read-only work.

choices.label: A
choices.explanation: Authorization protects access rather than defining a transaction's logical unit of work.

choices.label: B
choices.explanation: Optimization chooses execution strategies rather than defining transaction grouping.

choices.label: C
choices.explanation: Transactions participate in concurrency management, but this omits the defining logical-unit semantics.

choices.label: D
choices.explanation: Schema definition specifies structure rather than grouping database operations into one transaction.

reviews.answer_text: The particular threatened financial failure must identify the relevant ACID property.
reviews.hint: Read distinct ACID guarantees in ADB06.
reviews.explanation: Accurate recording may require all-or-none transfer effects, preserved balance rules, controlled concurrent interference and durable commits. ADB06 assigns those distinct guarantees to atomicity, consistency, isolation and durability. The stem identifies none of these failure modes, and consistency assumes correct business logic. No single property alone is uniquely established by accurate monetary recording.

evidence.quote: Atomicity means all effects or none; consistency means correct work preserves integrity rules; isolation controls concurrent interference; durability preserves committed effects despite failure.

choices.label: A
choices.explanation: Atomicity prevents only one side of a transfer from taking effect.

choices.label: B
choices.explanation: Consistency preserves declared financial rules when the transaction's business logic is correct.

choices.label: C
choices.explanation: Isolation controls concurrent interference that could damage the intended financial result.

choices.label: D
choices.explanation: Durability ensures committed monetary records survive subsequent failures.

reviews.answer_text: A speed comparison requires failure, data, logging and storage assumptions.
reviews.hint: Read cooperating recovery mechanisms in ADB26.
reviews.explanation: ADB26 treats rollback, redo, checkpoints and backups as cooperating mechanisms rather than exclusive complete methods. Checkpoints can shorten log scans, while backups consume separate storage but may take substantial time to restore. No failure type, history size, checkpoint policy or comparison baseline is given. Faster with additional storage therefore cannot uniquely identify one alternative.

evidence.quote: These are cooperating mechanisms, not four mutually exclusive complete alternatives.

choices.label: A
choices.explanation: Redo speed depends on missing committed page changes and the available log volume.

choices.label: B
choices.explanation: Checkpoint benefit depends on checkpoint type and the log history it safely bounds.

choices.label: C
choices.explanation: Backups require separate storage, but their restoration speed depends on data size and media.

choices.label: D
choices.explanation: Rollback speed depends on incomplete effects and available before-images rather than a universal ranking.

reviews.answer_text: Checkpoint-assisted recovery is part of restart recovery.
reviews.hint: Read checkpoints and crash restoration in ADB26/ADB30.
reviews.explanation: ADB30 records durable recovery state in checkpoints and uses relevant log history for active transactions and dirty pages. Restart recovery can combine those resources to restore valid state after a crash. B names the technique and C the broader activity, so both fit the wording. Rollback and backup restoration are not uniquely defined by that checkpoint/log combination.

evidence.quote: A checkpoint records enough durable recovery state to avoid scanning all old history.

choices.label: A
choices.explanation: Rollback specifically undoes incomplete effects rather than naming the checkpoint-plus-log restart procedure.

choices.label: B
choices.explanation: Checkpoint-assisted recovery uses durable checkpoint information with the relevant log history.

choices.label: C
choices.explanation: Restart recovery can use checkpoints and transaction logs to reconstruct valid state.

choices.label: D
choices.explanation: Backup recovery starts from a separate database copy, which the description does not mention.

reviews.answer_text: Recovery does not automatically rerun and commit transactions active at failure.
reviews.hint: Read controlled retries versus loser recovery in ADB32.
reviews.explanation: ADB32 explicitly states that transactions active at failure are not automatically restarted and committed. Crash recovery preserves durable commits and removes incomplete effects; business retries are new controlled attempts. C may be the intended name, but its actual behavior does not satisfy the literal claim. No listed method unconditionally re-executes every active transaction as stated.

evidence.quote: Transactions active at failure are not automatically restarted and committed.

choices.label: A
choices.explanation: Rollback reverses incomplete changes instead of re-executing the failed business work.

choices.label: B
choices.explanation: Checkpoints preserve recovery information rather than retrying active transactions.

choices.label: C
choices.explanation: Restart recovery restores state; it does not automatically rerun and commit every active transaction.

choices.label: D
choices.explanation: Backup recovery restores a copy and possibly logs rather than automatically re-executing active work.

reviews.answer_text: Restart recovery is the conventional overall answer; rollback and checkpoint-assisted recovery can also be suitable components.
reviews.hint: Read the overall crash-recovery process versus its cooperating mechanisms in ADB26.
reviews.explanation: ADB26 identifies restart recovery as restoring valid state after a crash, but also explicitly treats rollback, redo and checkpoints as cooperating mechanisms. The stem asks what is suitable, not exclusively what names the complete overall process. Rollback can remove incomplete persistent effects and checkpoints can guide recovery. C remains the conventional umbrella answer, conditional on that narrower interpretation; the literal wording does not make it unique.

evidence.quote: Restart recovery restores a valid database after a crash while preserving durable commits and removing incomplete effects.

Rollback handles failed/uncommitted work; redo preserves committed work missing from pages; checkpoints reduce log-search work; backups provide another stored copy. These are cooperating mechanisms, not four mutually exclusive complete alternatives.

choices.label: A
choices.explanation: Rollback is suitable when incomplete effects need undo during crash recovery; suitable does not exclude component mechanisms.

choices.label: B
choices.explanation: Checkpoint-assisted recovery can bound needed log processing and cooperate in restoring state after a crash.

choices.label: C
choices.explanation: Restart recovery is the conventional name for the overall crash-restoration process, but the stem does not restrict scope to that umbrella.

choices.label: D
choices.explanation: Backup restoration may be suitable if persistent data is damaged; that additional failure condition is not specified.

reviews.answer_text: Rollback, checkpoint-assisted recovery and restart can all rely on transaction logs.
reviews.hint: Read logged undo/redo and checkpoint history in ADB27/ADB30.
reviews.explanation: ADB27 uses before-images for undo and after-images for redo. ADB30 combines checkpoints with relevant log history, while log-based restart recovery can use both. Thus A, B and C are all supported log-based mechanisms. Backup restoration may replay archived logs too, but a backup itself starts from a separately stored copy, not logging alone.

evidence.quote: Undo restores before-images of incomplete effects

choices.label: A
choices.explanation: Log-based rollback uses before-images to undo incomplete transaction effects.

choices.label: B
choices.explanation: Checkpoint-assisted recovery combines durable recovery state with relevant logged updates.

choices.label: C
choices.explanation: Log-based restart uses durable history to preserve commits and remove incomplete effects.

choices.label: D
choices.explanation: A backup restore may replay archived logs, but the backup itself is a separate stored copy.

reviews.answer_text: Naming a fragment suggests location transparency; hiding fragmentation suggests another reading.
reviews.hint: Read exactly which distribution detail is hidden in ADB35.
reviews.explanation: ADB35 separates hiding an object's site from hiding its fragmentation and reconstruction. Accessing a specific fragment suggests the user knows that fragment exists but not its location. Yet unaware of distribution can also mean fragmentation itself is hidden. The stem must clarify what users name and which detail is concealed before B and C can be distinguished.

evidence.quote: If users explicitly name a fragment but need not specify its site, fragmentation is visible while location can remain transparent.

choices.label: A
choices.explanation: Local data transparency is not the note's defined distinction among hidden sites, fragments and copies.

choices.label: B
choices.explanation: This fits if users query a logical relation without awareness of the fragments themselves.

choices.label: C
choices.explanation: This fits if a fragment is named but its physical site need not be known.

choices.label: D
choices.explanation: Replication transparency hides copy management, which the stem does not describe.

reviews.answer_text: Interoperable networks and coherent schema mappings are both important.
reviews.hint: Read heterogeneous semantic integration in ADB33/ADB40.
reviews.explanation: ADB33 requires reconciliation of naming, types, identifiers and transaction semantics across differing systems. ADB40 preserves different DBMSs through mappings. Communication compatibility and coherent schema semantics are therefore both important. D means consistency through mappings, not identical local schemas; full replication and universal DBMS replacement are not inherent requirements of a heterogeneous architecture.

evidence.quote: Heterogeneous design must reconcile naming, types, units, identifiers, query capabilities and transaction semantics.

choices.label: A
choices.explanation: Replication everywhere is an optional placement strategy rather than a heterogeneous-integration requirement.

choices.label: B
choices.explanation: Replacing every DBMS with one standard removes DBMS heterogeneity rather than being mandatory.

choices.label: C
choices.explanation: Compatible communication interfaces are required for exchanging requests, results and coordination messages.

choices.label: D
choices.explanation: Schema meanings need coherent mappings, although local schemas need not be identical.

reviews.answer_text: All four factors can affect query-strategy cost and placement.
reviews.hint: Read local and distributed cost inputs in ADB19/ADB38.
reviews.explanation: ADB19 estimates I/O, CPU, memory, temporary storage and network cost, using relation sizes and distributions. ADB38 adds transferred bytes, bandwidth and fragment/replica localization. Every listed factor can therefore change the cost or placement of a candidate strategy. They are complementary evaluation inputs rather than mutually exclusive alternatives for a unique answer.

evidence.quote: A cost model estimates resources for a candidate plan: page I/O, CPU, memory, temporary storage and network traffic.

choices.label: A
choices.explanation: Estimated execution cost is the explicit basis for comparing candidate strategies.

choices.label: B
choices.explanation: Database and relation sizes affect scan work, intermediate sizes and algorithm feasibility.

choices.label: C
choices.explanation: Bandwidth affects transfer time when data or results move between sites.

choices.label: D
choices.explanation: Replica locations affect which copy can serve a query and its communication cost.

reviews.answer_text: Homogeneous systems use compatible DBMS technology; heterogeneous systems integrate differing DBMSs, models, schemas or interfaces.
reviews.hint: Read what heterogeneity means in ADB33.
reviews.explanation: ADB33 defines the distinction through compatibility of database technology and representation. Operating-system differences can occur but do not define heterogeneity. Homogeneous sites need not have identical schemas or automatic replication. Heterogeneous integration requires explicit mappings for names, types and semantics, rather than assuming that common connectivity alone reconciles their meanings.

evidence.quote: A homogeneous system uses compatible DBMS technology across sites; a heterogeneous system integrates differing DBMSs, data models, schemas or interfaces.

reviews.answer_text: Fragmentation improves locality, manageable placement and parallelism by splitting data across useful site boundaries.
reviews.hint: Read horizontal/vertical fragments and reconstruction in ADB36.
reviews.explanation: ADB36 splits rows with predicates and columns with projections while preserving reconstruction through unions or key joins. This can place frequently used data near its consumers and allow independent work on pieces. Correct fragments must preserve completeness and required disjointness. Fragmentation alone creates no spare copy, so losing the only site containing a fragment still makes it unavailable.

evidence.quote: Partitioning improves locality and parallelism but alone creates no spare copy.

reviews.answer_text: 2PL guarantees conflict serializability by separating lock acquisition from release.
reviews.hint: Read growing and shrinking phases in ADB12.
reviews.explanation: During the growing phase a transaction acquires or upgrades locks; after it releases any lock, the shrinking phase forbids acquiring new ones. For well-formed transactions this guarantees conflict serializability. Basic 2PL can still deadlock and permit cascading aborts, so strict or conservative variants add different protections. It is distinct from distributed two-phase commit.

evidence.quote: 2PL guarantees conflict serializability for well-formed transactions, but can deadlock and basic 2PL alone need not prevent cascading aborts.

reviews.answer_text: WAL makes recovery information durable before its changed data pages, enabling safe undo/redo after crashes.
reviews.hint: Read durable log ordering and commit records in ADB27.
reviews.explanation: ADB27 requires needed update logs to reach stable storage before corresponding changed pages. A durable commit also forces required log records, including commit. Recovery can then use before-images for undo and after-images for redo if buffered data was lost. WAL orders durable writes; modifying an in-memory buffer before the log flush does not itself violate it.

evidence.quote: Write-ahead logging requires the update log needed for recovery to reach stable storage before the corresponding changed data page reaches disk.

reviews.answer_text: A warehouse integrates historical data for analysis; an operational database serves frequent business transactions.
reviews.hint: Read OLTP versus OLAP/warehouses in ADB41.
reviews.explanation: ADB41 contrasts OLTP account updates and other frequent operational transactions with OLAP scans and summaries over large datasets. A warehouse commonly integrates sources through extraction, transformation and loading for historical analysis. These are workload tendencies rather than absolute restrictions: operational databases may retain history, and warehouses may receive updates. Schema and storage choices should follow the actual workload.

evidence.quote: A warehouse integrates data for historical analysis, often through extraction, transformation and loading.

reviews.answer_text: Atomicity, Consistency, Isolation, Durability.
reviews.hint: Read the four transaction guarantees in ADB06.
reviews.explanation: ADB06 names all four ACID properties and assigns distinct roles: all-or-none effects, preserved invariants, controlled interference and durable commits. Only A lists those names in the correct order. Accuracy, integrity, concurrency, data and availability are related database concepts but do not replace the letters of this established transaction acronym.

evidence.quote: Atomicity means all effects or none; consistency means correct work preserves integrity rules; isolation controls concurrent interference; durability preserves committed effects despite failure.

choices.label: A
choices.explanation: It lists the four ACID properties in the proper acronym order.

choices.label: B
choices.explanation: Accuracy and Integrity replace Atomicity and Isolation, changing the defined acronym.

choices.label: C
choices.explanation: Concurrency and Data incorrectly replace Consistency and Durability.

choices.label: D
choices.explanation: Availability is not the A in the ACID transaction acronym.

reviews.answer_text: Atomicity.
reviews.hint: Read all-or-none effects in ADB06.
reviews.explanation: The question specifies indivisibility of the transaction effects: partial success must not remain if the transaction fails. ADB06 assigns that guarantee to atomicity. Consistency concerns valid invariants, isolation controls interference, and durability protects already committed work. Those properties support correctness too, but none directly means all-or-none effects.

evidence.quote: Atomicity means all effects or none

choices.label: A
choices.explanation: Consistency concerns preserving integrity rules rather than specifically making effects indivisible.

choices.label: B
choices.explanation: Isolation controls interactions between concurrent transactions rather than partial transaction application.

choices.label: C
choices.explanation: Atomicity applies every transaction effect together or discards the incomplete work.

choices.label: D
choices.explanation: Durability protects committed effects after failure rather than defining all-or-none completion.

reviews.answer_text: A = 4,250 Birr and B = 8,750 Birr.
reviews.hint: Read successful transfer effects versus merely preserved totals in ADB06.
reviews.explanation: The requested transfer subtracts 750 from 5000 and adds 750 to 8000, giving 4250 and 8750. The invariant total remains 13000. A and C also sum to 13000, but implement a different amount or the reverse direction. Preserving the total alone does not implement the specified successful transfer; D loses the credit.

evidence.quote: consistency means correct work preserves integrity rules

choices.label: A
choices.explanation: The sum remains 13000, but the changes transfer 1000 rather than the requested 750.

choices.label: B
choices.explanation: It debits 750 from A, credits 750 to B and preserves the 13000 total.

choices.label: C
choices.explanation: It preserves the total but transfers 750 in the reverse direction.

choices.label: D
choices.explanation: It debits A without crediting B, reducing the total to 12250.

reviews.answer_text: Durability.
reviews.hint: Read committed effects after failure in ADB06.
reviews.explanation: ADB06 defines durability as preserving committed effects despite failure. A system may leave data pages buffered at commit provided durable recovery information can restore the changes after a crash. Atomicity controls partial outcomes, consistency protects declared invariants and isolation controls concurrent interference; they do not name this persistence guarantee.

evidence.quote: durability preserves committed effects despite failure.

choices.label: A
choices.explanation: Atomicity means all-or-none effects, not specifically persistence after a successful commit.

choices.label: B
choices.explanation: Consistency concerns valid integrity rules before and after correct work.

choices.label: C
choices.explanation: Isolation controls concurrent interference rather than persistence across a crash.

choices.label: D
choices.explanation: Durability ensures committed changes survive failures through the supported recovery mechanisms.

reviews.answer_text: Copy X from the buffer into the program variable x.
reviews.hint: Read read_item movement in ADB07.
reviews.explanation: ADB07 first locates the page containing X, brings it into a buffer if absent and then copies X into a program variable. Thus D is the final conceptual read step. Locating and loading precede it, and storing an updated block to disk belongs to writing/flushing rather than completing read_item. A buffer hit can avoid physical I/O.

evidence.quote: read_item(X) locates X's page, brings it into a buffer if absent, and copies X into a program variable.

choices.label: A
choices.explanation: A read does not update and write the block back to disk.

choices.label: B
choices.explanation: Locating the containing page is the first conceptual step, not the final one.

choices.label: C
choices.explanation: Loading the page into a buffer precedes copying the item into the program variable.

choices.label: D
choices.explanation: The final read step copies the requested item from its buffer into x.

reviews.answer_text: Active.
reviews.hint: Read transaction states in ADB06.
reviews.explanation: ADB06 defines Active as the state while transaction operations are executing. Partially committed follows completion of the last operation but precedes assured durable commitment. Committed means commitment succeeded, while Failed means execution encountered a failure. Merely starting and continuing its operations therefore places this transaction in Active.

evidence.quote: Active means operations are executing.

choices.label: A
choices.explanation: Committed requires successful commitment, which has not occurred while operations are still executing.

choices.label: B
choices.explanation: Partially committed follows the last operation rather than ordinary ongoing execution.

choices.label: C
choices.explanation: Active is the state during execution of the transaction operations.

choices.label: D
choices.explanation: Failed requires an execution failure, which the stem does not report.

reviews.answer_text: Partially committed.
reviews.hint: Read the last-operation versus durable-commit boundary in ADB06.
reviews.explanation: Finishing all operations does not yet establish durable commitment. ADB06 names this intermediate state Partially committed. The transaction becomes Committed only after commitment succeeds, or can fail before that boundary. Active describes operations still running, while Aborted means rollback completed, so neither matches successful operations awaiting finalized commit.

evidence.quote: Partially committed means the last operation finished but durable commitment is not yet assured.

choices.label: A
choices.explanation: Active means operations are still executing, whereas the last operation has finished here.

choices.label: B
choices.explanation: Partially committed means execution finished but durable commitment is not yet assured.

choices.label: C
choices.explanation: Committed requires the commit itself to have succeeded, which the stem excludes.

choices.label: D
choices.explanation: Aborted follows rollback rather than successful execution awaiting a commit decision.

reviews.answer_text: T is aborting/aborted and its transaction effects must be discarded.
reviews.hint: Read conceptual ABORT records and rollback completion in ADB07.
reviews.explanation: ADB07 includes ABORT among conceptual log records and warns that it can mark the start of rollback rather than prove every undo step is already complete. C is correct because it says the changes must be discarded, not that all undo has finished. START, COMMIT and ordinary read activity have different meanings.

evidence.quote: an ABORT record can mark the start of rollback rather than prove every undo step is complete.

choices.label: A
choices.explanation: A START record, rather than ABORT, marks beginning transaction execution.

choices.label: B
choices.explanation: COMMIT records successful completion; ABORT means the opposite outcome.

choices.label: C
choices.explanation: Abort requires discarding transaction effects, though this record need not prove all undo is already complete.

choices.label: D
choices.explanation: The record denotes abort handling rather than a read_item operation.

reviews.answer_text: Sort.
reviews.hint: Read primitive item access/modification versus query processing in ADB07.
reviews.explanation: ADB07 distinguishes read_item and write_item and notes that inserts and deletes also modify data. Sorting is instead an operation used in query processing, not a primitive item update in this classification. The exact count four is a teaching convention, but the note directly supplies the relevant distinction that singles out Sort.

evidence.quote: Insert and delete also modify data; sorting is a query-processing operation rather than a primitive item update.

choices.label: A
choices.explanation: Reading is an explicitly defined primitive database item operation.

choices.label: B
choices.explanation: Writing is an explicitly defined primitive database item modification operation.

choices.label: C
choices.explanation: Sorting is a query-processing operation rather than the primitive item access/update category.

choices.label: D
choices.explanation: Delete modifies stored data and belongs with the listed primitive data operations.

reviews.answer_text: Concurrent work is isolated from improper interference.
reviews.hint: Read isolation rather than success or commit-order guarantees in ADB06.
reviews.explanation: ADB06 defines isolation as controlling interference between concurrent transactions. B captures logical independence under the specified isolation guarantee; it does not mean transactions literally use separate hardware or never wait. Isolation does not require identical reads, start-order commits or universal successful completion. Strong serializable isolation makes behavior equivalent to some serial order.

evidence.quote: isolation controls concurrent interference

choices.label: A
choices.explanation: Isolation does not require all transactions to read identical values at the same time.

choices.label: B
choices.explanation: Isolation controls interference so concurrent transactions retain the promised logical execution semantics.

choices.label: C
choices.explanation: Isolation does not require commit order to match transaction start order.

choices.label: D
choices.explanation: Conflicts and failures can still cause aborts; isolation is not a success guarantee.

reviews.answer_text: A disk flush may follow, but write_item itself need not immediately write the buffer to disk.
reviews.hint: Read buffered writes and later page flushing in ADB07.
reviews.explanation: ADB07 defines write_item as copying the program value into the buffered page and marking it dirty. A disk write can happen later under the buffer policy. C would be the final step only in a simplified model that includes an immediate flush, which the stem does not state. The other options are read/setup steps, so the asserted final step needs a policy clarification.

evidence.quote: Writing that page to disk can occur later according to the buffer policy; write_item is not inherently an immediate disk flush.

choices.label: A
choices.explanation: Copying from the buffer into a variable describes reading, not completion of a buffered write.

choices.label: B
choices.explanation: Locating the block precedes access and cannot be the final step after buffer modification.

choices.label: C
choices.explanation: A later disk flush is possible, but it is not an inherent immediate final write_item step.

choices.label: D
choices.explanation: Reading an old value is not the mandatory final step after modifying the buffer.

reviews.answer_text: Failed.
reviews.hint: Read failure before completed rollback in ADB06.
reviews.explanation: ADB06 places a transaction in Failed when an error prevents successful execution. After rollback removes its effects it reaches Aborted. The stem reports the execution error but does not say rollback has completed, so Failed is the precise state. Partially committed follows successful final operation execution, not an error that prevents completion.

evidence.quote: A failure leads to Failed, then Aborted after rollback

choices.label: A
choices.explanation: Aborted requires completed rollback, which is not stated after the execution error.

choices.label: B
choices.explanation: Failed is the immediate state when an error prevents completing the transaction.

choices.label: C
choices.explanation: Termination is later lifecycle handling rather than the immediate error state.

choices.label: D
choices.explanation: Partially committed follows completion of the last operation rather than failed execution.

reviews.answer_text: Enable recovery by recording the information needed to undo or redo changes.
reviews.hint: Read conceptual log before/after images in ADB07.
reviews.explanation: ADB07 records starts, updates, commits and aborts, with before-images for undo and after-images for redo. That makes recovery the primary purpose among the choices. Actual log formats may be physical or logical and need not record every read, so all changes should be understood as the change information required by the recovery design, not every operation indiscriminately.

evidence.quote: Before-images support undo; after-images support redo.

choices.label: A
choices.explanation: The primary log purpose here is recovery rather than speeding query execution.

choices.label: B
choices.explanation: Transaction logging does not inherently encrypt the stored sensitive data.

choices.label: C
choices.explanation: Logged update and transaction-state information supports recovery of valid committed state after failures.

choices.label: D
choices.explanation: Access privileges control authorization; transaction log records are not themselves that enforcement mechanism.

reviews.answer_text: Parallel processing.
reviews.hint: Read simultaneous workers versus single-CPU interleaving in ADB22.
reviews.explanation: ADB22 distinguishes concurrency by interleaving on one CPU from actual simultaneous work on multiple cores. The stem explicitly uses multiple CPUs to execute different transactions at the same time, making Parallel the correct classification. Batch describes grouping work, and sequential processing performs work in order; neither guarantees the stated simultaneous execution.

evidence.quote: Interleaving on one CPU is concurrency; simultaneous cores provide parallelism.

choices.label: A
choices.explanation: Sequential processing does not execute different transactions simultaneously on multiple CPUs.

choices.label: B
choices.explanation: Interleaving alternates execution and need not provide simultaneous CPU work.

choices.label: C
choices.explanation: Multiple CPUs working simultaneously provide parallel execution.

choices.label: D
choices.explanation: Batch describes grouped submission or handling, not necessarily simultaneous multi-CPU execution.

reviews.answer_text: Transactions support consistent, reliable work through ACID guarantees.
reviews.hint: Read logical units and correct transaction logic in ADB06.
reviews.explanation: ADB06 groups operations into a logical unit with all-or-none effects, invariant preservation, isolation and durable commits. These guarantees support consistent and reliable database behavior when application logic is correct. They do not inherently speed queries, expand storage capacity or simplify syntax. In particular a DBMS cannot make an incorrect business operation consistent merely by wrapping it in a transaction.

evidence.quote: A DBMS cannot automatically make incorrect business logic consistent.

choices.label: A
choices.explanation: Transactions can add coordination costs and do not inherently make queries faster.

choices.label: B
choices.explanation: ACID guarantees support valid and recoverable logical work, provided business logic is correct.

choices.label: C
