choices.explanation: Transaction semantics do not increase the database's physical storage capacity.

choices.label: D
choices.explanation: Grouping work atomically does not inherently simplify the SQL language for users.

reviews.answer_text: Lost update: T1 overwrites T2’s increment with its stale calculation.
reviews.hint: Trace each read and write in ADB08.
reviews.explanation: Both transactions read 500. T2 writes 700 after adding 200, but T1 then writes its previously computed 600, erasing T2’s increment. A serial execution would produce 800. This matches the lost-update trace in ADB08; no waiting cycle or aggregate calculation is described, and reading an uncommitted value is not the stated cause.

evidence.quote: Correct serial execution yields 800.

choices.label: A
choices.explanation: Neither transaction is described as reading the other's uncommitted write.

choices.label: B
choices.explanation: T1's stale write of 600 overwrites T2's added 200; the correct combined result is 800.

choices.label: C
choices.explanation: No aggregate over mutually inconsistent versions is being calculated.

choices.label: D
choices.explanation: No circular waiting or blocked resource requests are present.

reviews.answer_text: Read another transaction’s uncommitted modification.
reviews.hint: Read dirty read versus reading one’s own changes in ADB08.
reviews.explanation: ADB08 defines dirty read as consuming a value written by an uncommitted other transaction. If that writer aborts, the dependent read used a value that should not survive. Reading one’s own changes is allowed and is not this anomaly; the age of a value or a completed permanent deletion does not define dirty reading.

evidence.quote: Reading one's own changes is not a dirty read.

choices.label: A
choices.explanation: Reading changes made earlier by the same transaction is not a dirty read.

choices.label: B
choices.explanation: The read depends on T2's uncommitted update, which may later need undo.

choices.label: C
choices.explanation: Permanent deletion is not the defining uncommitted-value dependency.

choices.label: D
choices.explanation: Elapsed time since a read does not determine whether the writer committed.

reviews.answer_text: Shared lock.
reviews.hint: Read S/S compatibility in ADB11.
reviews.explanation: ADB11 states that a shared lock permits reading and multiple shared holders can coexist on the same item. Exclusive/write locks conflict with another transaction’s shared or exclusive lock on that item. Thus shared locking provides the requested concurrent-reader behavior. A generic binary locked/unlocked label does not establish shared-reader compatibility in the supplied model.

evidence.quote: A shared (S) lock permits reading; multiple S locks on the same item can coexist.

choices.label: A
choices.explanation: An exclusive lock conflicts with other transactions' read locks on the same item.

choices.label: B
choices.explanation: A write/exclusive lock does not grant multiple independent readers the requested shared ownership.

choices.label: C
choices.explanation: Shared locks are compatible with other shared locks, permitting multiple readers.

choices.label: D
choices.explanation: The binary label does not provide the explicit S/S compatibility defined in the note.

reviews.answer_text: Growing phase.
reviews.hint: Read acquisition before the first release in ADB12.
reviews.explanation: Basic 2PL separates acquiring/upgrading locks from releasing/downgrading them. ADB12 permits acquisition only in the growing phase; after any release, no new lock may be acquired. Termination is a transaction boundary and validation belongs to a different control approach. The growing/shrinking rule is what distinguishes 2PL from unrestricted use of locks.

evidence.quote: Once any lock is released, no new lock may be acquired.

choices.label: A
choices.explanation: The shrinking phase releases or downgrades locks and forbids new acquisitions.

choices.label: B
choices.explanation: Termination is not the 2PL phase in which new locks are acquired.

choices.label: C
choices.explanation: Growing permits acquiring and upgrading locks before any release begins.

choices.label: D
choices.explanation: Validation is an optimistic-control stage, not the lock-acquisition phase of 2PL.

reviews.answer_text: Conflict serializability for well-formed transactions.
reviews.hint: Read the guarantee and limits of basic 2PL in ADB12.
reviews.explanation: ADB12 explicitly guarantees conflict serializability for well-formed 2PL transactions. Locking without its phase discipline need not provide that ordering guarantee. Basic 2PL can still deadlock and may permit cascading aborts, so it does not guarantee successful completion. Nor does serializability require every read to observe the latest wall-clock update.

evidence.quote: 2PL guarantees conflict serializability for well-formed transactions, but can deadlock and basic 2PL alone need not prevent cascading aborts.

choices.label: A
choices.explanation: Basic 2PL can deadlock, so deadlock freedom is not its general guarantee.

choices.label: B
choices.explanation: The phase discipline guarantees conflict-serializable schedules for well-formed transactions.

choices.label: C
choices.explanation: Deadlock resolution or failures can still abort transactions.

choices.label: D
choices.explanation: Serializability does not require every read to see the newest wall-clock version.

reviews.answer_text: A circular wait among transactions holding resources needed by others.
reviews.hint: Read wait-for cycles in ADB13.
reviews.explanation: ADB13 defines deadlock through a waiting cycle: each participant holds a resource another needs, so none can advance without an intervention. Slow work alone can still make progress and is not deadlock. Hardware loss and consistency violations are distinct problems that do not require a resource-wait cycle.

evidence.quote: Deadlock requires a waiting cycle

choices.label: A
choices.explanation: A slow transaction may still make progress and need not participate in a wait cycle.

choices.label: B
choices.explanation: Circular hold-and-wait prevents the involved transactions from progressing without intervention.

choices.label: C
choices.explanation: Hardware failure is a different failure category and does not define a lock wait cycle.

choices.label: D
choices.explanation: A consistency violation concerns invalid data states rather than necessarily circular waiting.

reviews.answer_text: Abort the younger requester; retry with its original timestamp.
reviews.hint: Identify requester and holder before applying wait–die in ADB14.
reviews.explanation: The requester is younger and the resource holder older. ADB14 says wait–die permits an older requester to wait but aborts a younger requester needing an older holder. C therefore gives the correct action. Restart should retain the original timestamp to improve relative priority; immediately aborted does not require an immediate successful retry or resource grant.

evidence.quote: a younger requester needing an older holder aborts itself.

choices.label: A
choices.explanation: Wait–die does not let the younger requester abort the older holder.

choices.label: B
choices.explanation: In wait–die, the younger requester dies rather than waiting for the older holder.

choices.label: C
choices.explanation: The younger requester is aborted and may restart using its original timestamp.

choices.label: D
choices.explanation: The older holder retains priority; the younger requester does not receive the resource immediately.

reviews.answer_text: The older requester aborts the younger holder.
reviews.hint: Read wound–wait requester/holder rules in ADB14.
reviews.explanation: ADB14 distinguishes wound–wait from wait–die: an older requester wounds the younger holder, while a younger requester waits for an older holder. Here the requester is explicitly older, so B applies. The rule prevents waiting cycles through age-based action; it does not require detecting an existing deadlock first or aborting both participants.

evidence.quote: In wound–wait, an older requester aborts the younger holder; a younger requester waits for the older holder.

choices.label: A
choices.explanation: An older requester wounds the younger holder rather than waiting under wound–wait.

choices.label: B
choices.explanation: The older requester causes the younger resource holder to abort and release its lock.

choices.label: C
choices.explanation: The protocol aborts the younger holder, not both transactions.

choices.label: D
choices.explanation: This is a prevention action based on ages, not a requirement to run cycle detection first.

reviews.answer_text: Low-conflict workloads.
reviews.hint: Read validation success and contention costs in ADB16.
reviews.explanation: Optimistic control computes privately and validates before publication, retrying when conflicts invalidate the work. ADB16 says it works well when conflicts are uncommon and wastes work under high contention. C states that decisive condition; read-heavy is only a useful tendency, since actual overlap/conflict still matters. Strict timestamp completion is not the defining optimistic-control requirement.

evidence.quote: It works well when conflicts are uncommon, but high contention wastes work on aborts.

choices.label: A
choices.explanation: Frequent writes to the same items increase validation conflicts and wasted retries.

choices.label: B
choices.explanation: Persistent read/write conflicts make optimistic retries expensive rather than especially suitable.

choices.label: C
choices.explanation: Rare conflicts let most private work validate and commit without costly retries.

choices.label: D
choices.explanation: Optimistic validation is not defined by completing every transaction in strict timestamp order.

reviews.answer_text: Shared → Exclusive.
reviews.hint: Read lock conversion direction in ADB11.
reviews.explanation: ADB11 explicitly names S→X an upgrade and X→S a downgrade. The stronger exclusive lock permits writing and can be granted only after conflicting other holders leave. Acquiring a new shared lock is initial acquisition rather than conversion, while releasing an exclusive lock is unlocking. Thus B alone names a lock upgrade.

evidence.quote: S→X is an upgrade, possible only after conflicting other holders leave.

choices.label: A
choices.explanation: Exclusive-to-shared weakens permissions and is a downgrade.

choices.label: B
choices.explanation: Shared-to-exclusive strengthens the held lock to permit writing, subject to compatibility.

choices.label: C
choices.explanation: No-lock-to-shared is initial acquisition, not conversion of an already held lock.

choices.label: D
choices.explanation: Exclusive-to-no-lock is release rather than upgrade.

reviews.answer_text: B is a possible setting, but an actual inconsistent mix must be shown; nonrepeatable read is distinct.
reviews.hint: Read incorrect summaries versus repeated-row changes in ADB08.
reviews.explanation: ADB08 distinguishes nonrepeatable reads from incorrect summaries. An aggregate becomes incorrect when it mixes mutually inconsistent versions, such as the old debit balance and new credit balance. Merely running an aggregate concurrently with an update does not prove that mix; a consistent snapshot may avoid it. B suggests the setting, but the parenthetical synonym and missing timing make the definition imprecise.

evidence.quote: Incorrect summary mixes mutually inconsistent versions

choices.label: A
choices.explanation: Concurrent deletion alone does not define either a mixed-version aggregate or a repeated-row read.

choices.label: B
choices.explanation: This can cause an incorrect summary if the aggregate mixes inconsistent versions; concurrency alone is insufficient.

choices.label: C
choices.explanation: Reading another transaction's uncommitted value specifically defines a dirty read.

choices.label: D
choices.explanation: Failure to acquire a lock concerns waiting or abort handling rather than the stated read anomaly.

reviews.answer_text: Indefinite postponement while other transactions keep progressing.
reviews.hint: Read starvation versus deadlock in ADB13.
reviews.explanation: ADB13 defines starvation as indefinite postponement while other work proceeds, without requiring any waiting cycle. Repeatedly favoring higher-priority work can prevent a transaction from executing, matching B. Memory consumption, a full log or a long deadlock are different resource/failure conditions; none alone defines the fairness failure of starvation.

evidence.quote: Starvation is indefinite postponement while other work proceeds, without a required cycle.

choices.label: A
choices.explanation: Excessive memory use is a resource problem rather than the definition of indefinite postponement.

choices.label: B
choices.explanation: Repeated bypass by other transactions can indefinitely postpone this transaction while work continues.

choices.label: C
choices.explanation: Deadlock requires a waiting cycle; starvation can occur without one.

choices.label: D
choices.explanation: A full log can block work but does not itself define unfair indefinite postponement.

reviews.answer_text: Timestamp-based concurrency control.
reviews.hint: Read transaction and item timestamp tests in ADB15.
reviews.explanation: ADB15 assigns TS(T) to each transaction and compares it with item read_TS and write_TS values. Those tests reject operations that would violate timestamp order, so C matches the start-time ordering technique. 2PL orders locking, optimistic control validates private work, and shadow paging is a recovery/storage technique rather than this conflict-ordering protocol.

evidence.quote: A read by T aborts if TS(T)<write_TS(X); otherwise it succeeds and updates read_TS. A write aborts if TS(T)<read_TS(X) or TS(T)<write_TS(X); otherwise it succeeds and sets write_TS.

choices.label: A
choices.explanation: 2PL orders lock acquisition and release rather than defining the timestamp validity tests.

choices.label: B
choices.explanation: Shadow paging preserves page versions for recovery rather than ordering concurrent transaction operations by timestamp.

choices.label: C
choices.explanation: Timestamp ordering compares transaction timestamps with item read/write timestamps to resolve conflicts.

choices.label: D
choices.explanation: Optimistic control validates private read/write work rather than being defined by these timestamp-order tests.

reviews.answer_text: Acquire the appropriate lock before accessing the item.
reviews.hint: Read well-formed lock access in ADB11.
reviews.explanation: ADB11 requires ownership of an appropriate lock before access and permits releasing only one’s own locks. Reads therefore need shared or suitable stronger locks in this basic model; writes need exclusive ownership. Alphabetical acquisition may be a separate prevention convention, but it is not the general well-formedness rule and locks cannot be postponed until after access.

evidence.quote: A transaction must own the appropriate lock before access and can release only its own locks.

choices.label: A
choices.explanation: Locking only at the end leaves the earlier accesses unprotected.

choices.label: B
choices.explanation: A well-formed transaction holds an appropriate lock before reading or writing an item.

choices.label: C
choices.explanation: Basic lock-based access also requires an appropriate read lock, not only locks for writes.

choices.label: D
choices.explanation: A fixed resource order can help prevention, but alphabetical order is not the general well-formedness definition.

reviews.answer_text: Abort a transaction after its lock wait exceeds the timeout.
reviews.hint: Read timeout limitations in ADB13.
reviews.explanation: ADB13 describes timeout as aborting long waits, while warning it may mistake slow progress for deadlock. C directly states that mechanism. Detecting cycles is a different method; acquiring all needed locks first is conservative locking; a priority queue alone neither defines a timeout nor guarantees elimination of waiting cycles.

evidence.quote: A timeout aborts long waits but may mistake slow progress for deadlock.

choices.label: A
choices.explanation: Cycle detection is graph-based deadlock detection rather than a wait-duration timeout.

choices.label: B
choices.explanation: A priority queue alone does not enforce the stated wait-duration abort policy.

choices.label: C
choices.explanation: The policy aborts work whose lock wait exceeds the chosen threshold.

choices.label: D
choices.explanation: Obtaining all locks before execution is conservative locking, not timeout handling.

reviews.answer_text: Parsing/translation → optimization → evaluation.
reviews.hint: Read query representation before execution in ADB17.
reviews.explanation: ADB17 checks grammar and semantics, constructs a logical representation, chooses an equivalent efficient execution plan and evaluates it. B groups parsing and translation into the first phase and preserves that dependency order. Plans cannot sensibly be evaluated before construction and selection, and optimization does not precede understanding the query’s syntax and meaning.

evidence.quote: Translation constructs a logical representation, typically relational algebra or a logical query tree.

choices.label: A
choices.explanation: Optimization cannot precede parsing and understanding the query in the stated pipeline.

choices.label: B
choices.explanation: It preserves analysis/translation, plan optimization and then execution/evaluation.

choices.label: C
choices.explanation: Evaluation cannot be the first phase before the query is represented and planned.

choices.label: D
choices.explanation: It executes before selecting the optimized plan, reversing optimization and evaluation.

reviews.answer_text: Relational algebra expressions or a logical query tree.
reviews.hint: Read the logical translation representation in ADB17.
reviews.explanation: ADB17 states that translation constructs a logical representation, typically relational algebra or a logical query tree. This allows equivalent rewrites and plan choice before physical execution. Machine code or bytecode may appear in particular execution implementations, but they are not the general logical translation target asked for here; a binary decision tree is also not the defined representation.

evidence.quote: Translation constructs a logical representation, typically relational algebra or a logical query tree.

choices.label: A
choices.explanation: Machine code is not the logical relational representation described for query translation.

choices.label: B
choices.explanation: A binary decision tree is not the note's general query-algebra representation.

choices.label: C
choices.explanation: Relational algebra expresses the logical operators that can be rewritten and optimized.

choices.label: D
choices.explanation: Compressed bytecode is not the stated general logical query representation.

reviews.answer_text: Choose a low-cost equivalent execution plan.
reviews.hint: Read candidate-plan cost objectives in ADB19.
reviews.explanation: ADB19 estimates resource costs such as I/O, CPU, memory, temporary storage and communication for candidate plans. Optimization compares equivalent ways to return the same result and chooses a suitable low-cost strategy. It does not seek index count, force textual table order or impose sorting that the query never requested. The estimate need not prove a global real-world minimum.

evidence.quote: A cost model estimates resources for a candidate plan: page I/O, CPU, memory, temporary storage and network traffic.

choices.label: A
choices.explanation: Sorting is required only when query semantics need it, not as the universal optimizer goal.

choices.label: B
choices.explanation: The optimizer seeks an efficient equivalent plan under the selected resource-cost model.

choices.label: C
choices.explanation: More indexes used does not necessarily mean lower cost or better execution.

choices.label: D
choices.explanation: Equivalent join reordering can reduce cost; SQL textual order need not dictate access order.

reviews.answer_text: The dominant cost depends on whether the workload is disk-based, in-memory or distributed.
reviews.hint: Read cost-model context in ADB19.
reviews.explanation: ADB19 explicitly makes disk I/O dominant in many local-disk textbook cases, CPU dominant in some in-memory work and network cost dominant in distributed plans. The stem gives no system or workload assumption. B is the conventional local-disk answer, but it is not universally most significant; choosing it unconditionally would turn a stated contextual tendency into a rule.

evidence.quote: Disk I/O often dominates textbook local-disk examples; CPU can dominate in-memory work and network can dominate distributed plans.

choices.label: A
choices.explanation: CPU processing can dominate in-memory or computation-heavy queries.

choices.label: B
choices.explanation: Disk I/O often dominates the conventional local-disk model, which the stem does not specify.

choices.label: C
choices.explanation: Memory overhead can matter for some workloads, but no cost breakdown establishes its dominance here.

choices.label: D
choices.explanation: Network latency can dominate distributed queries or remote communication-heavy workloads.

reviews.answer_text: The number of transferred disk blocks.
reviews.hint: Read count × unit-time disk cost in ADB19.
reviews.explanation: ADB19 computes disk cost as seeks times seek duration plus transferred blocks times per-block transfer time. Therefore B in the formula is a block count, making B×tT the total transfer time. Block size, buffer capacity and search-operation count are different quantities and would not have the units required by this expression.

evidence.quote: cost = seeks×seek_time + transferred_blocks×block_transfer_time.

choices.label: A
choices.explanation: Block size is bytes per block rather than the number multiplied by per-block transfer time.

choices.label: B
choices.explanation: B counts transferred blocks, so B×tT gives their total transfer time.

choices.label: C
choices.explanation: Buffer-pool capacity is not the transferred-block count in this formula.

choices.label: D
choices.explanation: Binary-search operation count is not the disk-block transfer term.

reviews.answer_text: Reverse incomplete or aborted transaction effects.
reviews.hint: Read before-image undo in ADB27.
reviews.explanation: ADB27 uses undo to restore before-images of incomplete effects, usually traversing a transaction’s updates backward. This removes changes that must not survive. Reapplying committed changes is redo, checkpoint records bound recovery searches, and transferring dirty buffers to storage is page flushing. Only C describes undo rather than another recovery or storage operation.

evidence.quote: Undo restores before-images of incomplete effects

choices.label: A
choices.explanation: Reapplying missing committed updates is redo rather than undo.

choices.label: B
choices.explanation: Checkpoint creation records recovery state and is not reversal of incomplete effects.

choices.label: C
choices.explanation: Undo restores old values to remove incomplete or aborted transaction changes.

choices.label: D
choices.explanation: Writing a buffer to disk is flushing rather than restoring before-images.

reviews.answer_text: Reapply required logged after-images, including committed changes missing from pages.
reviews.hint: Read redo and its algorithm-dependent scope in ADB27.
reviews.explanation: ADB27 describes redo as installing logged after-images when necessary. In the simple teaching model it preserves committed work not yet on disk, matching C. ARIES may repeat history more broadly before loser undo, so C describes the ordinary purpose rather than every algorithm’s full phase. Aborting transactions and reversing failed changes are different actions.

evidence.quote: Redo installs logged after-images when necessary, usually forward.

choices.label: A
choices.explanation: Aborting active transactions is not the operation of applying logged after-images.

choices.label: B
choices.explanation: Reversing incomplete effects is undo rather than redo.

choices.label: C
choices.explanation: Redo can restore committed changes whose data pages were not durable at the crash.

choices.label: D
choices.explanation: Shadow-page creation is a separate copy-on-write technique rather than logged redo.

reviews.answer_text: WAL orders durable log writes before corresponding durable data-page writes.
reviews.hint: Read durable writes versus buffer modification in ADB27.
reviews.explanation: ADB27 requires recovery logs to be stable before the corresponding changed page reaches disk. A buffer can already have been modified before that log flush. B is correct only if actual data changes means durable database-page writes; taken as every memory modification it is too strong. The stem needs that distinction, while the other options reverse or abandon WAL.

evidence.quote: A buffer can be changed before that log flush; WAL orders durable writes, not every CPU assignment.

choices.label: A
choices.explanation: Writing the changed data page first reverses the required durable log-before-data order.

choices.label: B
choices.explanation: This fits durable data-page writes, but incorrectly forbids earlier buffer changes if read literally as every modification.

choices.label: C
choices.explanation: Update logs can precede commit; successful commit does not precede all log creation.

choices.label: D
choices.explanation: Logs must already be durable before failure to support recovery afterward.

reviews.answer_text: Checkpoints bound recovery history, but the exact starting point depends on checkpoint type.
reviews.hint: Read active transactions and fuzzy checkpoints in ADB30.
reviews.explanation: ADB30 says checkpoints avoid scanning all old history, but active transactions may have earlier updates requiring undo. A fuzzy checkpoint need not produce one fully flushed consistent data image, and redo may start earlier than the checkpoint. C captures a simplified quiescent model but overstates the general mechanism without specifying that model. Checkpoints do not prevent failures or commit active transactions.

evidence.quote: Recovery may start analysis at the checkpoint but redo from an earlier required log position.

choices.label: A
choices.explanation: A checkpoint records recovery state; it does not prevent hardware failures.

choices.label: B
choices.explanation: Encryption is not the checkpoint mechanism that reduces recovery search work.

choices.label: C
choices.explanation: This fits a simplified consistent checkpoint, but fuzzy checkpoints and earlier active work need qualifications.

choices.label: D
choices.explanation: Checkpointing does not automatically commit active transactions.

reviews.answer_text: After successful commit, in the deferred-update model.
reviews.hint: Read why deferred update avoids undo in ADB29.
reviews.explanation: ADB29 keeps uncommitted changes outside the persistent database. Only committed effects may therefore be installed in its actual database pages, which is the property B expresses. This does not require every committed page to be flushed immediately. Checkpoints and periodic timers cannot independently authorize writing uncommitted changes while retaining the claimed No-Undo model.

evidence.quote: Deferred update keeps uncommitted changes outside the persistent database

choices.label: A
choices.explanation: Immediate per-statement persistent writes can expose uncommitted effects and do not define deferred update.

choices.label: B
choices.explanation: The model does not install uncommitted effects in the persistent database; committed changes can be written later.

choices.label: C
choices.explanation: A checkpoint alone does not make an uncommitted transaction eligible for persistent installation.

choices.label: D
choices.explanation: A fixed timer cannot ignore transaction commit status while preserving deferred-update semantics.

reviews.answer_text: Write changed data to new pages while preserving the committed page map.
reviews.hint: Read shadow/copy-on-write and commit maps in ADB29.
reviews.explanation: ADB29 preserves the committed version and writes changed data at new locations. Shadow paging keeps the old page map plus a modified map; commit atomically installs the new durable root after needed pages are durable. B captures the copy-on-write preservation, although the unchanged old map is the shadow rather than the name of each newly modified page.

evidence.quote: Shadow/copy-on-write update writes a new location while preserving the committed version.

choices.label: A
choices.explanation: A separate-server backup is not the page-map copy-on-write mechanism of shadow paging.

choices.label: B
choices.explanation: Changes use new pages, preserving the originals until the new committed map is safely installed.

choices.label: C
choices.explanation: Encryption does not preserve the old page mapping or provide the stated rollback mechanism.

choices.label: D
choices.explanation: Sorting pages is an access-layout choice rather than preserving committed copies.

reviews.answer_text: Human error.
reviews.hint: Read mistaken operations versus system/media failures in ADB26.
reviews.explanation: The described cause is an accidental user action, not faulty hardware, a natural event or a software defect. ADB26 treats human mistakes separately and notes they may need point-in-time restoration before a bad committed operation. Ordinary crash redo would otherwise preserve a committed deletion rather than recognize the user’s intention.

evidence.quote: Human mistakes may require point-in-time restoration before the bad committed operation.

choices.label: A
choices.explanation: No hardware malfunction is stated; the cause is the user's mistaken deletion.

choices.label: B
choices.explanation: A natural disaster is not the cause described in the prompt.

choices.label: C
choices.explanation: The software may have executed the requested deletion correctly; the stated mistake belongs to the user.

choices.label: D
choices.explanation: Accidental deletion by a user is a human error.

reviews.answer_text: Undo with old values and redo with logged new values.
reviews.hint: Read before- and after-images in ADB27.
reviews.explanation: ADB27 restores before-images when undoing incomplete work and installs after-images when redoing logged effects. Recording both values therefore supports reversal and reapplication after failure. Query costing uses catalog statistics, access control uses privileges, and compression is a different storage concern; none explains the specific recovery value pair as directly.

evidence.quote: Undo restores before-images of incomplete effects

choices.label: A
choices.explanation: Query optimization estimates plan cost rather than restoring old/new transaction values.

choices.label: B
choices.explanation: Access control checks privileges rather than using before/after images to authorize users.

choices.label: C
choices.explanation: Old values support reversal and new values support necessary reapplication during recovery.

choices.label: D
choices.explanation: Recording two values can add storage overhead and is not primarily a compression mechanism.

reviews.answer_text: Homogeneous distributed database.
reviews.hint: Read compatible DBMS technology in ADB33.
reviews.explanation: ADB33 identifies homogeneous systems by compatible DBMS technology across sites. Using the same DBMS software fits that classification. Heterogeneous systems integrate differing engines, models or interfaces. Middleware describes integration architecture and partial replication describes placement of copies, so neither substitutes for the homogeneity classification asked for here.

evidence.quote: A homogeneous system uses compatible DBMS technology across sites

choices.label: A
choices.explanation: Heterogeneous systems integrate differing database technologies rather than the same DBMS throughout.

choices.label: B
choices.explanation: Using the same DBMS at each site fits homogeneous distributed database technology.

choices.label: C
choices.explanation: Middleware describes communication/integration responsibilities, not whether DBMS technology is the same.

choices.label: D
choices.explanation: Partial replication describes where selected copies reside rather than which DBMS software sites use.

reviews.answer_text: Split rows by predicates.
reviews.hint: Read horizontal versus vertical fragmentation in ADB36.
reviews.explanation: ADB36 defines horizontal fragmentation as selecting row subsets using predicates and reconstructing the relation by union. Column subsets belong to vertical fragmentation. Combining tables is not fragmentation, and copying a whole table is replication. Thus B identifies both the item being split and the rule used to decide fragment membership.

evidence.quote: Horizontal fragmentation selects row subsets by predicates; their union reconstructs the relation.

choices.label: A
choices.explanation: Column splitting is vertical fragmentation rather than horizontal fragmentation.

choices.label: B
choices.explanation: Horizontal fragments contain rows selected by stated predicates.

choices.label: C
choices.explanation: Combining tables increases the combined relation rather than splitting one table into row subsets.

choices.label: D
choices.explanation: Replicating copies preserves the whole table at more sites rather than partitioning its rows.

reviews.answer_text: A repeated key or row identifier lets vertical pieces join back losslessly.
reviews.hint: Read reconstruction of column fragments in ADB36.
reviews.explanation: ADB36 repeats a key or row identifier across vertical fragments so attributes from the same original row can be matched during reconstruction. C states that purpose. The general requirement is a suitable identifier, not necessarily the particular declared primary key if another row identifier is used. It is unrelated to mandatory replication or inherently faster inserts.

evidence.quote: Vertical fragmentation projects column subsets and repeats a key or row identifier so joining on it reconstructs the original rows without spurious matches.

choices.label: A
choices.explanation: Faster insertion is not why vertical fragments share a row identifier.

choices.label: B
choices.explanation: Avoiding duplicate values is not sufficient to align column pieces from the same original row.

choices.label: C
choices.explanation: The shared key identifies matching original rows when the column fragments are joined.

choices.label: D
choices.explanation: Replication copies data and is distinct from reconstructing vertical column fragments.

reviews.answer_text: No replication, or nonredundant allocation.
reviews.hint: Read copy placement policies in ADB37.
reviews.explanation: ADB37 explicitly calls storing each fragment once nonredundant allocation. Full replication places the whole database at every relevant site, while partial replication copies selected fragments to selected sites. A hybrid can mix strategies, but the stem specifies exactly one location and no copies for every fragment, so C is the precise classification.

evidence.quote: nonredundant allocation stores each fragment once.

choices.label: A
choices.explanation: Full replication stores copies throughout the relevant sites rather than one copy per fragment.

choices.label: B
choices.explanation: Partial replication still copies selected fragments and therefore does not mean no copies.

choices.label: C
choices.explanation: Nonredundant allocation stores each fragment at one site without replicas.

choices.label: D
choices.explanation: A hybrid can combine policies, but the stated universal no-copy arrangement is specifically nonreplicated.

reviews.answer_text: Hide distribution details behind a single logical database experience.
reviews.hint: Read location, fragmentation and replication transparency in ADB35.
reviews.explanation: ADB35 defines transparency through which distribution details are hidden: sites, fragment reconstruction or replica selection/maintenance. Together these can let clients work with a single logical database abstraction. B captures that broad meaning. Transparency is not encryption, disclosure of every technical detail or a requirement that operating systems be identical.

evidence.quote: The broad single-logical-database experience may involve all three.

choices.label: A
choices.explanation: Encryption protects content; transparency here concerns hiding distribution complexity from legitimate users.

choices.label: B
choices.explanation: Distribution details can be hidden so users work with one logical database abstraction.

choices.label: C
choices.explanation: Transparency hides selected implementation details rather than exposing all of them.

choices.label: D
choices.explanation: Operating-system uniformity does not define distribution transparency.

reviews.answer_text: Horizontal and vertical fragmentation.
reviews.hint: Read hybrid splits and inverse reconstruction in ADB36.
reviews.explanation: ADB36 defines hybrid fragmentation as combining row and column splits in a suitable order. Reconstructing reverses those operations using unions for horizontal pieces and key joins for corresponding vertical pieces. Replication, deployment architectures and DBMS homogeneity are different design dimensions rather than the two fragmentation types combined by hybrid fragmentation.

evidence.quote: Hybrid fragmentation combines row and column splits in either suitable order.

choices.label: A
choices.explanation: Replication copies data and is not the second fragmentation dimension in the hybrid definition.

choices.label: B
choices.explanation: Hybrid fragmentation combines horizontal row splits with vertical column splits.

choices.label: C
choices.explanation: Client-server and middleware classify architectures rather than fragmentation operations.

choices.label: D
choices.explanation: Homogeneous/heterogeneous classifies system technology compatibility rather than row/column splitting.

reviews.answer_text: Copy-maintenance overhead is real, but biggest and very slow depend on replication policy and workload.
reviews.hint: Read eager/lazy propagation and storage costs in ADB37.
reviews.explanation: Full replication requires propagating updates and maintaining copies, supporting B’s central concern. But ADB37 distinguishes synchronous propagation, which increases acknowledgment latency, from asynchronous propagation, which permits later updates. Storage cost and stale reads may dominate instead. The stem gives no synchronization policy or workload, so B’s universal very slow and biggest wording is not established.

evidence.quote: Full replication does not inherently mean every copy is updated simultaneously; its synchronization rule must be stated.

choices.label: A
choices.explanation: Usable replicas can improve availability after a site failure rather than make all data unavailable.

choices.label: B
choices.explanation: Update propagation and coordination add costs, but latency and the biggest disadvantage depend on policy and workload.

choices.label: C
choices.explanation: Full replication does not inherently require all sites to use identical DBMS technology.

choices.label: D
choices.explanation: Replicas can serve queries; full replication does not limit queries to one primary site.

reviews.answer_text: Atomicity, Consistency, Isolation, Durability.
reviews.hint: Read the four ACID transaction guarantees in ADB06.
reviews.explanation: ADB06 gives all-or-none effects, preservation of declared rules, controlled interference and persistence after failure as the four ACID properties. B names them correctly. The other options substitute concurrency, availability, integrity, correctness or distribution for the defined terms, changing the acronym rather than describing an equivalent expansion.

evidence.quote: Atomicity means all effects or none; consistency means correct work preserves integrity rules; isolation controls concurrent interference; durability preserves committed effects despite failure.

choices.label: A
choices.explanation: Concurrency incorrectly replaces Consistency in the acronym.

choices.label: B
choices.explanation: The expansion exactly matches the four ACID property names.

choices.label: C
choices.explanation: Availability and Integrity replace Atomicity and Isolation, which are the defined terms.

choices.label: D
choices.explanation: Correctness and Distribution do not replace Consistency and Durability in ACID.

reviews.answer_text: Atomicity.
reviews.hint: Read all effects or none in ADB06.
reviews.explanation: The requested property concerns whether partial transaction effects can survive. ADB06 assigns all-or-none application to atomicity. A correct transaction also preserves consistency, concurrency needs isolation and completed commits need durability, but those are different guarantees. C is therefore the property matching the explicit ALL or NONE condition.

evidence.quote: Atomicity means all effects or none

choices.label: A
choices.explanation: Consistency concerns preservation of integrity rules rather than the indivisible effect boundary itself.

choices.label: B
choices.explanation: Isolation governs concurrent interference rather than all-or-none transaction effects.

choices.label: C
choices.explanation: Atomicity makes the transaction effects succeed together or be removed together.

choices.label: D
choices.explanation: Durability protects committed effects rather than defining partial-success handling.

reviews.hint: Compute the requested debit and credit using ADB06.
reviews.explanation: Subtracting 750 from A gives 4250 and adding it to B gives 8750; their total remains 13000. A implements both the specified operation and its total-balance invariant. B and C apply only one side. D preserves the initial total but does not perform the requested transfer, so invariant preservation alone does not make it the successful-transfer result.

evidence.quote: consistency means correct work preserves integrity rules

choices.label: A
choices.explanation: It performs the 750 debit and credit and preserves the total of 13000.

choices.label: B
choices.explanation: The debit occurs without its credit, reducing the total to 12250.

choices.label: C
choices.explanation: The credit occurs without its debit, increasing the total to 13750.

choices.label: D
choices.explanation: It preserves the starting total but leaves both accounts unchanged rather than performing the transfer.

reviews.answer_text: Isolation.
reviews.hint: Read interference between concurrent transactions in ADB06.
reviews.explanation: ADB06 assigns concurrent-interference control to isolation. That is the distinguishing phrase in the stem. Atomicity handles partial effects, durability handles committed persistence, and consistency means correct work preserves declared rules. Different isolation levels provide different detailed guarantees, so this classification does not imply that all implementations offer serializability by default.

evidence.quote: isolation controls concurrent interference

choices.label: A
choices.explanation: Atomicity governs partial effects within a transaction rather than concurrent interference.

choices.label: B
choices.explanation: Durability concerns persistence of committed changes after failures.

choices.label: C
choices.explanation: Consistency concerns declared integrity rules under correct business logic.

choices.label: D
choices.explanation: Isolation controls interference among concurrently executing transactions.

reviews.answer_text: Durability.
reviews.hint: Read committed effects despite failure in ADB06.
reviews.explanation: ADB06 defines durability by persistence of committed effects despite failure. Recovery information can provide this even when changed data pages were buffered at the instant of commit. All-or-none application, invariant preservation and concurrent isolation serve different transaction guarantees, so only durability matches survival of successful commits after a crash.

evidence.quote: durability preserves committed effects despite failure.

choices.label: A
choices.explanation: Atomicity concerns all-or-none application rather than the persistence of completed commits.

choices.label: B
choices.explanation: Consistency concerns validity of declared invariants rather than crash survival of commits.

choices.label: C
choices.explanation: Isolation controls concurrent interactions rather than persistence after a crash.

choices.label: D
choices.explanation: Durability preserves committed effects across system failures.

reviews.answer_text: Partially committed.
reviews.hint: Read the operation-completion versus commit boundary in ADB06.
reviews.explanation: ADB06 places a transaction in Partially committed after its last operation finishes but before durable commitment is assured. The stem states exactly that boundary. Active means operations are still executing; Committed needs successful commit; Failed needs an error. Finishing the operation list alone does not establish the committed state.

evidence.quote: Partially committed means the last operation finished but durable commitment is not yet assured.

choices.label: A
choices.explanation: Active describes ongoing operation execution, not the interval after the last operation finishes.

choices.label: B
choices.explanation: The last operation finished, but commitment is not yet assured.

choices.label: C
choices.explanation: The stem explicitly says the transaction has not yet committed.

choices.label: D
choices.explanation: No execution or commit failure is reported.

reviews.answer_text: Its effects have been rolled back; other committed transactions remain.
reviews.hint: Read Failed followed by Aborted in ADB06.
reviews.explanation: ADB06 reaches Aborted after rollback. Thus the aborted transaction’s own changes are removed rather than permanently saved. Restoring pre-transaction state must be understood relative to its effects, not erasing unrelated concurrent commits. A restart can be a new attempt, but is not automatic merely because the aborted state was reached.

evidence.quote: A failure leads to Failed, then Aborted after rollback

choices.label: A
choices.explanation: Permanent saving is a committed outcome, not an aborted outcome.

choices.label: B
choices.explanation: Rollback removes this transaction's effects while retaining other transactions' legitimate committed work.

choices.label: C
choices.explanation: Waiting for a lock describes a blocked executing transaction rather than completed rollback.

choices.label: D
choices.explanation: An aborted transaction may be retried, but automatic restart is not guaranteed.

reviews.answer_text: [commit, T].
reviews.hint: Read transaction-state log records in ADB07.
reviews.explanation: ADB07 identifies COMMIT as the record of successful transaction completion. START begins work, UPDATE records a data change and ABORT marks failed termination/rollback handling. A data write by itself does not prove the enclosing transaction committed, and an abort record can begin rollback rather than confirm it has completed.

evidence.quote: COMMIT records successful completion

choices.label: A
choices.explanation: The start record indicates beginning work rather than successful completion.

choices.label: B
choices.explanation: Abort records failure/rollback handling instead of successful commitment.

choices.label: C
choices.explanation: An update record describes one changed item, not successful transaction completion.

choices.label: D
choices.explanation: The commit record signals successful completion of transaction T.

reviews.answer_text: Disk page → buffer → program variable.
reviews.hint: Read the conceptual read_item path in ADB07.
reviews.explanation: ADB07 locates X’s page, loads it into a buffer if absent and copies the item from that buffer into the program variable. C gives that conceptual data movement order. A cached page may avoid the physical disk read, but the program still reads through the buffer. The reverse direction describes a write path rather than read_item.

evidence.quote: read_item(X) locates X's page, brings it into a buffer if absent, and copies X into a program variable.

choices.label: A
choices.explanation: The page is buffered before the item is copied to the program variable.

choices.label: B
choices.explanation: A read does not first send the buffer to disk before obtaining the variable value.

choices.label: C
choices.explanation: The page enters the buffer if needed, then its item is copied into the program variable.

choices.label: D
choices.explanation: Program-variable-to-buffer-to-disk describes writing, not reading into a variable.

reviews.answer_text: Locks, timestamp rules and transaction scheduling.
reviews.hint: Read concurrency mechanisms in ADB11/ADB15.
reviews.explanation: ADB11 defines compatible shared/exclusive locks and ADB15 orders conflicting operations with timestamp tests. These are actual concurrency-control mechanisms that constrain transaction schedules. Backups provide copies for recovery, and file permissions determine access rather than safe interleavings. Physical separation of people also does not coordinate their concurrent database operations.

evidence.quote: The lock manager decides requests; the lock table stores granted locks and waiting requests.

choices.label: A
choices.explanation: Backups support restoration rather than scheduling safe concurrent reads and writes.

choices.label: B
choices.explanation: Locks and timestamp rules control conflicting accesses and permissible schedules.

choices.label: C
choices.explanation: Separating users physically does not coordinate their concurrent operations on shared database items.

choices.label: D
choices.explanation: File permissions alone do not enforce isolation among authorized concurrent transactions.

reviews.answer_text: Write-write problem, as shorthand for a lost-update overwrite.
reviews.hint: Trace stale overwrite versus read anomalies in ADB08.
reviews.explanation: ADB08 illustrates both transactions reading 500, one writing 700 and the other later overwriting it with stale 600. The conflict is between their writes, which explains the offered write-write shorthand. This is not a claim that every pair of writes loses an update: the stale calculation and overwrite are essential. Read/read and phantom behavior describe different situations.

evidence.quote: T1 adds 100 to its stale value and writes 600.

choices.label: A
choices.explanation: Two reads alone do not overwrite and lose an update.

choices.label: B
choices.explanation: The stale write overwrites another write, motivating this write-write shorthand.

choices.label: C
choices.explanation: The defining loss is the later stale overwrite, not merely an arbitrary read/write pair.

choices.label: D
choices.explanation: A phantom changes a predicate query's qualifying row set rather than overwriting one balance.

reviews.answer_text: Reading another transaction’s uncommitted data.
reviews.hint: Read dirty-read dependencies in ADB08.
reviews.explanation: ADB08 defines dirty read through another transaction’s uncommitted write. The value can disappear if its writer aborts, leaving dependent work based on invalid data. Reading committed data or two readers accessing one item is not inherently dirty. Invalid-format writes concern data validity rather than whether the read-from transaction has committed.

evidence.quote: Dirty read: T2 reads a value written by uncommitted T1

choices.label: A
choices.explanation: Reading only committed values avoids the defining uncommitted-writer dependency.

choices.label: B
choices.explanation: The read consumes another transaction's modification before that writer commits.

choices.label: C
choices.explanation: Multiple readers alone do not create an uncommitted data dependency.

choices.label: D
choices.explanation: Invalid format concerns validation or integrity rather than the definition of a dirty read.

reviews.answer_text: A mixed-version aggregate is required; concurrent updates alone do not establish it.
reviews.hint: Read incorrect summary separately from nonrepeatable read in ADB08.
reviews.explanation: ADB08 distinguishes a repeated row read seeing a committed change from an aggregate mixing inconsistent versions. B gives a possible setting for the latter but not the necessary inconsistent read trace; a snapshot can produce a valid aggregate during updates. The parenthetical synonym also conflates distinct anomalies. The stem needs the actual version timing or a corrected definition.

evidence.quote: Incorrect summary mixes mutually inconsistent versions

choices.label: A
choices.explanation: Reading after another commit alone does not imply any inconsistent aggregate or repeated-row anomaly.

choices.label: B
choices.explanation: This can cause a mixed-version summary, but concurrency alone does not prove one occurred.

choices.label: C
choices.explanation: Concurrent deletion alone does not specify the inconsistent aggregate described by this anomaly.

choices.label: D
choices.explanation: Reading one's own uncommitted changes is not another transaction's dirty read or a summary anomaly.

reviews.answer_text: Compatible readers, with no writing under a shared lock.
reviews.hint: Read shared and exclusive permissions in ADB11.
reviews.explanation: ADB11 permits multiple shared locks on one item, each for reading. Writing requires a suitable exclusive lock, which conflicts with other shared holders. Thus B describes shared-lock behavior in the basic lock-based model. Exclusive read/write ownership and multiple simultaneous writers are not shared locking; multiversion snapshot rules are a separate model.

evidence.quote: A shared (S) lock permits reading; multiple S locks on the same item can coexist.

choices.label: A
choices.explanation: More than one transaction may hold compatible shared read locks on the same item.

choices.label: B
choices.explanation: Shared locks permit multiple readers but do not authorize writes under that lock mode.

choices.label: C
choices.explanation: Sole read/write ownership describes an exclusive lock.

choices.label: D
choices.explanation: Shared locks do not allow multiple transactions to write simultaneously.

reviews.answer_text: The exclusive holder may read and write; conflicting access to that item is blocked.
reviews.hint: Read same-item X/S and X/X conflicts in ADB11.
reviews.explanation: ADB11 permits an exclusive lock holder to read and write and makes that item’s X lock conflict with another S or X. C is correct in this basic model. Blocking all other access means conflicting access to the same item, not the entire database; locks on other items remain independent and multiversion systems can have additional snapshot-reader behavior.

evidence.quote: An exclusive (X) lock permits its holder to read and write and conflicts with another S or X on that item.

choices.label: A
choices.explanation: Other transactions' shared reads conflict with an exclusive lock on the same item in this model.

choices.label: B
choices.explanation: Two exclusive writers cannot hold compatible locks on the same item.

choices.label: C
choices.explanation: One holder can read/write the locked item while incompatible same-item accesses wait or abort.

choices.label: D
choices.explanation: Concurrent same-item shared readers conflict with this exclusive writer under the basic rules.

reviews.answer_text: Acquire or upgrade locks without releasing them.
reviews.hint: Read the 2PL phase boundary in ADB12.
reviews.explanation: ADB12 defines growing as the acquisition/upgrade phase and shrinking as the release/downgrade phase. Once any lock is released, no further acquisition is allowed. B therefore matches growing. Freely mixing acquisition and release would abandon the two-phase discipline that guarantees conflict serializability for well-formed transactions.

evidence.quote: Basic 2PL has a growing phase that acquires/upgrades locks and a shrinking phase that releases/downgrades them.

choices.label: A
choices.explanation: Releasing locks belongs to shrinking rather than growing.

choices.label: B
choices.explanation: Growing acquires or upgrades locks before any release occurs.

choices.label: C
choices.explanation: Freely acquiring after release violates the defining 2PL phase restriction.

choices.label: D
choices.explanation: Growing is precisely the phase in which lock requests may be made.

reviews.answer_text: Timestamp-based concurrency control.
reviews.hint: Read transaction start timestamps and item timestamps in ADB15.
reviews.explanation: ADB15 assigns each transaction a timestamp and checks reads and writes against item read/write timestamps. These checks preserve timestamp order and can abort stale operations. Locking instead uses ownership compatibility, optimistic control validates private work and shadow paging concerns recovery page maps. Only C names the start-time ordering technique described.

evidence.quote: A read by T aborts if TS(T)<write_TS(X); otherwise it succeeds and updates read_TS. A write aborts if TS(T)<read_TS(X) or TS(T)<write_TS(X); otherwise it succeeds and sets write_TS.

choices.label: A
choices.explanation: Locking uses lock compatibility and protocols rather than being defined by transaction start-time ordering.

choices.label: B
choices.explanation: Optimistic control validates private read/write sets rather than applying these timestamp-order tests.

choices.label: C
choices.explanation: Timestamp-based control orders valid conflicting operations using transaction timestamps.

choices.label: D
choices.explanation: Shadow paging preserves committed page maps for recovery rather than ordering concurrent operations.

reviews.answer_text: Read-heavy, low-conflict workloads.
reviews.hint: Read the validation/retry trade-off in ADB16.
reviews.explanation: ADB16 computes privately, validates and publishes, retrying failed validation. Low-conflict workloads let most work succeed; high write contention wastes computation on aborts. B states that criterion explicitly. Single-user systems do not need intertransaction conflict control, and OCC is not restricted to distributed transactions. Actual conflict frequency matters more than the read-heavy label alone.

evidence.quote: It works well when conflicts are uncommon, but high contention wastes work on aborts.

choices.label: A
choices.explanation: High conflicts cause validation failures and repeated wasted work.

choices.label: B
choices.explanation: Rare conflicts allow optimistic private work to validate successfully with few retries.

choices.label: C
choices.explanation: A single-user setting lacks the concurrent conflict problem motivating this choice.

choices.label: D
choices.explanation: Optimistic control is not limited to distributed transaction environments.

reviews.answer_text: A circular resource-wait chain.
reviews.hint: Read the wait-for-cycle definition in ADB13.
reviews.explanation: ADB13 requires a waiting cycle: participants hold resources needed by others and cannot make progress without a victim release or another intervention. Waiting for an unheld resource does not state such a cycle. Slow commit and simultaneous reads can occur without deadlock; compatible shared readers in particular need not block one another.

evidence.quote: Deadlock requires a waiting cycle

choices.label: A
choices.explanation: A resource held by no one does not create the stated circular hold-and-wait dependency.

choices.label: B
choices.explanation: Each participant waits for another holder in a cycle, preventing independent progress.

choices.label: C
choices.explanation: A slow commit may still progress and need not form a waiting cycle.

choices.label: D
choices.explanation: Compatible shared reads of the same data do not inherently deadlock.

reviews.answer_text: The younger requester aborts.
reviews.hint: Compare requester and holder ages in wait–die, ADB14.
reviews.explanation: The requester is younger and the holder older. ADB14 makes that requester die in wait–die; only an older requester may wait for a younger holder. On retry the aborted transaction retains its original timestamp. Wounding a holder belongs to a different protocol, and both participants need not be aborted.

evidence.quote: a younger requester needing an older holder aborts itself.

choices.label: A
choices.explanation: Wait–die aborts the younger requester when the needed resource is held by an older transaction.

choices.label: B
choices.explanation: The older holder keeps its resource; this protocol does not kill it for a younger requester.

choices.label: C
choices.explanation: Waiting is allowed for an older requester facing a younger holder, not this case.

choices.label: D
choices.explanation: The policy aborts the younger requester, not both participants.

reviews.answer_text: Abort the younger holder so the older requester can proceed.
reviews.hint: Read the wound–wait age action in ADB14.
reviews.explanation: ADB14 says an older requester wounds a younger holder, while a younger requester waits. B is therefore the rule for the given ages. The protocol uses priority to prevent cycles rather than arbitrarily aborting both or handing the work to a new transaction. Any retry should preserve the original timestamp to reduce starvation.

evidence.quote: In wound–wait, an older requester aborts the younger holder

choices.label: A
choices.explanation: An older requester wounds the younger holder rather than waiting under this policy.

choices.label: B
choices.explanation: The younger holder is aborted, releasing the resource for the older requester.

choices.label: C
choices.explanation: Aborting both is unnecessary and is not the wound–wait rule.

choices.label: D
choices.explanation: No replacement transaction takes over; the older requester continues after the conflicting holder releases.

reviews.answer_text: Abort a transaction whose wait exceeds the configured limit.
reviews.hint: Read timeout versus detection and prevention in ADB13.
reviews.explanation: ADB13 defines timeout by excessive wait duration and warns it can mistake slow progress for deadlock. B matches that mechanism. Wait-for graphs detect cycles, conservative locking obtains all locks before execution and age priorities define wait–die/wound–wait decisions. Those are distinct policies rather than implementations of a time limit.

evidence.quote: A timeout aborts long waits but may mistake slow progress for deadlock.

choices.label: A
choices.explanation: Graph analysis detects cycles rather than deciding from elapsed lock-wait time.

choices.label: B
choices.explanation: Timeout aborts a waiting transaction after its configured wait limit is exceeded.

choices.label: C
choices.explanation: Preacquiring all locks is conservative locking rather than timeout handling.

choices.label: D
choices.explanation: Age-based priorities define other prevention policies, not an elapsed-wait threshold.

reviews.answer_text: Equivalent behavior to some serial execution, even if interleaved.
reviews.hint: Read serial versus serializable schedules in ADB09.
reviews.explanation: ADB09 defines a serializable schedule as equivalent to a serial order while permitting interleaving. B matches when same result means the required full transaction equivalence, not an accidental equality of one final value. A describes a serial schedule, which is a special case but not the general definition. Commit simultaneity and disjoint tables are not required.

evidence.quote: A serializable schedule is equivalent to some serial order; it may interleave transactions.

choices.label: A
choices.explanation: This defines serial execution, a stricter special case that omits permitted serializable interleavings.

choices.label: B
choices.explanation: Serializable behavior is equivalent to some serial ordering; coincidental equality of one value alone is insufficient.

choices.label: C
choices.explanation: Simultaneous commits do not establish the required transaction-execution equivalence.

choices.label: D
choices.explanation: Serializable transactions may access the same tables if their operations are correctly ordered.

reviews.answer_text: Convert Shared to Exclusive.
reviews.hint: Read S→X upgrade versus X→S downgrade in ADB11.
reviews.explanation: ADB11 identifies S→X as an upgrade, possible only after incompatible other holders leave. It strengthens an existing read lock to permit writing. X→S is a downgrade, releasing all locks is transaction cleanup and granting compatible readers is shared acquisition. Only B names the requested conversion of a held lock.

evidence.quote: S→X is an upgrade, possible only after conflicting other holders leave.

choices.label: A
choices.explanation: Exclusive-to-shared is a downgrade rather than an upgrade.

choices.label: B
choices.explanation: Shared-to-exclusive strengthens the lock to permit writing when compatibility allows.

choices.label: C
choices.explanation: Removing locks is release rather than conversion to a stronger mode.

choices.label: D
choices.explanation: Granting compatible shared readers is not the upgrade of one existing lock.

reviews.answer_text: Indefinite postponement caused by repeated priority to other work.
reviews.hint: Read fairness versus waiting cycles in ADB13.
reviews.explanation: ADB13 defines starvation as indefinite postponement while other transactions progress, without requiring a deadlock cycle. B states that repeated bypass precisely. Holding many locks can create contention but does not itself prove starvation. Storage exhaustion and premature commit are different failures, so neither supplies the scheduling-fairness definition.

evidence.quote: Starvation is indefinite postponement while other work proceeds, without a required cycle.

choices.label: A
choices.explanation: Holding many locks describes resource use rather than being perpetually denied execution.

choices.label: B
choices.explanation: Repeated priority to others can indefinitely postpone the transaction while other work continues.

choices.label: C
choices.explanation: Running out of storage is a capacity failure rather than the defined scheduling starvation.

choices.label: D
choices.explanation: Premature commit concerns transaction correctness rather than indefinite postponement.

reviews.answer_text: Parsing and translation.
reviews.hint: Read representation before plan selection in ADB17.
reviews.explanation: ADB17 first checks syntax and semantics and constructs a logical query representation, before optimization and evaluation. C groups those initial activities. Result delivery follows execution, while optimization needs an understood query to compare valid plans. The phase grouping is conventional, but the ordering dependency is explicit in the complete note.

evidence.quote: Parsing checks SQL grammar; semantic analysis resolves names, types and access permissions.

choices.label: A
choices.explanation: Optimization follows understanding and representing the query rather than preceding it.

choices.label: B
choices.explanation: Evaluation executes a selected plan and is not the first processing activity.

choices.label: C
choices.explanation: Parsing/translation establishes query meaning and logical representation before optimization.

choices.label: D
choices.explanation: Results can be delivered only after the required evaluation produces them.

reviews.answer_text: Relational algebra.
reviews.hint: Read the typical logical query representation in ADB17.
reviews.explanation: ADB17 translates a query into relational algebra or a logical query tree for equivalent rewrites and plan selection. B names that logical representation. A particular engine may later compile execution code, but machine code, Python scripts and XML documents are not the general logical translation target taught here. Logical meaning precedes implementation-specific execution choices.

evidence.quote: Translation constructs a logical representation, typically relational algebra or a logical query tree.

choices.label: A
choices.explanation: Machine code may be an implementation detail but is not the stated logical translation target.

choices.label: B
choices.explanation: Relational algebra represents the logical operations used for rewriting and planning.

choices.label: C
choices.explanation: Python scripts are not the general internal representation specified by the note.

choices.label: D
choices.explanation: XML documents are not the defined general relational query representation.

reviews.answer_text: Overall execution cost under the chosen resource model.
reviews.hint: Read plan-cost inputs in ADB19.
reviews.explanation: ADB19 measures candidate plans using I/O, CPU, memory, temporary storage and network traffic. The aim is a suitable low-cost equivalent plan, not syntactic brevity or indiscriminate removal of joins and tables. Required tables and semantics must be preserved; even fewer operations do not necessarily imply lower runtime or resource cost.

evidence.quote: A cost model estimates resources for a candidate plan: page I/O, CPU, memory, temporary storage and network traffic.

choices.label: A
choices.explanation: Required tables cannot be discarded merely to reduce the table count.

choices.label: B
choices.explanation: Optimization compares equivalent plans using estimated time and resource costs.

choices.label: C
choices.explanation: Join count alone ignores access paths, cardinalities and the cost of each join.

choices.label: D
choices.explanation: Short SQL text does not necessarily produce a cheaper execution plan.

reviews.answer_text: Disk I/O in the conventional local-disk query-cost model.
reviews.hint: Read the context of typical cost dominance in ADB19.
reviews.explanation: ADB19 says disk I/O often dominates textbook local-disk examples, matching the question’s typical teaching model. C includes both seek and transfer work. This is a contextual tendency, not a universal claim: CPU can dominate in-memory work and communication can dominate distributed plans. The answer should retain that local-disk qualification rather than extend it to every system.

evidence.quote: Disk I/O often dominates textbook local-disk examples

choices.label: A
choices.explanation: CPU can dominate in-memory work but is not the typical local-disk-model answer.

choices.label: B
choices.explanation: Network cost can dominate distributed plans rather than the conventional local-disk model.

choices.label: C
choices.explanation: Seek and transfer I/O often dominate the conventional disk-based cost model.

choices.label: D
choices.explanation: Memory allocation is not the dominant term specified for the textbook local-disk model.

reviews.answer_text: 35 ms.
reviews.hint: Apply count × unit-time disk cost in ADB19.
reviews.explanation: ADB19 adds seeks times seek duration to blocks times per-block transfer duration. Five seeks cost 5×5=25 ms and ten block transfers cost 10×1=10 ms. Their sum is 35 ms. The terms must be added, not multiplied together or considered separately; this is the supplied simple disk model rather than a measured universal query runtime.

evidence.quote: cost = seeks×seek_time + transferred_blocks×block_transfer_time.

choices.label: A
choices.explanation: Fifty does not equal the sum of 25 ms seeking and 10 ms transfer.

choices.label: B
choices.explanation: Five times five plus ten times one gives 35 ms.

choices.label: C
choices.explanation: Fifteen omits the correct five-seek multiplication.

choices.label: D
choices.explanation: Twenty-five counts only seek time and omits ten milliseconds of transfer.

reviews.answer_text: A valid recovered state preserving durable commits and removing incomplete effects.
reviews.hint: Read restart recovery goals in ADB26.
reviews.explanation: ADB26 defines restart recovery by preserving durable commits and removing incomplete effects after failure. B matches the simple undo/redo teaching model. The detailed work depends on buffer policy and algorithm; not every committed update needs physical redo if already installed. Recovery does not reset the database to creation, last login or an empty replacement state.

evidence.quote: Restart recovery restores a valid database after a crash while preserving durable commits and removing incomplete effects.

choices.label: A
choices.explanation: Returning to creation would discard legitimate later durable commits.

choices.label: B
choices.explanation: Recovery preserves committed work and removes incomplete effects to restore valid state.

choices.label: C
choices.explanation: User login time is not the transaction recovery boundary.

choices.label: D
choices.explanation: Emptying the database would destroy committed data rather than recover it.

reviews.answer_text: Software error.
reviews.hint: Distinguish stated cause from hardware/media failures in ADB26.
reviews.explanation: The stem directly identifies DBMS software bugs as the cause. That is a software error rather than failed hardware, a natural event or broken communication. ADB26 separates transaction/system/media failure concerns so the recovery resource can be chosen appropriately; an observed crash alone would not identify its cause, but this question explicitly supplies it.

evidence.quote: Transaction failures include invalid operations, constraint violations and concurrency-control aborts.

choices.label: A
choices.explanation: The stated cause is faulty software behavior rather than a malfunctioning hardware component.

choices.label: B
choices.explanation: No natural event is described; the prompt names a software bug.

choices.label: C
choices.explanation: Unexpected behavior caused by DBMS bugs is a software error.

choices.label: D
choices.explanation: No failed network connection is given as the cause of the behavior.

reviews.answer_text: The required order is stable log before corresponding changed data-page disk writes.
reviews.hint: Read WAL durable ordering versus buffer changes in ADB27.
reviews.explanation: ADB27 allows a buffer to change before its log flush, but requires recovery information to become durable before the changed page reaches disk. B is the intended rule if corresponding data changes means durable writes; it is too strong if it includes in-memory assignments. Since that scope is unstated, the literal wording needs clarification rather than an unconditional log-before-every-change claim.

evidence.quote: A buffer can be changed before that log flush; WAL orders durable writes, not every CPU assignment.

choices.label: A
choices.explanation: Data-before-log reverses WAL's required durable ordering.

choices.label: B
choices.explanation: It matches durable page writes, but not all in-memory data modifications; the scope is unstated.

choices.label: C
choices.explanation: WAL logs updates before necessary data flushes and does not wait to create all logs until after commit.

choices.label: D
choices.explanation: A checkpoint before every write is not the WAL requirement.

reviews.answer_text: Reapply missing logged committed effects in the simple undo/redo model.
reviews.hint: Read after-image redo in ADB27.
reviews.explanation: ADB27 uses redo to install logged after-images when necessary. B describes preserving committed work missing from disk pages in the simple teaching model. It does not mean re-running application side effects or blindly adding an amount twice. ARIES has a broader repeat-history phase before undo, but that does not make reversal, checkpoint creation or lock acquisition the definition of redo.

evidence.quote: Redo installs logged after-images when necessary, usually forward.

choices.label: A
choices.explanation: Reversing incomplete changes is undo rather than redo.

choices.label: B
choices.explanation: Redo installs required logged effects missing from data pages, preserving committed work in the simple model.

choices.label: C
choices.explanation: Checkpoint creation records recovery state rather than reapplying update after-images.

choices.label: D
choices.explanation: Locking may coordinate access but is not the operation of logged redo.

reviews.answer_text: Restore before-images of incomplete or aborted work.
reviews.hint: Read logged reversal in ADB27.
reviews.explanation: ADB27 restores before-images when undoing incomplete effects, normally following that transaction’s updates backward. B states both the affected work and the supporting log information. Applying committed after-images is redo, forcing logs is a WAL durability action, and copying pages is part of a different update/recovery approach. None is the reversal operation itself.

evidence.quote: Undo restores before-images of incomplete effects

choices.label: A
choices.explanation: Reapplying committed effects is the redo purpose in the simple model.

choices.label: B
choices.explanation: Undo restores logged old values to remove incomplete or aborted transaction effects.

choices.label: C
choices.explanation: Forcing the log supports durable ordering but does not itself reverse data changes.

choices.label: D
choices.explanation: Shadow-page copies preserve versions instead of defining logged before-image undo.

reviews.answer_text: Copy changed pages and atomically install the new durable map on commit.
reviews.hint: Read shadow paging maps in ADB29.
reviews.explanation: ADB29 keeps the committed page map unchanged while modifications use new locations and a modified map. Commit durably installs the new root/map pointer after required pages are durable. B captures that preservation-and-switch mechanism. Timestamp ordering, mandatory per-transaction checkpoints and universal log-based rollback are not the defining shadow-paging steps.

evidence.quote: commit durably installs a new root/map pointer atomically after required pages are durable.

choices.label: A
choices.explanation: Timestamp ordering controls concurrent operations rather than defining shadow page-map replacement.

choices.label: B
choices.explanation: Copy-on-write preserves originals and commit safely installs the new page map.

choices.label: C
choices.explanation: Shadow paging is an alternative to conventional log-based recovery, not mandatory logged rollback for all changes.

choices.label: D
choices.explanation: A checkpoint every transaction is not the mechanism that preserves the old page map.

reviews.answer_text: A checkpoint supplies recovery state that avoids scanning all historical logs from the beginning.
reviews.hint: Read checkpoint entry points and earlier active work in ADB30.
reviews.explanation: ADB30 uses durable checkpoint state to avoid processing all old history. B describes that benefit if start means entering recovery analysis, not assuming every earlier update is irrelevant. Active transactions can span a checkpoint and fuzzy-checkpoint redo may require earlier log positions. A checkpoint is not a full backup, universal stop or lock grant.

evidence.quote: A checkpoint records enough durable recovery state to avoid scanning all old history.

choices.label: A
choices.explanation: Fuzzy checkpoints permit ongoing transactions, so stopping all work is not required.

choices.label: B
