choices.explanation: Recorded recovery state provides a bounded starting point, while earlier necessary undo/redo must still be considered.

choices.label: C
choices.explanation: A checkpoint stores recovery metadata and is not a full separate database backup.

choices.label: D
choices.explanation: Checkpointing does not grant every active transaction exclusive locks.

reviews.answer_text: REDO only and NO UNDO/REDO are synonymous here.
reviews.hint: Read deferred-update classification in ADB29.
reviews.explanation: ADB29 explicitly classifies usual deferred update with no-force as NO-UNDO/REDO, because uncommitted changes do not reach the persistent database but committed changes may need replay. REDO only describes the same requirement. Therefore both C and D are correct, rather than separate alternative algorithms. The classification is under the stated usual deferred model.

evidence.quote: Redo-only and NO-UNDO/REDO mean the same thing, so those cannot be separate unique answers.

choices.label: A
choices.explanation: Usual deferred update does not require undo of uncommitted persistent database changes.

choices.label: B
choices.explanation: Undo only gives the opposite recovery requirement from the usual deferred no-force model.

choices.label: C
choices.explanation: REDO only is the usual deferred-update recovery classification.

choices.label: D
choices.explanation: NO UNDO/REDO is another spelling of the same redo-only requirement.

reviews.answer_text: Shadow update, or copy-on-write.
reviews.hint: Read update location separately from commit timing in ADB29.
reviews.explanation: ADB29 distinguishes where an update is written from when it may become persistent. Shadow/copy-on-write uses a new location while retaining the committed version, matching C. Immediate and deferred classify commit timing, not necessarily a separate location. In-place update overwrites the original location, which directly contradicts the preservation condition in the stem.

evidence.quote: Shadow/copy-on-write update writes a new location while preserving the committed version.

choices.label: A
choices.explanation: Immediate update concerns allowing persistent changes before commit rather than requiring new locations.

choices.label: B
choices.explanation: Deferred update concerns withholding uncommitted persistent effects rather than necessarily copying pages.

choices.label: C
choices.explanation: Shadow/copy-on-write preserves the original and writes the changed value at a separate location.

choices.label: D
choices.explanation: In-place update overwrites the original location rather than preserving it intact.

reviews.answer_text: Both values are present in the conceptual undo/redo log, but real log formats vary.
reviews.hint: Read conceptual UPDATE records versus physical/logical implementations in ADB07.
reviews.explanation: ADB07 gives a conceptual UPDATE(T,X,old,new) record, making C correct in that teaching model. It also explicitly allows physical or logical real-system records. A redo-only or undo-focused design may store different information, so an unqualified claim about every transaction log is too broad. The stem needs the assumed recovery/log format to establish a unique universal answer.

evidence.quote: Real systems may use physical or logical records, and need not log every read.

choices.label: A
choices.explanation: After-image-only records can support redo-oriented formats, but the log model is not specified.

choices.label: B
choices.explanation: Before-image information can support undo-oriented designs; the assumed format is unstated.

choices.label: C
choices.explanation: The note's conceptual undo/redo UPDATE record includes both old and new values.

choices.label: D
choices.explanation: Identifiers and timestamps alone omit the update information required for the described value recovery.

reviews.answer_text: Logically related data across networked sites under coordinated database management.
reviews.hint: Read the distributed database definition in ADB33.
reviews.explanation: ADB33 defines logically related data across networked sites managed as a coordinated system. B matches that architecture and its logical abstraction. Full replication is only one placement choice, not a defining requirement. A single powerful server is centralized, and generic web file storage does not establish coordinated database semantics across related distributed data.

evidence.quote: A distributed database contains logically related data across networked sites, managed as a coordinated system.

choices.label: A
choices.explanation: A database confined to one server is centralized rather than distributed across networked sites.

choices.label: B
choices.explanation: Networked, logically related data with coordinated management fits the distributed database definition.

choices.label: C
choices.explanation: A distributed database need not replicate every row at every network location.

choices.label: D
choices.explanation: Generic web file storage does not by itself establish coordinated distributed database management.

reviews.answer_text: The same compatible DBMS technology at the sites.
reviews.hint: Read homogeneous versus heterogeneous technology in ADB33.
reviews.explanation: ADB33 defines homogeneity through compatible DBMS technology across sites. B is the listed form of that condition. It does not imply identical local schemas, replication or immediate synchronization. Different DBMSs describe heterogeneity, while removing the network or demanding full independence contradicts coordinated distributed management rather than defining homogeneity.

evidence.quote: A homogeneous system uses compatible DBMS technology across sites

choices.label: A
choices.explanation: Different DBMS technologies characterize heterogeneous integration rather than homogeneity.

choices.label: B
choices.explanation: The same DBMS software supplies the compatible database technology described by homogeneous systems.

choices.label: C
choices.explanation: Distributed sites need network communication for coordinated management.

choices.label: D
choices.explanation: Full local independence is an autonomy choice rather than a homogeneity requirement.

reviews.answer_text: ODBC and JDBC connectivity interfaces.
reviews.hint: Read connectivity versus semantic integration in ADB33.
reviews.explanation: ADB33 explicitly names ODBC and JDBC as connectivity interfaces for differing systems. C therefore identifies the offered communication interfaces. They do not automatically reconcile schemas, units or transaction semantics and do not create a distributed transaction by themselves. Identical DBMS software is not heterogeneity, and generic LAN protocols do not replace database-level connectivity interfaces.

evidence.quote: ODBC and JDBC provide connectivity interfaces; they do not automatically solve semantic differences or create one distributed transaction.

choices.label: A
choices.explanation: Requiring the same DBMS removes the differing-engine situation rather than identifying its connectivity interfaces.

choices.label: B
choices.explanation: Direct SQL alone does not identify the generic cross-system connectivity standards named in the note.

choices.label: C
choices.explanation: ODBC and JDBC provide generic database connectivity while semantic mappings remain necessary.

choices.label: D
choices.explanation: LAN protocols alone do not supply the database API/interface compatibility described.

reviews.answer_text: Rows selected by conditions.
reviews.hint: Read horizontal row predicates in ADB36.
reviews.explanation: ADB36 defines horizontal fragmentation by selecting row subsets with predicates. B directly states that operation. Column division is vertical fragmentation, and combining both dimensions is hybrid fragmentation. Schema names and geographic placement can influence a design, but are not the definition of what is split by horizontal fragmentation.

evidence.quote: Horizontal fragmentation selects row subsets by predicates; their union reconstructs the relation.

choices.label: A
choices.explanation: Splitting attributes is vertical rather than horizontal fragmentation.

choices.label: B
choices.explanation: Horizontal fragmentation partitions rows according to stated predicates or criteria.

choices.label: C
choices.explanation: Splitting both dimensions combines horizontal and vertical operations in hybrid fragmentation.

choices.label: D
choices.explanation: Schemas are not the row units divided by the defined horizontal operation.

reviews.answer_text: UNION.
reviews.hint: Read reconstruction of horizontal row subsets in ADB36.
reviews.explanation: Horizontal fragments contain selected subsets of the original relation’s rows. ADB36 reconstructs the relation by their union, assuming completeness and the intended overlap rules. Joining is used to align vertical column pieces by a key; intersection would keep only shared rows and difference would remove rows, so neither reconstructs all horizontal fragments.

evidence.quote: Horizontal fragmentation selects row subsets by predicates; their union reconstructs the relation.

choices.label: A
choices.explanation: Key joins reconstruct matching vertical column pieces, not ordinary horizontal row partitions.

choices.label: B
choices.explanation: Union collects the rows from every complete horizontal fragment.

choices.label: C
choices.explanation: Intersection keeps only common rows and would discard rows unique to individual fragments.

choices.label: D
choices.explanation: Difference removes rows instead of recombining all fragment members.

reviews.answer_text: Column subsets with a repeated key or row identifier.
reviews.hint: Read vertical reconstruction identifiers in ADB36.
reviews.explanation: ADB36 splits a relation by columns and repeats a key or row identifier so the pieces can be joined without spurious matches. B describes that usual primary-key form. Rows are split horizontally; transaction counts and geography concern workload or placement rather than the attribute-level split defining vertical fragmentation. The shared identifier can be an appropriate equivalent key.

evidence.quote: Vertical fragmentation projects column subsets and repeats a key or row identifier

choices.label: A
choices.explanation: Row subsets define horizontal rather than vertical fragmentation.

choices.label: B
choices.explanation: Vertical fragments contain column subsets plus a repeated identifier for reconstruction.

choices.label: C
choices.explanation: Concurrent transaction count is a workload property rather than the dimension being split.

choices.label: D
choices.explanation: Geographic placement does not define the column projection used for vertical fragments.

reviews.answer_text: Propagating each update across all copies adds maintenance overhead.
reviews.hint: Read replication benefits and update cost in ADB37.
reviews.explanation: ADB37 says copies improve locality and can improve availability but require storage and update propagation. B names that maintenance burden for full replication. Propagation timing may be synchronous or asynchronous, so the answer does not imply every copy is updated simultaneously. Fast reads are a possible benefit, and concurrency control becomes more involved rather than inherently simple.

evidence.quote: Copies improve read locality and can improve availability but require storage and update propagation.

choices.label: A
choices.explanation: Usable replicas can improve availability rather than inherently making it low.

choices.label: B
choices.explanation: All copies must eventually reflect relevant updates, creating propagation and coordination overhead.

choices.label: C
choices.explanation: Fast reads are a potential benefit rather than the listed disadvantage.

choices.label: D
choices.explanation: Maintaining consistent copies does not inherently simplify concurrency control.

reviews.answer_text: Users query the logical relation without knowing its fragments.
reviews.hint: Read fragmentation transparency separately from location/copy hiding in ADB35.
reviews.explanation: ADB35 defines fragmentation transparency as hiding the existence and reconstruction of fragments. B states that user-facing abstraction directly. It does not require literally only DBAs to know the implementation; developers and administrators may also need that knowledge. Exposing fragment tables or all fragmentation details to users would make fragmentation visible instead of transparent.

evidence.quote: Fragmentation transparency hides the existence and reconstruction of fragments: users query the whole logical relation.

choices.label: A
choices.explanation: Showing all fragmentation details is the opposite of hiding them from ordinary queries.

choices.label: B
choices.explanation: Users operate on the whole logical relation without managing its fragment reconstruction.

choices.label: C
choices.explanation: Transparency describes the user abstraction, not exclusive knowledge restricted to DBAs alone.

choices.label: D
choices.explanation: Naming fragments separately exposes fragmentation rather than concealing it from the querying user.

reviews.answer_text: Middleware mediates between clients and independent database servers.
reviews.hint: Read middleware communication responsibilities in ADB34.
reviews.explanation: ADB34 lets middleware translate requests, locate data, coordinate operations and combine results across independent servers. C describes that mediating tier. The logical responsibility does not require exactly one physical machine in every implementation. Direct connections omit this mediator, universal server collaboration is a different arrangement, and one centralized server is not the stated distributed middleware design.

evidence.quote: Middleware can translate requests, locate data, coordinate operations and combine results across independent servers.

choices.label: A
choices.explanation: Direct client-server links alone omit the middleware mediation that defines the requested architecture.

choices.label: B
choices.explanation: Every server need not participate in every query; relevant sources depend on the request.

choices.label: C
choices.explanation: A middleware tier mediates client requests across multiple independent database servers.

choices.label: D
choices.explanation: One centralized database server does not describe mediation across independent distributed servers.

reviews.answer_text: Horizontal and vertical fragmentation.
reviews.hint: Read hybrid row/column splitting in ADB36.
reviews.explanation: ADB36 explicitly defines hybrid fragmentation as combining row and column splits in an appropriate order. B names those two operations. Replication changes copy placement, locking and timestamps control concurrent access, and client-server/middleware describe architecture responsibilities. They can coexist with hybrid fragmentation but are not its two component fragmentation techniques.

evidence.quote: Hybrid fragmentation combines row and column splits in either suitable order.

choices.label: A
choices.explanation: Full/no replication concerns copies rather than the row and column splits of hybrid fragmentation.

choices.label: B
choices.explanation: Hybrid fragmentation combines horizontal row subsets with vertical column subsets.

choices.label: C
choices.explanation: Locking and timestamps are concurrency-control mechanisms, not fragmentation types.

choices.label: D
choices.explanation: These are architecture forms rather than the two data-fragmentation operations.

reviews.answer_text: Manage shared data, process requests and enforce supported transaction/integrity guarantees.
reviews.hint: Read server responsibilities in ADB34.
reviews.explanation: ADB34 assigns clients request submission and servers shared-data management, operation execution and supported integrity/transaction enforcement. C matches those responsibilities. User interfaces usually belong to clients, while initiating all connections, polling every client or caching all sessions for offline use are not the server role defined by this architecture. Guarantees still depend on supported mechanisms and correct application use.

evidence.quote: servers manage shared data, execute operations and enforce supported integrity/transaction rules.

choices.label: A
choices.explanation: The user-facing GUI is normally a client responsibility rather than the database server's primary role.

choices.label: B
choices.explanation: The server need not initiate every connection or poll clients for every update.

choices.label: C
choices.explanation: Shared-data management, query execution and supported integrity/transaction enforcement are server duties.

choices.label: D
choices.explanation: Caching every session for offline access is not the defined database-server responsibility.

reviews.answer_text: Growing phase.
reviews.hint: Read acquire-before-release discipline in ADB12.
reviews.explanation: ADB12 allows acquiring or upgrading locks during growing and releasing or downgrading them during shrinking. Once any lock is released, a transaction may not acquire another. A is therefore the phase described. Commit is a transaction event, validation belongs to optimistic control and shrinking has the opposite lock-release role.

evidence.quote: Basic 2PL has a growing phase that acquires/upgrades locks and a shrinking phase that releases/downgrades them.

choices.label: A
choices.explanation: Growing permits acquisitions and upgrades before any release starts.

choices.label: B
choices.explanation: Commit is not the general 2PL phase for new lock acquisition.

choices.label: C
choices.explanation: Validation is an optimistic-control stage rather than the 2PL growing phase.

choices.label: D
choices.explanation: Shrinking releases or downgrades locks and forbids acquiring new ones.

reviews.answer_text: Access control.
reviews.hint: Read permitted read versus forbidden update privileges in ADB24.
reviews.explanation: ADB24 explicitly describes a user allowed to view but not change a record as having restricted access privileges. That is authorization/access control. Integrity concerns valid values, availability concerns readiness for use and non-repudiation concerns attributable actions rather than whether a particular read or write is permitted. A matches the actual permission distinction.

evidence.quote: A user who can view but cannot change a record has restricted access privileges.

choices.label: A
choices.explanation: Access control grants reading while denying modification for the specified user.

choices.label: B
choices.explanation: Availability concerns service readiness rather than the read-versus-write privilege distinction.

choices.label: C
choices.explanation: Non-repudiation does not define whether this user is authorized to modify a record.

choices.label: D
choices.explanation: Integrity restricts valid data states rather than assigning user-specific read/update permissions.

reviews.answer_text: Long-running log scans can make recovery expensive.
reviews.hint: Read why deferred update still needs recovery boundaries in ADB30.
reviews.explanation: ADB30 warns that without checkpoints or another valid truncation boundary, a long-running system may scan expensive amounts of log history. Deferred update removes uncommitted persistent effects but does not remove that search problem. Page copying belongs to shadow approaches, while shared locks and serializability are independent concurrency concerns rather than consequences of omitting checkpoints.

evidence.quote: Without checkpoints or another valid truncation boundary, long-running systems may need expensive log scans; deferred update does not avoid that problem.

choices.label: A
choices.explanation: High transaction volume and long uptime can produce costly recovery log scans without a valid boundary.

choices.label: B
choices.explanation: Frequent copy-on-write pages characterize shadow updating rather than the absence of checkpoints in deferred update.

choices.label: C
choices.explanation: Omitting checkpoints does not inherently prohibit shared locks.

choices.label: D
choices.explanation: View serializability is a concurrency-order property, not inherently lost by this checkpoint omission.

reviews.answer_text: ARIES and deferred database modification are both log-based techniques.
reviews.hint: Read ARIES WAL and deferred redo in ADB29/ADB31.
reviews.explanation: ADB31 explicitly builds ARIES on WAL and logged recovery metadata. ADB29’s usual deferred-update model logs committed work for redo without undo. Both therefore satisfy the category, as ADB45 warns. Shadow paging is a page-map alternative, while multidatabase recovery identifies a system scope rather than a specific log-based algorithm.

evidence.quote: ARIES uses WAL, page log sequence numbers (pageLSN), a transaction table and a dirty-page table.

choices.label: A
choices.explanation: Multidatabase recovery describes an environment rather than one specific recovery technique.

choices.label: B
choices.explanation: ARIES explicitly uses WAL and log-driven analysis, redo and undo.

choices.label: C
choices.explanation: Shadow paging preserves committed page maps rather than being the conventional log-based technique.

choices.label: D
choices.explanation: Deferred modification can use logged changes for redo after commitment.

reviews.answer_text: The operation is vertical fragmentation, not a transparency level.
reviews.hint: Distinguish the column split from hiding that split in ADB35/ADB36.
reviews.explanation: ADB36 defines splitting columns into reconstructable subrelations as vertical fragmentation. ADB35 separately names hiding that split fragmentation transparency. D identifies the intended operation, but the stem incorrectly asks for a type of transparency, and the correct transparency name is absent. The conceptual answer is therefore supported, but the category in the literal question and choices needs repair.

evidence.quote: Vertical fragmentation projects column subsets and repeats a key or row identifier

choices.label: A
choices.explanation: Replication copies data rather than splitting its columns into fragments.

choices.label: B
choices.explanation: Location transparency hides physical sites rather than performing a column projection.

choices.label: C
choices.explanation: Horizontal fragmentation selects rows rather than columns and is not itself a transparency level.

choices.label: D
choices.explanation: Vertical describes the fragmentation operation, but it is not a named transparency level as the stem claims.

reviews.answer_text: After repairing the sets and normalizing case, fghe is absent; the literal item is defective.
reviews.hint: Read language concatenation and the case sensitivity of alphabet symbols.
reviews.explanation: AUT02 computes {e,fgh}{c,d}={ec,ed,fghc,fghd}, excluding fghe. However, the stem has broken set delimiters and all options begin with uppercase letters while its languages use lowercase. Under literal case sensitivity every displayed choice is absent. Only an explicit transcription repair makes C the intended unique exclusion, so this question cannot support a unique literal key.

evidence.quote: Symbols are case-sensitive; uppercase choices cannot literally equal lowercase words without a declared transcription repair.

choices.label: A
choices.explanation: Fghc is absent literally; normalizing its initial letter gives fghc, which belongs to the repaired product.

choices.label: B
choices.explanation: Ed is absent literally; normalizing its initial letter gives ed, which belongs to the repaired product.

choices.label: C
choices.explanation: Fghe is absent literally and fghe remains absent after case normalization, making it the intended repaired exclusion.

choices.label: D
choices.explanation: Ec is absent literally; normalizing its initial letter gives ec, which belongs to the repaired product.

reviews.answer_text: The concatenation L1L2 is regular, as the saved image clarifies.
reviews.hint: Read closure of regular languages and distinguish reversal from equivalence.
reviews.explanation: AUT14 states closure under concatenation, so any two regular languages have a regular concatenation. The source image resolves the OCR fragment LiL in C as L1L2 and shows D as reversal, not the garbled star notation. Reversal preserves regularity but need not preserve the original language. Union needs no exclusion of the empty word, and arbitrary closures need not coincide.

evidence.quote: Regular languages are closed under union, concatenation, star, reversal, intersection, difference and complement.

choices.label: A
choices.explanation: Union is regular even if it contains the empty word; the only-if restriction is false.

choices.label: B
choices.explanation: Both stars are regular, but arbitrary regular languages need not have equal Kleene closures.

choices.label: C
choices.explanation: The image reads L1L2; regular languages are closed under this concatenation operation.

choices.label: D
choices.explanation: The image reads reversal: it remains regular but need not equal L1, for example {ab} reverses to {ba}.

reviews.answer_text: The optional expression r? = r|ε.
reviews.hint: Read the difference between optionality, star and positive closure.
reviews.explanation: AUT12 defines r? as r|ε: one occurrence of a word matching r or no occurrence. Positive closure requires one or more occurrences; star permits arbitrarily many including zero. Their identities may be valid, but only the optional expression denotes the requested zero-or-one repetition count, so the aggregate is false.

evidence.quote: r? means r|ε; r⁺=rr*.

choices.label: A
choices.explanation: Positive closure rr* requires at least one repetition and also allows more than one.

choices.label: B
choices.explanation: Star allows zero or arbitrarily many repetitions, not just zero or one.

choices.label: C
choices.explanation: The union with ε makes r optional: either one r match or none.

choices.label: D
choices.explanation: The positive and Kleene closures do not impose the zero-or-one bound.

reviews.answer_text: Always context-free, but not necessarily regular.
reviews.hint: Read CFL intersection with a regular language and its counterexample.
reviews.explanation: AUT23 constructs the intersection by combining PDA control with DFA control and retaining the original stack. It therefore guarantees a CFL. Regularity does not follow: intersecting {aⁿbⁿ} with a*b* gives the same nonregular CFL. Some individual intersections can be regular, but the question’s general result cannot assert that extra property.

evidence.quote: The result is guaranteed context-free, not necessarily regular: intersect aⁿbⁿ with a*b* to get aⁿbⁿ.

choices.label: A
choices.explanation: Closure under intersection with a regular language guarantees that the result is context-free.

choices.label: B
choices.explanation: The stated closure theorem directly rules out a result outside the context-free family.

choices.label: C
choices.explanation: Every regular language is context-free, so regular but not context-free is impossible.

choices.label: D
choices.explanation: Some intersections are regular, but the counterexample in AUT23 shows regularity is not guaranteed.

reviews.answer_text: Linear Bounded Automaton (LBA).
reviews.hint: Read AUT25 and AUT26. Compare regular, context-free and context-sensitive languages, then identify the memory needed to match three equal counts.
reviews.explanation: The clarified language contains equal numbers of a, b and c in that order. AUT26 identifies this family as context-sensitive but not context-free. Restricting n to integers greater than 1 does not remove the unbounded equal-count requirement. AUT25 describes an LBA that checks the order and repeatedly marks one a, one b and one c, using only the input-sized tape region. B therefore recognizes the stated language; DFA, NFA and single-stack PDA cannot.

evidence.quote: aⁿbⁿcⁿ is CSL but not CFL, and therefore decidable.
For aⁿbⁿcⁿ first verify a*b*c* order, repeatedly mark one unmarked a, b and c, and reject missing/excess symbols.

choices.label: A
choices.explanation: A DFA recognizes regular languages; this three-equal-count language is not even context-free.

choices.label: B
choices.explanation: An LBA can mark matching a, b and c symbols while staying within space proportional to the input length.

choices.label: C
choices.explanation: An NFA recognizes exactly the regular languages, so nondeterminism does not give it the memory needed here.

choices.label: D
choices.explanation: A standard single-stack PDA recognizes context-free languages; the stated three-equal-count language is not context-free.

question_revision.original_stem: Which automaton is powerful enough to recognize the language L = {a"b"c" | n> 1}?
question_revision.stem: Which automaton is powerful enough to recognize the language L = {aⁿbⁿcⁿ | n > 1}, where n is an integer?
question_revision.note: Clarified practice version: the corrupted powers are restored as aⁿbⁿcⁿ.
assumptions: Each of a, b and c is repeated n times, with integer n > 1.

reviews.answer_text: The first step depends on the chosen GNF conversion algorithm.
reviews.hint: Read the GNF construction route and whether CNF is mandatory.
reviews.explanation: The source image confirms both CNF conversion and left-recursion elimination are offered. AUT20 describes a constructive route involving simplification, ordering and substitution, and says some algorithms first convert to CNF. Left recursion must eventually be removed, but that does not make it the universal first step. Without naming an algorithm, the question cannot select one mandatory starting operation.

evidence.quote: Some algorithms first convert to CNF; this is a method choice, not a universally mandatory first step.

choices.label: A
choices.explanation: CNF is the initial normalization in some algorithms, but not a mandatory first step for every route.

choices.label: B
choices.explanation: This restates the overall conversion task without specifying a concrete initial operation.

choices.label: C
choices.explanation: Converting to GNF is the goal, not an algorithmic first step explaining how to reach it.

choices.label: D
choices.explanation: Eliminating left recursion is necessary when present, but its position depends on the selected construction route.

reviews.answer_text: PDAs characterize Type 2 languages and also accept the included Type 3 languages.
reviews.hint: Read the exact NPDA family and the inclusion of regular languages.
reviews.explanation: AUT05 identifies Type 2 CFG languages with NPDA recognition and places regular languages strictly inside CFLs. The literal wording asks which language is accepted, not which family is exactly characterized. Consequently Type 3 languages are accepted as well as Type 2. Entire Type 0 or Type 1 families exceed PDA power; an exact-family question would single out Type 2.

evidence.quote: Type 3 regular grammars correspond to finite automata; type 2 CFGs to nondeterministic PDAs;

choices.label: A
choices.explanation: PDAs do not recognize every Type 0 language; unrestricted TM recognition exceeds context-free power.

choices.label: B
choices.explanation: The Type 1 family includes non-CFLs such as three-equal-count languages, beyond ordinary PDA recognition.

choices.label: C
choices.explanation: Nondeterministic PDAs recognize exactly the context-free, Type 2 language family.

choices.label: D
choices.explanation: Every regular Type 3 language is context-free, so it too is accepted by a suitable PDA.

reviews.answer_text: Both consistently left-linear and right-linear grammars can be converted to DFAs.
reviews.hint: Read the expressiveness of both orientations of regular grammars.
reviews.explanation: AUT14 states that both consistent linear orientations generate regular languages. Its right-linear construction produces an NFA, and AUT09/AUT10 give equivalence and subset conversion to DFA; left-linear languages are regular too. Generic grammar is undefined and cannot mean that arbitrary CFGs or unrestricted grammars are convertible. Thus B and C are supported, but All is not.

evidence.quote: Both consistent orientations generate REG;

choices.label: A
choices.explanation: Generic grammar is undefined; arbitrary grammars can generate nonregular languages and need not have equivalent DFAs.

choices.label: B
choices.explanation: Consistently left-linear grammars generate regular languages, which have equivalent DFAs.

choices.label: C
choices.explanation: Right-linear grammars convert to NFAs and then, by subset construction, to equivalent DFAs.

choices.label: D
choices.explanation: The undefined generic-grammar choice is not guaranteed regular, so all choices cannot be accepted.

reviews.answer_text: FORTRAN needs a specified syntax, semantic-constraint or computational-power interpretation.
reviews.hint: Read why a programming language’s name does not determine one formal-language classification.
reviews.explanation: AUT31 explicitly separates CFG-style programming syntax, semantic restrictions and Turing-complete computation. These are different questions. Calling FORTRAN context-free may refer to a syntactic approximation; Turing language may refer to computational power, while context-sensitive constraints concern well-formed programs. The stem states none of these scopes, so no unique formal classification can be justified from its name alone.

evidence.quote: FORTRAN/programming-language questions must distinguish CFG-style syntax, semantic restrictions and Turing-complete computation; a language's name alone does not choose one formal classification.

choices.label: A
choices.explanation: This may refer to Turing-complete computation, but it does not classify the set of syntactically valid source strings.

choices.label: B
choices.explanation: Context-sensitive restrictions may arise in program well-formedness, but the stem defines no such source-language set.

choices.label: C
choices.explanation: CFG-style syntax is a common interpretation, but the stem does not restrict itself to that syntax.

choices.label: D
choices.explanation: Regular token patterns do not classify the complete nested syntax or computational behavior of a programming language.

reviews.answer_text: An off-line Turing machine.
reviews.hint: Read the organization of the off-line TM’s input and work tapes.
reviews.explanation: AUT28 directly defines an off-line TM as having a read-only input tape and a separate read/write work tape. The question gives that architecture. Multiple heads, nondeterministic transition choices and multidimensional tape geometry are independent variants; none defines this input/work separation. The number of tape roles alone does not imply those other variants.

evidence.quote: An off-line TM has a read-only input tape and separate read/write work tape.

choices.label: A
choices.explanation: Multi-head describes head multiplicity rather than this read-only input and writable work-tape separation.

choices.label: B
choices.explanation: The off-line model explicitly separates a read-only input tape from a read/write work tape.

choices.label: C
choices.explanation: Nondeterministic describes transition choices, not which tape permits writes.

choices.label: D
choices.explanation: Multidimensional describes tape geometry rather than the two tape roles specified here.

reviews.answer_text: The singleton set {λ}.
reviews.hint: Read zero-length words versus zero powers of languages or alphabets.
reviews.explanation: AUT03 defines Σⁿ as all words of length n, including Σ⁰={ε}; AUT01 identifies λ with ε. There is exactly one length-zero word, so its set is {λ}. Σ, positive closure and Kleene closure contain nonempty words for the given nonempty alphabet and therefore are not equal to the zero power.

evidence.quote: including Σ⁰={ε}.

choices.label: A
choices.explanation: Σ⁺ contains positive-length words over the alphabet and excludes the empty word.

choices.label: B
choices.explanation: Σ* contains every finite-length word, not just the single empty word.

choices.label: C
choices.explanation: Σ contains four alphabet symbols, each forming a length-one word rather than a length-zero word.

choices.label: D
choices.explanation: λ denotes the empty word, and its singleton set is exactly the alphabet’s zero power.

reviews.answer_text: A null (epsilon) production.
reviews.hint: Read null and unit production definitions.
reviews.explanation: AUT19 defines a null production as A→ε, while AUT01 identifies λ as another notation for the empty word. Substituting S for A gives the displayed S→λ rule. A unit production instead has one nonterminal on the right; secondary and sigma production are not the defined names for an empty right-hand side.

evidence.quote: A null production is A→ε; a unit production is A→B with one variable.

choices.label: A
choices.explanation: The right-hand side is the empty word, exactly the definition of a null production.

choices.label: B
choices.explanation: A unit production has one nonterminal on the right, not the empty word.

choices.label: C
choices.explanation: Secondary production is not the defined term for a rule deriving the empty word.

choices.label: D
choices.explanation: Sigma denotes an alphabet conventionally, not the null-production category described here.

reviews.answer_text: Context-sensitive, regular and context-free languages are all subsets of recursive languages.
reviews.hint: Read the containment chain and apply transitivity.
reviews.explanation: AUT05 gives REG⊊CFL⊊CSL⊊DECIDABLE⊊RE. Recursive means decidable under AUT29, so context-sensitive languages lie inside recursive languages, and transitivity places regular and context-free languages there too. A reverses the strict regular/CFL inclusion. The wording asks which statement is true, and three options independently satisfy that condition.

evidence.quote: Use REG ⊊ CFL ⊊ CSL ⊊ DECIDABLE ⊊ RE,

choices.label: A
choices.explanation: The inclusion is reversed: regular languages are a proper subset of context-free languages.

choices.label: B
choices.explanation: Every context-sensitive language is decidable, hence recursive, as the hierarchy states.

choices.label: C
choices.explanation: Regular languages are inside CFL, CSL and then decidable languages by transitivity.

choices.label: D
choices.explanation: Context-free languages are inside CSL and therefore inside recursive languages.

reviews.answer_text: NP-complete problems belong to NP and admit deterministic exponential-time exhaustive search.
reviews.hint: Read both parts of NP-completeness and the certificate-search upper bound.
reviews.explanation: AUT36 explicitly states both membership in NP and an exponential-time exhaustive certificate decision procedure. These are compatible truths: an exponential upper bound does not establish an exponential lower bound. Deterministic search refutes the claim of only nondeterministic solvability. The note’s SAT, TSP and coloring examples also do not support dismissing the entire class as having no applications.

evidence.quote: Thus NP-complete languages lie inside NP and can be decided by finite exhaustive certificate search in exponential time; both statements can be true options.

choices.label: A
choices.explanation: Finite deterministic certificate enumeration decides NP-complete languages; nondeterministic algorithms are not the only possibility.

choices.label: B
choices.explanation: Membership in NP is a necessary part of the definition of NP-completeness.

choices.label: C
choices.explanation: Exhaustive search over polynomial-size certificates gives an exponential-time deterministic upper bound, not a proven lower bound.

choices.label: D
choices.explanation: No such exclusion follows from NP-completeness; the note includes substantive SAT, tour and coloring formulations.

reviews.answer_text: NP-complete: the problems both in NP and NP-hard.
reviews.hint: Read the distinction between NP-hardness and membership in NP.
reviews.explanation: AUT36 defines NP-complete as NP membership together with hardness for every NP problem under polynomial reductions. That is the precise class described by hardest problems in NP. NP-hard alone can extend beyond NP, even to undecidable problems; PSPACE is a larger resource class, and P does not impose the required hardness.

evidence.quote: X is NP-complete if X∈NP and X is NP-hard.

choices.label: A
choices.explanation: P means deterministic polynomial time and does not define hardness for every NP language.

choices.label: B
choices.explanation: NP-completeness combines being in NP with being at least as hard as every NP problem.

choices.label: C
choices.explanation: NP-hardness alone does not ensure membership in NP, so it is broader than the class requested.

choices.label: D
choices.explanation: PSPACE is defined by polynomial space and can contain languages outside the specified NP-complete class.

reviews.answer_text: The general halting problem is undecidable.
reviews.hint: Read the diagonal contradiction for a hypothetical halting decider.
reviews.explanation: AUT30 constructs a machine that contradicts a hypothetical universal halting decider when run on its own description. Hence no decider answers halting correctly for all machine/input pairs. HALT is recognizable by simulation, but that process need not terminate on nonhalting instances; recognizing some yes-instances is not solving the general decision problem.

evidence.quote: Thus HALT is undecidable and witnesses RE beyond DECIDABLE.

choices.label: A
choices.explanation: Simulation recognizes halting yes-instances but no TM decides the general halting problem on every input.

choices.label: B
choices.explanation: The diagonal argument rules out a decider correct for all programs and inputs.

choices.label: C
choices.explanation: Undecidability is the exact result proved by the halting diagonalization argument in AUT30.

choices.label: D
choices.explanation: HALT concerns arbitrary computations and is not confined to regular languages or finite automata.

reviews.answer_text: Determining whether an arbitrary TM halts on its given input.
reviews.hint: Read what undecidable means and the general halting theorem.
reviews.explanation: AUT30 proves HALT undecidable, directly matching D. The other choices describe ordinary finite mathematical computation: primality can test finitely many candidate divisors, a finite list can be sorted, and an exact finite linear system can be processed by elimination. Their cost can vary, but no general undecidability follows from those ordinary formulations.

evidence.quote: Undecidable means no general decider exists, not merely no algorithm is currently known.

choices.label: A
choices.explanation: For an integer, testing finitely many candidate divisors decides primality; AUT26 uses bounded divisor testing.

choices.label: B
choices.explanation: A finite numeric list can be sorted by a terminating comparison procedure.

choices.label: C
choices.explanation: An ordinarily encoded finite linear system can be decided and solved by finite elimination steps.

choices.label: D
choices.explanation: This is the general halting decision problem proved undecidable in AUT30.

reviews.answer_text: Context-sensitive and unrestricted grammars can generate the three-equal-count language.
reviews.hint: Read the least family for three equal counts and upward inclusion in the hierarchy.
reviews.explanation: Reading the conventional flattened powers as 0ⁿ1ⁿ2ⁿ with n≥0, renaming the symbols in AUT26 gives a CSL that is not a CFL. AUT05 permits the isolated-start epsilon convention for n=0. Context-sensitive is therefore the least sufficient listed family, while unrestricted grammars can also generate it. The stem does not request the least family, so both are valid.

evidence.quote: aⁿbⁿcⁿ is CSL but not CFL, and therefore decidable.

choices.label: A
choices.explanation: Three unbounded equal counts are not regular; the language is outside even the context-free family.

choices.label: B
choices.explanation: Renaming aⁿbⁿcⁿ to 0ⁿ1ⁿ2ⁿ preserves its non-context-free character.

choices.label: C
choices.explanation: A context-sensitive grammar suffices, with the isolated-start epsilon convention covering n=0.

choices.label: D
choices.explanation: Unrestricted grammars include the context-sensitive capability and can generate the same language.

reviews.answer_text: Both context-sensitive and unrestricted grammars can generate unary prime-length words.
reviews.hint: Read unary prime length, pumping and the unary-CFL property.
reviews.explanation: Interpreting an as the conventional flattened aⁿ notation, AUT26 proves unary prime length nonregular by pumping and excludes CFL status because every unary CFL is regular. It also gives bounded-workspace divisor testing, establishing context sensitivity. Unrestricted grammars are stronger and can generate the same language. Without a least-family qualifier, both C and D work.

evidence.quote: Every unary CFL is regular, so this language is not CFL either. It is nevertheless context-sensitive: count the input in bounded workspace and test divisors.

choices.label: A
choices.explanation: The prime-length pumping argument in AUT26 proves the unary language nonregular.

choices.label: B
choices.explanation: Every unary CFL is regular, contradicting the established nonregularity of prime lengths.

choices.label: C
choices.explanation: Bounded-workspace counting and divisor testing establish the context-sensitive classification.

choices.label: D
choices.explanation: The unrestricted family can generate all context-sensitive languages, including unary prime length.

reviews.answer_text: PSPACE is the exact polynomial-space class; EXPTIME also contains it.
reviews.hint: Read the definition of PSPACE and distinguish defining membership from broad containment.
reviews.explanation: AUT38 defines PSPACE by deterministic polynomial workspace, making C the intended exact class. AUT39 also places PSPACE inside EXPTIME, so D contains every polynomial-space decision problem as well. If contains problems means merely some problems, even P and NP overlap. The missing exact-class qualifier prevents a unique answer under the literal containment wording.

evidence.quote: Use L⊆NL⊆P⊆NP⊆PSPACE⊆EXPTIME⊆EXPSPACE.

choices.label: A
choices.explanation: P languages use polynomial space, but P is not the class defined by all polynomial-space decisions.

choices.label: B
choices.explanation: NP is contained in PSPACE, so it contains polynomial-space-solvable problems without defining the full space class.

choices.label: C
choices.explanation: PSPACE is precisely the class of languages decidable using polynomial workspace.

choices.label: D
choices.explanation: EXPTIME contains PSPACE, so broad containment wording does not exclude this larger class.

reviews.answer_text: Reductions.
reviews.hint: Read the transformation and the direction required for hardness proofs.
reviews.explanation: AUT35 defines a polynomial reduction as a computable transformation preserving yes/no membership and explains how reducing a known hard problem to a new target proves target hardness. AUT32 supplies the computable version for undecidability. Thus reductions name the proof concept itself, while hierarchy, completeness and classes describe relationships or resulting properties rather than the transformation method.

evidence.quote: To prove a new target X hard, reduce a known hard problem Y to X, not X to Y.

choices.label: A
choices.explanation: A reduction transforms instances while preserving membership, enabling hardness or completeness arguments with the stated resource bound.

choices.label: B
choices.explanation: A hierarchy organizes classes; it does not itself supply the instance transformation used in a hardness proof.

choices.label: C
choices.explanation: Completeness is the property proved using membership and hardness, not the reduction method itself.

choices.label: D
choices.explanation: Complexity classes group problems by resources; reductions establish the required relationships between individual problems.

reviews.answer_text: ZW = cddcababb.
reviews.hint: Read the order-preserving definition of string concatenation.
reviews.explanation: AUT02 defines xy as all of x followed by all of y, preserving order and every symbol. Appending ababb to cddc yields cddcababb, of length 4+5=9. Reversing the operands produces a different string; selecting prefixes or first letters discards symbols and is not concatenation.

evidence.quote: Concatenation xy writes x followed by y: cddc·ababb=cddcababb;

choices.label: A
choices.explanation: This preserves cddc followed by ababb, giving the required nine-symbol concatenation.

choices.label: B
choices.explanation: cdab discards symbols from both operands instead of retaining both complete strings.

choices.label: C
choices.explanation: ababbcddc is WZ, reversing the specified operand order.

choices.label: D
choices.explanation: ca retains only initial symbols and is not the concatenation of the full strings.

reviews.answer_text: L⁰ is {λ}, not the word λ itself.
reviews.hint: Read the set-valued definition of language powers.
reviews.explanation: AUT02 defines L⁰={ε}; AUT01 equates λ with ε. Thus the literal equality L⁰=λ confuses a set with its sole word and is false unless braces are explicitly understood. Reading the binary stars in A as the displayed concatenation separators, A is the third-power definition; C and D are the unions defining star and positive closure in AUT03.

evidence.quote: A language power is a set, so L⁰=ε is a type error unless braces are understood.

choices.label: A
choices.explanation: With the displayed binary stars denoting concatenation, three copies of L form L³, so this is true.

choices.label: B
choices.explanation: This is the false statement: the zeroth power is the singleton language {λ}, not the word λ.

choices.label: C
choices.explanation: The union of all nonnegative language powers is the definition of Kleene closure, so this is true.

choices.label: D
choices.explanation: The union of positive language powers is positive closure, even if L itself contains ε.

reviews.answer_text: ac.
reviews.hint: Read alphabet powers as words of exactly the exponent’s length.
reviews.explanation: AUT03 defines Σⁿ as the words containing exactly n alphabet symbols. The given alphabet includes a and c, so ac has two permitted symbols and belongs to Σ². Single-symbol choices have length one; aabbccdd has length eight. Membership depends on length and symbol validity, not on including all alphabet symbols.

evidence.quote: Σⁿ contains words of exactly n symbols;

choices.label: A
choices.explanation: b uses an allowed symbol but has length one rather than the required two.

choices.label: B
choices.explanation: c is a one-symbol word and therefore belongs to Σ¹, not Σ².

choices.label: C
choices.explanation: ac has exactly two symbols, both drawn from the given alphabet.

choices.label: D
choices.explanation: aabbccdd has eight symbols; using each symbol twice does not make it a length-two word.

reviews.answer_text: None of the four strings is generated from either possible start, A or B.
reviews.hint: Apply each production to a shrinking residual and check the start-variable declaration.
reviews.explanation: The image confirms A→aB|bA|bBa and B→bB|cA|b. Exhaustively testing their shrinking residuals rejects every offered string from both A and B. Every recursive step removes terminals, so the test terminates and covers all productions. AUT40 supports the no-member result. Although the start variable is undeclared, neither possible choice changes the rejection, so the defect is no valid offered option.

evidence.quote: Every recursive residual is shorter. Checking all four offered words yields no member, contradicting the marked source choice.
The language is L(G)={w∈Σ*:S⇒*w}.

choices.label: A
choices.explanation: The exhaustive shrinking recurrence rejects this exact string from both A and B.

choices.label: B
choices.explanation: This exact string fails every permitted terminal-prefix or b…a wrapper decomposition.

choices.explanation: Despite source emphasis, its residuals fail the displayed grammar for both possible start variables.

choices.label: D
choices.explanation: The recurrence rejects it; a c before the required A-to-B a transition also exposes failure.

reviews.answer_text: A path records a derivation in a sentential-form graph; a whole parse tree records derivation structure.
reviews.hint: Identify whether graph vertices are sentential forms or grammar symbols.
reviews.explanation: The image confirms generic graph wording without specifying its vertices. AUT16 distinguishes a parse tree from a derivation graph. A path through sentential forms records successive rewrites, whereas a branch of a parse tree does not capture the whole derivation. C is valid under the first graph interpretation, but the omitted graph model prevents a unique unconditional selection.

evidence.quote: The whole tree represents derivation structure; a path in a derivation graph is a different object.

choices.label: A
choices.explanation: A root identifies the starting object, not the full sequence of derivation steps.

choices.label: B
choices.explanation: Vertex degree counts incident connections and does not record the rewrite sequence.

choices.label: C
choices.explanation: A root-to-vertex path records steps if vertices are sentential forms; that graph model is not specified.

choices.label: D
choices.explanation: One parent records only a local predecessor relationship, not the complete derivation history.

reviews.answer_text: All four membership statements hold under the image-restored CFG notation.
reviews.hint: Read a CFG production’s single-variable left side and string-valued right side.
reviews.explanation: The image restores a∈(V+Σ), a∈V, a∈(V+Σ)* and b∈(V+Σ)*, with + denoting union. AUT16 says a CFG left side is one variable and the right side is any finite variable/terminal string. A variable also belongs to the union and its string closure. The stronger B condition therefore does not make the weaker A or C false.

evidence.quote: In a context-free grammar (CFG) each production has one variable on the left, A→α with α∈(V∪Σ)*.

choices.label: A
choices.explanation: A single variable belongs to V and hence to the union V∪Σ restored in the image.

choices.label: B
choices.explanation: The CFG left-hand side is exactly one variable, so it belongs to V.

choices.label: C
choices.explanation: A variable is also a length-one word over V∪Σ, satisfying this weaker condition.

choices.label: D
choices.explanation: The right side is a finite string of terminals and variables, including epsilon where allowed.

reviews.answer_text: No offered expression matches both ε and ab, which the diagram accepts.
reviews.hint: Test an accepting start and the shortest return cycle before deriving a complete expression.
reviews.explanation: Both saved images show the start state accepting and an a edge out followed by b back. AUT41 therefore requires ε and ab in the language. A, C and D lack ε because of their mandatory prefixes. B includes ε through its outer star but its shortest nonempty block has four symbols, excluding ab. No source-highlighted choice can satisfy both tests.

choices.explanation: Its mandatory (a+b)ab prefix prevents epsilon, which the accepting start must accept.

choices.explanation: The outer star admits epsilon, but every nonempty block has length at least four, so ab is absent.

reviews.answer_text: Input is data, not a separate hardware component.
reviews.hint: Read the TM’s finite control, head and tape architecture.
reviews.explanation: AUT27 lists finite control, a read/write head and an unbounded tape as the standard TM architecture. Input is initial tape content rather than a separate hardware organ. Thus input is the distinction requested by not part, under that structural reading; the other three options are actual machine components, not merely values processed by them.

evidence.quote: The standard machine has finite control, a read/write head and an unbounded tape. Input is initial tape content, not a separate hardware organ; no separate stack is required.

choices.explanation: Finite control is explicitly part of the standard machine’s architecture.

choices.label: B
choices.explanation: Input is initial tape content rather than a separate machine hardware component.

choices.label: C
choices.explanation: The unbounded tape is the standard TM’s storage component.

choices.label: D
choices.explanation: The read/write head is an explicit machine component used for tape access.

reviews.answer_text: No grammar family is determined by an unspecified formal language.
reviews.hint: Read grammar-generated languages and the limits of unrestricted grammars.
reviews.explanation: The source image adds no language specification. AUT04 defines a grammar as generating its own language, and AUT05 orders expressive families. Regular, CFG and context-sensitive grammars each generate all words of their respective language, while unrestricted grammars cover RE languages, not arbitrary non-RE sets. The missing language or most-general-listed-family qualifier prevents one unique grammar category.

evidence.quote: The language is L(G)={w∈Σ*:S⇒*w}.

choices.label: A
choices.explanation: A CFG suffices if the specified language is context-free, but no such property is supplied.

choices.label: B
choices.explanation: A context-sensitive grammar suffices for CSLs; the language here is not classified.

choices.label: C
choices.explanation: RE names a language family associated with unrestricted grammars, not a guarantee for every possible formal language.

choices.label: D
choices.explanation: Regular grammars suffice for regular languages, which the unspecified language might be.

reviews.answer_text: The formula ww is the non-CFL copy language; even palindromes require wwᴿ.
reviews.hint: Distinguish copying a word from appending its reversal.
reviews.explanation: AUT26 explicitly separates ww from wwᴿ over two symbols. The literal formula denotes copying, so D fits that reading. The parenthetical even-length palindromes instead denotes wwᴿ, for which B fits under AUT22. These contradictory descriptions cannot both define the same language. The author must choose the formula or the verbal description before one label is certified.

evidence.quote: Over a two-symbol alphabet, wwᴿ is CFL, ww is not CFL; both are decidable.

choices.label: A
choices.explanation: Both binary copy and binary unmarked even-palindrome languages are nonregular.

choices.label: B
choices.explanation: This fits wwᴿ, the parenthetical palindrome reading, but not the literal ww formula.

choices.label: C
choices.explanation: Binary unmarked even palindromes are not deterministic CFL, and binary copying is not CFL at all.

choices.label: D
choices.explanation: This fits the literal binary copy language ww, contradicting the parenthetical palindrome description.

reviews.answer_text: n+1 states for a fixed valid suffix word.
reviews.hint: Read suffix-prefix state invariants and the minimality argument.
reviews.explanation: AUT08 gives n+1 states for a valid fixed suffix of length n: states remember the longest suffix of the consumed input that is a prefix of the target. Distinguishable prefixes establish the lower bound. The answer presumes the target word uses the declared alphabet; no extra rejecting sink is needed for a suffix matcher.

evidence.quote: For a fixed valid word w of length n, a DFA for strings ending in w needs n+1 states representing the longest consumed suffix that is a prefix of w.

choices.label: A
choices.explanation: n states omit one of the n+1 necessary prefix-match stages.

choices.label: B
choices.explanation: The note gives one state for each matched-prefix length from zero through n.

choices.label: C
choices.explanation: An extra rejecting sink is unnecessary because later input may always form the required suffix.

choices.label: D
choices.explanation: Doubling n is not the general suffix-matching state bound; accidental numeric equality does not define it.

reviews.answer_text: A DFA may have no final states, and it need not have only one transition.
reviews.hint: Read accepting-set emptiness and per-state/symbol determinism.
reviews.explanation: AUT06 permits F=∅ and specifies exactly one successor for each state/symbol pair, not one transition in the whole machine. Hence B and D are both false under the literal wording. A describes acceptance after consuming the complete word and C matches the required start state. D would be repairable by adding per state/input pair.

evidence.quote: Exactly one next state is specified per state/symbol pair; this does not mean the whole machine has one transition. F may be empty, recognizing ∅.

choices.label: A
choices.explanation: Final-state acceptance is correct when evaluated after all input has been consumed.

choices.label: B
choices.explanation: This is false: an empty accepting set is permitted and recognizes the empty language.

choices.label: C
choices.explanation: The standard automaton has a designated initial state, satisfying at least one.

choices.label: D
choices.explanation: This is false literally: determinism gives one successor per state/symbol pair, not one total transition.

reviews.answer_text: Type 0 is most general overall but absent; context-sensitive is largest among the explicitly named families.
reviews.hint: Read the hierarchy and specify the comparison domain.
reviews.explanation: AUT05 makes unrestricted Type 0 the most expressive grammar family, but the options omit it. If the question means largest among the named families, context-sensitive exceeds CFG and regular. If all structured grammars is intended, that answer is incomplete. Phase is also undefined here, so the comparison domain must be repaired before an exclusive answer is justified.

evidence.quote: Use REG ⊊ CFL ⊊ CSL ⊊ DECIDABLE ⊊ RE,

choices.label: A
choices.explanation: Context-sensitive is largest among the three explicitly named families, but not most general overall.

choices.label: B
choices.explanation: CFGs are properly below context-sensitive grammars in expressive power.

choices.label: C
choices.explanation: Regular grammars are the weakest of the listed named families.

choices.label: D
choices.explanation: The three listed families are not equally most general, and unrestricted grammars are absent.

reviews.answer_text: a is not generated.
reviews.hint: Read the matching-pair recursion and empty-word base case.
reviews.explanation: The image restores S→aSb|λ and option C as λ, not the extracted X. AUT17 derives exactly aⁿbⁿ for n≥0. Two recursions generate aabb, one generates ab, and the base rule gives λ. A lone a has unequal counts and cannot arise. The readable source resolves the OCR damage rather than changing the grammar by assumption.

choices.label: A

choices.label: B

choices.label: C

choices.label: D

reviews.answer_text: Grammars generate languages and automata recognize those languages; no option states that relation unambiguously.

reviews.explanation: AUT04 explicitly says automata recognize languages, not grammars. A is the likely intended relation if which refers back to languages, but its immediate grammatical antecedent is formal grammars. B and D reverse the roles, while C changes the generative object to automata. The relation itself is clear; A needs a repaired pronoun before a unique literal statement is certified.

evidence.quote: Grammars generate languages; automata recognize languages, not grammars.

choices.label: B
choices.explanation: Languages do not recognize automata; recognition is performed by a machine on words.

choices.label: C
choices.explanation: Formal grammars generate languages, not automata as the statement asserts.

choices.label: D
choices.explanation: Grammars generate rather than recognize languages, and languages do not generate automata.

reviews.answer_text: None names a formal language as a precisely specified set of words.

English, Spanish and French are natural-language names; regular expressions name a notation, not a particular precisely specified word set here. The question needs an actual language example or must ask for a formal specification notation instead.

evidence.quote: A regular expression denotes a language but is not itself the set of matched words.

choices.explanation: French is a natural language rather than a formally specified set of strings in this item.

reviews.answer_text: Finite automata characterize REG; stronger models can also recognize regular languages.

reviews.explanation: AUT05 pairs regular grammars with finite automata, making C the characteristic least model. But PDAs and TMs also recognize regular languages by the hierarchy. D does not identify the nondeterministic model; it could mean NFA, which also recognizes REG. Since the stem asks what is used rather than the least or exact model family, its choices overlap.

evidence.quote: Type 3 regular grammars correspond to finite automata; type 2 CFGs to nondeterministic PDAs; type 1 context-sensitive/noncontracting grammars to nondeterministic LBAs; type 0 unrestricted grammars to Turing recognizers.

A is unconditionally true while D is also true under the existential reading and false under an all-CFL reading. The stem does not resolve that ambiguity; multiple successors and epsilon moves are not ordinary DFA behavior.

reviews.answer_text: PDA fits; “context-sensitive automaton” also fits if it means LBA.

D is undefined, yet under the conventional LBA interpretation it also satisfies that interval. NFA is equivalent to DFA and TM reaches the upper endpoint. Asking specifically for stack memory or defining D would resolve the overlap.

evidence.quote: Type 3 regular grammars correspond to finite automata; type 2 CFGs to nondeterministic PDAs; type 1 context-sensitive/noncontracting grammars to nondeterministic LBAs; type 0 unrestricted grammars to Turing recognizers.

choices.explanation: A PDA recognizes CFLs, properly beyond regular languages and below Turing-recognizable languages.

choices.label: B

choices.label: C
choices.explanation: TM is the upper endpoint and is not less powerful than itself.

choices.label: D
choices.explanation: If context-sensitive automaton means LBA, it too lies strictly between finite automata and unrestricted TM power.

A CFG is the exact defining grammar family, but stronger grammars can generate its languages too. The question asks capability rather than least sufficient family, so B, C and D work; regular grammars cannot generate every CFL.

choices.label: B
choices.explanation: Context-free grammars define the context-free family directly.

choices.label: D

The language aⁿbⁿcⁿ demonstrates why the reverse containment fails. Strict inclusion does not invalidate the weaker inclusion, so both true choices must be retained rather than selecting only the more informative statement.

This is defective option scope, not a missing CSL theorem.

evidence.quote: Type 3 regular grammars correspond to finite automata; type 2 CFGs to nondeterministic PDAs; type 1 context-sensitive/noncontracting grammars to nondeterministic LBAs; type 0 unrestricted grammars to Turing recognizers.

A question asking for an example cannot exclude valid subfamilies merely because another option is more general.

An NFA cannot recognize this nonregular language, but nondeterministic automaton alone could denote a stronger model. Without least-model wording and a definition of D, the item cannot support one exclusive answer.

evidence.quote: For aⁿbⁿ, push one X per a, switch to a b-reading phase, pop one X per b, and accept when input ends at the bottom marker.

choices.label: D

reviews.answer_text: Binary mirror palindromes are CFL and belong to stronger families; the alphabet is unspecified.

reviews.answer_text: PDA and TM recognize mirror palindromes; alphabet and generic automaton scope are missing.

evidence.quote: For even palindromes wwᴿ over {a,b}, push the first half, nondeterministically guess its midpoint, then pop matching symbols.

choices.label: D
choices.explanation: Nondeterminism without a machine model is insufficient; NPDA works while binary NFA recognition does not.

reviews.answer_text: A TM recognizes the three-equal-count language; the nondeterministic option lacks a model.

It is not CFL, excluding PDA and finite automata. C is supported, but D could mean an NLBA or NTM rather than NFA. That undefined model prevents an exclusive answer.

evidence.quote: For aⁿbⁿcⁿ first verify a*b*c* order, repeatedly mark one unmarked a, b and c, and reject missing/excess symbols.

choices.label: A

choices.explanation: A single-stack PDA recognizes only CFLs, and three matched blocks are not CFL.

choices.label: D

reviews.answer_text: A TM decides unary prime length; nondeterministic automaton is not a specified model.
reviews.hint: Read bounded counting and divisor testing for prime lengths.
reviews.explanation: AUT26 proves unary prime length nonregular and non-CFL, then establishes context sensitivity via bounded counting and divisor testing. Therefore finite automata and PDAs fail, while a TM succeeds. D remains undefined: an NFA fails but a sufficiently strong nondeterministic machine works. The missing machine noun prevents making C exclusive.

evidence.quote: It is nevertheless context-sensitive: count the input in bounded workspace and test divisors.

choices.label: A
choices.explanation: The pumping argument establishes that unary prime length is nonregular.

choices.label: B
choices.explanation: Every unary CFL is regular, so a PDA cannot recognize this nonregular unary language.

choices.label: C
choices.explanation: A TM counts the finite input and performs a terminating primality test.

choices.label: D
choices.explanation: NFA fails but NLBA/NTM can work; nondeterministic alone does not specify recognizer power.

reviews.answer_text: All listed grammar families can generate aⁿb.
reviews.hint: Read the regular example and upward grammar containment.
reviews.explanation: AUT26 directly calls {aⁿb:n≥0} regular. A regular grammar can repeatedly add a and terminate with b. AUT05 places REG inside CFL and CSL and RE, so every stronger listed grammar family can generate it too. Without asking for the weakest sufficient family, all four labels satisfy the literal question.

evidence.quote: a*b* and {aⁿb:n≥0} are regular.

choices.label: A
choices.explanation: A right-linear grammar can generate any number of a symbols followed by one b.

choices.label: B
choices.explanation: Regular grammars are a special context-free case, so a CFG also generates it.

choices.label: C
choices.explanation: Regular languages lie within CSL and admit context-sensitive generation.

choices.label: D
choices.explanation: Unrestricted grammars can generate every regular language, including this one.

reviews.answer_text: P is the defining class; NP, PSPACE and EXPTIME also contain it.
reviews.hint: Read P membership and transitive resource-class containment.
reviews.explanation: AUT34 defines deterministic polynomial-time decision as P. AUT39 gives P⊆NP⊆PSPACE⊆EXPTIME. The question asks contains, so each larger listed class also contains polynomial-time languages. This does not assert their equality or strict separation; replacing contains with is defined by would isolate P.

evidence.quote: Use L⊆NL⊆P⊆NP⊆PSPACE⊆EXPTIME⊆EXPSPACE.

choices.label: A
choices.explanation: P is exactly the deterministic polynomial-time decision class.

choices.label: B
choices.explanation: NP contains P because a verifier may simply run the deterministic polynomial algorithm.

choices.label: C
choices.explanation: PSPACE contains NP and hence all P languages by transitivity.

choices.label: D
choices.explanation: EXPTIME contains PSPACE and therefore contains polynomial-time languages too.

reviews.answer_text: Hardest means completeness relative to a specified class and reduction.
reviews.hint: Read membership plus hardness rather than comparing class names in isolation.
reviews.explanation: AUT36 defines NP-completeness relative to NP and polynomial reductions; AUT38 gives PSPACE-completeness relative to PSPACE. The stem names neither the reference class nor the reduction and offers no complete-class alternative. P, NP, PSPACE and EXPTIME are resource classes, not a generic synonym for hardest problems in whichever class is intended.

evidence.quote: X is NP-complete if X∈NP and X is NP-hard.

choices.label: A
choices.explanation: P names polynomial-time decisions and is not the general completeness concept.

choices.label: B
choices.explanation: NP membership does not make every member among the hardest problems in NP.

choices.label: C
choices.explanation: PSPACE includes easier problems as well as PSPACE-complete ones; it is not a generic hardest-class label.

choices.label: D
choices.explanation: EXPTIME is a resource upper-bound class, not the undefined completeness notion requested.

reviews.answer_text: |Z|²=36; no option supplies it.

reviews.explanation: AUT01 counts six symbols in caddba, giving |Z|=6 and |Z|²=36. Choice 12 instead equals |Z²|, the length of concatenating two copies. The exponent is outside the length bars in the literal stem, so moving it changes the question. None of the choices is the required squared numeric length.

evidence.quote: Length counts occurrences, not distinct symbols: |caddba|=6, so |caddba|²=36.

choices.label: A
choices.explanation: Three neither counts all six occurrences nor squares the resulting length.

choices.label: B

choices.label: C

reviews.answer_text: The empty word is not numeric zero.
reviews.hint: Read empty-word identity, zeroth string powers and alphabet closure.
reviews.explanation: AUT01 distinguishes the empty word λ from the numeric symbol 0. AUT02 gives λx=x and Z⁰=λ, while AUT03 includes the empty word in Σ*. Thus the first three claims express the standard empty-word identities under the displayed concatenation notation, and D is the false equality.

evidence.quote: Neither ε nor ∅ is the numeric symbol 0.

choices.label: A
choices.explanation: Reading the displayed star as concatenation, the empty word followed by ab is ab.

choices.label: B
choices.explanation: Every string’s zeroth concatenation power is the empty word.

choices.label: D

reviews.answer_text: DFA has one successor per state/symbol; NFA permits sets. They recognize the same languages.
reviews.hint: Read determinism and subset construction.
reviews.explanation: AUT09 permits an NFA to have zero, one or several next states and states that DFA and NFA recognize exactly REG. Subset construction simulates the simultaneous NFA possibilities by DFA states.

evidence.quote: An NFA is not more expressive than a DFA: both recognize exactly REG.

reviews.answer_text: The regular pumping lemma can disprove regularity, for example for aⁿbⁿ.
reviews.hint: Read the quantifiers and defeat every permitted split.
reviews.explanation: AUT15 chooses aᵖbᵖ after assuming a pumping length p. Every legal nonempty y in the first p symbols contains only a, so pumping it out changes the a count without changing b. That contradicts regularity.

evidence.quote: Every allowed y=aᵏ with k≥1; pumping i=0 leaves fewer a's than b's.

reviews.answer_text: P is deterministic polynomial-time decision; NP admits polynomial certificates. Equality remains open.
reviews.hint: Read solving versus verifying and P⊆NP.
reviews.explanation: AUT34 defines P by deterministic polynomial running time and NP by nondeterministic polynomial time or polynomial-size verifiable certificates. P is included in NP, and equality is unresolved. This matters for converting efficiently checked witnesses into efficiently found decisions.

evidence.quote: P consists of deterministic polynomial-time decidable languages; NP consists of nondeterministic polynomial-time decidable languages, equivalently polynomially verifiable yes-instances with polynomial-size certificates.

reviews.answer_text: A proposed halting decider yields a program contradicting its own prediction.
reviews.hint: Read diagonal self-application to a hypothetical halting decider.
reviews.explanation: AUT30 constructs D(x) to loop when H(x,x) predicts halting and to halt otherwise. On D’s own description, either prediction is contradicted. Therefore no general halting decider exists, although simulation recognizes halting instances.

evidence.quote: Construct D(x) that loops if H(x,x) says halt, otherwise halts. Running D on its own description contradicts H in both cases.

reviews.answer_text: REG⊊CFL⊊CSL⊊RE by increasing generative power; separating examples witness proper inclusions.
reviews.hint: Read grammar/machine correspondence and separating languages.

evidence.quote: Use REG ⊊ CFL ⊊ CSL ⊊ DECIDABLE ⊊ RE,

reviews.answer_text: DFA=NFA < PDA < LBA < TM in language-recognition power.
reviews.hint: Read the machine correspondences of the strict language hierarchy.
reviews.explanation: AUT09 equates DFA and NFA power. AUT05 assigns finite automata, nondeterministic PDAs, nondeterministic LBAs and Turing recognizers to successively stronger language families. That gives C under the standard nondeterministic PDA/LBA family convention. The comparison is expressiveness, not a statement that stronger models always run faster.

evidence.quote: Type 3 regular grammars correspond to finite automata; type 2 CFGs to nondeterministic PDAs; type 1 context-sensitive/noncontracting grammars to nondeterministic LBAs; type 0 unrestricted grammars to Turing recognizers.

choices.label: A
choices.explanation: NFA and DFA have equal power rather than the strict order shown.

choices.label: B

choices.label: C
choices.explanation: This gives equal finite-automaton power followed by the standard strictly increasing PDA/LBA/TM families.

choices.label: D
choices.explanation: This reverses the standard language-recognition power hierarchy.

reviews.answer_text: Time and space resources for computational problems.

Complexity studies these resource requirements as a function of encoded input size. Designing automata or transforming grammars may be objects of study, but neither is the general defining purpose.

evidence.quote: Time counts computation steps; space counts cells/memory used, specifying whether read-only input is excluded.

choices.label: A
choices.explanation: Finite-automaton design is one specific task rather than the general study of computational resources.

choices.label: B
choices.explanation: Complexity theory classifies time and space requirements relative to input size.

choices.label: C
choices.explanation: NFA determinization is a particular construction, not the broad subject of complexity theory.

choices.label: D
choices.explanation: Grammar syntax concerns formal language description rather than resource requirements in general.

Stack alphabets and write/direction outputs belong to richer models and are not components of the ordinary DFA transition signature.

evidence.quote: total δ:Q×Σ→Q.

choices.label: A
choices.explanation: This is the exact state/symbol to unique next-state signature of a DFA.

choices.label: B

evidence.quote: Complement is Σ*−L and needs a fixed alphabet.

evidence.quote: δ:Q×Σ→𝒫(Q).

choices.explanation: Write-symbol and direction outputs are tape-machine operations, not NFA state-set transitions.
