evidence.quote: A transfer between a register and memory does not uniquely specify addressing mode; either direct, indexed or indirect addressing may produce it.

choices.label: A
choices.explanation: Direct addressing can supply the memory operand, but indexed or indirect addressing can produce the same transfer.

choices.label: B
choices.explanation: Immediate addressing uses an instruction-field value rather than locating a memory operand by the stated transfer alone.

choices.label: C
choices.explanation: Register addressing uses the register value as operand; it does not determine the memory-side effective address.

choices.label: D
choices.explanation: No listed mode is uniquely implied, but none would be misleading if interpreted as denying valid direct-address transfers.

reviews.answer_text: Test instructions, as named in main option A.
reviews.hint: Read TEST/CMP semantics and compare the actual source image with the damaged extraction.
reviews.explanation: The saved image shows the stem and the textual alternative Test instructions clearly. Despite extraction debris, main option A retains that phrase. COA19 independently states that TEST/CMP examine values and set condition information, so A answers the literal main choices. Data instruction has slipped into the stem, and option D is a next-question heading; these extraction faults do not make another main option describe testing.

evidence.quote: TEST/CMP examine values and set condition information, often without retaining the arithmetic result.

choices.label: A
choices.explanation: The recognizable Test instructions phrase matches examining a data word or computation status; source image confirms its text.

choices.label: B
choices.explanation: Branch instructions choose control-flow targets, rather than naming the instruction class that performs the test.

choices.label: C
choices.explanation: All includes branches and a displaced heading, so it cannot be the correct class definition.

choices.label: D
choices.explanation: The source image shows 40 - True or false is the next item’s heading, not an instruction alternative.

reviews.answer_text: PC or address register can hold an instruction address at different phases.
reviews.hint: Read next-fetch position versus the address of the current memory access.
reviews.explanation: COA14 explicitly warns that address of the instruction without a phase can describe PC or MAR. PC identifies the next instruction to fetch, while the address register contains the location for the current memory access, including an instruction fetch. The stem lacks next/current and phase qualifiers. IR holds the instruction itself, and the accumulator holds operands/results rather than the requested address role.

evidence.quote: “Address of the instruction” without a phase can describe PC or MAR.

choices.label: A
choices.explanation: The accumulator holds operands or results, not the defined instruction-address role in the fetch sequence.

choices.label: B
choices.explanation: IR holds the fetched instruction itself, rather than serving as the instruction-address register.

choices.label: C
choices.explanation: The address register holds the memory address during an instruction fetch, so the unqualified phrase can fit.

choices.label: D
choices.explanation: PC identifies the next instruction to fetch, but next is missing from the stem’s address description.

reviews.answer_text: Performance improved across several generations; the stem is not exclusive.
reviews.hint: Read broad historical trends rather than selecting one era for a repeated improvement.
reviews.explanation: COA38 explicitly says several generations improved performance. The question names no metric, comparison machine or distinctive technology, so improved compared with previous generations does not isolate one era. The first era also lacks a defined previous-computer baseline. The source therefore establishes nonexclusivity, not an exact generation subset that could be safely emitted as multiple labels.

evidence.quote: Several generations improved performance.

choices.label: A
choices.explanation: A first-era comparison requires a defined earlier-machine baseline, which the question does not provide.

choices.label: B
choices.explanation: Second-era improvement is compatible with the repeated trend, but is not uniquely distinguished.

choices.label: C
choices.explanation: Third-era improvement is likewise compatible with the repeated trend and does not exclude other eras.

choices.label: D
choices.explanation: Fourth-era performance growth is compatible with the note, but improved speed is not an exclusive era marker.

reviews.answer_text: No offered statement is necessarily false from the definitions.
reviews.hint: Separate architecture/organization meanings from unsupported lifetime assumptions.
reviews.explanation: COA01 distinguishes programmer-visible architecture from internal implementation and explicitly says neither definition imposes a maximum lifetime. A single architecture can therefore span models and organizations, supporting A–C. D is not necessarily false either: an organization can persist for a long time. The stem needs a qualified typical-change-rate claim or a repaired alternative before a unique not-correct answer follows.

evidence.quote: Different organizations can implement the same architecture; neither definition imposes a maximum lifetime.

choices.label: A
choices.explanation: Architecture can persist while implementation changes; the definitions support rather than refute this statement.

choices.label: B
choices.explanation: Different implementations can share one architecture, exactly as the note explicitly permits.

choices.label: C
choices.explanation: An architecture can encompass multiple models over time; no lifetime bound prevents this.

choices.label: D
choices.explanation: Likely intended as false, but neither definition prevents an organization lasting a long time.

reviews.answer_text: Both aggregate control and data buses can be bidirectional.
reviews.hint: Read data transfers and the directions of aggregate control signals.
reviews.explanation: COA12 explicitly permits both data and control in an unrestricted bidirectionality question. Data moves on reads and writes; aggregate control combines CPU outputs and device inputs. The address bus is outward under the stated simple CPU-master model. Uni-bus supplies no signal-direction definition in this packet, so that name cannot displace the two directly supported choices.

evidence.quote: Aggregate control signals include both CPU outputs and device inputs, so an unrestricted “which bus is bidirectional?” item can admit both data and control.

choices.label: A
choices.explanation: Control includes CPU-generated commands and device-generated requests or acknowledgements, so aggregate signaling runs both ways.

choices.label: B
choices.explanation: Memory reads and writes transfer data in opposite directions on the data bus.

choices.label: C
choices.explanation: The packet does not define Uni-bus signal direction; its name alone cannot establish a distinct answer.

choices.label: D
choices.explanation: Addresses flow outward from CPU in the simple CPU-master model, rather than carrying read/write data both ways.

reviews.answer_text: Fetching several instructions increases supply bandwidth; it does not by itself reduce access latency.
reviews.hint: Distinguish latency, bandwidth, fetch width and issue width.
reviews.explanation: COA34 distinguishes one-job latency from completed-work throughput, and COA36 explicitly says wider fetch improves instruction supply rather than necessarily individual memory latency. The stem conflates those properties. Caching can lower access delay, while superscalar/multiple-issue resources consume wider instruction supply; neither makes the claimed causal definition correct. A memory hierarchy or explicit bandwidth question would resolve the intended concept.

evidence.quote: wider fetch improves instruction supply, not necessarily individual memory latency.

choices.label: A
choices.explanation: Pipeline overlap increases throughput but does not define multiple-instruction fetch as reduced memory latency.

choices.label: B
choices.explanation: Caching can reduce effective access delay, but multiple-instruction fetch per cycle is not its defining rule.

choices.label: C
choices.explanation: Superscalar issue benefits from wider supply, but multiple issue is not itself a reduction in memory-request latency.

choices.label: D
choices.explanation: Instruction-level parallelism concerns independent operations; it does not equate fetch bandwidth with access latency.

reviews.answer_text: The fundamental logic-gate answer is absent.
reviews.hint: Read structural components versus fundamental hardware logic elements.
reviews.explanation: COA01 says gates are fundamental logic building blocks and explicitly warns that offering only CPU, memory, disk and motherboard gives no unique technical answer. All four listed objects are substantial components assembled from lower-level elements. The stem does not define a higher structural level at which one should be called basic, so choosing CPU or motherboard would import an unstated criterion.

evidence.quote: Gates are fundamental logic building blocks, so an item asking for the basic building block while offering only CPU, memory, disk and motherboard has no unique technical answer.

choices.label: A
choices.explanation: CPU is a major structural component composed of lower-level logic, not the omitted fundamental logic-gate answer.

choices.label: B
choices.explanation: Memory is a major storage component, not uniquely the fundamental building block of all hardware.

choices.label: C
choices.explanation: A hard disk is a storage device built from many parts rather than the fundamental logic element.

choices.label: D
choices.explanation: A motherboard physically connects components; that does not make it the fundamental hardware logic building block.

reviews.answer_text: Hard disk and nonvolatile forms of memory retain contents without power.
reviews.hint: Read whether memory is restricted to volatile RAM.
reviews.explanation: COA24 says ROM and flash retain contents without power, while COA28 says an HDD does not need continuous power to preserve bits. The option Memory is unrestricted, so it includes those nonvolatile types rather than necessarily meaning RAM. Consequently both memory and hard disk fit the literal capability. CPU and motherboard do not name the retention mechanisms defined by the note.

evidence.quote: ROM and flash retain contents without power;
It does not need continuous power to preserve stored bits.

choices.label: A
choices.explanation: CPU registers are not identified as the persistent storage mechanism; ordinary powered state is volatile.

choices.label: B
choices.explanation: Unqualified memory includes ROM/flash, which the note explicitly says retain contents without power.

choices.label: C
choices.explanation: Hard disks preserve their stored magnetic data without continuous operating power.

choices.label: D
choices.explanation: A motherboard’s defining role is connecting components, not itself being the specified persistent storage medium.

reviews.answer_text: Memory and CPU execution storage fit different scopes of currently processed.
reviews.hint: Read main-memory working data versus CPU operand and instruction registers.
reviews.explanation: COA02 describes addressed memory holding instructions/data, while COA14 assigns fetched instructions and operands/results to CPU registers. The phrase holds instructions and data currently being processed does not distinguish main-memory residence from immediate execution storage. Therefore Memory is the likely general-system answer, but CPU storage also fits a narrower execution interpretation. The stem needs a memory-versus-register role qualifier.

evidence.quote: IR holds the fetched instruction; MAR holds an address used for the current memory access; MDR holds transferred data. The accumulator holds operands/results,

choices.label: A
choices.explanation: CPU instruction and operand registers hold information actively used during execution, fitting a narrow processing interpretation.

choices.label: B
choices.explanation: Main memory holds program instructions and working data, fitting the conventional system-level interpretation.

choices.label: C
choices.explanation: Hard disk is persistent backing storage rather than the directly executing CPU/main-memory working-storage role.

choices.label: D
choices.explanation: The motherboard connects components rather than serving as the instruction/data working-store component.

reviews.answer_text: Both cache and registers provide temporary processing storage.
reviews.hint: Read register execution roles versus cached copies of memory blocks.
reviews.explanation: COA14 expressly says registers and cache both store temporary information. Registers serve explicit execution operands and cache retains memory-block copies. The stem says only temporarily stores data and instructions, without requiring programmer-visible operands, so both named storage units fit. The ALU computes and the control unit sequences operations; neither is the storage class requested.

evidence.quote: Registers and cache both store temporary information, but registers are explicit execution operands and cache holds copies of memory blocks.

choices.label: A
choices.explanation: The ALU performs arithmetic/logic computation rather than naming the temporary instruction/data storage unit.

choices.label: B
choices.explanation: The control unit sequences transfers and operations rather than serving as the storage category requested.

choices.label: C
choices.explanation: Cache retains temporary copies of memory blocks, including data or instructions, near the CPU.

choices.label: D
choices.explanation: Registers temporarily hold instructions, operands and results used directly during CPU execution.

reviews.answer_text: Reading the PC during fetch and changing it during execution are different interpretations.
reviews.hint: Read sequential fetch progression versus branch target calculation.
reviews.explanation: COA15 explicitly warns that which phase determines the next instruction requires distinguishing reading the current PC from computing a branch target. Fetch obtains the instruction at the selected address and advances the sequential PC; executing a branch can replace that PC. Without sequential/branch and selection/reading qualifiers, the question cannot uniquely choose fetching or execution.

evidence.quote: Thus “which phase determines the next instruction?” needs to distinguish reading the current PC from calculating a branch target.

choices.label: A
choices.explanation: Decoding identifies control-flow fields, but the stem does not distinguish recognizing a branch from calculating or using its target.

choices.label: B
choices.explanation: Executing a branch can replace the sequential PC, thereby choosing a different next instruction.

choices.label: C
choices.explanation: Fetching uses the current PC and may advance it sequentially, matching another interpretation of determining next.

choices.label: D
choices.explanation: Result storage/write-back is not itself another fetch or the general next-PC selection rule.

reviews.answer_text: Textbook direct access and informal random-access usage both occur for disk.
reviews.hint: Read the access-taxonomy convention before contrasting direct with random.
reviews.explanation: COA28 calls disk direct access in the textbook taxonomy but explicitly notes that random-access disk is common informal usage. Since the question offers both labels without specifying the taxonomy, direct is the likely textbook answer but not an exclusive literal description. Disk is not limited to tape-like sequential streaming, and associative access instead matches content.

evidence.quote: “Random-access disk” is also common informal usage; an item offering both direct and random must specify its taxonomy.

choices.label: A
choices.explanation: Associative access matches content; the note does not classify ordinary magnetic disks that way.

choices.label: B
choices.explanation: Sequential is the tape taxonomy; disk can address blocks without traversing every earlier record.

choices.label: C
choices.explanation: Random-access disk is accepted informal usage according to the note, so it cannot be excluded without a convention.

choices.label: D
choices.explanation: Direct is the textbook disk-access category, conditional on using the taxonomy that contrasts it with RAM.

reviews.answer_text: The opcode specifies the operation.
reviews.hint: Separate operation selection from operand-reference and next-instruction fields.
reviews.explanation: COA16 defines the opcode as specifying the operation and operand fields as locating data/registers. In the given 16-bit format, the 4-bit opcode therefore selects an operation, while the two 6-bit references identify operands under the machine’s interpretation. The bit widths are not evidence that the opcode stores a source/destination address or next-PC reference.

evidence.quote: An opcode specifies the operation; operand fields locate data or registers, and a mode field explains interpretation.

choices.label: A
choices.explanation: A destination operand reference belongs in an operand field, not in the operation-selecting opcode.

choices.label: B
choices.explanation: The opcode determines which operation the processor should perform for this instruction.

choices.label: C
choices.explanation: A source operand reference is an operand-field role rather than the opcode’s operation role.

choices.label: D
choices.explanation: The next-instruction reference is a control-flow/PC concern, not the general purpose of this opcode field.

reviews.answer_text: A bus topology and connection role are needed.
reviews.hint: Distinguish storage connections, peripheral expansion and bridge/controller hardware.
reviews.explanation: COA32 distinguishes PCI expansion connectivity, SCSI storage connections and bridge/controller logic joining unlike bus segments. It explicitly rejects uniquely identifying PCI or Multibus from extends processor-bus connectivity alone. The question supplies no host/expansion buses or whether it wants a standard or physical bridge component. Therefore several roles remain plausible rather than one verified answer.

evidence.quote: “Extends processor-bus connectivity” without topology does not uniquely identify PCI or Multibus.

choices.label: A
choices.explanation: SCSI is a storage connection rather than a general processor-bus extension mechanism in the note.

choices.label: B
choices.explanation: PCI supplies peripheral expansion, but the processor/expansion topology needed to select it is absent.

choices.label: C
choices.explanation: Bridge/controller logic can connect unlike bus segments, but the generic label does not specify the required design.

choices.label: D
choices.explanation: Multibus cannot be uniquely identified without a stated bus standard or topology requirement.

reviews.answer_text: Combinational output depends on present inputs rather than stored history.
reviews.hint: Read the state-based distinction between combinational and sequential circuits.
reviews.explanation: COA05 defines combinational output through present inputs after propagation delay, while sequential output also depends on stored state. B expresses that distinction. Combinational circuits are built from logic, not prohibited from it; the feedback statement reverses the usual state relationship. Nor do combinational circuits inherently require a clock, while clocked sequential circuits update at clock events.

evidence.quote: A combinational output depends on present inputs after propagation delay.

choices.label: A
choices.explanation: Combinational circuits are logic circuits; the statement incorrectly denies their ordinary implementation basis.

choices.label: B
choices.explanation: Present inputs determine combinational outputs, whereas sequential circuits additionally depend on retained state.

choices.label: C
choices.explanation: This reverses the state/feedback distinction; sequential storage can involve feedback, not its categorical absence.

choices.label: D
choices.explanation: Combinational logic does not inherently require a clock; clock events characterize clocked sequential updates.

reviews.answer_text: Fetch the instruction.
reviews.hint: Read the conceptual instruction-cycle order.
reviews.explanation: COA15 begins the conceptual instruction cycle with fetch, then decode, operand acquisition, execution and any result write-back. Fetch must obtain the instruction before its opcode can be decoded and operation performed. Permitted interrupt checks are a separate stage/transition in that conceptual model, not the first ordinary instruction-processing step among these choices.

evidence.quote: A conceptual instruction cycle fetches an instruction, decodes opcode/addressing fields, obtains operands, executes, writes results where required and checks permitted interrupts.

choices.label: A
choices.explanation: Execution follows obtaining and decoding the instruction, rather than being the cycle’s first conceptual step.

choices.label: B
choices.explanation: Interrupt checks/service are distinct from the first ordinary fetch step in the note’s conceptual cycle.

choices.label: C
choices.explanation: Decoding requires an already fetched instruction, so it follows rather than precedes fetch.

choices.label: D
choices.explanation: Fetching obtains the instruction and is explicitly first in the conceptual instruction-cycle sequence.

reviews.answer_text: Direct Memory Access (DMA).
reviews.hint: Read per-word CPU transfer versus controller-managed block transfer.
reviews.explanation: COA30 says DMA lets a controller transfer a block directly between device and memory after CPU setup. The stem’s without CPU involvement must mean without CPU moving every item, not no configuration/completion involvement whatsoever. Polling and interrupt-driven I/O still require CPU transfer work; asynchronous transfer describes timing coordination rather than this block-moving mechanism.

evidence.quote: DMA lets a controller move a block directly between device and memory after CPU setup.

choices.label: A
choices.explanation: Asynchronous transfer describes coordination/timing rather than specifically controller-managed movement directly between device and memory.

choices.label: B
choices.explanation: DMA transfers the block through a controller after CPU setup, avoiding per-item CPU copying.

choices.label: C
choices.explanation: Interrupt-driven handlers still consume CPU time to service and move device data in this comparison.

choices.label: D
choices.explanation: Programmed I/O repeatedly checks status and has the CPU move each item rather than using DMA.

reviews.answer_text: AND gate.
reviews.hint: Read the all-inputs-high truth-table condition.
reviews.explanation: COA03 states that AND is 1 only when all inputs are 1. This is exactly the condition in the stem. OR needs any high input, NAND complements AND, and two-input XOR is high when inputs differ. Thus none of the other truth functions has the specified all-high-only output rule.

evidence.quote: AND is 1 only when all inputs are 1; OR is 1 if any input is 1.

choices.label: A
choices.explanation: OR becomes high when any input is high, so it does not require all inputs to be one.

choices.label: B
choices.explanation: AND outputs one exactly for the all-inputs-one combination required by the stem.

choices.label: C
choices.explanation: NAND inverts AND and therefore outputs zero, not one, when all its inputs are one.

choices.label: D
choices.explanation: Two-input XOR outputs one when inputs differ, not when both inputs are one.

reviews.answer_text: XOR gate.
reviews.hint: Read the exclusive-OR symbol and differing-input truth rule.
reviews.explanation: The expression A⊕B is the exclusive-OR operation. COA03 defines its two-input output as 1 when the inputs differ and contrasts XNOR as agreement. NOR and NAND complement OR and AND instead. Thus XOR is the operation represented by the given symbol, with no extra circuit diagram or numeric assumption needed.

evidence.quote: For two inputs XOR is 1 when inputs differ, and XNOR when they agree.

choices.label: A
choices.explanation: XNOR is the complement of XOR, giving one when the two inputs agree.

choices.label: B
choices.explanation: NOR complements OR; it is not the exclusive-OR operation denoted by the circled plus.

choices.label: C
choices.explanation: The circled-plus expression denotes exclusive OR, whose output is one for differing inputs.

choices.label: D
choices.explanation: NAND complements AND rather than implementing the given exclusive-OR expression.

reviews.answer_text: NAND, the only universal gate offered.
reviews.hint: Read how universal NAND/NOR gates construct other logic operations.
reviews.explanation: COA04 explicitly states that NAND and NOR are each universal and explains constructing NOT by tying inputs together, then building AND/OR combinations. Of those two universal families, only NAND is offered. AND and OR alone cannot provide inversion under this rule, and XOR is not identified as a universal family. Thus the correct offered gate is NAND.

evidence.quote: NAND and NOR are each universal: feeding the same input to both inputs constructs NOT; combine complemented gates to construct AND or OR.

choices.label: A
choices.explanation: AND alone is not the universal family described; it does not supply the required inversion construction.

choices.label: B
choices.explanation: OR alone is not the universal family described and cannot generate the stated NOT construction.

choices.label: C
choices.explanation: NAND is explicitly universal and can be combined to construct NOT, AND and OR.

choices.label: D
choices.explanation: XOR is not the NAND/NOR universal family; tied inputs produce zero rather than inversion.

reviews.hint: Apply OR first, then invert for NOR.
reviews.explanation: COA03 defines OR as high when any input is high and NOR as its complement. At A=1, B=0, the OR value is 1, so NOR produces 0. The input combination is completely specified in ordinary Boolean logic; it is neither undefined nor dependent on an unspecified analog voltage model.

evidence.quote: NOT complements a bit. NAND complements AND; NOR complements OR.

choices.label: A
choices.explanation: OR of 1 and 0 is 1; complementing that for NOR yields zero.

choices.label: B
choices.explanation: One is the OR result before inversion, not the NOR output for these inputs.

choices.label: C
choices.explanation: The Boolean NOR truth table fully defines this ordinary input combination.

choices.label: D
choices.explanation: The stem supplies Boolean input values, so no additional voltage threshold assumption is required.

reviews.answer_text: NOT(A·B) = NOT(A) + NOT(B).
reviews.hint: Read De Morgan’s complement-of-product identity.
reviews.explanation: COA04 gives (AB)'=A'+B'. Complementing a product changes AND to OR and complements each operand. B matches that exact transformation. A instead gives the complement of A+B, C omits the operand complements, and D leaves the complement attached to a sum, which represents NOR rather than the requested NAND function.

evidence.quote: De Morgan gives (AB)'=A'+B' and (A+B)'=A'B'.

choices.label: A
choices.explanation: The product of complements equals NOT(A+B), rather than the complement of the original product.

choices.label: B
choices.explanation: Complement each operand and change AND to OR, exactly as De Morgan’s product rule states.

choices.label: C
choices.explanation: A+B omits both required complements and is not generally equal to NOT(A·B).

choices.label: D
choices.explanation: NOT(A+B) is NOR and differs from NOT(A·B), for example when only one input is high.

reviews.hint: Read the Boolean complement identity.
reviews.explanation: COA04 explicitly lists A+A'=1. If A is 0 then A' is 1, and if A is 1 then A' is 0; either way their Boolean OR is 1. Neither A nor A' remains fixed across both assignments, and zero is the product-of-complements result rather than their sum.

choices.label: A
choices.explanation: Zero is A AND NOT A; the given operation is OR, so one input is always high.

choices.label: B
choices.explanation: A can be zero while the expression remains one, so the identity is not simply A.

choices.label: C
choices.explanation: A bit OR its complement is always one for both possible assignments.

choices.label: D
choices.explanation: A complement can be zero while the full expression is one, so it is not the constant result.

reviews.answer_text: 16 rows.
reviews.hint: Read the truth-table row count for independent binary inputs.
reviews.explanation: COA03 gives 2^n rows for n binary inputs. For four independent variables, each has two assignments, so the total combinations are 2×2×2×2=16. The options 8 and 32 correspond to three and five binary variables respectively; 12 does not enumerate all four-variable combinations.

evidence.quote: With n binary inputs, enumerate 2^n truth-table rows.

choices.label: A
choices.explanation: Eight is 2^3, the number of assignments for three inputs rather than four.

choices.label: B
choices.explanation: Twelve omits four of the sixteen possible combinations of four independent binary inputs.

choices.label: C
choices.explanation: Four independent binary inputs yield 2^4=16 distinct truth-table rows.

choices.label: D
choices.explanation: Thirty-two is 2^5 and would require five independent binary input variables.

reviews.answer_text: F = 0; the symbolic option x also equals 0 under the supplied assignment.
reviews.hint: Apply NOT before AND before OR, then evaluate every option using the given values.
reviews.explanation: COA03 evaluates this exact expression: y'=0, so F=0 OR (0 AND 1)=0. The numeric answer is A. However, literal main option C is x, and the stem explicitly sets x=0, so it denotes the same result under this assignment. B and D denote 1. The duplicated value makes A and C both valid unless numeric-only answers are explicitly required.

evidence.quote: F=x+y'z at x=0,y=1,z=1: y'=0, so F=0 OR (0 AND 1)=0.

choices.label: A
choices.explanation: Complementing y gives zero, so x OR y′z evaluates to the numeric value zero.

choices.label: B
choices.explanation: One contradicts the computed zero: neither x nor y′z is high under the supplied assignment.

choices.label: C
choices.explanation: The option x equals zero under the explicitly supplied x=0 assignment, duplicating the numeric answer.

choices.label: D
choices.explanation: The option z equals one under the assignment, whereas the computed expression equals zero.

reviews.answer_text: A bistable one-bit storage element.
reviews.hint: Read flip-flop state storage versus combinational circuits and assembled counters.
reviews.explanation: COA05 says a flip-flop stores one bit while powered and classifies flip-flops as sequential circuits with stored state. B is the option describing that storage element. A combinational circuit lacks stored logical state; a four-bit counter requires a multi-bit state structure, and an arithmetic unit computes rather than defining this one-bit storage component.

evidence.quote: A flip-flop stores one bit while powered.

choices.label: A
choices.explanation: A combinational circuit has no stored logical state, whereas a flip-flop retains a bit.

choices.label: B
choices.explanation: Bistable one-bit storage matches the powered state-retention role of a flip-flop.

choices.label: C
choices.explanation: One flip-flop stores one bit; a four-bit counter requires a multi-bit state organization.

choices.label: D
choices.explanation: An arithmetic unit computes values rather than defining the one-bit sequential storage element.

reviews.answer_text: Flip-flops retain stored state during powered operation.
reviews.hint: Read stored state versus a gate’s present-input function.
reviews.explanation: COA05 distinguishes sequential state from combinational outputs determined by present inputs. A flip-flop can retain its bit when inputs change without a qualifying update, giving the memory distinction in B. This does not imply nonvolatile retention after power-off. Power, speed and AC-supply claims are neither the defining property nor guarantees established by the note.

evidence.quote: A sequential circuit depends on stored state as well as inputs; registers, counters and flip-flops are examples.

choices.label: A
choices.explanation: Power consumption is implementation-dependent and does not define whether a circuit has logical memory.

choices.label: B
choices.explanation: Stored state persists between valid updates while powered, unlike a purely present-input combinational gate.

choices.label: C
choices.explanation: Speed is not the defining memory distinction and is not guaranteed by the flip-flop label.

choices.label: D
choices.explanation: The note specifies powered storage, not a requirement for an AC rather than another supply.

reviews.hint: Read binary place values.
reviews.explanation: Using COA08’s base-position rule, 1011₂ has weights 8, 4, 2 and 1. Its high bits contribute 8+2+1=11, while the 4-place is zero. The note’s worked example confirms the same sum. Nine, ten and thirteen correspond to different low-order bit patterns, not the supplied 1011.

choices.label: A
choices.explanation: Nine equals 8+1, corresponding to 1001₂ and omitting the given two-place bit.

choices.label: B
choices.explanation: Ten equals 8+2, corresponding to 1010₂ and omitting the given one-place bit.

choices.label: C
choices.explanation: The set bit positions contribute 8+2+1=11 in decimal.

choices.label: D
choices.explanation: Thirteen equals 8+4+1, corresponding to 1101₂ rather than the supplied 1011₂.

reviews.answer_text: F₁₆ = 15₁₀.
reviews.hint: Read the hexadecimal digit alphabet.
reviews.explanation: COA08 defines hexadecimal digits as 0–9,A–F and explicitly gives F=15. These sixteen symbols represent values zero through fifteen, so sixteen itself requires the two-digit hexadecimal representation 10. Fourteen is E, and ten is A, leaving fifteen as the only value of the single digit F.

evidence.quote: Binary uses 0–1, octal 0–7 and hexadecimal 0–9,A–F; F=15.

choices.label: A
choices.explanation: Fourteen corresponds to the preceding hexadecimal digit E, not the final digit F.

choices.label: B
choices.explanation: The note explicitly assigns decimal value fifteen to the hexadecimal digit F.

choices.label: C
choices.explanation: Sixteen requires hexadecimal 10; it is outside the value range of a single hexadecimal digit.

choices.label: D
choices.explanation: Ten corresponds to hexadecimal A rather than the later digit F.

reviews.answer_text: Base 8.
reviews.hint: Count the digit values allowed in octal.
reviews.explanation: COA08 gives octal digits 0–7: eight possible digit values, so octal has base eight. Binary has two digits, decimal ten and hexadecimal sixteen. Place weights in octal are therefore powers of eight, not powers of two, ten or sixteen, even though octal digits can be grouped with three binary bits.

evidence.quote: Binary uses 0–1, octal 0–7 and hexadecimal 0–9,A–F; F=15.

choices.label: A
choices.explanation: Base two is binary; octal allows eight digit values rather than only zero and one.

choices.label: B
choices.explanation: Octal uses digits zero through seven, giving a base of eight.

choices.label: C
choices.explanation: Base ten is decimal, not the eight-digit octal number system.

choices.label: D
choices.explanation: Base sixteen is hexadecimal, which uses the additional A–F digits absent from octal.

reviews.answer_text: Binary matches the two logical states used by digital logic.
reviews.hint: Connect Boolean bit states with the binary digit set.
reviews.explanation: COA03 defines digital gates using the two Boolean values 0 and 1, and COA08 defines binary using exactly those two digits. That direct correspondence explains why binary is fundamental to the digital representation described here. Octal and hexadecimal group binary bits for convenience, while decimal’s human familiarity does not supply the two-state circuit correspondence.

evidence.quote: AND is 1 only when all inputs are 1; OR is 1 if any input is 1.
Group binary bits in threes for octal and fours for hexadecimal, outward from the radix point.

choices.label: A
choices.explanation: Human decimal familiarity does not match the two Boolean states used by the note’s digital gates.

choices.label: B
choices.explanation: Octal groups three binary bits and is a convenient notation rather than the underlying two-state representation.

choices.label: C
choices.explanation: Binary digits zero and one directly correspond to the two logical values used by digital circuits.

choices.label: D
choices.explanation: Hexadecimal compactly groups four binary bits; compact notation does not replace the underlying binary states.

reviews.answer_text: 4 bits: F₁₆ = 1111₂.
reviews.hint: Read binary grouping for hexadecimal and the unsigned n-bit range.
reviews.explanation: COA08 groups four binary bits for each hexadecimal digit and gives F=15. COA09’s unsigned range shows three bits reach only 7, while four bits reach 15. Therefore the minimum representation of F is four bits, 1111. Eight bits can contain the value but are not the number needed for one hexadecimal digit.

evidence.quote: Group binary bits in threes for octal and fours for hexadecimal, outward from the radix point.

choices.label: A
choices.explanation: Two bits encode only zero through three, insufficient for hexadecimal F’s decimal value fifteen.

choices.label: B
choices.explanation: Three bits encode only zero through seven, so they cannot represent the value fifteen.

choices.label: C
choices.explanation: Four bits encode zero through fifteen; F is represented by the four-bit pattern 1111.

choices.label: D
choices.explanation: Eight bits could contain fifteen but exceed the minimum four bits needed for a hexadecimal digit.

reviews.answer_text: RAM and ordinary SRAM-based cache are volatile.
reviews.hint: Read volatility separately from the functional role of a cache.
reviews.explanation: COA24 states that ordinary SRAM and DRAM lose contents without power, while ROM/flash retain them. RAM therefore fits. Ordinary processor cache implemented in SRAM fits the same volatility rule as well; cache describes a hierarchy role, not a separate nonvolatile technology. Thus RAM and ordinary SRAM cache are both valid under the conventional implementation, rather than a unique RAM-only answer. The wording should specify a technology or exclude cache to make the choice unique.

evidence.quote: Both are ordinarily volatile. ROM and flash retain contents without power;
Cache copies memory blocks near the CPU.

choices.label: A
choices.explanation: ROM retains contents without power according to the note, so it does not fit the volatility condition.

choices.label: B
choices.explanation: Flash explicitly retains contents without power, unlike the requested volatile storage.

choices.label: C
choices.explanation: Both SRAM and DRAM are explicitly described as ordinarily volatile, so RAM satisfies the condition.

choices.label: D
choices.explanation: Ordinary SRAM-based processor cache loses its powered state, satisfying the same volatility rule as SRAM elsewhere.

reviews.answer_text: Small, fast storage near the CPU between it and main memory.
reviews.hint: Read cache’s hierarchy position, relative capacity and reuse role.
reviews.explanation: COA23 places cache above DRAM in the usual speed/cost hierarchy and says faster levels are generally smaller and more expensive per bit. It defines cache as copied memory blocks near the CPU. B captures that role. Cache is not the large slow backup layer or disk-based virtual-memory backing store; its useful speed derives from proximity/reuse, not guaranteed persistence.

evidence.quote: Faster levels are generally smaller and more expensive per bit.
Cache copies memory blocks near the CPU.

choices.label: A
choices.explanation: Large slow cheap storage describes lower hierarchy levels rather than the small fast cache layer.

choices.label: B
choices.explanation: Cache is a small fast near-CPU copy of memory blocks used to accelerate access.

choices.label: C
choices.explanation: The note defines cache for accelerated reuse, not as nonvolatile backup storage.

choices.label: D
choices.explanation: Disk-backed virtual memory is a different address-space/backing-store mechanism from the CPU cache.

reviews.answer_text: A placement conflict: only one block can occupy that direct-mapped slot.
reviews.hint: Read direct mapping’s single permitted line for each block.
reviews.explanation: COA25 states that two blocks with the same direct-mapped index cannot reside together. When the requested block differs from the valid block at that slot, the cache must replace the slot’s contents, producing a conflict miss. This is ordinary cache operation, not a crash or merging of block contents; direct mapping offers no alternate placement for the same index.

evidence.quote: Two blocks with the same direct-mapped index cannot reside together.

choices.label: A
choices.explanation: One direct-mapped line holds one block at a time, so the colliding blocks cannot coexist there.

choices.label: B
choices.explanation: The shared index causes a placement conflict; installing the requested block replaces the current one.

choices.label: C
choices.explanation: Conflict replacement is ordinary cache behavior and does not imply a system crash.

choices.label: D
choices.explanation: Cache replacement preserves separate memory-block identities; it does not merge their contents into one block.

reviews.answer_text: Fully associative mapping.
reviews.hint: Compare the number of legal cache locations for a memory block.
reviews.explanation: COA25 says direct mapping fixes one line, set associativity permits any way within one indexed set, and fully associative placement permits any line. Allowing every line gives the most placement flexibility for a fixed cache. The sequential-mapping option is not one of the cache placement rules defined by the supplied note.

evidence.quote: Fully associative placement permits any line.

choices.label: A
choices.explanation: Direct mapping restricts a block to a single line and therefore has the least placement freedom.

choices.label: B
choices.explanation: Set associativity permits several ways in one set, fewer locations than the entire fully associative cache.

choices.label: C
choices.explanation: Fully associative placement allows any cache line, maximizing placement freedom for each block.

choices.label: D
choices.explanation: Sequential mapping is not a cache-placement policy defined by the supplied mapping rules.

reviews.answer_text: Direct and fully associative mapping.
reviews.hint: Read fixed set selection with a choice of ways inside that set.
reviews.explanation: COA25 defines W-way set associativity as fixing a set by the block index while allowing any of W ways inside it. That combines direct indexing with an associative choice within the selected set, placing it between one-line direct mapping and unrestricted fully associative placement. RAM/ROM and primary/secondary are technology/hierarchy contrasts, not the two placement endpoints.

evidence.quote: A W-way set-associative cache has S=L/W sets and set=block mod S; any of W ways in that set may hold the block.

choices.label: A
choices.explanation: RAM and ROM describe memory types rather than the placement-policy endpoints combined by set associativity.

choices.label: B
choices.explanation: Set indexing restricts placement like direct mapping while allowing an associative choice among the selected set’s ways.

choices.label: C
choices.explanation: Primary and secondary describe hierarchy roles, not the direct versus associative cache-placement alternatives.

choices.label: D
choices.explanation: Cache and virtual memory are different mechanisms rather than the two placement extremes defining set associativity.

reviews.answer_text: Hard disk / SSD as backing storage.
reviews.hint: Read nonresident-page backing separately from address translation itself.
reviews.explanation: COA27 says backing storage can hold nonresident pages while virtual memory provides translated protected address spaces. COA28 identifies HDDs and SSDs as persistent storage devices, matching that backing role. ROM, cache and registers are not the nonresident-page backing tier described. Apparent extension does not mean physical RAM is added or that virtual memory is only disk disguised as RAM.

evidence.quote: Virtual memory gives processes translated address spaces and protection; backing storage can hold nonresident pages.

choices.label: A
choices.explanation: ROM stores persistent firmware/data but is not the writable nonresident-page backing role described here.

choices.label: B
choices.explanation: Cache holds near-CPU copies of memory blocks rather than serving as the mass backing store.

choices.label: C
choices.explanation: Persistent HDD/SSD storage can hold nonresident page contents for the virtual-memory system.

choices.label: D
choices.explanation: Registers hold immediate execution state and cannot serve as the large backing store for nonresident pages.

reviews.answer_text: Access to a disk-backed page that is not resident causes a page fault.
reviews.hint: Read the nonresident-page case without treating disk reads as universal to every fault.
reviews.explanation: COA27 says a valid nonresident page access faults and may require loading data. Thus B describes the ordinary disk-backed nonresident-page case and is the only offered cause fitting a page fault. Its disk-loading phrase is not a universal definition: zero-fill, already-resident shared pages and invalid/protection accesses can fault differently. None of the register, cache-capacity or arithmetic options identifies virtual-page residency.

evidence.quote: A valid nonresident page access faults and may require loading data; invalid or forbidden accesses can also fault.

choices.label: A
choices.explanation: Register allocation pressure is not an access to a missing or forbidden virtual page.

choices.label: B
choices.explanation: The described disk-backed nonresident access is a page-fault case, although not all faults require a disk read.

choices.label: C
choices.explanation: A full cache leads to cache replacement, not necessarily a virtual-memory page fault.

choices.label: D
choices.explanation: Arithmetic overflow is an instruction arithmetic condition rather than a virtual-page access event.

reviews.answer_text: HDD is generally slower and nonvolatile.
reviews.hint: Read memory-hierarchy speed and power-off retention separately.
reviews.explanation: COA23 places DRAM above HDD in the usual speed hierarchy. COA28 says an HDD does not require continuous power to preserve stored bits, while COA24 calls ordinary SRAM/DRAM volatile. Combining the independent speed and retention rules gives slower and nonvolatile. The answer concerns the usual hierarchy comparison rather than every conceivable workload or specialized memory device.

evidence.quote: A usual speed/cost-per-bit order is registers, L1/L2/L3 cache, DRAM, SSD, HDD and archival tape.
It does not need continuous power to preserve stored bits.

choices.label: A
choices.explanation: It reverses both usual properties: HDD is slower than RAM and retains data without power.

choices.label: B
choices.explanation: The hierarchy places HDD below RAM in speed, and magnetic storage preserves bits without continuous power.

choices.label: C
choices.explanation: Nonvolatility is right, but the claim that HDD is faster than RAM reverses the usual hierarchy.

choices.label: D
choices.explanation: Slower is right, but volatile contradicts the note’s explicit HDD power-off retention statement.

reviews.answer_text: 100–300 ms is a historical example, not a universal typical range.
reviews.hint: Read why access timing needs an optical drive/model and era.
reviews.explanation: COA28 explicitly names 100–300 ms as historical optical-access examples rather than universal specifications. The question supplies no drive generation, model, measurement definition or historical scope. C can match that example, but typically cannot be established for all optical disks from it. The other ranges likewise cannot be evaluated as general typical values without the missing device context.

evidence.quote: Optical access ranges such as 100–300 ms are historical examples, not universal device specifications.

choices.label: A
choices.explanation: The note does not establish 1–5 ms as typical for the unspecified optical device and access measurement.

choices.label: B
choices.explanation: The note does not establish 10–30 ms as typical without the drive model and era.

choices.label: C
choices.explanation: This matches the note’s historical example, but the question does not restrict its typical claim to that context.

choices.label: D
choices.explanation: The note provides no basis to call 500–1000 ms typical for an unspecified optical system.

reviews.answer_text: Magnetic tape.
reviews.hint: Read sequential streaming versus addressed-block access.
reviews.explanation: COA28 classifies tape as sequential and suited to streaming/archives. Disk provides direct addressed-block access, while SSD provides nonmechanical persistent storage rather than a tape-style stream. The question asks the medium whose access is characteristically sequential, so magnetic tape is the supported choice. Physical streaming inside another device does not make its logical access interface tape-like.

evidence.quote: In textbook access taxonomy, tape is sequential, disk is direct access with positioning delay, RAM is random access with broadly address-independent timing, and associative access matches content.

choices.label: A
choices.explanation: SSD is addressed nonvolatile semiconductor storage rather than the sequential tape-access medium described.

choices.label: B
choices.explanation: HDD permits addressed-block direct access rather than requiring tape-like sequential record traversal.

choices.label: C
choices.explanation: Tape is explicitly the sequential streaming/archive medium in the note’s access taxonomy.

choices.label: D
choices.explanation: Optical disk uses addressed disk access rather than being the sequential tape medium requested.

reviews.answer_text: Hold temporary values for immediate CPU operations.
reviews.hint: Read execution operands/results versus persistent bulk storage.
reviews.explanation: COA14 distinguishes registers as explicit execution operands and assigns them fetched instructions, transferred data and operands/results. That supports the immediate temporary-storage role in B. Registers are small execution state rather than permanent bulk data storage. Some registers participate in I/O or translation, but those specialized uses do not replace the primary execution-storage role asked here.

evidence.quote: Registers and cache both store temporary information, but registers are explicit execution operands and cache holds copies of memory blocks.

choices.label: A
choices.explanation: Registers are small temporary execution storage rather than permanent bulk storage for large datasets.

choices.label: B
choices.explanation: Registers hold operands, instruction state and intermediate results used directly by current CPU operations.

choices.label: C
choices.explanation: Some registers support I/O, but general I/O communication is not their primary execution-storage purpose.

choices.label: D
choices.explanation: Translation can use specialized state, but managing virtual pages is not the primary role of CPU registers generally.

reviews.answer_text: Specify the addressed memory location.
reviews.hint: Read address, data and control signal roles separately.
reviews.explanation: COA12 says address signals select a location, data signals carry values and control signals coordinate read/write and timing. Therefore B directly matches the address bus. Actual payload data belongs to the data bus, while timing and operation commands belong to control signaling. The distinction does not depend on address width or the value being transferred.

evidence.quote: Address signals select a location; data signals carry values; control signals coordinate read/write, timing, requests and acknowledgements.

choices.label: A
choices.explanation: Actual payload values travel on the data bus rather than the address signals selecting a location.

choices.label: B
choices.explanation: The address bus identifies the memory location selected for the CPU’s access.

choices.label: C
choices.explanation: Timing belongs to control signaling, not the location-selection role of address signals.

choices.label: D
choices.explanation: Read/write and other operation commands belong to control signaling rather than the address bus.

reviews.answer_text: 32 address bits select 2^32 locations; bytes per location must be specified.
reviews.hint: Read the addressable-unit assumption before converting locations to byte capacity.
reviews.explanation: COA12 says a address bits give 2^a locations and requires multiplying by bytes per location before claiming byte capacity. Here 32 bits gives 2^32 locations. B follows only with byte addressing, yielding 4 GiB (often called 4 GB). Since the stem omits the addressable-unit size, selecting a unique byte capacity would silently add the key assumption.

evidence.quote: With a address bits there are 2^a addressable locations. Multiply by bytes per location before calling this a byte capacity.

choices.label: A
choices.explanation: Two GB is not implied by the stated address count; the missing addressable-unit convention prevents a capacity answer.

choices.label: B
choices.explanation: Four GiB follows for one byte per location, but byte addressing is not specified.

choices.label: C
choices.explanation: Eight GiB could follow for two bytes per location; the addressable unit is missing.

choices.label: D
choices.explanation: Sixteen GiB could follow for four bytes per location; the stem gives no unit width.

reviews.answer_text: Control signals coordinate operations, including read/write timing.
reviews.hint: Read control signaling as a collection rather than only one request type.
reviews.explanation: COA12 defines control signals as coordinating read/write, timing, requests and acknowledgements. C expresses that general role. The data and address alternatives belong to distinct signal groups. Interrupt requests may be part of aggregate control, but the word only makes D too restrictive because read/write and timing controls are also included.

evidence.quote: control signals coordinate read/write, timing, requests and acknowledgements.

choices.label: A
choices.explanation: Actual transferred data belongs to the data bus rather than the control-signal group.

choices.label: B
choices.explanation: Location selection belongs to address signals rather than the control bus’s coordination role.

choices.label: C
choices.explanation: Read/write coordination and timing are explicitly among the functions assigned to control signals.

choices.label: D
choices.explanation: Interrupt requests are only one possible control input; the bus also carries other coordination signals.

reviews.answer_text: Bits specifying the operation.
reviews.hint: Read operation selection separately from operands and PC.
reviews.explanation: COA16 defines the opcode as the operation-specifying field. Operand fields locate registers/data and mode fields explain their interpretation. Thus B names the correct format role; next-instruction addresses, result-register identity and operand values are separate quantities. Their presence elsewhere in a machine does not change what opcode means.

evidence.quote: An opcode specifies the operation; operand fields locate data or registers, and a mode field explains interpretation.

choices.label: A
choices.explanation: Next-instruction position is a PC/control-flow role, not the opcode’s operation-selection role.

choices.label: B
choices.explanation: Opcode bits select the operation the processor should perform for the instruction.

choices.label: C
choices.explanation: Result-register selection belongs to an operand/destination field rather than defining the opcode.

choices.label: D
choices.explanation: An operand data value is distinct from the code selecting the operation to apply.

reviews.answer_text: Implicit top-of-stack operands.
reviews.hint: Read zero explicit operand fields in stack arithmetic.
reviews.explanation: COA16 says zero-address stack ADD uses two implicit top-of-stack operands. The absence of written operand addresses therefore relies on stack organization, not immediate constants or direct memory fields. Generic implicit register addressing is too broad and does not identify the stack discipline specified for this format; PUSH/POP may still have explicit addresses.

evidence.quote: Zero-address stack ADD uses two implicit top-of-stack operands.

choices.label: A
choices.explanation: Implicit register addressing alone does not identify the stack operand convention defining zero-address arithmetic here.

choices.label: B
choices.explanation: Operands come implicitly from the top of the stack, so arithmetic needs no explicit operand-address fields.

choices.label: C
choices.explanation: Immediate values require encoded operand information; zero-address stack arithmetic is not restricted to constants.

choices.label: D
choices.explanation: Direct memory addressing would use an explicit operand address, contrary to the stated zero-address arithmetic format.

reviews.answer_text: Three-address format.
reviews.hint: Count explicit destination and source operand fields.
reviews.explanation: COA16 defines three-address ADD X,Y,Z as X←Y+Z, allowing a separately named destination and two sources. This matches the stem’s three separate operands. Two-address form overwrites one source, one-address uses an implicit accumulator, and zero-address uses stack operands. Most expressive is interpreted here through the explicit three-operand criterion rather than a universal comparison of complete instruction sets.

evidence.quote: Three-address ADD X,Y,Z means X←Y+Z under destination-first notation.

choices.label: A
choices.explanation: Zero-address arithmetic names no explicit operands and instead uses the implicit stack top.

choices.label: B
choices.explanation: One-address accumulator arithmetic names only one explicit operand and relies on an implicit accumulator.

choices.label: C
choices.explanation: Two-address arithmetic overwrites a named source and lacks a separately named third operand field.

choices.label: D
choices.explanation: Three explicit fields allow one destination and two independently named source operands.

reviews.answer_text: LIFO: last in, first out.
reviews.hint: Read which stack item PUSH and POP operate on.
reviews.explanation: COA17 defines a stack as last-in, first-out: PUSH adds at the logical top and POP removes that top item. The most recently pushed remaining item is therefore the next removed. FIFO describes queue ordering, while arbitrary indexed access or priority selection does not define the stack discipline.

evidence.quote: A stack is last-in, first-out. PUSH adds an item and POP removes the logical top.

choices.label: A
choices.explanation: FIFO removes the oldest inserted item, the opposite order from normal stack removal.

choices.label: B
choices.explanation: The last item pushed becomes the top and is the first item popped.

choices.label: C
choices.explanation: Random access does not enforce removal of the most recently pushed remaining item.

choices.label: D
choices.explanation: Stack removal follows insertion order in reverse, not a priority ranking assigned to items.

reviews.answer_text: A reference whose stored contents supply the effective address.
reviews.hint: Read indirect EA=M[A] versus direct EA=A and immediate value A.
reviews.explanation: COA18 defines memory-indirect addressing as EA=M[A], followed by operand M[EA]. Thus the instruction’s field identifies a pointer location rather than directly containing the operand value or final operand address. C is the pointer/indirection description. A describes immediate, B direct, and a plain register number identifies a register-based mode rather than this memory-indirect convention.

evidence.quote: indirect uses EA=M[A] then operand M[EA].

choices.label: A
choices.explanation: An actual value encoded in the instruction is immediate addressing rather than memory indirection.

choices.label: B
choices.explanation: Using the field directly as the operand’s address is direct addressing, without the intermediate pointer lookup.

choices.label: C
choices.explanation: The field identifies a pointer-bearing location; its contents supply the address of the operand data.

choices.label: D
choices.explanation: A register number names register-based addressing rather than the memory-indirect field defined in this note.

reviews.answer_text: RISC emphasizes simple regular, load/store, pipeline-friendly operations; no option states a valid universal distinguishing rule.
reviews.hint: Distinguish one-per-cycle throughput from instruction latency.
reviews.explanation: COA20 explicitly warns that a pipeline completing one instruction each cycle does not make every instruction single-cycle; modern RISC instructions can take multiple cycles. The other alternatives describe CISC tendencies or an unsupported instruction-count range. Therefore C is a familiar oversimplification rather than a valid general characteristic as written. The actual supported RISC traits are absent from the choices.

evidence.quote: One instruction completing per pipeline cycle is throughput, not proof that every instruction has one-cycle latency. Modern RISC instructions can take multiple cycles

choices.label: A
choices.explanation: Variable instruction lengths are listed as a CISC tendency, not the regular-encoding RISC trait requested.

choices.label: B
choices.explanation: The supplied numerical range is not a defining RISC property established by the note.

choices.label: C
choices.explanation: Single-cycle latency for every instruction is explicitly not implied by RISC or pipeline throughput.

choices.label: D
choices.explanation: Complex microcoded control is not the simple, pipeline-friendly RISC tendency identified by the note.

reviews.answer_text: CISC commonly supports richer complex instructions, potentially with multi-cycle execution.
reviews.hint: Read RISC/CISC tendencies without turning them into absolute implementation rules.
reviews.explanation: COA20 associates CISC with complex operations, richer addressing and variable lengths, and rejects universal one-cycle latency claims. C therefore gives the matching tendency and permits, rather than requires, multi-cycle execution. The remaining claims either reverse the usual complexity contrast or impose unsupported only/no restrictions. The answer does not claim modern RISC instructions can never take multiple cycles.

evidence.quote: CISC commonly supplies more complex operations, richer addressing modes and variable lengths.

choices.label: A
choices.explanation: Fewer instructions reverses the usual simple-versus-rich instruction-set contrast rather than stating the note’s CISC tendency.

choices.label: B
choices.explanation: Only register-to-register operations contradicts the richer addressing modes associated with CISC in the note.

choices.label: C
choices.explanation: Complex operations and possible multi-cycle latency fit the CISC tendency without claiming exclusivity of multi-cycle execution.

choices.label: D
choices.explanation: The note does not define CISC by absence of microcode; control implementation is a separate design dimension.

reviews.answer_text: Registers.
reviews.hint: Read the plentiful-register tendency in textbook RISC.
reviews.explanation: COA20 explicitly lists plentiful registers among textbook RISC characteristics, alongside load/store access and simple operations. C is therefore the supported tendency. More addressing modes and instruction bytes are not the stated compensating mechanism, and more cycles per instruction is not a defining guarantee. The typically qualifier matters because the labels alone do not impose a register count on every implementation.

evidence.quote: Textbook RISC emphasizes simple operations, regular encodings, load/store memory access, plentiful registers and pipeline-friendly control.

choices.label: A
choices.explanation: More cycles per instruction is not the plentiful-register mechanism or a guaranteed RISC property.

choices.label: B
choices.explanation: Richer addressing modes are associated with CISC tendencies, not the stated RISC compensating feature.

choices.label: C
choices.explanation: Plentiful registers are explicitly one of the textbook RISC traits named by the complete note.

choices.label: D
choices.explanation: More instruction bytes is not the feature identified as supporting simple RISC operations.

reviews.answer_text: Poll the status register.
reviews.hint: Read programmed/polled I/O versus event-driven notification.
reviews.explanation: COA30 defines programmed/polled I/O as repeatedly checking device status while the CPU moves each item. B names that readiness/completion checking mechanism. Interrupt notification belongs to interrupt-driven I/O, and a DMA controller is a separate transfer mechanism. The OS may arrange when polling code runs, but that broad scheduling statement does not replace the actual status check.

evidence.quote: Programmed/polled I/O repeatedly checks status and lets the CPU move each item.

choices.label: A
choices.explanation: An interrupt signal names interrupt-driven notification rather than programmed I/O’s polling mechanism.

choices.label: B
choices.explanation: The CPU reads device status repeatedly to determine readiness or completion in programmed I/O.

choices.label: C
choices.explanation: DMA-controller completion notification belongs to a DMA transfer rather than programmed CPU-driven I/O.

choices.label: D
choices.explanation: Scheduling a check is broader software organization; polling the status register is the actual completion-detection method.

reviews.answer_text: The CPU can do other work while the device operates.
reviews.hint: Read polling overhead versus interrupt notification, including handler cost.
reviews.explanation: COA30 says interrupt-driven I/O lets the CPU do other work until the device requests service. That removes continuous status polling, which is the principal advantage in B. Service still consumes CPU time and needs device support/software. Therefore it does not universally increase device transfer speed, eliminate hardware requirements or remove drivers.

evidence.quote: Interrupt-driven I/O lets the CPU do other work until an event requests service; the handler still consumes CPU time to service the device.

choices.label: A
choices.explanation: Avoiding polling does not by itself guarantee that the device or bus transfers data at a higher rate.

choices.label: B
choices.explanation: The CPU can execute other useful work between setup and the device’s service request.

choices.label: C
choices.explanation: Interrupt notification requires suitable device/controller support; the note does not promise no special hardware.

choices.label: D
choices.explanation: A handler/driver must still service the device; interrupt-driven operation does not remove that software role.

reviews.answer_text: Controller-managed device–memory transfer avoids CPU work per item.
reviews.hint: Read the limited meaning of without CPU involvement in DMA.
reviews.explanation: COA30 defines DMA as controller movement directly between device and memory after CPU setup. B describes that transfer-phase advantage, provided without involvement means without per-word CPU copying. The same section explicitly retains CPU configuration/completion duties. DMA does not require increasing CPU frequency, compressing the data or changing to a faster bus; its benefit is reduced per-item processor work.

evidence.quote: DMA reduces per-word CPU work but competes for memory bandwidth.

choices.label: A
choices.explanation: DMA changes who performs transfer work, not the processor’s clock frequency.

choices.label: B
choices.explanation: The controller transfers the block directly after setup, avoiding CPU copying for each item; setup/completion still involve CPU.

choices.label: C
choices.explanation: Data compression is not part of the DMA definition or its stated per-word CPU-work reduction.

choices.label: D
choices.explanation: DMA may use the existing bus and does not inherently replace it with a faster one.

reviews.answer_text: Device registers occupy memory addresses and use suitable memory access instructions.
reviews.hint: Read MMIO versus isolated port I/O and device access caveats.
reviews.explanation: COA31 says memory-mapped I/O assigns device registers addresses in the memory address space and uses suitable loads/stores. C matches, but like regular memory refers to address/instruction access rather than identical side effects: MMIO widths, ordering and status-read behavior still matter. Special IN/OUT and a separate port space instead describe isolated I/O; DMA is independent of address-space choice.

evidence.quote: Memory-mapped I/O assigns device registers addresses in the memory address space and uses suitable load/store operations.

choices.label: A
choices.explanation: Special IN/OUT instructions describe isolated/port-mapped I/O rather than the defining memory-mapped access mechanism.

choices.label: B
choices.explanation: A separate port space is the isolated I/O arrangement, not device registers in memory address space.

choices.label: C
choices.explanation: MMIO places device registers at memory-space addresses accessed through suitable loads/stores, with device-specific side-effect rules.

choices.label: D
choices.explanation: MMIO specifies addressing and access, not an exclusive requirement to transfer all device data through DMA.

reviews.answer_text: Transmit system data to the peripheral.
reviews.hint: Read command direction from the system’s perspective.
reviews.explanation: COA29 defines write/output commands as sending system data to the device. C matches that direction: data from the system bus is handed to the peripheral. Reading brings device data toward the system, status testing inspects readiness/errors, and reset is a control action. These are distinct command functions even when one controller implements them all.

evidence.quote: write/output commands send system data to the device.

choices.label: A
choices.explanation: Moving peripheral data into a system buffer is the input/read direction rather than write/output.

choices.label: B
choices.explanation: Checking readiness or errors is a test/status command rather than transferring output data.

choices.label: C
choices.explanation: A write/output command sends data from the system side to the peripheral device.

choices.label: D
choices.explanation: Reset is a device-control action, not the ordinary data-output direction defining a write command.

reviews.answer_text: DMA for substantial block transfers.
reviews.hint: Compare CPU work per item with block setup/completion overhead.
reviews.explanation: COA30 explicitly recommends DMA for substantial blocks because it reduces per-word CPU work to setup and completion duties. This matches disk-like large transfers. Polling and interrupt transfer still involve CPU servicing of individual items, while memory-mapped I/O is an address-space design choice that may coexist with DMA. The answer assumes the substantial-block context, not a universal fastest mechanism for every tiny transfer.

evidence.quote: Choose it for substantial blocks; mapping devices to addresses is a separate design dimension.

choices.label: A
choices.explanation: Programmed I/O makes the CPU check status and move each item, adding substantial work for large blocks.

choices.label: B
choices.explanation: Interrupt-driven transfer avoids continuous polling but still consumes CPU service work for transferred items.

choices.label: C
choices.explanation: DMA replaces much per-item CPU work with block setup/completion, matching the substantial-transfer recommendation.

choices.label: D
choices.explanation: Memory mapping specifies device addressing and can coexist with DMA; it does not itself offload block movement.

reviews.answer_text: Peer processors sharing memory and I/O.
reviews.hint: Read symmetric shared-memory roles versus distributed address spaces.
reviews.explanation: COA37 defines SMP processors as sharing memory/I/O and having peer roles under one OS. B is the conventional matching description; identical is read as the compatible symmetric processor model, not a claim that every physical property must match. The other choices describe specialized asymmetry, an incoherent chip/core formulation, or networked/distributed organization rather than the stated shared-memory model.

evidence.quote: SMP processors share memory/I/O and have peer roles under an OS.

choices.label: A
choices.explanation: Specialized different roles describe asymmetry rather than the peer roles used to define SMP here.

choices.label: B
choices.explanation: The conventional symmetric processor arrangement shares memory and I/O with peer roles under one OS.

choices.label: C
choices.explanation: A single processor with cores on different chips does not state the peer shared-memory SMP definition.

choices.label: D
choices.explanation: Network connection alone does not establish shared memory/I/O or the symmetric peer-processor organization.

reviews.answer_text: Overlap stages of different instructions.
reviews.hint: Read throughput improvement rather than assuming reduced single-instruction latency.
reviews.explanation: COA35 defines pipelining by overlapping stages from different instructions and says it primarily improves throughput. C directly states that mechanism. It does not require faster stages, larger registers or a single instruction completing all work faster. Pipeline fill/drain, stalls and the slowest stage constrain actual gains, so overlap rather than guaranteed latency reduction is the supported explanation.

evidence.quote: A pipeline overlaps stages of different instructions; it primarily improves throughput.

choices.label: A
choices.explanation: Pipeline performance does not require increasing each stage’s clock speed; clock choice is limited by the slowest stage.

choices.label: B
choices.explanation: An instruction still spans several stages, so lower single-instruction latency is not the defining improvement.

choices.label: C
choices.explanation: Overlapping stages lets different instructions progress concurrently, increasing completed-work throughput.

choices.label: D
choices.explanation: Larger register width does not define stage overlap or directly explain pipelining’s throughput benefit.

reviews.answer_text: Compare exponents first.
reviews.hint: Read floating-point addition’s alignment-before-addition sequence.
reviews.explanation: COA10 orders floating addition as compare exponents, shift the smaller significand to align, add/subtract, normalize and round. Comparing exponents must precede alignment because their difference determines the required shift. Adding before alignment combines unequal place weights, and normalization happens after arithmetic. Therefore D is the first named sub-operation.

evidence.quote: For floating addition, compare exponents, shift the smaller significand to align, add or subtract, normalize and round.

choices.label: A
choices.explanation: Normalization follows aligned addition/subtraction rather than initiating the floating-point addition sequence.

choices.label: B
choices.explanation: Significands must first be aligned to a common exponent before their values can be added correctly.

choices.label: C
choices.explanation: Alignment follows exponent comparison, which determines which significand to shift and by how much.

choices.label: D
choices.explanation: Exponent comparison is explicitly first and supplies the information needed for subsequent alignment.

reviews.answer_text: A vector operation covers multiple elements, but the whole array need not execute at one instant.
reviews.hint: Distinguish vector instruction semantics from physical lane concurrency.
reviews.explanation: COA37 defines a vector instruction as an operation over a sequence of elements and explicitly allows physical lanes to process them in batches. B captures multi-element semantics but overstates them if simultaneously means every array element executes at once. The other choices make unsupported speed/transistor claims. A repaired B should say one instruction operates over multiple data elements, potentially in lane-sized batches.

evidence.quote: A vector instruction describes an operation over a sequence of elements; physical lanes may process them in batches, not all in one instant.

choices.label: A
choices.explanation: Faster single-element processing does not state the multi-element operation semantics defining vector processing.

choices.label: B
choices.explanation: This fits one multi-element instruction logically, but entire-array simultaneous physical execution is not guaranteed.

choices.label: C
choices.explanation: The note gives no transistor-count guarantee distinguishing vector from scalar processing.

choices.label: D
choices.explanation: Higher clock frequency is not a defining vector-processing property and is not guaranteed.

reviews.answer_text: One instruction per cycle is the ideal single-issue case; issue width is unstated.
reviews.hint: Read the single-issue assumption in the ideal pipeline model.
reviews.explanation: COA35 derives one completion per cycle for an ideal single-issue pipeline. COA36 separately permits superscalar multiple issue, and a RISC label does not specify issue width. Thus B is the conventional intended result only under the omitted single-issue assumption; C can describe an ideal two-issue design. The question should state pipeline width and steady-state/no-stall conditions to give one numerical throughput.

evidence.quote: In an ideal k-stage single-issue pipeline, n instructions take k+n−1 cycles when stages are balanced and there are no stalls.
Superscalar execution issues multiple instructions to multiple functional units in a cycle when dependencies permit.

choices.label: A
choices.explanation: One every two cycles is not the ideal completion rate of the note’s balanced unstalled single-issue pipeline.

choices.label: B
choices.explanation: One per cycle is the ideal steady-state single-issue result, conditional on an issue-width assumption.

choices.label: C
choices.explanation: Two per cycle is possible for an ideal two-issue design; RISC alone does not exclude such a pipeline.

choices.label: D
choices.explanation: The missing issue width is the decisive ambiguity; instruction complexity alone does not define the ideal numerical rate.

reviews.answer_text: Instruction streams and data streams.
reviews.hint: Read the two axes in SISD, SIMD, MISD and MIMD.
