reviews.explanation: COA37 explicitly defines Flynn classification by instruction and data streams. SISD has one of each, SIMD one instruction stream with multiple data elements, and MIMD multiple streams of each. Processor count, capacity, clock and register/cache sizes are implementation properties rather than the two classification axes. Therefore B directly matches the taxonomy.

evidence.quote: Flynn classifies instruction and data streams: SISD has one of each; SIMD applies one instruction stream to multiple data elements; MIMD uses multiple instruction and data streams;

choices.label: A
choices.explanation: Processor count and memory size do not define the instruction-stream/data-stream axes of Flynn’s taxonomy.

choices.label: B
choices.explanation: Flynn classifies the number of instruction streams and data streams, producing SISD/SIMD/MISD/MIMD categories.

choices.label: C
choices.explanation: Clock and bus width measure implementation characteristics rather than Flynn’s stream-count classification.

choices.label: D
choices.explanation: Cache capacity and register count are not the two axes used by Flynn’s taxonomy.

reviews.answer_text: Throughput: completed processing per unit time.
reviews.hint: Read available parallel work and the definition of throughput.
reviews.explanation: COA37 says more cores increase available parallel work while serial dependencies and coordination limit speedup. COA34 defines throughput as completed work per unit time. Parallel processing aims to raise that work rate, matching C, rather than inherently increasing physical memory, clock frequency or register width. Actual gains still depend on enough independent work and manageable overhead.

evidence.quote: Throughput counts completed work per unit time; latency measures one job’s delay.
More cores increase available parallel work, but serial dependencies and coordination limit speedup.

choices.label: A
choices.explanation: Parallel execution does not inherently increase the system’s installed memory capacity.

choices.label: B
choices.explanation: Additional concurrent work can improve throughput without increasing any processor’s clock frequency.

choices.label: C
choices.explanation: Concurrent useful work aims to increase completed processing per unit time, subject to serial and coordination limits.

choices.label: D
choices.explanation: Register width is an architectural data-size property, not the primary objective of parallel execution.

reviews.answer_text: A is the conventional historical-category answer; literal AI usage does not identify a unique generation.
reviews.hint: Read CP03’s historical taxonomy and distinguish an association from an exclusive application domain.
reviews.explanation: CP03 associates fifth generation with declarative logic, constraints and AI/expert systems, making A the conventional answer if the question asks for that historical category. The literal stem instead asks which languages are used in AI. A generation classification does not restrict applications or exclude third-generation high-level implementations. The wording therefore does not support a unique generation; this is question ambiguity, not a missing note rule.

evidence.quote: Fifth generation is a loose historical category associated with declarative logic, constraints and AI/expert systems.
general high-level languages such as C++ and Java are third.

choices.label: A
choices.explanation: The historical AI/logic association supports this conditional intended answer, without making fifth generation the exclusive AI implementation category.

choices.label: B
choices.explanation: Second generation denotes assembly; that classification alone does not establish an exclusion from AI applications.

choices.label: C
choices.explanation: Fourth generation denotes queries/application generators; CP03 does not turn that taxonomy into an exclusive application-domain restriction.

choices.label: D
choices.explanation: Third generation includes general high-level languages; their classification does not prohibit AI or expert-system implementations.

reviews.answer_text: Preprocessor → compiler → assembler → linker/loader.
reviews.hint: Follow the conventional C++ translation stages in CP04.
reviews.explanation: CP04 explicitly places preprocessing before compilation proper and compilation before assembly. The assembler produces object files, which are linked into an executable and then loaded. D preserves that order, although it compresses linking/loading into one label and describes the final result loosely as target machine code.

evidence.quote: source → preprocessing → compilation proper → assembly → object files → linking → executable → loading → execution.

choices.label: A
choices.explanation: Places the assembler before the compiler, reversing their stated order in CP04.

choices.label: B
choices.explanation: Attempts linking/loading before compilation and assembly have produced the required object files.

choices.label: C
choices.explanation: Places preprocessing after compilation and assembly, contrary to the conventional toolchain order.

choices.label: D
choices.explanation: Preserves preprocessing, compilation, assembly, linking and loading in the required sequence.

reviews.answer_text: Machine language is first generation.
reviews.hint: Read the machine/assembly/high-level generation sequence in CP03.
reviews.explanation: CP03 calls machine instructions first generation and symbolic assembly second generation. The question asks specifically about machine language, so the first-generation option follows directly. Third and fourth generations refer to higher-level languages and query/application generators, respectively; they do not classify native machine instructions.

evidence.quote: Machine instructions are conventionally first generation; symbolic assembly is second; general high-level languages such as C++ and Java are third.

choices.label: A
choices.explanation: Second generation identifies symbolic assembly, whose instructions still require assembly into machine code.

choices.label: B
choices.explanation: Third generation identifies general high-level languages such as C++ and Java.

choices.label: C
choices.explanation: Fourth generation identifies query languages and application generators, rather than machine instructions.

choices.label: D
choices.explanation: First generation is the note’s explicit conventional classification for machine instructions.

reviews.answer_text: Finding and correcting errors in program code.
reviews.hint: Read the distinction between a bug and debugging in CP32.
reviews.explanation: CP32 defines a bug as a defect and debugging as locating and correcting it. Defining the task, designing an algorithm and creating code are other development activities. They may expose defects, but none of them states the specific error-finding and correction purpose of debugging.

evidence.quote: A bug is a defect; debugging locates and corrects it.

choices.label: A
choices.explanation: Identifying the task defines requirements; it does not locate and repair defects in code.

choices.label: B
choices.explanation: Creating code is implementation, whereas debugging investigates and corrects defects in that code.

choices.label: C
choices.explanation: Creating an algorithm is design; debugging concerns finding and correcting defects.

choices.label: D
choices.explanation: Finding and correcting program errors directly matches the definition of debugging in CP32.

reviews.answer_text: Small, frequently used functions are reasonable inline optimization candidates.
reviews.hint: Read CP19 alongside the typedef distinction in CP06.
reviews.explanation: CP19 recommends small, frequently used functions as possible optimization candidates, while stressing that inline never forces expansion at the call site. CP06 says typedef creates an alias rather than a distinct new type. Thus D is defensible as a recommendation; the mandatory-expansion and distinct-type claims cannot make all choices correct.

evidence.quote: Small frequently used functions may be good optimization candidates, but actual expansion is the optimizer’s decision.
typedef creates an alias, not a distinct new type.

choices.label: A
choices.explanation: A typedef supplies an alternative name for an existing type, not a distinct new type.

choices.label: B
choices.explanation: Declaring inline does not require the compiler to expand the body at each call.

choices.label: C
choices.explanation: The distinct-type and mandatory-expansion claims are false, so all choices cannot be correct.

choices.label: D
choices.explanation: Simple, frequently called functions can be reasonable candidates, although expansion remains an optimizer decision.

choices.label: E
choices.explanation: The recommendation in D is supported, so it is false that none is correct.

reviews.hint: Trace the persistent static local separately from main’s accumulator in CP20.
reviews.explanation: The function’s static x is initialized once, then persists across calls. Its five returns are 1, 3, 5, 7 and 9: after the first update it stays odd and increases by two. Main has a separate x and accumulates all five returns, giving 25.

evidence.quote: A static local is initialized once and retains its value across calls even though its name remains local.

choices.label: A
choices.explanation: One is only the first function return, not the sum accumulated by main.

choices.label: B
choices.explanation: The five return values sum to 25; a total of 19 omits or miscomputes updates.

choices.label: C
choices.explanation: The function does not reset or simply count calls; its persistent values are odd.

choices.label: D
choices.explanation: The five odd returns total 25, not the sum of five even values.

choices.label: E
choices.explanation: Adding the five persistent-state returns gives 1+3+5+7+9, which equals 25.

reviews.answer_text: ExitExam and exitExam are distinct identifiers.
reviews.hint: Read CP05 on letter case in C++ names.
reviews.explanation: Case sensitivity means changing uppercase to lowercase can change the identifier. ExitExam and exitExam therefore name different entities in C++. Claims about headers, variable terminology or semicolon placement do not explain case sensitivity; the universal header and semicolon assertions also overstate C++ syntax requirements.

evidence.quote: C++ is case sensitive: exitExam and ExitExam differ; delete and float are keywords, but FLOAT is a legal identifier.

choices.label: A
choices.explanation: Variable names are identifiers, but this does not describe the effect of changing letter case.

choices.label: B
choices.explanation: Header inclusion is unrelated to case sensitivity, and headers are not included in every statement.

choices.label: C
choices.explanation: The differing initial letter case makes ExitExam and exitExam distinct C++ identifiers.

choices.label: D
choices.explanation: Semicolon rules concern grammar, not identifier case, and do not apply uniformly to every construct.

reviews.answer_text: Parentheses ().
reviews.hint: Compare grouping with unary, multiplicative and shift precedence in CP10.
reviews.explanation: CP10 places grouping/postfix at the top of its precedence ladder. Parentheses explicitly group an expression before surrounding operations are applied. Increment, multiplication or dereference, and right shift do not override that grouping. The precise role of * or ++ in an expression does not make it outrank explicit parentheses.

evidence.quote: The precedence ladder is grouping/postfix, unary, multiplicative, additive, shifts, relations, equality, bitwise &, ^, |, &&, ||, conditional, assignment, comma.

choices.label: A
choices.explanation: Parentheses explicitly group expressions and occupy the highest grouping level in the note.

choices.label: B
choices.explanation: Increment does not override parentheses; prefix increment is unary and postfix increment follows grouping rules.

choices.label: C
choices.explanation: Multiplication is below grouping; unary dereference also does not override parenthesized grouping.

choices.label: D
choices.explanation: Right shift ranks below both grouping and arithmetic operations in the stated ladder.

reviews.answer_text: delete and the literal . followed by jan2025 are invalid identifiers.
reviews.hint: Apply CP05’s keyword and permitted-character rules to the printed options.
reviews.explanation: CP05 prohibits keywords and characters other than letters, digits and underscores in an ASCII identifier. delete is a keyword. C is printed with a dot before jan2025; that complete text is not a single valid identifier either. If the dot is an extraction artifact, jan2025 alone is valid, but the packet supplies no image establishing that repair.

evidence.quote: In the basic ASCII identifier rules, start with a letter or underscore; continue with letters, digits or underscores. Do not use a keyword.

choices.label: A
choices.explanation: delete is a reserved C++ keyword and cannot serve as an ordinary identifier.

choices.label: B
choices.explanation: for_cpp starts with a letter, contains allowed characters, and is not the keyword for.

choices.label: C
choices.explanation: As printed, the leading dot makes this text invalid as one identifier; jan2025 alone would be valid.

choices.label: D
choices.explanation: Hello begins with a letter and contains only letters, so it is a valid identifier.

reviews.answer_text: SQL is conventionally fourth generation.
reviews.hint: Read CP03’s SQL classification separately from execution strategy.
reviews.explanation: CP03 explicitly classifies SQL with fourth-generation query languages and application generators. The question’s description of interpreted languages is imprecise: interpretation is not what determines a language generation. Nevertheless, the named example SQL has a clear conventional classification, making fourth generation the supported answer.

evidence.quote: Database query and application generators such as SQL are conventionally fourth generation.
Generations do not determine whether an implementation uses an interpreter.

choices.label: A
choices.explanation: Fourth generation is the note’s explicit conventional classification for SQL and query languages.

choices.label: B
choices.explanation: Second generation refers to assembly; interpretation alone does not move SQL into this category.

choices.label: C
choices.explanation: Third generation describes general high-level languages, rather than SQL’s stated query-language category.

choices.label: D
choices.explanation: SQL is not classified into all these generations merely because implementations can interpret it.

reviews.answer_text: Bug is the conventional term; Error also satisfies the literal wording.
reviews.hint: Read CP32’s bug/debugging terminology.
reviews.explanation: CP32 defines a bug as a defect, making Bug the conventional completion. However, the unrestricted literal statement also accepts Error: an error is an error in a program. The source image clarifies misplaced OCR text but its highlight cannot make the main Error option false. The literal options therefore admit A and C; the garbled D cannot be interpreted reliably.

evidence.quote: A bug is a defect; debugging locates and corrects it.

choices.label: A
choices.explanation: Bug is the conventional term for a defect or error in a program.

choices.label: B
choices.explanation: A debugger is a tool used to investigate defects, rather than the defect itself.

choices.label: C
choices.explanation: Error also satisfies the literal blank, although it repeats the definition rather than supplying the conventional term Bug.

choices.label: D
choices.explanation: The printed characters are corrupted and do not form a meaningful programming term.

reviews.answer_text: Assembler.
reviews.hint: Read CP04’s separate compiler and assembler roles.
reviews.explanation: CP04 states that compilation may emit assembly and the assembler emits machine instructions in an object file. The saved source image confirms the extracted words Compiler, Assembler, Interpreter and None of the above. The decorative OCR symbols have no semantic role; the translator named by the question is the assembler.

evidence.quote: compilation may emit assembly; the assembler emits machine instructions in an object file.

choices.label: A
choices.explanation: The compiler can produce assembly from higher-level source; that is the preceding stage in CP04.

choices.label: B
choices.explanation: The assembler translates assembly instructions into machine instructions contained in an object file.

choices.label: C
choices.explanation: An interpreter executes a program representation instead of performing the stated assembly-to-object translation.

choices.label: D
choices.explanation: Assembler is present and directly matches the translator role, so none of the above is false.

reviews.answer_text: Boolean.
reviews.hint: Read CP06’s mapping of C++ types to represented values.
reviews.explanation: CP06 assigns bool to logical values, whereas int represents whole numbers and float/double represent fractional approximations. Boolean is therefore the intended type category. Numeric values can participate in truth conversion, but that does not make their numeric types the dedicated representation of logical true/false values.

evidence.quote: Use int for whole numbers, float/double for fractional approximations, char for a character and bool for logical values in C++.

choices.label: A
choices.explanation: Integer represents whole numbers; possible conversion to truth does not make it the logical type.

choices.label: B
choices.explanation: Boolean represents logical true/false values, matching bool in the note’s C++ type mapping.

choices.label: C
choices.explanation: Double represents fractional numeric approximations rather than the dedicated logical type.

choices.label: D
choices.explanation: Float represents fractional numeric approximations rather than the dedicated logical type.

reviews.answer_text: Compiler.
reviews.hint: Read CP04’s distinction between compilation and assembly.
reviews.explanation: CP04 describes compilation as a stage that may emit assembly from source. The assembler then translates that assembly into object-file machine instructions, and linking combines objects and libraries. Thus the question asks for the compiler, without implying that every compiler implementation must produce assembly as its output.

evidence.quote: compilation may emit assembly; the assembler emits machine instructions in an object file.

choices.label: A
choices.explanation: An interpreter executes a representation rather than being the stated high-level-to-assembly translation stage.

choices.label: B
choices.explanation: The linker resolves external symbols and combines objects and libraries after their translation.

choices.label: C
choices.explanation: The assembler consumes assembly and emits machine instructions, rather than consuming high-level source.

choices.label: D
choices.explanation: A compiler can translate high-level source into assembly, as described in the conventional toolchain.

reviews.answer_text: Object file.
reviews.hint: Read CP04 on what an assembler emits.
reviews.explanation: In CP04’s toolchain the assembler emits machine instructions in an object file. Linking subsequently combines object files and libraries into an executable. The question therefore asks for the object file, rather than an unspecified program, data or task file; those other names do not identify the assembler’s defined output stage.

evidence.quote: the assembler emits machine instructions in an object file.

choices.label: A
choices.explanation: Program file is a vague description and does not identify the assembler’s specified object-file output.

choices.label: B
choices.explanation: The assembler emits an object file containing translated machine instructions for later linking.

choices.label: C
choices.explanation: Data file does not identify the translated instruction object produced at the assembly stage.

choices.label: D
choices.explanation: Task file is not a stage output identified for the assembler in CP04.

reviews.answer_text: No unique choice without a comparison baseline and compiler model.
reviews.hint: Separate CP04’s translation stages from unsupported performance comparisons.
reviews.explanation: The question does not specify what execution time is compared against, which debugging workflow is assumed, or whether compiler descriptions are simplified or universal. A may be the intended exception under a conventional compiled-versus-interpreted execution comparison, but that condition is unstated. B is also unqualified, and CP04 warns against universal one-step compiler descriptions. These are question assumptions, not a demonstrated omission from the complete note.

evidence.quote: Compilation uses multiple passes, so “whole program in one step” is not literally universal.

choices.label: A
choices.explanation: Execution time needs a comparison and workload; CP04 supplies no rule proving this the unique false characteristic.

choices.label: B
choices.explanation: Debugging speed is not characterized in the note, and slow is an unspecified comparison.

choices.label: C
choices.explanation: Successful translation normally precedes execution, but this alone cannot settle the unsupported timing claims.

choices.label: D
choices.explanation: This is a simplified compiler description, not a universal process guaranteed by the multiple-pass discussion.

reviews.answer_text: The floating-point remainder expression is invalid in C++.
reviews.hint: Read CP08’s operand restriction for % and CP10’s Boolean grouping.
reviews.explanation: The expression (8.0 * 3) has floating type, so applying % to it is invalid under CP08; it does not evaluate to 4. The integer multiplication/division in B gives 8. C is true because its left disjunct is true. D uses floating division and gives 21.0/5 = 4.2.

evidence.quote: % requires integral operands in C++; (8.0*3)%5 is invalid.
&& evaluates its right operand only if the left is true; || only if the left is false.

choices.label: A
choices.explanation: This is the false statement: floating-point operands cannot be used with the C++ remainder operator.

choices.label: B
choices.explanation: Equal-precedence multiplication and division group left to right: 24/3 gives the stated 8.

choices.label: C
choices.explanation: The first comparison is true, so the disjunction is true regardless of its right operand.

choices.label: D
choices.explanation: 7.0 makes the computation floating point, and 21.0 divided by 5 gives 4.2.

reviews.answer_text: ios::out is the default ofstream mode argument.
reviews.hint: Distinguish the default argument from truncation behavior in CP29.
reviews.explanation: CP29 explicitly identifies ios::out as the constructor’s default mode argument. Ordinary output-only opening also creates or truncates a file, but that effective behavior does not change the default argument’s spelling. C additionally prints trunk rather than trunc. Under the literal default-mode question, B is the supported choice.

evidence.quote: The constructor’s default ofstream mode argument is ios::out; its ordinary effect is to create/truncate the file.

choices.label: A
choices.explanation: ios::in requests input; ofstream is the output stream class with a default out mode argument.

choices.label: B
choices.explanation: ios::out is exactly the default ofstream constructor mode argument stated in CP29.

choices.label: C
choices.explanation: ios::trunk is misspelled; even out|trunc describes effective behavior rather than the default argument.

choices.label: D
choices.explanation: Input combined with truncation is not the stated default argument of the output stream class.

reviews.hint: Read CP03’s conventional scripting-language examples.
reviews.explanation: CP03 identifies Python, Perl and PHP as commonly called scripting languages and C++ as conventionally compiled. This supports C++ as the intended exception. The classification describes common use rather than an absolute prohibition on interpreting C++ or compiling languages normally used for scripting.

evidence.quote: Python, Perl and PHP are commonly called scripting languages; C++ is conventionally compiled.

choices.label: A
choices.explanation: Python is explicitly included among the note’s commonly called scripting languages.

choices.label: B
choices.explanation: Perl is explicitly included among the note’s commonly called scripting languages.

choices.label: C
choices.explanation: PHP is explicitly included among the note’s commonly called scripting languages.

choices.label: D
choices.explanation: C++ is the conventionally compiled language contrasted with the three scripting-language examples.

reviews.answer_text: Check the nearby code for typos and incorrect syntax.
reviews.hint: Read CP32’s diagnostic, repair and rebuild sequence.
reviews.explanation: CP32 recommends reading the first useful compiler diagnostic and inspecting nearby tokens and declarations before repairing and rebuilding. Among the offered actions, checking for typos or incorrect syntax matches that early repair step. Ignoring the error cannot fix translation, and a debugger is most useful once a runnable program exists.

evidence.quote: Read the first useful compiler diagnostic, inspect nearby tokens and declarations, repair and rebuild; a debugger is useful after a runnable program exists.

choices.label: A
choices.explanation: Rewriting everything is unnecessary; the note recommends diagnosing and repairing the relevant local code.

choices.label: B
choices.explanation: Ignoring a syntax error neither corrects grammar nor establishes that an executable can be built.

choices.label: C
choices.explanation: A debugger is useful after a runnable program exists; compiler diagnostics guide syntax repair first.

choices.label: D
choices.explanation: Inspecting tokens and declarations for syntax mistakes matches the first useful action among these options.

reviews.answer_text: 3, 4, 5, each on a separate line with a trailing space.
reviews.hint: Trace Java array indices using the exclusive loop bound in CP14 and CP23.
reviews.explanation: The saved source image resolves the OCR: the initializer is {3,4,5,6,7}, i starts at 0, and the condition is i < arr.length - 2. Length 5 makes the bound 3, so indices 0,1,2 print 3,4,5. Source option D is 345; the packet’s 3:45 is corrupted. println actually places each value on its own line.

evidence.quote: for(initialization; condition; update) executes initialization once, then condition → body → update → condition.
In Java, length belongs to each array; a traversal ending at arr.length-2 visits fewer elements than a full traversal.

choices.label: A
choices.explanation: All five values would require visiting indices 0 through 4, but this loop stops before index 3.

choices.label: B
choices.explanation: Four values would include index 3; the strict bound i<3 excludes that iteration.

choices.label: C
choices.explanation: Two values stop too early; index 2 also satisfies i<3 and prints 5.

choices.label: D
choices.explanation: The image shows 345 in D, resolving the packet typo; the actual println output uses separate lines.

reviews.answer_text: Conditional is a construct rather than a programming paradigm.
reviews.hint: Read CP02’s paradigm examples and its treatment of conditionals.
reviews.explanation: CP02 distinguishes procedural, object oriented and functional programming as ways of organizing computation. A conditional is a selection construct used inside programs rather than a separate paradigm in this classification. Thus the first three options name paradigms, while Conditional is the requested exception.

evidence.quote: A conditional statement is a construct, not a separate programming paradigm.

choices.label: A
choices.explanation: Procedural programming is a paradigm organizing operations into procedures, as described in CP02.

choices.label: B
choices.explanation: Object oriented programming is a paradigm organizing state and behavior in objects.

choices.label: C
choices.explanation: Functional programming is a paradigm emphasizing function evaluation, as described in CP02.

choices.label: D
choices.explanation: Conditional denotes a selection construct used within paradigms rather than a separate paradigm here.

reviews.answer_text: High-level languages are easier to read and write.
reviews.hint: Read CP03’s readability and portability distinction.
reviews.explanation: CP03 says high-level source is easier to read and often portable after recompilation when platform assumptions are avoided. Readability is the advantage stated in A. The note does not promise universally faster execution or greater hardware control, and platform specificity conflicts with the portability advantage rather than explaining it.

evidence.quote: High-level source is easier to read and often portable after recompilation, provided it avoids platform assumptions.

choices.label: A
choices.explanation: Easier source reading and writing is the abstraction benefit directly supported by CP03.

choices.label: B
choices.explanation: The note gives no universal speed or efficiency guarantee for high-level languages over low-level ones.

choices.label: C
choices.explanation: Direct hardware control is not the high-level readability advantage described by the note.

choices.label: D
choices.explanation: Platform specificity contradicts the potential source portability discussed in CP03.

reviews.answer_text: A method is a function associated with a class or object; no option states that precisely.
reviews.hint: Read CP17’s definition of method without adding return-value restrictions.
reviews.explanation: CP17 defines a method by its association with a class or object, and explicitly says methods can return values. A and C are loose pedagogical contrasts: ordinary functions also occur in object oriented programs, and methods also operate on data. Neither states the defining relationship accurately enough for a unique literal answer.

evidence.quote: A method is a function associated with a class or object; methods can return values.

choices.label: A
choices.explanation: This describes common teaching contexts, but functions also occur within object oriented programs, so the contrast is not exclusive.

choices.label: B
choices.explanation: Methods can return values, and void functions need not; this proposed distinction is false.

choices.label: C
choices.explanation: Object association is relevant, but methods also operate on data and ordinary functions can accept objects.

choices.label: D
choices.explanation: The note identifies a specific class/object association for methods, so the terms are not completely interchangeable.

reviews.answer_text: Find and fix errors in programs.
reviews.hint: Read CP32’s definition of debugging.
reviews.explanation: A bug is a defect, and CP32 says debugging locates and corrects it. Executing or writing programs describes broader activities; optimizing performance has a different primary aim. Debugging can involve running code and editing it, but those steps serve its specific purpose of finding and fixing errors.

evidence.quote: A bug is a defect; debugging locates and corrects it.

choices.label: A
choices.explanation: Execution can reveal defects, but simply running a program does not define debugging’s purpose.

choices.label: B
choices.explanation: Writing programs is implementation; debugging specifically investigates and corrects defects in them.

choices.label: C
choices.explanation: Performance optimization aims at efficiency, whereas debugging aims at correcting erroneous behavior.

choices.label: D
choices.explanation: Finding and fixing program errors directly matches CP32’s stated debugging purpose.

reviews.answer_text: Manage and track code changes over time.
reviews.hint: Read CP32 on version history, comparison and rollback.
reviews.explanation: CP32 says version control records changes and supports comparison and rollback. That is the management of code history described by C. A version-control system may support a development workflow, but it does not itself define the process of writing code, executing a program or optimizing its runtime performance.

evidence.quote: Version control records changes, supports comparison and rollback; documentation explains use, design and maintenance assumptions.

choices.label: A
choices.explanation: Developers write programs; version control records and manages the resulting revisions rather than creating program logic.

choices.label: B
choices.explanation: Execution is performed by the program’s runtime or machine, not by revision-history management.

choices.label: C
choices.explanation: Tracking revisions, comparing changes and rolling back are the version-control purposes explicitly stated in CP32.

choices.label: D
choices.explanation: Runtime performance optimization changes program efficiency; version control manages the history of such changes.

reviews.answer_text: Handle exceptional runtime conditions and recover where appropriate.
reviews.hint: Read CP32’s matching-handler rule and its limits.
reviews.explanation: CP32 describes exceptions as transferring control to a matching handler for exceptional conditions. This supports handling and possible recovery from runtime errors. It does not promise that every runtime fault is recoverable: arbitrary undefined behavior is specifically excluded. Input/output, optimization and declarations are not exception handling’s defining purpose.

evidence.quote: Exceptions transfer control to a matching handler for exceptional conditions; they do not make arbitrary undefined behavior recoverable.

choices.label: A
choices.explanation: Input/output may raise exceptional conditions, but performing I/O is not the defining purpose of exception handling.

choices.label: B
choices.explanation: Exception handling routes exceptional control flow rather than being a mechanism for performance optimization.

choices.label: C
choices.explanation: Matching handlers support handling and possible recovery from runtime exceptions, subject to the note’s stated limits.

choices.label: D
choices.explanation: Variables and constants are introduced by declarations, not by exception-handling control flow.

reviews.answer_text: No fully accurate distinction is offered; static types can be inferred.
reviews.hint: Read CP33’s distinction between type checking time and explicit annotations.
reviews.explanation: CP33 says static typing checks types before execution and can infer them, as with C++ auto. Dynamic typing checks operations using runtime values. B incorrectly makes explicit declarations mandatory for static typing. A gives an unsupported universal efficiency comparison, C confuses typing with paradigms, and D denies the real distinction. No option is fully correct.

evidence.quote: Static typing checks types before execution; type inference can still infer a static type, as with C++ auto.

choices.label: A
choices.explanation: Typing discipline alone does not establish a universal performance ranking; the note provides no such guarantee.

choices.label: B
choices.explanation: Static types can be inferred without explicit annotations, so its mandatory-declaration claim is false.

choices.label: C
choices.explanation: Typing discipline is not determined by whether a program uses objects or procedures.

choices.label: D
choices.explanation: The note distinguishes before-execution type checks from checks using runtime values; they are not interchangeable.

reviews.answer_text: Improve code readability and maintainability while preserving behavior.
reviews.hint: Read CP32’s definition of refactoring.
reviews.explanation: CP32 defines refactoring as improving internal structure while preserving observable behavior. Better readability and maintainability are the offered purpose that matches this definition. Performance tuning can accompany other changes, but is not the defining aim; runtime-error recovery belongs to exception handling rather than refactoring.

evidence.quote: Refactoring improves internal structure while preserving observable behavior.

choices.label: A
choices.explanation: Writing efficient code is broader than refactoring and does not specify preserving existing observable behavior.

choices.label: B
choices.explanation: Performance optimization has a different primary aim; refactoring concerns structure and maintainability.

choices.label: C
choices.explanation: Readability and maintainability improve through internal restructuring while observable program behavior is preserved.

choices.label: D
choices.explanation: Handling exceptional runtime conditions belongs to exception handling, not to refactoring’s structural purpose.

reviews.hint: Read CP08 on division when both operands are integers.
reviews.explanation: Both x and y have type int, so CP08’s integer-division rule applies: 10/3 truncates toward zero to 3. The stream prints that integer value. No floating conversion occurs before division, and no decimal formatting is requested, so neither a fractional quotient nor the literal output 3.0 is correct.

evidence.quote: Integer division truncates toward zero.

choices.label: A
choices.explanation: 3.33333 is a fractional approximation, but division of these int operands discards the fractional part.

choices.label: B
choices.explanation: Integer division gives 3, and cout prints the resulting integer without a decimal suffix.

choices.label: C
choices.explanation: 3.0 is not the printed representation of the int quotient in this code.

choices.label: D
choices.explanation: An indefinitely repeating decimal is not produced by integer division or this stream insertion.

reviews.answer_text: The integer value 2.
reviews.hint: Read CP07’s integer-literal division example.
reviews.explanation: Both literals in 5/2 are integers. CP07 states that the integer quotient is 2, and even assigning that already-computed quotient to double would not restore the lost fraction. The question asks for the expression’s result, so the integer 2 is the precise choice rather than a floating representation or fractional quotient.

evidence.quote: With int x=5,y=2, x/y is 2. Assigning that quotient to double gives 2.0, not 2.5.

choices.label: A
choices.explanation: Two integer operands produce the integer quotient 2 after truncating the fractional part.

choices.label: B
choices.explanation: 2.5 requires floating division, which these uncast integer literals do not perform.

choices.label: C
choices.explanation: 2.0 is a floating representation, while this expression itself has an integer result.

choices.label: D
choices.explanation: 2.25 follows neither integer truncation nor the ordinary mathematical quotient of five divided by two.

reviews.hint: Read CP07 on casting an operand before division.
reviews.explanation: static_cast<double>(x) converts 5 to a floating value before the division takes place. CP07 explicitly gives this form as yielding 2.5 when x=5 and y=2. The result therefore retains the fractional part; storing it in double does not first perform an integer quotient.

evidence.quote: static_cast<double>(x)/y performs floating division and yields 2.5.

choices.label: A
choices.explanation: Casting x before division prevents the integer truncation that would have produced 2.

choices.label: B
choices.explanation: The converted floating operand makes the quotient 2.5, which is stored and printed.

choices.label: C
choices.explanation: 2.0 would result from first computing the integer quotient and then converting it, unlike this code.

choices.label: D
choices.explanation: The floating quotient of 5 by 2 is 2.5, not 2.25.

reviews.answer_text: x becomes 7.
reviews.hint: Read CP08’s compound-update rules in execution order.
reviews.explanation: The initial x is 10. x+=5 updates it to 15; x/=2 then performs integer division because x is int, truncating 15/2 toward zero to 7. CP08 provides this exact sequence and result. The updates happen in order, so the second operation acts on 15 rather than the original 10.

evidence.quote: Starting x=10, x+=5 then x/=2 gives 7.

choices.label: A
choices.explanation: Five divides the original value by two and ignores the preceding addition of five.

choices.label: B
choices.explanation: The sequence gives 10+5=15, then integer 15/2=7.

choices.label: C
choices.explanation: Integer division truncates 7.5 to 7 rather than rounding it to 8.

choices.label: D
choices.explanation: Both compound assignments update x; it does not retain its initial value of 10.

reviews.hint: Read CP08’s integer-division truncation rule.
reviews.explanation: x and y are int variables with values 15 and 2. Their division therefore produces integer 7 before assignment to z, as CP08 specifies truncation toward zero. z also has type int and cout prints 7. None of the fractional or unrelated numerical options follows from this expression.

evidence.quote: Integer division truncates toward zero.

choices.label: A
choices.explanation: 7.5 is the mathematical fractional quotient, but these int operands produce an integer quotient.

choices.label: B
choices.explanation: The integer quotient 15/2 truncates toward zero to 7, which z stores and cout prints.

choices.label: C
choices.explanation: Three is not the quotient obtained by dividing the stated values 15 and 2.

choices.label: D
choices.explanation: 12.5 is neither the integer quotient nor the fractional quotient of 15 divided by 2.

reviews.answer_text: No offered final step: repair, rebuild and retest the program.
reviews.hint: Read CP32’s full syntax-repair sequence and CP35’s final-step wording warning.
reviews.explanation: The stem says final step. CP32 places inspection before repair and rebuilding, and CP35 explicitly says rebuilding and retesting complete the repair. D is useful inspection but is not the final step asked for. None of the remaining options supplies rebuild/retest, so the literal wording has no correct unique offered answer.

evidence.quote: Read the first useful compiler diagnostic, inspect nearby tokens and declarations, repair and rebuild; a debugger is useful after a runnable program exists.
CS0092 says final step while its useful option describes inspection; rebuilding and retesting complete the repair.

choices.label: A
choices.explanation: Rewriting the entire program is unnecessary and is not the final verification step stated in the note.

choices.label: B
choices.explanation: Ignoring an error leaves it unresolved and does not complete the repair process.

choices.label: C
choices.explanation: A debugger does not replace rebuilding and retesting syntax corrections as the final repair check.

choices.label: D
choices.explanation: Checking syntax is a sensible early diagnostic step, but it fails the stem’s literal final-step requirement.

reviews.answer_text: Literal code is invalid; repairing += and /= gives 2.
reviews.hint: Read CP08’s compound assignment syntax.
reviews.explanation: The packet separates + from = and / from =, so the displayed text does not contain the compound assignment operators defined in CP08. It has no literal numeric output. If those two tokenization errors are explicitly repaired, p starts at 8, becomes 16 and then 2. B is the intended repaired trace, not an output of the printed fragment.

evidence.quote: Starting p=q=n=8, p+=n gives 16 and p/=q gives 2.

choices.label: A
choices.explanation: 16 is only the intermediate value after a repaired += operation, before the repaired division.

choices.label: B
choices.explanation: Two is correct only after replacing the split token pairs with += and /=.

choices.label: C
choices.explanation: 24 does not follow the two updates, even under the explicitly repaired interpretation.

choices.label: D
choices.explanation: One ignores the addition before division and still cannot describe the invalid literal code.

reviews.answer_text: Linker combines objects; loader places the executable in memory.
reviews.hint: Separate the two roles described in CP04.
reviews.explanation: The question merges two distinct actions. CP04 assigns combining object files and libraries to the linker, but placing the executable and required components in memory to the loader. C fits puts together object files; D fits into memory for execution. Without specifying which action is intended, neither should be forced as a unique answer.

evidence.quote: The linker resolves external symbols and combines object files and libraries. The loader places an executable and required components in memory and starts it.

choices.label: A
choices.explanation: An editor changes source text, rather than combining objects or loading an executable into memory.

choices.label: B
choices.explanation: A debugger investigates execution and defects; it does not define either build/loading role asked here.

choices.label: C
choices.explanation: Linker fits the combining-object-files wording but not the separate memory-placement role.

choices.label: D
choices.explanation: Loader fits placement in memory for execution but not the combining-object-files wording.

reviews.answer_text: Only Graduating and fourth print; every offered output wrongly includes Year.
reviews.hint: Follow the goto target in CP15.
reviews.explanation: Entry at a prints Graduating, then goto b skips the c block entirely. b prints lowercase fourth and reaches the end. Year is unreachable under this fragment’s normal entry, and the literal spaces in the string constants also remain part of output. No offered sequence correctly describes these executed statements.

evidence.quote: entry at a prints Graduating fourth and reaches the end. Year is not printed.

choices.label: A
choices.explanation: Year is unreachable because goto b skips c, and Fourth also changes the printed capitalization.

choices.label: B
choices.explanation: It adds Year after fourth even though the fragment ends after printing at b.

choices.label: C
choices.explanation: It starts with unreachable Year and reverses the actual control-flow order.

reviews.answer_text: = assigns a value; == compares values for equality.
reviews.hint: Read CP06 assignment and CP10 equality/truth conversion together.
reviews.explanation: CP06 describes assignment as replacing a variable’s value; CP10 describes equality as a value test. Confusing them can change state instead of testing it. In C++ a numeric assigned result can also convert to a condition, allowing an unintended assignment to alter control flow.

evidence.quote: later assignment replaces a value.
Relational and equality operators test values; && and || combine truth values; ! negates. In C++, zero converts to false and a nonzero number to true.

reviews.answer_text: while tests first; do-while runs once before testing. Use do-while for a mandatory first menu/input attempt.
reviews.hint: Read CP14’s pre-test and post-test mechanics.
reviews.explanation: CP14 allows a while body to execute zero times because its condition is checked first. A do-while body executes before its first check, making it suitable for a menu or input attempt that must happen at least once.

evidence.quote: while(condition) checks before each body execution and may run zero times. do {body;} while(condition); runs the body once before checking; it repeats while the condition remains true. Use it when a menu or input attempt must occur at least once.

reviews.answer_text: Index 5 is out of bounds: Java throws; C++ access has undefined behavior.
reviews.hint: Read CP22’s zero-based bounds and language-specific consequences.
reviews.explanation: Five elements occupy indices 0 through 4, so array[5] is outside the array. CP22 distinguishes Java’s bounds exception from C++ undefined behavior; an adjacent-memory value must not be guessed. The question does not specify a language, so both consequences are stated.

evidence.quote: Java checks bounds and throws ArrayIndexOutOfBoundsException. Do not predict a C++ out-of-range value from nearby memory.
a[4] is outside the array; accessing it has undefined behavior.

reviews.answer_text: Functions decompose named tasks, enable reuse, reduce duplication and simplify understanding/testing.
reviews.hint: Read CP17’s function and reusable-module purpose.
reviews.explanation: CP17 defines a function as grouping a named task and explains that reuse reduces duplication while independent functions are easier to understand and test. Decomposition localizes responsibilities and supports maintenance through those clearer units.

evidence.quote: Reuse reduces duplication; independent functions are easier to understand and test.

reviews.answer_text: C++ value parameters copy; reference parameters alias caller variables. Java passes copied values, including references.
reviews.hint: Read CP18’s value, alias and copied-reference distinctions.
reviews.explanation: CP18 makes a value parameter a separate initialized object, while int& aliases the caller variable and can change it directly. Passing a pointer copies an address and can change its target without rebinding the caller’s pointer. Java copies object references by value.

evidence.quote: A C++ value parameter is a separate object initialized from the argument.
An int& parameter aliases the caller variable, so swap(int& a,int& b) changes both originals.
Java always passes by value, including a copy of an object reference; it does not pass caller variables by reference.

reviews.answer_text: Literal code is invalid; the conventional repaired trace leaves a=6, b=7, c=4.
reviews.hint: Read CP11’s conditional/comma rule and CP34’s documented syntax defects.
reviews.explanation: Int and Cout have incorrect case, smart quotes are not ordinary string delimiters, and semicolons cannot separate the two subexpressions inside each branch. After explicitly repairing those defects to comma expressions, x>y is false, b decrements to 7 and c receives y=4 while a stays 6. D names those intended values, but the first literal also lacks =.

evidence.quote: c=(x>y ? (a--,x) : (b--,y)) takes the false branch. b becomes 7, c receives 4 and a remains 6.
NS0301 needs Int/Cout case, quotes and comma-expression punctuation repaired.

choices.label: A
choices.explanation: The repaired false branch decrements b only to 7, not to 5.

choices.label: B
choices.explanation: The branch yields y=4 to c, not 5, even after all necessary syntax repairs.

choices.label: C
choices.explanation: The false branch does not change a, and it leaves b=7 and c=4.

choices.label: D
choices.explanation: These are the repaired variable values; the literal malformed program has no such output and its first string lacks =.

reviews.answer_text: A high-level language, with portability constraints checked.
reviews.hint: Read CP03’s readability, recompilation and platform-assumption rules.
reviews.explanation: CP03 says high-level source is easier to read and often portable after recompilation if platform assumptions are avoided. That fits rapid development of a large program and a portable result better than instruction-set-dependent machine or assembly code. Portability remains conditional on the target environment; the answer is a preference, not an unconditional guarantee.

evidence.quote: High-level source is easier to read and often portable after recompilation, provided it avoids platform assumptions.
Machine and assembly code depend on an instruction set.

choices.label: A
choices.explanation: Low-level code retains instruction-set details and does not best match the stated readability/development and portability goals.

choices.label: B
choices.explanation: Machine-level code depends directly on the instruction set, opposing the requested portable-source preference.

choices.label: C
choices.explanation: High-level source offers the note’s readability and conditional portability advantages for the stated scenario.

choices.label: D
choices.explanation: Assembly depends on the instruction set and is not the preferred abstraction for these development goals.

reviews.answer_text: delete is a reserved keyword.
reviews.hint: Read CP05’s permitted identifier characters and keyword exclusion.
reviews.explanation: CP05 directly identifies delete as a C++ keyword, which cannot be used as an ordinary identifier. for_cpp is not the keyword for, and jan2025 and Hello use letters followed only by permitted letters or digits. Unlike the earlier dotted extraction, this packet prints jan2025 without an invalid punctuation prefix.

evidence.quote: Do not use a keyword. C++ is case sensitive: exitExam and ExitExam differ; delete and float are keywords, but FLOAT is a legal identifier.

choices.label: A
choices.explanation: delete is a reserved C++ keyword and therefore invalid as an ordinary identifier.

choices.label: B
choices.explanation: for_cpp is a distinct permitted name containing letters and underscore, rather than the keyword for.

choices.label: C
choices.explanation: jan2025 begins with a letter and contains only permitted letters and trailing digits.

choices.label: D
choices.explanation: Hello contains permitted letters and is not a reserved keyword identified by the question.

reviews.answer_text: Overloads share a name and differ in their parameter lists.
reviews.hint: Read CP19’s overload signature rule.
reviews.explanation: CP19 requires a shared name with differences in parameter count or types/order. A states that relationship. Return type alone does not distinguish overloads, and neither different return types nor equal parameter counts are mandatory. Thus the other statements either deny supported overloading or impose restrictions contradicted by the note.

evidence.quote: Overloads share a name but differ in parameter count or types/order. Return type alone cannot distinguish them.

choices.label: A
choices.explanation: This states the shared-name and differing-parameter-list relationship required by CP19.

choices.label: B
choices.explanation: CP19 explicitly describes supported C++ function overloading, contradicting this blanket denial.

choices.label: C
choices.explanation: Different return types are not required and return type alone cannot distinguish overloads.

choices.label: D
choices.explanation: Parameter count may differ between overloads, so equal counts are not mandatory.

reviews.answer_text: UPS is normally protective, but “cannot affect” is absolute
reviews.hint: Read Physical protection and resilient design and distinguish definitions from possible effects.
reviews.explanation: Heat, humidity and electrical surges can harm operation. A properly functioning UPS normally protects against power problems, making D the likely intended contrast. However SEC11 explicitly permits UPS installation/battery hazards. Consequently none of these devices or conditions is categorically incapable of affecting operation, and the literal absolute question has no unconditional unique answer.

evidence.quote: A UPS supplies temporary conditioned power; it is normally protective, but faulty installation/battery failure can itself be hazardous.

choices.label: A
choices.explanation: An improperly placed heater can expose equipment to harmful heat.

choices.label: B
choices.explanation: Humidity is explicitly among the environmental conditions equipment must be protected against.

choices.label: C
choices.explanation: Lightning can cause electrical surges, a physical hazard addressed by protective design.

choices.label: D
choices.explanation: A working UPS is protective, but faulty installation or battery failure can itself affect system operation.

reviews.answer_text: Trojan
reviews.hint: Read Malware: propagation, disguise and payload and distinguish definitions from possible effects.
reviews.explanation: The defining clue is apparent legitimacy hiding malicious behavior. SEC04 assigns that disguise property to a Trojan. Malware is the broad umbrella, while viruses and worms are distinguished by replication mechanisms. Because the stem asks what best describes the program, Trojan is more specific than the umbrella term and requires no unmentioned replication behavior.

evidence.quote: A Trojan disguises malicious behavior as something useful and does not require self-replication.

choices.label: A
choices.explanation: A Trojan presents useful or legitimate behavior as cover for concealed malicious actions.

choices.label: B
choices.explanation: Malware is the broad umbrella and does not specifically capture the deceptive legitimate appearance asked for.

choices.label: C
choices.explanation: A virus is defined by attaching to a host and replicating, neither of which the stem specifies.

choices.label: D
choices.explanation: A worm independently replicates; that is different from the concealed malicious disguise described.

reviews.answer_text: Keylogger
reviews.hint: Read Malware: propagation, disguise and payload and distinguish definitions from possible effects.
reviews.explanation: SEC04 directly assigns keystroke recording to a keylogger. Recording every entered character can capture passwords and other secrets typed by the user. Rootkits hide malicious presence, worms replicate independently and Trojans conceal malicious behavior under useful appearances; none of those names specifically denotes keystroke collection.

evidence.quote: Spyware monitors users; a keylogger records keystrokes.

choices.label: A
choices.explanation: A rootkit hides malicious presence or privileged activity; keystroke capture is not its defining function.

choices.label: B
choices.explanation: Worms are defined by independent replication, not by collecting typed information.

choices.label: C
choices.explanation: A keylogger records keystrokes and can capture the sensitive values entered through the keyboard.

choices.label: D
choices.explanation: A Trojan describes deceptive packaging; it does not specifically name the keystroke-recording function.

reviews.answer_text: Intrusion detection system
reviews.hint: Read Detection, prevention and diagnostic measures and distinguish definitions from possible effects.
reviews.explanation: The stem describes observing traffic and alerting on suspicious patterns rather than enforcing a block. SEC24 defines that as an IDS role. Antivirus focuses on malicious software, a firewall enforces traffic policy and a router forwards packets. A product can combine functions, but detection/alerting is the specific function requested.

evidence.quote: An IDS observes and alerts; an IPS can enforce blocking, usually inline.

choices.label: A
choices.explanation: Antivirus targets malicious software; it is not the generic traffic-pattern detection system defined by the stem.

choices.label: B
choices.explanation: An IDS observes activity and alerts personnel about suspected intrusion patterns.

choices.label: C
choices.explanation: A firewall’s defining role is traffic-policy enforcement rather than the stated intrusion-alerting function.

choices.label: D
choices.explanation: A router forwards packets between networks and is not defined by suspicious-pattern alerting.

reviews.answer_text: Ordinary IP fragmentation is not itself an attack; SYN flooding is traffic-based
reviews.hint: Read DoS, wireless attacks and layer-specific defenses and distinguish definitions from possible effects.
reviews.explanation: SYN flooding uses network traffic to consume handshake state, so D’s denial is false. B literally calls IP fragmentation an attack, although fragmentation is an ordinary IP operation; SEC06 instead identifies fragment floods as abuse. DNS/NXDOMAIN floods can exhaust resolver resources, including in distributed attacks. If B were repaired to “fragmentation flood,” only D would be false, but that is not its wording.

evidence.quote: A SYN flood leaves many incomplete TCP handshakes occupying state.

choices.label: A
choices.explanation: NXDOMAIN query flooding can be used in distributed denial-of-service against resolver capacity.

choices.label: B
choices.explanation: Ordinary IP fragmentation is a protocol operation; fragment flooding or abusive reassembly traffic is the attack.

choices.label: C
choices.explanation: DNS flooding stresses query capacity through traffic, consistent with a traffic-based denial-of-service attack.

choices.label: D
choices.explanation: SYN flooding sends connection attempts that occupy TCP state, so denying its traffic-based nature is false.

reviews.answer_text: Strong-star permits writes only at the matching level
reviews.hint: Read Confidentiality and integrity models and distinguish definitions from possible effects.
reviews.explanation: SEC10 separates the properties: simple security is no read up, star is no write down and strong-star restricts writing to the same level. C correctly names the strong-star condition. A and D exchange the names of the simple and star properties, while B states no write up, contrary to Bell–LaPadula’s confidentiality direction.

evidence.quote: The strong-star variant permits writing only at the same level.

choices.label: A
choices.explanation: No read up is the simple-security rule, not the star property.

choices.label: B
choices.explanation: Bell–LaPadula prohibits writing down; this option instead asserts no write up and allows downward disclosure.

choices.label: C
choices.explanation: Strong-star permits writes only to objects at the subject’s matching level.

choices.label: D
choices.explanation: No write down is the star rule, not the simple-security rule.

reviews.answer_text: Missing bounds checks permit overflow; the other claims lack needed scope
reviews.hint: Read Memory safety and secure input handling and distinguish definitions from possible effects.
reviews.explanation: D states the clear underlying defect: absent bounds checks can leave an overflow bug. A describes one possible injected-code exploit, but not every overflow places executable instructions in the excess data. B broadly attributes vulnerability to old OS families without identifying a vulnerable component/version. The singular true-statement question therefore needs qualifiers before A/B/C can be judged as a unique full selection.

evidence.quote: A buffer overflow writes beyond allocated bounds and can corrupt data or control information; code execution is a possible consequence, not its definition or an inevitable outcome.

choices.label: A
choices.explanation: Some exploits inject instructions, but overflow can corrupt data/control information without injecting executable payload bytes.

choices.label: B
choices.explanation: Particular old components can be vulnerable, but the note does not establish a universal OS-family/version claim.

choices.label: C
choices.explanation: All would require the unqualified exploit and OS claims to be accepted; the stem supplies no such scope.

choices.label: D
choices.explanation: Incomplete length/index bounds checks can leave writes beyond the allocated buffer.

reviews.answer_text: Configure access limits by protocol and port
reviews.hint: Read Firewalls and protected boundaries and distinguish definitions from possible effects.
reviews.explanation: SEC23 explicitly gives protocol/port matching as a firewall function. It also describes bypass paths, insiders and infected removable media as limits, so firewall deployment does not guarantee all hijacking, malware or same-segment attacks are prevented. C is the configurable capability supported without those absolute guarantees.

evidence.quote: Stateless packet filtering matches headers such as source/destination, protocol and ports.

choices.label: A
choices.explanation: A firewall does not universally prevent every session hijack, especially traffic outside its inspected or enforced paths.

choices.label: B
choices.explanation: Malware can arrive through bypass paths or permitted traffic; a firewall cannot guarantee excluding all malicious code.

choices.label: C
choices.explanation: Protocol and port fields can be matched in traffic-policy rules to restrict access.

choices.label: D
choices.explanation: An attacker sharing an internal segment may bypass the firewall’s traffic path; detection/prevention is not guaranteed.

reviews.answer_text: Behavioral characteristics: voice/handwriting/typing patterns
reviews.hint: Read Identification, authentication and factors and distinguish definitions from possible effects.
reviews.explanation: SEC07 distinguishes knowledge, possession and inherence, and recognizes behavioral biometrics under the textbook “does” category. A matches that classification, including handwriting and typing rhythm. The remaining options exchange possession and biometrics or call a possessed token knowledge. Voice-pattern recognition is biometric behavior/characteristic recognition, not possession of an external object.

evidence.quote: Behavioral biometrics include typing rhythm or handwriting; some textbooks call these “something one does.”

choices.label: A
choices.explanation: The examples describe biometric behavior/patterns consistent with the textbook something-one-does category.

choices.label: B
choices.explanation: Fingerprints, retina and face are body characteristics, not possessed token/card objects.

choices.label: C
choices.explanation: Keycards, smart cards and physical keys are possession factors, not inherent body characteristics.

choices.label: D
choices.explanation: Possessing a token is a possession factor; knowledge means a secret such as a password or PIN.

reviews.answer_text: HTTPS does not fix buffer overflows
reviews.hint: Read DoS, wireless attacks and layer-specific defenses and distinguish definitions from possible effects.
reviews.explanation: SEC06 matches protections to the attacked layer: authenticated IPsec can resist IP impersonation, DNSSEC authenticates DNS data and TLS protects application transport against interception/tampering. HTTPS is HTTP over TLS; it cannot make an unsafe server memory copy bounds-safe. Thus D is the mismatched attack/defense pairing, without treating the other mechanisms as unconditional guarantees.

evidence.quote: HTTPS cannot fix an unsafe memory copy in a server.

choices.label: A
choices.explanation: Authenticated IPsec can resist IP impersonation, so this is a relevant defense pairing.

choices.label: B
choices.explanation: TLS protects authenticated transport against interception/tampering relevant to session hijacking, under correct endpoint validation.

choices.label: C
choices.explanation: DNSSEC authenticates DNS data and is relevant to resisting false cached DNS answers.

choices.label: D
choices.explanation: HTTPS protects the channel but does not repair writes beyond a server buffer’s allocated bounds.

reviews.answer_text: Spyware-like monitoring capability
reviews.hint: Read Malware: propagation, disguise and payload and distinguish definitions from possible effects.
reviews.explanation: The capability described is monitoring user activity, which SEC04 associates with spyware. Ransomware locks or encrypts for extortion, worms replicate and adware displays unwanted advertisements. SEC05 adds an important context limit: monitoring with authorization is not automatically an attack. A matches the functionality, but the child-monitoring use alone does not establish malicious intent.

evidence.quote: Spyware monitors users; a keylogger records keystrokes.

choices.label: A
choices.explanation: Spyware’s monitoring function matches collection of user activity, subject to the authorization caveat.

choices.label: B
choices.explanation: Ransomware denies access and extorts payment rather than primarily monitoring user activity.

choices.label: C
choices.explanation: A worm independently replicates; monitoring is not the defining capability.

choices.label: D
choices.explanation: Adware primarily displays unwanted advertisements, although some packages may also track activity.

reviews.answer_text: ARP spoofing
reviews.hint: Read Social engineering, spoofing and sessions and distinguish definitions from possible effects.
reviews.explanation: ARP spoofing targets the local mapping between IPv4 and link-layer MAC addresses, making A the data-link-oriented attack among these choices. DNS spoofing targets name resolution rather than local link associations, and SYN flooding abuses TCP handshake state. D incorrectly includes DNS spoofing in the data-link category.

evidence.quote: ARP spoofing poisons local IPv4-to-MAC associations; DNS spoofing/cache poisoning supplies false name resolutions; IP spoofing falsifies a source address.

choices.label: A
choices.explanation: ARP spoofing poisons the local IPv4-to-MAC mapping at the network/link addressing boundary.

choices.label: B
choices.explanation: DNS spoofing falsifies name-resolution data rather than manipulating the local data-link association.

choices.label: C
choices.explanation: The likely SYN-flood reference concerns TCP handshake state at transport scope, not link addressing.

choices.label: D
choices.explanation: This includes DNS spoofing, which is not a data-link mapping attack.

reviews.answer_text: A virus needs a host; a worm replicates independently
reviews.hint: Read Malware: propagation, disguise and payload and distinguish definitions from possible effects.
reviews.explanation: SEC04 distinguishes the replication mechanisms rather than universal speed or user-interaction rules. A virus attaches to a host program/document and spreads when that infected host executes. A worm replicates independently. C gives that direction correctly; the other options reverse it or impose unsupported absolute speed/action comparisons.

evidence.quote: A virus replicates by attaching to a host program or document; execution of the infected host spreads it. A worm replicates independently, commonly across networks.

choices.label: A
choices.explanation: This reverses the host dependency: viruses attach to hosts, whereas worms replicate independently.

choices.label: B
choices.explanation: The note does not define worms by requiring user action; independent replication is their defining distinction.

choices.label: C
choices.explanation: Viruses depend on infected host execution while worms replicate independently.

choices.label: D
choices.explanation: There is no universal worm-versus-virus spreading-speed ranking in the note.

reviews.answer_text: Evaluator
reviews.hint: Read Independent evaluation, certification and assurance and distinguish definitions from possible effects.
reviews.explanation: SEC29 assigns technical examination of developer evidence, testing and vulnerability analysis against Security Target claims to evaluators. The certification body oversees/reviews evaluation and issues the certification decision; sponsors commission the work and developers supply the product/evidence. A therefore names the party performing the actual technical evaluation rather than those adjacent roles.

evidence.quote: Evaluators examine developer evidence, test and analyze vulnerabilities against those claims.

choices.label: A
choices.explanation: Evaluators review developer evidence and perform tests/analysis against the stated functional and assurance claims.

choices.label: B
choices.explanation: The certifier oversees/reviews evaluation and issues the certification decision rather than being the named technical evaluator.

choices.label: C
choices.explanation: The sponsor commissions the work; that role does not itself perform the technical evaluation.

choices.label: D
choices.explanation: The developer supplies the product and supporting evidence for independent examination.

reviews.answer_text: Masquerade
reviews.hint: Read Social engineering, spoofing and sessions and distinguish definitions from possible effects.
reviews.explanation: Negesa presents himself as Dereje so the registrar attributes the message to the wrong person. That is an identity impersonation, defined as masquerade in SEC05. The scenario does not state that service is denied, an existing message is modified, or a previously valid message is replayed; those mechanisms should not be inferred.

evidence.quote: Masquerade claims another identity.

choices.label: A
choices.explanation: No service interruption or resource exhaustion is described; the harm is false identity attribution.

choices.label: B
choices.explanation: The stem does not describe altering an existing message; it describes claiming another sender’s identity.

choices.label: C
choices.explanation: Negesa claims Dereje’s identity, directly matching masquerade.

choices.label: D
choices.explanation: No captured old valid message is reused, so replay is not established.

reviews.answer_text: Packet filters, stateful firewalls and NGFWs can filter ports/protocols
reviews.hint: Read Firewalls and protected boundaries and distinguish definitions from possible effects.
reviews.explanation: SEC23 explicitly warns that port-filtering capability is not exclusive to stateless packet filtering. Packet filters inspect headers, and stateful/next-generation firewalls also enforce such fields while adding context or inspection. Thus A, C and D satisfy the capability question. A proxy primarily terminates/relays application exchanges; its exact port-policy implementation is not specified here.

evidence.quote: Stateful and next-generation devices also filter ports, so a stem asking merely which device “can filter ports” is nonexclusive.

choices.label: A
choices.explanation: Stateless packet filtering directly matches protocol and port header fields.

choices.label: B
choices.explanation: A proxy can mediate application connections, but its specific incoming header-filter capability depends on implementation.

choices.label: C
choices.explanation: Stateful inspection adds connection context without losing port/protocol filtering capability.

choices.label: D
choices.explanation: Next-generation firewalls also filter ports/protocols and add further inspection capabilities.

reviews.answer_text: A genuine one-time pad provides stronger secrecy than repeated-key Vigenère
reviews.hint: Read Transposition and one-time pads and distinguish definitions from possible effects.
reviews.explanation: A genuine one-time pad meets strict randomness, secrecy, length and nonreuse conditions, giving perfect secrecy unlike repeated-key Vigenère. Symmetric encryption is not inherently slower than asymmetric encryption. Hill’s known-plaintext linear weakness does not establish easy brute-force search for every matrix size. Therefore A is supported, subject to all one-time-pad conditions.

evidence.quote: A one-time pad XORs bits with an independent uniformly random secret key at least as long as the message and never reused. Its perfect secrecy depends on every condition.

choices.label: A
choices.explanation: A properly implemented one-time pad has perfect secrecy, whereas repeated-key Vigenère leaks periodic structure.

choices.label: B
choices.explanation: SEC16 describes symmetric encryption as efficient for bulk data; the proposed universal slowdown is unsupported.

choices.label: C
choices.explanation: Hill is vulnerable to sufficient known plaintext, but that is not the same as universally easy brute-force search.

choices.label: D
choices.explanation: The symmetric-speed and blanket Hill brute-force claims are not supported, so all cannot hold.

reviews.answer_text: Mandatory Access Control
reviews.hint: Read Access control and least privilege and distinguish definitions from possible effects.
reviews.explanation: Security labels and clearances identify the mandatory policy mechanism in SEC09, elaborated for multilevel databases in SEC32. Owners cannot override that centrally enforced label policy. RBAC assigns role permissions and DAC allows owner grants; generic ABAC can evaluate attributes, but the specified clearance/classification mechanism is the named mandatory control model.

evidence.quote: mandatory control enforces labels and policy that ordinary owners cannot override.

choices.label: A
choices.explanation: Mandatory control compares classifications/clearances under a policy ordinary owners cannot override.

choices.label: B
choices.explanation: ABAC evaluates general attributes; the named security-label/clearance mechanism specifically identifies mandatory control.

choices.label: C
choices.explanation: DAC allows owners to grant permissions rather than enforcing nonoverridable classification labels.

choices.label: D
choices.explanation: RBAC bases permissions on roles and user-role assignments rather than security-label clearance comparisons.

reviews.answer_text: DNS hijacking/spoofed resolution
reviews.hint: Read Social engineering, spoofing and sessions and distinguish definitions from possible effects.
reviews.explanation: Wrong name-to-address answers redirecting users match falsified DNS resolution, described as spoofing/cache poisoning in SEC05 and called hijacking in D. DNS and NXDOMAIN floods instead stress query capacity; they need not provide a malicious replacement destination. No SNMP reflection mechanism is described by the stem.

evidence.quote: DNS spoofing/cache poisoning supplies false name resolutions

choices.label: A
choices.explanation: DNS flooding exhausts query-processing capacity rather than specifically supplying false destination records.

choices.label: B
choices.explanation: NXDOMAIN attacks generate nonexistent-name queries to stress resolvers, not the false successful answers described.

choices.label: C
choices.explanation: The stem describes DNS answer manipulation, not reflected traffic using a different management protocol.

choices.label: D
choices.explanation: Hijacking DNS resolution redirects a name to an attacker-controlled destination through false resolution data.

reviews.answer_text: Input fuzzing is testing, not an injection-attack category
reviews.hint: Read SQL injection, XSS and request forgery and distinguish definitions from possible effects.
reviews.explanation: SEC26 directly distinguishes fuzzing from injection: fuzzing varies unexpected inputs to discover defects. SQL injection changes SQL syntax and XSS introduces attacker-controlled script into a browser context. Command injection likewise names unsafe interpretation of input as commands. Fuzzing may discover those defects but does not itself identify that attack mechanism.

evidence.quote: Fuzzing sends unexpected inputs to discover faults; it is a testing technique, not itself a category of injection.

choices.label: A
choices.explanation: XSS injects attacker-controlled script/content into a browser execution context, so it is an injection-type attack.

choices.label: B
choices.explanation: Input fuzzing is a technique for finding faults with varied unexpected inputs, not an injection category.

choices.label: C
choices.explanation: SQL injection explicitly alters query syntax through unsafe handling of untrusted values.

choices.label: D
choices.explanation: Command injection names untrusted input interpreted as executable commands rather than merely a testing technique.

reviews.answer_text: D fits verification by the user only if “prove” means verify the host’s proof
reviews.hint: Read Identification, authentication and factors and distinguish the mechanism from general consequences.
reviews.explanation: The note defines the arrow as prover to verifier. A–C describe a different entity than the indicated prover would authenticate. D could intend the user verifying the host’s identity, but literally says the user proves the machine’s identity, reversing who supplies proof.
