Therefore a unique answer requires an IPv4 assumption; neither version supports reassembly by intermediate routers as claimed in C or D.

evidence.quote: IPv4 sources and routers may fragment when allowed; reassembly occurs at the destination.

choices.label: A
choices.explanation: Source-only fragmentation and destination reassembly matches IPv6; it omits permitted IPv4 router fragmentation.

choices.label: B
choices.explanation: This matches IPv4 when fragmentation is permitted, but is not true of IPv6 router behavior.

choices.label: C
choices.explanation: Neither cited IP fragmentation rule places reassembly at intermediate routers.

choices.label: D
choices.explanation: Destination reassembly is required; the additional router reassembly claim is unsupported for either version.

choices.label: E
choices.explanation: Both version-specific rules support fragmentation and reassembly, although the allowed fragmenting nodes differ.

reviews.answer_text: Both IP addresses and both port numbers
reviews.hint: Read Transport choice, ports and connections, focusing on the distinction in the question.
reviews.explanation: All packets under discussion are already TCP, so their protocol identity is common. Distinguishing arbitrary simultaneous connections needs the endpoint four-tuple: source IP, destination IP, source port and destination port. Addresses alone cannot distinguish separate applications between the same hosts; ports alone can repeat between different hosts. C supplies all four required fields.

evidence.quote: A TCP connection is identified by source/destination IP and source/destination port, with TCP understood.

choices.label: A
choices.explanation: Ports and protocol can repeat between different host pairs, so this omits necessary IP addresses.

choices.label: B
choices.explanation: Two hosts can have several simultaneous TCP connections; addresses and TCP protocol alone do not distinguish them.

choices.label: C
choices.explanation: The source/destination IP addresses and source/destination ports form the TCP connection four-tuple.

choices.label: D
choices.explanation: An IP-address pair cannot distinguish multiple connections between the same two hosts.

choices.label: E
choices.explanation: The same source/destination port pair can be used with different IP-address endpoints.

choices.label: F
choices.explanation: Every connection in the stem uses TCP, so protocol number alone distinguishes none of them.

reviews.answer_text: Travel distance is not an explicit channel-capacity formula variable
reviews.hint: Read Bit rate, baud and channel capacity and apply its stated assumptions.
reviews.explanation: NET05 gives Nyquist in terms of bandwidth and signal states, and Shannon in terms of bandwidth and signal-to-noise ratio. Distance is not an independent variable in those simplified capacity formulas, so A is the intended comparison. It can still affect practical achievable rate through attenuation and delay. The image confirms travel distance despite noise in another extracted option.

evidence.quote: Distance affects attenuation, delay and often achievable rate, but is not a separate variable in these simplified capacity formulas.

choices.label: A
choices.explanation: Distance is absent as an independent variable in the simplified formulas, although it affects real links indirectly.

choices.label: B
choices.explanation: The number of signal levels appears explicitly in Nyquist through log2(M).

choices.label: C
choices.explanation: Available bandwidth directly appears as B in both Nyquist and Shannon capacity expressions.

choices.label: D
choices.explanation: Noise affects signal-to-noise ratio and therefore the Shannon capacity limit.

reviews.hint: Read Find subnet bounds and usable hosts and apply its stated assumptions.
reviews.explanation: A /21 groups eight third-octet values, here 128–135. The network is 172.17.128.0 and its broadcast is 172.17.135.255. B sets every host bit to one and cannot be assigned to an ordinary host. The other choices are inside the usable range; ending in .0 or .255 alone does not make an address reserved.

choices.label: A
choices.explanation: 172.17.128.1 is one above the network boundary and is a valid usable host.

choices.label: B
choices.explanation: 172.17.135.255 sets all eleven host bits to one and is the subnet broadcast address.

choices.label: C
choices.explanation: 172.17.135.0 is inside the /21 block; its host bits are not all zero or all one.

choices.label: D
choices.explanation: 172.17.128.255 is an interior host; the .255 ending alone does not make it /21 broadcast.

reviews.answer_text: Switch-to-PC normally uses straight-through cable in legacy Ethernet
reviews.hint: Read Cables, wireless and connectors and apply its stated assumptions.
reviews.explanation: Under the legacy MDI/MDI-X convention, a switch port and PC have unlike roles and use straight-through cable. PCs and router Ethernet endpoints conventionally share the endpoint role, while two switches share the switch role, so those like-role links use crossover. Auto-MDI-X can remove the practical requirement; the question is testing the conventional cable-role distinction.

evidence.quote: Legacy Ethernet straight-through cables join unlike MDI/MDI-X roles; crossover joins like roles, such as PC–PC or switch–switch. Auto-MDI-X can remove that requirement.

choices.label: A
choices.explanation: A legacy router Ethernet endpoint and PC have like interface roles, so crossover is appropriate.

choices.label: B
choices.explanation: Two legacy switch ports have like roles and conventionally require crossover.

choices.label: C
choices.explanation: Switch and PC have unlike legacy interface roles and normally use straight-through cable.

choices.label: D
choices.explanation: Two PCs have like legacy interface roles; NET07 explicitly names PC–PC as a crossover example.

reviews.answer_text: Stop and retry after random backoff
reviews.hint: Read Access control and reliable-link procedures and apply its stated assumptions.
reviews.explanation: NET14 gives the collision sequence: detect, jam, stop and retry after random backoff. The jam indicates the collision itself, not that it has cleared. There is no router-coordinated clearance procedure or electrical clearance pulse in the stated rule. Therefore waiting for a delay and attempting transmission again is the supported host behavior.

evidence.quote: In legacy half-duplex Ethernet, CSMA/CD detects collision, sends a jam indication, stops, and retries after random backoff.

choices.label: A
choices.explanation: The defined procedure uses collision indication and backoff; it does not include a collision-cleared electrical pulse.

choices.label: B
choices.explanation: Ethernet collision recovery is performed by the hosts’ MAC procedure, not a router clearance signal.

choices.label: C
choices.explanation: A jam announces the collision; it does not certify that the shared medium is clear.

choices.label: D
choices.explanation: After stopping, hosts retry following random backoff, matching a delay before another transmission attempt.

reviews.answer_text: Switch ports separate collision domains
reviews.hint: Read Bridges, switches and access points and apply its stated assumptions.
reviews.explanation: NET10 says each switch port separates collision domains, whereas a half-duplex hub repeats traffic into one shared collision domain. Switches still flood broadcasts within their VLAN, and hubs do not inspect and filter destination frames. The note gives no universal switch-versus-hub processing-time advantage, so A is the supported claim.

evidence.quote: Each switch port separates collision domains; full-duplex point-to-point Ethernet has no collisions and does not use CSMA/CD.

choices.label: A
choices.explanation: Replacing a shared hub segment with separate switch ports divides the network into additional collision domains.

choices.label: B
choices.explanation: The note establishes no universal lower switch processing time; a hub simply repeats signals.

choices.label: C
choices.explanation: Switches flood broadcasts within the VLAN unless another control filters them.

choices.label: D
choices.explanation: Hubs repeat physical signals and neither learn MAC destinations nor filter frames.

reviews.answer_text: Flow control is not a primary network-layer duty
reviews.hint: Read OSI layers and encapsulation and apply its stated assumptions.
reviews.explanation: The network layer supplies logical addressing/routing and, for IPv4, fragmentation when permitted. Flow control instead protects a receiver in transport or hop-local link procedures, as NET14 and NET17 explain. Thus C is not a primary network-layer function in this layer model, without claiming that all control mechanisms belong exclusively to one layer.

evidence.quote: Logical addressing and routing

choices.label: A
choices.explanation: Routing is explicitly a main network-layer duty in the NET12 layer table.

choices.label: B
choices.explanation: Logical addressing is explicitly assigned to the network layer.

choices.label: C
choices.explanation: Receiver flow control is described at link and transport scope rather than as a primary network duty.

choices.label: D
choices.explanation: NET16 supports IPv4 fragmentation by sources and routers, a network-protocol function.

reviews.answer_text: Modem
reviews.hint: Read Routers, gateways and traffic controls and apply its stated assumptions.
reviews.explanation: The stem asks about conversion for a telephone-line carrier, which is modem modulation. NET11 separates this signal-conversion function from routing IP packets, switching link frames and applying firewall traffic policy. These functions can coexist in one appliance, but the functional component asked for remains the modem.

evidence.quote: A modem modulates outgoing and demodulates incoming carrier signals.

choices.label: A
choices.explanation: A modem modulates outgoing carrier signals and demodulates incoming ones, supplying the requested conversion.

choices.label: B
choices.explanation: A router selects next hops between networks; that role is distinct from telephone-carrier modulation.

choices.label: C
choices.explanation: A switch forwards link-layer frames and is not the component defined by carrier modulation.

choices.label: D
choices.explanation: A firewall applies security policy to traffic rather than converting data onto a telephone-line carrier.

reviews.answer_text: DHCP
reviews.hint: Read DNS, DHCP and address resolution and apply its stated assumptions.
reviews.explanation: NET20 assigns dynamic address-setting leases to DHCP, whose basic exchange is discover, offer, request and acknowledge. DNS instead resolves names to records. HTTP and FTP are application services for web exchanges and file transfer; neither is the automatic host-address lease protocol.

evidence.quote: DHCP dynamically leases IPv4 settings, commonly address, mask, gateway and DNS server.

choices.label: A
choices.explanation: HTTP provides web request/response semantics rather than automatic IP-address leases.

choices.label: B
choices.explanation: DNS resolves names into records, including addresses, but does not lease the host’s own address.

choices.label: C
choices.explanation: DHCP dynamically leases an IP address and related host-network configuration.

choices.label: D
choices.explanation: FTP transfers files; it does not provide the address-assignment exchange described.

reviews.answer_text: 255.255.255.0, the historical Class C default
reviews.hint: Read IPv4 notation and classful defaults and apply its stated assumptions.
reviews.explanation: In the classful convention requested, Class C has a /24 default. Twenty-four leading one bits give three full 255 octets followed by zero: 255.255.255.0. This is a historical default rather than a restriction that every modern address in that range must use /24; CIDR can specify another prefix.

evidence.quote: Historical classes use leading patterns: A 0 with /8, B 10 with /16, C 110 with /24; D 1110 is multicast and E 1111 reserved.

choices.label: A
choices.explanation: 255.0.0.0 is /8, the historical Class A default rather than Class C.

choices.label: B
choices.explanation: 255.255.0.0 is /16, the historical Class B default.

choices.label: C
choices.explanation: 255.255.255.0 is /24, matching the historical Class C default prefix.

choices.label: D
choices.explanation: 255.255.255.255 is /32, identifying one address rather than the Class C default network.

reviews.answer_text: 30 usable hosts
reviews.hint: Read Find subnet bounds and usable hosts and apply its stated assumptions.
reviews.explanation: The mask 255.255.255.224 has 27 one bits and five host bits. Five bits yield 32 total addresses; reserving the subnet identifier and directed broadcast leaves 30 assignable ordinary hosts. This is an ordinary broadcast-subnet calculation, so the special /31 point-to-point exception is not relevant.

evidence.quote: /27 gives 32 total and 30 usable, not 32 usable.

choices.label: A
choices.explanation: Eight does not equal the usable count from five host bits and two reserved addresses.

choices.label: B
choices.explanation: Sixteen is not the /27 usable-host count; this block has 32 total addresses.

choices.label: C
choices.explanation: A /27 has 32 total addresses and 30 ordinary assignable host addresses.

choices.label: D
choices.explanation: Sixty-two usable hosts requires six host bits, corresponding to /26 rather than /27.

reviews.answer_text: 16 subnets
reviews.hint: Read Borrow bits and choose a mask and apply its stated assumptions.
reviews.explanation: The question explicitly supplies a Class B parent, so use its historical /16. The given mask 255.255.240.0 is /20. Borrowing 20−16=4 bits yields 2^4=16 equal subnets under modern practice. The note says not to subtract two subnets; host capacity is a different calculation.

evidence.quote: To split parent /a into equal /p blocks, borrow b=p-a bits and obtain 2^b subnets.

choices.label: A
choices.explanation: Eight subnets would borrow three bits and produce /19 from a /16 parent.

choices.label: B
choices.explanation: The /20 mask borrows four bits from /16, yielding sixteen equal subnets.

choices.label: C
choices.explanation: Thirty-two subnets would borrow five bits and require /21 from the Class B parent.

choices.label: D
choices.explanation: Sixty-four subnets would borrow six bits and require /22 rather than /20.

reviews.hint: Read IPv4 notation and classful defaults and apply its stated assumptions.
reviews.explanation: The historical Class A default is /8. Eight leading mask ones fill only the first octet, giving 255.0.0.0. The other choices correspond to /16, /24 and /32; they can be explicit CIDR prefixes, but they are not the historical default asked for.

evidence.quote: Historical classes use leading patterns: A 0 with /8, B 10 with /16, C 110 with /24; D 1110 is multicast and E 1111 reserved.

choices.label: A
choices.explanation: 255.0.0.0 contains eight leading ones and is the historical Class A default.

choices.label: B
choices.explanation: 255.255.0.0 is /16, the historical default for Class B.

choices.label: C
choices.explanation: 255.255.255.0 is /24, the historical default for Class C.

choices.label: D
choices.explanation: 255.255.255.255 is /32 and describes one address, not the Class A default.

reviews.answer_text: 30 usable host addresses
reviews.hint: Read Find subnet bounds and usable hosts and apply its stated assumptions.
reviews.explanation: 224 in the final mask octet is 11100000. That yields /27 and h=5. Computing 2^5−2 gives 30 ordinary usable host addresses after network and directed-broadcast reservations. The distractors correspond to different host-bit counts; none changes the explicit mask in this question.

evidence.quote: For ordinary broadcast LANs let h=32-p. Total addresses=2^h; usable hosts=2^h-2, reserving network and directed broadcast.

choices.label: A
choices.explanation: Six usable hosts would use three host bits, normally /29 rather than /27.

choices.label: B
choices.explanation: Fourteen usable hosts would use four host bits, normally /28.

choices.label: C
choices.explanation: Five host bits give 32 addresses minus two reservations, yielding 30 usable hosts.

choices.label: D
choices.explanation: Sixty-two usable hosts would use six host bits and a /26 mask.

reviews.hint: Read IPv4 notation and classful defaults and apply its stated assumptions.
reviews.explanation: NET22 gives historical Class B a /16 default. The first sixteen mask bits are ones, producing 255.255.0.0. This answers the requested default-mask question; it does not imply that a modern Class B-range address cannot have a different explicit CIDR prefix.

evidence.quote: Historical classes use leading patterns: A 0 with /8, B 10 with /16, C 110 with /24; D 1110 is multicast and E 1111 reserved.

choices.label: A
choices.explanation: 255.0.0.0 is /8, the historical default for Class A.

choices.label: B
choices.explanation: 255.255.0.0 has sixteen leading ones and is the historical Class B default.

choices.label: C
choices.explanation: 255.255.255.0 is /24, the historical default for Class C.

choices.label: D
choices.explanation: 255.255.255.255 is /32, a single-address prefix rather than a Class B default.

reviews.answer_text: 30 host addresses per ordinary subnet
reviews.hint: Read Find subnet bounds and usable hosts and apply its stated assumptions.
reviews.explanation: The mask 255.255.255.224 is /27, leaving five host bits. A block therefore contains 32 addresses. Because the question asks addresses available to hosts, exclude its network and broadcast addresses, leaving 30. Treating all 32 as usable would confuse block size with conventional broadcast-LAN host capacity.

evidence.quote: /27 gives 32 total and 30 usable, not 32 usable.

choices.label: A
choices.explanation: Six usable addresses corresponds to /29, not the stated /27 mask.

choices.label: B
choices.explanation: Fourteen usable addresses corresponds to /28 and four host bits.

choices.label: C
choices.explanation: The /27 block has five host bits and 32−2=30 conventional usable addresses.

choices.label: D
choices.explanation: Sixty-two usable addresses would require /26 and six host bits.

reviews.answer_text: 4 subnets
reviews.hint: Read Borrow bits and choose a mask and apply its stated assumptions.
reviews.explanation: A historical Class C parent is /24. The supplied 255.255.255.192 mask is /26, borrowing two bits. Modern counting gives 2^2=4 equal subnets, not two: NET26 explicitly rejects subtracting two subnets under modern practice. Here the parent is given, unlike the under-specified standalone-prefix questions.

evidence.quote: To split parent /a into equal /p blocks, borrow b=p-a bits and obtain 2^b subnets.

choices.label: A
choices.explanation: Two would incorrectly exclude two subnets under an obsolete unstated convention; modern counting gives four.

choices.label: B
choices.explanation: Borrowing two bits from /24 to /26 produces four equal subnets.

choices.label: C
choices.explanation: Eight subnets requires borrowing three bits, producing /27 rather than /26.

choices.label: D
choices.explanation: Sixteen subnets requires four borrowed bits and a /28 prefix.

reviews.answer_text: 30 assignable host IP addresses
reviews.hint: Read Find subnet bounds and usable hosts and apply its stated assumptions.
reviews.explanation: With /27, 32−27=5 host bits produce 2^5=32 addresses. For an ordinary subnet, network and broadcast are reserved, so 30 can be assigned to hosts. The alternative values are usable-host counts for /28, /26 and /25, rather than the supplied /27.

evidence.quote: /27 gives 32 total and 30 usable, not 32 usable.

choices.label: A
choices.explanation: Fourteen usable hosts requires /28, leaving only four host bits.

choices.label: B
choices.explanation: A /27 leaves five host bits and therefore 30 assignable ordinary host addresses.

choices.label: C
choices.explanation: Sixty-two usable hosts is the /26 result, not /27.

choices.label: D
choices.explanation: 126 usable hosts requires /25 and seven host bits.

reviews.answer_text: 169.254.0.0/16 link-local/APIPA range
reviews.hint: Read Special ranges, private addresses and IPv6 and apply its stated assumptions.
reviews.explanation: NET23 assigns link-local/APIPA to 169.254.0.0/16, the range printed in C. That identifies the reserved overall block; the first and last /24 blocks are excluded from normal automatic selection. The private RFC1918 blocks and loopback block offered elsewhere have different purposes and are not the APIPA range.

evidence.quote: Link-local/APIPA uses 169.254.0.0/16, with edge /24 blocks excluded from normal automatic selection.

choices.label: A
choices.explanation: 10/8 is RFC1918 private space, not the link-local/APIPA allocation.

choices.label: B
choices.explanation: 127/8 is loopback for local protocol access, not automatic link-local addressing.

choices.label: C
choices.explanation: 169.254/16 is the APIPA block; normal automatic host selection excludes its edge /24 blocks.

choices.label: D
choices.explanation: 192.168/16 is RFC1918 private space rather than the APIPA block.

reviews.answer_text: DHCP
reviews.hint: Read DNS, DHCP and address resolution and apply its stated assumptions.
reviews.explanation: DHCP is the address-configuration service in NET20, dynamically leasing an address together with other settings. DNS resolves names rather than assigning a client’s host address. HTTP and FTP handle web exchanges and file transfers. Therefore B matches dynamic assignment rather than name resolution or application-data transfer.

evidence.quote: DHCP dynamically leases IPv4 settings, commonly address, mask, gateway and DNS server.

choices.label: A
choices.explanation: DNS resolves names to records and does not perform the dynamic lease assignment asked about.

choices.label: B
choices.explanation: DHCP dynamically leases host addresses and related network configuration.

choices.label: C
choices.explanation: HTTP provides web request/response exchanges rather than dynamic IP-address allocation.

choices.label: D
choices.explanation: FTP transfers files and is not a host-address lease protocol.

reviews.answer_text: Larger address space, 128-bit addresses and encryption support
reviews.hint: Read Special ranges, private addresses and IPv6 and apply its stated assumptions.
reviews.explanation: NET23 gives IPv6 128-bit addressing, implying a much larger address space than IPv4’s 32 bits. It also permits encryption support, while explicitly warning that IPv6 does not automatically encrypt traffic. These support A, B and D. The note provides no universal rule that IPv6 routes slower or is necessarily memory-intensive, so C is not established.

evidence.quote: Several choices saying larger address space, 128 bits and encryption support can all be true; the requested comparison must be specific.

choices.label: A
choices.explanation: A 128-bit address space can represent far more addresses than IPv4’s 32-bit space.

choices.label: B
choices.explanation: NET23 explicitly states that IPv6 addresses contain 128 bits.

choices.label: C
choices.explanation: The note establishes no universal slower-routing or memory-cost conclusion merely from choosing IPv6.

choices.label: D
choices.explanation: Encryption is supported, but IPv6 does not automatically encrypt traffic and this is not unique to IPv6.

reviews.answer_text: Loopback is local self-reference, not an external address
reviews.hint: Read Special ranges, private addresses and IPv6 and apply its stated assumptions.
reviews.explanation: Loopback lets a host address itself and access local services through networking protocols without an external link. NET23 identifies 127/8 and common 127.0.0.1 for that purpose. Describing it as external contradicts this local scope, whereas the remaining choices all describe supported loopback uses or notation.

evidence.quote: 127.0.0.0/8 is IPv4 loopback, commonly 127.0.0.1, for local protocol access without an external link.

choices.label: A
choices.explanation: Referring to the host itself is precisely the loopback function, so this statement does describe it.

choices.label: B
choices.explanation: Local programs can use networking protocols to access local services through loopback.

choices.label: C
choices.explanation: External contradicts loopback’s local self-reference without an external network link.

choices.label: D
choices.explanation: 127.0.0.1 is explicitly given as the common IPv4 loopback address.

reviews.answer_text: Travel distance is not explicit in the simplified capacity formulas
reviews.hint: Read Bit rate, baud and channel capacity and apply its stated assumptions.
reviews.explanation: In the simplified capacity comparison taught in NET05, Nyquist uses bandwidth and signal levels, while Shannon uses bandwidth and signal-to-noise ratio. Travel distance is not a separate formula parameter, making A the intended choice. The qualification matters: distance can affect attenuation, delay and real achievable rates, so the answer is not physical independence from distance.

evidence.quote: Bandwidth, signal levels and noise appear explicitly. Distance affects attenuation, delay and often achievable rate, but is not a separate variable in these simplified capacity formulas.

choices.label: A
choices.explanation: Travel distance is absent as an independent variable in the taught formulas, despite indirect real-link effects.

choices.label: B
choices.explanation: Bandwidth appears directly in both Nyquist and Shannon expressions and limits channel capacity.

choices.label: C
choices.explanation: Noise enters Shannon capacity through the signal-to-noise ratio.

choices.label: D
choices.explanation: Signal levels enter Nyquist capacity through the number of bits represented per symbol.

reviews.answer_text: Multiplexing is missing from the options
reviews.hint: Read Multiplexing and channelization and distinguish the relevant scope/function.
reviews.explanation: Combining multiple analogue/digital streams over one shared medium is multiplexing. None of the main options names it. Point-to-point specifies endpoints, broadcast/multicast specify destination sets and synchronization concerns coordination. NET32 explicitly identifies this defective option set, so the missing term must not be replaced by a supplied but unrelated choice.

evidence.quote: Multiplexing combines multiple input streams onto a shared link; demultiplexing separates them at the receiver.

choices.label: A
choices.explanation: Point-to-point joins two endpoints and does not mean combining input signals onto a shared link.

choices.label: B
choices.explanation: Broadcast sends a message to all destinations in scope rather than combining multiple input streams.

choices.label: C
choices.explanation: Synchronization coordinates timing; it is not the multiplexing operation defined by the stem.

choices.label: D
choices.explanation: Multicast targets a subscribed group rather than combining signals onto one medium.

reviews.answer_text: OSI is a reference model, not itself an implemented protocol suite
reviews.hint: Read Protocols, standards and layers and distinguish the relevant scope/function.
reviews.explanation: NET03 distinguishes an abstract reference model from an implemented protocol suite. D incorrectly calls OSI a protocol model in that distinction. TCP/IP supplies the implemented suite, and designers can use models as architectural guides. B is valid when understood as the model itself not providing executable implementation details, rather than denying all interface descriptions.

evidence.quote: OSI is a seven-layer reference model; TCP/IP describes an implemented protocol suite, usually taught with four layers.

choices.label: A
choices.explanation: TCP/IP describes an implemented protocol suite, consistent with calling it a protocol model.

choices.label: B
choices.explanation: A reference model divides responsibilities/interfaces without itself being executable implementation software.

choices.label: C
choices.explanation: Models can guide network design; using one or both perspectives is compatible with their reference purpose.

choices.label: D
choices.explanation: OSI is the reference model in the stated contrast, not itself the implemented TCP/IP-style protocol suite.

reviews.answer_text: Both allocated public 9.0.0.1 and private 172.16.1.27 can be LAN hosts
reviews.hint: Read Special ranges, private addresses and IPv6 and distinguish the relevant scope/function.
reviews.explanation: D is private unicast space commonly used on a LAN. B is syntactically valid public unicast and can also be used on a LAN with legitimate allocation and suitable subnetting; LAN does not imply private-only. A is loopback and C has an impossible octet 256. Thus both B and D are possible host assignments under appropriate allocation, not all or none.

evidence.quote: A LAN may also use legitimately assigned public addresses; private is common, not mandatory.

choices.label: A
choices.explanation: 127/8 is reserved for loopback and is not an ordinary LAN interface assignment.

choices.label: B
choices.explanation: Public unicast can be used on a LAN when legitimately allocated and correctly subnetted.

choices.label: C
choices.explanation: An IPv4 octet must be 0–255; 256 makes this address syntactically invalid.

choices.label: D
choices.explanation: 172.16.1.27 lies in private 172.16/12 and can be an ordinary LAN host under a suitable prefix.

choices.label: E
choices.explanation: All fails because loopback and the impossible .256 octet are not valid ordinary LAN host assignments.

choices.label: F
choices.explanation: At least B conditionally and D commonly are valid LAN host candidates.

reviews.answer_text: Packet switching divides a message into packets
reviews.hint: Read Circuit, message and packet switching and distinguish the relevant scope/function.
reviews.explanation: The defining packet-switching property is dividing data into packets for shared-link forwarding. Routing may seek good paths, but packets do not guarantee the most efficient or geometrically shortest path, as NET31 warns. C directly states the definition; D includes unsupported universal route claims and therefore fails.

evidence.quote: Packet switching divides data into packets that share links statistically; queueing can add variable delay and loss.

choices.label: A
choices.explanation: Routing chooses next hops, but packet switching does not guarantee packets discover the globally most efficient route.

choices.label: B
choices.explanation: NET31 explicitly rejects a guarantee that every packet takes the geometrically shortest route.

choices.label: C
choices.explanation: Breaking a message into data packets is the packet-switching operation defined in NET31.

choices.label: D
choices.explanation: The all option includes unsupported route-optimality and necessary-shortest-path claims.

reviews.answer_text: Both include application and corresponding transport/network responsibilities
reviews.hint: Read Upper layers and the TCP/IP correspondence and distinguish the relevant scope/function.
reviews.explanation: NET19 establishes application layers and comparable transport/network responsibilities in both models, supporting A and B. C treats both models as operating technologies; NET03 instead says a reference model is not executable software. The note does not restrict every OSI-guided implementation to packet switching. Thus A/B are established similarities and D overstates the technology claim.

evidence.quote: The four-layer TCP/IP model folds OSI layers 5–7 into application, retains transport, calls layer 3 Internet, and combines link/physical as network access.

choices.label: A
choices.explanation: Both models include an application layer, although TCP/IP folds several OSI upper-layer functions into it.

choices.label: B
choices.explanation: TCP/IP retains transport and maps OSI network responsibilities to its Internet layer.

choices.label: C
choices.explanation: A reference model does not itself use a switching technology or restrict every implementation to one.

choices.label: D
choices.explanation: The implemented-technology claim in C is not a property established for both abstract models.

reviews.answer_text: A layer-1 device such as a repeater/hub is absent
reviews.hint: Read NICs, repeaters and hubs and distinguish the relevant scope/function.
reviews.explanation: NET09 identifies repeaters and active hubs as layer-1 signal devices. The supplied options instead contain a router, switch and duplicated firewall; none names the required physical-layer device. Ordinary routers/switches enforce higher-layer forwarding decisions and firewall is a policy function. Duplicating the distractor does not supply the missing correct answer.

evidence.quote: A repeater regenerates layer-1 signals without inspecting destination addresses.

choices.label: A
choices.explanation: A router’s defining forwarding function is network-layer IP routing rather than layer-1 signal repetition.

choices.label: B
choices.explanation: An ordinary Ethernet switch performs layer-2 MAC frame forwarding.

choices.label: C
choices.explanation: A firewall enforces traffic policy rather than being the layer-1 repeater/hub requested.

choices.label: D
choices.explanation: This duplicates Firewall and still does not offer a physical-layer repeater or hub.

reviews.answer_text: Security is required; role universality and administrator scope are also unclear
reviews.hint: Read Network size, access and architecture and distinguish the relevant scope/function.
reviews.explanation: D is false because peer networks still need security. A says all computers function as both roles, while NET02 says peers may do both, not necessarily every host at all times. B can refer either to a dedicated centralized administrator or simply someone responsible for operating a peer network. These unstated universality/role assumptions prevent a uniquely false option.

evidence.quote: Peer systems may perform both roles. Dedicated servers concentrate on service workloads but can still be clients of DNS, backup or update services.

choices.label: A
choices.explanation: Peer capability to serve and request does not prove every computer actively performs both roles in every deployment.

choices.label: B
choices.explanation: A peer network can have administrative responsibility, but need not have a dedicated centralized administrator.

choices.label: C
choices.explanation: Absence of a required client/server hierarchy is compatible with peer architecture.

choices.label: D
choices.explanation: Peer-to-peer systems still require security; saying security is not an issue is false.

reviews.answer_text: OSI guides understanding of layered communication
reviews.hint: Read Protocols, standards and layers and distinguish the relevant scope/function.
reviews.explanation: OSI is a seven-layer reference model used to explain responsibilities and communication interfaces. C matches that teaching/reference role. It has more layers than the usual four-layer TCP/IP model. B is too literal if it means an executable implementation used to build the network; the model guides design rather than itself supplying network software.

evidence.quote: A reference model divides responsibilities and interfaces; it is not itself executable networking software.

choices.label: A
choices.explanation: Seven OSI layers are more than the usual four TCP/IP layers, not fewer.

choices.label: B
choices.explanation: OSI can guide design, but the model itself is not executable networking software or a built implementation.

choices.label: C
choices.explanation: A layered reference model helps learners understand communication responsibilities and interfaces.

choices.label: D
choices.explanation: The reversed layer count in A prevents all statements from being true.

reviews.answer_text: Every listed item is a communication component
reviews.hint: Read Communication components and quality and distinguish the relevant scope/function.
reviews.explanation: NET01 explicitly includes message, medium, sender and protocol among the required communication components, along with the omitted receiver. The negative stem offers no noncomponent and no none-of-the-above response. Therefore the question lacks a correct option, even though the relevant concept is fully covered.

evidence.quote: Communication requires a message, sender, receiver, medium and agreed protocol.

choices.label: A
choices.explanation: Message is explicitly one of the required components.

choices.label: B
choices.explanation: The medium carries signals and is explicitly a communication component.

choices.label: C
choices.explanation: The sender is explicitly included among communication components.

choices.label: D
choices.explanation: An agreed protocol is explicitly required, so it is not a noncomponent.

reviews.answer_text: Link and transport reliability procedures can use these mechanisms
reviews.hint: Read Access control and reliable-link procedures and distinguish the relevant scope/function.
reviews.explanation: NET14 gives link stop-and-wait sequence bits, acknowledgments and sliding windows. NET17 gives TCP sequence numbers, ACKs and windows at transport scope. The question does not specify hop-local versus end-to-end reliability, so both layer 2 and layer 4 fit. These mechanisms are not universally supplied by every protocol in either layer.

evidence.quote: Link reliability/flow control is hop-local; transport reliability/flow control is end-to-end.

choices.label: A
choices.explanation: Reliable link procedures can use ACKs, sequence bits and hop-local flow control.

choices.label: B
choices.explanation: TCP transport uses sequence numbers, acknowledgments and receiver flow-control windows end to end.

choices.label: C
choices.explanation: IP best-effort delivery does not provide the indicated ordered acknowledgment/retransmission service.

choices.label: D
choices.explanation: Application services can build reliability, but the standard link/transport mechanisms named here are not layer-7 duties.

reviews.answer_text: IPv6 is logical addressing; IPv4 is 32-bit and IPv6 128-bit
reviews.hint: Read Special ranges, private addresses and IPv6 and distinguish the relevant scope/function.
reviews.explanation: IPv4 uses 32-bit logical addresses and IPv6 uses 128-bit logical addresses. C correctly identifies IPv6 addressing as logical, and D correctly compares widths. A has both widths wrong and B confuses network addresses with physical/link addresses. The singular question therefore has two independent true statements.

evidence.quote: IPv6 has 128-bit hexadecimal addresses, flexible prefixes and no IPv4-style broadcast.

choices.label: A
choices.explanation: IPv4 is 32 bits and IPv6 is 128 bits; neither printed width is correct.

choices.label: B
choices.explanation: IPv4 is network-layer logical addressing, not a physical/MAC address.

choices.label: C
choices.explanation: IPv6 addresses identify network-layer endpoints logically rather than physical link interfaces.

choices.label: D
choices.explanation: This gives the correct address lengths: 32 bits for IPv4 and 128 for IPv6.

reviews.answer_text: Neither induced nor crosstalk names a transmission medium
reviews.hint: Read Cables, wireless and connectors and distinguish the relevant scope/function.
reviews.explanation: The note identifies cables and unguided radio/microwave/infrared as transmission media. Crosstalk instead names interference from nearby channels in NET06, and induced alone does not name a medium in the note. Regardless of the vague direct-transmission phrase, none of A–C supplies a listed medium, so D is the supported exclusion response.

evidence.quote: Radio, microwave and infrared are unguided media.

choices.label: A
choices.explanation: Induced is not a transmission-medium category established by the note.

choices.label: B
choices.explanation: Crosstalk is unwanted coupling/interference, not a medium for intentional direct transmission.

choices.label: C
choices.explanation: Combining two nonmedium terms does not supply the requested transmission medium.

choices.label: D
choices.explanation: Neither induced nor crosstalk names a transmission medium among the choices.

reviews.answer_text: Bus uses a shared multipoint backbone
reviews.hint: Read Topology and failure reasoning and distinguish the relevant scope/function.
reviews.explanation: A multipoint connection shares one medium among endpoints. NET08 describes bus as a shared backbone, while a full mesh consists of separate point-to-point links. Ordinary star and ring link layouts connect endpoints through separate adjacent links rather than requiring a common shared bus. D is therefore the topology matching multipoint sharing.

evidence.quote: Bus uses a shared backbone; an unterminated break can disrupt the segment.

choices.label: A
choices.explanation: A star connects endpoints through a central device using individual edge links rather than requiring a shared backbone.

choices.label: B
choices.explanation: A full mesh consists of point-to-point links, explicitly correcting the old contradictory multipoint claim.

choices.label: C
choices.explanation: A ring forms successive neighboring links, not the common shared backbone requested.

choices.label: D
choices.explanation: A bus shares one backbone among multiple endpoints, matching a multipoint connection.

reviews.answer_text: All are physical-medium/signaling specifications
reviews.hint: Read NICs, repeaters and hubs and distinguish the relevant scope/function.
reviews.explanation: Mechanical connectors, electrical signal levels and optical signaling specifications all concern how the physical medium transports symbols. NET09 defines that PHY scope, and NET07 covers guided light in fiber. C should be read as specifying a chosen infrared optical link, not as claiming every fiber uses the same wavelength. D includes all listed physical specification types.

evidence.quote: Physical specifications include connectors, signaling, voltage, timing and physical coding/modulation

choices.label: A
choices.explanation: Connector/cable mechanical specifications are explicitly part of the physical interface.

choices.label: B
choices.explanation: Transmission-line signal levels are electrical signaling specifications at the physical layer.

choices.label: C
choices.explanation: Specifying optical signaling over fiber is a physical-medium requirement when that optical wavelength is chosen.

choices.label: D
choices.explanation: All listed specifications concern physical media/interfaces or signaling, so the aggregate is the inclusive response.

reviews.answer_text: Process-to-process, also application-endpoint communication
reviews.hint: Read Transport choice, ports and connections and distinguish the relevant scope/function.
reviews.explanation: NET12 names transport process delivery, while NET17 identifies ports as transport endpoints. Application communication builds on those process endpoints, so A is a broad description and B the precise layer term. Node-to-node framing instead belongs to link delivery, and man-to-man is not the layer definition. The stem does not require only the most precise wording.

evidence.quote: Ports identify transport endpoints

choices.label: A
choices.explanation: Application endpoints communicate through transport processes/ports, making this a valid broader description.

choices.label: B
choices.explanation: Process-to-process delivery is the precise transport-layer responsibility in NET12.

choices.label: C
choices.explanation: Hop/node-to-node frame delivery is a link-layer responsibility rather than transport process delivery.

choices.label: D
choices.explanation: Human-to-human interaction is not the protocol endpoint service defining transport.

reviews.answer_text: End-to-end and process service labels need a defined scope
reviews.hint: Read Upper layers and the TCP/IP correspondence and distinguish the relevant scope/function.
reviews.explanation: NET19 distinguishes application service from the process-to-process transport beneath it, while acknowledging overlapping end-to-end terminology. A can describe the application service boundary and B the transport service applications use. The stem supplies no definition of service scope, so C may combine unlike meanings. A unique layer assignment cannot be obtained from these broad labels.

evidence.quote: End-to-end application service builds on process-to-process transport; vague service labels can overlap.

choices.label: A
choices.explanation: Application services can be end to end, but the phrase alone is not an exclusive layer classification.

choices.label: B
choices.explanation: Applications use process-to-process transport, but the question does not distinguish offered service from underlying service.

choices.label: C
choices.explanation: Both can describe parts of the full service stack under broad usage, requiring the missing scope definition.

choices.label: D
choices.explanation: At least end-to-end application service is described in the note, so neither label being meaningful is not supported.

reviews.answer_text: The internal-access term is intranet, which is absent
reviews.hint: Read Network size, access and architecture and distinguish the relevant scope/function.
reviews.explanation: The decisive fact is access by university members to private organizational networks, describing an intranet. The options instead mix geographic size categories with the public Internet. Multiple LANs/WANs do not reveal a single geographic category for the whole organization, and no external global Internet is stated. The best access-scope term is missing.

evidence.quote: An intranet serves an organization internally; an extranet exposes selected services to approved outsiders.

choices.label: A
choices.explanation: The stem explicitly includes wide-area networks as well as LANs, so LAN alone does not describe the whole system.

choices.label: B
choices.explanation: The public global Internet is not the university’s internally restricted network.

choices.label: C
choices.explanation: WAN may describe distant components, but distance is unspecified and it does not name the internal-access scope.

choices.label: D
choices.explanation: No metropolitan geographic span is given, so MAN cannot be inferred.

reviews.answer_text: Data-link forwarding functions, with NICs also implementing PHY
reviews.hint: Read Bridges, switches and access points and distinguish the relevant scope/function.
reviews.explanation: Bridges and ordinary switches inspect MAC frames at layer 2. A NIC commonly implements both physical and data-link functions, as NET09 explains; listing NICs here does not force all NIC work into one layer. D is the common frame/addressing layer for the listed devices’ relevant network-interface forwarding functions.

evidence.quote: A bridge or ordinary Ethernet switch operates at layer 2.

choices.label: A
choices.explanation: A NIC has physical functions, but bridges/switches make layer-2 forwarding decisions beyond signal repetition.

choices.label: B
choices.explanation: These devices’ MAC/frame operations are below application-service semantics.

choices.label: C
choices.explanation: Ordinary bridges and Ethernet switches do not route IP prefixes as their defining function.

choices.label: D
choices.explanation: Bridges/switches operate at layer 2, and NICs also implement link-layer MAC/frame functions.

reviews.answer_text: The Internet
reviews.hint: Read Network size, access and architecture and distinguish the relevant scope/function.
reviews.explanation: The Internet names the particular global network of networks, while WAN, MAN and LAN name scope categories. NET02 explicitly gives the Internet as the largest common WAN example. Thus C is the intended largest actual network in the comparison, even though WAN includes Internet-scale networks rather than being a disjoint smaller category.

evidence.quote: The Internet is a global network of networks, commonly the largest example of a WAN.

choices.label: A
choices.explanation: WAN is a category that includes the Internet, not a separate specific network shown to be larger.

choices.label: B
choices.explanation: MAN spans a metropolitan area rather than the global network of networks.

choices.label: C
choices.explanation: NET02 identifies the global Internet as the largest common WAN example.

choices.label: D
choices.explanation: LAN covers a local building/campus and is much narrower in geographic scope.

reviews.answer_text: Classless prefixes, subnetting and CIDR terminology overlap
reviews.hint: Read Special ranges, private addresses and IPv6 and distinguish the relevant scope/function.
reviews.explanation: IPv6 uses flexible network prefixes rather than IPv4’s historical A/B/C class allocations. Classless addressing and CIDR describe that prefix approach, while subnetting divides prefixes for networks. Thus B, C and D are compatible descriptions of the broad addressing scheme. The question provides no distinction that makes classless addressing and its classless-routing notation mutually exclusive.

evidence.quote: IPv6 has 128-bit hexadecimal addresses, flexible prefixes

choices.label: A
choices.explanation: Historical classful A/B/C IPv4 defaults are not the IPv6 flexible-prefix scheme.

choices.label: B
choices.explanation: IPv6 uses flexible prefixes rather than fixed historical address classes.

choices.label: C
choices.explanation: IPv6 prefixes can be subdivided into subnets; the term overlaps the broad scheme wording.

choices.label: D
choices.explanation: Classless prefix/CIDR terminology applies to flexible-prefix allocation and routing rather than historical class boundaries.

reviews.answer_text: Switch and bridge
reviews.hint: Read Bridges, switches and access points and apply the stated scope.
reviews.explanation: NET10 explicitly places both an ordinary Ethernet switch and a bridge at layer 2. A hub repeats physical signals, and a router forwards IP packets between networks. The stem asks only which operates at the data-link layer, so B and D independently meet it; no additional qualifier makes either exclusive.

evidence.quote: A bridge or ordinary Ethernet switch operates at layer 2.

choices.label: A
choices.explanation: A hub repeats layer-1 signals rather than making MAC/frame forwarding decisions.

choices.label: B
choices.explanation: An ordinary Ethernet switch is explicitly a layer-2 forwarding device.

choices.label: C
choices.explanation: A router’s defining forwarding function is network-layer IP routing.

choices.label: D
choices.explanation: A bridge is explicitly a layer-2 device, like an ordinary Ethernet switch.

reviews.answer_text: SMTP sends/relays mail; end-user retrieval needs POP3/IMAP
reviews.hint: Read Web, file, mail and remote-login protocols and apply the stated scope.
reviews.explanation: A fits sending and server-to-server receipt/relay of mail. If receiving means end-user mailbox retrieval, SMTP is not sufficient and neither POP3 nor IMAP is offered. The stem does not distinguish relay receipt from mailbox access. Thus the combined sending/receiving claim depends on an unstated mail-system role, rather than supporting an unconditional SMTP selection.

evidence.quote: SMTP submits and relays mail; POP3 retrieves messages and IMAP accesses/synchronizes server mailboxes.

choices.label: A
choices.explanation: SMTP sends and relays mail, including server receipt, but does not provide end-user mailbox retrieval.

choices.label: B
choices.explanation: HTTP can serve application resources, but the stem does not specify a webmail application or its mailbox behavior.

choices.label: C
choices.explanation: FTP transfers files and is not the mail submission/relay or mailbox access protocol in the note.

choices.label: D
choices.explanation: DNS resolves records; it does not transport or retrieve the user’s messages.

reviews.answer_text: Hub and switch can connect LAN devices
reviews.hint: Read NICs, repeaters and hubs and apply the stated scope.
reviews.explanation: A hub interconnects LAN endpoints by repeating signals, and a switch interconnects them by MAC-based frame forwarding. The stem supplies neither collision isolation nor selective forwarding to distinguish them. A router instead joins IP networks and a modem performs carrier conversion. A and C therefore both meet the broad connection function.

evidence.quote: An active hub is a multiport repeater: it repeats incoming signals onto other ports, placing half-duplex endpoints in one collision domain.

choices.label: A
choices.explanation: A multiport hub joins LAN devices into a shared repeated-signal segment.

choices.label: B
choices.explanation: A router’s defining function is connecting/routing between IP networks rather than this shared LAN-device role.

choices.label: C
choices.explanation: A switch connects LAN endpoints and forwards frames among its ports.

choices.label: D
choices.explanation: A modem modulates/demodulates carrier signals rather than providing the offered multiport LAN interconnection function.

reviews.answer_text: Session dialogs and transport connections are distinct meanings
reviews.hint: Read Upper layers and the TCP/IP correspondence and apply the stated scope.
reviews.explanation: D fits session/dialog lifecycle management in the OSI model. C also fits establishing and terminating TCP transport connections when connection means protocol endpoint state. The stem says only connections between devices, without specifying dialog versus transport association. Physical/link functions do not resolve that scope, so the missing qualifier makes C/D competing interpretations.

evidence.quote: OSI session roles establish/manage dialogs and can coordinate checkpoints so transfer resumes after interruption.

choices.label: A
choices.explanation: Physical-layer signaling does not supply the session/dialog or TCP connection lifecycle described.

choices.label: B
choices.explanation: Some link protocols establish link associations, but the generic connection scope is not defined.

choices.label: C
choices.explanation: TCP establishes logical transport connections, so this fits a transport-connection interpretation.

choices.label: D
choices.explanation: Session-layer dialogs fit the textbook session-management interpretation, which the stem does not explicitly state.

reviews.answer_text: SMTP handles submission/relay, not end-user mailbox retrieval
reviews.hint: Read Web, file, mail and remote-login protocols and apply the stated scope.
reviews.explanation: If receiving means the mail server accepting a relay/submission, SMTP applies. If it means users retrieving mail, the required POP3/IMAP protocols are missing. The Internet qualifier does not resolve those distinct operations. A is therefore conditional; none of the other named protocols supplies the note’s end-user mailbox service as stated.

evidence.quote: Saying SMTP handles both sending and end-user mailbox retrieval is inaccurate.

choices.label: A
choices.explanation: SMTP submits/relays messages and accepts them at servers, but does not retrieve end-user mailbox contents.

choices.label: B
choices.explanation: FTP transfers files through a separate protocol rather than the mail flow defined here.

choices.label: C
choices.explanation: HTTP may carry web resources, but no webmail application behavior is specified by this generic mail-protocol stem.

choices.label: D
choices.explanation: DNS supplies records such as mail-exchanger names rather than delivering or retrieving message contents.

reviews.answer_text: Presentation layer for representation/format translation
reviews.hint: Read Upper layers and the TCP/IP correspondence and apply the stated scope.
reviews.explanation: The word format identifies representation translation rather than routing or connection management. NET19 assigns encoding translation and other representation work to presentation. Physical signaling maps bits to medium symbols, but does not supply the application-data format translation asked for. Thus A matches the intended formatting responsibility.

evidence.quote: Presentation roles translate encodings and handle compression/encryption.

choices.label: A
choices.explanation: Presentation translates representations/encodings into suitable data formats.

choices.label: B
choices.explanation: Session manages dialogs and checkpoints rather than data representation formats.

choices.label: C
choices.explanation: Physical maps bits/symbols to signals, a different responsibility from representation-format translation.

choices.label: D
choices.explanation: Application supplies network services to applications rather than the distinct presentation-format function.

reviews.answer_text: /30 is the conventional small offered choice, but larger subnets can also contain a link
reviews.hint: Read Point-to-point links and route aggregation and apply the stated scope.
reviews.explanation: D is the conventional efficient two-endpoint /30 choice. The question asks only which mask is used, not the smallest or most efficient offered mask. Larger /24, /25 or /26 networks also have room for two endpoints, and supported /31 links exist though absent here. A unique D selection therefore requires the missing conventional-smallest-choice qualifier.

evidence.quote: A conventional /30 has four addresses and two usable endpoints, often the smallest offered choice for a WAN link.

choices.label: A
choices.explanation: A /24 can contain two link endpoints but allocates far more addresses than needed.

choices.label: B
choices.explanation: A /25 also has sufficient endpoint addresses, though inefficient for a two-node link.

choices.label: C
choices.explanation: A /26 can address two endpoints but is larger than the conventional efficient offered choice.

choices.label: D
choices.explanation: A /30 is the conventional smallest offered two-usable-endpoint block, but smallest is not requested.

reviews.answer_text: Public or private unicast, and dynamically assigned addresses, can be used locally
reviews.hint: Read Special ranges, private addresses and IPv6 and apply the stated scope.
reviews.explanation: LAN use is not restricted to RFC1918 addresses. Legitimately allocated public unicast can also be used, and dynamic describes how an address is assigned rather than a mutually exclusive address scope. Thus A, B and D can all describe local-network host addressing. Reserved space is not a general permission to assign addresses such as loopback or broadcast to LAN hosts.

evidence.quote: A LAN may also use legitimately assigned public addresses; private is common, not mandatory.

choices.label: A
choices.explanation: Legitimately allocated public unicast addresses can be used inside a LAN under the correct prefix.

choices.label: B
choices.explanation: RFC1918 private unicast is commonly used for local-network communication.

choices.label: C
choices.explanation: Reserved addresses have specific purposes and are not a generic ordinary-LAN host address category.

choices.label: D
choices.explanation: A DHCP-leased dynamic address can be used locally; assignment method is separate from public/private scope.

reviews.answer_text: UDP and IP are both connectionless
reviews.hint: Read Transport choice, ports and connections and apply the stated scope.
reviews.explanation: UDP sends independent datagrams without connection setup. NET16 likewise gives IP connectionless best-effort packet delivery, so A and B both satisfy the general TCP/IP-suite question. TCP instead establishes a reliable logical connection, and OSI is a reference model rather than one TCP/IP protocol. No transport-only qualifier narrows the answer to UDP.

evidence.quote: UDP sends independent datagrams with ports and a checksum but no built-in setup, delivery guarantee, retransmission or ordering.

choices.label: A
choices.explanation: UDP has no built-in connection setup and treats datagrams independently.

choices.label: B
choices.explanation: IP also supplies connectionless best-effort packet delivery at the network layer.

choices.label: C
choices.explanation: TCP establishes logical transport connection state before its reliable stream transfer.

choices.label: D
choices.explanation: OSI is a reference model, not a connectionless TCP/IP-suite protocol.

reviews.answer_text: Network-layer PDU is packet, not frame
reviews.hint: Read OSI layers and encapsulation and apply the stated scope.
reviews.explanation: NET12 directly maps the PDUs: application data, transport segment/datagram, network packet, link frame and physical bits. D assigns the link-layer frame to the network layer, making it the mismatch. Transport segment is appropriate for TCP, so B remains a valid conventional example rather than a claim about every transport protocol.

evidence.quote: Sending proceeds from application data to transport segment/datagram, network packet, link frame and physical bits/symbols

choices.label: A
choices.explanation: Application data is the conventional PDU designation, so this match is valid.

choices.label: B
choices.explanation: TCP uses transport segments; this is a valid conventional transport PDU example.

choices.label: C
choices.explanation: Bits/symbols belong to physical transport, making this match valid.

choices.label: D
choices.explanation: A frame is link-layer; the network-layer unit is a packet.

reviews.answer_text: Presentation layer
reviews.hint: Read Upper layers and the TCP/IP correspondence and apply the stated scope.
reviews.explanation: The three listed operations are representation functions: encoding translation, compression and encryption. NET19 groups them under the OSI presentation role. Link handles frames, transport process delivery and network logical routing; none is the named OSI representation layer. Real implementations may distribute these functions, but the reference-model answer is presentation.

evidence.quote: Presentation roles translate encodings and handle compression/encryption.

choices.label: A
choices.explanation: Presentation explicitly covers encoding translation, compression and encryption roles.

choices.label: B
choices.explanation: Data link handles hop frames/access rather than the OSI representation-function grouping.

choices.label: C
choices.explanation: Transport delivers between process endpoints, not the named presentation representation roles.

choices.label: D
choices.explanation: Network handles logical addressing/routing rather than compression/encoding translation.

reviews.hint: Read IPv4 notation and classful defaults and apply the stated scope.
reviews.explanation: Using octet weights 128,64,32,16,8,4,2,1 gives 11000001=193, 10000011=131, 00011011=27 and 11111111=255. Combining the four decimal octets gives 193.131.27.255. This is a notation conversion, not a claim about whether that address is assignable as a host under an unspecified prefix.

choices.label: A
choices.explanation: The first octet should be 193 and the second 131, not 192 and 174.

choices.label: B
choices.explanation: All four printed octets differ from the binary-derived values 193,131,27,255.

choices.label: C
choices.explanation: Only the first octet matches; the correct remaining values are 131,27,255.

choices.label: D
choices.explanation: Each decimal octet matches its eight-bit sum: 193, 131, 27 and 255.

reviews.answer_text: LAN
reviews.hint: Read Network size, access and architecture and apply the stated scope.
reviews.explanation: All computers are in one building, the geographic scope of a LAN in NET02. The count of 500 devices or ten floors does not itself make a MAN/WAN; the note explicitly separates device count from geographic category. No metropolitan or distant-region interconnection is supplied.

evidence.quote: LAN covers a local building or campus; MAN spans a metropolitan region; WAN connects distant regions.

choices.label: A
choices.explanation: WAN concerns distant regions, not simply many devices on floors of one building.

choices.label: B
choices.explanation: MAN requires metropolitan scope rather than a single-building deployment.

choices.label: C
choices.explanation: A single building falls within the LAN scope defined by NET02.

choices.label: D
choices.explanation: The Internet is the global network of networks, not the building network described.

reviews.answer_text: Data link, layer 2
reviews.hint: Read Link control, framing and error detection and apply the stated scope.
reviews.explanation: MAC addressing identifies link-layer frame endpoints and forwarding scope. NET13 assigns medium-dependent addressing/access to MAC in the data-link layer. Physical transports signals, network uses logical IP prefixes and transport identifies process endpoints by ports. The word physical in physical address must not be confused with a layer-1 functional assignment.

evidence.quote: MAC handles medium-dependent addressing/access and frame delivery.

choices.label: A
choices.explanation: Network-layer addressing uses logical IP addresses rather than the link MAC address.

choices.label: B
choices.explanation: Physical transports signals; the conventional physical-address nickname does not move MAC addressing to layer 1.

choices.label: C
choices.explanation: MAC addressing and frame delivery are data-link functions at layer 2.

choices.label: D
choices.explanation: Transport identifies process endpoints by ports rather than MAC frame addresses.

reviews.answer_text: Loss of signal strength
reviews.hint: Read Delay, impairments and transmission modes and apply the stated scope.
reviews.explanation: NET06 defines attenuation as reduced signal strength. Different delays among frequency components describe distortion, adjacent-channel leakage describes crosstalk and maximum rate concerns capacity. B gives the strength-loss mechanism rather than those separate impairments or performance measures.

evidence.quote: Attenuation reduces signal strength. Distortion changes shape, often because frequencies have different delays.

choices.label: A
choices.explanation: Different component delays change waveform shape, describing distortion rather than attenuation.

choices.label: B
choices.explanation: A reduction in signal strength during propagation is attenuation.

choices.label: C
choices.explanation: Adjacent-channel interference is crosstalk, a separate noise source.

choices.label: D
choices.explanation: Maximum data rate is channel capacity, not signal-strength loss.

reviews.answer_text: Borrow 3 bits to obtain at least six equal subnets
reviews.hint: Read Borrow bits and choose a mask and apply the stated scope.
reviews.explanation: For equal-sized subnets of a /24 parent, borrowing b bits yields 2^b blocks. Two bits give only four; three give eight, the minimum power-of-two count that accommodates six required subnets. The resulting mask is /27 with 30 conventional hosts per block. Exactly six equal blocks would not fill the parent; two blocks remain unused.

evidence.quote: For at least six equal subnets choose b=3. A Class C /24 split to /27 yields eight subnets.

choices.label: A
choices.explanation: Two borrowed bits yield only four blocks, fewer than the six required.

choices.label: B
choices.explanation: Three borrowed bits yield eight blocks and are the minimum satisfying at least six.

choices.label: C
choices.explanation: Four bits yield sixteen blocks and are not the minimum required.

choices.label: D
choices.explanation: Six bits yield sixty-four blocks, substantially more than the minimum.

reviews.answer_text: Full mesh among the conventional topology choices
reviews.hint: Read Topology and failure reasoning and apply the stated scope.
reviews.explanation: A full mesh connects every pair of nodes, offering multiple alternate paths compared with the basic star, single ring and shared bus. NET08 explains the additional links/interfaces and improved fault tolerance. D assumes the conventional full-mesh interpretation; actual protected rings or partial mesh designs would require more detail for a quantitative comparison.

evidence.quote: Redundant paths improve fault tolerance at greater cable and interface cost.

choices.label: A
choices.explanation: A basic star depends on its central device and lacks the full mesh’s many alternate paths.

choices.label: B
choices.explanation: A basic single ring is vulnerable to a break, unlike a full mesh’s multiple paths.

choices.label: C
choices.explanation: A shared bus depends on one backbone rather than redundant pairwise paths.

choices.label: D
choices.explanation: A full mesh supplies pairwise links and multiple alternate paths, at increased cable/interface cost.

reviews.hint: Read Masks, prefixes and binary AND and apply the stated scope.
reviews.explanation: A /24 prefix fixes the first three octets and leaves eight host bits. Setting them all to one gives final octet 255, so the broadcast is 192.168.17.255. The .0 address is the network boundary and .254 is the last ordinary host; 192.168.16.255 belongs outside the specified /24.

evidence.quote: Host bits zero identify the block start; host bits one give broadcast.

choices.label: A
choices.explanation: 192.168.17.0 has all host bits zero and identifies the network, not broadcast.

choices.label: B
choices.explanation: 192.168.17.254 is the last ordinary host, one below broadcast.

choices.label: C
choices.explanation: The final eight host bits are all one, giving the /24 broadcast .255.

choices.label: D
choices.explanation: The third octet 16 lies outside network 192.168.17.0/24.

reviews.answer_text: Router
reviews.hint: Read Routers, gateways and traffic controls and apply the stated scope.
reviews.explanation: IP destination-prefix forwarding between networks is the router function in NET11. Hubs repeat signals and bridges/ordinary switches forward MAC frames at layer 2. Some marketed switches include routing, but the unqualified ordinary switch function in this option set is layer 2; router is the explicit matching device.

evidence.quote: Routers forward IP packets between networks using destination prefixes and next hops.

choices.label: A
choices.explanation: A hub repeats layer-1 signals rather than forwarding on IP prefixes.

choices.label: B
choices.explanation: A bridge makes layer-2 frame-forwarding decisions using MAC addresses.

choices.label: C
choices.explanation: An ordinary switch is layer 2; a specifically layer-3 switch would require the missing routing qualifier.

choices.label: D
choices.explanation: Routers inspect destination IP prefixes and choose next hops at layer 3.

reviews.answer_text: No setup and no built-in delivery guarantee
reviews.hint: Read Transport choice, ports and connections and apply the stated scope.
reviews.explanation: UDP’s connectionlessness means independent datagrams without built-in setup, not an inability to carry video or an enforced physical duplex mode. It is a transport protocol. B correctly combines no connection establishment with absence of built-in reliable delivery; applications may add their own recovery mechanisms.

evidence.quote: UDP sends independent datagrams with ports and a checksum but no built-in setup, delivery guarantee, retransmission or ordering.

choices.label: A
choices.explanation: UDP can carry live media; connectionlessness does not forbid video data.

choices.label: B
choices.explanation: UDP sends independent datagrams without setup or built-in delivery guarantees.

choices.label: C
choices.explanation: UDP does not impose simplex physical transmission; transport service and physical duplex mode are distinct.

choices.label: D
choices.explanation: UDP is transport-layer, not exclusively a network-layer protocol.

reviews.answer_text: Host capacity requires a prefix; /16 would give 65534
reviews.hint: Read Resolve ambiguous and damaged networking items; apply the relevant definition or calculation.
reviews.explanation: 185 is historically Class B, but the stem supplies only a host address and no classful assumption or current prefix. A /16 would yield 65534 usable hosts, while a /24 or /8 yields different offered counts. Modern CIDR cannot infer capacity from the first octet alone. Therefore B is conditional rather than a uniquely determined answer.

evidence.quote: A host address without a prefix does not determine capacity unless the question explicitly assumes historical classful addressing.

choices.label: A
choices.explanation: 254 is the ordinary /24 usable count, but no /24 prefix is supplied.

choices.label: B
choices.explanation: 65534 follows from historical Class B /16, an assumption the stem never requests.

choices.label: C
choices.explanation: 16777214 follows from /8; the given host address alone does not specify its prefix.

choices.label: D
choices.explanation: 65536 is a /16 total count before reserving ordinary network and broadcast addresses.

reviews.answer_text: Full duplex
reviews.hint: Read Delay, impairments and transmission modes; apply the relevant definition or calculation.
reviews.explanation: The decisive condition is simultaneous communication in both directions. NET06 defines full duplex exactly that way. Half duplex permits both directions at different times and simplex only one. Multipoint describes sharing a medium among endpoints, not whether two endpoints can send and receive at the same instant.

evidence.quote: Simplex is one way, half duplex alternates directions, and full duplex permits simultaneous sending/receiving.

choices.label: A
choices.explanation: Simplex permits communication in one direction only.

choices.label: B
choices.explanation: Half duplex alternates directions and does not permit simultaneous transmission both ways.

choices.label: C
choices.explanation: Full duplex supports sending and receiving simultaneously.

choices.label: D
choices.explanation: Multipoint describes medium sharing among endpoints rather than a bidirectional timing mode.

reviews.answer_text: Compression, encryption and representation translation
reviews.hint: Read Upper layers and the TCP/IP correspondence; apply the relevant definition or calculation.
reviews.explanation: NET19 assigns these three representation functions to the OSI presentation layer. Routing belongs to network, dialogs to session and raw bit signaling to physical. Real software can combine roles, but within the stated OSI model C is the specific matching responsibility set.

evidence.quote: Presentation roles translate encodings and handle compression/encryption.

choices.label: A
choices.explanation: Routing between networks is the network-layer responsibility.

choices.label: B
choices.explanation: Session setup/ending belongs to the session role rather than presentation representation handling.

choices.label: C
choices.explanation: Compression, encryption and format translation are the presentation roles explicitly listed in NET19.

choices.label: D
choices.explanation: Physical signaling transports bits/symbols rather than translating data representations.

reviews.answer_text: Fiber cost and tapping claims need specification and threat context
reviews.hint: Read Cables, wireless and connectors; apply the relevant definition or calculation.
reviews.explanation: The note supports EMI resistance and high capacity/long reach, but explicitly refuses material-only cost conclusions and warns fiber can be tapped. C is a common intended distractor, yet lower installation cost can depend on actual optics, distance and installation. D also overstates security without a threat model. No specific cost/security context establishes one uniquely false characteristic.

evidence.quote: Exact speed, cost and reach depend on the specification, not the material alone. Fiber can still be tapped.

choices.label: A
choices.explanation: Fiber guides light and resists electromagnetic interference, a supported characteristic.

choices.label: B
choices.explanation: The note supports high capacity and long reach, with exact performance depending on the specification.

choices.label: C
choices.explanation: Relative initial cost depends on optics, reach and installation; no universal copper-versus-fiber cost ordering is proved.

choices.label: D
choices.explanation: Tapping difficulty may affect exposure, but fiber can still be tapped and high security is not automatic.

reviews.answer_text: A dedicated server concentrates on service workloads; it may still be a client
reviews.hint: Read Network size, access and architecture; apply the relevant definition or calculation.
reviews.explanation: The supported definition is concentration on service workloads, not an absolute ban on making client requests. B’s never-used-as-client wording contradicts NET02, while A merely describes a possibility without defining dedication. C limits the server to files and D switches to peer architecture. None states the complete-note definition accurately.

evidence.quote: Dedicated servers concentrate on service workloads but can still be clients of DNS, backup or update services.

choices.label: A
choices.explanation: A dedicated server may act as a DNS/backup client, but that incidental capability is not its defining dedicated workload.

choices.label: B
choices.explanation: The absolute never is false: dedicated servers can request DNS, backups or updates.

choices.label: C
choices.explanation: Dedicated service workloads need not be limited to file storage.

choices.label: D
choices.explanation: An arbitrary peer computer is not thereby a dedicated service-workload server.

reviews.answer_text: DNS
reviews.hint: Read DNS, DHCP and address resolution; apply the relevant definition or calculation.
reviews.explanation: DNS is the name-resolution application protocol in NET20. A/AAAA records provide address data for names. SMTP submits/relays mail, FTP transfers files and HTTP serves web requests; none provides the requested general domain-name record service. Its lookup role is separate from DHCP address assignment.

evidence.quote: DNS resolves names to records, including IPv4 A and IPv6 AAAA addresses

choices.label: A
choices.explanation: SMTP submits and relays mail rather than resolving hostnames to addresses.

choices.label: B
choices.explanation: FTP transfers files and does not supply the name-resolution record service.

choices.label: C
choices.explanation: HTTP defines web exchanges, not the general hostname-to-address service.

choices.label: D
choices.explanation: DNS resolves names into records such as A and AAAA address records.

reviews.answer_text: Leakage from an adjacent communication channel
reviews.hint: Read Delay, impairments and transmission modes; apply the relevant definition or calculation.
reviews.explanation: Crosstalk is unwanted coupling from a neighboring communication channel, directly matching B. Strength loss is attenuation, random thermal motion creates thermal noise and differential frequency delay produces distortion. These impairments can coexist but their definitions are distinct, so the question’s mechanism identifies crosstalk specifically.

evidence.quote: thermal noise comes from random thermal motion, crosstalk leaks from nearby channels, and impulse noise is a short disturbance.

choices.label: A
choices.explanation: Signal-strength loss is attenuation rather than coupling from a neighboring channel.

choices.label: B
choices.explanation: Signals leaking into an adjacent channel are crosstalk.

choices.label: C
