choices.explanation: Random electron/thermal motion describes thermal noise.

choices.label: D
choices.explanation: Different component-frequency delays distort waveform shape rather than defining crosstalk.

reviews.answer_text: 62 usable hosts
reviews.hint: Read Find subnet bounds and usable hosts; apply the relevant definition or calculation.
reviews.explanation: A /26 leaves six host bits, so the block has 64 addresses. In the specified block, .64 is the network and .127 the broadcast; usable hosts span .65–.126 inclusive, totaling 62. The question asks usable hosts, not block size, and /31 point-to-point exceptions do not apply.

choices.label: A
choices.explanation: Thirty-two is not the usable count of this /26 block; /26 has 64 total addresses.

choices.label: B
choices.explanation: Sixty-four is the total block size before network/broadcast reservations.

choices.label: C
choices.explanation: Six host bits give 64 total addresses minus two reservations, leaving 62 usable hosts.

choices.label: D
choices.explanation: Thirty usable hosts is the /27 result, not /26.

reviews.answer_text: Session layer
reviews.hint: Read Upper layers and the TCP/IP correspondence; apply the relevant definition or calculation.
reviews.explanation: The stem explicitly specifies communication sessions, matching the OSI session role rather than merely a TCP connection. NET19 assigns dialog management and checkpoints to that layer. Transport serves process endpoints, application supplies services and presentation handles representations. B is therefore the specific reference-model lifecycle role.

evidence.quote: OSI session roles establish/manage dialogs and can coordinate checkpoints so transfer resumes after interruption.

choices.label: A
choices.explanation: Transport connection state is distinct from the explicitly named OSI session/dialog lifecycle.

choices.label: B
choices.explanation: Session manages dialogs and their setup, maintenance and recovery/end lifecycle.

choices.label: C
choices.explanation: Application supplies user/application network services rather than the distinct session-layer lifecycle.

choices.label: D
choices.explanation: Presentation translates/compresses/encrypts representations instead of managing dialogs.

reviews.answer_text: A main-backbone break can disrupt the whole basic bus segment
reviews.hint: Read Topology and failure reasoning; apply the relevant definition or calculation.
reviews.explanation: In the conventional single-backbone bus assumed by these options, a main-cable break disrupts the shared segment, affecting the network rather than just one endpoint. NET08 qualifies the physical mechanism as an unterminated break. Redundant segmentation or protected designs are not specified, so C expresses the standard basic-bus failure consequence.

evidence.quote: Bus uses a shared backbone; an unterminated break can disrupt the segment.

choices.label: A
choices.explanation: A main-backbone fault affects shared signaling, not merely the two closest nodes.

choices.label: B
choices.explanation: A broken unterminated backbone does not preserve normal basic-bus operation.

choices.label: C
choices.explanation: The shared basic bus segment can fail as a whole when its main backbone is broken.

choices.label: D
choices.explanation: A backbone break differs from an isolated endpoint spur failure and need not be limited to one node.

reviews.answer_text: Ongoing synchronized clock recovery rather than per-character start/stop
reviews.hint: Read Delay, impairments and transmission modes; apply the relevant definition or calculation.
reviews.explanation: NET06 contrasts character start/stop framing with ongoing clock recovery in synchronous transmission. B is the intended synchronized-transfer description; “same clock” should mean synchronized timing, not necessarily a single physical clock device. The note gives no universal speed ordering, and both methods can transmit digital/binary data.

evidence.quote: Character-oriented asynchronous serial adds start/stop bits; synchronous framing uses ongoing clock recovery.

choices.label: A
choices.explanation: Per-character start/stop bits describe character-oriented asynchronous serial transmission.

choices.label: B
choices.explanation: Synchronous transfer maintains coordinated timing through ongoing clock recovery rather than character start/stop framing.

choices.label: C
choices.explanation: No universal slower-than-asynchronous rule follows from the timing method.

choices.label: D
choices.explanation: Synchronous framing can carry binary data; the timing convention does not prohibit it.

reviews.answer_text: Logical IP addressing and routing across networks
reviews.hint: Read OSI layers and encapsulation; apply the relevant definition or calculation.
reviews.explanation: NET12 gives network-layer logical addressing and routing; NET11 explains forwarding IP packets among networks by destination prefixes. C directly states that responsibility. The other options assign physical signaling, link MAC/error detection and session-dialog management, which belong to different model layers.

evidence.quote: Logical addressing and routing

choices.label: A
choices.explanation: Transporting raw physical bits/symbols is the physical-layer function.

choices.label: B
choices.explanation: MAC addressing and hop frame error detection are data-link responsibilities.

choices.label: C
choices.explanation: Network-layer logical addressing and routing carry IP packets between networks.

choices.label: D
choices.explanation: Establishing application dialogs is a session-layer role rather than IP routing.

reviews.answer_text: 10.256.0.1 has an impossible octet
reviews.hint: Read IPv4 notation and classful defaults; apply the relevant definition or calculation.
reviews.explanation: An IPv4 decimal octet must fit eight bits, from 0 through 255. D has 256 and is therefore syntactically invalid. A–C each meet that range condition. B’s .255 ending alone does not establish a broadcast without a prefix, so it cannot be rejected merely by its last octet.

evidence.quote: Write IPv4 as four decimal octets 0–255, or as 32 binary bits.

choices.label: A
choices.explanation: All four octets are within 0–255, so this notation is valid.

choices.label: B
choices.explanation: Every octet is valid; a .255 ending alone does not determine broadcast status without a prefix.

choices.label: C
choices.explanation: All four values fit eight-bit octets and form valid dotted-decimal notation.

choices.label: D
choices.explanation: The second octet 256 exceeds the maximum representable eight-bit value 255.

reviews.answer_text: 128 bits
reviews.hint: Read Special ranges, private addresses and IPv6; apply the relevant definition or calculation.
reviews.explanation: NET23 explicitly gives IPv6 addresses a 128-bit width. IPv4 uses 32 bits; 64 may describe a common subnet interface boundary but is not the whole IPv6 address length. Ninety-six bits is likewise not the full width. D therefore answers the requested address size.

evidence.quote: IPv6 has 128-bit hexadecimal addresses

choices.label: A
choices.explanation: Thirty-two bits is the IPv4 address width, not IPv6.

choices.label: B
choices.explanation: Sixty-four bits is not the complete IPv6 address width.

choices.label: C
choices.explanation: Ninety-six bits does not match the specified 128-bit IPv6 address length.

choices.label: D
choices.explanation: IPv6 addresses contain 128 bits as explicitly stated in NET23.

reviews.answer_text: Learn source MACs and forward according to destination MAC
reviews.hint: Read Bridges, switches and access points; apply the relevant definition or calculation.
reviews.explanation: A bridge learns which sources are reachable through each port and consults the destination MAC when forwarding/filtering a frame. C names the relevant link addresses. IP, transport ports and TTL belong to higher-layer packet/segment processing, not the ordinary bridge forwarding decision. Unknown destinations may be flooded, so learning does not imply always-one-port forwarding.

evidence.quote: It learns source-MAC-to-port mappings, looks up the destination, forwards a known unicast to its port

choices.label: A
choices.explanation: Destination IP prefixes drive routing, not ordinary layer-2 bridge frame forwarding.

choices.label: B
choices.explanation: Transport ports identify process endpoints and are not the bridge MAC-table lookup key.

choices.label: C
choices.explanation: Source MAC informs learning and destination MAC informs forwarding/filtering to the appropriate segment.

choices.label: D
choices.explanation: TTL is an IP header field used in routed packet lifetime, not ordinary bridging.

reviews.answer_text: Reserved bandwidth can be wasted during silence
reviews.hint: Read Circuit, message and packet switching; apply the relevant definition or calculation.
reviews.explanation: Circuit switching holds resources for the call even while endpoints are silent, so unused reservation cannot be statistically shared as packet traffic would be. B gives that cost. The note does not identify inherent out-of-order packet delivery or inability to carry voice; traditional telephone calls are its standard circuit example.

evidence.quote: Predictable allocated bandwidth trades against setup/blocking and wasted reservation during silence.

choices.label: A
choices.explanation: Reserved circuits can offer predictable transfer behavior; setup cost is distinct from universally high transfer latency.

choices.label: B
choices.explanation: Capacity remains reserved during silence and can be wasted when no data is sent.

choices.label: C
choices.explanation: Independent out-of-order packet routing is not the defining reserved-circuit disadvantage.

choices.label: D
choices.explanation: Traditional telephone calls are the note’s standard circuit-switching example, so voice is supported.

reviews.answer_text: Microwave and infrared under the conventional line-of-sight assumption
reviews.hint: Read Cables, wireless and connectors; apply the relevant definition or calculation.
reviews.explanation: The intended textbook contrast is directional microwave and infrared paths, both obstructed by unsuitable visibility/solid barriers. D combines those choices. NET07 warns that microwaves are themselves radio waves and propagation depends on antennas/path conditions, so this is not a universal claim that every radio link behaves differently or every microwave path needs direct visual sight.

evidence.quote: line-of-sight paths require suitable visibility. Microwaves are radio waves in the broader physical classification. Infrared generally does not penetrate walls.

choices.label: A
choices.explanation: Radio is a broad category with several propagation modes; it is not uniquely limited to the stated line-of-sight paths.

choices.label: B
choices.explanation: Conventional directional microwave links need suitable path visibility and can be blocked by terrain/buildings.

choices.label: C
choices.explanation: Infrared generally does not penetrate walls, matching the obstructed-path description.

choices.label: D
choices.explanation: Both B and C fit the conventional line-of-sight/obstruction comparison, making the aggregate inclusive.

reviews.answer_text: Classless Inter-Domain Routing; flexible prefixes reduce rigid class allocation waste
reviews.hint: Read Point-to-point links and route aggregation; apply the relevant definition or calculation.
reviews.explanation: NET28 gives the exact expansion and says CIDR replaces rigid class allocation. Flexible prefixes allow blocks sized to requirements and aggregation of aligned blocks, addressing waste from fixed historical class sizes. The other expansions are incorrect and their proposed packet-loss, loop or latency cures are not the defined purpose.

evidence.quote: CIDR, Classless Inter-Domain Routing, replaces rigid class allocation and supports aggregation.

choices.label: A
choices.explanation: This gives the correct expansion and relates flexible prefix allocation to avoiding rigid class-size waste.

choices.label: B
choices.explanation: Classful Internet Domain Routing is the wrong expansion, and CIDR is not defined as a packet-loss cure.

choices.label: C
choices.explanation: Centralized IP Domain Routing is not the acronym expansion or the stated mechanism.

choices.label: D
choices.explanation: Classless Internet Data Routing is incorrect; CIDR is not defined as a general WAN-latency cure.

reviews.answer_text: 32 subnets
reviews.hint: Read Borrow bits and choose a mask; apply the relevant definition or calculation.
reviews.explanation: Borrowing five bits yields 2^5=32 equal subnets under modern counting. The parent Class B /16 would become /21, but the direct subnet count only needs the specified five borrowed bits. NET26 says not to subtract two subnets under modern practice.

evidence.quote: To split parent /a into equal /p blocks, borrow b=p-a bits and obtain 2^b subnets.

choices.label: A
choices.explanation: Five is the number of borrowed bits, not the exponential number of resulting subnet combinations.

choices.label: B
choices.explanation: Sixteen subnets would use four borrowed bits rather than five.

choices.label: C
choices.explanation: Five borrowed bits have 32 distinct combinations and therefore produce 32 subnets.

choices.label: D
choices.explanation: Sixty-four subnets would require six borrowed bits.

reviews.answer_text: MAC table
reviews.hint: Read Bridges, switches and access points; apply the relevant definition or calculation.
reviews.explanation: The bridge forwarding database records MAC-to-port associations learned from source addresses and used for destination lookups. MAC table is therefore the matching name. A routing table maps IP prefixes to next hops; ARP associates on-link IPv4 addresses with link addresses. Those are different tables even if one device maintains several of them.

evidence.quote: It learns source-MAC-to-port mappings

choices.label: A
choices.explanation: Routing tables describe destination IP prefixes and next hops rather than bridge MAC-to-port mappings.

choices.label: B
choices.explanation: ARP caches associate IPv4 next hops with link addresses, not MAC addresses with bridge ports.

choices.label: C
choices.explanation: The bridge’s learned source-MAC-to-port forwarding database is its MAC table.

choices.label: D
choices.explanation: IP table does not name the layer-2 learned MAC forwarding database described in NET10.

reviews.answer_text: Physical layer
reviews.hint: Read NICs, repeaters and hubs and retain its scope qualifications.
reviews.explanation: Voltage, cable/interface characteristics and signal transport are the physical-layer scope in NET09. Data-link functions operate on frames and MAC access, network handles IP routing and transport handles process delivery. The wording explicitly asks how bits are physically represented and carried, so C is the corresponding layer.

evidence.quote: Physical specifications include connectors, signaling, voltage, timing and physical coding/modulation

choices.label: A
choices.explanation: Data link manages frames/access rather than defining the physical voltage and cable interface.

choices.label: B
choices.explanation: Network manages logical addressing/routing rather than electrical signal specifications.

choices.label: C
choices.explanation: Physical-layer specifications include connectors, signaling, voltage and timing.

choices.label: D
choices.explanation: Transport supplies process delivery rather than cable and voltage definitions.

reviews.answer_text: The dependent star loses connectivity when its center fails
reviews.hint: Read Topology and failure reasoning and retain its scope qualifications.
reviews.explanation: In a basic star every endpoint depends on the central hub for communication with other endpoints. Failure of that common center therefore affects the whole star. No alternate center or automatic topology reconfiguration is specified; the network does not become a bus or ring merely because the hub stops functioning.

evidence.quote: Star connects endpoints through a central device: one edge failure isolates that endpoint, whereas central failure affects the star.

choices.label: A
choices.explanation: The center serves all star endpoints, so its failure is not limited to the nearest neighbor.

choices.label: B
choices.explanation: All endpoints depend on the central hub, so the basic star loses inter-endpoint connectivity.

choices.label: C
choices.explanation: A hub failure does not physically or logically rewire the star into an operational bus.

choices.label: D
choices.explanation: No automatic ring reconnection mechanism follows from the basic star topology.

reviews.answer_text: Thermal noise
reviews.hint: Read Delay, impairments and transmission modes and retain its scope qualifications.
reviews.explanation: The stated cause—random motion associated with temperature—is thermal noise in NET06. Crosstalk is neighboring-channel coupling and impulse noise is a short disturbance. D names a different noise phenomenon not defined by random thermal motion. The cause identifies C without requiring a claim that all other real noise can be perfectly eliminated.

evidence.quote: thermal noise comes from random thermal motion

choices.label: A
choices.explanation: Crosstalk arises from coupling between nearby communication channels, not the stated thermal-motion cause.

choices.label: B
choices.explanation: Impulse noise is a short disturbance rather than persistent random thermal motion.

choices.label: C
choices.explanation: Thermal noise is explicitly caused by random thermal motion, matching the temperature-dependent clue.

choices.label: D
choices.explanation: This option does not match the random thermal-motion definition supplied in NET06.

reviews.answer_text: Class B
reviews.hint: Read IPv4 notation and classful defaults and retain its scope qualifications.
reviews.explanation: NET22 gives first-octet 128–191 for historical Class B, corresponding to leading bits 10. Ordinary Class A is 1–126, Class C is 192–223 and Class D uses leading 1110 for multicast. Since the question explicitly asks classes, the historical categorization is appropriate rather than inferring a current CIDR prefix.

evidence.quote: B spans 128–191 and C 192–223.

choices.label: A
choices.explanation: Ordinary historical Class A uses first octets 1–126 rather than 128–191.

choices.label: B
choices.explanation: Historical Class B spans first octets 128–191, with leading bits 10.

choices.label: C
choices.explanation: Historical Class C spans 192–223, above the supplied interval.

choices.label: D
choices.explanation: Class D multicast begins with 1110, outside the Class B 128–191 interval.

reviews.answer_text: Checkpoint state supports resuming after interruption
reviews.hint: Read Upper layers and the TCP/IP correspondence and retain its scope qualifications.
reviews.explanation: A checkpoint records recoverable progress/state so interrupted work can resume from an agreed point. NET19 assigns such coordination to the session role. Encryption, compression and encoding translation belong to representation handling and do not by themselves preserve resumable dialog progress. C matches the checkpoint recovery purpose.

evidence.quote: OSI session roles establish/manage dialogs and can coordinate checkpoints so transfer resumes after interruption.

choices.label: A
choices.explanation: Encryption conceals content and does not define saving resumable session progress.

choices.label: B
choices.explanation: Compression reduces representation size rather than recording recovery checkpoints.

choices.label: C
choices.explanation: Saving agreed progress/state enables continuation after interruption rather than restarting from the beginning.

choices.label: D
choices.explanation: Encoding translation changes representation format, not checkpoint recovery state.

reviews.answer_text: A formally approved standard
reviews.hint: Read Protocols, standards and layers and retain its scope qualifications.
reviews.explanation: NET03 defines de jure by formal approval. B directly states official approval, while industry adoption without that approval is de facto. Corporate origin does not alone decide status, but C specifically lacks formal approval and D emphasizes informal use. Therefore B is the option establishing the defining approval condition.

evidence.quote: De facto means established through use; de jure means formally approved.

choices.label: A
choices.explanation: Widespread adoption alone demonstrates de facto use rather than formal de jure approval.

choices.label: B
choices.explanation: Official approval matches the defining de jure criterion in NET03.

choices.label: C
choices.explanation: A corporate format without the stated formal approval does not meet the offered de jure definition.

choices.label: D
choices.explanation: Widespread informal use without formal approval is de facto rather than de jure.

reviews.answer_text: More conductors and interline impairments
reviews.hint: Read Delay, impairments and transmission modes and retain its scope qualifications.
reviews.explanation: Parallel transfer needs several conductors to carry simultaneous bits. Those paths can experience skew and neighboring-channel coupling, as NET06’s impairment definitions explain. C states the extra-line and interference burden. No universal slower-speed claim, inability to carry digital data or fiber-only restriction follows from parallel transmission.

evidence.quote: Serial sends sequential bits; parallel uses multiple conductors and may suffer skew.

choices.label: A
choices.explanation: Parallel is not universally slower; performance depends on implementation, distance and synchronization.

choices.label: B
choices.explanation: Parallel transmission can carry digital bits simultaneously, exactly as the stem states.

choices.label: C
choices.explanation: Multiple conductors add wiring and can suffer skew or coupled interference between adjacent lines.

choices.label: D
choices.explanation: Parallel transmission is not restricted to fiber and commonly concerns multiple electrical conductors.

reviews.answer_text: Variable delay and packet loss can disturb real-time audio
reviews.hint: Read Circuit, message and packet switching and retain its scope qualifications.
reviews.explanation: Real-time audio is sensitive to late or missing data. Packet networks may introduce variable queueing delay and loss, so B gives a plausible suitability issue. NET31 explicitly says modern voice over packets remains possible with buffering, scheduling and capacity planning; it is not intrinsically prohibited or dependent on reserved circuits.

evidence.quote: Packet switching divides data into packets that share links statistically; queueing can add variable delay and loss.

choices.label: A
choices.explanation: Datagram packet switching does not require a dedicated circuit before every communication.

choices.label: B
choices.explanation: Variable queueing latency and loss can make audio arrive late or incomplete.

choices.label: C
choices.explanation: NET31 explicitly allows voice over packets with suitable engineering.

choices.label: D
choices.explanation: Statistical link sharing differs from reserving all bandwidth for established circuits.

reviews.answer_text: 30 usable hosts
reviews.hint: Read Find subnet bounds and usable hosts and retain its scope qualifications.
reviews.explanation: A /27 leaves five host bits regardless of the historical class of its parent. Those bits provide 32 total addresses. On an ordinary broadcast subnet, network and broadcast reserve two, leaving 30 usable host addresses. Parent classification matters for subnet counting, not this explicit-prefix host calculation.

evidence.quote: /27 gives 32 total and 30 usable, not 32 usable.

choices.label: A
choices.explanation: Thirty-two is the total address count before reserving network and broadcast.

choices.label: B
choices.explanation: Five host bits give 32−2=30 ordinary usable hosts.

choices.label: C
choices.explanation: Twenty-eight does not follow from the stated five host bits and two standard reservations.

choices.label: D
choices.explanation: Sixty-two usable hosts corresponds to /26 rather than the supplied /27.

reviews.answer_text: Anycast
reviews.hint: Read Routing algorithms and destination sets and retain its scope qualifications.
reviews.explanation: Anycast routes to one member of a set sharing the address, typically the nearest by routing metrics. That is not necessarily geographic distance. Multicast targets a subscribed group, broadcast all in scope and ordinary unicast a single designated destination. D uniquely matches the shared-address nearest-member rule.

evidence.quote: anycast one member sharing an address, normally nearest under routing metrics.

choices.label: A
choices.explanation: Multicast targets a subscribed group rather than selecting only one nearest shared-address member.

choices.label: B
choices.explanation: Broadcast targets all destinations within its scope, not the nearest member.

choices.label: C
choices.explanation: Ordinary unicast targets one designated destination without the shared-address nearest-member semantics.

choices.label: D
choices.explanation: Anycast selects one shared-address member, normally nearest according to routing metrics.

reviews.answer_text: The conductor and shield share an axis
reviews.hint: Read Cables, wireless and connectors and retain its scope qualifications.
reviews.explanation: The name coaxial refers to a common geometric axis for the inner conductor and surrounding shield. NET07 states this directly. Neither identical material, opposite signal directions nor a particular insulation covering defines the term; those are separate construction or usage details rather than the shared-axis relationship.

evidence.quote: Coax has an inner conductor and outer shield sharing an axis.

choices.label: A
choices.explanation: The definition concerns geometric arrangement, not whether both conductive parts use the same material.

choices.label: B
choices.explanation: The inner conductor and outer shield share a central axis, giving the coaxial name.

choices.label: C
choices.explanation: Opposite signal directions are not the defining common-axis geometry.

choices.label: D
choices.explanation: Insulation details do not define coaxial; sharing an axis does.

reviews.answer_text: Default IP gateway and protocol-translating gateway are different senses
reviews.hint: Read Routers, gateways and traffic controls and retain its scope qualifications.
reviews.explanation: C describes a protocol gateway joining unlike systems, while B can describe a default IP gateway/router joining networks that both use IP. NET11 explicitly distinguishes these meanings and rejects a single universal all-layer device definition. Since the stem says only gateway, best depends on which functional sense is intended.

evidence.quote: A default gateway is usually a router, while a protocol gateway can translate application formats

choices.label: A
choices.explanation: Signal regeneration/strength extension is a repeater function rather than either gateway meaning defined here.

choices.label: B
choices.explanation: A default IP gateway/router can connect networks using the same IP protocol.

choices.label: C
choices.explanation: A protocol gateway can translate between unlike protocols/formats, matching this sense of gateway.

choices.label: D
choices.explanation: MAC-address frame filtering describes bridging/switching rather than the gateway distinction in NET11.

reviews.answer_text: 10.0.0.0 under the explicitly requested Class A default
reviews.hint: Read IPv4 notation and classful defaults and retain its scope qualifications.
reviews.explanation: Because the question explicitly assigns Class A, its historical default /8 supplies the intended network/host boundary. Keep first octet 10 and zero the remaining 24 host bits to obtain 10.0.0.0. If a different CIDR prefix were supplied it would override the default, but none is given in this class-specific question.

evidence.quote: Historical classes use leading patterns: A 0 with /8

choices.label: A
choices.explanation: The Class A /8 default keeps first octet 10 and clears the remaining three octets.

choices.label: B
choices.explanation: This assumes a /16 boundary instead of the explicitly invoked Class A /8 default.

choices.label: C
choices.explanation: This assumes /24, retaining host bits that the Class A default would clear.

choices.label: D
choices.explanation: Clearing the network octet too loses the assigned Class A network identifier 10.

reviews.answer_text: EMI and crosstalk
reviews.hint: Read Cables, wireless and connectors and retain its scope qualifications.
reviews.explanation: UTP is unshielded copper: twisting reduces coupled interference but does not remove all electromagnetic coupling. NET06 identifies crosstalk as leakage from nearby channels. B names the relevant ordinary interference types, whereas thermal-only excludes other sources and infrared/gamma are not the note’s cabling-susceptibility mechanism.

evidence.quote: Twisted pairs reduce coupled interference; UTP has no added shield and STP adds shielding.

choices.label: A
choices.explanation: Thermal noise is not the only impairment; unshielded pairs can experience coupled electromagnetic interference.

choices.label: B
choices.explanation: EMI and adjacent-pair/channel crosstalk are relevant to unshielded copper, though twisting reduces coupling.

choices.label: C
choices.explanation: Infrared is an optical/unguided signaling category rather than the stated ordinary copper-coupling issue.

choices.label: D
choices.explanation: Gamma radiation is not the interference mechanism identified for UTP in the supplied note.

reviews.answer_text: Hub repeats signals; switch learns MAC ports and may forward or flood
reviews.hint: Read Bridges, switches and access points and retain its scope qualifications.
reviews.explanation: B is the intended simplification but its “only” is false: switches flood unknown unicasts and broadcasts within a VLAN. The supported distinction is a hub repeating signals versus a switch learning MAC-to-port mappings and making conditional forwarding decisions. A/C/D also contain false layer/address/media claims. The options omit that correctly qualified contrast.

evidence.quote: A switch does not always send only to one destination port.

choices.label: A
choices.explanation: Hubs are layer-1 repeaters, not layer-3 routers; ordinary switches are layer 2.

choices.label: B
choices.explanation: Switches can flood broadcasts and unknown unicasts, so only the intended device is an invalid absolute.

choices.label: C
choices.explanation: Hubs do not use IP addresses to decide forwarding; they repeat signals without address inspection.

choices.label: D
choices.explanation: A fiber-versus-switch prohibition is not established; switch roles are not restricted by this media contrast.

reviews.answer_text: A subscribed/interested receiver group
reviews.hint: Read Routing algorithms and destination sets and retain its scope qualifications.
reviews.explanation: NET30 distinguishes multicast group delivery from unicast, broadcast and anycast. Receivers express membership/interest in a group, rather than every network device receiving by definition or only one nearest destination being selected. D matches that destination-set meaning. Delivery still depends on the deployed network’s forwarding and membership mechanisms.

evidence.quote: Unicast targets one destination, broadcast all in a scope, multicast a subscribed group and anycast one member sharing an address, normally nearest under routing metrics.

choices.label: A
choices.explanation: All devices regardless of interest describes broadcast scope rather than multicast group selection.

choices.label: B
choices.explanation: One specific destination is ordinary unicast rather than a receiver group.

choices.label: C
choices.explanation: One nearest shared-address member is anycast.

choices.label: D
choices.explanation: Multicast targets a subscribed group of receivers that expressed interest.

reviews.answer_text: Class D
reviews.hint: Read IPv4 notation and classful defaults and retain its scope qualifications.
reviews.explanation: Historical IPv4 Class D begins with bits 1110 and is designated for multicast. Classes A, B and C describe historical unicast network allocations, with differing default prefixes. The question explicitly asks that historical class designation, so D is supported independently of how modern unicast prefixes are allocated.

evidence.quote: D 1110 is multicast and E 1111 reserved.

choices.label: A
choices.explanation: Class A is historical unicast network space rather than the multicast class.

choices.label: B
choices.explanation: Class B is historical unicast space with a /16 default, not multicast.

choices.label: C
choices.explanation: Class C is historical unicast space with a /24 default.

choices.label: D
choices.explanation: Class D, identified by leading 1110, is designated for IPv4 multicast.

reviews.answer_text: Reliable link procedures and TCP transport can both supply these mechanisms
reviews.hint: Read Access control and reliable-link procedures and retain its scope qualifications.
reviews.explanation: The listed sequence, ACK and flow-control mechanisms occur in reliable link procedures and TCP transport. NET14 gives sequence bits and acknowledgments for stop-and-wait/sliding windows; NET17 gives TCP sequencing/ACKs/windows. The question omits hop-local versus end-to-end scope, so B and C both fit. Reliability is protocol-dependent rather than guaranteed by every layer-4 protocol.

evidence.quote: Link reliability/flow control is hop-local; transport reliability/flow control is end-to-end.

choices.label: A
choices.explanation: IP is best effort and does not supply the listed reliable acknowledgment/retransmission service.

choices.label: B
choices.explanation: Reliable link protocols can use sequencing, ACKs and hop-local flow control.

choices.label: C
choices.explanation: TCP transport uses sequence numbers, acknowledgments and flow-control windows end to end.

choices.label: D
choices.explanation: Session manages dialogs/checkpoints rather than the specifically listed link/TCP reliability machinery.

reviews.hint: Read Find subnet bounds and usable hosts and retain its scope qualifications.
reviews.explanation: A /26 has blocks of 64 addresses. Starting at .64, this block runs through .127; the final address has all six host bits one and is broadcast. .65 and .126 are ordinary first/last hosts. .255 belongs to another /26 block, so it is not this subnet’s broadcast.

choices.label: A
choices.explanation: 192.168.2.65 is the first usable host, not the all-host-bits-one address.

choices.label: B
choices.explanation: 192.168.2.126 is the last usable host, one address below broadcast.

choices.label: C
choices.explanation: The .64–.127 /26 block ends at .127, its directed broadcast.

choices.label: D
choices.explanation: The .255 address is outside this .64–.127 subnet block.

reviews.answer_text: SMTP submits and relays email
reviews.hint: Read Web, file, mail and remote-login protocols and retain its scope qualifications.
reviews.explanation: NET21 assigns SMTP mail submission and relay. A client sending a message to a mail server is therefore a correct SMTP role. DNS resolves names, HTTP serves web requests and FTP transfers files. This does not assign end-user mailbox retrieval to SMTP; POP3/IMAP serve that separate task.

evidence.quote: SMTP submits and relays mail

choices.label: A
choices.explanation: DNS resolves domain names to address records rather than SMTP.

choices.label: B
choices.explanation: HTTP governs web requests/responses, not SMTP.

choices.label: C
choices.explanation: SMTP submits mail from a client to a server and relays messages between mail servers.

choices.label: D
choices.explanation: File transfer is the FTP service role in this comparison, not SMTP’s defining mail role.

reviews.answer_text: 360-degree azimuth coverage, with a nonuniform vertical pattern
reviews.hint: Read Cables, wireless and connectors and retain its scope qualifications.
reviews.explanation: NET07 defines omnidirectional as broad azimuth coverage. C is correct when its 360 degrees refers to the horizontal plane, not equal power in every three-dimensional direction. Directional beams or upward-only radiation do not describe this pattern. Antenna elevation patterns can still have lobes/nulls, so the answer retains that scope qualification.

evidence.quote: omnidirectional means broad azimuth coverage, not equal radiation in every 3-D direction.

choices.label: A
choices.explanation: A narrow targeted beam is directional rather than omnidirectional azimuth coverage.

choices.label: B
choices.explanation: Upward-only radiation does not provide the broad around-the-antenna azimuth pattern.

choices.label: C
choices.explanation: 360-degree azimuth coverage is the intended meaning, without asserting equal power in all three-dimensional directions.

choices.label: D
choices.explanation: A single focused path describes a directional antenna pattern.

reviews.answer_text: Uniformity
reviews.hint: Distinguish even distribution from repeatable mapping.
reviews.explanation: DSA25 defines uniformity as spreading expected keys evenly among addresses. That directly matches the question’s wording. Determinism is a different obligation: repeated equal keys receive the same address for the chosen function. Continuity and data normalization do not name this distribution property, so only Uniformity answers the literal stem.

evidence.quote: Determinism means repeated equal keys get the same address for the chosen function. Uniformity means expected keys spread evenly.

choices.label: A
choices.explanation: Uniformity describes spreading expected input keys evenly across the output address range, exactly as the stem requires.

choices.label: B
choices.explanation: Determinism requires repeated equal keys to map identically; it does not require an even address distribution.

choices.label: C
choices.explanation: Continuity is not the key-distribution property defined for hash functions in DSA25.

choices.label: D
choices.explanation: Data normalization does not name the even-distribution requirement of a hash function.

reviews.answer_text: Queue
reviews.hint: Read how BFS keeps pending vertices in distance layers.
reviews.explanation: DSA41 repeatedly dequeues a vertex and enqueues its undiscovered neighbors. FIFO ordering ensures earlier distance layers are processed before later ones. Arrays or linked nodes can store this frontier, but Queue names its required access discipline. A stack instead serves latest pending work. The saved source image confirms the literal options without adding another algorithm.

evidence.quote: FIFO ensures vertices at distance d are explored before later distance layers.

choices.label: A
choices.explanation: A stack serves the latest pending vertex first and does not preserve BFS distance-layer order.

choices.label: B
choices.explanation: An array can store a queue, but an array alone specifies no FIFO frontier discipline.

choices.label: C
choices.explanation: Linked nodes can represent a queue, but Linked List alone does not specify breadth-first processing.

choices.label: D
choices.explanation: A FIFO queue processes discovered vertices by distance layer, the standard BFS frontier rule.

reviews.answer_text: O(N²), tightly Θ(N²)
reviews.hint: Include the cost of each indexed access in a LinkedList.
reviews.explanation: The loop visits about N/2 even indices, but LinkedList.get(i) walks from the nearer endpoint. A linear number of those indices lie near the middle, each requiring linear traversal. DSA07 analyzes exactly this access pattern and obtains Θ(N²) total work. Incrementing by two changes a constant factor, not the quadratic order.

evidence.quote: Summing get(0), get(2), get(4), … over a length-N list still gives Theta(N²), because a linear number of middle indices each require linear traversal.

choices.label: A
choices.explanation: O(N) would require constant-cost indexed access; LinkedList.get(i) instead traverses nodes.

choices.label: B
choices.explanation: A growing number of accesses and additions prevents a constant bound on total work.

choices.label: C
choices.explanation: A linear number of middle-index accesses each traverse a linear number of nodes, yielding quadratic time.

choices.label: D
choices.explanation: Neither the iteration count nor the accumulated linked-node traversal has logarithmic growth.

choices.label: E
choices.explanation: Quadratic traversal grows faster than N log N, so this is not a valid upper bound.

reviews.answer_text: Specify optimal-BST construction versus searching, and the case.
reviews.hint: Separate probability-optimal construction from searching by tree height.
reviews.explanation: DSA19 gives search cost O(height), with constant root hits and possible linear chains. An optimal BST minimizes probability-weighted expected search cost, not necessarily height. Its standard construction is cubic, absent from these options. The inspected image still says only time complexity; its displayed logarithmic answer supplies no missing operation, probability model, or case.

evidence.quote: An optimal BST minimizes expected search cost using access probabilities; constructing it is a different problem from searching it.

choices.label: A
choices.explanation: Linear worst-case search can occur in a chain; the stem does not identify an operation or analysis case.

choices.label: B
choices.explanation: Quadratic is a loose search bound but not the standard cubic construction complexity described in the note.

choices.label: C
choices.explanation: Logarithmic search requires a suitable height; probability-optimal does not universally mean height-balanced.

choices.label: D
choices.explanation: Factorial is a loose bound for several interpretations, not a uniquely justified tight complexity here.

reviews.answer_text: Stack conversion and expression-tree conversion are both possible.
reviews.hint: Compare pending-operator stacks with expression-tree preorder.
reviews.explanation: DSA13 supports an operator stack for precedence and parentheses, but also explains expression trees whose preorder emits prefix notation. Thus Stack is conventional and Binary tree is another offered representation. The word required specifies no conversion algorithm that would make either structure uniquely mandatory. Queue and Linked list alone do not supply the missing grouping discipline.

evidence.quote: Build an expression tree for either prefix (preorder) or postfix (postorder); a stack is useful but is not the only possible conversion representation.

choices.label: A
choices.explanation: A stack manages pending operators and parentheses in conventional expression-conversion algorithms.

choices.label: B
choices.explanation: FIFO storage alone does not describe how to maintain operator precedence and grouping during prefix conversion.

choices.label: C
choices.explanation: An expression binary tree records grouping and yields prefix notation through preorder traversal.

choices.label: D
choices.explanation: A linked list alone provides storage links without an operator-grouping or conversion rule.

reviews.answer_text: Three: best, average, worst.
reviews.hint: Read the ordinary equal-size input-case classification.
reviews.explanation: DSA05 names best, average, and worst as the ordinary cases for comparing costs on inputs of equal size. Average additionally needs an input distribution. Counting these cases gives three. This is a classification of input cases, rather than a count of resources, data structures, or asymptotic bound notations.

evidence.quote: Best, average and worst compare equal-size inputs; average needs a distribution.

choices.label: A
choices.explanation: Two omits one of the three named categories: best, average, and worst case.

choices.label: B
choices.explanation: The note lists three ordinary fixed-size input cases: best, average, and worst.

choices.label: C
choices.explanation: Four does not match the three ordinary input-case categories listed in DSA05.

choices.label: D
choices.explanation: Five adds categories outside the stated best, average, and worst input-case classification.

reviews.answer_text: Worst case
reviews.hint: Choose the maximum cost among inputs of equal size.
reviews.explanation: DSA05 distinguishes best, average, and worst over inputs of the same size. Worst selects the largest runtime; best selects the smallest, while average takes an expectation under a distribution. Therefore Worst Case directly matches maximum time. This input-case distinction is independent of whether the resulting cost function is described with O, Ω, or Θ notation.

evidence.quote: Best, average and worst compare equal-size inputs; average needs a distribution.

choices.label: A
choices.explanation: Worst case takes the maximum operation cost over valid inputs of the same size.

choices.label: B
choices.explanation: Average case computes an expected cost under a distribution instead of selecting the maximum.

choices.label: C
choices.explanation: Best case selects the minimum cost, the opposite extremum from the question.

choices.label: D
choices.explanation: Worst Case is offered and directly identifies the requested maximum-time input case.

reviews.answer_text: No exclusive characteristics taxonomy is defined.
reviews.hint: Separate correctness obligations from cost measures and undefined classification terms.
reviews.explanation: DSA04 warns that omission from a teaching list does not make a characteristic false. Correctness and resource costs are legitimate concerns, but the stem never defines Completeness in this context or supplies an exhaustive characteristics list. Therefore the note cannot establish one uniquely false characteristic. Selecting Completeness solely because its name is unfamiliar would be unsupported.

evidence.quote: An unfamiliar characteristic is not false merely because a teaching list omits it.

choices.label: A
choices.explanation: Completeness is undefined in this classification; its omission from the note does not establish that it is invalid.

choices.label: B
choices.explanation: Correctness concerns meeting specified results and is a legitimate obligation for operations on a structure.

choices.label: C
choices.explanation: Time complexity measures the cost of operations and is a relevant resource characteristic.

choices.label: D
choices.explanation: Space complexity measures memory consumption and is a relevant resource characteristic.

reviews.answer_text: Radix sort is a conditional candidate; key assumptions are missing.
reviews.hint: Check digit count, radix, and key accessibility before applying radix-sort costs.
reviews.explanation: DSA39 gives radix sorting O(d(n+r)) time and extra O(n+r) storage. This can be efficient for large eligible datasets, but the stem specifies neither accessible digits nor key length or radix. Large size alone therefore does not prove its efficiency. The other methods normally use constant extra element storage, making Radix the likely intended but incompletely qualified choice.

evidence.quote: With d digits and radix r, counting-based passes take O(d(n+r)) time and O(n+r) auxiliary storage.

choices.label: A
choices.explanation: Ordinary bubble sort uses constant extra element storage and quadratic average or worst work.

choices.label: B
choices.explanation: Ordinary selection sort uses constant extra element storage, failing the extra-memory distinction.

choices.label: C
choices.explanation: Radix sort uses extra storage and can be efficient when digit accessibility, lengths, and radix meet its assumptions.

choices.label: D
choices.explanation: Ordinary array insertion sort uses constant extra element storage and can require quadratic shifts.

reviews.answer_text: Strings are comparable; the premise does not identify a unique method.
reviews.hint: Distinguish lexicographic comparisons from digit-based key processing.
reviews.explanation: DSA39 explicitly states that strings are lexicographically comparable. Bubble, selection, and merge sorting can consequently sort them with comparisons. Radix sorting can use characters as digits under explicit encoding and length conventions. If the keys really lack both comparisons and accessible digit structure, no ordering method follows from the stem. The misleading string example prevents a unique justified answer.

evidence.quote: Strings are lexicographically comparable. Radix methods require accessible digits and length/signed-value conventions, not arbitrary unstructured keys.

choices.label: A
choices.explanation: Bubble sort can compare strings lexicographically; genuinely non-comparable keys would require an additional ordering rule.

choices.label: B
choices.explanation: Selection sort can select lexicographically smallest strings, so the example does not exclude it.

choices.label: C
choices.explanation: Merge sort can merge lexicographically sorted strings and is not excluded by string-valued keys.

choices.label: D
choices.explanation: Radix sort can use characters as digits with defined encoding and length conventions, absent from the stem.

reviews.answer_text: Sorting using external storage such as disk or tape.
reviews.hint: Read how external sorting builds and merges buffered runs.
reviews.explanation: DSA37 defines external sorting through datasets beyond main memory and buffered disk runs. Option A captures this distinguishing external-storage use. Main memory may still hold buffers, but using it alone does not define external sorting. Swapping and being in place are separate implementation properties and do not identify whether the working dataset resides externally.

evidence.quote: External sorting builds sorted runs and merges buffered streams from disk, aiming to reduce I/O.

choices.label: A
choices.explanation: Tape or disk stores external runs when the working dataset does not fit wholly in main memory.

choices.label: B
choices.explanation: Main-memory use alone does not distinguish external sorting; external algorithms also use memory for buffers.

choices.label: C
choices.explanation: Swapping is an operation used by many sorts and does not define external storage use.

choices.label: D
choices.explanation: In-place concerns auxiliary element storage, independently of whether sorting accesses an external dataset.

reviews.answer_text: O(n²) under the usual average-case model.
reviews.hint: Read repeated adjacent-pass costs and distinguish average from best case.
reviews.explanation: DSA32 identifies quadratic average and worst work from repeated adjacent comparisons. Under the usual random-permutation average model, bubble sort therefore takes Θ(n²), which implies O(n²). Early stopping makes an already sorted input linear, but that is the optimized best case rather than the ordinary average over input arrangements.

evidence.quote: Quadratic worst/average work comes from up to n(n-1)/2 pair comparisons.

choices.label: A
choices.explanation: Quadratic average work grows faster than n log n, so this bound is too small.

choices.label: B
choices.explanation: Repeated adjacent passes do not have logarithmic average growth under the usual input model.

choices.label: C
choices.explanation: Linear work is the optimized sorted-input best case, not ordinary average-case bubble sorting.

choices.label: D
choices.explanation: Quadratic average work is bounded by O(n²), matching the adjacent-pass analysis in DSA32.

reviews.answer_text: Linear merge sort is nonstandard terminology; a naming convention is needed.
reviews.hint: Distinguish recursive and iterative sorting from the linear merge operation.
reviews.explanation: DSA37 recognizes top-down, bottom-up, and in-place merging variants. It describes linear merge as an operation, not a universally standardized sort-variant name. Thus D is a plausible terminology exclusion, but the question supplies no exhaustive naming convention making it uniquely invalid. The absence of a standardized name is weaker than proof that no such variant can exist.

evidence.quote: In-place merging variants exist with different tradeoffs; linear merge names an operation, not a universally standardized sort variant.

choices.label: A
choices.explanation: In-place merging variants exist, although their runtime and storage tradeoffs differ from ordinary buffered merge sort.

choices.label: B
choices.explanation: Bottom-up merge sort iteratively merges runs of increasing widths and is explicitly recognized in DSA37.

choices.label: C
choices.explanation: Top-down merge sort recursively splits and sorts halves before combining them, a recognized variant.

choices.label: D
choices.explanation: This is not a standardized variant name; uniquely excluding it requires a supplied naming convention.

reviews.answer_text: Standard quicksort is unstable.
reviews.hint: Compare partition exchanges with strict adjacent swaps and left-first merge ties.
reviews.explanation: The DSA31 sorting table identifies quicksort as unstable. Cocktail and bubble sorts preserve equal-key order when swapping only strict adjacent inversions. Ordinary merge sort preserves equal-key order when ties are taken from the left run first. Under these usual implementations, quicksort is the single listed algorithm that does not guarantee stability.

evidence.quote: stack usually log n average, n worst; unstable

choices.label: A
choices.explanation: Standard quicksort partition exchanges can move equal keys past one another and do not guarantee stability.

choices.label: B
choices.explanation: Cocktail sort is stable with strict adjacent swaps, as described in DSA32.

choices.label: C
choices.explanation: Bubble sort preserves equal-key order when it swaps only strict adjacent inversions.

choices.label: D
choices.explanation: Merge sort preserves equal-key order by taking equal elements from the left run first.

reviews.answer_text: No universally most effective pivot rule.
reviews.hint: Compare partition balance, input assumptions, and selection overhead.
reviews.explanation: DSA36 explicitly gives random and median-of-three pivot choices different tradeoffs, with neither universally best. First and last elements may produce repeated extreme splits on structured input. Effectiveness depends on the input distribution, adversarial patterns, and selection overhead. Because no comparison criterion or workload is supplied, the four methods cannot be ranked uniquely.

evidence.quote: Random and median-of-three choices have different tradeoffs; neither is universally best.

choices.label: A
choices.explanation: The first element is cheap to select but may cause highly unbalanced partitions on some inputs.

choices.label: B
choices.explanation: The last element is cheap to select but may repeatedly be an extreme on structured inputs.

choices.label: C
choices.explanation: Median-of-three can improve ordinary balance, but its overhead and adversarial behavior prevent a universal ranking.

choices.label: D
choices.explanation: Random pivots support expected balance under a model but do not universally minimize total practical cost.

reviews.answer_text: Unordered direct search fails the prerequisite; broad application labels need context.
reviews.hint: Check ordered intervals or monotone good/bad boundaries.
reviews.explanation: DSA29 requires ordered search data and restricts binary debugging to an ordered good/bad boundary. Direct search in an unordered list therefore fails the ordinary prerequisite. However, generic debugging and union of intervals also name tasks without stating a monotone or ordered formulation. Their unspecified meanings prevent proving that only one of the literal application claims should be excluded.

evidence.quote: Binary debugging needs an ordered good/bad boundary, not arbitrary fault locations.

choices.label: A
choices.explanation: Binary-search boundary variants can find lower or upper bounds in an ordered sequence.

choices.label: B

choices.label: C

choices.label: D
choices.explanation: Unordered direct search lacks the ordering needed to discard half of the remaining positions safely.

reviews.answer_text: Binary search loses its usual advantage on linked lists.
reviews.hint: Include midpoint-location costs in pointer chains.
reviews.explanation: DSA29 explains that linked midpoint traversal loses logarithmic total time. That makes an ordinary linked list unsuitable for the usual efficient binary-search implementation, although an algorithm can still be written. The other tasks do not require constant-time midpoint access: insertion sort can relink nodes, polynomial terms can occupy nodes, and radix digit buckets can retain stable node sequences.

evidence.quote: Linked midpoint traversal loses logarithmic total time.

choices.label: B

reviews.answer_text: All listed applications.

Without metadata and a cost criterion, an array implementation cannot be declared uniquely best for the nth logical item.

reviews.answer_text: Queue

A linked list may store the queue but does not alone define this ordering; a stack chooses latest pending work and instead supports the depth-first discipline.

Pending interrupts can be buffered for processing; this does not mean every interrupt policy must be FIFO. reviews.answer_text: Array

Singly, doubly, and circular linked lists normally need traversal to logical position n. The damaged all-above option does not change the clear contrast between array indexing and ordinary pointer-chain access.

evidence.quote: This arithmetic gives constant-time positional access in the usual RAM cost model.

choices.label: A
choices.explanation: Singly linked lists reach a logical position by following next links, taking linear worst-case time.

choices.label: B
choices.explanation: Doubly linked lists may start from a nearer endpoint, but arbitrary positional access remains linear in the worst case.

choices.label: C
choices.explanation: The text ONo is garbled, and the all-above claim does not provide a valid constant-access answer.

choices.label: D
choices.explanation: Circular links permit wraparound but do not provide constant-time arbitrary logical-position access.

choices.label: E
choices.explanation: Array address arithmetic gives direct positional access in constant time under the note’s RAM cost model.

reviews.answer_text: Sorting whose working dataset fits in main memory.
reviews.hint: Separate storage location from swapping and in-place behavior.
reviews.explanation: DSA37 defines internal sorting by fitting the working dataset in memory. Option B expresses that main-memory setting. In contrast, external sorting handles disk-backed runs when data exceeds memory. Swapping is an operation used by some algorithms, and in-place describes auxiliary storage; neither determines whether a sort is internal.

evidence.quote: Internal sorting fits the working dataset in memory.

choices.label: A
choices.explanation: Tape or disk working data characterizes external sorting rather than the main-memory internal setting.

choices.label: B
choices.explanation: Internal sorting keeps its working dataset in main memory, matching the definition in DSA37.

choices.label: C
choices.explanation: Swapping is an implementation operation and does not define the location of the working dataset.

choices.label: D
choices.explanation: In-place concerns auxiliary element storage; an internal sort may still use a separate memory buffer.

reviews.answer_text: Both per-key function selection and universal fixed-function superiority are false.
reviews.hint: Read when the random hash function is chosen and what its guarantee means.
reviews.explanation: DSA25 chooses one random family member for the table independently of the fixed key set. It does not choose a fresh unrelated function for every key. Its random choice controls collision probability, so claiming that a single fixed function is universally better for collision reduction is also false. Both A and C fail; B and D describe the intended randomization principle.

evidence.quote: Universal hashing chooses one function randomly from a suitable family for the table, independently of a fixed key set; it does not choose a fresh unrelated function for each lookup.

choices.label: A
choices.explanation: The random function is chosen for the table, not independently for every key, so this statement is false.

choices.label: B
choices.explanation: Choosing the table function independently of the fixed key set is the principle explicitly described in DSA25.

choices.label: C
choices.explanation: No single fixed function is universally superior; random family choice controls collision probability against a fixed key set.

choices.label: D
choices.explanation: Universal hashing controls collision probability rather than guaranteeing zero collisions; this is a valid qualitative benefit.

reviews.answer_text: Stack
reviews.hint: Read the latest-pending-work rule of DFS.
reviews.explanation: DSA42 says DFS recursively explores an unvisited neighbor to completion before returning. The recursive call stack stores return points; an explicit stack can store pending work instead. Both implement latest-pending-work-first order. A queue would change that discipline, while a priority queue or tree alone does not encode the required depth-first frontier behavior.

evidence.quote: An explicit stack can store pending work instead. Both implement latest-pending-work first; a queue would change that discipline.

choices.label: A
choices.explanation: Priority service follows priority keys and does not guarantee finishing the latest active branch first.

choices.label: B
choices.explanation: A tree may represent traversal results, but it does not identify the standard DFS pending-work discipline.

choices.label: C
choices.explanation: FIFO queue order produces breadth-first pending work rather than the required latest-pending-work behavior.

choices.label: D
choices.explanation: A stack, explicit or supplied by recursion, preserves return points and latest-pending-work-first order.

reviews.answer_text: Auxiliary algorithm storage is a plausible intended indirect use; the classification is undefined.
reviews.hint: Read queue applications and identify whether direct versus indirect has been defined.
reviews.explanation: DSA14 supports equal-priority scheduling and real-world waiting, while DSA41 uses a queue inside BFS. Calling algorithmic auxiliary storage indirect is a possible teaching convention, but the note provides no exhaustive direct/indirect taxonomy. Multiprogramming can also involve scheduling queues. The broad labels therefore do not establish one uniquely indirect application without a definition.

evidence.quote: FIFO suits equal-priority printer jobs, shared-resource waiting, asynchronous buffers and level-order exploration.

choices.label: A
choices.explanation: Arrival-order scheduling directly models FIFO waiting, but the note does not assign it a formal direct/indirect category.

choices.label: B
choices.explanation: Real-world line simulation preserves FIFO service, but no formal direct/indirect classification is supplied.

choices.label: C
choices.explanation: BFS auxiliary frontier storage is a plausible indirect application under a teaching convention not defined here.

choices.label: D
choices.explanation: Multiprogramming can involve scheduling queues, but its broad label does not determine a direct/indirect category.

reviews.answer_text: Queue
reviews.hint: Read FIFO layer processing in BFS.
reviews.explanation: DSA41 enqueues discovered neighbors and dequeues the next pending vertex. This FIFO discipline preserves distance-layer ordering. A linked list can store the queue but does not by itself state the policy. Stack service is latest-first, while a binary tree is not the standard frontier discipline. Queue is therefore the specific suitable ADT among the choices.

evidence.quote: FIFO ensures vertices at distance d are explored before later distance layers.

choices.label: A
choices.explanation: Stack order selects the latest pending vertex and does not preserve the BFS layer invariant.

choices.label: B
choices.explanation: Queue FIFO ordering processes earlier distance layers before later discoveries, as BFS requires.

choices.label: C
choices.explanation: A linked list may represent a queue, but linked-list links alone specify no BFS service order.

choices.label: D
choices.explanation: A binary tree does not supply the standard FIFO pending-vertex discipline used by breadth-first search.

reviews.answer_text: Doubly linked lists support both directions; generic linked lists do not promise it.
reviews.hint: Compare next-only nodes with nodes carrying both next and prev.
reviews.explanation: DSA08 defines singly linked nodes using next only. DSA10 adds prev for doubly linked nodes, enabling both-direction traversal. The option merely says Linked list and does not identify this variant. Stacks and queues specify removal policies rather than unrestricted traversal, while tree visitation also needs a defined order. The missing representation and traversal contract prevent a unique literal claim.

evidence.quote: Doubly linked nodes add prev; head and tail enable constant-time operations at both ends.

choices.label: A
choices.explanation: The stack ADT specifies top access and LIFO removal, not a general forward-and-backward traversal interface.

choices.label: B
choices.explanation: The queue ADT specifies FIFO endpoint operations, not unrestricted traversal in both directions.

choices.label: C
choices.explanation: A doubly linked list has next and prev links; a generic singly linked list lacks the backward-link guarantee.

choices.label: D
choices.explanation: Tree traversal can be defined in different orders, but forward and backward require a stated traversal contract.

reviews.answer_text: A stack directly supports DFS; a linked list can implement that stack.
reviews.hint: Separate DFS pending-work discipline from the representations that can implement it.
reviews.explanation: DSA42 uses an explicit or runtime stack to keep the latest unfinished branch pending first. DSA01 permits linked nodes to implement the same LIFO stack, and DSA11 gives constant-time head insertion and deletion for linked stacks. Therefore both A and C satisfy the literal can be used to implement wording. A alone is the conventional answer if the question asks for the frontier ADT rather than its representation.

evidence.quote: Arrays or linked nodes can implement the same LIFO stack.
Linked stacks achieve constant time by inserting and deleting at the head;
An explicit stack can store pending work instead.

choices.label: A
choices.explanation: An explicit stack directly supplies latest-pending-work-first service for depth-first search.

choices.label: B
choices.explanation: Ordinary FIFO queue service changes the DFS frontier order; the question supplies no stack-emulation procedure.

choices.label: C
choices.explanation: A linked list with head insertion and deletion implements the LIFO stack needed by DFS.

choices.label: D
choices.explanation: A tree can be traversal input, but the note supplies no tree-based LIFO frontier implementation for this choice.

reviews.answer_text: Linked lists and heap-shaped binary trees can both implement priority queues.
reviews.hint: Separate the priority-queue contract from its storage representation.
reviews.explanation: DSA17 explicitly allows arrays and lists to implement priority queues and also gives binary heaps logarithmic insertion and extraction. A binary heap is a complete binary tree with heap order, as DSA23 explains. Therefore both Linked list and a suitably organized Binary tree can implement the ADT. A bare stack or FIFO queue provides a different selection rule.

evidence.quote: Arrays and lists can also implement priority queues: an unordered sequence gives cheap insertion but linear extremum removal; an ordered sequence reverses that tradeoff.

choices.label: A
choices.explanation: An unmodified LIFO stack removes the latest item, not necessarily the item with extremal priority.

choices.label: B
choices.explanation: An unmodified FIFO queue serves arrival order rather than selecting by priority.

choices.label: C
choices.explanation: An ordered or unordered linked list can implement priority service with different insertion and extraction costs.

choices.label: D
choices.explanation: A binary heap is a complete binary tree with heap order and supports efficient priority-queue operations.

reviews.answer_text: Stack
reviews.hint: Read the latest-pending-work invariant of DFS.
reviews.explanation: DSA42 describes recursively finishing an unvisited neighbor before returning to the parent. Explicit stack storage or the runtime call stack preserves this latest-pending-work-first behavior. A FIFO queue changes the exploration order. Linked lists can store frames but do not themselves define stack order, and a binary tree alone is not a frontier policy.

evidence.quote: Both implement latest-pending-work first; a queue would change that discipline.

choices.label: A
choices.explanation: A stack stores pending frames or vertices so the latest unfinished branch is resumed first.

choices.label: B
choices.explanation: A queue serves the oldest pending work and changes the depth-first exploration discipline.

choices.label: C
choices.explanation: A linked list may store a stack, but its name alone supplies no depth-first service order.

choices.label: D
choices.explanation: A binary tree is not the standard pending-work ADT needed to preserve DFS return points.

reviews.answer_text: A bounded cache needs an eviction and lookup policy before choosing storage.
reviews.hint: Compare FIFO eviction with LRU recency maintenance.
reviews.explanation: DSA27 says a bounded cache also needs eviction rules: FIFO uses a queue, whereas LRU can combine hashing and a doubly linked recency list. Capacity alone imposes no eviction order. Consequently Queue and Linked list already have supported uses under different policies, and the stem gives no policy or lookup requirement to justify a unique representation.

evidence.quote: A bounded cache also needs eviction rules: FIFO uses a queue; LRU can combine hash lookup with a doubly linked recency list.

choices.label: A
choices.explanation: A bounded stack supplies a LIFO policy, but the question gives no cache eviction contract requiring that order.

choices.label: B
choices.explanation: A queue can maintain FIFO eviction order when that policy is selected.

choices.label: C
choices.explanation: A doubly linked list can maintain LRU recency, commonly combined with hash-based lookup.

choices.label: D
choices.explanation: An ordered tree might hold cache entries, but neither ordering needs nor an eviction policy is specified.

reviews.answer_text: A circular buffer is natural, but fixed capacity alone does not force it.
reviews.hint: Specify buffer access order and what happens when storage is full.
reviews.explanation: DSA15 defines a circular queue over fixed capacity and DSA16 requires a reject, block, or overwrite policy. Fixed arrays can also implement bounded stacks or queues. The stem gives only a storage bound and no access or full-buffer behavior. Circular buffer is a natural intended implementation, but the literal requirements do not uniquely exclude other bounded structures.

evidence.quote: A fixed-capacity buffer also needs a full-policy choice: reject, block or overwrite. Capacity alone does not choose a policy.

choices.label: A
choices.explanation: A fixed-array stack can buffer a bounded number of items if LIFO access is the intended contract.

choices.label: B
choices.explanation: A bounded queue can buffer items with FIFO service; fixed capacity does not require circular representation.

choices.label: C
choices.explanation: A linked structure can enforce a capacity limit, though it is not automatically a fixed circular array.

choices.label: D
choices.explanation: A circular buffer efficiently reuses fixed slots, but the stem states no access or overwrite policy making it unique.

reviews.answer_text: Stable radix and merge-sort implementations both preserve equal-key order.
reviews.hint: Read stable digit passes and left-first merge tie handling.
reviews.explanation: DSA39 requires stable intermediate passes for LSD radix sorting; equal full keys remain tied in every digit and retain order. DSA37 gives merge-sort stability with left-first tie handling. Both thus satisfy the stated stability property under the described implementations. Standard quicksort and heapsort do not. The unqualified single-choice wording does not distinguish the two stable candidates.

evidence.quote: Stable intermediate passes preserve the ordering already established by less-significant digits.

choices.label: A
choices.explanation: Standard quicksort partition exchanges can reorder equal keys and are not guaranteed stable.

choices.label: B
choices.explanation: Ordinary heapsort’s long root-to-end exchanges can reorder equal keys, so it is generally unstable.

choices.label: C
choices.explanation: LSD radix sorting with stable digit passes preserves the order of equal full keys throughout all passes.

choices.label: D
choices.explanation: Merge sort with left-first handling of equal keys preserves their original relative order.

reviews.answer_text: Binary search
reviews.hint: Read the midpoint comparison and shrinking-interval rule.
reviews.explanation: DSA29 computes the midpoint of the current ordered interval, compares it with the target, and discards the half that cannot contain the target. That is exactly the midpoint-based procedure in the stem. Linear search scans successive elements, interpolation estimates a position from values, and DFS follows graph branches rather than ordered-array midpoints.

evidence.quote: Compute mid=lo+(hi-lo)//2. Equality finishes; if target<A[mid], set hi=mid-1; otherwise set lo=mid+1.

choices.label: A
choices.explanation: Linear search compares successive elements rather than repeatedly choosing the midpoint of a shrinking ordered interval.

choices.label: B
choices.explanation: Binary search explicitly compares the target with the current interval midpoint and keeps one half.

choices.label: C
choices.explanation: Interpolation search estimates a probe from numeric values and their distribution, rather than always using the midpoint.

choices.label: D
choices.explanation: Depth-first search explores graph neighbors and branches, not ordered-array midpoint intervals.

reviews.answer_text: Both binary and interpolation search require sorted input.
reviews.hint: Compare prerequisites of midpoint search and value-estimated search.
reviews.explanation: DSA29 defines binary search on an ascending sequence, with reversed comparisons for descending order. DSA30 likewise requires sorted numeric data for interpolation search. Thus both B and C satisfy the stem’s sorted-array prerequisite. Linear search allows unsorted data, and DFS works on graph adjacency rather than requiring a sorted array. The question does not distinguish the two ordered searches.

evidence.quote: Interpolation also needs sortedness, so prerequisite questions can overlap binary search.

choices.label: A
choices.explanation: Linear search scans successive items and explicitly permits unsorted input.

choices.label: B
choices.explanation: Binary search needs ordered values so a comparison can safely eliminate half the remaining interval.

choices.label: C
choices.explanation: Interpolation search also requires sorted data before value-based index estimation is meaningful.

choices.label: D
choices.explanation: Depth-first search follows graph or tree edges and does not require a sorted array.

reviews.answer_text: Interpolation search under the stated uniform-data model.
reviews.hint: Read how a value-based probe exploits a suitable distribution.
reviews.explanation: DSA30 gives interpolation search expected O(log log n) probes on sorted, suitably uniform numeric data. Binary search has logarithmic worst-case probes without that distribution assumption, while linear search scans. The stem supplies the distribution and sortedness conditions that motivate interpolation. The expected advantage does not promise faster finite runs or logarithmic worst-case behavior on arbitrary distributions.

evidence.quote: On sorted, suitably uniform data its expected probes can be O(log log n); pathological distributions can require linear time.

choices.label: A
choices.explanation: Linear search still examines successive elements and does not exploit uniform numeric distribution for sublinear expected probing.

choices.label: B
choices.explanation: Binary search gives logarithmic worst-case probing, but does not exploit uniform values for the stated expected advantage.

choices.label: C
choices.explanation: Interpolation estimates positions from uniformly distributed sorted numeric values, supporting the note’s expected O(log log n) probes.

choices.label: D
choices.explanation: DFS explores graph or tree branches and is not the distribution-based ordered-array search described here.

reviews.answer_text: Both depth-first and breadth-first search traverse graphs and trees.
reviews.hint: Compare branch-first and layer-first traversal disciplines.
reviews.explanation: DSA41 describes BFS as a graph traversal using a FIFO frontier, and DSA42 describes DFS using recursion or a stack. Trees are graphs, so both apply to trees too. The stem gives neither a depth-first order nor a shortest-edge-distance requirement that would distinguish them. Both named graph traversals are therefore valid answers among these choices.

evidence.quote: Mark a vertex, then recursively visit each unmarked neighbour before continuing with later neighbours.

choices.label: A
choices.explanation: Linear search scans a sequence and is not the named neighbor-based graph/tree traversal requested here.

choices.label: B
choices.explanation: Binary search needs an ordered search interval and is not a general traversal of arbitrary graph connections.

choices.label: C
choices.explanation: DFS follows each unvisited branch to completion and is a standard graph and tree traversal.

choices.label: D
choices.explanation: BFS explores successive distance layers and is also a standard graph and tree traversal.

reviews.answer_text: Binary search
reviews.hint: Read the ordered-input precondition for safely discarding half an interval.
reviews.explanation: DSA29 defines binary search over an ascending random-access sequence and reverses comparisons for descending data. Sortedness makes the half-elimination step sound. Linear scanning works without order; hashing needs a built table rather than sorted positions; DFS follows adjacency. Only Binary search among this option set requires a sorted input sequence for its ordinary operation.

evidence.quote: On an ascending random-access sequence, set lo=0, hi=n-1.

choices.label: A
choices.explanation: Linear search explicitly permits unsorted data and compares items one after another.

choices.label: B
choices.explanation: Binary search relies on ordered values to determine which half can still contain the target.

choices.label: C
