choices.explanation: Hash lookup needs a hash-table organization, not values arranged in sorted-array order.

choices.label: D
choices.explanation: Depth-first search follows graph or tree adjacency and does not require a sorted input array.

reviews.answer_text: Binary search has logarithmic worst-case time.
reviews.hint: Compare worst-case interval halving with scans and adverse hash collisions.
reviews.explanation: DSA29 bounds binary-search probes by floor(log₂n)+1 on nonempty random-access input. This supplies logarithmic worst-case time under constant-cost comparisons. Linear search may scan all items; adverse hash collisions may require linear work; DFS can inspect all vertices and edges. Their ordinary worst cases do not share binary search’s logarithmic bound.

evidence.quote: Worst probes are floor(log₂n)+1 for n>0: seven for 100 keys, about twenty for one million.

choices.label: A
choices.explanation: Linear search can inspect every item when the target is absent or last, giving linear worst-case time.

choices.label: B
choices.explanation: Each comparison discards about half the ordered interval, giving logarithmic worst-case probes.

choices.label: C
choices.explanation: Ordinary hash lookup can degrade to linear time under adverse collisions, despite expected constant-time performance.

choices.label: D
choices.explanation: DFS may visit all graph vertices and edges, rather than guarantee logarithmic worst-case work.

reviews.answer_text: Linear search directly searches an unsorted sequence.
reviews.hint: Distinguish direct scanning from preprocessing into a hash table.
reviews.explanation: DSA28 explicitly allows unsorted data for linear search: compare successive elements until the target is found or the sequence ends. Binary search requires sortedness. Hash lookup can be useful after building a table, but it does not directly search the supplied ordinary list without that preprocessing. DFS presumes graph or tree adjacency rather than a simple sequence query.

evidence.quote: Compare the target with successive elements until equal or exhausted. Unsorted data is allowed; sorted data is allowed too.

choices.label: A
choices.explanation: Linear search can inspect an unsorted array or list directly without sorting or building another structure.

choices.label: B
choices.explanation: Binary search needs ordering to safely eliminate half the remaining candidate positions.

choices.label: C
choices.explanation: Hash search needs a constructed hash table; the stem supplies an ordinary unsorted array or list.

choices.label: D
choices.explanation: DFS explores graph or tree adjacency and is not the direct unsorted-sequence scan described here.

reviews.answer_text: Depth-first search
reviews.hint: Read how recursive neighbor exploration traverses a graph or tree.
reviews.explanation: DSA42 describes marking a vertex and recursively visiting each unmarked neighbor before resuming later neighbors. That procedure is standard depth-first traversal and applies to graphs and trees. Linear search scans a sequence, binary search uses an ordered interval, and hash search queries table addresses. None of those alternatives names the adjacency-following traversal in this option set.

evidence.quote: Mark a vertex, then recursively visit each unmarked neighbour before continuing with later neighbours.

choices.label: A
choices.explanation: Linear search scans sequence elements and is not the named adjacency-following graph/tree traversal.

choices.label: B
choices.explanation: Binary search reduces an ordered interval rather than visiting arbitrary graph or tree connections.

choices.label: C
choices.explanation: Hash search probes key-derived table addresses rather than traversing graph or tree edges.

choices.label: D
choices.explanation: DFS follows unvisited neighbors recursively or through an explicit stack, providing a standard traversal.

reviews.answer_text: Ternary search
reviews.hint: Read the ordered-array search using two split points.
reviews.explanation: DSA30 explicitly describes sorted-array ternary search as comparing two split points and retaining the relevant third. The three candidate regions give the technique its name. Binary search uses one midpoint and two regions, linear search scans successively, and DFS explores graph branches. Thus Ternary search uniquely matches the described three-part split.

evidence.quote: Sorted-array ternary search compares two split points and keeps the relevant third, still logarithmic.

choices.label: A
choices.explanation: Linear search advances through successive items and does not divide the remaining interval into thirds.

choices.label: B
choices.explanation: Binary search uses one midpoint and retains one of two halves, not one of three regions.

choices.label: C
choices.explanation: Ternary search uses two split points to divide the ordered search interval into three candidate parts.

choices.label: D
choices.explanation: DFS explores graph or tree branches rather than repeatedly trisecting an ordered search interval.

reviews.answer_text: Binary search
reviews.hint: Read the reduction from an ordered interval to one half.
reviews.explanation: DSA29 compares the middle value with the target and continues only in the half that can contain it. This solves a smaller instance of the same ordered-search problem and is the divide-and-conquer reduction intended here. Linear scanning removes one candidate at a time, hashing computes addresses, and DFS follows adjacency without this ordered half-elimination rule.

evidence.quote: Equality finishes; if target<A[mid], set hi=mid-1; otherwise set lo=mid+1.

choices.label: A
choices.explanation: Linear search scans successive candidates rather than repeatedly solving a half-size ordered-search instance.

choices.label: B
choices.explanation: Binary search divides the ordered interval and continues in the only half that can contain the target.

choices.label: C
choices.explanation: Hash search derives an address and resolves collisions rather than recursively dividing an ordered problem.

choices.label: D
choices.explanation: DFS follows adjacency branches and does not inherently apply the ordered half-elimination strategy described here.

reviews.answer_text: Merge sort using buffered external runs.
reviews.hint: Read external sorting’s run-generation and sequential-merge strategy.
reviews.explanation: DSA37 describes external sorting by building sorted runs and merging buffered disk streams to reduce I/O. Merge sort naturally supports that strategy even when the whole dataset does not fit RAM. Bubble and insertion sorting repeatedly move local data, while ordinary quicksort assumes partition access rather than the external sequential-run pattern specified by the note.

evidence.quote: External sorting builds sorted runs and merges buffered streams from disk, aiming to reduce I/O.

choices.label: A
choices.explanation: Bubble sort’s repeated adjacent passes do not provide the buffered sorted-run strategy used for efficient external sorting.

choices.label: B
choices.explanation: Ordinary quicksort partitioning is not the sequential buffered-run merging strategy identified for external data here.

choices.label: C
choices.explanation: Merge sorting combines buffered sorted runs sequentially and is directly suited to disk-backed external sorting.

choices.label: D
choices.explanation: Insertion sort’s repeated local insertion work does not provide the note’s efficient external-run merging mechanism.

reviews.answer_text: Hash table for expected fast dictionary lookup and insertion.
reviews.hint: Read dictionary lookup costs and the assumptions behind hashing.
reviews.explanation: DSA27 explicitly names hashing as a dictionary implementation with expected constant lookup. DSA26 qualifies this by a suitable distribution and controlled load; insertion is likewise expected fast under those conditions. Arrays and linked lists lack the same ordinary key-lookup performance, while a stack specifies LIFO access. This is an expected-performance recommendation, not a universal worst-case guarantee.

evidence.quote: A dictionary or compiler symbol table can use hashing for expected constant lookup, or a balanced tree for logarithmic lookup with ordering.

choices.label: A
choices.explanation: An ordinary array lacks key-derived lookup and may require scanning or maintaining a sorted order with costly insertions.

choices.label: B
choices.explanation: An ordinary linked list needs traversal to locate an arbitrary dictionary key, giving linear worst-case lookup.

choices.label: C
choices.explanation: A well-sized hash table offers expected fast key lookup and insertion under suitable hashing and load assumptions.

choices.label: D
choices.explanation: A stack exposes LIFO top operations and does not directly provide efficient arbitrary-key dictionary lookup.

reviews.answer_text: BFS for unweighted paths and Dijkstra for nonnegative weighted paths.
reviews.hint: Check graph weights before choosing a shortest-path algorithm.
reviews.explanation: DSA41 gives BFS minimum-edge paths in unweighted graphs. DSA43 gives Dijkstra source shortest paths when weights are nonnegative. Both are shortest-path algorithms under stated conditions, and the stem specifies neither weight model. DFS does not generally minimize path length, and Prim minimizes total spanning-tree weight. Thus the literal unqualified question has two supported answers.

evidence.quote: BFS is enough when every edge has equal cost; negative edges require another justified method, such as Bellman–Ford.

choices.label: A
choices.explanation: A DFS reachability path need not minimize either edge count or total edge weight.

choices.label: B
choices.explanation: BFS finds shortest paths by edge count in unweighted or equal-cost graphs.

choices.label: C
choices.explanation: Dijkstra finds source shortest paths in graphs with nonnegative weights, as described in DSA43.

choices.label: D
choices.explanation: Prim minimizes total spanning-tree connection cost, which differs from minimizing source-to-vertex path lengths.

reviews.answer_text: Choose cache lookup and eviction requirements before selecting a structure.
reviews.hint: Compare FIFO eviction with the hash-plus-recency-list LRU design.
reviews.explanation: DSA27 describes FIFO caches using queues and LRU caches combining hash lookup with a doubly linked recency list. Lists give efficient known-node insertion and removal; hashing supplies expected key access. An array may suit fixed slots, but capacity and eviction policy determine movement costs. The stem states no lookup contract, removal target, or replacement rule, so no structure is uniquely best.

evidence.quote: LRU can combine hash lookup with a doubly linked recency list.

choices.label: A
choices.explanation: Fixed array slots can hold cache entries, but removal movement and lookup costs depend on the unspecified policy.

choices.label: B
choices.explanation: A doubly linked list supports efficient known-node removal and recency updates, commonly paired with hashing.

choices.label: C
choices.explanation: Hashing supports expected key lookup and updates, but does not alone specify recency or eviction order.

choices.label: D
choices.explanation: A queue supports efficient endpoint operations for FIFO eviction, if that is the intended policy.

reviews.answer_text: Kadane’s algorithm
reviews.hint: Read the best-sum-ending-here recurrence.
reviews.explanation: DSA44 directly identifies Kadane as the contiguous maximum-sum-subarray algorithm. It updates the best sum ending at the current item and the best sum seen overall, using linear time and constant working storage. Binary search does not optimize contiguous sums, and quicksort or merge sort reorder values rather than preserve the original adjacency needed by this problem.

evidence.quote: Kadane’s algorithm finds a contiguous maximum-sum subarray.

choices.label: A
choices.explanation: Binary search locates targets or ordered boundaries; it does not compute a contiguous maximum-sum subarray.

choices.label: B
choices.explanation: Quicksort reorders values and does not preserve the original adjacency required for maximum subarray sum.

choices.label: C
choices.explanation: Merge sort orders values; the named sorting algorithm is not the maximum-subarray recurrence.

choices.label: D
choices.explanation: Kadane maintains the best sum ending here and the best anywhere, directly solving the stated problem.

reviews.answer_text: Adjacency list
reviews.hint: Read the complete graph representations, separating them from underlying containers.
reviews.explanation: DSA40 describes adjacency lists as storing each vertex’s neighbors in Θ(V+E) space. This names a complete graph representation among the choices. Arrays, linked lists, or maps may store parts of a representation, but those container names alone do not specify how vertices and their edges are encoded. The answer identifies the graph-specific organization.

evidence.quote: Adjacency lists use Theta(V+E) space and enumerate neighbours.

choices.label: A
choices.explanation: An array can store a matrix or adjacency containers, but its name alone does not specify a graph representation.

choices.label: B
choices.explanation: A linked list can hold neighbor records, but alone does not describe the vertex-to-neighbor organization.

choices.label: C
choices.explanation: Hash tables may index vertices or neighbors, but do not by themselves name the graph representation supplied here.

choices.label: D
choices.explanation: An adjacency list explicitly associates vertices with their neighbors and is a standard graph representation.

reviews.answer_text: Prim’s algorithm
reviews.hint: Separate total spanning-tree cost from source shortest-path distances.
reviews.explanation: DSA43 defines an MST as a minimum-total-cost connection of all vertices in a connected undirected weighted graph. Prim repeatedly adds the cheapest edge crossing from its current tree to an outside vertex. Dijkstra minimizes source-path distances instead, while BFS and DFS are traversals without a general minimum-weight spanning-tree guarantee. Thus Prim is the listed MST algorithm.

evidence.quote: Prim adds the cheapest edge crossing from its current tree to an outside vertex.

choices.label: A
choices.explanation: DFS can produce a spanning tree but does not generally minimize total edge weight.

choices.label: B
choices.explanation: BFS produces minimum-edge source layers in unweighted graphs, not a general minimum-weight spanning tree.

choices.label: C
choices.explanation: Dijkstra minimizes source-to-vertex distances, a different objective from total spanning-tree connection cost.

choices.label: D
choices.explanation: Prim grows a spanning tree by repeatedly choosing a cheapest edge crossing to an outside vertex.

reviews.answer_text: Heap is a balanced-cost choice; best depends on operation mix.
reviews.hint: Compare insertion and extremum-removal costs across priority-queue representations.
reviews.explanation: DSA17 gives heaps constant peek and logarithmic insertion/extraction. It also permits arrays and lists, with cheap insertion versus expensive extremum removal in unordered storage and the reverse tradeoff when ordered. Therefore Heap is a strong conventional choice for mixed operations, but the question provides no operation frequency or required bounds to establish a universal best.

evidence.quote: Arrays and lists can also implement priority queues: an unordered sequence gives cheap insertion but linear extremum removal; an ordered sequence reverses that tradeoff.

choices.label: A
choices.explanation: An unordered or ordered array can implement priorities, trading insertion against extremum-removal cost.

choices.label: B
choices.explanation: An ordered or unordered linked list also implements priority service with a different operation-cost tradeoff.

choices.label: C
choices.explanation: A heap balances insert and extraction at logarithmic cost, but the stem specifies no workload proving it best.

choices.label: D
choices.explanation: An ordinary FIFO queue selects arrival order rather than priority unless its contract is changed.

reviews.answer_text: Knuth–Morris–Pratt
reviews.hint: Read prefix/suffix reuse after a pattern mismatch.
reviews.explanation: DSA44 explicitly defines KMP as finding a pattern inside text. It preprocesses longest proper prefix/suffix lengths and uses them to avoid restarting comparisons after mismatch, giving linear combined pattern-and-text work. DFS, BFS, and Dijkstra concern graph exploration or paths, rather than this specialized substring-matching mechanism. KMP uniquely matches the question among these choices.

evidence.quote: Knuth–Morris–Pratt (KMP) finds a pattern inside text.

choices.label: A
choices.explanation: DFS explores graph or tree branches; it is not the substring-pattern algorithm identified in DSA44.

choices.label: B
choices.explanation: BFS explores graph distance layers rather than applying prefix/suffix reuse for text matching.

choices.label: C
choices.explanation: Dijkstra computes nonnegative weighted shortest paths, not substring pattern occurrences.

choices.label: D
choices.explanation: KMP is the pattern-matching algorithm using preprocessed prefix/suffix lengths to avoid repeated text comparisons.

reviews.answer_text: C is the intended false allocation claim; A also lacks a justified universal ranking.
reviews.hint: Compare universe size, stored-key density, collision costs, and the criterion meant by better.
reviews.explanation: DSA25 reserves one position per possible universe key for direct addressing, so C falsely describes hashing. But A claims hashing is better from large universe size alone. Sparse storage can favor hashing; dense occupancy with sufficient memory can favor direct lookup without collisions. Neither key density nor a comparison criterion is stated. Therefore C remains the conventional sparse-universe/storage answer, while the literal question does not establish a uniquely false statement.

evidence.quote: Direct addressing reserves a position for every possible key in a finite universe U, costing Theta(|U|) slots. A hash table uses h(key) in 0..m-1 and stores only actual entries plus bucket capacity.
Load alpha=n/m is average chain length; expected operations are O(1+alpha) under suitable distribution assumptions, with O(n) worst cases.

choices.label: A
choices.explanation: Large U alone does not rank storage or performance; occupancy, memory availability, and the comparison criterion matter.

choices.label: B
choices.explanation: Direct addressing uses a key-specific universe position rather than compressing keys through a hash function; this statement is true.

choices.label: C
choices.explanation: One slot per possible universe key describes direct addressing, making this the clear intended false hashing claim.

choices.label: D
choices.explanation: Direct addressing assigns each universe key its own position, so this statement is true.

reviews.answer_text: Home address 0; final storage depends on occupied slots and collision resolution.
reviews.hint: Distinguish the computed home address from the final slot after collision resolution.
reviews.explanation: DSA25 gives h(36)=36 mod 6=0 as the home address, but explicitly allows collision displacement. With linear probing from DSA26, an occupied slot 0 and free slot 1 would place the key at 1, while an empty home slot permits 0. The stem gives neither table state nor collision policy, so D is conditional rather than a unique final-storage answer.

evidence.quote: With h(k)=k mod 6, key 36 has home address 0; collisions may move its final storage position.
Linear probing tries (h(k)+j)%m.

choices.label: A
choices.explanation: Index 35 is outside the six-slot array, regardless of the collision policy.

choices.label: B
choices.explanation: Linear probing can place 36 at index 1 when home slot 0 is occupied and slot 1 is free.

choices.label: C
choices.explanation: Index 6 is outside the zero-based six-slot range 0 through 5.

choices.label: D
choices.explanation: Zero is the computed home address and final slot only when collision handling does not displace the key.

reviews.answer_text: Open addressing, specifically linear probing.
reviews.hint: Read the collision strategy that probes subsequent array slots.
reviews.explanation: DSA26 defines open addressing as keeping entries within the array and probing until an available slot is found. Checking successive positions is its linear-probing form. Multiple hashing changes probe steps, chaining stores collisions in bucket lists, and cluster indexing is not this insertion procedure. Therefore Open addressing is the matching general method among the options.

evidence.quote: Open addressing keeps entries inside the array and probes until a key or an available slot is found.

choices.label: A
choices.explanation: Open addressing searches alternative table positions; checking successive positions is its linear-probing form.

choices.label: B
choices.explanation: Multiple or double hashing derives another probe step rather than the stated simple successive-slot scan.

choices.label: C
choices.explanation: Chaining puts colliding entries in a bucket list instead of searching successive array slots.

choices.label: D
choices.explanation: Cluster indexing does not name the collision insertion strategy described by the successive-position probing rule.

reviews.answer_text: Heap-file insertion is not required to occur at the beginning.
reviews.hint: Distinguish unordered record heap files from binary heaps.
reviews.explanation: DSA45 defines a heap file as unordered database records, unrelated to a binary heap. It inserts into available space and permits scans; ordered output needs sorting or an index. Therefore new records are not required to be placed at the beginning. The other options describe ordinary unordered-file operations, although an index can provide ordered access without sorting each query.

evidence.quote: A heap file is an unordered database record file, unrelated to a binary heap: insertion uses available space, scanning can find records, and ordered output requires sorting or an index.

choices.label: A
choices.explanation: Without a suitable index, a heap scan has no field order and ordered output requires sorting; an index is an alternative.

choices.label: B
choices.explanation: An unordered heap file can be scanned linearly to find a required record.

choices.label: C
choices.explanation: Placing a record into available space avoids maintaining sorted order, supporting efficient ordinary insertion.

choices.label: D
choices.explanation: Heap files use available space and impose no rule requiring every new record at the beginning.

reviews.answer_text: Indexing convention missing; one-based gives 2*i+1, zero-based gives absent 2*i+2.
reviews.hint: Read heap order and zero-based versus one-based indexing.
reviews.explanation: DSA23 gives different child formulas for zero-based and one-based heaps. The question specifies neither convention. A is the right-child formula only for one-based indexing; under zero-based indexing it is the left child and the actual right formula is absent. A unique literal answer therefore requires the missing origin.

evidence.quote: Zero-based array representation: root index 0, left=2i+1, right=2i+2, parent=floor((i-1)/2) for i>0.

choices.label: A
choices.explanation: Right child is 2*i+1 only with one-based heap indexing, which is not specified.

choices.label: B
choices.explanation: i/2 is associated with parent calculation under one-based indexing, not a right child.

choices.label: C
choices.explanation: (i+1)/2 is not the stated right-child formula under either standard convention.

choices.label: D
choices.explanation: 2*i is the one-based left child, not its right child.

reviews.answer_text: Memory comparison depends on iterative versus recursive implementations.
reviews.hint: Read ordered intervals and binary-search probe bounds.
reviews.explanation: DSA28 permits linear search on sorted or unsorted data, and DSA29 permits descending binary search with reversed comparisons. Binary search has fewer worst-case probes on sorted random-access data, but its stack space differs between iterative and recursive versions. Thus B is false for two iterative implementations but can describe recursive binary search versus iterative scanning.

evidence.quote: Worst probes are floor(log₂n)+1 for n>0: seven for 100 keys, about twenty for one million.

choices.label: A
choices.explanation: Descending binary search works when its comparison direction is reversed consistently.

choices.label: B
choices.explanation: Iterative searches both use constant auxiliary storage; recursive binary search needs a logarithmic stack.

choices.label: C
choices.explanation: Sequential scanning is valid for both sorted and unsorted sequences, as DSA28 states.

choices.label: D
choices.explanation: Logarithmic versus linear worst probes favors binary search under random access; finite runtime still depends on costs.

reviews.answer_text: Both insertion at the front and deletion of the front node.
reviews.hint: Read head, tail, and predecessor update costs.
reviews.explanation: With only a head pointer, prepending changes the new node’s link and head; deleting head advances head and releases the old node. Both require constant work. Appending must find the last node, and tail deletion must find its predecessor. E explicitly combines the two valid constant-time operations, so it is the complete aggregate answer.

evidence.quote: Prepend with new.next=head; head=new.

choices.label: A
choices.explanation: Prepending changes only the new node link and head, requiring constant work.

choices.label: B
choices.explanation: Without a tail pointer, insertion at the end must traverse the chain.

choices.label: C
choices.explanation: Deleting head advances one link and releases one node, requiring constant work.

choices.label: D
choices.explanation: Finding the last node’s predecessor requires a linear traversal in a head-only singly linked list.

choices.label: E
choices.explanation: This aggregate includes exactly the two constant-time endpoint operations supported by the representation.

reviews.answer_text: Logical FIFO gives 13,15,17,19,21,9; a noncircular implementation can overflow.
reviews.hint: Read circular slots, logical order, and capacity conventions.
reviews.explanation: DSA15 distinguishes the queue sequence from fixed-array storage policy. Dequeue removes 11 and a successful enqueue appends 9, yielding B logically. But a noncircular array can reject insertion when rear already reaches its final slot despite space at the front. Without circularity, compaction, or a rear convention, B and D reflect different valid implementations.

evidence.quote: Physical array: [9,13,15,17,19,21]; logical front-to-rear queue: [13,15,17,19,21,9]. A noncircular version can instead overflow.

choices.label: A
choices.explanation: This prepends nine and removes twenty-one, contrary to successful FIFO operations.

choices.label: B
choices.explanation: This is the logical FIFO sequence if the freed capacity can be reused.

choices.label: C
choices.explanation: This removes the rear item rather than the front eleven.

choices.label: D
choices.explanation: A noncircular rear-at-final-index queue can report overflow despite the freed front slot.

reviews.answer_text: Logical queue is B; physical slots are D under the stated full-array convention.
reviews.hint: Read circular slots, logical order, and capacity conventions.
reviews.explanation: DSA15 works this exact capacity-six example. Removing the front 11 and appending 9 gives the logical sequence 13,15,17,19,21,9. Circular reuse places 9 in physical slot zero, yielding 9,13,15,17,19,21 in memory. The question asks for elements without identifying logical front-to-rear order or physical array order, so both interpretations must be distinguished.

evidence.quote: Physical array: [9,13,15,17,19,21]; logical front-to-rear queue: [13,15,17,19,21,9]. A noncircular version can instead overflow.

choices.label: A
choices.explanation: This retains the removed eleven and drops twenty-one, fitting neither correct order.

choices.label: B
choices.explanation: This lists the correct logical front-to-rear queue after the two operations.

choices.label: C
choices.explanation: This removes twenty-one instead of eleven and does not describe the circular update.

choices.label: D
choices.explanation: This lists physical array slots after nine reuses the freed slot zero.

reviews.answer_text: No uniquely defined additional requirement among the options.
reviews.hint: Read ordered intervals and binary-search probe bounds.
reviews.explanation: DSA29 requires comparable ordered keys and valid finite bounds; DSA02 explains array representation and resizable storage. Homogeneous elements and contiguous storage describe ordinary arrays rather than separate binary-search requirements. A resizable array need not fix capacity before population. Finiteness matters to the interval, but the stem already calls the input an array and does not distinguish representation from algorithmic prerequisites.

evidence.quote: Comparable keys and valid finite bounds matter; fixed allocation before population is not an extra algorithmic requirement.

choices.label: A
choices.explanation: Homogeneous type is an ordinary array property, not the essential extra binary-search condition of comparability.

choices.label: B
choices.explanation: All fails because fixing size before population is not required for binary search.

choices.label: C
choices.explanation: Contiguous storage describes an ordinary array; binary-search logic fundamentally needs ordered accessible positions.

choices.label: D
choices.explanation: Valid finite bounds matter, but they are already implicit in an ordinary finite array input.

choices.label: E
choices.explanation: Resizable arrays can be populated before searching; compile-time or prior fixed capacity is unnecessary.

choices.label: F
choices.explanation: This fits a reading where array properties are already assumed, but comparability and valid bounds still matter.

reviews.answer_text: n-1 distinct-position exchanges; n calls if a final self-swap is counted.
reviews.hint: Read selection passes, exchanges, and record-move costs.
reviews.explanation: DSA33 explicitly distinguishes meaningful exchanges from swap calls. Selection sort needs at most n-1 exchanges of distinct positions, because the final position is then forced. A loop may nevertheless call swap on the last item with itself, giving n calls. The question does not specify its loop or counting convention, so A and C reflect different counts.

evidence.quote: At most n-1 exchanges of distinct positions are needed. A loop that also swaps the last item with itself can count n swap calls.

choices.label: A
choices.explanation: n-1 bounds actual exchanges between distinct positions in the ordinary selection-sort implementation.

choices.label: B
choices.explanation: One is not the maximum for arbitrary growing input size.

choices.label: C
choices.explanation: A version counting the final self-swap can execute n swap calls.

choices.label: D
choices.explanation: n-2 omits a possible meaningful exchange and is not the general bound.

reviews.answer_text: Both queues and deques allow front deletion and rear insertion.
reviews.hint: Read deque endpoint capabilities.
reviews.explanation: DSA14 defines the queue using those two operations. DSA16 gives a deque insertion and removal at both ends, which necessarily includes front deletion and rear insertion too. The stem says allows, rather than only allows, so it does not exclude the more capable deque. A stack and BST have different operation contracts.

evidence.quote: A deque permits both-end insertion/removal without guaranteeing middle access.

choices.label: A
choices.explanation: A stack exposes one top end and LIFO service rather than the specified two-end FIFO operations.

choices.label: B
choices.explanation: Queues explicitly enqueue at rear and dequeue at front.

choices.label: C
choices.explanation: Deques permit both-end insertion and removal, including the two operations named here.

choices.label: D
choices.explanation: BST operations follow keys and subtree order rather than front/rear service endpoints.

reviews.answer_text: Insertion and quicksort have tight quadratic worst cases; merge also satisfies the loose Big-O bound.
reviews.hint: Read sorting resource tables and overlapping bounds.
reviews.explanation: DSA31 distinguishes tight sorting growth from overlapping upper bounds. Insertion and quicksort have quadratic worst cases. Merge sort’s n log n worst cost is also O(n²), so the literal upper-bound wording includes A. Radix cost depends on digits and radix, neither specified here. If a tight bound was intended, B and C still both qualify.

evidence.quote: For eventually nonnegative functions, f(n)=O(g(n)) means f(n)≤c g(n) for some positive c beyond a threshold k.
Balanced partitions give n log n work; repeated extreme pivots sum n+(n-1)+… to quadratic work.

choices.label: A
choices.explanation: Merge sort’s n log n cost is also bounded above by n²; Big-O need not be tight.

choices.label: B
choices.explanation: Reverse-order insertion sort performs quadratic shifts and comparisons in the worst case.

choices.label: C
choices.explanation: Repeated extreme quicksort partitions give quadratic worst-case work.

choices.label: D
choices.explanation: Radix worst cost depends on digit count and radix, which the stem does not bound.

reviews.answer_text: Optimized bubble sort and insertion sort both have linear best cases.
reviews.hint: Read strict adjacent swaps and early stopping.
reviews.explanation: DSA32 stops optimized bubble sorting after a no-swap pass, giving linear sorted-input work. DSA34 gives insertion sorting one check per insertion on sorted input, also linear. Ordinary quicksort and merge sort have n log n best growth in the listed implementations. The alternate set replaces quicksort with selection sort, which remains quadratic even when sorted.

evidence.quote: Early stopping makes a sorted input linear: one no-swap pass finishes. A fixed pass schedule stays quadratic.

choices.label: A
choices.explanation: Early-exit bubble sort finishes a sorted input after one linear no-swap pass.

choices.label: B
choices.explanation: Ordinary quicksort has n log n best work rather than linear best growth.

choices.label: C
choices.explanation: Ordinary merge sort still performs linear merging at logarithmically many levels.

choices.label: D
choices.explanation: Insertion sort does one ordering check per pass with no shifts on sorted input.

variant_reviews.answer_text: Optimized bubble sort and insertion sort
variant_reviews.explanation: The alternate set replaces quicksort with selection sort. DSA33 gives selection quadratic comparisons in every input order, while DSA32 and DSA34 still give optimized bubble and insertion linear sorted-input work. The two valid best-case choices are therefore independently A and D.

choices.label: A
choices.explanation: An early-exit no-swap pass makes optimized bubble sort linear on sorted input.

choices.label: B
choices.explanation: Selection sort still scans each suffix and makes quadratic comparisons even when sorted.

choices.label: C
choices.explanation: Ordinary merge sorting does n log n work across input orders.

choices.label: D
choices.explanation: Insertion sort is linear on sorted input because each pass needs no shifts.

reviews.answer_text: Bubble, selection, and insertion are ordinarily in place.
reviews.hint: Read sorting resource tables and overlapping bounds.
reviews.explanation: DSA31’s table gives constant extra element storage for bubble, selection, and insertion sorting. Their ordinary array implementations rearrange values inside the original array. Ordinary merge sort instead uses a linear buffer, although specialized in-place variants exist. Nothing in the stem identifies one of the three standard in-place choices as uniquely intended.

evidence.quote: An in-place element algorithm uses a fixed amount of extra element storage; a recursive call stack may still matter when total auxiliary space is requested.

choices.label: A
choices.explanation: Ordinary bubble sort swaps adjacent elements within the original array using constant temporary storage.

choices.label: B
choices.explanation: Selection sort exchanges the selected minimum in place using constant temporary storage.

choices.label: C
choices.explanation: Ordinary array merge sort uses a linear auxiliary buffer; special variants would require qualification.

choices.label: D
choices.explanation: Insertion sort shifts within the array and uses constant extra element storage.

reviews.answer_text: Strict-swap bubble and left-first merge sort are stable.
reviews.hint: Read strict adjacent swaps and early stopping.
reviews.explanation: DSA32 preserves equal-key order by swapping only strict adjacent inversions. DSA37 preserves that order by choosing from the left run first on equal merge keys. Standard selection can reverse equal records through a distant exchange, and standard quicksort is unstable. Thus two listed algorithms satisfy the stability description under their ordinary implementations.

evidence.quote: Strict swaps preserve equal-key order.

choices.label: A
choices.explanation: Strict adjacent bubble swaps do not move equal keys past one another.

choices.label: B
choices.explanation: Standard selection sort’s distant minimum exchange can reverse equal-key records.

choices.label: C
choices.explanation: Standard quicksort partition exchanges do not guarantee preservation of equal-key order.

choices.label: D
choices.explanation: Merge sort preserves equal-key order with left-first tie handling.

reviews.answer_text: Merge qualifies; fixed-width, fixed-radix sorting also satisfies the literal upper bound.
reviews.hint: Distinguish a tight n log n comparison bound from a loose upper bound on digit-based sorting.
reviews.explanation: DSA37 gives merge sort n log n work across input orders, supporting C. DSA39 gives radix sorting O(d(n+r)); fixed digit count and radix make this O(n), which also satisfies O(n log n) under DSA06. The stem specifies neither tightness nor key bounds, so D cannot be uniquely excluded. C remains the conventional tight comparison-sort answer. The separately reviewed variant omits merge and radix and keeps its independent analysis.

evidence.quote: There are logarithmically many levels with linear merge work per level, giving n log n time even on sorted input unless an optimization skips merges.
With d digits and radix r, counting-based passes take O(d(n+r)) time and O(n+r) auxiliary storage.
For eventually nonnegative functions, f(n)=O(g(n)) means f(n)≤c g(n) for some positive c beyond a threshold k.

choices.label: A
choices.explanation: Ordinary bubble sort has quadratic average and worst work, exceeding an n log n upper bound.

choices.label: B
choices.explanation: Selection sort makes quadratic comparisons in every order, exceeding the stated bound.

choices.label: C
choices.explanation: Ordinary merge sort has n log n average and worst work and satisfies the stated upper bound.

choices.label: D
choices.explanation: Fixed digits and radix make radix sorting linear, which also satisfies O(n log n); those key restrictions are unspecified.

variant_reviews.answer_text: No offered ordinary algorithm has both stated bounds.
variant_reviews.explanation: This variant replaces merge sort with quicksort and radix with insertion. Bubble, selection, and insertion have quadratic worst costs. Quicksort has n log n expected average work under its model but can still be quadratic in the worst case. Therefore the main C label cannot be reused: this alternate option set has no matching algorithm.

choices.label: A
choices.explanation: Bubble sort’s average and worst work are quadratic rather than n log n.

choices.label: B
choices.explanation: Selection sort’s quadratic comparisons exceed n log n in both cases.

choices.label: C
choices.explanation: Quicksort can have quadratic worst work despite n log n expected average behavior.

choices.label: D
choices.explanation: Insertion sort has quadratic average and worst work under the usual model.

reviews.answer_text: Large records with cheap keys favor few exchanges, but the movement model is unstated.
reviews.hint: Read selection passes, exchanges, and record-move costs.
reviews.explanation: DSA33 recommends selection when record moves are expensive relative to comparisons. C fits if large values means large records and small keys means cheap comparisons. But those words can also mean numeric magnitudes, which do not imply movement cost. Already sorted input does not reduce selection comparisons, and large file size alone supplies no selection advantage.

evidence.quote: Selection suits expensive record moves with cheap key comparisons, not every large dataset.

choices.label: A
choices.explanation: Already sorted data still requires the same quadratic suffix comparisons in selection sort.

choices.label: B
choices.explanation: Large file size alone does not justify selection’s quadratic comparisons or address external I/O.

choices.label: C
choices.explanation: This fits expensive large-record movement with cheap small-key comparisons, an unstated cost interpretation.

choices.label: D
choices.explanation: Expensive large-key comparisons are not the condition favoring selection’s many comparisons.

reviews.answer_text: Constant extra element storage, conventionally called in-place sorting.
reviews.hint: Read selection passes, exchanges, and record-move costs.
reviews.explanation: DSA33 says selection uses constant extra element storage, which is the conventional meaning of A’s no-additional-storage phrasing. It still needs a few temporary values, so literally zero bytes would be inaccurate. Its quadratic comparisons do not improve on already sorted input, and the note gives no universal scalability or fastest-algorithm claim. A names the valid conventional benefit.

evidence.quote: Constant extra element storage is shared by several sorts.

choices.label: A
choices.explanation: Interpreted conventionally as in-place, selection uses constant extra element storage rather than an auxiliary array.

choices.label: B
choices.explanation: Quadratic comparisons do not provide an unqualified scalability advantage for growing datasets.

choices.label: C
choices.explanation: Selection makes the same quadratic comparisons even on already sorted input.

choices.label: D
choices.explanation: No universal fastest claim follows; selection trades few moves for many comparisons.

reviews.answer_text: Tight merge growth is n log n; loose bounds and the last option’s typography overlap.
reviews.hint: Read sorting resource tables and overlapping bounds.
reviews.explanation: DSA37 gives n log n worst growth. A is tight, while B and C are also valid but loose upper bounds. D may mean n log(n²), which is the same order as A, or n(log n)², another loose bound. The stem says Big-O without tightest and its final notation is unclear, so no unique literal answer follows.

evidence.quote: There are logarithmically many levels with linear merge work per level, giving n log n time even on sorted input unless an optimization skips merges.
For eventually nonnegative functions, f(n)=O(g(n)) means f(n)≤c g(n) for some positive c beyond a threshold k.

choices.label: A
choices.explanation: n log n is the tight ordinary merge-sort worst growth and a valid upper bound.

choices.label: B
choices.explanation: n² is a valid looser upper bound on n log n growth.

choices.label: C
choices.explanation: n² log n is also a valid looser upper bound on ordinary merge sorting.

choices.label: D
choices.explanation: If log n2 means log(n²), it duplicates A; another parsing gives a looser bound.

reviews.answer_text: Ordinary best growth is n log n; several offered upper bounds remain valid.
reviews.hint: Read sorting resource tables and overlapping bounds.
reviews.explanation: DSA37 says ordinary merge sort still performs n log n work on sorted input unless an optimization skips merges. Therefore A is the tight best bound, but B and C also bound it from above. D’s n log n2 typography can duplicate A or mean another loose bound. Without tightness and unambiguous notation, a single Big-O choice is not justified.

evidence.quote: There are logarithmically many levels with linear merge work per level, giving n log n time even on sorted input unless an optimization skips merges.
For eventually nonnegative functions, f(n)=O(g(n)) means f(n)≤c g(n) for some positive c beyond a threshold k.

choices.label: A
choices.explanation: n log n is the tight best growth for ordinary unoptimized merge sorting.

choices.label: B
choices.explanation: A quadratic upper bound is true but looser than the ordinary best growth.

choices.label: C
choices.explanation: n² log n also upper-bounds the ordinary n log n best cost.

choices.label: D
choices.explanation: The final notation can mean log(n²) or squared log; neither establishes a unique answer.

reviews.answer_text: Iterative heapsort and bottom-up merge sort avoid recursion.
reviews.hint: Read max-heap extraction for ascending sorting.
reviews.explanation: DSA37 explicitly contrasts recursive top-down merging with iterative bottom-up run merging. DSA38 describes iterative sinking for heapsort, so heapsort can also avoid recursion. Standard quicksort and top-down merge sort recurse. Since no recursive heapify implementation is mandated, both C and D meet the question’s nonrecursive description under the note’s implementations.

evidence.quote: Iterative sinking needs constant auxiliary storage.

choices.label: A
choices.explanation: The ordinary quicksort in the note recursively sorts its partition ranges.

choices.label: B
choices.explanation: Top-down merge sort recurses, while a bottom-up implementation is explicitly nonrecursive.

choices.label: C
choices.explanation: Heapsort with iterative sinking uses no recursion, as described in DSA38.

choices.label: D
choices.explanation: Bottom-up merge sort iteratively merges runs of increasing widths without recursion.

reviews.answer_text: Both short lists and a single unsorted-list query favor scanning.
reviews.hint: Read linear scanning and early-stop cases.
reviews.explanation: DSA28 says small lists may favor scanning because setup matters, and sorting first is rarely justified for one unsorted query. Thus A and B are individually supported use cases, and D explicitly combines them. C is an unjustified universal choice. The aggregate D is the most complete answer rather than evidence that the individual use cases are false.

evidence.quote: Compare the target with successive elements until equal or exhausted. Unsorted data is allowed; sorted data is allowed too.

choices.label: A
choices.explanation: Scanning can suit short lists because preprocessing and setup may dominate.

choices.label: B
choices.explanation: A single query on unsorted data can be answered directly without sorting first.

choices.label: C
choices.explanation: Linear search is not universally preferable; ordered or repeated-query structures can offer better costs.

choices.label: D
choices.explanation: This aggregate includes both supported scanning scenarios from DSA28.

reviews.answer_text: Insertion is linear; D additionally requires immediate reclamation when emptying.
reviews.hint: Separate endpoint traversal from the ownership and reclamation contract of clearing a queue.
reviews.explanation: DSA14 requires head-only insertion to traverse to the tail, while one front deletion is constant. DSA09 makes clearing an owned chain linear when it visits and releases all nodes. The stem does not require that contract: logical clear can reset front in constant time when reclamation is deferred or ownership is elsewhere. Thus D is conventional for immediate owned-node cleanup; A alone identifies the linear operation under logical-clear semantics.

evidence.quote: An abstract data type (ADT) defines values and operations; representation supplies implementation.
Clearing an owned n-node chain visits and releases every node.
With head alone, insertion must traverse to the tail.

choices.label: A
choices.explanation: Head-only enqueue must find the tail and therefore takes linear worst-case traversal.

choices.label: B
choices.explanation: Removing one front node updates a constant number of links and takes constant work.

choices.label: C
choices.explanation: Immediate owned-node reclamation is linear; logical reference reset can be constant with deferred or external reclamation.

choices.label: D
choices.explanation: Both are linear only when emptying includes visiting and reclaiming the whole owned chain.

reviews.answer_text: At-most-two children is true; uniqueness and left-equality depend on wording and duplicate policy.
reviews.hint: Read the global BST order invariant.
reviews.explanation: DSA18 defines binary as at most two children. DSA19 states strict subtree ordering with distinct keys but requires a separate policy for duplicates. A may mean at most two or exactly two; B can fit a left-duplicate convention but not strict distinct keys; C fits only the distinct-key model. The unspecified conventions prevent a stable single true option.

evidence.quote: With distinct keys, every key in a node’s left subtree is smaller and every key in its right subtree is larger.

choices.label: A
choices.explanation: At most two children is true, but exactly two would incorrectly exclude leaves and one-child nodes.

choices.label: B
choices.explanation: Equal left-subtree keys require a stated duplicate-placement policy and violate the distinct-key invariant.

choices.label: C
choices.explanation: Uniqueness holds in the note’s distinct-key model but is not mandatory for every duplicate-aware BST.

choices.label: D
choices.explanation: All cannot be justified without resolving the conflicting uniqueness and left-equality conventions.

reviews.answer_text: Go left for a smaller target only if this is a binary search tree.
reviews.hint: Read the global BST order invariant.
reviews.explanation: DSA19’s subtree ordering allows a BST search to go left when the target is smaller than the current root. An arbitrary binary tree has no such key order, so the question’s literal binary tree cannot justify that direction. If BST was intended, A is correct; otherwise None may describe the absence of a general key-directed rule.

evidence.quote: With distinct keys, every key in a node’s left subtree is smaller and every key in its right subtree is larger.

choices.label: A
choices.explanation: This is correct under the BST ordering invariant, but not for an arbitrary binary tree.

choices.label: B
choices.explanation: A larger target goes right in an ascending BST; arbitrary binary trees provide no such guarantee.

choices.label: C
choices.explanation: Equality is a successful match in ordinary BST lookup rather than a reason to continue left.

choices.label: D
choices.explanation: None fits arbitrary binary trees lacking an ordering invariant, but not the likely BST interpretation.

reviews.answer_text: Array, queue, and linked list are all linear.
reviews.hint: Read the ADT and linear/nonlinear structure distinction.
reviews.explanation: DSA01 explicitly classifies arrays, linked lists, stacks, and queues as linear structures and trees as hierarchical. B, C, and D therefore all satisfy the stem. The stray character in C does not obscure the word Queue. The singular Which one wording cannot make one of these three valid linear structures uniquely correct.

evidence.quote: Arrays, linked lists, stacks and queues are linear. Trees model hierarchies; graphs model general connections.

choices.label: A
choices.explanation: Trees model hierarchical branching and are not classified as linear structures in DSA01.

choices.label: B
choices.explanation: Arrays are explicitly classified as linear structures in the complete note.

choices.label: C
choices.explanation: The readable Queue option is explicitly a linear structure despite its stray OCR character.

choices.label: D
choices.explanation: Linked lists are explicitly included among linear structures in DSA01.

reviews.answer_text: LIFO and FILO name the same stack policy.
reviews.hint: Read stack service policy and top conventions.
reviews.explanation: DSA11 explicitly states that stack policy is LIFO, equivalently FILO. The last item inserted is removed first, which also means the first inserted is removed last. FIFO and FCFS instead describe arrival-order queues. Therefore A and C are synonymous correct choices; the OCR character before FILO does not change its readable meaning.

evidence.quote: Stack policy is LIFO, equivalently FILO. Push inserts, pop removes/returns top, and peek only observes.

choices.label: A
choices.explanation: LIFO names last-in-first-out stack service, directly matching DSA11.

choices.label: B
choices.explanation: FIFO serves oldest arrivals first and describes queue service rather than stacks.

choices.label: C
choices.explanation: FILO is explicitly equivalent to LIFO and therefore also names the stack policy.

choices.label: D
choices.explanation: FCFS is arrival-order queue service rather than the stack’s latest-in-first-out policy.

reviews.answer_text: A, C, D, and E satisfy the final-pivot invariant; exact order needs a partition algorithm.
reviews.hint: Read partition invariants and algorithm-dependent traces.
reviews.explanation: DSA36 says the ten distinct values contain five keys below pivot 5 and four above it. A, C, D, and E place those groups on the appropriate sides of 5. Different partition procedures can leave different internal orders, so the invariant does not choose one exact array. F leaves 5 at the start and fails final-position ordering.

evidence.quote: Internal orders depend on the partition algorithm; several candidate arrays can satisfy the invariant.

choices.label: A
choices.explanation: All five smaller keys precede five and all larger keys follow; this is a valid partition arrangement.

choices.label: B
choices.explanation: Several arrays satisfy the partition invariant, so None is not justified merely from the stated conditions.

choices.label: C
choices.explanation: This also has the correct smaller/pivot/larger grouping, though internal order depends on the algorithm.

choices.label: D
choices.explanation: This satisfies the final-pivot grouping but cannot be uniquely predicted without a partition procedure.

choices.label: E
choices.explanation: This also satisfies the invariant and differs only in the order within a partition.

choices.label: F
choices.explanation: Five remains first despite smaller keys after it, so it is not at its final sorted position.

reviews.answer_text: Merge worst comparisons depend on interleaving, not merely sortedness or distinctness.
reviews.hint: Read merge levels, buffers, and external runs.
reviews.explanation: DSA37 says ordinary merge sorting has n log n growth across orders and that reverse order alone does not characterize maximum comparisons. Exact worst comparisons depend on how the two sorted halves interleave at each merge. None of the broad labels uniquely fixes that pattern; choosing None also depends on whether worst means exact comparisons or asymptotic growth.

evidence.quote: There are logarithmically many levels with linear merge work per level, giving n log n time even on sorted input unless an optimization skips merges.

choices.label: A
choices.explanation: Reverse order still has n log n growth but does not by itself force maximum merge comparisons.

choices.label: B
choices.explanation: Already sorted input still has ordinary n log n growth, though not necessarily maximum comparisons.

choices.label: C
choices.explanation: Equal elements still undergo ordinary merge levels but can reduce comparisons with left-first ties.

choices.label: D
choices.explanation: Distinctness permits worst interleavings but does not guarantee them.

choices.label: E
choices.explanation: None fits an exact-characterization reading, but several inputs share the worst asymptotic order.

reviews.answer_text: Balanced BSTs and sorted random-access arrays both allow logarithmic search.
reviews.hint: Read ordered intervals and binary-search probe bounds.
reviews.explanation: DSA19 gives BST search O(height), which becomes logarithmic only with balance. DSA29 gives sorted random-access arrays logarithmic binary search. A generic BST can be a chain and a generic array can be unsorted. The stem specifies neither prerequisite, so A and E are conditional candidates rather than a unique guaranteed logarithmic ADT.

evidence.quote: Worst probes are floor(log₂n)+1 for n>0: seven for 100 keys, about twenty for one million.

choices.label: A
choices.explanation: A balanced BST qualifies; a chain-shaped BST can require linear search.

choices.label: B
choices.explanation: Singly linked midpoint traversal does not supply the usual logarithmic total time.

choices.label: C
choices.explanation: Ordinary singly linked lists require traversal and do not guarantee logarithmic target lookup.

choices.label: D
choices.explanation: Heap order does not give logarithmic arbitrary-key lookup; only extremes are privileged.

choices.label: E
choices.explanation: A sorted random-access array supports logarithmic binary search; unsortedness is not ruled out.

reviews.answer_text: Quicksort needs an input case and a tightness convention.
reviews.hint: Read partition invariants and algorithm-dependent traces.
reviews.explanation: DSA36 gives n log n work for balanced or expected partitions and n² for repeated extreme partitions. B and D therefore describe different cases. C is also a loose upper bound on either polynomial cost, while A is too small for ordinary sorting. No case or tightest-bound requirement is stated, so one complexity order cannot be selected uniquely.

evidence.quote: Internal orders depend on the partition algorithm; several candidate arrays can satisfy the invariant.

choices.label: A
choices.explanation: Ordinary quicksort does not have a general linear sorting cost across growing inputs.

choices.label: B
choices.explanation: Quadratic is its tight worst growth and also a loose bound for expected n log n.

choices.label: C
choices.explanation: Exponential is a valid very loose upper bound on polynomial quicksort work.

choices.label: D
choices.explanation: n log n describes balanced or expected behavior, not the general worst case.

reviews.answer_text: Head-only append is Θ(n), hence also O(n).
reviews.hint: Read head, tail, and predecessor update costs.
reviews.explanation: DSA09 says appending with only head requires finding the tail. Traversing n nodes and then changing constant links gives Θ(n) time. DSA06 makes Θ a tight bound and O an upper bound, so the same cost satisfies both C and A. The constant choices would require a maintained tail reference that the question does not provide.

evidence.quote: Prepend with new.next=head; head=new.

choices.label: A
choices.explanation: O(n) is a valid upper bound on the required head-to-tail traversal.

choices.label: B
choices.explanation: A head-only chain does not provide constant-time access to the append position.

choices.label: C
choices.explanation: Θ(n) tightly describes traversing the chain before attaching the new node.

choices.label: D
choices.explanation: Constant time would need a maintained tail reference, absent from the stated representation.

reviews.answer_text: Array queues can use index updates, shifting, or resizing; the implementation is missing.
reviews.hint: Read circular slots, logical order, and capacity conventions.
reviews.explanation: DSA15 uses circular front/size indices for constant endpoint updates. A shifting dequeue instead moves survivors and can be linear; a resizing enqueue can also be linear. Merely saying arrays does not choose among these algorithms or state fixed capacity. Thus C is valid for the fixed circular implementation but not a guaranteed pair for every array queue.

evidence.quote: Physical array: [9,13,15,17,19,21]; logical front-to-rear queue: [13,15,17,19,21,9]. A noncircular version can instead overflow.

choices.label: A
choices.explanation: Linear enqueue and constant dequeue can arise when enqueue resizes or shifts storage.

choices.label: B
choices.explanation: Constant enqueue and linear dequeue fit a representation that shifts survivors after removal.

choices.label: C
choices.explanation: Both are constant for a fixed circular queue with index updates and capacity checks.

choices.label: D
choices.explanation: Both linear bounds are loose possibilities; representation alone supplies no tight universal pair.

reviews.answer_text: The meaning of access and the endpoint representation are unspecified.
reviews.hint: Read FIFO endpoint operations.
reviews.explanation: DSA14 gives queue insertion at rear and removal at front. DSA10 permits both endpoint references in a linked list, and DSA16 gives deques both-end operations. Access could mean peeking, inserting, removing, or traversing; those are different contracts. The offered generic names do not identify which contract or maintained pointers are intended.

evidence.quote: An ordinary queue enqueues at rear, dequeues at front, and peeks at front. This is FIFO or first-come, first-served.

choices.label: A
choices.explanation: A standard stack exposes its top rather than a two-end access contract.

choices.label: B
choices.explanation: A queue operates at front and rear, but not every operation is allowed at both ends.

choices.label: C
choices.explanation: A doubly linked list with head and tail can access both ends directly.

choices.label: D
choices.explanation: A binary tree does not define beginning and end as standard service endpoints.

reviews.answer_text: A doubly linked list with head and tail qualifies; generic linked lists do not guarantee it.
reviews.hint: Read doubly linked and circular variants.
reviews.explanation: DSA10 states that doubly linked nodes plus head and tail allow constant-time operations at both ends. Singly linked tail deletion still needs a predecessor. Therefore C is true under a specific variant, but the generic Linked list option omits the representation essential to the guarantee. The other ADT names do not provide all four endpoint operations by contract.

evidence.quote: Doubly linked nodes add prev; head and tail enable constant-time operations at both ends.

choices.label: A
choices.explanation: A stack provides top insertion/removal, not arbitrary constant operations at both ends.

choices.label: B
choices.explanation: An ordinary queue provides rear insertion and front removal rather than all both-end operations.

choices.label: C
choices.explanation: Doubly linked nodes with both endpoint pointers qualify; a generic singly linked list does not.

choices.label: D
choices.explanation: A binary tree has no standard guarantee for constant-time insertion/deletion at two sequence endpoints.

reviews.answer_text: Multiple structures have both indexed and linked representations.
reviews.hint: Read the ADT and linear/nonlinear structure distinction.
reviews.explanation: DSA01 separates ADTs from their representations. DSA11 supplies array and linked stacks, DSA14/15 array and linked queues, DSA08 array-linked chains, and DSA23 indexed binary heaps. Pointer-based trees also use linked nodes. Thus the broad can be implemented wording admits every offered structure under a suitable representation; it cannot uniquely identify Stack.

evidence.quote: Arrays, linked lists, stacks and queues are linear. Trees model hierarchies; graphs model general connections.

choices.label: A
choices.explanation: Stacks have both array-top and linked-head implementations explicitly described in the note.

choices.label: B
choices.explanation: Queues can use circular arrays or linked head/tail nodes.

choices.label: C
choices.explanation: An array-linked list stores links as indices, while ordinary linked nodes store references.

choices.label: D
choices.explanation: Binary trees can use indexed heap storage or linked child-node representations.

reviews.answer_text: All can use dynamically allocated linked nodes.
reviews.hint: Read node links and chain termination.
reviews.explanation: DSA08 allocates linked nodes as needed. DSA11 implements stacks at a linked head, DSA14 implements queues with linked endpoints, and pointer-based tree insertion attaches nodes. Therefore all four can allocate nodes dynamically. Dynamic allocation describes an implementation choice rather than an exclusive ADT property; array variants do not invalidate the existence of the linked variants.

evidence.quote: A singly linked node contains data and next. Head points to the first node; null ends a noncircular chain.

choices.label: A
choices.explanation: A linked stack allocates nodes as needed for pushes and releases them on pops.

choices.label: B
choices.explanation: A linked queue can allocate new rear nodes as requests arrive.

choices.label: C
choices.explanation: Linked-list nodes are explicitly allocated as needed, permitting dynamic growth.

choices.label: D
choices.explanation: A pointer-based binary tree can allocate a new node when attaching a leaf.

reviews.answer_text: Several array implementations exist; easily has no defined criterion.
reviews.hint: Read array address arithmetic and shifting costs.
reviews.explanation: DSA11 describes an array stack, DSA15 a circular array queue, DSA08 array-stored links, and DSA23 an array binary heap. These establish several implementations. The adjective easily supplies no space, time, or complexity measure that would rank them. The question therefore cannot select a unique structure merely from array storage being possible.

evidence.quote: This arithmetic gives constant-time positional access in the usual RAM cost model.

choices.label: A
choices.explanation: An array stack is straightforward, using a top index, but is not the only array implementation.

choices.label: B
choices.explanation: A circular array queue is explicitly described and also provides direct index updates.

choices.label: C
choices.explanation: Links can be stored as array indices, although the ease criterion is undefined.

choices.label: D
choices.explanation: A complete binary heap has simple child-index arithmetic; arbitrary tree layout needs further choices.

reviews.answer_text: Endpoint references or indices determine the guarantee, not the generic ADT name.
reviews.hint: Read doubly linked and circular variants.
reviews.explanation: DSA10 gives head/tail direct endpoints for doubly linked lists, and DSA14 uses both pointers in linked queues. A head-only list cannot access the last node in constant time. Array stacks can know their first and last occupied positions, but the stack interface normally exposes top only. The stem omits both representation and what access means.

evidence.quote: Doubly linked nodes add prev; head and tail enable constant-time operations at both ends.

choices.label: A
choices.explanation: An array stack can retain endpoint positions internally, but its abstract interface normally exposes only top.

choices.label: B
choices.explanation: A head/tail or indexed queue can reach endpoints directly; a front-only implementation cannot reach rear instantly.

choices.label: C
choices.explanation: A list with head and tail qualifies, but a generic head-only singly linked list does not.

choices.label: D
choices.explanation: A generic binary tree does not guarantee constant access to first and last traversal elements.

reviews.answer_text: A stack reverses output, while link reversal can avoid an auxiliary structure.
reviews.hint: Read stepwise stack traces and nested calls.
reviews.explanation: DSA12 reverses a sequence by pushing then popping. DSA09 also reverses a chain in linear time with constant extra pointers. Thus A is a conventional reversal tool, but C’s underlying links can be reversed with less extra storage. Best requires a specified input representation, output contract, and memory criterion, none of which is given.

evidence.quote: Reversal pushes input then pops it.

choices.label: A
choices.explanation: Pushing then popping reverses order, but requires auxiliary storage proportional to the sequence.

choices.label: B
choices.explanation: Ordinary FIFO service preserves arrival order rather than directly reversing it.

choices.label: C
choices.explanation: An existing linked list can be reversed in place with constant extra pointers.

choices.label: D
choices.explanation: A binary tree provides no stated advantage for the required sequence-reversal task.

reviews.answer_text: Queue is the likely endpoint policy; access is not defined precisely.
reviews.hint: Read FIFO endpoint operations.
reviews.explanation: DSA14 limits an ordinary queue to rear insertion and front removal or peek. If access means those operations, B fits. If it means arbitrary reading or all insertion/removal operations at either end, that is a different contract, such as deque. The stem’s beginning-and-end phrasing does not identify which operations it permits or restricts.

evidence.quote: An ordinary queue enqueues at rear, dequeues at front, and peeks at front. This is FIFO or first-come, first-served.

choices.label: A
choices.explanation: A stack conventionally exposes only one top end, not distinct beginning and end operations.

choices.label: B
choices.explanation: A queue fits front removal and rear insertion, but unrestricted access at either end is not its contract.

choices.label: C
choices.explanation: A general linked list permits traversal to interior nodes and is not restricted to endpoint access.

choices.label: D
choices.explanation: A tree’s branch structure is not an endpoint-restricted sequence interface.

reviews.answer_text: Linked implementations of all four can use pointer-connected nodes.
reviews.hint: Read node links and chain termination.
reviews.explanation: DSA08 explicitly defines payload-and-next linked nodes. DSA11 and DSA14 use such linked nodes for stacks and queues. A binary tree can similarly link parent/child nodes instead of using indexed heap storage. The statement describes a representation that more than one structure can use, so it cannot uniquely identify Linked list.

evidence.quote: A singly linked node contains data and next. Head points to the first node; null ends a noncircular chain.

choices.label: A
choices.explanation: A linked stack uses node pointers at its head, although an array stack is also possible.

choices.label: B
choices.explanation: A linked queue connects nodes through pointers and maintains endpoint references.

choices.label: C
choices.explanation: An ordinary linked list is explicitly a chain of pointer-connected nodes.

choices.label: D
choices.explanation: A pointer-based binary tree connects child nodes through links, although indexed trees also exist.

reviews.answer_text: LIFO, FIFO, and priority service each impose a specific order.
reviews.hint: Read stack service policy and top conventions.
reviews.explanation: DSA11 gives stacks LIFO order, DSA14 queues FIFO order, and DSA17 priority queues an extremal-key order with a tie policy. These are all specific disciplines. DSA20 gives several possible tree traversals rather than one inherent binary-tree access order. Without naming the desired discipline, at least A, B, and C independently satisfy the description.

evidence.quote: Stack policy is LIFO, equivalently FILO. Push inserts, pop removes/returns top, and peek only observes.

choices.label: A
choices.explanation: Stacks impose LIFO, a specific service order for their elements.

choices.label: B
choices.explanation: Queues impose FIFO, another specific service order.

choices.label: C
choices.explanation: Priority queues serve an extremal key under a chosen direction and tie rule.

choices.label: D
choices.explanation: A binary tree needs a specified traversal; its shape alone does not enforce one access order.

reviews.answer_text: Local child inequalities neither define a full BST nor distinguish balanced BST subclasses.
reviews.hint: Read the global BST order invariant.
reviews.explanation: DSA19 requires every descendant in a left or right subtree to obey the ancestor bound, not merely the immediate children. AVL and red-black trees are ordered balanced BST disciplines in DSA22, so they also satisfy the local comparisons. Equal-key handling needs a policy. The weak local definition and overlapping subclasses prevent a unique defining structure.

evidence.quote: With distinct keys, every key in a node’s left subtree is smaller and every key in its right subtree is larger.

choices.label: A
choices.explanation: An AVL tree is an ordered balanced BST and satisfies the local child inequalities.

choices.label: B
choices.explanation: BST is the intended family, but the stated immediate-child inequalities are weaker than its global invariant.

choices.label: C
choices.explanation: A red-black ordered tree also satisfies the local inequalities, so it overlaps the BST choice.

choices.label: D
choices.explanation: A general B-tree is not a binary tree, so it does not fit the stated structural description.

reviews.answer_text: A circular-array deque may qualify; the deque contract does not guarantee middle indexing.
reviews.hint: Read deque endpoint capabilities.
reviews.explanation: DSA16 says a deque supports both-end operations but not guaranteed middle access. A linked deque needs linear indexing; a circular-array deque may provide constant indexed access. Therefore C fits only a specified implementation. The other ADT names do not promise the combined endpoint and middle-index guarantees, and the stem omits the representation needed to establish them.

evidence.quote: A deque permits both-end insertion/removal without guaranteeing middle access.

choices.label: A
choices.explanation: The stack interface lacks both-end insertion/removal and arbitrary constant middle access.

choices.label: B
choices.explanation: An ordinary queue lacks the full both-end operation set and arbitrary middle access.

choices.label: C
choices.explanation: A circular-array deque can support indexing; a linked deque does not guarantee constant middle access.

choices.label: D
choices.explanation: A generic binary tree does not guarantee constant-time access by middle sequence position.

reviews.answer_text: Every listed ordinary comparison sort satisfies the literal O(n²) upper bound.
reviews.hint: Read sorting resource tables and overlapping bounds.
reviews.explanation: DSA31 gives n log n worst bounds for merge and heap, and n² worst costs for quick and insertion. Because Big-O is an upper bound rather than necessarily tight, the first two also satisfy O(n²). If the question intended tightly quadratic, B and C remain two valid main choices. The alternate set similarly needs independent interpretation.

evidence.quote: For eventually nonnegative functions, f(n)=O(g(n)) means f(n)≤c g(n) for some positive c beyond a threshold k.
Balanced partitions give n log n work; repeated extreme pivots sum n+(n-1)+… to quadratic work.

choices.label: A
choices.explanation: Merge’s n log n worst cost is below a quadratic upper bound, though not tightly quadratic.

choices.label: B
choices.explanation: Quicksort can have repeated extreme partitions and tight quadratic worst work.

choices.label: C
choices.explanation: Insertion sort has tight quadratic worst work on reverse-ordered arrays.

choices.label: D
choices.explanation: Heapsort’s n log n worst bound also satisfies the looser quadratic upper bound.

variant_reviews.answer_text: All four satisfy O(n²); bubble, quick, and insertion are tightly quadratic.
variant_reviews.explanation: The alternate set contains bubble, quick, merge, and insertion. Bubble, quick, and insertion each have quadratic worst costs. Merge remains n log n, which is also O(n²) as a loose upper bound. Therefore all four satisfy the literal notation, while A, B, and D satisfy the intended tight-quadratic reading.

choices.label: A
choices.explanation: Bubble sort has quadratic worst-case adjacent-pass work.

choices.label: B
choices.explanation: Quicksort has quadratic worst work under repeatedly extreme partitions.

choices.label: C
choices.explanation: Merge sort has n log n worst growth and hence also a looser O(n²) bound.

choices.label: D
choices.explanation: Insertion sort performs quadratic shifts in reverse order.

reviews.answer_text: Merge sort; the alternate set also includes quicksort.
reviews.hint: Read merge levels, buffers, and external runs.
reviews.explanation: DSA37 splits the input into halves, recursively sorts them, and merges the results, which is divide and conquer. Bubble and selection use repeated local passes or minima, while the described LSD radix method sorts digit passes. Thus C is the main answer. The variant adds quicksort, whose independent recursive partitions provide a second valid divide-and-conquer choice.

evidence.quote: Split into halves, sort them, then merge by advancing the smaller current front.

choices.label: A
choices.explanation: Bubble sort uses repeated adjacent passes rather than recursive independent subproblem decomposition.

choices.label: B
choices.explanation: Selection repeatedly chooses a suffix minimum instead of recursively sorting and combining halves.

choices.label: C
choices.explanation: Merge sort recursively sorts halves and combines them through merging.

choices.label: D
choices.explanation: The described LSD radix method uses stable digit passes rather than this divide-and-conquer decomposition.

variant_reviews.explanation: This variant substitutes quicksort for selection and insertion for radix. DSA36 partitions and recursively sorts smaller ranges, while DSA37 recursively sorts halves and merges. Both are divide-and-conquer algorithms. Bubble and ordinary insertion lack that recursive decomposition, so the variant has two supported answers, B and C.

choices.label: A
choices.explanation: Bubble sorting repeatedly swaps adjacent inversions instead of recursively decomposing subinstances.

choices.label: B
choices.explanation: Quicksort partitions around a pivot and recursively sorts the smaller ranges.

choices.label: C
choices.explanation: Merge sort recursively sorts halves and combines their sorted results.

choices.label: D
choices.explanation: Ordinary insertion sort extends a sorted prefix instead of applying recursive divide and conquer.

reviews.answer_text: Quicksort and merge sort have n log n average growth under their usual models.
reviews.hint: Read merge levels, buffers, and external runs.
reviews.explanation: DSA36 gives expected n log n quicksort under an input or random-pivot model. DSA37 gives ordinary merge sort n log n across input orders, hence also on average. Bubble and insertion have quadratic ordinary average work. The stem specifies neither a distinguishing distribution nor another requirement, so B and C both fit.

evidence.quote: There are logarithmically many levels with linear merge work per level, giving n log n time even on sorted input unless an optimization skips merges.

choices.label: A
choices.explanation: Bubble sort has quadratic average work under the usual random-order model.

choices.label: B
