choices.explanation: Quicksort has expected n log n work under the usual input or random-pivot assumptions.

choices.label: C
choices.explanation: Merge sort has n log n work across input orders and therefore also on average.

choices.label: D
choices.explanation: Insertion sort has quadratic ordinary average work, although nearly sorted inputs can be faster.

reviews.answer_text: Bubble, quicksort, and insertion are in-place comparison methods under element-storage convention.
reviews.hint: Read sorting resource tables and overlapping bounds.
reviews.explanation: DSA31 defines in-place in terms of constant extra element storage and warns that recursion stacks can still matter. Bubble and insertion use constant working storage; quicksort ordinarily partitions within the array but uses a call stack. Ordinary merge uses a linear buffer. Under the common element-storage interpretation, three options qualify; total-space interpretation would exclude ordinary recursive quicksort.

evidence.quote: An in-place element algorithm uses a fixed amount of extra element storage; a recursive call stack may still matter when total auxiliary space is requested.

choices.label: A
choices.explanation: Bubble compares adjacent keys and swaps them in the original array using constant extra storage.

choices.label: B
choices.explanation: Quicksort partitions in the original array; its recursion stack must be counted separately for total auxiliary space.

choices.label: C
choices.explanation: Ordinary merge sorting uses a linear merge buffer; special in-place variants need explicit qualification.

choices.label: D
choices.explanation: Insertion compares keys and shifts within the same array using constant extra element storage.

reviews.answer_text: Unit intervals suggest linear scanning; larger regular jumps suggest an omitted jump search.
reviews.hint: Read interpolation and ternary-search assumptions.
reviews.explanation: DSA28 compares successive elements, which are regularly spaced by one position. DSA30 says regular intervals could also refer to jump search probing block boundaries. The stem supplies no stride, sortedness, or block-scan behavior. A is plausible for unit-step scanning, but the wording does not uniquely identify that interpretation or include the alternative jump algorithm.

evidence.quote: Sorted-array ternary search compares two split points and keeps the relevant third, still logarithmic.

choices.label: A
choices.explanation: Linear scanning compares consecutive items at unit intervals, one possible meaning of regular intervals.

choices.label: B
choices.explanation: Binary-search midpoints move by shrinking, nonconstant distances rather than a fixed regular stride.

choices.label: C
choices.explanation: Hash probes depend on hash addresses and collision strategy rather than a general ordered interval scan.

choices.label: D
choices.explanation: DFS follows graph adjacency and does not define fixed positional comparison intervals.

reviews.answer_text: Bubble, merge, and insertion are stable with the described strict/tie rules.
reviews.hint: Read strict adjacent swaps and early stopping.
reviews.explanation: DSA32 preserves ties through strict adjacent bubble swaps, DSA34 shifts only strictly larger keys for stable insertion, and DSA37 takes equal merge keys left-first. Those are three standard stable implementations. Standard quicksort does not preserve ties through arbitrary partition exchanges. Stability alone therefore cannot distinguish one of A, C, and D.

evidence.quote: Strict swaps preserve equal-key order.

choices.label: A
choices.explanation: Strict adjacent bubble swaps preserve the original order of equal keys.

choices.label: B
choices.explanation: Standard quicksort partition exchanges do not preserve equal-key relative order.

choices.label: C
choices.explanation: Left-first handling of equal keys makes ordinary merge sort stable.

choices.label: D
choices.explanation: Shifting only strictly larger keys makes insertion sort stable.

reviews.answer_text: Insertion sort
reviews.hint: Read sorted-prefix insertion and shifts.
reviews.explanation: DSA34 explicitly favors insertion for small arrays or few inversions. Each inversion corresponds to shifting work, so nearly sorted data requires few shifts; sorted input is linear. This low-setup incremental algorithm is the conventional match among the choices. The other algorithms can sort these inputs, but their mere applicability does not identify the specific use case emphasized in the note.

evidence.quote: On sorted input each pass needs one ordering check and no shifts: linear time.

choices.label: A
choices.explanation: Bubble can exploit early stopping but is not the note’s specific small-array/few-inversions recommendation.

choices.label: B
choices.explanation: Quicksort incurs partition and recursive setup and is not the cited small-subarray method.

choices.label: C
choices.explanation: Ordinary merge sorting uses its merge levels and buffer even on nearly sorted input.

choices.label: D
choices.explanation: Insertion has low setup and few shifts on nearly sorted or small arrays.

reviews.answer_text: Bubble and insertion both use O(1) auxiliary space.
reviews.hint: Read sorting resource tables and overlapping bounds.
reviews.explanation: DSA31’s table gives constant extra storage for bubble and insertion in all input cases. Ordinary quicksort uses a recursion stack, usually logarithmic on average; ordinary merge sorting uses a linear buffer. Thus A and D satisfy the stated best-and-average auxiliary-space bound. Counting only quicksort’s element temporaries would be a different, unstated storage convention.

evidence.quote: An in-place element algorithm uses a fixed amount of extra element storage; a recursive call stack may still matter when total auxiliary space is requested.

choices.label: A
choices.explanation: Bubble sort uses a fixed number of temporaries, independent of input order.

choices.label: B
choices.explanation: Ordinary quicksort’s recursion stack is not constant on average when total auxiliary space is counted.

choices.label: C
choices.explanation: Ordinary array merge sort uses a linear auxiliary merge buffer.

choices.label: D
choices.explanation: Insertion sort stores a key and indices, giving constant auxiliary space across cases.

reviews.answer_text: Dataset size alone does not select an appropriate search.
reviews.hint: Read map/set contracts and cache policies.
reviews.explanation: DSA27 permits expected constant hash lookup and ordered tree alternatives; DSA29 permits binary search on sorted random-access sequences; DSA28 supports direct scans without preprocessing. Large dataset or database does not state key indexes, ordering, update patterns, storage I/O, or the number of queries. Those requirements determine suitability, so no offered algorithm is uniquely justified.

evidence.quote: A map associates unique keys with values; different keys may share values, and entries can be traversed.

choices.label: A
choices.explanation: Scanning can suit a one-off unindexed query or full-record processing even on a large dataset.

choices.label: B
choices.explanation: Binary search suits sorted random-access records but requires ordering and suitable access costs.

choices.label: C
choices.explanation: Hash search suits indexed equality queries under distribution and load assumptions.

choices.label: D
choices.explanation: DFS suits graph-shaped data, but dataset size alone does not supply graph relationships or objectives.

reviews.answer_text: Quicksort and merge tie at n log n average asymptotic growth.
reviews.hint: Read merge levels, buffers, and external runs.
reviews.explanation: DSA36 gives expected n log n quicksort under its usual model, and DSA37 gives n log n merge sorting across orders. Bubble and insertion are quadratic on ordinary average inputs. Therefore B and C tie in asymptotic average growth. No workload distribution, implementation constants, or measured time is supplied to decide which tied algorithm runs faster in practice.

evidence.quote: There are logarithmically many levels with linear merge work per level, giving n log n time even on sorted input unless an optimization skips merges.

choices.label: A
choices.explanation: Bubble’s ordinary quadratic average growth is worse than n log n.

choices.label: B
choices.explanation: Quicksort has expected n log n growth under the usual model, tying merge asymptotically.

choices.label: C
choices.explanation: Merge sorting has n log n average growth and ties the expected quicksort order.

choices.label: D
choices.explanation: Insertion’s ordinary quadratic average growth is worse than the two n log n choices.

reviews.answer_text: Arrays and linked lists are both standard stack representations.
reviews.hint: Read stack service policy and top conventions.
reviews.explanation: DSA11 describes an indexed array stack and a linked stack inserting and deleting at head. Both implement the same LIFO contract with ordinary constant endpoint operations. Queue and tree name different ADTs rather than the two standard representations described. The word typically does not establish a prevalence measure that would eliminate either supported implementation.

evidence.quote: Stack policy is LIFO, equivalently FILO. Push inserts, pop removes/returns top, and peek only observes.

choices.label: A
choices.explanation: An array and top index directly implement stack pushes, pops, and peeks.

choices.label: B
choices.explanation: A linked-head implementation also provides constant-time stack pushes and pops.

choices.label: C
choices.explanation: An ordinary queue follows FIFO rather than directly supplying the standard LIFO stack representation.

choices.label: D
choices.explanation: A tree is not one of the standard array/linked-head stack representations described in DSA11.

reviews.answer_text: Every listed comparison sort can compare a priority field.
reviews.hint: Read max-heap extraction for ascending sorting.
reviews.explanation: DSA38 explicitly warns that heapsort is not uniquely sorting by priorities: any comparison sort can compare a priority field. A heap becomes distinctive only when the stem specifies repeated root extraction. Because the question merely asks for ordering by priorities, bubble, quick, merge, and heap all satisfy the broad requirement under a consistent priority comparator.

evidence.quote: Iterative sinking needs constant auxiliary storage.

choices.label: A
choices.explanation: Bubble sort can compare priority keys instead of another field.

choices.label: B
choices.explanation: Quicksort can partition and recursively sort using the same priority comparator.

choices.label: C
choices.explanation: Merge sort can merge runs by priority and retain equal-priority order when stable.

choices.label: D
choices.explanation: Heapsort can repeatedly extract priority extremes, but priorities alone do not make it unique.

reviews.answer_text: Array, queue, and linked list are linear.
reviews.hint: Read the ADT and linear/nonlinear structure distinction.
reviews.explanation: DSA01 explicitly lists arrays, linked lists, stacks, and queues as linear structures while assigning trees a hierarchical role. Hence B, C, and D all satisfy the literal classification question. Tree is the exclusion. There is no combined option, so the singular wording cannot remove the other two independently correct linear choices.

evidence.quote: Arrays, linked lists, stacks and queues are linear. Trees model hierarchies; graphs model general connections.

choices.label: A
choices.explanation: Trees model hierarchical branching rather than the linear sequence category used here.

choices.label: B
choices.explanation: Array is explicitly included among linear data structures in DSA01.

choices.label: C
choices.explanation: Queue is explicitly included among linear data structures in DSA01.

choices.label: D
choices.explanation: Linked list is explicitly included among linear data structures in DSA01.

reviews.answer_text: LIFO and FILO
reviews.hint: Read stack service policy and top conventions.
reviews.explanation: DSA11 explicitly equates LIFO and FILO. A stack removes the most recently inserted item first, meaning the earliest inserted item is removed last. FIFO and FCFS instead serve arrivals in original order. Therefore A and C are equivalent correct answers; the question supplies no distinction that could make only one valid.

evidence.quote: Stack policy is LIFO, equivalently FILO. Push inserts, pop removes/returns top, and peek only observes.

choices.label: A
choices.explanation: LIFO is the explicit stack policy: last inserted, first removed.

choices.label: B
choices.explanation: FIFO serves oldest arrivals first and describes a queue policy.

choices.label: C
choices.explanation: FILO is explicitly equivalent to LIFO and therefore also describes a stack.

choices.label: D
choices.explanation: FCFS preserves arrival order and is not the stack’s latest-first policy.

reviews.answer_text: D is tightest, but every listed conventional upper bound includes logarithmic search.
reviews.hint: Read ordered intervals and binary-search probe bounds.
reviews.explanation: DSA29 gives logarithmic worst probes on sorted random-access data. D is the tight conventional answer. However, Big-O need not be tight: linear, quadratic, and the larger n-times-log expression also upper-bound a logarithmic function. Without a tightest qualifier, all four conventional readings are valid upper bounds, not four different actual running times.

evidence.quote: Worst probes are floor(log₂n)+1 for n>0: seven for 100 keys, about twenty for one million.

choices.label: A
choices.explanation: Either ordinary reading of n times the log expression grows faster than logarithmic search and is a loose upper bound.

choices.label: B
choices.explanation: Quadratic growth is a valid but loose upper bound on logarithmic binary-search work.

choices.label: C
choices.explanation: Linear growth also upper-bounds logarithmic search, though it is not tight.

choices.label: D
choices.explanation: Logarithmic is the tight worst-case bound under sorted random-access assumptions.

reviews.answer_text: Bubble sort with early stopping
reviews.hint: Read strict adjacent swaps and early stopping.
reviews.explanation: DSA32 describes adjacent comparisons, swapping strict inversions, and repeating passes until a pass performs no swaps. That matches every part of the stem, including its stopping condition. Insertion grows a sorted prefix, selection chooses a suffix minimum, and Shell uses separated gap subsequences, so none has this exact adjacent full-pass mechanism.

evidence.quote: Early stopping makes a sorted input linear: one no-swap pass finishes. A fixed pass schedule stays quadratic.

choices.label: A
choices.explanation: Insertion places each next value into a sorted prefix rather than repeating full adjacent passes.

choices.label: B
choices.explanation: Adjacent inversion swaps and repetition until no swaps identify optimized bubble sort.

choices.label: C
choices.explanation: Selection finds a suffix minimum and exchanges it with the prefix boundary.

choices.label: D
choices.explanation: Shell sorts gap-separated subsequences before its final gap-one insertion pass.

reviews.answer_text: Depth-first search uses stack discipline rather than the ordinary queue.
reviews.hint: Read branch-first traversal and pending work.
reviews.explanation: DSA42 finishes a branch using a stack or recursion and explicitly says a queue changes that discipline. DSA14 gives FIFO waiting, play sequences, and asynchronous buffering as queue uses. Interrupt work can also be buffered pending service. Thus the standard DFS claim is the non-queue application among the offered ordinary examples.

evidence.quote: An explicit stack can store pending work instead. Both implement latest-pending-work first; a queue would change that discipline.

choices.label: A
choices.explanation: Pending interrupts can be buffered for later service; queue use need not imply one universal interrupt priority policy.

choices.label: B
choices.explanation: A FIFO play queue can preserve the order of media items.

choices.label: C
choices.explanation: Standard DFS uses latest-pending-work-first stack or recursion rather than FIFO queue service.

choices.label: D
choices.explanation: Waiting for one shared resource is a direct FIFO queue application.

reviews.answer_text: Stack
reviews.hint: Read stack service policy and top conventions.
reviews.explanation: DSA11 explicitly assigns LIFO to a stack. Arrays and linked lists can represent that stack, but neither storage structure inherently fixes its removal order. A queue instead supplies FIFO. The question asks for the service-policy ADT, so Stack is the specific answer rather than one of the possible underlying representations.

evidence.quote: Stack policy is LIFO, equivalently FILO. Push inserts, pop removes/returns top, and peek only observes.

choices.label: A
choices.explanation: A queue follows FIFO, not the latest-in-first-out order requested.

choices.label: B
choices.explanation: An array is a representation and does not inherently impose LIFO service.

choices.label: C
choices.explanation: A stack is explicitly defined by LIFO, equivalently FILO.

choices.label: D
choices.explanation: A linked list can implement several policies and does not inherently require LIFO.

reviews.answer_text: Dynamic structures can change size at runtime; static structures have fixed capacity.
reviews.hint: Read array address arithmetic and shifting costs.
reviews.explanation: DSA02 distinguishes fixed arrays from resizable arrays, and DSA08 allocates linked nodes as needed. Runtime growth or shrinkage is the key distinction; fixed capacity need not mean compile-time allocation.

evidence.quote: A fixed array has a chosen capacity; the choice need not occur at compile time. A resizable array allocates a larger block and copies when needed.

reviews.answer_text: Non-linear
reviews.hint: Read the ADT and linear/nonlinear structure distinction.
reviews.explanation: DSA01 treats arrays, lists, stacks, and queues as linear sequences, trees as hierarchies, and graphs as general connections. Trees and graphs therefore belong to the nonlinear relationship category. Homogeneity describes element types and static describes storage capacity; neither classifies both by their branching relationship structure. C is the appropriate shared category.

evidence.quote: Arrays, linked lists, stacks and queues are linear. Trees model hierarchies; graphs model general connections.

choices.label: A
choices.explanation: Linear describes sequence-like structures rather than branching trees and general graphs.

choices.label: B
choices.explanation: Homogeneous concerns uniform element types and does not identify their relationship structure.

choices.label: C
choices.explanation: Trees and graphs are nonlinear relationship structures, unlike the listed linear sequences.

choices.label: D
choices.explanation: Static concerns storage or capacity decisions, not whether connections branch.

reviews.answer_text: An ADT defines its values/data and permitted operations.
reviews.hint: Read the ADT and linear/nonlinear structure distinction.
reviews.explanation: DSA01 explicitly defines an abstract data type through values and operations, leaving representation to the implementation. The same LIFO stack can therefore use arrays or linked nodes without changing its contract.

evidence.quote: An abstract data type (ADT) defines values and operations; representation supplies implementation.

reviews.answer_text: Non-homogeneous, or heterogeneous
reviews.hint: Read the ADT and linear/nonlinear structure distinction.
reviews.explanation: DSA01 directly identifies a record grouping integer, character, and floating fields as heterogeneous. The different field types distinguish it from an ordinary same-element-type array. Linear describes relationships, and static describes storage behavior, neither of which follows merely from the field types. Thus Non-homogeneous is the requested classification.

evidence.quote: A record grouping integer, character and floating fields is heterogeneous; an ordinary array has one element type.

choices.label: A
choices.explanation: Homogeneous would mean a uniform element type, contrary to the mixed int, char, and float fields.

choices.label: B
choices.explanation: The record combines different field types and is therefore heterogeneous or non-homogeneous.

choices.label: C
choices.explanation: Linear concerns relationships or order, not the mixed-type classification asked here.

choices.label: D
choices.explanation: Static concerns allocation or lifetime and is not established merely by these field types.

reviews.answer_text: Abstraction preserves relevant behavior and hides irrelevant implementation detail.
reviews.hint: Read the ADT and linear/nonlinear structure distinction.
reviews.explanation: DSA01 illustrates abstraction using patient urgency and arrival order while ignoring hair colour. Programmers retain the data and operations needed for the task and separate that contract from representation details. This supports the substantive answer without additional facts.

evidence.quote: Abstraction keeps relevant details: patient urgency and arrival order matter for service; hair colour does not.

reviews.answer_text: Merging
reviews.hint: Read operation definitions and memory ownership.
reviews.explanation: DSA03 calls combining sequences merging and works through sorted inputs by repeatedly emitting the smaller current front. Advancing only the selected sequence preserves sorted output until the remaining suffix is appended. For mathematical sets, duplicate handling additionally follows the set contract.

evidence.quote: To merge sorted [1,4] and [2,3], repeatedly emit the smaller front, producing [1,2,3,4].

reviews.answer_text: Destruction or deallocation of owned storage.
reviews.hint: Read operation definitions and memory ownership.
reviews.explanation: DSA03 says destroying a structure releases owned storage. In a linked chain, DSA09 visits and releases each owned node; C++ allocation forms must be matched to their deletion forms, and freed nodes must not be dereferenced.

evidence.quote: Destroying a structure releases owned storage.

reviews.answer_text: O(n), tightly Θ(n).
reviews.hint: Read formal asymptotic bounds and overlapping upper bounds.
reviews.explanation: For n≥1, 6n+4≤10n, while 6n+4≥6n. These constant upper and lower multiples establish linear growth by DSA06. O(n) is the natural tightest-order response, though larger upper bounds also exist.

evidence.quote: For eventually nonnegative functions, f(n)=O(g(n)) means f(n)≤c g(n) for some positive c beyond a threshold k.

reviews.answer_text: One valid witness pair is c=8, k=1.
reviews.hint: Read formal asymptotic bounds and overlapping upper bounds.
reviews.explanation: For every n≥1, 4n≤4n² and 1≤n², so 3n²+4n+1≤8n². DSA06 supplies the same inequality, proving the required eventual upper bound with c=8 and k=1. Other larger constants may also work.

evidence.quote: For n≥1, 3n²+4n+1≤8n²: c=8,k=1 witness O(n²).

reviews.answer_text: Finiteness
reviews.hint: Read correctness, finiteness, and definite instructions.
reviews.explanation: DSA04 defines finiteness as terminating after finitely many steps for every valid input. It is distinct from definiteness, executable instructions, or correctness: a terminating procedure can still return a wrong answer. The required concept is directly covered.

evidence.quote: Finiteness means termination after finitely many steps for every valid input.

reviews.answer_text: For k independent n-iteration nesting levels, Θ(n^k); two levels give Θ(n²).
reviews.hint: Read loop counts and hidden access costs.
reviews.explanation: DSA05 multiplies independent nested iteration counts, and DSA07 gives two levels as Θ(n²). The stem does not state the number of nested loops or constant-cost body work, so a unique exponent cannot be established. The empty option set is secondary: even the free-response cost needs the missing nesting and body assumptions.

evidence.quote: Two independent n-iteration loops nested around constant work take Theta(n²).

reviews.answer_text: Both upper and lower asymptotic bounds.
reviews.hint: Read formal asymptotic bounds and overlapping upper bounds.
reviews.explanation: DSA06 defines Big-O as an eventual upper bound, Omega as the reverse bound, and Theta as requiring both. Thus Theta expresses a tight growth class up to positive constants. It is independent of choosing best, average, or worst input cases; Average case only confuses the bound relation with an input-distribution choice.

evidence.quote: Omega reverses the inequality; Theta requires both.

choices.label: A
choices.explanation: An upper bound alone is Big-O and does not supply Theta’s lower requirement.

choices.label: B
choices.explanation: A lower bound alone is Omega and does not supply Theta’s upper requirement.

choices.label: C
choices.explanation: Theta requires simultaneous eventual upper and lower constant-factor bounds.

choices.label: D
choices.explanation: Theta can describe any case or resource function, not only an average case.

reviews.answer_text: Representative n log n grows faster than n; Big-O classes themselves overlap.
reviews.hint: Read formal asymptotic bounds and overlapping upper bounds.
reviews.explanation: DSA06 orders representative rates with n before n log n. Their ratio is log n, which grows without bound, so the representative n log n rate grows faster. However an O(n) function is also O(n log n), so membership alone does not compare actual runtimes.

evidence.quote: Increasing representative rates: 1, log n, n, n log n, n², n³, 2^n, 3^n, n!, n^n.

reviews.answer_text: One constant time unit in the elementary-operation model.
reviews.hint: Read the cost model and input cases.
reviews.explanation: DSA05 explicitly treats a single assignment as one unit in an elementary model, not one physical second. The convention abstracts hardware and requires that evaluating the assigned expression itself be constant cost; complicated expressions need their own accounting.

evidence.quote: A single assignment is one unit in the elementary model, not literally one second.

reviews.answer_text: If f∈O(g) and g∈O(h), then f∈O(h); this composes upper bounds.
reviews.hint: Read formal asymptotic bounds and overlapping upper bounds.
reviews.explanation: DSA06 composes the eventual inequalities f≤c g and g≤d h to obtain f≤cd h beyond both thresholds. Choose the larger threshold and multiply the positive witness constants. This lets a complicated bound pass through a simpler intermediate function.

evidence.quote: Transitivity multiplies witnesses: f≤c g≤cd h beyond both thresholds.

reviews.answer_text: Increasing representative growth: 1, log n, n, n², 2^n.
reviews.hint: Read formal asymptotic bounds and overlapping upper bounds.
reviews.explanation: DSA06 gives the standard growth ordering, with constants below logarithms, then linear and quadratic functions, then exponential. The ranking compares representative rates, not disjoint Big-O classes, since loose upper bounds overlap.

evidence.quote: Increasing representative rates: 1, log n, n, n log n, n², n³, 2^n, 3^n, n!, n^n.

reviews.answer_text: Time, memory space, and—in distributed settings—communication volume.
reviews.hint: Read the cost model and input cases.
reviews.explanation: DSA05 measures operation counts and live memory, and adds communication volume for distributed algorithms. Thus the third resource is context-dependent rather than a universal resource needed by every local algorithm. These are the three supported categories in the note.

evidence.quote: Time counts chosen operations; space counts memory, including live recursive frames. Distributed algorithms may also measure communication volume.

reviews.answer_text: Θ(n) worst time, when absent or at the last position.
reviews.hint: Read linear scanning and early-stop cases.
reviews.explanation: DSA28 scans until equality or exhaustion. An absent target or one in the final position requires all n comparisons, giving linear worst time; a first-position match instead takes constant time. The operation and cases are directly supported.

evidence.quote: An absent target or last-position match needs n comparisons, giving Theta(n) worst time.

reviews.answer_text: Sorted
reviews.hint: Read ordered intervals and binary-search probe bounds.
reviews.explanation: DSA29 eliminates half an ordered interval according to the midpoint comparison. That elimination is valid only when comparable values follow a consistent order; descending input works with reversed comparisons. Circularity and links are representation properties, not substitutes for sortedness. An unsorted sequence gives no safe smaller-half decision. Therefore Sorted is the required prerequisite.

evidence.quote: On an ascending random-access sequence, set lo=0, hi=n-1.

choices.label: A
choices.explanation: Without order, a midpoint comparison cannot safely eliminate either half.

choices.label: B
choices.explanation: Consistent sorted order supports the midpoint half-elimination invariant.

choices.label: C
choices.explanation: Circular storage does not establish the value ordering needed by binary search.

choices.label: D
choices.explanation: Linked storage does not imply sortedness and also changes midpoint-access costs.

reviews.answer_text: About 20 worst-case midpoint probes.
reviews.hint: Read ordered intervals and binary-search probe bounds.
reviews.explanation: DSA29 gives floor(log₂n)+1 probes for n>0. Since 2^19=524288 and 2^20=1048576, one million lies between them, so the worst probe count is twenty under the ordinary interval algorithm. A root/midpoint hit can finish earlier.

evidence.quote: Worst probes are floor(log₂n)+1 for n>0: seven for 100 keys, about twenty for one million.

reviews.answer_text: Worst and usual average Θ(n²); early-stop best Θ(n).
reviews.hint: Read strict adjacent swaps and early stopping.
reviews.explanation: DSA32 sums repeated adjacent passes to at most n(n−1)/2 comparisons, yielding quadratic worst and ordinary average work. A no-swap early-stop pass makes sorted input linear, while a fixed pass schedule remains quadratic. The answer needs these implementation and case distinctions.

evidence.quote: Quadratic worst/average work comes from up to n(n-1)/2 pair comparisons.

reviews.answer_text: Select the remaining minimum and put it at the next prefix position.
reviews.hint: Read selection passes, exchanges, and record-move costs.
reviews.explanation: DSA33 scans the unsorted suffix for its minimum and exchanges it with A[i]. After each meaningful pass, the sorted prefix grows by one and contains the smallest keys placed so far. This differs from inserting the next encountered item into a prefix.

evidence.quote: At position i, scan the remaining suffix for its minimum, then exchange it with A[i].

reviews.answer_text: Selection finds a suffix minimum; insertion places the next item into a sorted prefix.
reviews.hint: Read sorted-prefix insertion and shifts.
reviews.explanation: DSA33 chooses the globally smallest remaining key for each next output position. DSA34 instead takes the next input item, shifts larger prefix values, and inserts it into their gap. Both grow sorted prefixes, but choose their next item differently.

evidence.quote: For each remaining item, save its value, shift larger preceding values right, and insert it into the gap.

reviews.answer_text: Already sorted input; Θ(n) with no-swap early stopping.
reviews.hint: Read strict adjacent swaps and early stopping.
reviews.explanation: DSA32 performs one pass over an already sorted array, makes no swaps, and stops when early-exit detection is enabled. That is linear best work. A fixed-pass implementation still executes its quadratic comparison schedule even on the same input.

evidence.quote: Early stopping makes a sorted input linear: one no-swap pass finishes. A fixed pass schedule stays quadratic.

reviews.answer_text: Payload/data and a next-node link.
reviews.hint: Read node links and chain termination.
reviews.explanation: DSA08 defines a singly linked node as data plus next. The head reference points to the first node, and a null next terminates an ordinary noncircular chain. Head is a list-level reference rather than a second payload field inside every node.

evidence.quote: A singly linked node contains data and next. Head points to the first node; null ends a noncircular chain.

reviews.answer_text: A circular tail links back to head instead of ending at null.
reviews.hint: Read doubly linked and circular variants.
reviews.explanation: DSA10 defines circularity by the tail-to-head link and stops traversal after returning to the start. This is independent of singly versus doubly linked: a singly linked list can itself be circular. Compared with the ordinary noncircular singly linked chain, termination changes from null to return-to-start.

evidence.quote: A circular tail links back to head; stop traversal on returning to the start, handling empty separately.

reviews.answer_text: Advance head to the old head’s next link, then reclaim the old node.
reviews.hint: Read head, tail, and predecessor update costs.
reviews.explanation: DSA09 saves old=head, sets head=head.next, and releases old in an owned C++ chain. The essential link update is advancing head; check empty before dereferencing, and clear tail too if the only node was removed. This answers the operation without hiding ownership work.

evidence.quote: Delete the head by saving old=head, advancing head=head.next and releasing old in C++.

reviews.answer_text: A prev link to the predecessor.
reviews.hint: Read doubly linked and circular variants.
reviews.explanation: DSA10 says doubly linked nodes add prev alongside next. That extra link permits backward traversal and supports endpoint updates when head and tail are maintained. It does not automatically give constant arbitrary positional access, which may still need traversal.

evidence.quote: Doubly linked nodes add prev; head and tail enable constant-time operations at both ends.

reviews.answer_text: Arrays compute addresses directly; linked positional access follows a chain.
reviews.hint: Read array address arithmetic and shifting costs.
reviews.explanation: DSA02 computes an element address from base, index, and element size in constant time. DSA08’s chain lacks direct index arithmetic, so reaching an arbitrary position may traverse linearly many links. This comparison concerns positional access rather than every operation: a known-head update can be constant.

evidence.quote: This arithmetic gives constant-time positional access in the usual RAM cost model.

reviews.answer_text: ABC*+DE/-
reviews.hint: Read operator order and expression conversions.
reviews.explanation: DSA13 works the exact expression. Multiplication groups B*C and division groups D/E before addition and subtraction. Emit A, then B C *, then +, then D E /, then −, producing ABC*+DE/-.

evidence.quote: A+B*C-D/E becomes ABC*+DE/-.

reviews.answer_text: Attempting push when the fixed array is full.
reviews.hint: Read stack service policy and top conventions.
reviews.explanation: DSA11 distinguishes full storage from the overflow attempt. Under zero-based top-as-last-occupied convention, full means top=C−1; a count convention uses size=C. A push must check this before writing beyond capacity.

evidence.quote: With zero-based occupied slots, top=-1 is empty and top=C-1 is full. Check before A[++top]=x or returning A[top--].

reviews.answer_text: Push, pop, and peek are O(1) for fixed-array or head-linked stacks.
reviews.hint: Read stack service policy and top conventions.
reviews.explanation: DSA11 defines push insertion, pop removal/return, and peek observation at top. Fixed-array indexing and linked-head updates take constant work. A resizing append or singly linked tail-pop implementation can change the cost, so the guarantee needs the stated representations.

evidence.quote: Stack policy is LIFO, equivalently FILO. Push inserts, pop removes/returns top, and peek only observes.

reviews.answer_text: Operator position and known arity determine grouping.
reviews.hint: Read operator order and expression conversions.
reviews.explanation: DSA13 places postfix operators after their operands. During stack evaluation, each binary operator consumes the two latest operand values in right-then-left order and pushes their result. The sequence therefore encodes grouping without precedence parentheses.

evidence.quote: Their fixed operator arity determines grouping.

reviews.answer_text: Circular wraparound reuses freed front slots; a simple noncircular queue may not.
reviews.hint: Read circular slots, logical order, and capacity conventions.
reviews.explanation: DSA15 distinguishes a rear index reaching the array end from circular modulo arithmetic. A circular queue can insert into positions freed at the front, while a simple noncircular version may report overflow despite those gaps. Capacity and empty/full conventions still must be consistent.

evidence.quote: A simple noncircular array queue may report overflow when rear reaches the final index despite released slots at the front. A circular queue reuses slots with modulo arithmetic.

reviews.answer_text: Equal-priority service order requires a tie policy; FIFO is not inherent.
reviews.hint: Read priority-queue costs and tie policies.
reviews.explanation: DSA17 explicitly denies an inherent FIFO guarantee among equal priorities. A stable queue can compare priority and arrival counter to preserve arrival order, while another implementation can break ties differently. The stem supplies no stability requirement or comparator, so the actual task order is genuinely ambiguous rather than a fact missing from the note.

evidence.quote: Equal priorities have no inherent FIFO guarantee. If stable service is required, compare (priority, arrival_counter).

reviews.answer_text: Dequeue on an empty queue causes underflow.
reviews.hint: Read stack service policy and top conventions.
reviews.explanation: DSA11 defines underflow as attempted removal from empty storage; DSA15’s count convention detects empty using size==0. This indicates that no item exists to return, not that the array is full or that an ordinary emptiness test itself failed.

evidence.quote: Empty means size==0; full means size==C.
Push inserts, pop removes/returns top, and peek only observes.

reviews.answer_text: Runtime call frames, undo/redo history, and string or sequence reversal.
reviews.hint: Read stepwise stack traces and nested calls.
reviews.explanation: DSA12 gives nested calls latest-first returns, moving latest actions between undo and redo stacks, and reversing input by pushing then popping. Each example uses the same latest-pending-item discipline. A new edit after undo normally clears redo history.

evidence.quote: Reversal pushes input then pops it. Undo moves the latest action from undo to redo; redo moves it back.

reviews.answer_text: Every left-subtree key is smaller and every right-subtree key larger, for distinct keys.
reviews.hint: Read the global BST order invariant.
reviews.explanation: DSA19 imposes this invariant over entire subtrees at every node, not only immediate children. A descendant can satisfy its parent comparison yet violate an ancestor bound. Duplicate keys require an explicit count or placement policy instead of silently weakening the distinct-key rule.

evidence.quote: With distinct keys, every key in a node’s left subtree is smaller and every key in its right subtree is larger.

reviews.hint: Read recursive tree visit orders.
reviews.explanation: DSA20 visits left subtree, node, then right subtree for inorder, and says BST inorder returns sorted keys. The supplied seven distinct keys therefore appear in increasing order even though the internal child shapes are not fully specified. Shape would matter to preorder or postorder.

evidence.quote: Inorder returns sorted keys only for a BST.

reviews.answer_text: Inorder predecessor or inorder successor.
reviews.hint: Read BST deletion methods and replacement nodes.
reviews.explanation: DSA21 identifies the maximum key in the left subtree and minimum key in the right subtree as valid replacement values. Copy one into the deleted node, then remove that value’s original node, which has at most one child. These preserve the subtree order invariant.

evidence.quote: For two children, copy the inorder predecessor (left-subtree maximum) or successor (right-subtree minimum), then delete that replacement from its original location.

reviews.answer_text: Best successful search Θ(1); arbitrary BST worst Θ(n), balanced worst Θ(log n).
reviews.hint: Read the global BST order invariant.
reviews.explanation: DSA19 gives a constant root hit and O(height) search. A chain has linear height, producing linear worst work; logarithmic height disciplines in DSA22 improve that worst bound. Calling every BST logarithmic would incorrectly assume balance.

evidence.quote: Operations cost O(height): logarithmic for balanced trees, linear for a chain. Best-case successful search is Theta(1), a root hit.

reviews.answer_text: BFS explores distance layers with FIFO; DFS finishes branches with a stack or recursion.
reviews.hint: Read branch-first traversal and pending work.
reviews.explanation: DSA41 enqueues discoveries in layer order, while DSA42 resumes the latest unfinished branch before later neighbors. Both can traverse all reachable vertices, but their pending-work discipline and visitation order differ. BFS also has the unweighted minimum-edge guarantee.

evidence.quote: An explicit stack can store pending work instead. Both implement latest-pending-work first; a queue would change that discipline.

reviews.answer_text: Directed: following accounts; undirected: a mutual friendship relationship.
reviews.hint: Read graph relationships and representations.
reviews.explanation: DSA40 gives following as directed because u following v need not imply v following u. It gives mutual friendship as undirected, representing a symmetric connection. The examples concern relation semantics rather than whether lines happen to be drawn with arrows.

evidence.quote: Following accounts is directed; a mutual friendship relation is undirected.

reviews.answer_text: Edge-processing algorithms do more work when E is larger.
reviews.hint: Read graph relationships and representations.
reviews.explanation: DSA40 says dense simple graphs approach quadratic edge counts and adjacency lists use Θ(V+E) space. Traversals or algorithms inspecting every edge therefore require more work as density increases. This is not universal: a vertex-only operation need not inspect edges.

evidence.quote: Examining every edge costs more on denser graphs; vertex-only operations need not inspect every edge.

reviews.answer_text: Full restricts each node to zero or two children; complete restricts level filling.
reviews.hint: Read binary-tree shape definitions and height conventions.
reviews.explanation: DSA18 defines full by each node’s child count and complete by filled earlier levels plus left-filled final level. Those are distinct conditions: completeness can allow one child at the boundary, while fullness alone need not keep every level filled.

evidence.quote: Full means each node has zero or two children. Complete means all earlier levels are filled and the last fills from left.

reviews.answer_text: Weighted edges carry differing costs; use them when edge costs matter.
reviews.hint: Read graph relationships and representations.
reviews.explanation: DSA40 assigns costs to weighted edges and says unweighted shortest-path questions count edges. Distances or travel costs can therefore justify weights when fewer edges is not the true objective. DSA43 then distinguishes weighted shortest paths from unweighted BFS.

evidence.quote: Weighted edges carry costs; unweighted shortest-path questions count edges.

reviews.answer_text: An ordinary unbalanced insertion forms a right chain; worst search is Θ(n).
reviews.hint: Read the global BST order invariant.
reviews.explanation: DSA19 explicitly traces sorted insertion 1,2,3,4,5 into a right chain. Each new larger key follows right links to the tail, making the height linear. Worst search follows that chain, while a root hit remains constant. Balanced insertion would rotate and is a different assumption.

evidence.quote: Sorted insertions 1,2,3,4,5 instead form a right chain.

reviews.answer_text: Choose links for frequent known-location updates, such as a doubly linked history cursor.
reviews.hint: Read doubly linked and circular variants.
reviews.explanation: DSA10 gives browser history with a doubly linked cursor as an application. With references to current insertion or removal positions, link changes avoid shifting an array’s later elements; arbitrary positional lookup can still be linear. This concrete scenario supports the choice without claiming universal superiority.

evidence.quote: Lists suit changing sequences when references to insertion positions are already available. Finding a position is still linear.

reviews.answer_text: Stack: LIFO for undo; queue: FIFO for equal-priority printer jobs.
reviews.hint: Read FIFO endpoint operations.
reviews.explanation: DSA11 gives latest-first stack service and DSA12 applies it to undoing the latest edit. DSA14 gives arrival-order queues for equal-priority printing. Both ADTs may use arrays or nodes; their service order, not that representation, is the distinction.

evidence.quote: An ordinary queue enqueues at rear, dequeues at front, and peeks at front. This is FIFO or first-come, first-served.

reviews.answer_text: Balance prevents linear-height chains and guarantees logarithmic worst search.
reviews.hint: Read height balance and rotations.
reviews.explanation: DSA22 maintains AVL balance factors through rotations that preserve inorder. DSA19 shows ordinary sorted insertion producing a chain, where a search can traverse all nodes. Maintaining logarithmic height prevents that worst degradation, though root-hit best time remains constant.

evidence.quote: Both prevent linear worst-case search; balanced trees also support ordered ranges unlike ordinary hashing.

reviews.answer_text: A collision maps different keys to one home address; compare chaining and open addressing.
reviews.hint: Read collision resolution and load factors.
reviews.explanation: DSA26 stores colliding entries in bucket lists for chaining, whereas open addressing probes other array slots. Chaining uses link or bucket overhead and expected O(1+α) work; probing keeps entries inside the table and requires careful load and deletion policies. Neither prevents all collisions.

evidence.quote: Open addressing keeps entries inside the array and probes until a key or an available slot is found.

reviews.answer_text: BFS uses FIFO layers and finds shortest unweighted paths; DFS uses branch-first stack order.
reviews.hint: Read FIFO graph distance layers.
reviews.explanation: DSA41 guarantees minimum-edge paths for BFS on unweighted graphs. DSA42 says DFS paths are reachability witnesses but need not be shortest. Differing edge weights require an appropriate weighted-path algorithm, such as Dijkstra under nonnegative weights.

evidence.quote: BFS finds minimum-edge paths in unweighted graphs, not arbitrary minimum-weight paths.

reviews.answer_text: Use an undo stack, with a second redo stack if needed.
reviews.hint: Read stepwise stack traces and nested calls.
reviews.explanation: DSA12 moves the latest action from undo to redo and reverses that movement for redo. Pushing each new edit and popping for undo naturally matches the most-recent-edit-first requirement. A new edit after undo normally clears redo history.

evidence.quote: Undo moves the latest action from undo to redo; redo moves it back. A new edit after undo normally clears redo.

reviews.answer_text: Heap sort
reviews.hint: Compare independent recursive decomposition with heap extraction.
reviews.explanation: DAA16 explicitly classifies heap sort as outside standard divide and conquer: it builds a heap and repeatedly extracts its maximum. Quicksort partitions and recursively sorts ranges; merge sort recursively sorts halves; binary search recursively or iteratively reduces to a smaller half. Thus heap sort is the single exclusion among the listed algorithms.

evidence.quote: Heap sort builds a max-heap in Θ(n), then extracts/restores in O(log n) per item: O(n log n) total, Θ(1) auxiliary space, ordinarily unstable. It is not standard D&C.

choices.label: A
choices.explanation: Quicksort partitions its input and recursively sorts the resulting smaller ranges, a standard divide-and-conquer pattern.

choices.label: B
choices.explanation: Binary search repeatedly reduces a sorted search interval to one half; the note treats this as divide-and-conquer.

choices.label: C
choices.explanation: Merge sort divides into halves, sorts each recursively, and combines them by merging.

choices.label: D
choices.explanation: Heap sort builds a heap and repeatedly restores it after extraction, rather than independently sorting and combining subinstances.

reviews.answer_text: No offered technique-and-reason pair is sound.
reviews.hint: Read the comparison decision-tree lower-bound proof.
reviews.explanation: DAA11 derives Ω(n log n) from a comparison decision tree with at least n! leaves. That makes both objections to decision trees false. Recurrences can analyze recursive sorting algorithms, but do not by themselves establish a lower bound for the entire class; option B gives a false reason. Ignoring constants also does not invalidate asymptotic lower bounds. No complete offered pair answers the literal question.

evidence.quote: A comparison decision tree needs at least n! leaves for distinct-key orderings. Height h allows at most 2^h leaves, so h≥log 2(n!)=Ω(n log n); merge sort matches this worst-case bound.

choices.label: A
choices.explanation: Decision trees model comparisons and outcomes; they do not assume that only array indexing is allowed.

choices.label: B
choices.explanation: Recursive sorting algorithms exist; the stated reason is false even though an algorithm-specific recurrence cannot bound the entire class.

choices.label: C
choices.explanation: An asymptotic lower bound deliberately ignores constants; that does not make the analysis inappropriate.

choices.label: D
choices.explanation: Providing the information-theoretic comparison lower bound makes the decision-tree model appropriate, despite the garbled displayed notation.

reviews.answer_text: All listed factors affect observed runtime.
reviews.hint: Distinguish abstract operation counts from elapsed execution time.
reviews.explanation: DAA02 makes runtime a function of input size and explains that elapsed measurements also depend on hardware and competing load. A faster processor changes execution speed; other running work changes available resources; larger inputs can require more operations. Therefore all three listed factors matter when trying to predict an exact elapsed time, so the combined option is appropriate.

evidence.quote: Elapsed measurements also depend on hardware, compiler, cache, I/O and competing load.

choices.label: A
choices.explanation: Processor speed affects elapsed time for a given amount of work, so this is one valid contributing factor.

choices.label: B
choices.explanation: Competing processor load changes scheduling and available execution resources, affecting the observed elapsed time.

choices.label: C
choices.explanation: Input size determines how many algorithmic operations may be required, even on the same processor.

choices.label: D
choices.explanation: All three preceding factors affect exact elapsed runtime; this combined option fully answers the question.

reviews.answer_text: No unique exclusion without a specified taxonomy.
reviews.hint: Compare growth analysis, measurements, and graph-based reasoning.
reviews.explanation: DAA02 recognizes asymptotic reasoning and experimental or dynamic measurement. It explicitly warns that no universal taxonomy makes graph analysis or dynamic analysis invalid. Graph-based analysis can have legitimate algorithmic uses, while dynamic analysis can mean observing runs. The question supplies no narrower definition of technique, so selecting a unique NOT option would depend on an unstated teaching classification.

evidence.quote: There is no universal taxonomy proving “graph analysis” or “dynamic analysis” is invalid.

choices.label: A
choices.explanation: Asymptotic analysis studies how resource cost grows with input size and is explicitly recognized in DAA02.

choices.label: B
choices.explanation: Experimental analysis measures actual runs; DAA02 explicitly recognizes such observations as analysis.

choices.label: C
choices.explanation: Dynamic analysis can mean measuring program executions, so its name alone cannot establish a valid exclusion.

choices.label: D
choices.explanation: Graph analysis may legitimately analyze graph algorithms or dependencies; an exclusive taxonomy would be needed to rule it out.

reviews.answer_text: Data type complexity is nonstandard terminology, not an established unique exclusion.
reviews.hint: Read what storage, I/O, representation, and bit costs measure.
reviews.explanation: DAA02 explicitly includes storage, auxiliary space, and I/O transfers. It calls data type complexity a nonstandard metric name, but also states that representation and arithmetic bit costs affect analysis. If the task meant standard metric names, D would be the intended exclusion; the literal word consideration is broader. Without defining that term, the note does not prove that data types are irrelevant.

evidence.quote: Auxiliary space excludes input; I/O complexity counts transfers. Representation affects costs; “data type complexity” is not a standard metric name.

choices.label: A
choices.explanation: Memory consumption is a standard resource consideration, so space complexity cannot be excluded.

choices.label: B
choices.explanation: Auxiliary space measures additional storage excluding the input; it is a legitimate analysis consideration.

choices.label: C
choices.explanation: Input-output complexity counts transfers and matters when storage or communication costs dominate.

choices.label: D
choices.explanation: The phrase is a nonstandard metric name, but data representation and arithmetic bit sizes still affect cost.

reviews.answer_text: No uniquely invalid technique among the supplied names.
reviews.hint: Distinguish empirical measurements from probabilistic expectations.
reviews.explanation: DAA02 describes asymptotic growth, observed runs, and probabilistic expectations as legitimate analyses. Dynamic analysis can denote those observed executions and overlap empirical analysis. The question does not identify a particular taxonomy or define commonly used, so it cannot establish that one of these labels is invalid. A supplied answer cannot replace that missing classification.

evidence.quote: Experimental/dynamic measurement observes actual runs; asymptotic analysis abstracts growth; probabilistic analysis studies expectations.

choices.label: A
choices.explanation: Asymptotic analysis is explicitly recognized as abstracting resource growth with increasing input size.

choices.label: B
choices.explanation: Empirical analysis observes executions and corresponds to the experimental measurement described in DAA02.

choices.label: C
choices.explanation: Dynamic analysis can mean actual-run measurement and is not inherently an invalid analysis technique.

choices.label: D
choices.explanation: Probabilistic analysis studies expected costs under distributions or randomness and is explicitly recognized by the note.

reviews.answer_text: Both divide and conquer and dynamic programming solve maximum subarray sum.
reviews.hint: Compare the crossing-subarray decomposition with the best-ending-here recurrence.
reviews.explanation: DAA18 gives two algorithms for exactly this problem. Divide and conquer compares the best left, right, and crossing intervals in Θ(n log n). Kadane uses a best-sum-ending-at-this-position recurrence in Θ(n). The stem specifies neither recurrence nor runtime, so both named techniques fit. Greedy and backtracking are not the two established constructions in the note.

evidence.quote: Both D&C and DP therefore solve the bank’s unqualified strategy question.

choices.label: A
choices.explanation: Divide and conquer combines the best left, right, and crossing subarrays, yielding a valid Θ(n log n) algorithm.

choices.label: B
choices.explanation: The note derives Kadane through a state recurrence, not an independently justified irrevocable local-choice rule.

choices.label: C
choices.explanation: Kadane uses the best sum ending at each index and the largest such value, a dynamic program.

choices.label: D
choices.explanation: The stated note algorithms do not grow and retract candidate assignments through a backtracking search.

reviews.answer_text: Dynamic programming using prefix-pair states.
reviews.hint: Read the LCS recurrence for equal and unequal final characters.
reviews.explanation: DAA30 defines a state for each pair of prefix lengths. A match extends a diagonal state; a mismatch takes the larger of two neighboring prefix solutions. Filling states in dependency order avoids recomputing overlapping subproblems and gives Θ(mn) time. This is the note’s dynamic-programming solution; no greedy safety rule or backtracking enumeration is supplied.

evidence.quote: If X[i−1]=Y[j−1], set L[i, j]=1+L[i−1, j−1]; otherwise use max(L[i−1, j], L[i, j−1]).

choices.label: A
choices.explanation: The given LCS construction reuses overlapping prefix states rather than only independently solving and combining disjoint pieces.

choices.label: B
choices.explanation: No rule for committing to a locally best character is justified; prefix alternatives must be compared.

choices.label: C
choices.explanation: The prefix-pair table and recurrence reuse optimal subproblem lengths, exactly the dynamic-programming technique described.

choices.label: D
choices.explanation: The note computes stored prefix states instead of exhaustively extending and undoing candidate subsequences.

reviews.answer_text: Whether efficiently verifiable decision problems also have efficient solving algorithms.
reviews.hint: Read the definitions of P and NP and the unresolved equality question.
reviews.explanation: DAA44 defines P by deterministic polynomial-time decision solving and NP by polynomial-time certificate verification, equivalently nondeterministic polynomial solving. The P-versus-NP problem asks whether these classes coincide. Option D captures the question of efficient algorithms for this particular class of problems, although its wording is broad. It does not concern parallelism, language comparisons, or timing one program.

evidence.quote: NP does not mean non-polynomial; P⊆NP. Whether P=NP remains open.

choices.label: A
choices.explanation: P and NP refer to polynomial solving and verification classes, not parallel versus non-parallel execution.

choices.label: B
choices.explanation: The question concerns equality of decision-problem classes, not merely determining a particular algorithm runtime.

choices.label: C
choices.explanation: Programming-language efficiency is unrelated to whether polynomial-time solvability and verifiability coincide.

choices.label: D
choices.explanation: This broadly expresses whether NP problems have deterministic polynomial-time solving algorithms, the P-versus-NP question.

reviews.answer_text: NP
reviews.hint: Read the nondeterministic polynomial-time definition, separating membership from completeness.
reviews.explanation: DAA44 identifies NP with decision problems solvable by a nondeterministic polynomial-time machine. P is a contained class defined using deterministic machines; NP-complete adds hardness, which the stem never requires. Exponential is a time-growth description rather than the requested definition. The alternate set replaces Exponential with NP-hard, which likewise does not change the defining NP answer.

evidence.quote: NP contains decision problems with polynomial-length certificates verifiable in polynomial time, equivalently solvable by a nondeterministic polynomial-time machine.

choices.label: A
choices.explanation: P is defined through deterministic polynomial time; it is contained in NP but does not name the full defined class.

choices.label: B
choices.explanation: NP exactly names decision problems solvable by a nondeterministic polynomial-time Turing machine.

choices.label: C
choices.explanation: NP-complete requires both NP membership and NP-hardness; hardness is absent from the stem.

choices.label: D
choices.explanation: Exponential describes time growth, not the class defined by nondeterministic polynomial-time computation.

variant_reviews.explanation: The variant retains P, NP, and NP-complete and replaces the fourth option with NP-hard. DAA44 still defines NP by nondeterministic polynomial-time computation. NP-hard is a reduction-based hardness property and need not imply NP membership, so the answer remains NP after independently examining this set.

choices.label: A
choices.explanation: P specifies deterministic polynomial solving, a subclass rather than the full nondeterministic polynomial class.

choices.label: B
choices.explanation: NP is exactly the class defined by nondeterministic polynomial-time decision computation.

choices.label: C
choices.explanation: NP-complete additionally requires NP-hardness; the stem imposes no such condition.

choices.label: D
choices.explanation: NP-hardness alone does not imply membership in NP or a nondeterministic polynomial-time algorithm.

reviews.answer_text: The literal C++ is invalid; repaired doubling would be logarithmic.
reviews.hint: Read specific damaged items and minimum clarifications and check its assumptions.
reviews.explanation: The image restores return 0 but still redeclares parameter n in the same function scope. The extracted return @;3 adds another defect. DAA07 and DAA45 require syntax repair before assigning executable runtime. If n is preserved and the declaration repaired, doubling gives Θ(log n), but none of the offered complexity labels describes the literal invalid program.

evidence.quote: Stray ini/inl or redeclared n needs syntax repair; exact counts also need a primitive-cost model.

choices.label: A
choices.explanation: n log n is only a loose bound after a repair, not a runtime for invalid C++.

choices.label: B
choices.explanation: The extracted n° is damaged; the image shows n², another loose bound only after repair.

choices.label: C
choices.explanation: Log n is the intended tight repaired-loop result, conditional on valid source and bounded arithmetic.

choices.label: D
choices.explanation: Linear is a loose bound after repair, not a runtime for the invalid source.

reviews.answer_text: Floyd–Warshall is Θ(n³), but best achievable needs graph and computation assumptions.
reviews.hint: Read floyd–warshall, reachability and negative cycles and check its assumptions.
reviews.explanation: The image confirms the broad best achievable wording, not a named Floyd algorithm. DAA28 gives Floyd–Warshall cubic cost but explicitly denies that this is a universal APSP optimum. Density, weight restrictions, and computation model can change available algorithms. C is also too small to explicitly materialize n² distances. Thus B is a taught algorithm’s cost, not a justified universal best.

evidence.quote: Floyd’s cost is not a universal best-achievable bound for all APSP settings; sparse nonnegative graphs permit repeated Dijkstra and other models permit other methods.

choices.label: A
choices.explanation: Quadratic relates to the number of explicit pair outputs, but is not a universal established algorithm bound here.

choices.label: B
choices.explanation: Cubic is Floyd–Warshall’s cost, not a universal best-achievable APSP theorem.

choices.label: C
choices.explanation: Linear cannot explicitly output all n² distances for arbitrary n-vertex inputs.

choices.label: D
choices.explanation: Quartic is a loose bound on cubic Floyd work, not a demonstrated optimum.

reviews.answer_text: Merge sort
reviews.hint: Read merge sort: invariant, trace and costs and check its assumptions.
reviews.explanation: DAA14 splits into halves, recursively sorts each, and merges the results, directly implementing divide and conquer. DAA16 excludes standard heap sort from that category and describes selection’s repeated minimum and bubble’s adjacent passes. Only Merge Sort among these options has the specified independent recursive decomposition and combination mechanism.

evidence.quote: Ordinary array merge sort has T(n)=2T(n/2)+Θ(n)=Θ(n log n) across input orders, Θ(n) auxiliary buffer and Θ(log n) recursion depth.

choices.label: A
choices.explanation: Merge sort recursively solves halves and combines them through a merge.

choices.label: B
choices.explanation: Standard heapsort builds and repeatedly restores a heap rather than applying the standard independent-subproblem decomposition.

choices.label: C
choices.explanation: Selection repeatedly finds a suffix minimum instead of recursively sorting halves.

choices.label: D
choices.explanation: Bubble repeatedly swaps adjacent inversions instead of recursively decomposing subinstances.

reviews.answer_text: Quicksort

An efficiency or missing-output defect would require a problem specification. All offered violation claims are unsupported; a no-violation answer is absent.

reviews.answer_text: An MST spans every vertex and is itself a graph.

Equal edge weights can produce multiple MSTs, so uniqueness is not universal. Cycles are forbidden. Thus both A and C are true, independently of the singular wording.

evidence.quote: For a connected weighted undirected graph, an MST spans every vertex without cycles and minimizes total edge weight; it has V−1 edges.

reviews.answer_text: Smallest input size is not the definition of best case.
reviews.hint: Read input cases and bound notation are independent and check its assumptions.
reviews.explanation: DAA03 defines best case as minimum cost among inputs of the same size and explicitly distinguishes smallest input size from best case. The stem instead changes the input set or its size. D is the likely intended answer only after replacing the wording with fastest legal input at fixed n; the literal definition is not one of the offered standard terms.

evidence.quote: O/Ω/Θ bound functions independently of case or resource.

choices.label: B

reviews.answer_text: No complete technique-and-reason pair is correct.
reviews.hint: Read comparison sorting lower bounds and check its assumptions.
reviews.explanation: DAA11 proves the comparison-sorting lower bound using decision-tree leaves and depth. Thus decision trees are appropriate, and obtaining an information-theoretic bound supports rather than disqualifies them. Sorting can be recursive, refuting B’s reason. Ignoring constants is inherent in asymptotic lower bounds, not a flaw. The options omit a sound inappropriate-technique/reason pair.

reviews.explanation: DAA45 requires syntax repair for the literal stray ini. DAA06 then counts two initializations, n+1 tests, n increments, two body operations per iteration, and one return, totaling 4n+4. Other conventions alter coefficients while retaining Θ(n). Therefore no exact answer is established without both corrections; a supplied marked coefficient is not sufficient evidence.

reviews.answer_text: Divide and conquer and memoized DP both fit recursive subproblem combination.
reviews.hint: Read choose a design from structural conditions and check its assumptions.
reviews.explanation: DAA12 solves smaller independent instances for divide and conquer, while DAA25/26 permit recursive memoized states for DP. Both recursively solve subproblems and combine results. The wording omits independence or repeated-state reuse, which would distinguish them. Greedy and backtracking have other defining conditions not supplied by the decomposition description alone.

evidence.quote: Divide and conquer solves smaller largely independent instances and combines results. DP reuses a defined set of subproblem states.

choices.label: A

choices.label: B

choices.label: C

choices.label: D

reviews.answer_text: f∈O(g) iff ∃c>0,k such that 0≤f(n)≤c g(n) for all n≥k.
reviews.hint: Read formal asymptotic bounds and constants and check its assumptions.
reviews.explanation: DAA04 requires one fixed positive multiplier and one threshold covering the entire tail of the eventually nonnegative functions. c permits constant-factor scaling; k excludes a finite initial prefix. Neither may be chosen anew for each n. This defines an eventual upper bound, independently of input case or whether the resource is time or space.

evidence.quote: f∈O(g) means f(n)≤c·g(n) for all n≥n 0, with fixed c>0.

reviews.answer_text: c=15 and k=1 work.
reviews.hint: Read formal asymptotic bounds and constants and check its assumptions.
reviews.explanation: For every n≥1, 5≤5n, so 10n+5≤15n. Choosing c=15 and k=1 therefore satisfies the Big-O upper inequality for the whole tail. DAA04 gives this exact worked example. These witnesses need not be unique; the goal is one valid fixed constant and threshold, not the smallest pair.

evidence.quote: 10n+5≤15n for n≥1, so c=15,n 0=1 works.

reviews.answer_text: c=8 and k=1 work.
reviews.hint: Read formal asymptotic bounds and constants and check its assumptions.
reviews.explanation: For n≥1, replace 4n by at most 4n² and 1 by at most n². The sum is then at most 8n², satisfying DAA04’s upper-bound definition. Thus c=8 and k=1 are valid witnesses. They are not uniquely required constants; larger multipliers or thresholds can also satisfy the inequality.

evidence.quote: Also 3n²+4n+1≤8n² for n≥1.

reviews.answer_text: Increasing representative growth: log n, n log n, n², 2^n, n!.
reviews.hint: Read growth ordering and loose bounds and check its assumptions.
reviews.explanation: DAA05 orders logarithmic, polynomial, exponential, and factorial rates. A log factor above n is still dominated by n²; fixed-base exponential eventually exceeds any fixed polynomial, and factorial exceeds fixed-base exponential. This ranks representative functions, not mutually exclusive Big-O sets, since a slower function can also satisfy a looser larger upper bound.

evidence.quote: Representative growth is 1,log n,n,n log n,n²,n³,…,b^n,n! for fixed b>1.

reviews.answer_text: A tight asymptotic bound: both upper and lower constant-factor bounds.
reviews.hint: Read formal asymptotic bounds and constants and check its assumptions.
reviews.explanation: DAA04 requires positive constants c1,c2 and a threshold k with c1 h(n)≤f(n)≤c2 h(n) for all n≥k. Theta therefore specifies growth up to constant factors, not exact seconds. It can describe best, average, worst, or space functions; choosing Theta does not itself choose an input case.

evidence.quote: Ω reverses that inequality; Θ requires both bounds.

reviews.answer_text: Ω is an eventual lower bound; O is an eventual upper bound.
reviews.hint: Read formal asymptotic bounds and constants and check its assumptions.
reviews.explanation: DAA04 gives f∈Ω(g) when f(n)≥c g(n) beyond a fixed threshold for some c>0, reversing the Big-O inequality. The relations describe functions independently of best or worst case. A function may satisfy both, giving Theta, or only one for a particular comparator; they are not literal fastest-versus-slowest input labels.

evidence.quote: Ω reverses that inequality; Θ requires both bounds.

reviews.answer_text: If f∈O(g) and g∈O(h), then f∈O(h).
reviews.hint: Read formal asymptotic bounds and constants and check its assumptions.
reviews.explanation: DAA04 permits chained upper bounds. If f≤c g past k1 and g≤d h past k2, then f≤cd h for every n beyond max(k1,k2). Multiplying constants and combining thresholds proves transitivity. It is useful for replacing a complicated intermediate expression by a simpler known bound without redoing the entire comparison.

evidence.quote: Transitivity allows chained upper bounds; sums are dominated by the largest nonnegative growth term.

reviews.answer_text: Increasing growth: k, log n, n, n log n, n², 2^n, n!.
reviews.hint: Read growth ordering and loose bounds and check its assumptions.
reviews.explanation: For fixed positive k, DAA05 places constant growth first, followed by logarithmic and linear rates, then n log n, quadratic, exponential, and factorial growth. The ordering is eventual, not a promise of speed for every small input. It concerns representative functions; Big-O memberships can overlap when upper bounds are loose.

evidence.quote: Representative growth is 1,log n,n,n log n,n²,n³,…,b^n,n! for fixed b>1.

reviews.answer_text: Validation checks required behavior; analysis measures resource costs.
reviews.hint: Read specify the problem and prove correctness and check its assumptions.
reviews.explanation: DAA01 specifies legal inputs, required outputs, and correctness proof through invariants or recursive induction. DAA02 counts operations and storage as input size grows. A procedure can be fast yet incorrect, or correct yet expensive. Testing can reveal failures but finite tests do not prove correctness for all inputs, so resource analysis does not replace validation.

evidence.quote: Testing finds failures but finite tests do not prove correctness for all inputs.

reviews.answer_text: For equal-size splits, T(n)=aT(n/b)+f(n), with an explicit base case.
reviews.hint: Read recursion trees and the master theorem and check its assumptions.
reviews.explanation: DAA10 uses a recursive subcalls of size n/b and f(n) nonrecursive divide/combine work, with a≥1 and b>1. Include a base such as T(1)=Θ(1). Unequal or decrementing subproblems require a more general sum of subproblem costs; the equal-split form is a common model, not every possible divide-and-conquer recurrence.

evidence.quote: For T(n)=aT(n/b)+f(n), a≥1, b>1, let p=log_b a.

reviews.answer_text: Ordinary array merge sort is Θ(n log n).
reviews.hint: Read merge sort: invariant, trace and costs and check its assumptions.
reviews.explanation: DAA14 gives T(n)=2T(n/2)+Θ(n): two half-size sorts and linear merging. There are logarithmically many levels, each totaling linear merge work, with linear total leaf work. Therefore the tight result is n log n across input orders, assuming the ordinary algorithm rather than a variant that skips already ordered merges.

evidence.quote: Ordinary array merge sort has T(n)=2T(n/2)+Θ(n)=Θ(n log n) across input orders, Θ(n) auxiliary buffer and Θ(log n) recursion depth.

reviews.answer_text: Split into halves, recursively sort each half, then merge the sorted halves.
reviews.hint: Read merge sort: invariant, trace and costs and check its assumptions.
reviews.explanation: DAA14 stops at empty or singleton ranges. During combination it repeatedly takes the smaller remaining front item, then appends the unexhausted suffix. Left-first equal-key selection preserves stability. These steps separate division, recursive solution, and combination; the merge assumes each half is already sorted rather than that the original full array was sorted.

evidence.quote: Split by indices, recursively sort each half, then repeatedly copy the smaller remaining front element into a temporary result.

reviews.answer_text: Take equal keys from the left half first while merging.
reviews.hint: Read merge sort: invariant, trace and costs and check its assumptions.
reviews.explanation: DAA14 explicitly requires left-first equal-key handling for stability. Recursive halves retain their internal equal-key order, and choosing a left equal before a right equal preserves their original cross-half order. Inductively the entire output retains the relative order of equal-key records. Choosing the right equal first can break that property.

evidence.quote: Equal keys must be taken from the left half first to preserve stability.

reviews.answer_text: Expected average Θ(n log n); worst Θ(n²) from repeated highly unbalanced partitions.
reviews.hint: Read quicksort: partition variants and worst cases and check its assumptions.
reviews.explanation: DAA15 gives logarithmic partition depth when splits are balanced and expected n log n with random pivots. Repeated extreme pivots leave sizes n−1,n−2,…, causing n+(n−1)+… work. Sorted input can trigger this with certain fixed endpoint pivots, but input order alone is not a universal worst-case characterization across partition rules.

evidence.quote: Balanced splits give Θ(n log n); repeatedly highly unbalanced splits give Θ(n²).

reviews.answer_text: Advance i over values below the pivot and j over values above; swap while i≤j, then advance both.
reviews.hint: Read quicksort: partition variants and worst cases and check its assumptions.
reviews.explanation: DAA15’s two-pointer partition bounds its scans and ensures progress even on equal values. After pointers cross, recurse on the resulting smaller ranges. Hoare-style boundaries need not put the pivot in its final position, whereas Lomuto commonly does. The chosen return convention and recursion ranges must match; mixing them can miss elements or fail to terminate.

evidence.quote: In a two-pointer scheme, advance i while values are below pivot and j while above; when i≤j, swap and advance both.

reviews.answer_text: Merge: stable, Θ(n log n) worst, Θ(n) buffer. Quick: unstable, Θ(n²) worst, expected Θ(log n) and worst Θ(n) stack.
reviews.hint: Read merge sort: invariant, trace and costs and check its assumptions.
reviews.explanation: DAA14 provides merge’s linear buffer and logarithmic recursion depth, with left-first ties for stability. DAA15 gives quicksort’s in-array partitioning but nonconstant recursive storage and potentially linear depth. Recursing only on the smaller side can bound that stack logarithmically. These describe ordinary implementations; ignoring recursive frames would misstate total auxiliary space.

evidence.quote: Ordinary array merge sort has T(n)=2T(n/2)+Θ(n)=Θ(n log n) across input orders, Θ(n) auxiliary buffer and Θ(log n) recursion depth.

reviews.answer_text: Each midpoint comparison reduces the ordered-search instance to one half.
reviews.hint: Read binary search and simultaneous minimum/maximum and check its assumptions.
reviews.explanation: DAA13 maintains sorted low/high bounds and excludes the half that cannot contain the target. The recurrence T(n)=T(n/2)+Θ(1) gives logarithmic worst work. Unlike sorting two halves, binary search solves only one surviving subinstance and requires no substantial combination step; this is the common divide-and-conquer or decrease-by-factor classification.

evidence.quote: T(n)=T(n/2)+Θ(1): worst Θ(log n), best Θ(1); iterative auxiliary space Θ(1), recursive Θ(log n).

reviews.answer_text: Repeatedly make a locally attractive feasible choice and keep it.
reviews.hint: Read greedy correctness, limits and counterexamples and check its assumptions.
reviews.explanation: DAA19 defines greedy decisions as irrevocable rather than exploring and undoing alternatives. To obtain a global optimum, the local choice needs a problem-specific safety argument, often an exchange proof. Optimal substructure alone is insufficient.
