This admits other code in the same package but does not admit an other-package subclass merely through inheritance. protected would be broader because it adds qualified cross-package subclass access; private would be narrower. The answer is omission, not a default keyword modifier.

evidence.quote: no modifier grants package access; protected grants same-package access plus qualified subclass access;

reviews.answer_text: Yes. A private constructor can support a factory or controlled singleton creation.
reviews.hint: Read OOP09’s private-constructor example.
reviews.explanation: OOP09 explicitly permits private constructors. Restricting constructor access prevents arbitrary outside callers from directly constructing the class, while its own permitted code can still instantiate it. A factory can control creation, or a singleton arrangement can expose a controlled instance. Private construction does not mean the class can never create any object internally.

evidence.quote: A private constructor can support a factory or controlled singleton creation; it does not mean the class can never create an object internally.

reviews.answer_text: == compares reference identity; equals uses the class’s equality policy.
reviews.hint: Read OOP22’s default and overridden equality distinction.
reviews.explanation: For object references, == asks whether they denote the same object. equals invokes a method whose policy may compare content or value; Object.equals remains identity-based unless overridden. String.equals compares character content. Therefore equals does not automatically mean value equality for every class, and two distinct objects may be equal under an appropriate override.

evidence.quote: For object references, == tests identity; equals invokes the class’s equality policy. Object.equals uses identity unless overridden; String.equals compares character content.

reviews.answer_text: Compilation fails: a Java class cannot extend two direct superclasses.
reviews.hint: Read OOP13’s single-superclass rule.
reviews.explanation: OOP13 explicitly prohibits class Dog extends Animal,Mammal. Java class inheritance permits one direct superclass, so the comma-separated extends clause is invalid rather than a runtime ambiguity to resolve. A class can instead implement multiple interfaces for multiple type contracts, and composition can combine separately held collaborators where multiple state/implementation sources are needed.

evidence.quote: A class extends one direct class and can implement multiple interfaces. Single, multilevel and hierarchical inheritance mean one parent, a chain, and several children of one parent. Java does not permit class Dog extends Animal,Mammal.

reviews.answer_text: The child declaration is independent; it does not override the private parent method.
reviews.hint: Read OOP14’s private-parent-method restriction.
reviews.explanation: OOP14 expressly treats a same-signature child method matching a private parent method as an independent declaration. The parent’s private method is not an eligible inherited method for runtime overriding. Thus equal spelling and parameters alone do not establish polymorphic replacement, and this is not ordinary static-method hiding either. Calls must follow each declaration’s own accessibility and context.

evidence.quote: A same-signature child method matching a private parent method is an independent declaration, not runtime overriding and not ordinary static-method hiding.

reviews.answer_text: Declared type: Animal. Actual/runtime type: Dog.
reviews.hint: Read OOP15’s declaration/object distinction.
reviews.explanation: Animal is the variable’s declared compile-time type, determining which member operations may be selected by source checking. new Dog() creates the object, making Dog its actual runtime class. Assignment to the Animal reference does not turn that object into an Animal-only instance. Eligible overridden calls still use the runtime Dog implementation.

evidence.quote: For Animal a=new Dog(), Animal is the declared type and Dog the actual type. The declared type determines which member operations compile.

reviews.answer_text: Compilation fails because fetch() is absent from the declared Animal type.
reviews.hint: Read OOP15’s compile-time member check before runtime dispatch.
reviews.explanation: Although the object is a Dog, the reference a has declared type Animal. OOP15 checks member availability using that declared type before considering runtime overriding. Because fetch() exists only in Dog, a.fetch() is rejected. A checked/safe narrowing to a suitable Dog reference could expose Dog-specific members, but the original expression does not perform that narrowing.

evidence.quote: If fetch() exists only in Dog, a.fetch() fails compilation.

reviews.answer_text: Eligible overridden instance methods are selected at runtime from the actual object class.
reviews.hint: Read OOP15’s three-stage dispatch procedure.
reviews.explanation: The compiler first verifies accessible members and selects the method signature from declared types. Runtime dispatch then selects the most specific eligible override in the object’s actual class. For Animal a=new Dog(), a.sound() can therefore invoke Dog.sound(). This rule does not make Dog-only methods compile through Animal, and static methods/fields follow different selection rules.

evidence.quote: check the declaration and visibility, determine the compile-time signature, then identify the object’s runtime class and its most specific override.

reviews.answer_text: The subclass must remain abstract unless it provides or inherits the third implementation; a concrete incomplete subclass fails compilation.
reviews.hint: Read OOP18’s complete abstract-contract obligation.
reviews.explanation: Implementing only two of three required methods leaves an abstract obligation. OOP18 requires a concrete subclass to provide or inherit implementations for every required method. If the third is still unimplemented, declaring the subclass abstract is permitted; declaring it concrete is not. Merely implementing a majority of the methods does not satisfy the parent contract.

evidence.quote: A concrete subclass must provide or inherit implementations of all required abstract methods; otherwise it must itself be abstract.

reviews.answer_text: Yes, it can have constructors; no, it cannot be directly instantiated.
reviews.hint: Read OOP18’s permitted abstract-class contents.
reviews.explanation: OOP18 allows an abstract class to define constructors alongside fields and concrete/abstract methods. Its constructor participates in initializing the inherited part of a concrete subclass object. That initialization role does not permit new of the abstract class itself. Direct instantiation remains prohibited even if the abstract class happens to contain no abstract methods.

evidence.quote: An abstract class cannot be directly instantiated but can define fields, constructors, abstract methods and concrete methods. It need not contain an abstract method.

reviews.answer_text: extends forms a single superclass relationship; implements fulfills one or more interface contracts.
reviews.hint: Read OOP19’s class/interface relationship rules.
reviews.explanation: A class can extend one superclass, gaining a subtype relationship and appropriate inherited implementation/state. It can also implement multiple interfaces, satisfying their required public operations through provided or inherited methods. Interfaces supply capability contracts rather than per-instance fields or constructors. Modern default/static interface methods mean the distinction cannot simply be summarized as interfaces never contain bodies.

evidence.quote: A class can extend a superclass and implement zero or more interfaces. An interface can extend several interfaces. No interface instance fields or constructors exist; fields are implicitly public static final.

reviews.answer_text: public and abstract for an ordinary interface method declaration without private, default or static.
reviews.hint: Read OOP19’s qualified implicit-method rule.
reviews.explanation: OOP19 gives public abstract for an unmodified abstract interface declaration such as double getPaymentAmount();. Those words are not a universal description of every modern interface method: default and static methods can have bodies, and Java 9+ allows private helpers. The two blanks are answerable only with that ordinary abstract-declaration qualification retained.

evidence.quote: A method declaration without private, default or static is implicitly public abstract.

reviews.answer_text: No. Interface fields are implicitly public static final, not per-instance variables.
reviews.hint: Read OOP19’s field and constructor restriction.
reviews.explanation: OOP19 explicitly excludes interface instance fields. Any field declared in an interface is a public static final class-level constant under the note’s rule, even when some modifiers are not written. Implementing classes may define their own instance fields, but those belong to the implementing objects rather than being instance state supplied by the interface.

evidence.quote: No interface instance fields or constructors exist; fields are implicitly public static final.

reviews.answer_text: Meow, from Cat.makeNoise(), assuming the inherited method is accessible and eligible for overriding.
reviews.hint: Read OOP15’s runtime-type dispatch rule.
reviews.explanation: The declared Animal type allows the makeNoise call under the stated override relationship. The actual object is a Cat, so runtime dispatch selects Cat’s overriding implementation and prints Meow. Assignment to a superclass reference does not suppress subclass behavior. The question does not specify an exact print API, so no additional punctuation or newline is invented.

evidence.quote: For an eligible overridden sound(), a.sound() invokes Dog.sound() at runtime.

reviews.answer_text: For a non-null value, when the actual object is Dog or a subtype; test instanceof when uncertain.
reviews.hint: Read OOP21’s cast check and null exception.
reviews.explanation: An Animal reference may denote a Dog, another subtype or a plain Animal. Downcasting succeeds for an actual Dog-compatible object and otherwise throws ClassCastException. OOP21 recommends instanceof before narrowing when uncertain. Casting null also succeeds and yields null, but using it as an object afterward fails; therefore successful casting and safe dereferencing are distinct questions.

evidence.quote: Use if(a instanceof Ferrari) before narrowing when the dynamic type is uncertain. null instanceof Ferrari is false; casting null yields null, although dereferencing it fails.

reviews.answer_text: It prevents subclasses from extending that class.
reviews.hint: Read OOP07’s separate final effects on variables, methods and classes.
reviews.explanation: OOP07 says final on a class prohibits extension. Developers therefore cannot declare a subclass of String. This differs from final on a variable, which prevents reassignment, and final on a method, which prevents overriding. A final class is not automatically immutable merely because subclassing is prohibited; String’s immutability is an additional property discussed in OOP22.

evidence.quote: final prevents reassignment of a variable, overriding of a method or extension of a class.

reviews.answer_text: No. A same-signature subclass static method hides the parent static method.
reviews.hint: Read OOP16’s static hiding versus runtime overriding.
reviews.explanation: OOP16 states that static methods hide rather than override. Selecting a static method through a reference uses the compile-time type, unlike eligible instance-method dispatch based on the object’s runtime class. Thus Animal a=new Dog(); a.staticMethod() selects Animal’s static declaration. ClassName.method() is the clearer recommended spelling and makes that selection explicit.

evidence.quote: Fields are hidden rather than dynamically overridden, and same-signature static methods hide rather than override.

reviews.answer_text: A subtype is a valid instance of its parent contract: Dog is an Animal.
reviews.hint: Read OOP13’s contract-based inheritance test.
reviews.explanation: OOP13 recommends inheritance when a subtype can satisfy its parent’s contract, as Dog satisfies Animal. That is the is-a relationship rather than mere code reuse. Car containing Engine is instead has-a composition. Reusing fields or methods alone does not justify declaring a subclass if its behavior cannot honor the parent’s promised operations.

evidence.quote: Use inheritance when a subtype can satisfy the parent’s contract: Dog is an Animal.

reviews.answer_text: Compilation fails unless an accessible matching no-argument superclass constructor exists.
reviews.hint: Read OOP10’s required parent-constructor match.
reviews.explanation: An explicit super() requests the immediate superclass’s no-argument constructor. OOP10 requires a matching accessible parent constructor, so a superclass with only parameterized constructors cannot satisfy that invocation. The subclass must instead call an appropriate super(arguments) or the superclass must provide an accessible no-argument constructor. Java does not synthesize one after another constructor has been declared.

evidence.quote: a matching accessible no-argument parent constructor must exist.

reviews.answer_text: It permits inherited access in subclasses across packages, and also same-package access.
reviews.hint: Read OOP08’s protected receiver restrictions.
reviews.explanation: protected supports subclass use of a parent member without making it universally public. OOP08 also grants access to unrelated code in the same package, so it is not subclasses-only. Across packages an instance member must be accessed in the inherited context or through an appropriate subclass-typed receiver, rather than any arbitrary superclass object.

evidence.quote: Across packages, a subclass accessing a protected instance member must do so through its own inherited context or an appropriate subclass-typed receiver, not any arbitrary superclass object.

reviews.answer_text: A concrete Circle must satisfy all inherited abstract operations from Drawable, Shape and Colorable.
reviews.hint: Read OOP19’s inherited interface-contract rule.
reviews.explanation: Drawable can extend both interfaces, combining their contracts. Circle implements Drawable and must therefore provide or inherit suitable public implementations of every remaining abstract operation from the full hierarchy. One compatible implementation can satisfy a shared signature; inherited defaults may supply implementations where applicable. If obligations remain unresolved, Circle must be abstract rather than an incomplete concrete class.

evidence.quote: Implementations must satisfy all inherited abstract contracts; they may inherit suitable public implementations.

reviews.answer_text: Compatible declarations can coexist; implementation obligations depend on abstract, concrete and default status.
reviews.hint: Read OOP20’s class-method precedence and compatibility conditions.
reviews.explanation: OOP20 says a concrete inherited class method takes precedence over an interface default. An abstract class declaration can instead leave an implementation obligation for a concrete subclass. A compatible public implementation may satisfy the interface contract, but incompatible signatures/return types may be impossible. Without declaration details, these conditional rules are the answer rather than one unconditional outcome.

evidence.quote: The answer to “same method in abstract class and interface” depends on whether each is abstract or implemented and whether their signatures are compatible.

reviews.answer_text: Not directly. Use an interface reference holding an implementing object, anonymous implementation or suitable lambda.
reviews.hint: Read OOP19’s instance-versus-reference distinction.
reviews.explanation: OOP19 prohibits direct interface instantiation while allowing a reference of interface type to hold an implementing object. Calls then use the interface contract with the object’s implementation. Anonymous class syntax still creates an implementing class instance, and a compatible functional-interface lambda supplies an implementation; neither means constructing a bare interface with no implementation.

evidence.quote: Interfaces cannot be instantiated directly, but references may hold implementing objects, anonymous implementations or suitable functional-interface lambdas.

reviews.answer_text: throw actively raises an exception value; throws declares a method’s possible checked-exception obligation.
reviews.hint: Read OOP30’s statement versus signature examples.
reviews.explanation: OOP30 contrasts throw new IOException("message") with throws IOException in a method signature. The first performs an action in control flow, skipping the remaining try body; the second declares an obligation that callers must handle or propagate. A throws clause does not itself throw anything, and throwing a checked exception still requires handling or declaration.

evidence.quote: throw new IOException("message") actively throws a value; throws IOException in a signature declares a possible checked exception.

reviews.answer_text: It propagates outward to a matching enclosing handler; if uncaught, its thread terminates.
reviews.hint: Read OOP30’s unmatched-handler propagation rule.
reviews.explanation: Without a matching local catch, the exception is not ignored and execution does not resume with the next ordinary statement in the try. OOP30 sends it outward through enclosing calls/handlers. Relevant finally blocks normally execute during that exit under OOP31’s limits. If no handler catches it, the uncaught exception terminates its thread, not necessarily every JVM thread.

evidence.quote: If no catch matches, the exception propagates outward and an uncaught exception terminates its thread.

reviews.answer_text: No catch-or-declare obligation applies: ArithmeticException is unchecked.
reviews.hint: Read OOP29’s unchecked hierarchy examples.
reviews.explanation: OOP29 lists ArithmeticException among unchecked exceptions, so Java does not require a surrounding catch or throws declaration merely because it may occur. A program can still catch it when that provides useful recovery. Unchecked means no mandatory compile-time handling obligation, not harmless behavior: an uncaught occurrence propagates and may terminate its thread.

evidence.quote: ArithmeticException, NullPointerException, ClassCastException and array bounds exceptions are unchecked.

reviews.answer_text: Run try, then a matching catch if thrown, then normally finally.
reviews.hint: Read OOP31’s normal finally guarantee and exceptional limits.
reviews.explanation: If try completes normally, no catch executes and finally follows. If an exception is thrown, the remaining try body is skipped, a matching catch runs if available, and finally normally executes before continuation or outward propagation. finally also normally runs on return. Process/JVM exit, a crash or control never leaving try prevents an unconditional always claim.

evidence.quote: finally normally executes after try and any selected catch, including when leaving by return or propagating an exception.

reviews.answer_text: Compilation fails because the IOException catch after Exception is unreachable.
reviews.hint: Read OOP30’s specific-before-general catch order.
reviews.explanation: Exception already catches IOException values because IOException is a subtype. The later subtype handler can never be selected, and OOP30 says this ordering prevents compilation rather than merely causing the general handler to win at runtime. Place the specific IOException catch before Exception if both handlers are needed.

evidence.quote: a general catch before a subtype catch makes that later handler unreachable and prevents compilation.

reviews.answer_text: Exception information plus recorded call-stack frames for diagnosis.
reviews.hint: Read OOP31’s message, textual representation and stack-trace distinctions.
reviews.explanation: OOP31 distinguishes getMessage, toString and printStackTrace. The stack trace reports exception information together with recorded call frames, helping locate the call path associated with the failure. It is more diagnostic context than the message alone and does not repair or handle the error by itself. Exact text depends on the exception and recorded frames.

evidence.quote: getMessage returns the message, toString normally includes type and message, and printStackTrace shows exception information and recorded call frames for diagnosis.

reviews.answer_text: Yes. A return from finally overrides the pending try/catch return; avoid it.
reviews.hint: Read OOP31’s return-expression evaluation order.
reviews.explanation: A try return expression is evaluated before finally runs. A return statement inside finally can replace that pending return and can even suppress an exception, which OOP31 warns against. Merely changing a local after a primitive return expression was evaluated does not automatically recompute that earlier result. The explicit finally return is the clear override mechanism.

evidence.quote: A return expression is evaluated before finally; a finally return overrides the pending return and can suppress an exception, so avoid that pattern.

reviews.answer_text: They are Throwable branches: Error usually denotes serious conditions; Exception contains checked and unchecked application exceptions.
reviews.hint: Read OOP29’s hierarchy and recovery qualifications.
reviews.explanation: OOP29 places Error and Exception below Throwable. Error normally signals serious conditions for which routine recovery is inappropriate and its subclasses are unchecked. Exception includes unchecked RuntimeException subclasses and other checked exceptions requiring catch-or-declare handling. It is technically possible to catch Error, so the distinction must not be stated as errors can never be caught.

evidence.quote: Error normally signals serious conditions for which routine recovery is inappropriate; it is not technically impossible to catch an Error.
RuntimeException and Error subclasses are unchecked; other throwable classes are checked.

reviews.answer_text: For FileNotFoundException, the first applicable catch wins; put it before IOException.
reviews.hint: Read OOP30’s required subtype-to-supertype ordering.
reviews.explanation: Both handler types can match a FileNotFoundException, so catch order matters. If FileNotFoundException is first, that specific block executes. If IOException is placed first with FileNotFoundException afterward, the latter is unreachable and compilation fails. If only IOException is present, it can handle the subclass. The prompt omits order, so these cases must be distinguished.

evidence.quote: Catch blocks are considered in source order. Place FileNotFoundException before IOException and IOException before Exception;

reviews.answer_text: An attempted reference cast is incompatible with the actual object type.
reviews.hint: Read OOP21’s plain-Car-to-Ferrari cast example.
reviews.explanation: A cast can be syntactically and type-checkably permitted between related reference types while still fail at runtime. OOP21’s plain Car cannot become a Ferrari merely by casting, so ClassCastException occurs before subsequent method calls. The exception reports an incompatible dynamic type, not object transformation, allocation or a numeric conversion failure.

evidence.quote: A downcast may pass compile-time type checks yet fail at runtime. Car a=new Car(); Ferrari f=(Ferrari)a; throws ClassCastException before subsequent drive() or brake() calls.

reviews.answer_text: Yes to both: use ordered catches or a multi-catch such as catch(IOException | SQLException e).
reviews.hint: Read OOP30’s multiple-handler and union-catch restrictions.
reviews.explanation: One try can have several catch blocks; source order and specific-before-general reachability still apply. A single multi-catch can also handle alternative exception types. OOP30 prohibits alternatives related by subclassing, so IOException and FileNotFoundException cannot be paired in one union catch. Their hierarchy instead calls for an appropriate common catch or ordered handlers.

evidence.quote: Multiple catch blocks are allowed; catch(IOException | SQLException e) handles alternatives, which must not be related by subclassing.

reviews.answer_text: 73. The expression leaves x=5 and y=36, then adds the space character’s value 32.
reviews.hint: Read OOP24’s single-quoted-space trap.
reviews.explanation: Java evaluates ++x first, changing 5 to 6 and supplying 6. x-- then supplies 6 and restores x to 5, so y=36. In x + ' ' + y the space is char, not String, and numeric promotion gives 5+32+36=73. Replacing it with a double-quoted space would instead concatenate separated values.

evidence.quote: System.out.println(x + ' ' + y) then adds char space’s numeric value 32, so it prints 73.

reviews.answer_text: Compilation fails for an ordinary separately declared Sphere: the inherited radius field is private.
reviews.hint: Read OOP11’s explicit private-field subclass example.
reviews.explanation: OOP11 says a separately declared subclass cannot normally access a private parent field directly, even through this.field. this denotes the current object but does not override member visibility. Sphere should use an accessible parent operation that validates or changes radius. This answer uses the ordinary separate-class context in the note rather than assuming an unspecified shared nest.

evidence.quote: A private field cannot normally be accessed directly by a separately declared subclass, even with this.field; use a permitted parent operation.

reviews.answer_text: A concrete class can be instantiated and must satisfy abstract obligations; an abstract class cannot be directly instantiated.
reviews.hint: Read OOP18’s contents and implementation requirements.
reviews.explanation: An abstract class can hold state, constructors, concrete methods and abstract methods, and need not contain an abstract method. A concrete subclass must provide or inherit implementations of every required abstract operation before it can serve as an instantiable class. Abstract is therefore a class-level instantiation/contract restriction, not a prohibition on implemented behavior.

evidence.quote: A concrete subclass must provide or inherit implementations of all required abstract methods; otherwise it must itself be abstract.
An abstract class cannot be directly instantiated but can define fields, constructors, abstract methods and concrete methods.

reviews.answer_text: Developers cannot subclass String; final prohibits extension.
reviews.hint: Read OOP07’s class-level final effect and OOP22’s immutability distinction.
reviews.explanation: Applying final to String prevents any class from extending String. It does not prevent constructing or referencing String instances, nor does the class modifier alone explain immutability of arbitrary objects. OOP22 treats String’s immutable content as a distinct property. Developers should use existing String operations rather than attempting a String subclass.

evidence.quote: final class String prevents subclassing; final alone does not make arbitrary objects immutable.

reviews.answer_text: A subclass static method hides a same-signature parent static method; overriding is runtime instance dispatch.
reviews.hint: Read OOP16’s compile-time static selection.
reviews.explanation: For static hiding, the selected declaration follows the compile-time type used to qualify the call. For eligible overridden instance methods, the object’s runtime class determines the implementation. OOP16’s Animal a=new Dog() static call therefore resolves to Animal, unlike a virtual instance sound call that could invoke Dog. Class qualification makes static selection clearer.

evidence.quote: With Animal a=new Dog(), a.staticMethod() resolves using Animal’s compile-time type.

reviews.answer_text: C must provide public void m1() and public void m2(), or inherit suitable implementations.
reviews.hint: Read OOP19’s implicit public contracts and all-inherited-method obligation.
reviews.explanation: Both unmodified interface declarations are implicitly public abstract. A concrete C implementing A and B must satisfy both signatures, not merely one. In the shown class with no suitable superclass implementation, define public void m1() and public void m2(). Package-private implementations would narrow the public contract; otherwise C must be declared abstract instead of concrete.

evidence.quote: Implementations must satisfy all inherited abstract contracts; they may inherit suitable public implementations.
A method declaration without private, default or static is implicitly public abstract.

reviews.answer_text: Throwable is the common root of Java’s throwable Error and Exception hierarchy.
reviews.hint: Read OOP29’s root-class definition.
reviews.explanation: OOP29 places both Error and Exception under Throwable, establishing the common type for Java throwable values. The distinction between checked and unchecked branches controls catch-or-declare obligations, not whether an exception happens during compilation. Throwable therefore unifies the hierarchy without implying that every subclass is an ordinary recoverable application exception.

evidence.quote: Throwable is the root of throwable values, with Exception and Error branches.

reviews.answer_text: Compilation fails because the checked exception is neither handled nor declared.
reviews.hint: Read OOP30’s checked catch-or-propagate obligation.
reviews.explanation: OOP30 requires callers and methods to handle or propagate checked obligations. A method that may throw a checked exception but neither catches it nor declares it in throws violates that compile-time requirement. The failure is not that checked exceptions occur during compilation: the compiler is checking a possible future runtime throw.

evidence.quote: A caller must handle or propagate checked obligations.

reviews.answer_text: New subtypes can supply behavior while existing common-type client code remains reusable.
reviews.hint: Read OOP15’s unchanged polymorphic-loop example.
reviews.explanation: OOP15 describes a common Animal array loop invoking speak on Dog and Cat objects. Adding another conforming Animal subtype can supply its own override without rewriting that generic loop. That ability is extensibility through polymorphism: clients depend on the shared contract, while runtime dispatch supplies subtype behavior. The new subtype must still satisfy that contract.

evidence.quote: New subclasses can supply behavior without rewriting this generic loop, which is the practical meaning of extensibility.

reviews.answer_text: Literal single-quoted Hello is invalid. With "Hello", the String cast succeeds and the Integer cast throws ClassCastException.
reviews.hint: Read OOP21’s exact quotation and dynamic-type distinctions.
reviews.explanation: A Java character literal cannot contain the multi-character text 'Hello', so the printed declaration fails before either cast executes. OOP21 explicitly separates that defect from the intended double-quoted version. After changing it to a String literal, obj refers to a String: narrowing back to String succeeds, but narrowing it to Integer fails at runtime.

evidence.quote: For Object obj="Hello", (String)obj succeeds and (Integer)obj throws ClassCastException. A literal 'Hello' is invalid Java syntax, so the bank’s single-quoted version must be clarified first.

reviews.answer_text: If no explicit this(...) or super(...) delegation exists, Java inserts super(); this(...) instead delegates within the class.
reviews.hint: Read OOP10’s conditional implicit-delegation rule.
reviews.explanation: Omitting explicit super() alone is insufficient to determine what happens. A constructor may explicitly call this(...), delegating to another same-class constructor that eventually reaches superclass construction. Only when there is no explicit constructor delegation does OOP10 insert super(), requiring an accessible matching parent no-argument constructor. Otherwise the program fails to compile.

evidence.quote: If there is no explicit delegation, an implicit super() is inserted; a matching accessible no-argument parent constructor must exist.

reviews.answer_text: A class defines common structure/behavior; an object is one instance, such as a particular Rectangle with width and height.
reviews.hint: Read OOP01’s Rectangle and object-identity example.
reviews.explanation: Rectangle can define width, height, getArea and getPerimeter for every rectangle. A particular rectangle object stores its own width and height values and responds to those operations. OOP01 distinguishes that instance from the type description: two objects can have equal field values and still have distinct identities. The class is shared structure, not one particular rectangle.

evidence.quote: A class defines their common structure and behavior; an object is a particular instance.

reviews.answer_text: Encapsulation protects invariants and stable interfaces by grouping state with validated operations and controlling access.
reviews.hint: Read OOP02’s grouping/interface rule and OOP11’s validation example.
reviews.explanation: OOP02 groups state and operations with controlled access, keeping representation decisions behind stable interfaces. A private account balance exposed through deposit(amount) can reject invalid negative changes rather than permitting unrestricted assignment. This localizes responsibility and lets clients use meaningful operations without depending on internal representation. OOP11 cautions that automatically exposing setters for every field is not required.

evidence.quote: a private balance plus deposit(amount) can demonstrate all three, depending on what the question emphasizes.
Encapsulation does not require blindly generating setters for every field: validate changes and expose only useful operations.

reviews.answer_text: Overloading changes parameter signatures; overriding replaces eligible inherited instance behavior with the same signature.
reviews.hint: Read OOP12’s compile-time overload rule and OOP14’s override rule.
reviews.explanation: For overloading, f(int), f(double) and f(int,int) share a name but have distinct signatures selected using declared arguments at compile time. For overriding, Dog extends Animal and supplies void sound() matching Animal’s eligible void sound(); a superclass reference can then dispatch to Dog at runtime. Changing only the return type cannot create an overload, and override return compatibility still matters.

evidence.quote: f(int), f(double) and f(int,int) are distinct, but changing a parameter name does not create an overload.
A subclass overrides an eligible inherited instance method with the same signature and a compatible return type;

reviews.answer_text: Java permits one direct superclass. Use multiple interfaces for type contracts and composition for cooperating implementation/state.
reviews.hint: Read OOP13’s single-superclass rule and OOP20’s conflict resolution.
reviews.explanation: The immediate reason the declaration is rejected is Java’s one-direct-superclass rule in OOP13. Multiple interfaces supply multiple type contracts, while contained collaborators model has-a reuse without multiple class inheritance. This does not eliminate every diamond problem: OOP20 requires explicit resolution of conflicting unrelated interface defaults. The note supplies these mechanisms, rather than a historical language-design rationale.

evidence.quote: A class extends one direct class and can implement multiple interfaces.
Unrelated interfaces providing conflicting defaults require an explicit resolution; interfaces do not remove every diamond ambiguity.

reviews.answer_text: Polymorphism lets a common-type reference invoke behavior appropriate to the actual subtype.
reviews.hint: Read OOP15’s Animal/Dog dispatch example.
reviews.explanation: Example: class Animal { void sound() { System.out.println("Animal"); } } class Dog extends Animal { void sound() { System.out.println("Bark"); } } Then Animal a=new Dog(); a.sound(); prints Bark. The declared Animal type makes sound available; the actual Dog object supplies its eligible override at runtime. A new Animal subtype can participate through the same common operation.

evidence.quote: For an eligible overridden sound(), a.sound() invokes Dog.sound() at runtime.

reviews.answer_text: Use an abstract class for shared state/construction/implementation; use an interface for capabilities across unrelated classes and multiple type contracts.
reviews.hint: Read OOP20’s explicit design-choice rule.
reviews.explanation: An abstract class can centralize common fields, constructor initialization and concrete operations while leaving selected operations abstract. An interface specifies a capability that otherwise unrelated classes can implement, and a class may implement several interfaces. Modern interface defaults do not supply per-instance fields or constructors, so shared object state/construction remains a reason to choose an abstract class.

evidence.quote: Use an abstract class for shared state, construction and common implementation; use an interface for a capability across unrelated classes and multiple type inheritance.

reviews.answer_text: Strict alternation (option misspells it as alteration).
reviews.hint: Read the turn-variable mutual-exclusion algorithm.
reviews.explanation: OS12 defines strict alternation using turn=0/1: each process waits until turn equals its identifier and passes the turn on leaving. That directly matches the described integer ownership variable. A naive lock variable instead records availability and can race during separate test/set operations. Disabling interrupts and a race condition do not implement the described turn-taking algorithm.

evidence.quote: Strict alternation uses turn=0/1: process i waits while turn≠i, then enters and sets turn to the other process on leaving.

choices.label: A
choices.explanation: A naive lock variable records free/busy status rather than assigning alternating ownership to process 0 or 1.

choices.label: B
choices.explanation: Disabling interrupts does not implement the integer turn-owner protocol described in the stem.

choices.label: C
choices.explanation: Strict alternation uses a turn variable initialized to one process and passed to the other.

choices.label: D
choices.explanation: A race condition is a concurrency failure, not a mechanism providing the described alternating access.

reviews.answer_text: Blocking send.
reviews.hint: Read which participant waits in rendezvous messaging.
reviews.explanation: OS09 explicitly identifies a sender blocked until receipt as blocking send under rendezvous semantics. The stem describes the sending process waiting, not a receiver awaiting an incoming message. Nonblocking sending returns promptly rather than waiting for receipt, and receive modes describe the other side. The receipt condition here supplies the relevant API assumption.

evidence.quote: “Sender blocked until received” identifies blocking send under rendezvous semantics.

choices.label: A
choices.explanation: Blocking receive waits on the receiving side, whereas the stem explicitly blocks the sender.

choices.label: B
choices.explanation: Nonblocking receive returns promptly on the receiving side and does not describe sender waiting.

choices.label: C
choices.explanation: Nonblocking sending returns promptly rather than keeping the sender blocked until the handoff completes.

choices.label: D
choices.explanation: Under the stated rendezvous condition, waiting until message receipt is blocking-send behavior.

reviews.answer_text: The claim that kernel modules cannot load while running is false.
reviews.hint: Review loadable kernel modules and the OS boot boundary.
reviews.explanation: OS03 states that loadable modules can add drivers to a running kernel, directly contradicting option C’s absolute prohibition. It describes the kernel as the core OS component and resident through the session. Option B is read as the first core OS component, rather than the first code executed at power-on: firmware and bootloader stages precede it.

evidence.quote: Loadable modules can add drivers to a running kernel; “kernel modules cannot be loaded while running” is false in modular systems.

choices.label: A
choices.explanation: The kernel implements core resource management, protection and system-call handling, so this statement is true.

choices.label: B
choices.explanation: As the first core OS component, the kernel is loaded at boot; firmware/bootloader execution precedes that OS boundary.

choices.label: C
choices.explanation: Modular kernels permit runtime module loading, directly refuting the statement that it cannot occur.

choices.label: D
choices.explanation: A resident kernel remains active throughout the session, matching the note’s ordinary kernel model.

reviews.answer_text: None: all four are I/O-software goals or supporting functions.
reviews.hint: Read I/O independence, naming, error handling and buffering.
reviews.explanation: OS34 identifies device independence, uniform naming and error handling as I/O services. OS35 explains buffering as holding in-transit data to absorb speed/size differences. Each listed feature therefore supports I/O software, so none is an exclusion. Calling buffering a supporting mechanism rather than a high-level objective does not make it unrelated to I/O software’s goals.

evidence.quote: Device independence and uniform naming hide brand-specific details; error handling reports/retries supported failures.
Buffering temporarily holds data in transit to absorb speed/transfer-size differences.

choices.label: A
choices.explanation: Buffering absorbs transfer-speed and size differences, directly supporting reliable and efficient I/O software.

choices.label: B
choices.explanation: Device independence is an explicit I/O service that hides device-specific details from higher layers.

choices.label: C
choices.explanation: Uniform naming is explicitly included among the I/O services described by the note.

choices.label: D
choices.explanation: Reporting or retrying supported device failures is the error-handling responsibility of I/O software.

choices.label: E
choices.explanation: All four listed functions support I/O software, leaving no listed function to exclude.

reviews.answer_text: No fit policy is universally best for both speed and storage utilization.
reviews.hint: Compare fit-policy selection rules under an actual allocation workload.
reviews.explanation: OS28 explicitly rejects a policy that universally optimizes both search time and future storage utilization. The source image confirms that the question provides no holes, requests, workload or weighting of those two objectives. First-fit, best-fit and worst-fit use different selection rules, so a blanket superiority claim cannot be established. The source’s emphasized options do not supply missing evaluation conditions.

evidence.quote: No policy universally optimizes both search time and future storage utilization.

choices.label: A
choices.explanation: First-fit chooses the first adequate hole, but its combined superiority requires a workload and comparison criterion.

choices.label: B
choices.explanation: Best-fit minimizes the selected adequate hole, which does not prove universally superior speed or future utilization.

choices.label: C
choices.explanation: Worst-fit selects the largest hole; any advantage depends on the allocation stream and measurement objective.

choices.label: D
choices.explanation: All three cannot each be unconditionally better under one unstated comparison; no universal superiority is established.

reviews.answer_text: Mutual exclusion is a desired safety property.
reviews.hint: Separate concurrency failures from the properties used to prevent them.
reviews.explanation: OS10 explicitly contrasts mutual exclusion, a desired safety property, with race conditions, starvation and deadlock as possible failures. Although a badly designed locking scheme can introduce deadlock, that does not turn the mutual-exclusion requirement itself into a concurrency failure. Therefore it is the single option that is not a problem in the sense used by the list.

evidence.quote: Mutual exclusion is a desired safety property; races, starvation and deadlock are possible failures.

choices.label: A
choices.explanation: A race is a concurrency failure caused by uncoordinated interleaving of conflicting accesses.

choices.label: B
choices.explanation: Starvation is a possible indefinite-delay failure of concurrent scheduling or resource competition.

choices.label: C
choices.explanation: Deadlock is a possible failure in which blocked participants cannot supply one another’s required events.

choices.label: D
choices.explanation: Mutual exclusion is a correctness property protecting shared state, rather than a failure to be avoided.

choices.label: E
choices.explanation: Mutual exclusion provides a clear non-failure option, so none of the choices is not appropriate.

reviews.answer_text: Process termination and rollback are both recovery methods.
reviews.hint: Read recovery methods separately from prevention conditions.
reviews.explanation: OS26 permits terminating selected processes or reclaiming safely preemptable resources while rolling affected work back to a checkpoint. Both killing a process and rollback can therefore participate in deadlock recovery. Non-preemption is a condition that can permit deadlock, and locking a process is not a recovery method. The single-answer shape does not remove the two supported choices.

evidence.quote: Recovery can terminate selected processes or reclaim safely preemptable resources and roll affected work back to a checkpoint.

choices.label: A
choices.explanation: Terminating a selected process can release its resources and break a deadlock dependency.

choices.label: B
choices.explanation: Rollback to a checkpoint can support recovery after resources are safely reclaimed from affected work.

choices.label: C
choices.explanation: Keeping resources non-preemptable preserves a deadlock condition rather than providing the listed recovery method.

choices.label: D
choices.explanation: Merely locking a process does not release dependencies or restore affected work to a recoverable checkpoint.

reviews.answer_text: The policy removes hold-and-wait.
reviews.hint: Ask whether a waiting process retains any resource.
reviews.explanation: The source image confirms the policy says the process drops all previously held resources when it must wait. OS24 states that release-all-and-retry removes simultaneous holding while waiting. The stem describes voluntary dropping, not forced withdrawal by another agent, so hold-and-wait is the directly attacked condition. It supplies no global ordering or resource-sharing rule.

evidence.quote: “If waiting, release all held resources and try again” removes simultaneous holding while waiting.

choices.label: A
choices.explanation: The policy does not impose a global acquisition order, which is the direct circular-wait prevention method.

choices.label: B
choices.explanation: The stem specifies the process dropping resources, not a general rule permitting forced resource preemption.

choices.label: C
choices.explanation: Resources may remain nonshareable; releasing holdings does not remove mutual-exclusion requirements.

choices.label: D
choices.explanation: A process no longer retains allocated resources while waiting to acquire the rest.

choices.label: E
choices.explanation: Hold-and-wait is explicitly removed by the release-all-before-waiting rule, so an identified condition fits.

reviews.answer_text: Both the universal filesystem claim and the critical-section definition are false.
reviews.hint: Read filesystem diversity and the distinction between shared resources and critical code.
reviews.explanation: OS36 names distinct filesystem formats, refuting the claim that all OS filesystem standards are the same. OS10 defines a critical section as code accessing protected shared state, not the resource itself. OS16/OS17 support possible SJF starvation and aging for waiting priority jobs. Thus both A and D are false under the literal wording, even if the source intended only one.

evidence.quote: FAT32, NTFS and ext4 are filesystem formats; HTTP is an application communication protocol.
A critical section is code accessing shared state that needs protection, not the resource itself.
Aging increases waiting jobs’ effective priority according to a rule, reducing indefinite postponement when the priority scheme and workload permit.

choices.label: A
choices.explanation: Different filesystem formats and OS-specific policies refute the absolute claim that their standards are all the same.

choices.label: B
choices.explanation: Repeated short arrivals can starve a long SJF job, so this statement is true.

choices.label: C
choices.explanation: Aging raises waiting jobs’ effective priority to address priority starvation under the stated policy assumptions.

choices.label: D
choices.explanation: A critical section is protected code, not the shared resource that the code accesses.

reviews.answer_text: fork().
reviews.hint: Distinguish child creation, image replacement and termination.
reviews.explanation: OS07 states that fork() creates a child in POSIX-style systems, returning zero in the child and its PID in the parent on success. exec replaces the current process image and does not itself create another process. exit and abort terminate execution normally and abnormally respectively. Creation therefore corresponds to fork among the literal listed calls.

evidence.quote: In POSIX-style systems fork() creates a child: zero is returned in the child and the child PID in the parent on success.

choices.label: A
choices.explanation: fork creates a child process rather than replacing or terminating the existing process image.

choices.label: B
choices.explanation: exit terminates normally through the runtime rather than creating a new process.

choices.label: C
choices.explanation: abort requests abnormal termination rather than allocating a new child execution instance.

choices.label: D
choices.explanation: exec replaces the current process image; it does not itself create another process.

reviews.answer_text: Semaphore.
reviews.hint: Compare software semaphore coordination with two-process algorithms and atomic hardware primitives.
reviews.explanation: OS12 explicitly says a semaphore can coordinate more than two processes, while classic Peterson’s algorithm is for two under its memory-model assumptions. OS11 explains counting semaphores as tracking several permits, fitting multiple resource instances. Compare-and-swap and test-and-set are atomic primitives rather than the named software coordination abstraction requested by the stem.

evidence.quote: Peterson’s classic algorithm uses flags plus turn for two processes under its memory-model assumptions; a semaphore can coordinate more than two.
A binary semaphore represents one permit; a counting semaphore tracks several.

choices.label: A
choices.explanation: Counting semaphores track multiple permits and coordinate more than two participating processes.

choices.label: B
choices.explanation: Compare-and-swap is an atomic checking/updating primitive, rather than the requested software semaphore abstraction.

choices.label: C
choices.explanation: Classic Peterson’s algorithm solves the two-process case, not the stated more-than-two configuration.

choices.label: D
choices.explanation: Test-and-set is an atomic primitive; the software multiple-permit coordination mechanism here is a semaphore.

reviews.answer_text: All listed causes can terminate a process.
reviews.hint: Read voluntary exits versus involuntary termination.
reviews.explanation: OS07 distinguishes voluntary normal completion from involuntary faults or being killed. Each named cause is therefore a genuine termination cause, although the causes differ in who initiates them and whether completion is normal. The aggregate choice includes all three. Selecting only one named cause would omit other valid termination paths supported by the complete note.

evidence.quote: Normal completion and a program-detected error exit are voluntary; an unrecoverable fault or being killed is involuntary.

choices.label: A
choices.explanation: Being killed can terminate a process, but this alone omits normal completion and fatal faults.

choices.label: B
choices.explanation: Normal exit is valid, but it is only one of the three supported termination causes.

choices.label: C
choices.explanation: Being killed, normal exit and fatal error all provide legitimate process-termination causes.

choices.label: D
choices.explanation: A fatal error can terminate execution, but the other two named causes are also valid.

reviews.answer_text: All named conditions are necessary conditions.
reviews.hint: Review the four standard deadlock conditions and distinguish necessity from sufficiency.
reviews.explanation: OS22 lists mutual exclusion, hold-and-wait, no resource preemption and circular wait as necessary in the standard reusable-resource model. The three substantive choices name the first three, so all of the mentioned is the comprehensive option. Circular wait is also required despite being omitted from the list. Having these policies does not prove a particular current allocation is already deadlocked.

evidence.quote: All four are necessary in the standard reusable-resource model.

choices.label: A
choices.explanation: Mutual exclusion is necessary, but selecting it alone omits the other two necessary conditions offered.

choices.label: B
choices.explanation: Each substantive option names a standard necessary deadlock condition; the aggregate includes all offered conditions.

choices.label: C
choices.explanation: Retaining resources while requesting more is hold-and-wait, one valid condition among the three offered.

choices.label: D
choices.explanation: No forced removal is no-preemption, which is necessary but does not exclude the other valid conditions.

reviews.answer_text: Tree directory structure, in the usual general-purpose OS sense.
reviews.hint: Read the hierarchical namespace model used by modern general-purpose systems.
reviews.explanation: OS37 states that modern general-purpose systems commonly present hierarchical namespaces and defines a tree as allowing nested directories and absolute/relative paths. That directly supports the conventional tree-directory choice. This is a general-purpose namespace convention, not a measured claim about every OS ever built; links can add graph structure without replacing the hierarchy as the basic user-visible organization.

evidence.quote: A tree allows nested directories and absolute/relative paths; links can create shared graphs. Modern general-purpose systems commonly present hierarchical namespaces,

choices.label: A
choices.explanation: A single namespace without nested directories does not match the common hierarchical organization described.

choices.label: B
choices.explanation: Separating user directories alone is less general than the nested hierarchy specified for modern general-purpose systems.

choices.label: C
choices.explanation: Nested directories and paths form the tree/hierarchical organization the note identifies as commonly presented.

choices.label: D
choices.explanation: Links can add graph sharing, but acyclic sharing is not the basic common directory organization identified.

reviews.answer_text: All four are standard necessary deadlock conditions.
reviews.hint: Read why each standard condition is necessary and none alone proves an actual deadlock.
reviews.explanation: OS22 lists mutual exclusion, hold-and-wait, no-preemption and circular wait as the four necessary conditions in the standard reusable-resource model. Each substantive choice therefore names a valid deadlock condition, making all of these the comprehensive answer. The wording causes must not be read as saying one condition alone is sufficient; actual allocation/request dependencies still require inspection.

evidence.quote: All four are necessary in the standard reusable-resource model. Their availability as general system policies does not prove a deadlock exists at this instant; inspect actual allocations/requests.

choices.label: A
choices.explanation: Mutual exclusion is one necessary condition, but the other three named conditions also belong to the standard set.

choices.label: B
choices.explanation: Hold-and-wait is necessary, but selecting it alone leaves out the other valid conditions.

choices.label: C
choices.explanation: Circular wait is part of the condition set, but it is not the sole valid listed condition.

choices.label: D
choices.explanation: No-preemption is necessary in this model, alongside the other three substantive choices.

choices.label: E
choices.explanation: All four substantive choices are standard necessary conditions; together their names give the complete condition set.

reviews.answer_text: Permanent blocking alone does not establish the required dependency set.
reviews.hint: Read deadlock as waiting on events only another blocked member can provide.
reviews.explanation: OS22 defines deadlock through a set of blocked participants waiting for events/resources that only other blocked members can provide. Option C describes indefinite blocking but omits that dependency, so it is the intended consequence rather than a sufficient literal definition. Unfair delay or an unavailable external event need not be deadlock. The question needs the closed dependency condition before C can be uniquely established.

evidence.quote: A set is deadlocked when each member waits for an event/resource that only another blocked member can provide. Mere waiting for another holder is normal blocking; indefinite unfair delay can be starvation without a cycle of dependencies.

choices.label: A
choices.explanation: Terminated processes are no longer waiting participants; termination is not the defining deadlock state.

choices.label: B
choices.explanation: Processes attempting to kill each other does not establish blocked resource dependencies or a deadlock.

choices.label: C
choices.explanation: This is the intended consequence, but indefinite blocking alone omits the required dependency on other blocked members.

choices.label: D
choices.explanation: If read as a strict sufficient definition, none states the complete dependency condition; the intended reading remains unclear.

reviews.answer_text: Worst-fit.
reviews.hint: Read which allocation rule selects the largest adequate hole.
reviews.explanation: OS28 defines worst-fit as selecting the largest hole, directly matching the stem. Best-fit chooses the smallest adequate hole, and first-fit stops at the first adequate one rather than comparing all sizes. The buddy label does not state this largest-hole rule in the provided note. No numeric trace is necessary because the selection criterion itself is explicit.

evidence.quote: First-fit selects the first adequate hole; next-fit continues from the previous search position; best-fit selects the smallest adequate hole; worst-fit selects the largest.

choices.label: A
choices.explanation: Best-fit chooses the smallest adequate hole, which is the opposite size-selection criterion from the stem.

choices.label: B
choices.explanation: First-fit selects the first adequate hole in search order, not necessarily the largest available hole.

choices.label: C
choices.explanation: Worst-fit is explicitly the policy that selects the largest available adequate hole.

choices.label: D
choices.explanation: The supplied largest-hole criterion is defined as worst-fit; the buddy label is not that rule.

reviews.answer_text: Plug-and-play functionality.
reviews.hint: Read automatic discovery/configuration of compatible hardware.
reviews.explanation: OS34 defines plug-and-play as discovering and configuring compatible new hardware, with the qualification that a driver may still be required. That is exactly the printer scenario. The automatic wording excludes the two manual alternatives. Resource allocation may occur during configuration, but it is broader than the specific automatic detection/configuration feature requested by the question.

evidence.quote: Plug-and-play discovers/configures compatible new hardware but may still require a driver.

choices.label: A
choices.explanation: Automatically discovering and configuring the installed printer is precisely the plug-and-play behavior described.

choices.label: B
choices.explanation: The scenario explicitly says automatic detection/configuration rather than manual driver installation by the user.

choices.label: C
choices.explanation: Manual hardware management conflicts with the automatic configuration behavior specified in the scenario.

choices.label: D
choices.explanation: Resources may be assigned during setup, but the specific automatic discovery feature is plug-and-play.

reviews.answer_text: No preemption.
reviews.hint: Read which condition requires the holder to release resources voluntarily.
reviews.explanation: OS22 directly defines no resource preemption as requiring voluntary release. The stem repeats that resources cannot be forcibly taken, so the match is exact. Hold-and-wait concerns retaining one resource while requesting another, mutual exclusion concerns exclusive possession, and circular wait concerns a closed dependency chain. None of those separately states the prohibition on forced withdrawal.

evidence.quote: No resource preemption means release must be voluntary.

choices.label: A
choices.explanation: Prohibiting forced withdrawal and requiring voluntary release is exactly the no-preemption resource condition.

choices.label: B
choices.explanation: Hold-and-wait concerns retaining a resource while requesting another, not whether forced removal is permitted.

choices.label: C
choices.explanation: Mutual exclusion limits concurrent holders; it does not itself require voluntary release.

choices.label: D
choices.explanation: Circular wait describes a closed chain of dependencies rather than the resource-withdrawal rule.

reviews.answer_text: C is the conventional fatal-fault answer; B also qualifies if Terminate exit means an external kill.
reviews.hint: Distinguish voluntary program exits from fault- or kill-imposed termination, and define the exit categories.
reviews.explanation: OS07 makes unrecoverable faults and being killed involuntary, so C is supported when fatal exit means a fatal fault. However, Terminate exit in B has no defined cause. If it means termination imposed by another process, B also qualifies; if the program chooses to terminate, it does not. Normal completion and program-detected error exit are voluntary. The undefined category prevents a unique label; define B before selecting C alone or B and C together.

evidence.quote: Normal completion and a program-detected error exit are voluntary; an unrecoverable fault or being killed is involuntary.
“Terminate exit” is not a precise standard category.

choices.label: A
choices.explanation: Normal completion is voluntary in the supplied exit taxonomy, rather than an imposed fault or kill.

choices.label: B
choices.explanation: Terminate exit could mean an external kill, which is involuntary; its cause is not defined.

choices.label: C
choices.explanation: Under the conventional fatal-fault meaning, an unrecoverable fault imposes involuntary termination.

choices.label: D
choices.explanation: A program-detected error exit is voluntary, unlike termination imposed by an unrecoverable execution fault.

reviews.answer_text: Detection frequency requires an overhead-versus-delay policy.
reviews.hint: Read the tradeoff between checking each request and periodic deadlock detection.
reviews.explanation: OS26 explicitly rejects a universal best detection interval. Checking on every request can reduce delay but increases overhead; periodic checking makes a different tradeoff. The source gives no deadlock rate, request rate, detection cost or acceptable delay. Option A also merges two schedules unclearly. Effective alone is not a measurable criterion from which one checking policy can be selected.

evidence.quote: Checking on every request versus periodically trades overhead against detection delay; no universal best interval exists.

choices.label: A
choices.explanation: This merges every-request checking and fixed intervals without specifying whether both triggers or another policy is intended.

choices.label: B
choices.explanation: Periodic checking is a valid policy whose suitability depends on acceptable delay and detection overhead.

choices.label: C
choices.explanation: Checking every request is another valid policy, but its overhead may outweigh its detection-latency benefit.

choices.label: D
choices.explanation: No universal schedule follows, but none is not a positive replacement for the missing cost/latency requirements.

reviews.answer_text: Disk responsibilities span OS tools, boot firmware and drive firmware.
reviews.hint: Read which layer initializes filesystems, starts boot and remaps bad sectors.
reviews.explanation: OS35 distinguishes disk initialization/filesystem creation as OS/tool work, firmware as beginning boot, and drive firmware as potentially remapping bad sectors. The broad responsible for wording does not say whether coordinating a multistage operation counts as performing it. Therefore the all alternative cannot be assumed, and a unique exclusive answer needs a defined abstraction level and disk-function scope.

evidence.quote: Disk initialization/filesystem creation is OS/tool work, firmware begins boot, and drive firmware may remap bad sectors.

choices.label: A
choices.explanation: Bad-block recovery may involve drive firmware and OS handling; the stem does not define the responsibility boundary.

choices.label: B
choices.explanation: Firmware begins boot before kernel control, although a broader boot sequence can involve OS-provided components.

choices.label: C
choices.explanation: Initialization/filesystem creation is explicitly OS/tool work, but the question does not exclude broader coordinated responsibilities.

choices.label: D
choices.explanation: All requires a broad coordinating meaning of responsibility; it is not justified as a direct OS-only implementation claim.

reviews.answer_text: A semaphore can enforce one-at-a-time access.
reviews.hint: Read binary semaphore initialization and wait/signal around critical work.
reviews.explanation: OS11 describes a binary semaphore as one permit and gives wait(m); critical work; signal(m) with m initialized to 1. This prevents competing threads/processes from entering the protected resource operation simultaneously; it does not mean nobody can ever use the resource. A PCB stores process state, a scheduler selects jobs, and allocation layout does not enforce this resource-access rule.

evidence.quote: A binary semaphore represents one permit; a counting semaphore tracks several.
Initialize a mutex semaphore to 1. Each thread does wait(m); critical work; signal(m).

choices.label: A
choices.explanation: A PCB records execution and resource state rather than supplying atomic mutual-exclusion operations.

choices.label: B
choices.explanation: A one-permit semaphore with atomic wait/signal can serialize entry to the protected resource operation.

choices.label: C
choices.explanation: A job scheduler selects admitted or ready work; it does not by itself protect shared resource accesses.

choices.label: D
choices.explanation: Noncontiguous memory placement changes allocation layout rather than synchronizing access to one shared resource.

reviews.answer_text: Microsoft Office is an application suite.
reviews.hint: Separate operating-system families from user applications.
reviews.explanation: OS40 explicitly identifies Microsoft Office as an application suite and discusses Windows, Linux and macOS as OS/kernel families. Office runs using OS services rather than providing the core resource-management platform. Thus Office is the exclusion in this list. The kernel-versus-distribution distinction for Linux does not turn it into an office application or invalidate the conventional OS-family contrast.

evidence.quote: Microsoft Office is an application suite.

choices.label: A
choices.explanation: Windows is identified as the Microsoft operating-system family, so it is not the application-suite exclusion.

choices.label: B
choices.explanation: Linux names a kernel used with distributions as operating systems, unlike the Office application suite.

choices.label: C
choices.explanation: macOS is an operating-system product rather than a user application suite in this classification.

choices.label: D
choices.explanation: Microsoft Office is explicitly described as an application suite, not an operating system.

reviews.answer_text: Virtualization, in the virtual-machine sense.
reviews.hint: Distinguish guest-machine virtualization from process memory techniques.
reviews.explanation: OS04 defines virtualization as presenting virtual machine environments and distinguishes it from virtual memory. OS27 describes swapping, OS30 paging and OS31 segmentation as memory-management mechanisms. Under the guest-machine sense used in this note, virtualization is therefore the option outside that list. The answer depends on that stated sense; the broader phrase memory virtualization would describe a different use of the word.

evidence.quote: Virtualization presents a virtual machine environment, often allowing guest operating systems on one host through a hypervisor. It differs from virtual memory, which translates a process’s addresses.

choices.label: A
choices.explanation: Paging maps fixed-size virtual pages to physical frames and is explicitly a memory-management mechanism.

choices.label: B
choices.explanation: Segmentation maps variable-length logical regions and is explicitly a memory-management mechanism.

choices.label: C
choices.explanation: Swapping moves a process to backing store and is a memory-management operation described by the note.

choices.label: D
choices.explanation: In the note’s guest-machine sense, virtualization presents virtual computers rather than naming these process-memory techniques.

reviews.answer_text: Binary Search Tree is a data structure.
reviews.hint: Read the distinction between queue implementation and CPU scheduling policy.
reviews.explanation: OS19 explicitly states that a binary search tree may implement a queue but is not itself a CPU selection policy. FCFS, Round Robin and SJF are actual scheduling algorithms described in OS15, OS18 and OS16. Consequently BST is the exclusion. Using a tree internally to maintain priorities would not change the selection policy into an algorithm called BST.

evidence.quote: A binary search tree is a data structure that might implement a queue; it is not itself a CPU selection policy.

choices.label: A
choices.explanation: FCFS is a scheduling policy that runs ready bursts in their arrival order.

choices.label: B
choices.explanation: Round Robin is a scheduling policy assigning cyclic ready-queue turns bounded by a quantum.

choices.label: C
choices.explanation: SJF is a scheduling policy selecting the shortest next burst among ready jobs.

choices.label: D
choices.explanation: BST is a data structure that can support queue operations rather than a CPU scheduling policy.

reviews.answer_text: HTTP is an application communication protocol.
reviews.hint: Separate filesystem formats from network application protocols.
reviews.explanation: OS36 explicitly names FAT32, NTFS and ext4 as filesystem formats and contrasts HTTP as an application communication protocol. Filesystems organize stored file content and metadata; a communication protocol does not become a filesystem merely because it transfers file contents. Therefore HTTP is the single option outside the stated filesystem-format category.

evidence.quote: FAT32, NTFS and ext4 are filesystem formats; HTTP is an application communication protocol.

choices.label: A
choices.explanation: FAT32 is explicitly identified as a filesystem format, making it a member of the requested category.

choices.label: B
choices.explanation: NTFS is explicitly identified as a filesystem format, not a communication-protocol exclusion.

choices.label: C
choices.explanation: ext4 is explicitly identified as a filesystem format in the complete study note.

choices.label: D
choices.explanation: HTTP is an application communication protocol rather than a filesystem format for organizing stored files.

reviews.answer_text: All four can be user-interface forms; no supported exclusion is supplied.
reviews.hint: Read whether the note treats interface examples as a closed list.

The question supplies no OS/version or scope that would exclude one. All substantive options are possible interface types, and there is no none-of-the-above alternative.

choices.label: D
choices.explanation: The note explicitly allows VR interfaces; the stem gives no product-specific restriction excluding them.

reviews.answer_text: Web browser.
reviews.hint: Distinguish core resource-management components from applications.
reviews.explanation: OS03 defines the kernel through core resource management, protection and system-call handling, while explicitly calling browsers applications. Scheduling, memory management and filesystem service are core resource-management functions in the textbook kernel sense. Some systems move services outside a kernel, but a web browser remains the clear application-level exclusion from the listed ordinary kernel responsibilities.

evidence.quote: The kernel implements core resource management, protection and system-call handling. A shell reads/interprets user commands; a GUI is another interface. Browsers, office tools and editors are applications.

choices.label: A
choices.explanation: Process scheduling is a core resource-management function in the textbook kernel model used here.

choices.label: B
choices.explanation: Memory management is a core resource-management function rather than the listed user application.

choices.label: C
choices.explanation: Filesystem service belongs to ordinary OS resource management in this textbook kernel-level comparison.

choices.label: D
choices.explanation: The note explicitly identifies browsers as applications rather than components implementing the kernel’s core role.

reviews.answer_text: Video editing is an application operation.
reviews.hint: Read generic protected-service categories versus user-task operations.
reviews.explanation: OS04 lists process control, file/device management, information retrieval and communication as service categories. Network communication falls within communication services, so it is not excluded merely because it uses sockets rather than local files. The category outside generic system calls is video editing.

choices.label: D
choices.explanation: Video editing is an application-level operation, not a standard generic system-call service category.

reviews.answer_text: Both macOS and Windows are proprietary products.
reviews.hint: Distinguish open-source components from an entire OS product.
reviews.explanation: OS40 explicitly identifies both Windows and macOS as proprietary products, while noting open-source components in macOS. Linux is an open-source kernel and Android’s AOSP base is open source, though shipped devices may include proprietary additions. Under the product-family interpretation, both C and D satisfy not open source; component availability does not make macOS as a whole an open-source product.

choices.label: D
