reviews.answer_text: Load the OS kernel into memory.
reviews.hint: Read the bootloader-to-kernel handoff.
reviews.explanation: OS03 places firmware/bootloader stages before transfer of control to a kernel loaded into RAM. This identifies loading the kernel as the bootloader purpose among the alternatives. Resource management is subsequently a kernel role, application management is a running-system function, and user interfaces are provided by shells/GUI components rather than defining the bootloader’s purpose.

evidence.quote: Firmware/bootloader stages execute before transferring control to a kernel loaded into RAM.

choices.label: A
choices.explanation: The bootloader prepares the kernel in memory and transfers control to it during the boot sequence.

choices.label: B
choices.explanation: Core hardware-resource management is the kernel’s role after the bootloader hands over control.

choices.label: C
choices.explanation: Managing running applications belongs to the operating system’s runtime services rather than defining the bootloader.

choices.label: D
choices.explanation: Shells and GUIs provide user interfaces; that is not the bootloader’s principal role here.

reviews.answer_text: Under strict terminology, none of the four is a deadlock-prevention algorithm.
reviews.hint: Distinguish prevention, avoidance, detection and unrelated search algorithms.
reviews.explanation: The source image confirms prevention, not the broader handling term. OS25 classifies Banker as avoidance, explicitly not prevention. OS23/OS26 describe wait-for/resource-allocation graphs for dependencies, detection and safety reasoning; OS24 defines prevention as breaking a necessary condition. Binary search trees are unrelated data structures. Consequently every option fails the literal prevention category, even though D is the likely intended broad-handling exclusion.

evidence.quote: Banker is avoidance, not CPU scheduling, detection or prevention by breaking a condition.
Prevention constrains how requests are made.
A binary search tree is a data structure that might implement a queue; it is not itself a CPU selection policy.

choices.label: A
choices.explanation: Banker is avoidance rather than strict deadlock prevention, so it satisfies the literal not-prevention wording.

choices.label: B
choices.explanation: Wait-for graph analysis detects dependency cycles rather than eliminating a necessary deadlock condition.

choices.label: C
choices.explanation: Ordinary resource-allocation graph analysis represents dependencies for detection/avoidance, rather than a specified condition-breaking prevention rule.

choices.label: D
choices.explanation: A binary search tree is a data structure, not a deadlock-prevention algorithm or deadlock-handling policy.

reviews.answer_text: Keyboard.
reviews.hint: Compare synchronization abstractions with physical input devices.
reviews.explanation: OS10 describes monitors as protected operations with condition synchronization, and OS11 explains mutex/semaphore exclusion mechanisms. These coordinate concurrent execution. A keyboard is an input device rather than such a coordination abstraction. Interrupts generated by hardware may participate in event handling, but that does not make the keyboard itself a mutex, semaphore or monitor mechanism.

evidence.quote: A barrier waits until a defined set of participants reaches a point; a monitor encapsulates protected operations with condition synchronization.
A binary semaphore represents one permit; a counting semaphore tracks several. A mutex normally has ownership rules that a general semaphore lacks.

choices.label: A
choices.explanation: A mutex provides owned mutual exclusion and is a synchronization mechanism in the note.

choices.label: B
choices.explanation: A semaphore coordinates participants through atomic wait and signal operations, so it is a synchronization mechanism.

choices.label: C
choices.explanation: A monitor combines protected operations and condition synchronization, making it a genuine synchronization abstraction.

choices.label: D
choices.explanation: A keyboard is a physical input device rather than a process/thread synchronization abstraction.

reviews.answer_text: HTTP requests can carry IPC; the list has no universal exclusion.
reviews.hint: Distinguish a communication protocol from the mechanism carrying it without assuming it cannot implement IPC.
reviews.explanation: OS09 names pipes, shared memory and message queues as IPC mechanisms, but also states that HTTP can carry interprocess communication. A narrow course taxonomy may separate application protocols from primitive OS mechanisms; the stem does not state that restriction. Therefore HTTP requests cannot be uniquely rejected as not IPC under the broad literal wording, and all four can support communication between processes.

evidence.quote: HTTP is an application protocol over a communication mechanism and can carry interprocess communication, so it is not universally “not IPC.”

choices.label: A
choices.explanation: Pipes provide streams between processes and are explicitly included in the note’s IPC mechanisms.

choices.label: B
choices.explanation: Shared memory lets processes access a common region and is explicitly an IPC mechanism.

choices.label: C
choices.explanation: Message queues preserve messages exchanged by processes and are explicitly an IPC mechanism.

choices.label: D
choices.explanation: HTTP is a higher-level protocol but can carry IPC; exclusion requires an unstated primitive-mechanism-only taxonomy.

reviews.answer_text: Infinite is not a scheduling-policy category.
reviews.hint: Read preemptive, non-preemptive and cooperative scheduling definitions.
reviews.explanation: OS14 distinguishes preemptive and non-preemptive scheduling and explains cooperative scheduling as relying on voluntary release. OS19 explicitly rejects Infinite as a standard scheduling-policy category. Thus the first three labels describe genuine scheduling approaches, whereas infinite does not identify a selection or preemption rule. It should not be confused with a possible unbounded waiting-time outcome.

evidence.quote: Cooperative describes relying on voluntary release.
“Infinite” is not a standard scheduling-policy category.

choices.label: A
choices.explanation: Preemptive scheduling can interrupt running work and return it to the ready state.

choices.label: B
choices.explanation: Non-preemptive scheduling retains a running burst until completion, blocking or voluntary release.

choices.label: C
choices.explanation: Cooperative scheduling is the recognized approach relying on voluntary release of execution.

choices.label: D
choices.explanation: Infinite names no scheduling selection or preemption policy in the provided note.

reviews.answer_text: Report performance and resource usage.

User-account administration, hardware allocation and application management are broader OS/administration functions, not the monitor’s defining reporting role. Observing a resource is distinct from allocating or increasing it.

That is exactly the complete description in D. Account, hardware and application management may occur within host or guest systems, but those broad administrative roles do not define why a virtual machine is provided.

An interrupt handler is privileged event-handling code in the conventional kernel context. Specify execution location or ask for multiple examples.

evidence.quote: Device drivers are commonly kernel components, although user-space drivers also exist.
Utilities such as antivirus and disk tools can combine user processes with privileged components.

choices.label: A
choices.explanation: Drivers are commonly kernel components, but the note explicitly allows user-space drivers in some architectures.

choices.label: B
choices.explanation: Antivirus software can include user processes and privileged components; its name alone does not fix execution mode.

choices.label: C
choices.explanation: Disk-management tools can likewise have user-process components, so antivirus is not the sole possible user program.

choices.label: D
choices.explanation: An interrupt handler belongs to the conventional privileged event-handling path rather than being the clear user-program example.

reviews.answer_text: Ignorance, the intentional ignoring/ostrich policy.
reviews.hint: Read which deadlock policy may be chosen when the problem is rare enough.
reviews.explanation: OS26 describes intentionally ignoring a sufficiently rare deadlock problem as the ostrich policy. This matches the stem’s rare and insignificant criterion, so Ignorance is the appropriate label. Recovery instead acts after detection, while waiting and presentation do not name this handling decision. The answer does not imply that real operating systems ignore every kind of deadlock.

evidence.quote: Ignoring a sufficiently rare problem is sometimes called the ostrich policy, but real systems still prevent or detect selected deadlocks.

choices.label: A
choices.explanation: Presentation is not a deadlock-handling policy described by the note; its literal wording does not fit.

choices.label: B
choices.explanation: Waiting is not the deliberate policy of accepting sufficiently rare deadlocks described by the stem.

choices.label: C
choices.explanation: Recovery actively resolves detected deadlocks rather than choosing to ignore the sufficiently rare problem.

choices.label: D
choices.explanation: Ignorance matches intentional ignoring, also called the ostrich policy for a sufficiently rare problem.

reviews.answer_text: Software versions and server implementation are needed to identify a non-threaded process.
reviews.hint: Read why application category names do not determine their threading model.
reviews.explanation: OS08 explicitly warns that browser and Excel names do not prove a version’s threading model. Server is even broader and specifies no implementation. Therefore none of A, B or C is verified as non-threaded, and D would require proving all three use multithreading. The missing concrete versions/program designs prevent a unique answer, even though multithreading is common in these categories.

evidence.quote: Application names such as browser or Excel do not prove a particular version’s threading model.

choices.label: A
choices.explanation: Excel’s version and implementation are unspecified, so its thread use cannot be established from the name alone.

choices.label: B
choices.explanation: A browser category does not specify which version or architecture uses threads or separate processes.

choices.label: C
choices.explanation: Server names a role, not an implementation; it could use different concurrency architectures.

choices.label: D
choices.explanation: None requires showing all three are multithreaded, which the absent versions and designs do not establish.

reviews.answer_text: None: modern OS families can support all three techniques.
reviews.hint: Read security capability support versus specific product configuration.
reviews.explanation: OS39 states that modern OS families can support cryptography, authentication and firewalls, while support/configuration depends on product. Therefore none of the three is categorically unsupported by modern operating systems. The answer is a capability-category statement, not a guarantee that every installation includes every feature or enables it by default. Each technique has a distinct security role.

evidence.quote: Modern OS families can support cryptography, authentication and firewalls, but support/configuration depends on product.

choices.label: A
choices.explanation: Cryptography is explicitly a capability that modern OS families can support, though configuration varies.

choices.label: B
choices.explanation: Authentication is explicitly supported as a modern OS capability for verifying identity.

choices.label: C
choices.explanation: Firewalls are explicitly within modern OS support capabilities, even though product and configuration matter.

choices.label: D
choices.explanation: All three techniques can be supported; none is categorically outside modern operating-system security capabilities.

reviews.answer_text: Modern hierarchical namespaces are common; the stem does not define whether it asks for the usual model or any supported structure.
reviews.hint: Read common directory presentation versus possible simpler structures.
reviews.explanation: OS37 says modern general-purpose systems commonly present hierarchical namespaces, supporting multilevel as the ordinary organization. It also warns that this does not prove every system excludes simpler arrangements. The stem asks used without a particular OS or a most-common criterion. Thus multilevel is the likely intended convention, while all requires a broader scope; neither interpretation is made exclusive by the wording.

evidence.quote: Modern general-purpose systems commonly present hierarchical namespaces, but a feature name alone does not prove that every system excludes simpler arrangements.

choices.label: A
choices.explanation: Multilevel is the common hierarchical organization, but common is stronger and more specific than the stem’s used wording.

choices.label: B
choices.explanation: All would require a broad existence interpretation; the note does not verify every listed structure for a specified system.

choices.label: C
choices.explanation: Two-level structures are defined, but no particular modern system or prevalence condition is supplied.

choices.label: D
choices.explanation: Single-level structures are defined and not universally excluded; the stem lacks the system and scope needed to decide.

reviews.answer_text: Several historical pairings can overlap; a reference taxonomy and dates are required.
reviews.hint: Read mechanism definitions separately from historical chronology.
reviews.explanation: OS02 defines mechanisms rather than assigning each exclusively to a generation, and OS40 warns that generation/function pairings require historical evidence. Introduced in, used in and became prominent in are different relations; batch, multiprogramming and real-time features can span eras. The stem gives no dated taxonomy or exclusivity criterion, so a unique wrongly coupled pair cannot be established from its broad era labels.

evidence.quote: “First widely used OS,” “first multitasking OS,” and generation/function pairings require a definition and historical evidence; UNIX was not the first system ever to multitask.

choices.label: A
choices.explanation: Multiprogramming is defined, but its second-generation pairing is not historically established in the provided note.

choices.label: B
choices.explanation: Real-time systems are defined, but the note supplies no evidence confirming or rejecting this fourth-generation pairing.

choices.label: C
choices.explanation: Single-user is an access classification; the note gives no historical first-generation pairing evidence.

choices.label: D
choices.explanation: Batch operation is defined, but no chronology establishes whether this third-generation coupling is wrong.

reviews.answer_text: Nonblocking receive.
reviews.hint: Read whether an operation waits for a message or returns promptly.
reviews.explanation: OS09 defines nonblocking operations as returning promptly with data, progress or a would-block result. Among the options, nonblocking receive therefore supplies the asynchronous/non-waiting behavior being contrasted. Blocking receive waits for a message, blocking send waits for its defined completion condition, and direct message concerns how endpoints are addressed rather than whether the call blocks.

evidence.quote: Nonblocking operations return promptly with data, progress or a would-block result.

choices.label: A
choices.explanation: Nonblocking receive returns promptly instead of waiting until a message arrives, matching this asynchronous contrast.

choices.label: B
choices.explanation: Blocking receive waits for a message rather than providing the non-waiting behavior requested.

choices.label: C
choices.explanation: Blocking send waits for its defined handoff or receipt condition rather than returning promptly.

choices.label: D
choices.explanation: Direct messaging describes endpoint addressing, not whether sending or receiving blocks.

reviews.answer_text: System throughput.
reviews.hint: Read completed work per unit time versus per-process delays.
reviews.explanation: OS13 defines throughput as completed jobs divided by elapsed time. Counting process completions per hour is exactly that rate. Waiting, turnaround and response are delays associated with an individual process or an average of such delays; they are not completion counts per hour. The stated measurement therefore identifies system throughput without any scheduling trace.

evidence.quote: Throughput=completed jobs/elapsed time; CPU utilization=busy time/elapsed time.

choices.label: A
choices.explanation: Waiting time measures ready-queue delay, not the number of processes completed in an hour.

choices.label: B
choices.explanation: Completed processes divided by hours elapsed is system throughput by the note’s definition.

choices.label: C
choices.explanation: Turnaround measures arrival-to-completion duration for a process rather than a system completion rate.

choices.label: D
choices.explanation: Response measures arrival-to-first-start delay, not the number of jobs finished per unit time.

reviews.answer_text: Fatal exit.
reviews.hint: Read fault termination versus a program choosing to exit after detecting an error.
reviews.explanation: OS07 explicitly identifies a reference to nonexistent/protected memory as a fatal fault. Here the OS terminates the process because of that fault, so this is involuntary fatal termination. It is not the program’s voluntary error exit, normal completion or a kill request by another ordinary process. The cause in the stem resolves the otherwise loose exit terminology.

evidence.quote: A reference to nonexistent/protected memory is a fatal fault, unlike an application deciding to exit after bad input.

choices.label: A
choices.explanation: Normal exit is voluntary completion, unlike OS-enforced termination for an invalid memory reference.

choices.label: B
choices.explanation: A program-detected error exit is voluntary; the stem specifies an unrecoverable memory-access fault.

choices.label: C
choices.explanation: The stated cause is a fault handled by the OS, not a kill request from another process.

choices.label: D
choices.explanation: The note explicitly classifies nonexistent-memory access as a fatal fault causing involuntary termination.

reviews.answer_text: Maximizing response time is the wrong optimization direction.
reviews.hint: Read which scheduling metrics should be minimized and which maximized.
reviews.explanation: OS13 says to minimize response, turnaround and waiting while maximizing useful throughput/utilization under the chosen objective. Thus maximum response time is the mismatched criterion: making first response later worsens responsiveness. The other alternatives name a standard metric or its conventional optimization direction. The question is about preferred direction, not whether response time itself is measurable.

evidence.quote: Minimize response/turnaround/waiting under the selected goal and maximize useful throughput/utilization.

choices.label: A
choices.explanation: CPU utilization is a standard scheduling metric measuring the fraction of elapsed time the CPU is busy.

choices.label: B
choices.explanation: Minimizing turnaround is the conventional goal for reducing arrival-to-completion delay.

choices.label: C
choices.explanation: Maximizing useful throughput is a conventional goal for increasing completed work per unit time.

choices.label: D
choices.explanation: Response delay should ordinarily be minimized; maximizing it reverses the responsiveness objective.

reviews.answer_text: Priority scheduling.
reviews.hint: Read how aging modifies waiting jobs’ effective priority.
reviews.explanation: OS17 describes aging as increasing waiting jobs’ effective priority to reduce indefinite postponement. That is a direct adjustment within a priority scheme and matches the stem exactly. RR rotates turns, SJN selects the shortest next burst, and SRTF selects the shortest remaining work. Those policies may be modified, but they are not the named priority-aging mechanism requested.

evidence.quote: Aging increases waiting jobs’ effective priority according to a rule, reducing indefinite postponement when the priority scheme and workload permit.

choices.label: A
choices.explanation: RR cycles ready jobs by quantum rather than defining aging through increasing priority.

choices.label: B
choices.explanation: SJN chooses shortest next bursts; aging refers specifically to adjusting the effective priority of waiting work.

choices.label: C
choices.explanation: Priority scheduling can raise a waiting task’s effective priority through aging to reduce starvation.

choices.label: D
choices.explanation: SRTF compares remaining bursts rather than increasing priority solely because a task has waited longer.

reviews.answer_text: Allocated resources cannot be forcibly withdrawn.
reviews.hint: Read the resource meaning of no-preemption rather than CPU time slicing.
reviews.explanation: OS22 defines no resource preemption as requiring voluntary release by the holder. C states that resources cannot be preempted while in use and therefore matches. A reverses the condition. B and D describe policies attacking hold-and-wait by limiting requests or requiring release; they are different from the no-preemption property itself.

evidence.quote: No resource preemption means release must be voluntary.

choices.label: A
choices.explanation: Permitting withdrawal and reassignment is resource preemption, directly reversing the condition requested.

choices.label: B
choices.explanation: Forbidding additional requests while holding resources attacks hold-and-wait rather than defining no-preemption.

choices.label: C
choices.explanation: The holder retains the resource until voluntary release, so it cannot simply be forcibly withdrawn.

choices.label: D
choices.explanation: Requiring release when blocked removes holding-while-waiting; it is not the no-preemption definition.

reviews.answer_text: Multiple execution is not itself a process-creation event.
reviews.hint: Read explicit creation triggers versus scheduling existing work.
reviews.explanation: OS07 lists initialization, user requests, service requests and a running process’s creation call as creation causes. B, C and D match that list. Multiple execution of processes describes work being run, not an explicit request or initialization event creating a new process. Existing processes can execute repeatedly without creating a child, so A is the unsupported creation trigger.

evidence.quote: Processes arise during initialization, user requests, service requests or a running process’s creation call.

choices.label: A
choices.explanation: Executing existing processes multiple times is not itself the explicit creation trigger identified by the note.

choices.label: B
choices.explanation: A running process’s creation system call is explicitly one of the listed process-creation causes.

choices.label: C
choices.explanation: System initialization is explicitly listed as a time when processes are created.

choices.label: D
choices.explanation: A user request to create a process is explicitly a valid process-creation cause.

reviews.answer_text: A is false as CPU scheduling; D also misstates request-check timing.
reviews.hint: Read the safety-test definition, then distinguish it from scheduling and detection.
reviews.explanation: OS25 defines Banker as avoidance rather than CPU scheduling, so A is false under that scheduling meaning. D says requests are considered before they occur, whereas the note checks a received request before granting it. B’s exact historical analogy and C’s extension-of-detection relationship remain unsupported secondary claims; verifying them would not remove the timing ambiguity. Because A itself does not specify CPU and D is imprecise, repair those meanings before asking for one false statement.

evidence.quote: Tentatively grant a request only if it is within Need and Available and the safety test succeeds. Unsafe does not mean already deadlocked. Banker is avoidance, not CPU scheduling, detection or prevention by breaking a condition.

choices.label: A
choices.explanation: False under CPU-scheduling meaning; the bare scheduling label is broader and should be narrowed in the question.

choices.label: B
choices.explanation: The historical customer/credit analogy is not established by the supplied course section.

choices.label: C
choices.explanation: The note distinguishes avoidance from detection but does not establish the asserted algorithm-extension relationship.

choices.label: D
choices.explanation: Requests are checked before being granted; before a request occurs is imprecise and can be read as another false claim.

reviews.answer_text: Linux kernel.
reviews.hint: Read Android’s base kernel layer versus its higher framework and applications.
reviews.explanation: OS40 directly states that Android’s base kernel layer is Linux and places framework and applications above it. Thus Linux Kernel is the lowest offered layer. A database is not identified as the kernel foundation in this model. The answer rests on Android’s architecture, not on a separate claim about Android’s current market share.

evidence.quote: Android’s base kernel layer is Linux; its framework and applications are higher layers.

choices.label: A
choices.explanation: Applications sit above the framework and kernel rather than forming Android’s base layer.

choices.label: B
choices.explanation: The application framework is explicitly a higher layer than the Linux kernel foundation.

choices.label: C
choices.explanation: A database is not the base kernel layer identified by the note’s Android architecture description.

choices.label: D
choices.explanation: The note explicitly names Linux as Android’s base kernel layer beneath framework and applications.

reviews.answer_text: Application development is not a core OS resource-management function.
reviews.hint: Read providing services to development tools versus developing applications.
reviews.explanation: OS01 explicitly distinguishes application-development tools using OS services from application development itself as a core OS function. Processes, files and communication resources are managed by the OS. Therefore D is the exclusion in the intended resource-management scope. Providing compilers, editors or development APIs does not mean the operating system itself performs application development as its defining resource function.

evidence.quote: Application development tools use OS services but application development itself is not a core resource-management function.

choices.label: A
choices.explanation: Managing execution/process resources belongs to the OS’s core resource-management responsibilities.

choices.label: B
choices.explanation: File and storage management are core OS services rather than the requested non-function.

choices.label: C
choices.explanation: Communication/network resource management belongs to the OS responsibilities described in the note.

choices.label: D
choices.explanation: The note explicitly separates developing applications from the OS functions used by development tools.

reviews.answer_text: Adapt to changing hardware configurations.
reviews.hint: Read maintainable evolution rather than virtualization, perfect compatibility or automatic updates.
reviews.explanation: OS01 defines ability to evolve as adding hardware support, features and repairs through maintainable interfaces/modules. Adaptation to hardware configurations is therefore the direct example. Running multiple guest OSs describes virtualization. Backward compatibility preserves supported behavior rather than guaranteeing every legacy binary, and automatic updating is not a defining property of all operating systems.

evidence.quote: Ability to evolve means adding hardware support, features and repairs through maintainable interfaces/modules.

choices.label: A
choices.explanation: Adding support for changing hardware is a direct example of maintainable OS evolution.

choices.label: B
choices.explanation: Supporting multiple guest operating systems describes virtualization rather than the definition of ability to evolve.

choices.label: C
choices.explanation: The absolute absence of compatibility issues is not guaranteed by evolution or supported backward compatibility.

choices.label: D
choices.explanation: Automatic updates may be provided, but the note explicitly rejects them as a defining property of every OS.

reviews.answer_text: Handle increasing workloads and resources.
reviews.hint: Compare scalability with portability and interface convenience.
reviews.explanation: OS01 directly defines scalability as handling greater workloads/resources. Running on different hardware platforms is portability, and providing an easy interface is convenience. Programming-language support does not itself establish either increasing capacity or workload handling. The wording in C matches the supplied definition without assuming scalability guarantees limitless growth or unchanged performance.

evidence.quote: Scalability means handling greater workload/resources; portability means adapting to other platforms.

choices.label: A
choices.explanation: Adapting to other hardware platforms is portability, explicitly distinguished from scalability.

choices.label: B
choices.explanation: Supporting programming languages does not define the ability to handle growing workload or resources.

choices.label: C
choices.explanation: Handling increasing workloads and resources directly matches the note’s definition of scalability.

choices.label: D
choices.explanation: A user-friendly interface concerns convenience rather than scaling capacity as demand grows.

reviews.answer_text: Automatic updates and patches can make software maintenance convenient.
reviews.hint: Read convenience as reducing administrative effort, not necessarily increasing execution speed.
reviews.explanation: OS01 defines convenience as making tasks easy and notes that updates help administration. Among the alternatives, offering automatic updates and patches directly reduces routine software-management effort. This is an example of a convenience feature, not a universal guarantee that every OS updates automatically. Development environments, speed optimization and appearance customization address different activities from installation/maintenance in the stem.

evidence.quote: Convenience means making tasks easy through consistent interfaces, files and device abstractions.
Updates and monitoring help administration, but automatic updates are not a defining property of every OS.

choices.label: A
choices.explanation: A development environment assists creating software rather than directly providing installation and maintenance convenience.

choices.label: B
choices.explanation: Automating updates and patches can reduce routine software-management work, though the feature is not universal.

choices.label: C
choices.explanation: Execution-speed optimization concerns performance, not the installation/maintenance convenience specifically requested.

choices.label: D
choices.explanation: Customizing GUI appearance changes presentation rather than automating software installation or maintenance tasks.

reviews.answer_text: The options omit fault tolerance’s defining continuation of service.
reviews.hint: Distinguish tolerating a specified fault from recovering after service fails.
reviews.explanation: OS01 defines fault tolerance as continuing correct service despite specified failures and distinguishes recovery as restoring service afterward. A describes quick recovery, not that continuation property. The other options concern concurrency, performance and security. None states the supplied definition, so selecting A would silently replace fault tolerance with recovery. A repaired option should explicitly describe continued correct service under the specified failures.

evidence.quote: Fault tolerance continues correct service despite specified failures; recovery restores service afterward.

choices.label: A
choices.explanation: This is the likely intended choice, but quick recovery is explicitly distinguished from continuing service despite a fault.

choices.label: B
choices.explanation: Handling simultaneous requests describes concurrency/capacity, not continued correct service under specified failures.

choices.label: C
choices.explanation: Optimizing intensive workloads describes performance rather than the fault-tolerance property.

choices.label: D
choices.explanation: A secure environment concerns protection rather than maintaining correct service through specified failures.

reviews.answer_text: Backward compatibility for supported legacy software.
reviews.hint: Read preserving supported older application behavior versus guaranteeing every old binary.
reviews.explanation: OS01 defines backward compatibility as preserving supported older application behavior. That is the software-compatibility aspect of evolution asked here. Preinstalled applications, execution speed and preference customization do not establish that older software’s supported behavior remains available. The answer must retain the support qualification; it does not promise all legacy binaries run without any compatibility issues.

evidence.quote: Backward compatibility preserves supported older application behavior; it is not a promise that every old binary works.

choices.label: A
choices.explanation: Preinstalling many applications does not establish compatibility with older applications or their supported behavior.

choices.label: B
choices.explanation: Backward compatibility preserves supported legacy behavior, directly matching the software-compatibility aspect of evolution.

choices.label: C
choices.explanation: Faster execution does not by itself preserve interfaces or behavior required by legacy software.

choices.label: D
choices.explanation: Customizing preferences changes configuration rather than establishing compatibility with older application behavior.

reviews.answer_text: Indefinite waiting alone is not the complete definition of deadlock.
reviews.hint: Read the closed dependency among blocked participants.
reviews.explanation: OS22 distinguishes deadlock from ordinary blocking and starvation. A describes indefinite waiting but omits that progress requires an event/resource only another blocked participant can supply. The remaining alternatives describe termination, concurrency or crashing, none of which defines deadlock. Thus A is a likely intended simplification, but the literal options do not supply a source-correct unique definition.

evidence.quote: A set is deadlocked when each member waits for an event/resource that only another blocked member can provide.

choices.label: A
choices.explanation: Indefinite waiting may occur in deadlock, but without the blocked dependency it can instead be starvation or external waiting.

choices.label: B
choices.explanation: Abrupt termination ends a process; it does not define a set of processes blocked on one another.

choices.label: C
choices.explanation: Concurrent execution is normal and does not by itself imply blocked resource dependencies.

choices.label: D
choices.explanation: An OS crash is not the definition of deadlock, which can affect processes while the OS continues running.

reviews.answer_text: Mutual exclusion, hold-and-wait, no-preemption and circular wait.
reviews.hint: Read the exact polarity of each necessary deadlock condition.
reviews.explanation: OS22 lists the four necessary conditions in the standard reusable-resource model. A preserves the exact set: exclusion, holding while requesting more, no forced resource withdrawal, and a wait cycle. B introduces preemption in place of no-preemption; C and D replace exclusion with inclusion. These are not harmless wording changes because they remove or reverse the relevant restrictions.

evidence.quote: Mutual exclusion allows at most one holder of a nonshareable resource. Hold-and-wait means retaining a resource while requesting another. No resource preemption means release must be voluntary. Circular wait forms a closed chain of such waits.

choices.label: A
choices.explanation: This option states all four standard necessary conditions with their correct meanings and polarity.

choices.label: B
choices.explanation: It substitutes preemption for no-preemption, reversing the required resource-withdrawal restriction.

choices.label: C
choices.explanation: It substitutes mutual inclusion for mutual exclusion, losing the nonshareable-resource condition.

choices.label: D
choices.explanation: It reverses both exclusion and no-preemption, so it is not the required condition set.

reviews.answer_text: At most one process holds the nonshareable resource at a time.
reviews.hint: Read mutual exclusion separately from hold-and-wait and indefinite postponement.
reviews.explanation: OS22 defines mutual exclusion as allowing at most one holder of a nonshareable resource. B states that one-at-a-time condition. A describes concurrent sharing, C describes holding while requesting another resource, and D describes indefinite waiting without establishing exclusivity. The definition concerns access safety, not a guarantee that every waiting process eventually obtains the resource.

evidence.quote: Mutual exclusion allows at most one holder of a nonshareable resource.

choices.label: A
choices.explanation: Simultaneous access by several processes contradicts the exclusive-holder condition for a nonshareable resource.

choices.label: B
choices.explanation: Only one process at a time may hold or use the nonshareable resource.

choices.label: C
choices.explanation: Retaining one resource while requesting another defines hold-and-wait rather than mutual exclusion.

choices.label: D
choices.explanation: Indefinite waiting describes a possible failure outcome and does not define exclusive resource possession.

reviews.answer_text: Retain a resource while waiting for another.
reviews.hint: Read simultaneous ownership and an outstanding resource request.
reviews.explanation: OS22 directly defines hold-and-wait as retaining a resource while requesting another. A contains both parts of that definition. Merely waiting indefinitely does not establish a retained allocation, simultaneous sharing contradicts exclusion, and one-at-a-time access describes mutual exclusion rather than a process holding one resource while requesting more.

evidence.quote: Hold-and-wait means retaining a resource while requesting another.

choices.label: A
choices.explanation: The process simultaneously retains an allocated resource and waits to acquire a further one.

choices.label: B
choices.explanation: Indefinite waiting does not establish that the process still holds another resource.

choices.label: C
choices.explanation: Simultaneous shared access is not the retained-allocation-plus-request condition defining hold-and-wait.

choices.label: D
choices.explanation: One process accessing a resource at a time defines mutual exclusion, not hold-and-wait.

reviews.answer_text: A resource may be forcibly taken from its holder.
reviews.hint: Read how prevention can attack the no-preemption condition.
reviews.explanation: OS22 defines no-preemption as voluntary release only, while OS24 permits safe withdrawal/restart as a way to attack that restriction. Preemption is the opposite permission: a resource can be forcibly reclaimed. D directly states it. The answer concerns resources that can safely be withdrawn, not a claim that every device or lock can be preempted without corruption.

evidence.quote: permit safe resource withdrawal/restart to attack no-preemption;

choices.label: A
choices.explanation: Holding one resource while waiting for another describes hold-and-wait rather than forced resource withdrawal.

choices.label: B
choices.explanation: Indefinite waiting is a possible outcome, not the permission to reclaim a held resource.

choices.label: C
choices.explanation: Concurrent sharing concerns resource shareability rather than withdrawing an existing allocation from its holder.

choices.label: D
choices.explanation: Forcibly taking a held resource is resource preemption, subject to safe withdrawal/restart support.

reviews.answer_text: A closed chain of resource waits.
reviews.hint: Read whether the dependency chain returns to its starting process.
reviews.explanation: OS22 defines circular wait as a closed chain of waits. D specifies that each process holds a resource requested by the next in a circular chain, which returns the dependency to the starting participant. C describes only one hold-and-wait relationship, which need not be cyclic. Indefinite waiting and simultaneous sharing likewise fail to establish a closed chain.

evidence.quote: Circular wait forms a closed chain of such waits.

choices.label: A
choices.explanation: Indefinite waiting does not identify a closed cycle of dependencies among resource holders.

choices.label: B
choices.explanation: Simultaneous resource sharing is not a chain of blocked requests and does not define circular wait.

choices.label: C
choices.explanation: One process holding while requesting another establishes hold-and-wait but not necessarily a cycle.

choices.label: D
choices.explanation: The circular chain of holdings and requests explicitly forms the required closed wait dependency.

reviews.answer_text: Acceptance can mean intentional ignoring, so no universally invalid handling method is listed.
reviews.hint: Read the ostrich policy alongside prevention, avoidance and recovery.
reviews.explanation: OS24–OS26 describe prevention, avoidance and detection/recovery as distinct approaches. OS26 also explicitly allows deadlock acceptance to mean intentional ignoring when the risk is judged sufficiently rare. Thus D cannot be rejected solely because acceptance is less active than the other methods. With no definition excluding the ignore policy, all four can describe handling choices and the not-method premise lacks a unique answer.

evidence.quote: “Deadlock acceptance” can mean intentional ignoring, not necessarily an invalid approach.

choices.label: A
choices.explanation: Avoidance checks that allocations remain safe and is an explicit deadlock-handling approach.

choices.label: B
choices.explanation: Detection followed by recovery is an explicit approach to identifying and resolving actual deadlocks.

choices.label: C
choices.explanation: Prevention constrains requests to remove a necessary condition and is an explicit handling approach.

choices.label: D
choices.explanation: Acceptance can mean the intentional ignore/ostrich policy; excluding it requires a narrower unstated taxonomy.

reviews.answer_text: A resource-allocation graph represents allocations/requests and can reveal circular wait.
reviews.hint: Read assignment/request edge directions and what cycles show.
reviews.explanation: OS23 defines assignment edges from resource instances to processes and request edges from processes to resources. This supports A as a representation of allocation and requests. Following the edges can also represent a circular wait, supporting C in the detection context. A cycle proves deadlock only in the single-instance model; with multiple instances it is insufficient. B omits processes and D concerns withdrawal rather than graph edges.

evidence.quote: In a resource-allocation graph, P→R is a request and an instance R→P is an assignment. Follow these directions to form waits. No cycle implies no deadlock; with one instance of every resource type, a cycle implies deadlock.

choices.label: A
choices.explanation: Assignment edges explicitly represent which process holds a resource instance, alongside request edges.

choices.label: B
choices.explanation: The graph relates processes and resource instances, rather than representing only dependencies between resources.

choices.label: C
choices.explanation: Following assignment and request edges can represent a circular wait; deadlock inference depends on resource-instance counts.

choices.label: D
choices.explanation: The stated edges represent requests and allocations, not a resource-preemption operation or permission.

reviews.answer_text: Banker’s algorithm, technically an avoidance policy.
reviews.hint: Read CPU scheduling versus safe resource-allocation decisions.
reviews.explanation: OS25 states that Banker grants requests only while preserving a safe state. That can prevent entry into a deadlocked state in the broad everyday sense used by can help prevent, although its technical category is avoidance rather than condition-breaking prevention. FCFS, RR and SJN are CPU scheduling policies and do not themselves test resource-allocation safety.

evidence.quote: Avoidance allows requests only if the resulting state remains safe. Banker requires maximum claims.

choices.label: A
choices.explanation: FCFS orders CPU bursts by arrival rather than testing maximum resource claims and safe allocations.

choices.label: B
choices.explanation: RR schedules CPU turns; time slicing does not establish safe allocation of locks or other resources.

choices.label: C
choices.explanation: SJN selects shortest next CPU bursts rather than performing a resource-state safety test.

choices.label: D
choices.explanation: Banker admits resource requests only when the resulting state is safe; its strict classification is avoidance.

reviews.answer_text: Ensure each granted request preserves a safe state.
reviews.hint: Read the Banker safety test rather than treating it as condition-breaking prevention.
reviews.explanation: OS25 defines the safety test using Need=Max−Allocation and grants only requests within Need and Available that keep the tentative state safe. That directly matches D. The stem misnames the technical category: Banker is avoidance, not prevention by breaking hold-and-wait. It also does not primarily guarantee fairness or detect and recover from an already deadlocked state.

evidence.quote: Tentatively grant a request only if it is within Need and Available and the safety test succeeds.

choices.label: A
choices.explanation: Banker does not require removing hold-and-wait; it checks whether tentative allocation remains safe.

choices.label: B
choices.explanation: Its safety criterion is not a guarantee of fair or equal allocation among processes.

choices.label: C
choices.explanation: Detection and recovery address actual deadlock, whereas Banker checks safety before granting a request.

choices.label: D
choices.explanation: Preserving a safe state after each grant is the purpose of the Banker avoidance test.

reviews.answer_text: Shortest Remaining Time First (SRTF).
reviews.hint: Distinguish next-burst length from remaining work after partial execution.
reviews.explanation: OS16 says SRTF reconsiders on arrivals and selects the shortest remaining work. This matches the estimated remaining-time criterion in the stem. SJN chooses the shortest next burst non-preemptively, while RR uses cyclic quanta and FCFS arrival order. The distinction matters after execution has begun: the originally shortest burst need not be the currently shortest remaining job.

evidence.quote: SRTF reconsiders on arrivals and selects the shortest remaining work; a shorter newcomer can preempt.

choices.label: A
choices.explanation: RR rotates bounded turns rather than selecting the job with the smallest estimated remaining execution.

choices.label: B
choices.explanation: FCFS follows arrival order rather than comparing estimated remaining CPU work.

choices.label: C
choices.explanation: Non-preemptive SJN compares next burst lengths when selecting, not continuously reconsidered remaining work.

choices.label: D
choices.explanation: SRTF explicitly selects the shortest remaining work and can preempt on a shorter arrival.

reviews.answer_text: D is the conventional proportional-share answer; A can be fair by arrival order for a finite queue.
reviews.hint: Define fairness, the participating entities and the workload before comparing allocation policies.
reviews.explanation: OS20 defines fair-share scheduling through stated weights and participant scope, making D the conventional proportional-entitlement answer. The stem does not define fairness that way. Under arrival-order fairness, FCFS serves a finite queue without later arrivals bypassing a waiting job; OS15 states that a finite burst with finitely many predecessors eventually starts. OS21 requires a workload and objective. Because those fairness definitions select different valid policies, the unqualified question cannot certify D uniquely.

evidence.quote: Fair-share scheduling allocates according to stated weights, potentially per user/group rather than per process.
A finite burst with finitely many jobs ahead eventually starts, but waiting can still be large.
State the workload and objective, apply the algorithm and compare measured results.

choices.label: A
choices.explanation: FCFS can be fair by arrival order and eventual service for finite bursts with finitely many predecessors.

choices.label: B
choices.explanation: SJN can indefinitely postpone long jobs under repeated short arrivals, so its rule supplies no general fairness guarantee.

choices.label: C
choices.explanation: Priority fairness depends on ranking and remedies such as aging; the bare policy name specifies no fairness criterion.

choices.label: D
choices.explanation: Fair-share is the intended policy for defined proportional entitlements, but the stem does not specify that fairness meaning.

reviews.answer_text: D names weighted fair-share; B also provides equal long-run turns for continuously ready equal-weight tasks.
reviews.hint: Specify whether shares apply equally per task or follow user/group weights, and state readiness assumptions.
reviews.explanation: OS20 assigns fair-share scheduling declared weights, potentially per user/group; D is the conventional named-policy answer. The stem instead leaves each task and fair share undefined. Under equal per-task entitlement with two continuously ready peers, OS18’s equal cyclic quanta give each half of long-run CPU service, so B also fits. RR need not implement unequal or user/group entitlements, but those are not stated. Define weights, entities and workload before selecting D alone or accepting B and D.

evidence.quote: Fair-share scheduling allocates according to stated weights, potentially per user/group rather than per process.
Proportional shares address that policy choice; fair need not mean equal.
RR serves a ready queue cyclically for at most quantum q per turn. Unfinished jobs return to the tail; completed/blocked jobs leave.

choices.label: A
choices.explanation: FCFS gives arrival-ordered bursts, not recurring CPU proportions for continuously competing tasks under declared share entitlements.

choices.label: B
choices.explanation: Equal cyclic quanta provide equal long-run service to continuously ready equal-weight tasks without priority bypass.

choices.label: C
choices.explanation: SJN can starve long work under repeated short arrivals rather than guarantee an ongoing CPU-share entitlement.

choices.label: D
choices.explanation: A defined fair-share policy implements its declared entitlements, but weights and participant scope are unstated here.

reviews.answer_text: Error exit, when the program detects an error and chooses to terminate.
reviews.hint: Read voluntary program exits versus imposed termination.
reviews.explanation: OS07 explicitly classifies program-detected error exits as voluntary. Being killed or terminated by another process is imposed, and a fatal unrecoverable fault is involuntary. The distinction is the termination decision’s origin, not whether the run succeeded: a program can voluntarily exit because its input is invalid or it detects another handled error.

evidence.quote: Normal completion and a program-detected error exit are voluntary; an unrecoverable fault or being killed is involuntary.

choices.label: A
choices.explanation: A program-detected error exit is a deliberate voluntary termination path, even though execution was unsuccessful.

choices.label: B
choices.explanation: Being killed by another process is imposed externally and is therefore involuntary.

choices.label: C
choices.explanation: Termination by another process is external rather than a voluntary exit chosen by the program.

choices.label: D
choices.explanation: A fatal unrecoverable fault causes involuntary termination rather than a deliberate program error exit.

reviews.answer_text: Critical section.
reviews.hint: Read protected code accessing shared state versus process lifecycle states.
reviews.explanation: OS10 defines a critical section as code accessing shared state that needs protection. The stem describes execution that may change shared data and therefore requires mutual exclusion, directly matching that definition. Deadlock and blocking are waiting states or failures, while termination means execution has ended. None identifies the protected shared-state code currently being executed.

evidence.quote: A critical section is code accessing shared state that needs protection, not the resource itself.

choices.label: A
choices.explanation: Deadlock involves blocked dependencies, whereas the stem describes protected code actively accessing shared data.

choices.label: B
choices.explanation: A terminated process has ended execution, contradicting the stem’s currently executing shared-data operation.

choices.label: C
choices.explanation: Code that accesses shared data and requires mutual exclusion is a critical section.

choices.label: D
choices.explanation: A blocked process cannot proceed pending an event; the stem instead identifies the code requiring protection.

reviews.answer_text: The normal MMU translation is logical to physical; the stem reverses it.
reviews.hint: Read translation direction before selecting an address-management component.
reviews.explanation: OS27 explicitly identifies this malformed physical-to-logical reversal. The image confirms the reversal is in the source, rather than merely extracted incorrectly. The supported ordinary operation is MMU logical/virtual-to-physical translation, not the requested inverse. None of the other options supplies a general inverse map either. A repaired stem should swap physical and logical, after which MMU would fit.

evidence.quote: An MMU translates logical to physical, not the reverse as one malformed bank stem says.

choices.label: A
choices.explanation: MMU performs the forward logical-to-physical translation, so it does not satisfy the literal reversed direction.

choices.label: B
choices.explanation: IRQ denotes interrupt signaling rather than an address-translation device implementing the requested inverse.

choices.label: C
choices.explanation: DMA transfers data between device and memory rather than mapping physical addresses back to process addresses.

choices.label: D
choices.explanation: Cache retains reusable contents or translations, not a general physical-to-logical inverse mapping device.

choices.label: E
choices.explanation: A relocation/base register participates in forward base-plus-offset translation rather than defining the requested inverse mapping.

reviews.answer_text: Execution times alone do not determine a submission-time maximum wait.
reviews.hint: Read the workload, arrival, policy and overhead assumptions needed for waiting bounds.
reviews.explanation: OS21 says maximum waiting at submission cannot be determined from burst times alone when future arrivals, priorities or overhead are unconstrained. The image confirms no extra workload conditions are supplied. SJF/SRTF/priority may postpone work indefinitely under continuing preferred arrivals; RR’s interval bound assumes n ready jobs and a quantum and is not a total lifetime waiting bound. The missing scheduling/workload parameters prevent selecting one option.

evidence.quote: Maximum waiting at submission is not determined from burst times alone if future arrivals, priorities or overhead are unconstrained.

choices.label: A
choices.explanation: A closed known ready set permits computation, but continued short arrivals can postpone a long SJF job.

choices.label: B
choices.explanation: SRTF waiting depends on future arrivals and preemptions, which execution lengths alone do not specify.

choices.label: C
choices.explanation: Priority waiting requires priority order, preemption rules and future higher-priority workload, none supplied here.

choices.label: D
choices.explanation: RR needs quantum and workload assumptions; its next-turn bound is not an unrestricted total waiting bound.

choices.label: E
choices.explanation: Knowing execution times alone is insufficient for every listed algorithm, so the aggregate claim does not follow.

reviews.answer_text: API/library and system calls are different interface layers.
reviews.hint: Read the application-facing wrapper versus the direct user/kernel boundary.
reviews.explanation: OS04 explicitly says a stem asking merely for the interface to OS services must distinguish the API from the direct kernel boundary. Applications often use API/library wrappers, which may issue system calls for protected services. The question names neither layer, so B and D remain plausible, with A describing a wrapper implementation. Assembly is not itself the general service-interface abstraction.

evidence.quote: Therefore a stem asking merely for the interface to OS services must distinguish the application API from the direct user/kernel boundary.

choices.label: A
choices.explanation: A library may provide wrappers through which applications request services; the stem does not specify the abstraction layer.

choices.label: B
choices.explanation: System calls are the direct protected-service boundary, which is one plausible intended interpretation.

choices.label: C
choices.explanation: Assembly instructions alone do not name the general OS-service API or system-call interface abstraction.

choices.label: D
choices.explanation: An API is the application-facing interface, another plausible reading of the unqualified service-interface wording.

reviews.answer_text: A process is an executing program instance with address space and resources.
reviews.hint: Read process identity rather than a particular application’s job.
reviews.explanation: OS05 defines a process as an executing instance of stored instructions with its address space/resources. It expressly rejects universal manage-applications or provide-interface purposes. A particular process may perform one of the listed jobs, but none states what a process generally is or its execution role. The fully answerable concept is absent from the alternatives.

evidence.quote: A program is stored instructions; a process is an executing instance with address space and resources.

choices.label: A
choices.explanation: Some processes administer accounts, but account management is not the general definition or purpose of a process.

choices.label: B
choices.explanation: Hardware management is an OS responsibility and not the universal role of every executing program instance.

choices.label: C
choices.explanation: The note explicitly rejects managing applications as a universal process purpose; processes execute individual program instances.

choices.label: D
choices.explanation: A UI process is one example, but many processes provide no user interface at all.

reviews.answer_text: A system call requests a protected kernel service.
reviews.hint: Read the purpose of the request mechanism versus examples of services.
reviews.explanation: OS04 defines a system call as requesting a protected kernel service such as process creation, file reading or socket opening. None of the four options states that purpose. Account, hardware or application administration can use system services, and a UI can request them, but these are particular uses rather than the general function of a system call. The requested concept is present in the note and absent from the choices.

evidence.quote: A system call requests a protected kernel service, such as creating a process, reading a file or opening a socket.

choices.label: A
choices.explanation: Account management is a possible service use, not the general purpose of the system-call mechanism.

choices.label: B
choices.explanation: Some services manipulate hardware resources, but a system call generally requests any protected kernel service.

choices.label: C
choices.explanation: Application management is a possible operation rather than the definition of why system calls exist.

choices.label: D
choices.explanation: A user interface may invoke syscalls, but providing the UI is not their general purpose.

reviews.answer_text: All four are OS-managed resources; no exclusion is offered.
reviews.hint: Read CPU, memory and device-resource management.
reviews.explanation: OS01 includes CPU, memory, devices and communications among OS resources. OS34 expressly identifies input devices and NICs as OS-managed hardware. Despite the truncated ending, the intended resource question is clear enough to solve: all listed items belong, so no not-managed option exists. The missing final word does not justify inventing a non-resource or choosing an unsupported unique key.

evidence.quote: Input/output/storage/NIC devices are OS-managed hardware; user accounts are identities.

choices.label: A
choices.explanation: CPU time is explicitly an OS-managed resource, so CPU is not the requested exclusion.

choices.label: B
choices.explanation: Memory allocation is explicitly within OS resource management rather than outside it.

choices.label: C
choices.explanation: A keyboard is an input device, and input devices are explicitly OS-managed hardware.

choices.label: D
choices.explanation: The note explicitly includes NIC devices among hardware resources managed by the OS.

reviews.answer_text: Kernel mode and supervisor mode both denote privileged execution.
reviews.hint: Read synonymous privileged-mode names.
reviews.explanation: OS03 says kernel mode has privileged operations and supervisor mode often means the same privileged mode. With no architecture that distinguishes those names, both A and C fit. User mode is restricted. Protected mode is not identified as a synonym for always executing with kernel privileges, so it cannot replace the two explicitly equivalent privileged-mode labels.

evidence.quote: Kernel mode has privileged operations; supervisor mode often means the same privileged mode, so offering both as exclusive answers is ambiguous.

choices.label: A
choices.explanation: Kernel mode is explicitly the privileged mode with access to protected operations.

choices.label: B
choices.explanation: User mode is the restricted execution mode rather than the privileged kernel-service mode.

choices.label: C
choices.explanation: Supervisor mode commonly names the same privileged mode, making it another valid offered answer.

choices.label: D
choices.explanation: The note does not define protected mode as the execution privilege synonymous with kernel/supervisor mode.

reviews.answer_text: Priority can cause preemption only under a specified preemptive policy.
reviews.hint: Read running-to-ready versus completion or blocking transitions.
reviews.explanation: OS06 maps running→ready to time-slice expiry or preemption and warns that bare priority causes this only when a preemptive policy chooses another process. Priority is therefore the likely intended option but insufficient as written. Completion terminates, and an I/O request blocks. Suspend waiting also fails to state ordinary ready eligibility. Specify a higher-priority arrival under preemptive scheduling to make A definite.

evidence.quote: A bare “priority” causes running→ready only if a preemptive policy chooses another process.

choices.label: A
choices.explanation: A higher-priority arrival can preempt, but only if the unspecified scheduling policy permits preemption.

choices.label: B
choices.explanation: Completion transitions to terminated rather than placing the process back in the ready state.

choices.label: C
choices.explanation: Suspended/waiting work is not ordinary CPU-ready work; this label does not state a running-to-ready event.

choices.label: D
choices.explanation: A blocking I/O request takes running work to waiting, not immediately to ready.

reviews.answer_text: A, B and C are all true basic paging/segmentation contrasts.
reviews.hint: Read unit size, fragmentation and translation-table differences.
reviews.explanation: OS31 explicitly contrasts fixed pages/page tables/internal waste with variable logical segments/segment tables/external fragmentation. Thus A, B and C each state a valid basic-model difference. D reverses the visibility relationship: segments reflect program structure, while ordinary paging is largely transparent. The question’s single-answer shape cannot make three true contrasts exclusive.

evidence.quote: Under the basic models, paging uses fixed units/page tables and can waste space internally; segmentation uses variable logical units/segment tables and can fragment externally.

choices.label: A
choices.explanation: Basic paging can waste space within a final frame, while variable-length segmentation can leave external holes.

choices.label: B
choices.explanation: Pages/frames have fixed size; logical segments may have different variable lengths.

choices.label: C
choices.explanation: Paging uses page tables, while segment translation uses segment-table entries with base and limit.

choices.label: D
choices.explanation: The note says the opposite: segments reflect program structure and ordinary pages are largely transparent.

reviews.answer_text: Resource management spans CPU/process, memory and device managers.
reviews.hint: Read the umbrella OS resource-management function.
reviews.explanation: OS41 explicitly identifies this options defect: CPU/memory/I/O management spans several managers, and the list lacks the umbrella resource-management answer. Device management covers I/O but not the full CPU/memory scope; process management covers CPU scheduling but not all three. File and security management also have narrower roles. The concept is answerable, but no offered category fully states it.

evidence.quote: CPU/memory/I/O management spans multiple managers, so a question listing only device/process/file/security management lacks an umbrella answer.

choices.label: A
choices.explanation: File management is narrower than the combined CPU, memory and I/O resource-management scope.

choices.label: B
choices.explanation: Device management addresses I/O devices but does not cover the full CPU and memory scope as stated.

choices.label: C
choices.explanation: Process management includes CPU allocation but is not the umbrella covering all named memory and device functions.

choices.label: D
choices.explanation: Security management controls protection rather than naming the combined allocation of CPU, memory and I/O resources.

reviews.answer_text: Waiting on a held resource alone is ordinary blocking; deadlock needs a closed blocked dependency.
reviews.hint: Read the deadlock definition and inspect what the actual source says.
reviews.explanation: The source image confirms only waiting for a resource owned by another process; it adds no cycle or claim that the holder cannot progress. OS22 distinguishes such waiting from deadlock. Deadlock is possible if a closed blocked dependency exists, while queuing may describe normal waiting but is not specified as a required structure. The literal description therefore does not uniquely select the marked deadlock option.

evidence.quote: Mere waiting for another holder is normal blocking; indefinite unfair delay can be starvation without a cycle of dependencies.

choices.label: A
choices.explanation: Deadlock requires additional closed blocked dependencies that neither the stem nor image establishes.

choices.label: B
choices.explanation: Ordinary resource waiting may be queued, but the stem does not specify a queue implementation.

choices.label: C
choices.explanation: Preemption is forced withdrawal/reassignment rather than the fact that a process is waiting on another holder.

choices.label: D
choices.explanation: Overloading describes excessive demand, which is not implied merely by a held-resource wait.

reviews.answer_text: Resource efficiency, convenience and protection are OS objectives without a stated ranking.
reviews.hint: Read OS objectives and the workload-independent limits of fastest execution claims.
reviews.explanation: OS01 describes resource allocation and convenience, while OS03 adds protection among kernel functions. Therefore several listed goals are legitimate; the stem supplies no design context that makes one the main objective. B is a broad conventional summary, but A and C cannot be rejected as OS goals. D also overstates performance if read as guaranteeing maximum speed for every program.

evidence.quote: An OS allocates CPU time, memory, storage, devices and communication resources, and provides services to programs.
Convenience means making tasks easy through consistent interfaces, files and device abstractions.

choices.label: A
choices.explanation: Providing usable interfaces is a convenience objective, though no ranking against resource management is supplied.

choices.label: B
choices.explanation: Efficient resource management is a core objective, but the stem provides no criterion making it uniquely primary.

choices.label: C
choices.explanation: Protection is a genuine kernel objective; the question gives no scope excluding it from consideration.

choices.label: D
choices.explanation: Performance can be an objective, but fastest execution for every program is not synonymous with OS efficiency.

reviews.answer_text: Kernel and device drivers both manage I/O at different abstraction levels.
reviews.hint: Read the core OS layer versus device-specific request translation.
reviews.explanation: OS34 expressly warns that a broad I/O-responsibility question can name both kernel and drivers. The kernel provides resource/service management, while drivers convert its requests into device-specific operations. The stem does not select an abstraction level, so both fit. Scheduling and filesystems have narrower related duties and do not name the general/device-specific pairing established by the note.

evidence.quote: A broad question can name both the kernel and drivers as responsible for I/O; specify the abstraction level.

choices.label: A
choices.explanation: The kernel owns core resource/service management, including I/O coordination at the OS level.

choices.label: B
choices.explanation: The scheduler selects runnable work rather than being the general device-operation management component requested.

choices.label: C
choices.explanation: A filesystem manages file-related I/O but is not the general component for all input and output devices.

choices.label: D
choices.explanation: Drivers translate OS I/O requests into device-specific operations, directly managing the hardware-facing layer.

reviews.answer_text: Provide translated, protected per-process address spaces.
reviews.hint: Distinguish virtual address spaces from adding RAM or hosting guest operating systems.
reviews.explanation: OS32 defines virtual memory as translated/protected address spaces with nonresident portions backed by storage. D is the option matching separate process memory spaces. A describes machine virtualization; B falsely adds physical RAM and C falsely removes all memory constraints. Isolation and translation are the supported purpose, with backing storage providing flexibility within finite resource limits.

evidence.quote: Virtual memory provides translated, protected address spaces and allows nonresident portions of a program to be backed by storage.

choices.label: A
choices.explanation: Running multiple guest OSs describes machine virtualization, explicitly distinguished from process virtual memory.

choices.label: B
choices.explanation: Virtual memory does not physically add RAM; it maps address spaces using existing RAM and backing storage.

choices.label: C
choices.explanation: The note explicitly retains capacity constraints; virtual memory does not make execution memory-unlimited.

choices.label: D
choices.explanation: Separate translated/protected process address spaces match the virtual-memory purpose described by the note.

reviews.answer_text: Synchronization coordinates conflicting shared-state accesses and execution ordering.
reviews.hint: Read correctness of shared access rather than guaranteed deadlock freedom or parallelism.
reviews.explanation: OS10 defines synchronization through protected critical sections, mutual exclusion, progress and bounded waiting, and notes that locking can itself introduce deadlock. None of the options states this core coordination purpose. IPC can require synchronization, but merely facilitating communication is not a complete primary definition; fair allocation and parallel execution likewise are not guarantees. A repaired choice should state safe/ordered shared-state access.

evidence.quote: A correct exclusion solution requires mutual exclusion, progress and bounded waiting under stated assumptions.
Shared memory lets processes access a common region and requires synchronization for conflicting updates.

choices.label: A
choices.explanation: Synchronization can itself introduce deadlock if locking order is inconsistent, so preventing all deadlock is not its definition.

choices.label: B
choices.explanation: Fair resource allocation is a scheduling policy objective rather than the primary shared-access coordination rule.

choices.label: C
choices.explanation: Synchronization may serialize conflicting accesses and does not itself provide parallel execution resources.

choices.label: D
choices.explanation: IPC may use synchronization, but facilitating communication omits the primary safe coordination of conflicting shared-state operations.

reviews.answer_text: An easy-to-use interface is the convenience example.
reviews.hint: Read convenience separately from efficiency and protection.
reviews.explanation: OS01 defines convenience as making tasks easy through consistent interfaces and abstractions. A directly exemplifies that user-facing goal, although a GUI is one possible interface rather than a universal requirement. B and C concern speed/resource efficiency, and D protection. Those are worthwhile OS objectives but do not match the convenience dimension specifically named in the stem.

evidence.quote: Convenience means making tasks easy through consistent interfaces, files and device abstractions.

choices.label: A
choices.explanation: An easy-to-use GUI is an example of making user tasks convenient through an interface.

choices.label: B
choices.explanation: Optimizing execution speed concerns performance rather than the user-facing convenience dimension requested.

choices.label: C
choices.explanation: Efficient allocation is a resource-use objective, distinguished from convenience in the note.

choices.label: D
choices.explanation: Security/protection is a separate OS objective rather than the interface-usability example of convenience.

reviews.answer_text: FCFS and non-preemptive SJN.
reviews.hint: Read the named policy’s preemption variant.
reviews.explanation: OS14 explicitly identifies FCFS and non-preemptive SJF/SJN as non-preemptive, while RR is preemptive. Priority can be either, so its bare name does not determine a variant. Therefore B and C are both directly valid conventional choices, and D would require an added non-preemptive qualifier. The single-answer wording cannot distinguish the two established non-preemptive policies.

evidence.quote: FCFS and non-preemptive SJF are non-preemptive; RR and SRTF are preemptive. Priority can be either, so its name alone cannot decide.

choices.label: A
choices.explanation: RR uses timer-bounded turns and is explicitly classified as preemptive.

choices.label: B
choices.explanation: FCFS ordinarily runs a burst until completion/blocking rather than forcibly preempting it.

choices.label: C
choices.explanation: SJN is the non-preemptive shortest-next-burst policy under the note’s naming convention.

choices.label: D
choices.explanation: Priority scheduling can be non-preemptive or preemptive; the option does not select a variant.

reviews.answer_text: Equal per-process turns, total CPU consumption and weighted fair shares are different claims.
reviews.hint: Read continuous-backlog assumptions and the definition of share entitlement.
reviews.explanation: OS18 says RR gives recurring opportunities rather than identical total CPU consumption for jobs of different lengths. OS20 says fair-share follows stated weights and fair need not mean equal. The stem gives neither continuous readiness nor an equal-weight policy, and every task could mean processes or users. RR is the usual equal-turn interpretation, but the absolute equal-share guarantee lacks the necessary scope.

evidence.quote: RR gives recurring opportunities, not identical total CPU consumption for jobs of different lengths.
Proportional shares address that policy choice; fair need not mean equal.

choices.label: A
choices.explanation: RR gives equal cyclic quanta to continuously ready peers, not equal lifetime CPU for every task.

choices.label: B
choices.explanation: FCFS serves arrival-ordered bursts whose lengths can differ, without enforcing equal shares.

choices.label: C
choices.explanation: SJN prioritizes shorter bursts and can postpone long ones rather than enforce equal allocation.

choices.label: D
choices.explanation: Fair-share can use equal weights but also unequal ones; the required weights and participant scope are absent.

reviews.answer_text: RR and finite FCFS can avoid starvation; the claimed guaranteed policy is undefined.
reviews.hint: Read the workload assumptions behind no-indefinite-postponement guarantees.
reviews.explanation: OS20 explicitly warns that guaranteed scheduling needs an actual guarantee and assumptions, and finite FCFS/RR can also avoid indefinite postponement. Thus D’s name does not establish an exclusive property. RR needs no bypass and finite turns; FCFS needs finitely many finite jobs ahead. SJN can starve long work under repeated short arrivals. The stem leaves the workload and guarantee model unspecified.

evidence.quote: Any “guaranteed scheduling” answer needs the actual guarantee and assumptions; finite FCFS and RR can also avoid indefinite postponement.

choices.label: A
choices.explanation: RR grants recurring turns under finite-ready-work/no-bypass assumptions, which the stem does not state.

choices.label: B
choices.explanation: A finite FCFS job with finitely many finite bursts ahead eventually runs, so D is not exclusive.

choices.label: C
choices.explanation: Repeated short arrivals can indefinitely postpone a long SJN job, so no general guarantee follows.

choices.label: D
choices.explanation: The label Guaranteed Scheduling specifies neither an actual algorithm nor the assumptions of its claimed guarantee.

reviews.answer_text: Both SJN and fixed-priority scheduling can starve work.
reviews.hint: Read repeated short arrivals and continued high-priority load.
