reviews.explanation: OS17 explicitly says fixed-priority scheduling can starve low-priority jobs and SJF can starve long jobs. SJN names the non-preemptive SJF policy in OS16. Both C and D therefore meet prone to starvation under appropriate sustained arrivals. RR and finite FCFS have recurring-turn/eventual-start properties under the stated ordinary assumptions, rather than the preference-based starvation mechanisms here.

evidence.quote: Fixed-priority scheduling can starve low-priority jobs under continued high-priority load. SJF can also starve long jobs, so a single-choice question offering both as starvation-prone has multiple answers.

choices.label: A
choices.explanation: Ordinary RR cycles ready jobs without the continual short-job or high-priority bypass causing these starvation examples.

choices.label: B
choices.explanation: Finite FCFS work with finitely many finite predecessors eventually starts rather than being bypassed by new preferred jobs.

choices.label: C
choices.explanation: Repeated short arrivals can keep a long SJN job waiting indefinitely.

choices.label: D
choices.explanation: Continued high-priority arrivals can indefinitely postpone a low-priority job under fixed-priority scheduling.

reviews.answer_text: Optimality needs a workload and policy assumptions.
reviews.hint: Read the simultaneous-ready-set SJF theorem and SRTF’s arrival behavior.
reviews.explanation: OS16 restricts the familiar SJF minimum-average-waiting theorem to a fixed simultaneous ready set with known bursts and no switch cost; it is not a workload-independent comparison against every preemptive policy. The question omits arrival assumptions and overhead while offering both SJN and SRTF. C is the conventional theorem answer under its assumptions; D can improve waiting when short jobs arrive during a long running burst.

evidence.quote: SJF minimizes average waiting for the usual fixed simultaneous ready set with known bursts and no preemption/switch cost; that theorem is not a workload-independent comparison against every preemptive policy.

choices.label: A
choices.explanation: RR’s average depends on bursts, arrivals and quantum; no universal optimum or exclusion follows without a workload.

choices.label: B
choices.explanation: FCFS can tie an optimum when arrival order already matches suitable burst order, so workload matters.

choices.label: C
choices.explanation: SJN is optimal for the fixed simultaneous known-burst set under the note’s stated no-cost assumptions.

choices.label: D
choices.explanation: SRTF can outperform non-preemptive SJN with later short arrivals; the question omits the arrival model.

reviews.answer_text: B is definitely preemptive; D also qualifies when priority scheduling uses its preemptive variant.
reviews.hint: Read the preemption rules of each scheduling policy and identify which variant of priority is intended.
reviews.explanation: OS14 explicitly classifies RR as preemptive and FCFS/non-preemptive SJN as non-preemptive. It also says priority can be either variant. The stem asks which algorithm is preemptive, rather than which bare name necessarily denotes preemption under every variant. B is therefore the conventional definite example, but D is also valid under ordinary preemptive priority scheduling. Specify the priority variant or ask for the necessarily preemptive policy before selecting B uniquely.

evidence.quote: FCFS and non-preemptive SJF are non-preemptive; RR and SRTF are preemptive. Priority can be either, so its name alone cannot decide.

choices.label: A
choices.explanation: FCFS is ordinarily non-preemptive in the supplied model and does not end a burst merely for another arrival.

choices.label: B
choices.explanation: RR preempts an unfinished running turn at the quantum boundary, so it is a definite preemptive example.

choices.label: C
choices.explanation: SJN denotes the non-preemptive shortest-next-burst policy; its preemptive counterpart is SRTF.

choices.label: D
choices.explanation: Priority scheduling can preempt for a higher-priority arrival, but it can also use a non-preemptive variant.

reviews.answer_text: SJN and fixed-priority scheduling can both cause starvation.
reviews.hint: Read starvation from continual preference for short or high-priority arrivals.
reviews.explanation: OS16 describes long-job starvation under repeated short arrivals, and OS17 describes low-priority starvation under continued high-priority load. Hence C and D both satisfy can result in starvation. The loose if not implemented properly phrase does not make every imagined broken implementation a meaningful algorithm property; the answer uses starvation mechanisms inherent in the standard policies under the stated workloads.

evidence.quote: Repeated short arrivals can starve a long job.
Fixed-priority scheduling can starve low-priority jobs under continued high-priority load.

choices.label: A
choices.explanation: Ordinary finite FCFS does not let newly arriving jobs repeatedly bypass a waiting job with finite predecessors.

choices.label: B
choices.explanation: Ordinary RR supplies recurring turns rather than preference-based indefinite bypass under the standard assumptions.

choices.label: C
choices.explanation: SJN can repeatedly favor new short bursts and postpone an older long job indefinitely.

choices.label: D
choices.explanation: Without effective aging or another remedy, fixed priority can keep low-priority work waiting indefinitely.

reviews.answer_text: A workload and scheduling parameters are required to compare average turnaround.
reviews.hint: Read turnaround calculations on a concrete arrival/burst timeline.
reviews.explanation: OS21 explicitly says highest average turnaround requires a concrete workload and rejects memorizing FCFS as an absolute worst. The question provides no arrivals, bursts, RR quantum, priority assignments or overhead. Different data can change the ranking or produce ties. The missing workload prevents calculating any of the four policy averages, so no uniquely highest algorithm can be established.

evidence.quote: “Highest average turnaround” requires a concrete workload; do not memorize FCFS as an absolute.

choices.label: A
choices.explanation: FCFS can suffer convoy delays, but it is not universally the highest-turnaround policy for every workload.

choices.label: B
choices.explanation: RR turnaround depends on arrivals, bursts, quantum and switch costs, none supplied here.

choices.label: C
choices.explanation: SJN performance depends on the ready-set/arrival model and cannot be ranked highest without the data.

choices.label: D
choices.explanation: Priority averages require priorities and preemption rules as well as the workload, all missing.

reviews.answer_text: Threads need not execute sequentially, and independent processes can exist.
reviews.hint: Read shared process resources and concurrency mapping assumptions.
reviews.explanation: OS08 explicitly rejects mandatory sequential thread execution and says independent processes can exist, making B and C false. D can hold in one-to-one/many-to-many mappings, though not every many-to-one blocking kernel call permits it. A’s children language needs an API interpretation, but does not negate the two directly contradicted statements. The review preserves those model qualifications rather than assuming every thread model behaves identically.

evidence.quote: Threads are not a group of processes and need not execute sequentially. Independent processes can exist; cooperating ones communicate/share data.

choices.label: A
choices.explanation: Processes can create processes and threads can create threads, but children is an API-specific relationship not fully defined here.

choices.label: B
choices.explanation: The note explicitly says threads need not execute sequentially; they can be interleaved or run in parallel.

choices.label: C
choices.explanation: The note explicitly permits independent processes, contradicting the claim that all are dependent.

choices.label: D
choices.explanation: Another thread can run in suitable kernel mappings, but a many-to-one blocking kernel call may block all.

reviews.answer_text: A and C reverse the single-user/multiuser access definitions.
reviews.hint: Read concurrent users separately from concurrent applications or database clients.
reviews.explanation: OS02 defines single-user/multiuser by concurrent user access, not application count. A falsely allows many simultaneous users in a single-user system, and C falsely restricts a multiuser system to one user. B can describe concurrent application/database access by one user, so it is not contradicted merely by single-user status. D states the normal multiuser capability.

evidence.quote: Single-user and multiuser describe concurrent user access, not the number of applications.

choices.label: A
choices.explanation: Many users logging in simultaneously contradicts the single-user concurrent-access classification.

choices.label: B
choices.explanation: A single user can run several applications or accesses; database concurrency is not excluded by the user-count definition.

choices.label: C
choices.explanation: At most one concurrent user reverses the defining multiuser capability.

choices.label: D
choices.explanation: Concurrent access by several users is the multiuser capability and is therefore a correct statement.

reviews.answer_text: Allocate the CPU to a process.
reviews.hint: Read CPU/process management versus device and memory managers.
reviews.explanation: OS06 assigns selection of ready work to the short-term scheduler, matching processor allocation under process management. D names that precise role. A belongs to device management, C to memory management, and B is a broad deallocation statement spanning resource managers rather than a uniquely process-management function. The specific CPU allocation choice best matches the requested category.

evidence.quote: Long-term scheduling admits jobs; medium-term scheduling suspends/swaps them; short-term scheduling selects ready work.

choices.label: A
choices.explanation: Allocating a device belongs to device management rather than the specific CPU/process function requested.

choices.label: B
choices.explanation: Process termination may deallocate resources, but this generic statement spans several managers rather than uniquely identifying process management.

choices.label: C
choices.explanation: Allocating memory is the memory manager’s specific role rather than the CPU scheduling function.

choices.label: D
choices.explanation: Selecting a process to receive the CPU is the process-management/scheduling role explicitly described.

reviews.answer_text: Act as the service/resource intermediary between users/programs and hardware.
reviews.hint: Read resource services and consistent user-facing abstractions.
reviews.explanation: OS01 describes the OS allocating hardware resources and providing program services, with convenient interfaces and abstractions. D captures that intermediary role. Internet connectivity and document creation are narrower tasks, and hardware design is not a runtime OS service. The answer combines convenience and resource control rather than reducing the OS to one application or device function.

evidence.quote: An OS allocates CPU time, memory, storage, devices and communication resources, and provides services to programs.

choices.label: A
choices.explanation: Internet access is one supported communication activity rather than the general purpose of an operating system.

choices.label: B
choices.explanation: Document and spreadsheet creation are application tasks that use OS services rather than define the OS.

choices.label: C
choices.explanation: Designing hardware is not the runtime resource/service function described for an operating system.

choices.label: D
choices.explanation: The OS provides interfaces and controlled resource services linking users/programs to the underlying hardware.

reviews.answer_text: Plug-and-play functionality.
reviews.hint: Read automatic discovery and configuration of compatible hardware.
reviews.explanation: OS34 defines plug-and-play as discovering/configuring compatible new hardware, which directly matches automatic printer setup. A driver may still be needed, so automatic configuration does not imply driver-free operation. Manual driver installation and hardware management contradict the scenario’s automatic action. Resource allocation may occur during setup but is broader than the specific feature named.

evidence.quote: Plug-and-play discovers/configures compatible new hardware but may still require a driver.

choices.label: A
choices.explanation: Automatic detection and configuration of the printer is the note’s plug-and-play behavior.

choices.label: B
choices.explanation: The stem specifies automatic setup, not user-performed manual installation of a driver.

choices.label: C
choices.explanation: Manual hardware management does not match the automatic discovery/configuration described in the scenario.

choices.label: D
choices.explanation: Allocation can be part of setup, but it does not specifically name automatic device discovery/configuration.

reviews.answer_text: No preemption.
reviews.hint: Read voluntary resource release rather than priority-based CPU scheduling.
reviews.explanation: OS22 defines no resource preemption as voluntary release by the current holder. The stem repeats that resources cannot be forcibly taken, giving a direct match. Holding while requesting another resource, one-at-a-time ownership and a closed chain of waits are separate conditions and do not by themselves express the withdrawal restriction.

evidence.quote: No resource preemption means release must be voluntary.

choices.label: A
choices.explanation: The holder must release voluntarily, so the system cannot forcibly preempt the resource.

choices.label: B
choices.explanation: Hold-and-wait concerns retaining one resource while requesting another rather than whether withdrawal is allowed.

choices.label: C
choices.explanation: Mutual exclusion limits simultaneous ownership, not whether allocated resources can be forcibly reclaimed.

choices.label: D
choices.explanation: Circular wait concerns a closed dependency chain, not the resource-release rule specified here.

reviews.answer_text: Time-sharing and scheduling distribute CPU service among users/processes.
reviews.hint: Read interactive scheduling and the difference between fairness and equal resource consumption.
reviews.explanation: OS02 describes time-sharing as rapid scheduling/preemption supporting interactive users. OS20 explains that fair allocation needs a share policy and may operate per user/group. C describes those relevant mechanisms rather than disabling services or requiring manual intervention. Its fairly should be understood under a specified policy, not as an automatic equality guarantee from time-sharing alone.

evidence.quote: Time-sharing uses rapid scheduling/preemption to support interactive users.
Fair-share scheduling allocates according to stated weights, potentially per user/group rather than per process.

choices.label: A
choices.explanation: Restricting access to one user contradicts the multiuser setting rather than explaining its efficient sharing.

choices.label: B
choices.explanation: Disabling every background service is neither required nor the time-sharing/resource-allocation mechanism described.

choices.label: C
choices.explanation: Scheduling/time-sharing interleave useful work and can allocate service according to the system’s fairness policy.

choices.label: D
choices.explanation: Manual intervention for each task adds administration rather than explaining efficient automatic CPU allocation.

reviews.answer_text: Manage resources and provide interfaces/services.
reviews.hint: Read the OS’s combined resource-management and interface roles.
reviews.explanation: OS01 defines both allocation of CPU/memory/storage/devices/communications and services to programs, while describing convenient interfaces. B combines those core responsibilities. Running applications only, providing connectivity only or permanently storing files each captures a narrower task and omits the overall system-management role. The primary role is therefore the resource/interface combination, not a single service.

evidence.quote: An OS allocates CPU time, memory, storage, devices and communication resources, and provides services to programs.

choices.label: A
choices.explanation: Application execution is supported, but only excludes the OS’s other essential resource and service duties.

choices.label: B
choices.explanation: Resource management plus user/program interfaces matches the combined OS role defined by the note.

choices.label: C
choices.explanation: Internet connectivity is one communication service rather than the complete primary OS role.

choices.label: D
choices.explanation: Permanent file storage is a storage-device/filesystem service and not the complete operating-system purpose.

reviews.answer_text: Batch system.
reviews.hint: Read interaction after job submission.
reviews.explanation: OS02 defines batch jobs as running with little interaction after submission. That matches processing submitted similar jobs without user interaction during execution. Time-sharing targets interactive users, real-time targets timing correctness, and single-user classifies concurrent access rather than job interaction. The job-processing clue therefore selects batch rather than a user-count or deadline category.

evidence.quote: Batch jobs run with little interaction after submission.

choices.label: A
choices.explanation: Real-time classification concerns meeting deadlines rather than the absence of user interaction during submitted job processing.

choices.label: B
choices.explanation: Time-sharing supports interactive users through rapid scheduling, unlike the noninteractive batch description.

choices.label: C
choices.explanation: Batch processing runs submitted jobs with little interaction, directly matching the scenario.

choices.label: D
choices.explanation: Single-user describes concurrent user access, not whether a workload is submitted and processed as batches.

reviews.answer_text: The saved next-instruction position for resuming the process.
reviews.hint: Read the saved PC separately from scheduling, accounting and open-resource fields.
reviews.explanation: OS05 says the PCB records PC/registers alongside scheduling, memory/accounting and I/O information, and a saved PC identifies where execution resumes. Thus B describes its specific field role. Priority, CPU usage and open files can be other PCB information, but they are not the program-counter value. The question requires distinguishing fields within one record rather than excluding them from the PCB entirely.

evidence.quote: A saved PC identifies where execution resumes.

choices.label: A
choices.explanation: Priority is scheduling information in the PCB, not the saved next-instruction position held by PC.

choices.label: B
choices.explanation: The saved PC records the instruction position at which the process will resume execution.

choices.label: C
choices.explanation: CPU time consumed is accounting information rather than the program-counter address.

choices.label: D
choices.explanation: Open files belong to I/O/open-resource state, not to the saved instruction-pointer field.

reviews.answer_text: Waiting/blocked.
reviews.hint: Read readiness for CPU versus inability to proceed until an event.
reviews.explanation: OS06 defines waiting/blocked as unable to proceed until an event and maps blocking I/O from running to waiting. Therefore a process waiting for I/O completion is in Waiting. It is not ready while the event prevents progress, not running during the wait, and not terminated merely because its request is outstanding. Completion normally makes it ready afterward.

evidence.quote: Waiting/blocked means unable to proceed until an event; terminated means execution has ended.

choices.label: A
choices.explanation: Ready means eligible for CPU immediately; the outstanding blocking I/O prevents that eligibility.

choices.label: B
choices.explanation: Running means currently using a CPU, unlike the blocked interval awaiting I/O completion.

choices.label: C
choices.explanation: Waiting/blocked is the state for a process that cannot proceed until its I/O event completes.

choices.label: D
choices.explanation: Terminated means execution has ended, not temporarily paused pending completion of an I/O request.

reviews.answer_text: Save one execution context and restore another.
reviews.hint: Read context switching versus privilege changes or process termination.
reviews.explanation: OS05 directly defines a context switch as saving one execution context and restoring another, with overhead interrupting useful application work. B matches. A process may later resume, so switching does not permanently stop or kill it. Allocating memory is another management operation, and a privilege transition alone need not switch processes.

evidence.quote: A context switch saves one execution context and restores another; useful application work is interrupted by this overhead.

choices.label: A
choices.explanation: The outgoing process can resume later; permanent stopping is termination rather than context switching.

choices.label: B
choices.explanation: Saving current state and restoring the selected execution context is the defined context-switch purpose.

choices.label: C
choices.explanation: Memory allocation changes resource assignment, not the saved/restored execution context defining a switch.

choices.label: D
choices.explanation: A context switch need not terminate any process, regardless of priority.

reviews.answer_text: Short-term (CPU) scheduler.
reviews.hint: Read admission, suspension and ready-queue selection as distinct scheduler roles.
reviews.explanation: OS06 assigns admission to the long-term scheduler, suspension/swapping to the medium-term scheduler and ready-work selection to the short-term scheduler. The question specifically asks which ready process receives the CPU next, so C is exact. The dispatcher then performs the handoff; that is distinct from selecting the ready process. Device request ordering is not CPU ready-queue selection.

evidence.quote: Long-term scheduling admits jobs; medium-term scheduling suspends/swaps them; short-term scheduling selects ready work.

choices.label: A
choices.explanation: The long-term scheduler admits jobs rather than making each immediate ready-queue CPU selection.

choices.label: B
choices.explanation: The medium-term scheduler suspends/swaps work rather than choosing the next CPU-ready process.

choices.label: C
choices.explanation: The short-term CPU scheduler selects the next eligible process from ready work.

choices.label: D
choices.explanation: An I/O scheduler orders device work rather than selecting the next process for the CPU.

reviews.answer_text: Suspend/swap processes between resident and backing-store states.
reviews.hint: Read medium-term scheduling separately from admission and dispatch.
reviews.explanation: OS06 explicitly assigns suspension/swapping to the medium-term scheduler. OS27 distinguishes traditional whole-process swapping to backing storage from page movement. Thus C is the matching memory/load-control role. Admitting jobs belongs to long-term scheduling, picking the next ready process to short-term scheduling, and servicing drivers to device-management paths.

evidence.quote: medium-term scheduling suspends/swaps them; short-term scheduling selects ready work.

choices.label: A
choices.explanation: Deciding admission into the system is the long-term scheduler’s role in the supplied model.

choices.label: B
choices.explanation: Selecting the next CPU process belongs to the short-term scheduler, not the medium-term one.

choices.label: C
choices.explanation: Medium-term scheduling suspends/swaps processes to control resident load and memory use.

choices.label: D
choices.explanation: Device-driver requests concern I/O service rather than the scheduler’s suspension/swapping function.

reviews.answer_text: Uncoordinated conflicting shared accesses make results depend on interleaving.
reviews.hint: Read conflicting updates rather than merely simultaneous execution.
reviews.explanation: OS10 defines a race by results depending on uncoordinated interleaving of conflicting accesses. B is the intended match, with shared access understood to include a conflict such as an update; simultaneous read-only access alone is insufficient. Coincident completion, ordinary priority selection and preemption do not by themselves establish a shared-state race.

evidence.quote: A race occurs when results depend on uncoordinated interleaving of conflicting accesses.

choices.label: A
choices.explanation: Two completions at the same time need not involve conflicting shared accesses or interleaving-dependent results.

choices.label: B
choices.explanation: Unsynchronized conflicting shared accesses can make results depend on execution interleaving, which is the race condition.

choices.label: C
choices.explanation: Priority order alone is a scheduling choice and does not establish a conflicting shared-data race.

choices.label: D
choices.explanation: Preemption can expose a race but is not itself sufficient without conflicting unprotected accesses.

reviews.answer_text: Preemption is not a necessary condition; no-preemption is.
reviews.hint: Read the exact polarity of the resource-withdrawal condition.
reviews.explanation: OS22 names mutual exclusion, hold-and-wait, no resource preemption and circular wait as the necessary set. The option Preemption reverses one of those conditions. Therefore C is the exception, while the other three are genuine members. This resource-preemption rule is separate from whether CPU scheduling uses timer preemption.

evidence.quote: No resource preemption means release must be voluntary. Circular wait forms a closed chain of such waits.

choices.label: A
choices.explanation: Mutual exclusion is explicitly one of the four necessary conditions in the standard resource model.

choices.label: B
choices.explanation: Hold-and-wait is explicitly necessary: a process retains a resource while requesting another.

choices.label: C
choices.explanation: The required condition is no-preemption; permitting preemption is not one of the necessary conditions.

choices.label: D
choices.explanation: Circular wait is explicitly a required closed dependency chain in the standard model.

reviews.answer_text: 17 ms.
reviews.hint: Read OS13 and OS15. Draw the FCFS time line, compute each ready-queue waiting time, and average those waits rather than the completion times.
reviews.explanation: FCFS runs P1 from 0 to 24 ms, P2 from 24 to 27 ms, and P3 from 27 to 30 ms. Because every process arrives at 0, their waiting times are 0, 24 and 27 ms. The average is (0+24+27)/3 = 51/3 = 17 ms, so C is correct. The average turnaround is a different quantity: (24+27+30)/3 = 27 ms.

evidence.quote: All ready at time 0, tie order P1=24,P2=3,P3=3: schedule 0–24 P1,24–27 P2,27–30 P3.
Waiting times 0,24,27 average to 17.

choices.label: A
choices.explanation: 3 ms is the burst time of P2 or P3, not the average ready-queue wait.

choices.label: B
choices.explanation: The three waits total 51 ms, so dividing by three cannot give 9 ms.

choices.label: C
choices.explanation: The waits 0, 24 and 27 ms average to 17 ms.

choices.label: D
choices.explanation: 27 ms is the average turnaround time in this example, not the average waiting time.

question_revision.original_stem: In the FCFS scheduling algorithm, if processes P1(24ms), P2(3ms), P3(3ms) arrive in order P1, P2, P3, what is the average waiting time?
question_revision.stem: All three processes arrive at time 0 and are ready immediately. Their CPU burst times are P1 = 24 ms, P2 = 3 ms and P3 = 3 ms. Using non-preemptive FCFS with tie order P1, P2, P3, and ignoring context-switch overhead, what is the average waiting time?
question_revision.note: Clarified practice version: all arrivals are at time 0, with FCFS tie order P1, P2, P3.
assumptions: FCFS resolves the simultaneous-arrival tie as P1, P2, P3.
Each process has one CPU burst and context-switch overhead is ignored.

reviews.answer_text: Starvation of low-priority processes.
reviews.hint: Read raising effective priority as waiting increases.
reviews.explanation: OS17 defines aging as increasing waiting jobs’ effective priority to reduce indefinite postponement under suitable rules/workloads. Thus B names the problem it addresses. It does not remove a deadlock dependency cycle, coordinate conflicting memory updates or consolidate fragmented memory. The result still depends on the priority/aging policy; naming aging alone does not provide an unconditional deadline guarantee.

evidence.quote: Aging increases waiting jobs’ effective priority according to a rule, reducing indefinite postponement when the priority scheme and workload permit.

choices.label: A
choices.explanation: Aging changes priority rather than breaking the blocked resource dependencies of a deadlock.

choices.label: B
choices.explanation: Increasing effective priority of waiting low-priority jobs addresses their starvation under sustained higher-priority load.

choices.label: C
choices.explanation: Races require shared-access synchronization; priority aging is not a mutual-exclusion mechanism.

choices.label: D
choices.explanation: Memory fragmentation concerns allocation layout rather than the priority of waiting CPU jobs.

reviews.answer_text: Shortest Remaining Time First.
reviews.hint: Read the preemptive remaining-work variant of shortest-job scheduling.
reviews.explanation: OS16 distinguishes non-preemptive SJF/SJN from SRTF, which reconsiders at arrivals and can preempt for shorter remaining work. Therefore SRTF is the preemptive SJF variant. RR uses fixed cyclic turns, FCFS arrival order and generic priority an independently defined ranking. The original burst length and the remaining length must not be confused after a job has executed.

evidence.quote: SRTF reconsiders on arrivals and selects the shortest remaining work; a shorter newcomer can preempt.

choices.label: A
choices.explanation: RR selects cyclic quantum turns rather than the shortest remaining CPU work.

choices.label: B
choices.explanation: FCFS follows arrival order and is ordinarily non-preemptive rather than preemptive shortest-job scheduling.

choices.label: C
choices.explanation: SRTF chooses minimum remaining work and can interrupt a running job for a shorter arrival.

choices.label: D
choices.explanation: Generic priority scheduling does not specifically rank by remaining burst length and can be either variant.

reviews.answer_text: Choose an appropriate time quantum.
reviews.hint: Read the large-quantum versus small-quantum tradeoff.
reviews.explanation: OS18 says a large RR quantum approaches FCFS, while tiny quanta increase context-switch overhead. Selecting q therefore trades responsiveness against overhead, matching B. Priority management, deadlock policy and memory allocation are separate concerns rather than the defining parameter-selection challenge of ordinary Round Robin. The useful quantum depends on workloads and switching cost.

evidence.quote: A large quantum approaches FCFS; tiny quanta increase switch overhead.

choices.label: A
choices.explanation: Basic RR uses cyclic ready-queue turns rather than requiring a hierarchy of priority levels.

choices.label: B
choices.explanation: Quantum length controls responsiveness and switching overhead, creating RR’s characteristic tuning tradeoff.

choices.label: C
choices.explanation: Deadlock avoidance concerns resources and dependencies, not the defining RR quantum parameter.

choices.label: D
choices.explanation: Memory allocation is a separate management problem rather than the Round Robin selection rule’s main parameter.

reviews.answer_text: A synchronization variable with atomic wait and signal operations.
reviews.hint: Read permits and blocking rather than CPU selection or memory placement.
reviews.explanation: OS11 defines a semaphore through atomic wait/P/down and signal/V/up operations. Tokens control whether participants can proceed with shared resource work, with binary or counting forms. C identifies that synchronization role. Scheduling, memory-management and file-allocation policies solve different resource-selection/layout problems and do not define semaphore semantics.

evidence.quote: A semaphore provides atomic wait/P/down and signal/V/up operations.

choices.label: A
choices.explanation: A semaphore synchronizes participants; it is not itself a CPU-selection scheduling algorithm.

choices.label: B
choices.explanation: It controls coordination through permits, rather than choosing memory locations or translation layouts.

choices.label: C
choices.explanation: Atomic wait/signal on a synchronization variable controls permits for concurrent shared-resource operations.

choices.label: D
choices.explanation: File allocation chooses storage-block layout; that is separate from semaphore synchronization semantics.

reviews.answer_text: Binary tracks one permit; counting tracks several.
reviews.hint: Read the nonnegative-token model and avoid speed assumptions.
reviews.explanation: OS11 defines a binary semaphore as one permit and a counting semaphore as several, under the nonnegative-token model. Thus binary availability is 0/1 while a resource pool can have a larger count. B states this logical distinction. Internal negative-waiter encodings are implementation details, not a reason to claim speed guarantees, deadlock-only usage or no difference.

evidence.quote: A binary semaphore represents one permit; a counting semaphore tracks several.

choices.label: A
choices.explanation: The note gives no universal relative-speed guarantee; permit capacity is the defining distinction.

choices.label: B
choices.explanation: In the nonnegative-token model, binary availability is zero/one while counting semaphores track several available permits.

choices.label: C
choices.explanation: Counting semaphores coordinate resource pools and are not limited to preventing deadlock.

choices.label: D
choices.explanation: The allowed permit count is a substantive difference explicitly stated by the note.

reviews.answer_text: All four standard necessary conditions.
reviews.hint: Read necessity as a conjunction without claiming that policy availability proves a current deadlock.
reviews.explanation: OS22 says all four conditions are necessary in the standard reusable-resource model. C names that full set. Any two or a cycle alone does not state the complete conjunction. This is a necessary-condition answer, not an assertion that merely allowing all four policies proves a deadlock already exists in a particular allocation state.

evidence.quote: All four are necessary in the standard reusable-resource model.

choices.label: A
choices.explanation: It omits hold-and-wait and no-preemption, both necessary in the stated standard resource model.

choices.label: B
choices.explanation: An arbitrary pair does not supply all four necessary restrictions for the standard deadlock model.

choices.label: C
choices.explanation: This option lists mutual exclusion, hold-and-wait, no-preemption and circular wait together.

choices.label: D
choices.explanation: A cycle alone omits other necessary restrictions; it is not the complete standard condition set.

reviews.answer_text: Definite deadlock under single-instance resource assumptions.
reviews.hint: Read why resource-instance count changes the implication of a cycle.
reviews.explanation: OS23 says a cycle implies deadlock when every resource type has one instance. The stem supplies that decisive assumption, so C follows. With multiple instances a cycle would indicate only a possibility, but importing that different model would ignore the literal question. A graph cycle also says nothing by itself about high CPU utilization.

evidence.quote: with one instance of every resource type, a cycle implies deadlock.

choices.label: A
choices.explanation: Potential-only applies to the more general multiple-instance caveat, not the supplied single-instance case.

choices.label: B
choices.explanation: A cycle in the stated single-instance model establishes deadlock rather than excluding it.

choices.label: C
choices.explanation: The note explicitly gives cycle implies deadlock for a graph with one instance per resource type.

choices.label: D
choices.explanation: Resource dependency cycles do not measure CPU busy time or establish high processor utilization.

reviews.answer_text: Deadlock recovery.
reviews.hint: Read action after actual deadlock versus avoiding unsafe grants.
reviews.explanation: OS26 describes recovery through terminating selected processes or safely reclaiming resources and rolling work back after deadlock is detected. That matches allowing occurrence and then resolving it. Prevention removes a necessary condition, avoidance preserves safety before granting, and ignoring accepts risk without committing to recovery. The complete handling strategy is detection plus recovery; C is the offered recovery component.

evidence.quote: Detection asks whether the current state is deadlocked. Recovery can terminate selected processes or reclaim safely preemptable resources and roll affected work back to a checkpoint.

choices.label: A
choices.explanation: Prevention constrains requests so the targeted deadlock class cannot arise rather than accepting occurrence first.

choices.label: B
choices.explanation: Ignoring rare deadlock does not define active detection and subsequent recovery.

choices.label: C
choices.explanation: Recovery acts on an actual detected deadlock using termination, reclamation or rollback as appropriate.

choices.label: D
choices.explanation: Avoidance checks safe states before grants rather than deliberately permitting deadlock and then repairing it.

reviews.answer_text: Relocate addresses when the program is loaded.
reviews.hint: Read compile-time, load-time and execution-time binding separately.
reviews.explanation: OS27 defines load-time binding as relocation when placed into memory. That matches C’s final-address assignment at load when placement was unknown at compile time. Fixing absolute addresses during compilation is compile-time binding; translating while running is execution-time binding. Merely storing address bytes on a disk describes neither the placement decision nor its timing.

evidence.quote: Load-time binding relocates when placed into memory.

choices.label: A
choices.explanation: Fixing absolute addresses in the compiler is compile-time binding, not relocation on loading.

choices.label: B
choices.explanation: Translation during execution is execution-time binding rather than assignment during loading.

choices.label: C
choices.explanation: The loader resolves placement-dependent addresses when placing the program into memory.

choices.label: D
choices.explanation: Storing address information on disk does not define when placement-dependent address binding occurs.

reviews.answer_text: Fixed-size paging avoids external page-frame fragmentation; variable segments can fragment externally.
reviews.hint: Read the basic allocation model rather than claiming every allocator in a paging OS is fragmentation-free.
reviews.explanation: OS29/OS31 state that fixed-frame paging avoids external fragmentation of frame allocation but can waste the last page internally, while variable segments can leave external holes. B captures that basic distinction. A reverses unit sizes, C invents an exclusive-use restriction, and D ignores translation support. The no-external-fragmentation claim is confined to page-frame allocation, not every allocator inside an OS.

evidence.quote: Basic fixed-frame paging avoids external fragmentation of page-frame allocation but can waste the final page internally.

choices.label: A
choices.explanation: The sizes are reversed: pages are fixed units and segments are variable-length logical regions.

choices.label: B
choices.explanation: This matches the basic page-frame versus variable-segment allocation and fragmentation distinction.

choices.label: C
choices.explanation: The note does not impose an only-in-virtual-memory restriction as the defining segmentation contrast.

choices.label: D
choices.explanation: Paging uses address translation structures and checking; no-hardware-support is not its stated defining property.

reviews.answer_text: Free capacity is split across holes too small for a required contiguous allocation.
reviews.hint: Read external holes versus unused space inside an allocated unit.
reviews.explanation: OS29 defines external fragmentation as sufficient total free space split into holes unable to satisfy a contiguous allocation. B matches that definition, with large requests understood to require one continuous region. A instead describes internal fragmentation. CPU time and open-file counts may create other pressures but do not define the spatial fragmentation of free memory.

evidence.quote: External fragmentation is sufficient total free space split into holes that cannot satisfy a required contiguous allocation.

choices.label: A
choices.explanation: Unused space within an oversized allocated block is internal fragmentation, not external free-hole fragmentation.

choices.label: B
choices.explanation: Noncontiguous small holes can have enough total capacity yet fail to satisfy one contiguous request.

choices.label: C
choices.explanation: CPU execution time does not define the spatial layout of free memory holes.

choices.label: D
choices.explanation: Open-file count is a resource-use limit rather than the definition of external memory fragmentation.

reviews.answer_text: Map virtual/logical pages to physical frames.
reviews.hint: Read translation mappings and per-page status, not file permission records.
reviews.explanation: OS30 says the page table maps each virtual page to a frame with protection/status flags. B directly states the primary translation role. CPU time allocation belongs to scheduling; file permissions belong to filesystem metadata, despite page tables also having memory-protection bits. Disk I/O may service nonresident pages but does not define the page table’s mapping purpose.

evidence.quote: The page table maps a page to a frame and protection/status flags.

choices.label: A
choices.explanation: CPU time allocation is scheduling, not the page-to-frame translation recorded by a page table.

choices.label: B
choices.explanation: The table identifies the physical frame corresponding to each virtual page and records relevant flags.

choices.label: C
choices.explanation: Memory access-protection flags differ from filesystem file-access permissions; file permissions are not the page table’s purpose.

choices.label: D
choices.explanation: Page faults may cause I/O, but general disk-operation management is not the table’s translation role.

reviews.answer_text: Physical address = segment base + valid offset.
reviews.hint: Validate the segment and offset before adding the base.
reviews.explanation: OS31 gives segment-table base, limit and permissions, then validates (segment,offset) and adds base+offset. B matches, conditional on the offset passing the bound/protection checks. A and D mix in paging components and omit required scaling or displacement, while subtracting a limit is not the segment translation formula. An invalid offset traps rather than spilling into another segment.

evidence.quote: For (segment,offset), validate the segment and check the bound, then add base+offset.

choices.label: A
choices.explanation: Page number times frame size is not the segment base-plus-offset translation and omits required mapping.

choices.label: B
choices.explanation: After segment and bound checks, add the selected segment’s physical base to the offset.

choices.label: C
choices.explanation: The limit is a bound for validation, not a number subtracted to form the physical address.

choices.label: D
choices.explanation: Frame terminology belongs to paging, and adding an unscaled frame number is not the segmentation formula.

reviews.answer_text: Translated protected address spaces can use backing storage for nonresident portions.
reviews.hint: Read backing-store capacity separately from adding physical RAM.
reviews.explanation: OS32 describes virtual memory as protected translated address spaces with nonresident program portions backed by storage. B gives the disk-backed extension aspect and can allow programs exceeding resident physical memory to execute. It is not a complete definition of virtual memory, nor does it eliminate finite capacity constraints. The other alternatives confuse RAM installation, cache or an OS-only restriction.

evidence.quote: Virtual memory provides translated, protected address spaces and allows nonresident portions of a program to be backed by storage.

choices.label: A
choices.explanation: Installing RAM chips adds physical capacity; virtual-memory translation is a different mechanism.

choices.label: B
choices.explanation: Backing storage holds nonresident portions, permitting a program’s address space to exceed its currently resident physical memory.

choices.label: C
choices.explanation: CPU cache retains copied memory blocks and is not the virtual-address/backing-store mechanism.

choices.label: D
choices.explanation: Processes receive virtual address spaces; virtual memory is not restricted to storage used only by the OS.

reviews.answer_text: A page fault is a trap for a nonresident or invalid/protected page access; disk loading is not universal.
reviews.hint: Read nonresident faults, zero-fill/shared mappings and rejected illegal accesses.
reviews.explanation: OS32 explicitly says not every page fault reads a disk: zero-filled and shared mappings can be established without one, and illegal accesses are rejected. B therefore describes one disk-backed nonresident case rather than a valid general definition as written. Hardware failure, table corruption and exceeding an allocation also do not define page faults generally. The comprehensive supported definition is absent.

evidence.quote: Not every fault reads a disk: some allocate zero-filled pages or establish shared mappings. An illegal access is rejected, not automatically loaded.

choices.label: A
choices.explanation: A page fault is an address-translation/access trap and need not indicate a failed memory component.

choices.label: B
choices.explanation: This is a common disk-backed case, but requiring every fault to load from disk contradicts the note.

choices.label: C
choices.explanation: A page table can be correct while a legitimate page is nonresident or access is forbidden.

choices.label: D
choices.explanation: An out-of-range access can fault, but exceeding allocation is not the general definition of a page fault.

reviews.answer_text: Bring a page into memory when it is needed/accessed.
reviews.hint: Read demand paging versus eager whole-program loading and whole-process swapping.
reviews.explanation: OS32 defines demand paging as bringing a page in when accessed. B matches loading only the pages demanded during execution, with disk backing for the described stored portions. Not all pages must literally originate on disk because zero-fill/shared cases exist. Whole-program loading, fixed contiguous partitions and whole-process swapping do not name this per-page demand policy.

evidence.quote: Demand paging brings a page in when accessed.

choices.label: A
choices.explanation: Loading the entire program before execution is eager loading rather than fetching pages on demand.

choices.label: B
choices.explanation: Pages are brought in as execution needs them; disk backing is the described common stored-page case.

choices.label: C
choices.explanation: Fixed partitions are a contiguous-allocation arrangement rather than the page-access-triggered loading policy.

choices.label: D
choices.explanation: Moving an entire process is traditional swapping, not the individual-page demand mechanism.

reviews.answer_text: Internal waste is inside allocations; external holes are between them.
reviews.hint: Read the location of unused space and the contiguity requirement.
reviews.explanation: OS29 defines internal fragmentation as unused space inside an allocated unit and external fragmentation as free holes unable to serve a required contiguous request. B states the location distinction. C is not the general definition and needs allocator scope; D adds an unsupported virtual-memory-only restriction. These wastes can arise from allocation geometry rather than the program’s CPU behavior.

evidence.quote: Internal fragmentation is unused space inside an allocated unit. External fragmentation is sufficient total free space split into holes that cannot satisfy a required contiguous allocation.

choices.label: A
choices.explanation: The note explicitly distinguishes internal unused allocation space from external free-hole fragmentation.

choices.label: B
choices.explanation: Internal space is wasted within an allocation; external waste is free space split between allocations.

choices.label: C
choices.explanation: This does not define the contrast; basic page-frame allocation avoids external fragmentation, though other allocators may differ.

choices.label: D
choices.explanation: Unused space within an allocated unit is not limited by definition to virtual-memory systems.

reviews.answer_text: First-fit.
reviews.hint: Read selection order rather than smallest/largest-hole optimization.
reviews.explanation: OS28 defines first-fit as selecting the first adequate hole. This is exactly the stem’s first hole large enough. Best-fit searches for the smallest adequate hole, worst-fit for the largest, and next-fit resumes from a prior search position. The explicit first-hole condition selects first-fit without any numeric hole trace.

evidence.quote: First-fit selects the first adequate hole; next-fit continues from the previous search position; best-fit selects the smallest adequate hole; worst-fit selects the largest.

choices.label: A
choices.explanation: Best-fit minimizes adequate hole size rather than stopping at the first adequate hole.

choices.label: B
choices.explanation: Worst-fit selects the largest available hole rather than the first adequate one encountered.

choices.label: C
choices.explanation: First-fit stops at the first hole that can accommodate the requested allocation.

choices.label: D
choices.explanation: Next-fit continues from the previous search position; the stem gives the ordinary first-fit criterion.

reviews.answer_text: Temporarily move a whole process to backing store.
reviews.hint: Read whole-process swapping versus execution-context switching.
reviews.explanation: OS27 explicitly distinguishes traditional swapping of a whole process to backing store from paging individual pages and context switching execution state. B describes the whole-process memory-management operation. Saving registers is a context-switch task, file copying is a filesystem operation, and replacing instruction contents does not define swapping’s residence change.

evidence.quote: Swapping traditionally moves a whole process to backing store; paging moves individual pages.

choices.label: A
choices.explanation: Saving/restoring CPU register contexts is context switching rather than moving a whole process out of RAM.

choices.label: B
choices.explanation: Traditional swapping moves a process image to backing storage to free resident memory.

choices.label: C
choices.explanation: Copying files changes directory/storage contents rather than a process image’s memory residence.

choices.label: D
choices.explanation: Replacing instruction contents is not the defined transfer of a whole process between RAM and backing store.

reviews.answer_text: Load a routine only when needed.
reviews.hint: Read routine-level demand loading separately from linking and page movement.
reviews.explanation: OS27 directly defines dynamic loading as bringing a routine in when needed. B states the routine-on-call form of that rule. Eager startup loading is the opposite, priority changes are scheduling, and automatic page movement is a virtual-memory mechanism at a different granularity. Dynamic loading concerns when code routines become resident, not which process gets CPU priority.

evidence.quote: Dynamic loading brings a routine in when needed.

choices.label: A
choices.explanation: Loading all routines at startup is eager loading rather than bringing them in only on demand.

choices.label: B
choices.explanation: A routine is loaded when execution actually calls or needs it, matching dynamic loading.

choices.label: C
choices.explanation: Changing priority affects scheduling and does not load a routine’s code into memory.

choices.label: D
choices.explanation: Paging moves pages by virtual-memory demand, whereas dynamic loading names demand-driven routine loading.

reviews.answer_text: User-level threads are library-managed; kernel threads are OS-known. The options add unsupported performance/stability claims.
reviews.hint: Read management layer without assuming guaranteed speed or reliability.
reviews.explanation: OS08 defines the management-layer distinction and explicitly says speed and reliability depend on implementation. A includes that distinction but bundles faster creation and greater stability as unqualified consequences, so the full option is not supported. B adds an absolute speed claim, C invents direct privileged access, and D denies real differences. A repaired option should retain only library-managed versus kernel-known execution contexts.

evidence.quote: User-level threads are managed by a library; kernel threads are known to the OS.
Speed and reliability depend on implementation; the management layer alone guarantees neither.

choices.label: A
choices.explanation: The management distinction is right, but bundled creation-speed and stability guarantees are explicitly not guaranteed by the note.

choices.label: B
choices.explanation: Kernel threads are not guaranteed always faster; performance depends on implementation and operation.

choices.label: C
choices.explanation: User-level thread management does not grant user code direct privileged hardware access.

choices.label: D
choices.explanation: Management and mapping differences affect blocking and CPU use, so there are real practical differences.

reviews.answer_text: Mechanisms for exchanging information and coordinating processes.
reviews.hint: Read shared memory, message passing and synchronization within IPC.
reviews.explanation: OS09 describes shared-memory communication, send/receive, pipes, queues, sockets and RPC, including synchronization for conflicting updates. B summarizes the exchange and coordination role. IPC is not a CPU selection algorithm or a particular memory-allocation/file operation, even though shared memory and file-based mechanisms may be used to implement it.

evidence.quote: Shared memory lets processes access a common region and requires synchronization for conflicting updates. Message passing exchanges data through send/receive operations.

choices.label: A
choices.explanation: CPU scheduling selects execution opportunities, rather than defining communication and coordination among processes.

choices.label: B
choices.explanation: Exchanging information with appropriate synchronization/coordination captures the IPC mechanisms described by the note.

choices.label: C
choices.explanation: Shared memory can implement IPC, but memory allocation alone does not define interprocess communication.

choices.label: D
choices.explanation: Files can participate in communication, but IPC is not restricted to one filesystem operation.

reviews.answer_text: Mutually exclude conflicting critical-region execution.
reviews.hint: Read shared protected state and all critical-section correctness conditions.
reviews.explanation: OS10 defines a critical section as code accessing shared state needing protection and lists mutual exclusion, progress and bounded waiting as requirements. B states the exclusion aspect for critical sections protecting the same conflicting resource. The problem also includes progress/fair-waiting requirements, so exclusion is not its entire specification. CPU quotas, disk management and real-time scheduling are different topics.

evidence.quote: A correct exclusion solution requires mutual exclusion, progress and bounded waiting under stated assumptions.

choices.label: A
choices.explanation: CPU consumption limits are not the shared-access exclusion problem defining critical sections.

choices.label: B
choices.explanation: Conflicting critical regions must not execute simultaneously; this is the mutual-exclusion part of the correctness requirements.

choices.label: C
choices.explanation: Disk I/O can involve shared state, but managing it generally is not the critical-section problem definition.

choices.label: D
choices.explanation: Real-time selection addresses timing/scheduling, not the core shared-state exclusion requirement requested.

reviews.answer_text: B is the general definition; B and D both hold in the single-burst/no-I/O model.
reviews.hint: Separate the general elapsed-time definition from a formula that assumes no blocked or I/O time.
reviews.explanation: OS13 defines turnaround as completion minus arrival, so B always holds. The same section gives waiting = completion − arrival − burst for one CPU burst without I/O. Rearranging yields turnaround = waiting + burst, making D equally valid in that ordinary scheduling model. With blocked/I/O time, ready-queue waiting plus CPU burst omits that delay. The stem does not select a model: preserve B as the general definition and accept B/D only under the stated no-I/O convention.

evidence.quote: For arrival A, first start S and completion C, response=S−A and turnaround=C−A. For a single CPU burst B with no I/O, waiting=C−A−B.
With I/O, subtract all CPU and blocked time to isolate ready-queue waiting.

choices.label: A
choices.explanation: Burst minus waiting reverses the contribution of ready-queue delay and is not the turnaround identity.

choices.label: B
choices.explanation: Completion minus arrival is the general turnaround definition, including elapsed CPU, ready-wait and blocked time.

choices.label: C
choices.explanation: Start plus burst can give completion for an uninterrupted burst; it omits subtracting arrival and other delays.

choices.label: D
choices.explanation: Waiting plus burst equals turnaround for one CPU burst without I/O, but omits blocked time in the broader model.

reviews.answer_text: Short jobs wait behind a long FCFS burst.
reviews.hint: Read the arrival-order convoy example.
reviews.explanation: OS15 describes the convoy effect as long CPU-bound work making many short jobs wait under non-preemptive FCFS. C directly states that queueing effect and its high waiting-time consequence. FCFS does not use priority order or grant equal total CPU, and shared address space is unrelated to the arrival-order delay. The effect depends on a long burst preceding shorter ones.

evidence.quote: Long CPU-bound work can make many short jobs wait: the convoy effect.

choices.label: A
choices.explanation: Priority order does not define FCFS, which follows arrival order rather than high-priority completion.

choices.label: B
choices.explanation: FCFS serves entire bursts of possibly different lengths rather than enforcing equal CPU shares.

choices.label: C
choices.explanation: Short jobs are delayed behind the long non-preempted burst, producing the FCFS convoy effect.

choices.label: D
choices.explanation: Shared memory concerns address-space organization rather than the scheduling delay called a convoy.

reviews.answer_text: Voluntary release versus possible forced CPU preemption.
reviews.hint: Read non-preemptive burst retention and preemptive timer/arrival events.
reviews.explanation: OS14 says non-preemptive scheduling retains the CPU until completion, blocking or voluntary yielding, while preemptive scheduling may return running work to ready. B captures the voluntary-versus-forced distinction, with completion/blocking included among natural release events. C contradicts preemption, D claims an unsupported universal performance ranking, and A erases the defining difference.

evidence.quote: Non-preemptive scheduling keeps a running CPU burst until completion, blocking or voluntary yielding. Preemptive scheduling can return running work to ready, usually after a timer quantum or a more urgent arrival.

choices.label: A
choices.explanation: The policies differ in whether a running CPU burst can be forcibly interrupted for another process.

choices.label: B
choices.explanation: Non-preemptive work releases naturally/voluntarily; preemptive policy may forcibly reassign CPU execution time.

choices.label: C
choices.explanation: Forcibly interrupting running work is exactly what preemptive scheduling permits.

choices.label: D
choices.explanation: No policy universally performs better for all workloads and objectives, so the absolute performance claim fails.

reviews.answer_text: Throughput.
reviews.hint: Read completed jobs per unit time versus utilization and delay.
reviews.explanation: OS13 defines throughput as completed jobs divided by elapsed time. That exactly matches the stem’s process-completion rate. CPU utilization is busy-time fraction; response measures delay to first start, and turnaround delay to completion. The units therefore distinguish throughput from the other criteria without requiring a scheduling example.

evidence.quote: Throughput=completed jobs/elapsed time; CPU utilization=busy time/elapsed time.

choices.label: A
choices.explanation: CPU utilization measures busy-time fraction, not how many processes finish per unit time.

choices.label: B
choices.explanation: Response measures first-service delay for a process rather than a completion-count rate.

choices.label: C
choices.explanation: Throughput is explicitly the number of completed jobs divided by elapsed time.

choices.label: D
choices.explanation: Turnaround measures arrival-to-completion elapsed duration rather than completed jobs per time.

reviews.answer_text: All processes in the broad textbook system/job-queue sense.
reviews.hint: Read broad job queue versus narrower admission and device queues.
reviews.explanation: OS06 explicitly defines the broad textbook job queue as processes in the system and distinguishes a narrower admission queue awaiting memory. B matches that broad usage, including not-yet-admitted jobs. Ready/running or I/O-blocked work are subsets, not the whole category; already-ended processes are not the intended current job population. The answer retains the note’s terminology qualification.

evidence.quote: The broad textbook job queue contains processes in the system, while an admission queue more narrowly holds jobs awaiting memory/admission.

choices.label: A
choices.explanation: Currently running work is only a subset, not the broad population represented by the textbook job queue.

choices.label: B
choices.explanation: The broad textbook usage includes system processes/jobs, including those awaiting memory admission.

choices.label: C
choices.explanation: I/O waiting belongs to device queues and does not exhaust the broad job-queue population.

choices.label: D
choices.explanation: Already-terminated work is not the current job population intended by the note’s broad system queue.

reviews.answer_text: An offset tracks position; a file descriptor is the handle referring to open-file state.
reviews.hint: Read descriptor, open-file state and current offset separately.
reviews.explanation: OS36 explicitly distinguishes the process-local integer descriptor from associated open-file state containing an offset. B describes that offset/file-position pointer, but the stem conflates it with the descriptor itself using a slash. A descriptor does not numerically track the current byte position. The wording needs to select the offset or handle concept; the other choices describe different metadata/location information.

evidence.quote: A file descriptor is a process-local integer handle; the associated open-file state contains the current offset and access mode. Descriptor and offset are not synonyms.

choices.label: A
choices.explanation: Physical block location is not what the descriptor or current logical file-offset field directly denotes.

choices.label: B
choices.explanation: This is correct for the current offset/file-position pointer, but not as a definition of the descriptor handle.

choices.label: C
choices.explanation: Owner permissions are file metadata rather than the descriptor identity or current I/O position.

choices.label: D
choices.explanation: Creation time is metadata rather than the process-local handle or current read/write offset.

reviews.answer_text: Specify principals and permitted access rights.
reviews.hint: Read authorization policy rather than disk layout or I/O scheduling.
reviews.explanation: OS39 defines an ACL as listing principals and rights. B states that users/groups can receive different read/write/execute permissions for a file. Authentication verifies identity first; authorization uses these permitted operations. Space accounting, fragmentation and I/O ordering do not define an access-control list. The answer does not assume universal default rights or that every filesystem uses exactly the same permission model.

evidence.quote: An ACL lists principals and rights; owner/group/other bits are a simpler policy model,

choices.label: A
choices.explanation: Disk-space usage is storage accounting, not the list of principals and allowed operations.

choices.label: B
choices.explanation: An ACL associates users/groups or other principals with specified access rights on the resource.

choices.label: C
choices.explanation: Fragmentation concerns block placement and free-space layout rather than authorization entries.

choices.label: D
choices.explanation: Scheduling I/O requests controls service order, not which principal is authorized to access a file.

reviews.answer_text: A file occupies consecutive disk blocks.
reviews.hint: Read start+i mapping and its growth/fragmentation tradeoffs.
reviews.explanation: OS38 defines contiguous allocation through consecutive blocks, with logical block i at start+i. This permits sequential and direct access without following a chain. B matches. Scattered pointers describe linked allocation, a separate index describes indexed allocation, and fixed physical memory frames belong to paging rather than file-contiguity organization. Growth and external fragmentation remain drawbacks.

evidence.quote: Contiguous allocation uses consecutive blocks; logical block i is start+i and supports direct access, but growth and external fragmentation are problems.

choices.label: A
choices.explanation: Scattered blocks linked by pointers describe linked allocation rather than one consecutive run.

choices.label: B
choices.explanation: A consecutive block run supports start-plus-index lookup and sequential/direct file access.

choices.label: C
choices.explanation: A separate block-pointer index describes indexed allocation, not contiguous placement itself.

choices.label: D
choices.explanation: Physical memory frames are paging units rather than the disk-block contiguity rule for a file.

reviews.answer_text: Linked blocks permit growth without reserving a full contiguous run.
reviews.hint: Read the contiguity constraint removed and the traversal cost introduced.
reviews.explanation: OS38 says linked allocation supports growth without reserving a complete contiguous file. Since successive blocks can occupy separate free locations, it removes the external-contiguity problem and the need to reserve the final length beforehand. B captures that advantage. Random access still requires traversing earlier links, internal last-block waste may remain, and no universal smaller-metadata claim follows.

evidence.quote: Linked allocation chains blocks and supports growth without reserving a complete contiguous file; locating block i requires traversing preceding links.

choices.label: A
choices.explanation: Locating a later linked block requires traversal, so faster random access is not its general advantage.

choices.label: B
choices.explanation: Separate linked blocks allow incremental growth without a single reserved contiguous region or preknown final length.

choices.label: C
choices.explanation: A partially used final block can still waste space internally; linking does not specifically remove that waste.

choices.label: D
choices.explanation: Pointers add metadata, and the note gives no universal less-memory guarantee over contiguous allocation.

reviews.answer_text: A per-file block of data-block pointers in the simple indexed model.
reviews.hint: Read indexed metadata versus per-data-block chaining and global tables.
reviews.explanation: OS38 defines indexed allocation through a per-file array/tree of block pointers and gives an index-block capacity example. B describes the simple single-index-block form. Large files may need multiple index levels, so all addresses in one block is model-dependent rather than universal. A is linked allocation, C a global-table description, and D ordinary metadata without the defining data-block pointers.

evidence.quote: Indexed allocation uses a per-file array/tree of block pointers and supports direct lookup with metadata overhead.

choices.label: A
choices.explanation: A next pointer in each data block describes linked allocation rather than a separate per-file index.

choices.label: B
choices.explanation: In the simple indexed model, a dedicated per-file index contains pointers to the file’s data blocks.

choices.label: C
choices.explanation: A global table for all files is not the per-file index block described by indexed allocation.

choices.label: D
choices.explanation: Size/timestamps alone do not provide the data-block address index that defines this allocation structure.

reviews.answer_text: Sequential access proceeds in order; direct access selects a position.
reviews.hint: Read traversing preceding records versus directly locating a block.
reviews.explanation: OS38 contrasts linked traversal of preceding blocks with contiguous start+i and indexed direct lookup. These illustrate the access distinction in B: sequential progression versus selecting a numbered position without reading every preceding record. Nothing restricts direct access to text or requires sequential files to occupy more disk space merely because of their access method.

evidence.quote: logical block i is start+i and supports direct access,
locating block i requires traversing preceding links.

choices.label: A
choices.explanation: Order-dependent traversal and direct selection are different access behaviors, not identical methods.

choices.label: B
choices.explanation: Sequential access advances through records; direct access identifies a chosen block/position for access.

choices.label: C
choices.explanation: The direct block-lookup rule does not impose a text-file-only restriction.

choices.label: D
choices.explanation: Access order alone does not determine a greater storage-space requirement for sequential files.

reviews.answer_text: A rooted hierarchy of nested directories and files.
reviews.hint: Read tree organization separately from links that add graph sharing.
reviews.explanation: OS37 says a tree allows nested directories and absolute/relative paths. In the pure tree model, each entry has a path from the root, matching B. Flat lists instead describe single-level organization; sharing among users and deletion at reboot do not define tree structure. Links can add graph relationships, but that is an extension beyond the pure tree premise.

evidence.quote: A tree allows nested directories and absolute/relative paths; links can create shared graphs.

choices.label: A
choices.explanation: One flat file list is single-level organization rather than nested branches from a root.

choices.label: B
choices.explanation: A root with nested subdirectories and paths is the tree hierarchy described by the note.

choices.label: C
choices.explanation: Multiple users sharing a directory does not by itself define its structural hierarchy.

choices.label: D
choices.explanation: Deletion on reboot is a lifetime policy rather than the rooted directory-tree organization.

reviews.answer_text: Hard links name one file object; symbolic links store a pathname.
reviews.hint: Read link target identity and filesystem-boundary behavior.
reviews.explanation: OS37 defines a hard link as another name for the same file object, usually within one filesystem, and a symbolic link as storing a pathname that can cross filesystems or dangle. B matches that distinction; pointing to the same data blocks is shorthand for the same underlying object. The other options reverse boundaries or invent deletion/platform restrictions.

evidence.quote: A hard link is another name for the same underlying file object, usually within one filesystem; a symbolic link stores a pathname and can point across filesystems or become dangling.

choices.label: A
choices.explanation: This reverses the note’s rule: symbolic links can cross filesystems, while hard links normally cannot.

choices.label: B
choices.explanation: Hard links name the same underlying file object; symbolic links contain a path resolving to a target.

choices.label: C
choices.explanation: A symbolic link is a removable pathname entry; the note imposes no cannot-delete restriction.

choices.label: D
choices.explanation: The hard-link definition is not Windows-only; the supplied statement invents an unsupported exclusive platform restriction.

reviews.answer_text: Attach a filesystem at a mount point.
reviews.hint: Read attaching an existing filesystem versus creating/formatting one.
reviews.explanation: OS37 explicitly defines mounting as attaching a filesystem at a mount point and distinguishes it from formatting. B states that integration into the existing namespace. Creation/formatting establish a filesystem’s on-device structure; deleting files frees content space. None of those is the namespace attachment operation requested by mounting.

evidence.quote: Mounting attaches a filesystem at a mount point; it does not format the device.

choices.label: A
choices.explanation: Creating a new filesystem establishes storage structure rather than attaching it to an existing namespace.

choices.label: B
choices.explanation: Mounting makes a filesystem accessible at a chosen point in the directory hierarchy.

choices.label: C
choices.explanation: Deleting files changes contents/free space rather than attaching a filesystem to the namespace.

choices.label: D
choices.explanation: Formatting is explicitly distinguished from mounting in the supplied note.

reviews.answer_text: Restore an affected process to a prior checkpoint after reclaiming resources.
reviews.hint: Read recovery state restoration rather than reboot or termination.
reviews.explanation: OS26 describes reclaiming safely preemptable resources and rolling affected work back to a checkpoint. B states that restoration to a safe prior state after resources are withdrawn. Restarting the entire OS/computer and killing all involved processes are different coarse recovery actions, not the meaning of rollback. Safe checkpoints/restart semantics are required to make withdrawal and restoration coherent.

evidence.quote: Recovery can terminate selected processes or reclaim safely preemptable resources and roll affected work back to a checkpoint.

choices.label: A
choices.explanation: Restarting the whole OS is not the checkpoint restoration of affected work that defines rollback.

choices.label: B
choices.explanation: Rollback restores an affected process to a previous recoverable state after safe resource reclamation.

choices.label: C
choices.explanation: Terminating processes is a separate recovery tool rather than restoring their earlier execution state.

choices.label: D
choices.explanation: Rebooting frees broad machine state but is not the process-checkpoint restoration definition of rollback.

reviews.answer_text: Base/relocation stores the process’s physical start; limit stores its permitted length.
reviews.hint: Read the process-relative base/limit model and its bounds check.
reviews.explanation: OS28 explicitly says base is the process’s physical starting address and limit its permitted length, and rejects interpreting relocation as the OS base. B therefore attaches both registers to the wrong region. The actual mechanism checks 0≤offset<limit then forms base+offset, protecting the process’s allowed region. Scheduling, disk locations and page tables are unrelated purposes; no option states the supported answer.

evidence.quote: In the standard base/limit model, base is that process’s physical starting address and limit is its permitted length.
The relocation register does not normally hold the OS base.

choices.label: A
choices.explanation: Base/limit checks validate memory accesses rather than speeding CPU scheduling decisions.

choices.label: B
choices.explanation: It incorrectly assigns the registers to the OS base/size instead of the user process’s start and permitted length.

choices.label: C
choices.explanation: These registers describe allowed RAM address translation, not filesystem disk-block locations.

choices.label: D
choices.explanation: The simple contiguous base/limit model does not manage page-table mappings.

reviews.answer_text: Share suitable library code pages across programs.
reviews.hint: Read dynamic reference resolution versus copied statically linked code.
reviews.explanation: OS27 says dynamic linking resolves external-library references at load/runtime and allows suitable library code pages to be shared, whereas static linking copies selected code into the executable. B captures the potential memory saving. It is not an unconditional speed guarantee, does not remove address translation/page tables and cannot eliminate programming bugs. Only shareable code/pages are implied, not arbitrary writable library state.

evidence.quote: Dynamic linking resolves references to external libraries at load/runtime, allowing suitable library code pages to be shared; static linking copies selected code into the executable.

choices.label: A
choices.explanation: Dynamic resolution/sharing does not guarantee faster execution for every program or workload.

choices.label: B
choices.explanation: Several processes can share suitable library code pages rather than each embedding a separate static copy.

choices.label: C
choices.explanation: Library linking does not remove virtual-address translation or its page-table requirements.

choices.label: D
choices.explanation: Choosing dynamic rather than static linking cannot guarantee the absence of programming errors.

reviews.answer_text: Team inexperience alone does not determine a lifecycle model.
reviews.hint: Read process selection factors in SE02.
reviews.explanation: SE02 requires considering requirement stability, risk, urgency, stakeholder availability, skills and assurance needs together. An inexperienced team may benefit from learning iterations, risk experiments or reviewed staged work depending on its uncertainty. RAD additionally needs skilled developers and available users. Without the other project conditions, the stem cannot uniquely select one of these models.
