Unit, integration and system testing describe levels or scope; regression tests can be run at any of them, so the change-driven purpose uniquely identifies C.

evidence.quote: Regression testing checks for unintended effects after change

choices.label: A
choices.explanation: Unit testing defines a small-component scope rather than the purpose of checking change-induced defects.

choices.label: B
choices.explanation: Integration testing focuses on interfaces and interactions, which may be regression-tested but do not define regression.

choices.label: C
choices.explanation: Regression testing retests previously working behavior to detect unintended effects of modifications.

choices.label: D
choices.explanation: System testing addresses the complete integrated system rather than specifically the after-change purpose.

reviews.answer_text: Docker.
reviews.hint: Read container packaging in SE28.
reviews.explanation: SE28 explicitly says Docker packages an application and its runtime dependencies into containers. That matches the deployment packaging task in the question. Git tracks versions, Jira tracks issues and Jenkins automates checks; they can participate in a deployment pipeline, but none replaces Docker's specified container packaging responsibility.

evidence.quote: Docker packages application/runtime dependencies into containers.

choices.label: A
choices.explanation: Git manages version history rather than packaging the runtime into a container.

choices.label: B
choices.explanation: Jira manages work and defects rather than building application containers.

choices.label: C
choices.explanation: Jenkins automates checks and pipelines but is not the named container-packaging tool.

choices.label: D
choices.explanation: Docker packages the application and runtime dependencies into a deployable container.

reviews.answer_text: Single Responsibility Principle.
reviews.hint: Read focused responsibilities in SE25.
reviews.explanation: SE25 identifies Single Responsibility among the core design principles. The question asks directly for one responsibility per component, so D is the exact named rule. Encapsulation protects internal decisions, inheritance creates subtype relations, and polymorphism supports varying implementations through a common interface. Those can help a design but do not themselves define a single responsibility.

evidence.quote: SOLID includes Single Responsibility, Open–Closed, Liskov substitution, Interface Segregation and Dependency Inversion.

choices.label: A
choices.explanation: Encapsulation hides implementation details rather than requiring one responsibility per component.

choices.label: B
choices.explanation: Inheritance establishes superclass/subclass reuse rather than the focused-responsibility rule.

choices.label: C
choices.explanation: Polymorphism supports compatible varying implementations rather than defining responsibility count.

choices.label: D
choices.explanation: Single Responsibility explicitly calls for one focused responsibility in a software component.

reviews.answer_text: Singleton.
reviews.hint: Read instance-control versus creation and notification patterns in SE27.
reviews.explanation: SE27 describes Singleton as controlling access to one instance. That is the pattern requested by the one-instance condition. Factory patterns address how concrete objects are created, Observer notifies subscribers and Decorator adds behavior by wrapping. None of those other pattern responsibilities guarantees a single shared instance by itself.

evidence.quote: Singleton controls access to one instance

choices.label: A
choices.explanation: Singleton controls creation and access so that the intended class has one shared instance.

choices.label: B
choices.explanation: A factory selects or constructs products rather than inherently limiting a class to one instance.

choices.label: C
choices.explanation: Observer distributes notifications to subscribers rather than restricting object instance count.

choices.label: D
choices.explanation: Decorator adds behavior through wrapping rather than enforcing a single instance.

reviews.answer_text: Functional programming, for the side-effect emphasis.
reviews.hint: Read function evaluation and controlled side effects in SE01.
reviews.explanation: The phrase promotes the use of data is not distinctive because all these paradigms use data. The discriminating part is avoiding or controlling side effects. SE01 explicitly assigns function evaluation and controlled side effects to functional programming. Procedural, object-oriented and event-driven styles organize behavior differently and do not inherently impose that emphasis.

evidence.quote: Functional programming emphasizes function evaluation and controlled side effects; event-driven programs react to events.

choices.label: A
choices.explanation: Functional programming emphasizes evaluating functions and controlling side effects.

choices.label: B
choices.explanation: Procedural decomposition organizes functions or procedures without inherently avoiding state-changing effects.

choices.label: C
choices.explanation: Object-oriented decomposition combines state and behavior and does not inherently exclude side effects.

choices.label: D
choices.explanation: Event-driven programs react to events; that does not itself require avoiding side effects.

reviews.answer_text: Adaptive maintenance.
reviews.hint: Read maintenance categories by motive in SE40.
reviews.explanation: SE40 defines adaptive maintenance as responding to changes in the environment. New platforms or technologies therefore create an adaptive-maintenance need even when the original software is not faulty. Corrective maintenance fixes faults, perfective work improves useful capability or performance, and preventive work reduces future risk. The stated environmental motive makes B the appropriate category.

evidence.quote: adaptive maintenance responds to environment changes

choices.label: A
choices.explanation: Corrective work fixes faults rather than primarily accommodating changed environments or technology.

choices.label: B
choices.explanation: Adaptive maintenance changes software so it continues working in a new environment or technology context.

choices.label: C
choices.explanation: Perfective work improves capability or performance rather than specifically responding to an environmental change.

choices.label: D
choices.explanation: Preventive work reduces future maintenance risk rather than defining adaptation to a new environment.

reviews.answer_text: Agile methodology, specifically Scrum.
reviews.hint: Read Scrum timeboxed Sprints in SE05.
reviews.explanation: SE05 places Sprints in Scrum, an Agile framework. B is therefore the available category that contains the specific process described. Agile as a whole does not require every method to call its iterations Sprints. Waterfall, spiral and the V-model have other organizing principles, so none is the named Sprint-based method.

evidence.quote: Scrum uses timeboxed Sprints of at most one month

choices.label: A
choices.explanation: Classical waterfall uses planned phases rather than Scrum Sprints.

choices.label: B
choices.explanation: Scrum is an Agile framework whose iterative delivery cycles are called Sprints.

choices.label: C
choices.explanation: Spiral uses risk-driven cycles rather than specifically the Scrum Sprint mechanism.

choices.label: D
choices.explanation: The V-model pairs development stages with tests rather than organizing work into Sprints.

reviews.answer_text: An abstract use case specifies behavior for specialization and is not directly instantiated.
reviews.hint: Read abstract use cases versus inclusion and optional extension in SE16.
reviews.explanation: SE16 defines abstract use cases through specialization and non-instantiability. No choice states that rule accurately. C is a loose possible consequence if accessed means independently executed, but lack of a direct actor line is not the definition. Reuse can involve include, and optional behavior can involve extend. A merely unfinished use case is not abstract by definition.

evidence.quote: An abstract use case specifies behavior for specialization and is not directly instantiated as a complete use case.

choices.label: A
choices.explanation: An unfinished description is not what makes a use case abstract.

choices.label: B
choices.explanation: Optional behavior is not the defining property of an abstract use case.

choices.label: C
choices.explanation: It may loosely suggest non-instantiability, but direct actor access/association is not the defining UML criterion.

choices.label: D
choices.explanation: Reuse alone does not establish abstraction; included concrete behavior can also be reused.

reviews.answer_text: No testing level is universally the most time-consuming.
reviews.hint: Read test-level scope and effort caveats in SE35.
reviews.explanation: SE35 defines unit, integration, system and acceptance testing but explicitly says none is universally longest. Duration depends on system size, interface complexity, assurance goals, automation, environment readiness and acceptance procedures. The stem provides no project or effort basis, so selecting a familiar level as always most time-consuming would invent a universal rule absent from the note.

evidence.quote: None of these levels is universally the longest.

choices.label: A
choices.explanation: Many units or difficult isolation can make unit testing dominate, depending on the project.

choices.label: B
choices.explanation: Acceptance can dominate when user trials, approvals or operational validation require substantial time.

choices.label: C
choices.explanation: Broad end-to-end and nonfunctional checks can make system testing longest in some projects.

choices.label: D
choices.explanation: Complex interactions and environment dependencies can make integration testing the largest effort.

reviews.answer_text: Functional requirements can specify required and prohibited behavior; the negative options need clear wording.
reviews.hint: Read observable services and forbidden actions in SE09.
reviews.explanation: SE09 explicitly includes permitted and prohibited behavior in functional requirements. A fits required tasks, and B can fit forbidden tasks; C’s must not work wording is damaged. D becomes an inclusive answer only if all three are intended as meaningful observable obligations. The modal and grammatical wording does not establish a unique classification as printed.

evidence.quote: A functional requirement states an observable service or behavior, including reactions to inputs, errors and forbidden actions.

choices.label: A
choices.explanation: Required observable program tasks are functional obligations.

choices.label: B
choices.explanation: Prohibited observable tasks can also be functional requirements, if that is the intended obligation.

choices.label: C
choices.explanation: This may mean forbidden behavior, but must not work is too damaged to classify precisely.

choices.label: D
choices.explanation: All fits only if B and C are intended as clear prohibited functional behaviors.

reviews.answer_text: No option clearly states a nonfunctional quality or constraint.
reviews.hint: Read prohibited functions versus nonfunctional qualities in SE09/SE10.
reviews.explanation: A required task is functional, and prohibited tasks can be functional too. SE09 explicitly rejects classifying a negative statement as automatically nonfunctional. D merely says a description omits something; it does not specify a measurable quality or constraint. A genuine nonfunctional requirement is absent, and the damaged must not work wording should not be used to manufacture one.

evidence.quote: A negative statement is not automatically nonfunctional.

choices.label: A
choices.explanation: A required observable task is a functional requirement.

choices.label: B
choices.explanation: A prohibition on observable behavior can itself be functional.

choices.label: C
choices.explanation: If it means a forbidden task, it remains functional; the damaged wording does not establish a quality requirement.

choices.label: D
choices.explanation: An assertion that something is not specified does not state a nonfunctional obligation or quality.

reviews.answer_text: Feasibility study.
reviews.hint: Read worth, constraints and organizational impact in SE08.
reviews.explanation: SE08 asks whether a proposal is worth doing and deliverable, considering existing limitations, impacts on organization and personnel, benefits, costs, skills and integration risk. That matches the stem’s preliminary impact and constraint investigation. System analysis studies the detailed problem and behavior and informs feasibility, but the broad early viability assessment is the more specific match here.

evidence.quote: Examine existing limitations, organizational impacts, benefits, cost, available skills and integration risk.

choices.label: A
choices.explanation: Design chooses solution structures rather than primarily assessing preliminary viability and organizational impacts.

choices.label: B
choices.explanation: Feasibility investigates existing limitations, impacts and whether the proposal is worthwhile and deliverable.

choices.label: C
choices.explanation: Gathering needs is useful input but does not by itself cover the full viability assessment.

choices.label: D
choices.explanation: System analysis examines detailed problem behavior; feasibility is the more specific preliminary impact/viability activity.

reviews.answer_text: The software product includes code and relevant requirements, design, test and user documentation.
reviews.hint: Read software work products in SE01.
reviews.explanation: SE01 explicitly includes executable code plus requirements, designs, test assets, configuration and user documentation in a software product. A describes the implemented software, while B and C name relevant accompanying artifacts. All three descriptions are therefore compatible; none limits the product to code alone. D is the inclusive answer among these options.

evidence.quote: A software product includes executable code and relevant requirements, designs, test assets, configuration and user documentation.

choices.label: A
choices.explanation: Software built to meet client requirements forms part of the product.

choices.label: B
choices.explanation: Relevant design and testing documentation are included product artifacts.

choices.label: C
choices.explanation: Requirements specifications and user manuals are relevant product documentation.

choices.label: D
choices.explanation: All three descriptions are compatible with the complete software-product scope.

reviews.answer_text: Isolation with a sandbox and limiting structural complexity can support testability.
reviews.hint: Read testability conditions and the self-referential option in SE27.
reviews.explanation: SE27 links testability to controllable inputs, observable outputs, replaceable dependencies and limited structural complexity; a sandbox can isolate execution. A and D therefore identify mechanisms with explicit support. Refactoring may improve those conditions but is not automatically a testability improvement. B is self-referential and cannot define a coherent independent combination of alternatives.

evidence.quote: Testability improves with controllable inputs, observable outputs, replaceable dependencies and limited structural complexity.

choices.label: A
choices.explanation: A sandbox can isolate execution, improving control of the test environment.

choices.label: B
choices.explanation: A and B refers to this same option B and does not define a noncircular combination.

choices.label: C
choices.explanation: Refactoring can improve testability if it improves control, observation or structure, but the result is unspecified.

choices.label: D
choices.explanation: Limiting structural complexity directly supports easier control and observation during testing.

reviews.answer_text: A structure is the elements/relations; a view represents selected aspects of it.
reviews.hint: Read structures versus views in SE23.
reviews.explanation: SE23 distinguishes actual software/hardware elements and relations from a representation selecting aspects of that structure. C and D express those complementary true definitions. B wrongly makes views the designers of structures; architects create and document designs using views. A excludes the true C and includes false material, so it cannot be the inclusive answer.

evidence.quote: A structure is the elements/relations themselves; a view represents selected aspects.

choices.label: A
choices.explanation: It excludes true C while including false B, so the combination fails.

choices.label: B
choices.explanation: Views represent structures; they are not agents that design them.

choices.label: C
choices.explanation: A structure consists of the actual modeled elements and their relations.

choices.label: D
choices.explanation: A view is a representation selecting aspects of an underlying structure.

reviews.answer_text: White-box is a technique, not a required testing level.
reviews.hint: Read unit level versus structural techniques in SE35.
reviews.explanation: SE35 explicitly distinguishes a unit-testing level from a white-box technique. Structural test derivation can be used where internals are available at different scopes; unit is common but not a prerequisite. The question does not state the code scope or coverage goal. C is also self-referential, so the options do not establish a unique required level.

evidence.quote: Unit is a level, while white-box is a technique; a unit can be tested using black-box cases too.

choices.label: A
choices.explanation: System-level structural testing can use internal information when the scope and observability permit it.

choices.label: B
choices.explanation: Integration-level tests can target internal interaction structure; white-box is not restricted to one level.

choices.label: C
choices.explanation: A and C refers to its own option C, giving a circular combination.

choices.label: D
choices.explanation: Unit testing commonly uses white-box techniques, but it is not an exclusive prerequisite.

reviews.answer_text: Use cases describe behavior broadly; detailed dynamic interaction/state diagrams are absent.
reviews.hint: Read goals versus workflow, messages and state changes in SE14/SE20.
reviews.explanation: SE20 selects sequence diagrams for message order, state machines for state changes and activity diagrams for workflow. None appears in these options. B can fit a broad behavioral-model interpretation because use cases describe actor goals, but SE14 says they do not show detailed algorithms. The stem must clarify broad behavioral scope versus detailed dynamic evolution before a unique answer is defensible.

evidence.quote: Choose a sequence diagram for message order between participants, a state machine for event-dependent state changes, and activity for workflow.

choices.label: A
choices.explanation: A component diagram shows structural components, interfaces and dependencies rather than dynamic evolution.

choices.label: B
choices.explanation: Use cases model external behavior/goals broadly, but not detailed message timing or state changes.

choices.label: C
choices.explanation: A deployment diagram places artifacts on nodes rather than describing dynamic behavior.

choices.label: D
choices.explanation: A class diagram shows static types and relationships rather than behavior unfolding over time.

reviews.answer_text: Problem analysis and solution design are both invoked by the wording.
reviews.hint: Read problem clarification versus choosing the solution in SE02.
reviews.explanation: SE02 assigns clarifying the problem to analysis and choosing architecture/interfaces/algorithms to design. The stem combines recognizing and understanding a problem with methods of overcoming it, so it crosses that boundary. Calling the activity creative does not resolve which part is intended. It needs a clear emphasis on problem understanding or solution construction to distinguish C from D.

evidence.quote: Analysis clarifies the problem; system design chooses architecture; object/detail design specifies interfaces and algorithms

choices.label: A
choices.explanation: Implementation writes the selected solution rather than primarily recognizing and analyzing the problem.

choices.label: B
choices.explanation: Testing evaluates behavior rather than defining the initial problem and solution methods.

choices.label: C
choices.explanation: Recognizing the problem and its constraints describes analysis.

choices.label: D
choices.explanation: Choosing methods to overcome the problem describes design; the stem also includes analysis language.

reviews.answer_text: Early delivery, smaller test scope and feedback are benefits; major needs a project goal.
reviews.hint: Read incremental delivery trade-offs in SE04.
reviews.explanation: SE04 supports early usable capability, smaller changes that can be easier to test/debug and feedback from increments. Thus A, C and D name benefits, while B combines two of them. The stem supplies no objective for ranking one benefit as major. An aggregate that omits feedback cannot become uniquely correct merely because it lists two valid points.

evidence.quote: Smaller changes can be easier to debug and permit feedback, though architecture and integration still require planning.

choices.label: A
choices.explanation: Smaller increments can be easier to test and debug, but major depends on the project objective.

choices.label: B
choices.explanation: Both included points are supported, but the stem supplies no reason to prioritize this partial combination.

choices.label: C
choices.explanation: User response to usable increments is a supported feedback benefit.

choices.label: D
choices.explanation: Early delivery is a supported reason to choose incremental development, but not universally the sole major benefit.

reviews.answer_text: Prototype learning and risk-driven spiral both fit different readings of the uncertainty.
reviews.hint: Read prototype purpose and spiral risk emphasis in SE07/SE06.
reviews.explanation: SE07 uses prototypes to explore incomplete requirements or technical feasibility, making B a direct fit for learning. Spiral can also use prototypes to reduce major technical risks before commitment. The stem does not specify whether the goal is exploratory learning, risk management or staged delivery. Waterfall lacks its usual stable/familiar conditions, but the remaining uncertainty does not uniquely choose one model.

evidence.quote: A prototype explores requirements, usability or technical feasibility.

choices.label: A
choices.explanation: Increments can support feedback, but the technical uncertainty may require additional exploration before delivery.

choices.label: B
choices.explanation: Prototyping directly explores unclear requirements and technical feasibility.

choices.label: C
choices.explanation: Spiral can address important technical risks, but explicit risk/commitment conditions are unstated.

choices.label: D
choices.explanation: Classical waterfall fits stable understood requirements and familiar technology, unlike the stated uncertainty.

reviews.answer_text: Cohesive reusable components and functional decomposition are modularization benefits.
reviews.hint: Read modularity, cohesion and information hiding in SE22.
reviews.explanation: SE22 supports smaller modules for reuse, understanding and maintenance, with high cohesion and low coupling. Functional decomposition and reusable cohesive components therefore both qualify. A reverses the ordinary maintenance benefit. Security can benefit from deliberate boundaries, but simply creating modules does not enforce security; D needs a specified access-control design rather than a blanket promise.

evidence.quote: Smaller modules can aid understanding, independent work, reuse and maintenance, but too many interfaces also create complexity.

choices.label: A
choices.explanation: This reverses the usual benefit; manageable cohesive components can be easier to maintain.

choices.label: B
choices.explanation: A cohesive component with a clear interface can be reused in another suitable context.

choices.label: C
choices.explanation: Functional decomposition divides the program into modules with related responsibilities.

choices.label: D
choices.explanation: Security may benefit from enforced boundaries, but modularization alone does not establish access protection.

reviews.answer_text: Poor object design can be hard to maintain; that is not an inherent property of every object-oriented design.
reviews.hint: Read object design benefits and complexity caveats in SE01/SE22.
reviews.explanation: SE01 says reuse, encapsulation and consistent models can ease change, but poor object design can still be complex. D can therefore describe a badly designed system, not a universal disadvantage of objects. A and C are benefits, and B can aid understanding subject to dependencies. The question omits the design conditions needed to make D a supported general disadvantage.

evidence.quote: Reuse, encapsulation and consistent models can reduce duplication and ease change; poor object design can still be complex.

choices.label: A
choices.explanation: Easier maintenance is a potential benefit rather than a disadvantage.

choices.label: B
choices.explanation: Understanding a suitably encapsulated object through its interface can be beneficial.

choices.label: C
choices.explanation: Potential component reuse is a benefit of suitable object design.

choices.label: D
choices.explanation: Objects can be hard to maintain under poor design, but difficulty is not inherent to object orientation.

reviews.answer_text: A directly misdefines a subsystem; B is also false if application domain means the underlying problem domain.
reviews.hint: Read logical subsystems and distinguish domain analysis from solution/design decomposition in SE21.
reviews.explanation: SE21 defines a subsystem as a logical collection, so A is the direct conventional false statement. It separately places subsystem decomposition in design rather than analysis of domain needs. B literally claims reduced application-domain complexity, not better management of design complexity; that can make B false too. A is uniquely intended only if B is read as a claim about managing solution structure, a qualification absent from the printed choice.

evidence.quote: A subsystem is a manageable logical collection with services and an interface; it need not be a physical replaceable artifact.
Analysis describes domain needs; subsystem decomposition is principally a design result.

choices.label: A
choices.explanation: This is directly false as a subsystem definition: a logical subsystem need not be physical or replaceable.

choices.label: B
choices.explanation: Also false on a literal underlying application-domain reading; managing design complexity would be a different, qualified claim.

choices.label: C
choices.explanation: Subsystem decomposition does divide the designed system into simpler responsibility groups.

choices.label: D
choices.explanation: Defined service interfaces can encapsulate the implementation, state and behavior of the contained classes.

reviews.answer_text: Change management process.
reviews.hint: Read request, impact, decision and implementation in SE33.
reviews.explanation: SE33 assigns handling change requests, impact assessment, decisions, implementation and validation to change management. Configuration management coordinates versions and baselines of affected artifacts, which supports that work but is a different focus. Inspection and general project management also contribute, yet B specifically names how proposed software changes are evaluated and incorporated.

evidence.quote: Change management handles request, impact assessment, decision/prioritization, implementation and validation

choices.label: A
choices.explanation: Configuration management maintains controlled versions and baselines rather than primarily deciding and incorporating requested changes.

choices.label: B
choices.explanation: Change management evaluates, approves/prioritizes, implements and validates proposed changes.

choices.label: C
choices.explanation: Inspection evaluates artifacts rather than defining the complete change-handling process.

choices.label: D
choices.explanation: Project management is broader than the specific process for handling software change requests.

reviews.answer_text: 9 days; the correct result is absent.
reviews.hint: Read parallel successors and longest-path completion in SE29.
reviews.explanation: A finishes at day 5. B and C then proceed in parallel, finishing at days 8 and 9 respectively. The project must wait for both, so earliest completion is 5+max(3,4)=9 days. Summing all three durations would ignore the parallelism. None of the four offered values is 9; D counts only the shorter branch.

evidence.quote: If A takes 5 days and B=3,C=4 both follow A, project duration is 5+max(3,4)=9 days.

choices.label: A
choices.explanation: Three days counts only B and omits A and the longer successor.

choices.label: B
choices.explanation: Four days counts only C and omits its predecessor A.

choices.label: C
choices.explanation: Five days stops at A before either required successor finishes.

choices.label: D
choices.explanation: Eight is A+B; the project still waits until C finishes at day 9.

reviews.answer_text: All listed factors can change requirements, scope or priorities; no valid exception is offered.
reviews.hint: Read scope/priorities changing with business and resources in SE40.
reviews.explanation: SE40 explicitly says markets, technology, stakeholders and funding can change scope or priorities. A, B and C are ordinary sources of evolving needs. Reduced funding can also force scope reduction or reprioritization, so D is not an unconditional exception. The negative question requires a genuinely irrelevant factor or a narrower definition of requirements change.

evidence.quote: Markets, technology, stakeholders and funding can all change scope or priorities.

choices.label: A
choices.explanation: Changed stakeholder needs are a direct reason to revise requirements.

choices.label: B
choices.explanation: Technology changes can create new constraints, opportunities or compatibility needs.

choices.label: C
choices.explanation: Market changes can alter business goals and therefore required behavior or priorities.

choices.label: D
choices.explanation: Funding changes can reduce scope or reorder requirements, so this is not a guaranteed exception.

reviews.answer_text: Splitting responsibilities is modularization; if behavior is preserved it is also refactoring.
reviews.hint: Read overlapping design concepts in SE22.
reviews.explanation: SE22 explicitly says splitting an unrelated three-purpose component improves modularity, and behavior-preserving restructuring is refactoring. The stem describes the structural split without saying whether refactoring’s preserved-behavior condition is intended. B directly fits, while A also fits under that ordinary condition. These concepts are not mutually exclusive, so a unique answer needs the requested emphasis.

evidence.quote: If behavior is preserved, the restructuring is refactoring; the words are not mutually exclusive answers.

choices.label: A
choices.explanation: The split is refactoring if it preserves externally observable behavior.

choices.label: B
choices.explanation: Separating unrelated responsibilities into cohesive components improves modularity.

choices.label: C
choices.explanation: No hidden implementation decision or access boundary is specifically identified as the defining change.

choices.label: D
choices.explanation: Refinement can be broad, but the stated split specifically concerns modular responsibility boundaries.

reviews.answer_text: Validation relates the product to customer needs; verification checks specified obligations.
reviews.hint: Read verification versus validation in SE34.
reviews.explanation: SE34 separates correct implementation of specifications from fitness for intended stakeholder needs. D describes verification. C’s customer-requirement traceability is relevant to validation, though tracing links alone is not sufficient evidence that needs are satisfied. A’s human-only versus computer-only split is false because both activities can use reviews, analysis and execution, so B also fails.

evidence.quote: Verification asks whether specified obligations are implemented correctly; validation asks whether the product meets intended stakeholder needs.

choices.label: A
choices.explanation: Both verification and validation can use human reviews, analysis and execution; the exclusive split is false.

choices.label: B
choices.explanation: A is false, so all choices cannot be correct.

choices.label: C
choices.explanation: Validation relates the built product to customer needs; traceability supports that connection but alone is not sufficient.

choices.label: D
choices.explanation: Verification checks that the specified functions and obligations are implemented correctly.

reviews.answer_text: Both paths are critical, each totaling 11 days.
reviews.hint: Compute each complete path using SE29.
reviews.explanation: The first path contains B5+C6=11 days, and the second D8+E3=11 days. Start/end are zero-duration in this stated network. Since both are equally longest, both are critical and the project duration is 11 days. The alternatives giving 14 days miscalculate; a supplied key choosing only one equal path would omit another valid critical path.

evidence.quote: If paths B5+C6 and D8+E3 share a zero-duration start/end, both total 11; there are two critical paths, not one.

choices.label: A
choices.explanation: A→B→C totals 5+6=11 days and ties for longest duration.

choices.label: B
choices.explanation: A→D→E totals 8+3=11 days and is equally critical.

choices.label: C
choices.explanation: The D/E path totals 11 days, not 14.

choices.label: D
choices.explanation: The B/C path totals 11 days, not 14.

reviews.answer_text: Testing provides evidence and reveals defects; it cannot generally guarantee complete conformance.
reviews.hint: Read the limits of testing in SE34.
reviews.explanation: SE34 says tests increase confidence and reveal defects but cannot generally guarantee correctness over every input. D states an unjustified guarantee, though checking specified requirements is a real testing aim. A is project scheduling, B broad lifecycle monitoring and C requirements/design production. No option accurately states the supported testing goal without overstating certainty.

evidence.quote: Tests increase confidence and reveal defects but cannot generally guarantee correctness over every possible input.

choices.label: A
choices.explanation: Meeting deadlines is a project-management outcome rather than the primary evidential purpose of testing.

choices.label: B
choices.explanation: Monitoring the whole lifecycle is broader assurance/control work rather than the specific goal of software tests.

choices.label: C
choices.explanation: Requirements and design documents are test inputs, not the primary output of executing tests.

choices.label: D
choices.explanation: Testing assesses conformance and reveals failures; it cannot generally guarantee every specified behavior.

reviews.answer_text: All four are legitimate architectural concerns; no valid exclusion is supplied.
reviews.hint: Read architecture views and design choices in SE23.
reviews.explanation: SE23 explicitly includes allocation to processors, decomposition and style selection among architectural concerns. Choosing an organization to deliver required behavior is also architectural design. A project may emphasize some decisions more than others, but none of these categories is inherently outside the architect’s scope. The negative question needs another option or a narrower project responsibility boundary.

evidence.quote: processor allocation, decomposition and style selection can all be architectural concerns.

choices.label: A
choices.explanation: Architectural organization must support the required behavior and is a legitimate design concern.

choices.label: B
choices.explanation: Mapping execution onto processors or cores is an allocation/concurrency architectural concern.

choices.label: C
choices.explanation: Decomposition of structural responsibilities is part of architectural organization.

choices.label: D
choices.explanation: Selecting architectural styles or patterns is a central architectural design decision.

reviews.answer_text: Both Agile scope/timing claims are false as universal lifecycle descriptions.
reviews.hint: Read adaptive scope, timeboxes and planning in SE05.
reviews.explanation: SE05 allows scope to be discussed before and during Sprint planning, directly contradicting D. It also describes fixed timeboxes with adaptive content, rather than B’s early fixed scope and routinely changing time/cost model. A captures classical up-front waterfall planning, while C describes functionality added in increments. Agile still plans; it does not forbid early agreement.

evidence.quote: Scope is discussed before and during planning; it is not forbidden to agree scope.

choices.label: A
choices.explanation: This is a reasonable description of classical planned waterfall baselines, not the false Agile claim.

choices.label: B
choices.explanation: This is false as a general Agile rule: content adapts while timeboxes tend to remain fixed.

choices.label: C
choices.explanation: Adding usable functionality through successive increments is consistent with incremental delivery.

choices.label: D
choices.explanation: This is false: Agile permits outlining and agreeing scope before iteration planning and delivery.

reviews.answer_text: Sequence and state-machine diagrams both describe behavior over time.
reviews.hint: Read message order versus event-dependent state changes in SE20.
reviews.explanation: SE20 explicitly says sequence and state diagrams both describe behavior over time. Sequence emphasizes interactions among participants, while state machines emphasize states and event-triggered transitions. A use case summarizes goals and flows without detailed temporal evolution, and a class diagram is static. Without narrowing messages versus states, C and D are both correct.

evidence.quote: Both sequence and state diagrams describe behavior over time.

choices.label: A
choices.explanation: Use cases describe goals/scenarios rather than the detailed temporal evolution targeted by these dynamic diagrams.

choices.label: B
choices.explanation: Class diagrams describe static types and relationships.

choices.label: C
choices.explanation: Sequence diagrams show ordered interactions across participant lifelines.

choices.label: D
choices.explanation: State machines show event-triggered changes among states over an object's lifecycle.

reviews.answer_text: Classical waterfall fits directly; a sequential V-model is also compatible with the broad wording.
reviews.hint: Read planned phases and V-model test pairing in SE03.
reviews.explanation: SE03 defines classical waterfall through separated planned phases and reviewed deliverables, making A the direct conventional description. The V-model also organizes staged development with paired testing levels, though test planning begins early. The stem gives only sequential phase completion and does not distinguish simple waterfall from that related staged organization, so A cannot exclude D without a narrower convention.

evidence.quote: The V-model pairs specification/design stages with later test levels.

choices.label: A
choices.explanation: Classical waterfall directly matches the conventional sequential phase-completion description.

choices.label: B
choices.explanation: Agile adapts content through feedback rather than requiring the stated rigid phase sequence.

choices.label: C
choices.explanation: Spiral is organized around repeated risk-driven cycles rather than one simple sequential pass.

choices.label: D
choices.explanation: A V-model can be staged sequentially while pairing development and tests, so the broad wording overlaps.

reviews.answer_text: Normal conditions alone do not distinguish functional, performance or usability testing.
reviews.hint: Read test purpose separately from workload conditions in SE36.
reviews.explanation: SE36 explicitly warns that normal operating conditions do not distinguish functional from performance testing. Functional tests check required behavior; performance tests measure speed/resources at a workload, and usability can also be assessed under ordinary use. The stem provides no metric, specification obligation or user-task objective. Stress is the contrasting above-normal condition, but excluding it does not select one remaining purpose.

evidence.quote: “Normal operating conditions” alone does not distinguish functional from performance testing.

choices.label: A
choices.explanation: Stress testing exceeds normal limits rather than using only normal operating conditions.

choices.label: B
choices.explanation: Performance can be measured under normal load, but no speed/resource metric is stated.

choices.label: C
choices.explanation: Functional behavior can be checked under normal conditions, but no specified service is identified.

choices.label: D
choices.explanation: Usability can be evaluated during normal tasks, but the stem states no user-success criterion.

reviews.answer_text: An actor is an external role; person/system and user-role descriptions overlap imperfectly.
reviews.hint: Read roles rather than specific individuals in SE14.
reviews.explanation: SE14 defines an actor as an external interacting role and says one person may play several roles. B gives common actor participants but does not state that abstraction; D describes a user role but omits external systems and leaves in the system unclear. Both can fit the intended role under suitable boundary interpretation. The question needs the precise external-role definition to be unique.

evidence.quote: An actor is an external role interacting with the system; it can be a person, device or another system.

choices.label: A
choices.explanation: An internal component is not an external actor merely because it performs actions.

choices.label: B
choices.explanation: People and external systems can play actor roles, but actors model roles rather than individual participants.

choices.label: C
choices.explanation: A diagram is a model artifact, not the external role represented within it.

choices.label: D
choices.explanation: A user role can be an actor if external to the chosen system boundary; this is not limited to people.

reviews.answer_text: Extend adds conditional additional behavior to a meaningful base use case.
reviews.hint: Read extension points and base independence in SE16.
reviews.explanation: SE16 says extend adds conditional behavior at extension points and leaves the base meaningful independently. B captures the optional/conditional nature and C captures the added behavior, so both work. Required reused behavior is factored with include. Actor associations are a different relationship and do not describe the extension-to-base arrow.

evidence.quote: Extend adds conditional behavior at extension points

choices.label: A
choices.explanation: Factoring required shared steps is the include relationship, not the distinctive extend purpose.

choices.label: B
choices.explanation: Extend can represent conditional additional behavior that need not occur in every base execution.

choices.label: C
choices.explanation: Extend adds behavior to an existing independently meaningful base use case.

choices.label: D
choices.explanation: Actor/use-case association is distinct from the extend relation between use cases.

reviews.answer_text: An exception flow is an alternative path handling an error or failure.
reviews.hint: Read alternatives and failure flows in SE15.
reviews.explanation: SE15 assigns exception flows to failure handling, while alternate flows describe conditional variations. A states the defining error/exception purpose. B is also true in the broad sense that an error-handling path is an alternative to the main success flow; it is less specific and not every alternative is an exception. Exceptions need not terminate the entire use case.

evidence.quote: An alternate flow is a conditional variation; an exception flow handles a failure.

choices.label: A
choices.explanation: Handling an error or failure is the defining exception-flow purpose.

choices.label: B
choices.explanation: A failure-handling route is an alternative to the main success path, though not every alternative is exceptional.

choices.label: C
choices.explanation: An exception may request correction or recover; termination is not its universal purpose.

choices.label: D
choices.explanation: Relations among actors are not the failure-handling steps of an exception flow.

reviews.answer_text: Composition is intended, but diamond placement and absolute lifetime wording need clarification.
reviews.hint: Read whole-end filled diamonds and detachment in SE18.
reviews.explanation: SE18 places the composition diamond at the whole, Car, rather than describing it as pointing to Engine. It requires strong ownership and destruction of parts still owned, but permits model-defined detachment or transfer. C is the simplified intended answer yet overstates cannot exist without it; B can be true for a detached engine. The absent placement/lifecycle assumptions prevent a unique literal claim.

evidence.quote: Parts may be detached/transferred under a defined model. Thus “cannot ever exist independently” is an oversimplification.

choices.label: A
choices.explanation: Temporary use is a dependency rather than the strong ownership of composition.

choices.label: B
choices.explanation: A detached/transferred engine can survive under a defined model, so independence needs a lifecycle qualification.

choices.label: C
choices.explanation: It captures the intended whole/part relationship but overstates permanent lifetime dependence.

choices.label: D
choices.explanation: Inheritance uses a generalization triangle rather than the filled composition diamond.

reviews.answer_text: Poor suitability when requirements have substantial change risk.
reviews.hint: Read stable requirements and costly late feedback in SE03.
reviews.explanation: SE03 says waterfall fits stable understood requirements and familiar technology. Late feedback can make changes costly, so moderate-to-high requirement-change risk is a direct disadvantage. Simplicity and milestone visibility are advantages. Sequential phase organization characterizes the classical model; it can contribute to rigidity, but C explicitly identifies the adverse scenario asked for.

evidence.quote: It fits well-understood, stable requirements and familiar technology; late feedback makes changes costly.

choices.label: A
choices.explanation: Simplicity and ease of understanding are presented as advantages rather than the adverse scenario.

choices.label: B
choices.explanation: Manageable milestones can be an advantage of planned rigidity, despite its trade-offs.

choices.label: C
choices.explanation: Likely requirement changes make late feedback and rigid commitments costly.

choices.label: D
choices.explanation: Sequential phases describe the model; C more directly states the requested disadvantage.

reviews.answer_text: Respond within two seconds under normal load: a performance requirement.
reviews.hint: Read measurable response-time qualities in SE10.
reviews.explanation: SE10 identifies response time under a stated workload as measurable performance, a nonfunctional quality. B supplies that kind of target. Generating a PDF and submitting an emergency report are observable functions. C mixes a storage service with a technology constraint, but it does not state the clear measurable quality that B does; technology constraints may be classified separately.

evidence.quote: Performance concerns response time, throughput and resource use

choices.label: A
choices.explanation: Generating a PDF report is an observable system function.

choices.label: B
choices.explanation: A two-second response target under normal load specifies measurable performance quality.

choices.label: C
choices.explanation: This states a storage capability plus technology choice rather than the explicit performance quality in B.

choices.label: D
choices.explanation: Submitting an emergency report is an observable service and therefore functional.

reviews.answer_text: Structural things.
reviews.hint: Read static conceptual/physical elements in SE17.
reviews.explanation: SE17 explicitly describes structural things as conceptual or physical structural elements. They make up the static model in contrast with behavior over time. Behavioral things cover dynamic aspects, grouping organizes elements and annotations add explanatory information rather than being the static elements themselves. Thus A directly matches both parts of the definition.

evidence.quote: Structural things describe conceptual or physical structural elements.

choices.label: A
choices.explanation: Structural things are the static conceptual or physical building blocks described.

choices.label: B
choices.explanation: Behavioral things concern dynamic behavior rather than the static structural elements.

choices.label: C
choices.explanation: Annotations add explanatory information rather than defining the static structural building blocks.

choices.label: D
choices.explanation: Grouping organizes model elements rather than being the stated conceptual/physical structural category.

reviews.answer_text: Functional requirements specify observable behavior; nonfunctional requirements specify qualities or constraints. Example: generate a PDF report versus respond within two seconds under a stated load.
reviews.hint: Read behavior in SE09 and measurable qualities in SE10.
reviews.explanation: SE09 includes required and prohibited services, so generating a PDF report is functional. SE10 specifies qualities such as performance, usability and availability; a response-time threshold under defined load is nonfunctional. Security mechanisms can implement functional behavior as well as support quality goals, so a negative or security-related statement is not automatically nonfunctional.

evidence.quote: A functional requirement states an observable service or behavior, including reactions to inputs, errors and forbidden actions.

reviews.answer_text: Low coupling limits dependencies, so changes remain local and modules are easier to understand, replace, test and maintain.
reviews.hint: Read dependencies and stable interfaces in SE22.
reviews.explanation: SE22 measures coupling through dependencies between modules and recommends low coupling with high cohesion. Shared mutable data and knowledge of another module’s representation increase the chance that one change affects others. Stable interfaces and information hiding constrain that impact. More interfaces can add complexity, so minimizing harmful dependencies matters more than simply maximizing the number of modules.

evidence.quote: Shared mutable data and knowledge of another module’s internal representation increase coupling.

reviews.answer_text: Waterfall uses planned, reviewed stages and suits stable requirements; Agile emphasizes collaboration, working results, feedback and adaptation.
reviews.hint: Read waterfall trade-offs in SE03 and Agile values in SE05.
reviews.explanation: SE03 describes planned phases with costly late feedback, useful for stable requirements and familiar technology. SE05 values customer participation and adaptation with useful working increments. Agile still plans and documents; waterfall can revisit work under control. The practical difference is feedback and commitment organization, not a claim that one process forbids change or the other forbids documentation.

evidence.quote: Agile favors people collaborating, useful working results, customer participation and adaptation over rigid adherence to procedures, exhaustive documents, contracts or fixed plans.

reviews.answer_text: Include factors required reused behavior, with base→included; extend adds conditional behavior, with extension→base.
reviews.hint: Read arrow direction and independent base meaning in SE16.
reviews.explanation: SE16 uses include for reused required behavior incorporated when the inclusion point is reached. Extend adds behavior at extension points under a condition, and the base remains meaningful independently. The dashed arrows have different directions: including use case toward included, and extending use case toward base. Neither relation should be confused with actor association or specialization generalization.

evidence.quote: with the arrow from the extension to the base. The base is meaningful independently.

reviews.answer_text: Maintenance can dominate cost because it lasts years and repeatedly requires legacy understanding, changes, regression testing and release work.
reviews.hint: Read corrective, adaptive, perfective and preventive evolution in SE40.
reviews.explanation: SE40 says maintenance often spans years and includes understanding existing code plus regression effort. Work is not limited to bug fixes: environments, useful capabilities and future risks also change. Repeated impact analysis, implementation and testing accumulate across the operational lifetime, so maintenance may dominate lifecycle cost. This is a common outcome, not a guarantee for every project.

evidence.quote: Maintenance often lasts years and includes understanding legacy code and regression effort, so it may dominate lifecycle cost.

reviews.answer_text: Traditional/procedural decomposition.
reviews.hint: Read functions versus objects in SE01.
reviews.explanation: SE01 contrasts procedural decomposition organized around functions with object-oriented decomposition organized around objects combining state and behavior. B is the available traditional/procedural label for functions operating on data. Agile and iterative describe lifecycle organization rather than this decomposition paradigm, and either can be used with procedural or object-oriented programming.

evidence.quote: Procedural decomposition organizes functions; object oriented decomposition organizes objects with state and behavior.

choices.label: A
choices.explanation: Object orientation combines state and behavior in objects rather than organizing primarily around separate procedures.

choices.label: B
choices.explanation: Traditional/procedural decomposition organizes functions and procedures acting on data.

choices.label: C
choices.explanation: Agile concerns process adaptation rather than requiring function-based decomposition.

choices.label: D
choices.explanation: Iteration describes revisiting development work and does not determine procedural versus object decomposition.

reviews.answer_text: Reusability.
reviews.hint: Read reuse and encapsulation as distinct benefits in SE01.
reviews.explanation: The stem explicitly asks about using existing classes elsewhere without rewriting them, which is reuse. SE01 lists reuse alongside encapsulation and consistent models as ways to reduce duplication and ease change. Encapsulation and abstraction can make reuse safer, while polymorphism supports compatible varying implementations, but those are enabling concepts rather than the name of the capability described.

evidence.quote: Reuse, encapsulation and consistent models can reduce duplication and ease change

choices.label: A
choices.explanation: Encapsulation hides implementation and can enable reuse, but it is not the capability's name.

choices.label: B
choices.explanation: Polymorphism supports differing implementations through compatible interfaces rather than directly naming reuse.

choices.label: C
choices.explanation: Reusability means using suitable existing classes or components in other contexts without rewriting them.

choices.label: D
choices.explanation: Abstraction exposes relevant contracts and can assist reuse, but the requested property is reusability.

reviews.answer_text: Software evolution.
reviews.hint: Read postdeployment changes in SE40.
reviews.explanation: SE40 describes maintenance and evolution through change requests, impact analysis, planning, implementation/testing and release. Updating a deployed product to meet changing customer needs belongs to evolution among the four broad process activities. Specification, implementation and validation still occur within that work, but D names the lifecycle-wide change activity asked for rather than one constituent task.

evidence.quote: A typical evolution sequence is change request→impact analysis→release planning→implementation/testing→release.

choices.label: A
choices.explanation: Specification captures needs but does not name the overall postdeployment change activity.

choices.label: B
choices.explanation: Design/implementation is part of making a change rather than the broad evolution activity.

choices.label: C
choices.explanation: Validation checks the changed product against needs rather than naming ongoing adaptation itself.

choices.label: D
choices.explanation: Evolution updates existing software as stakeholder needs and operating conditions change.

reviews.answer_text: Plan-driven process.
reviews.hint: Read planned stages and controlled commitments in SE03/SE02.
reviews.explanation: The stem defines up-front planning and measurement against that plan. B names the plan-driven organization, illustrated by SE03’s planned phases and reviewed deliverables. Incremental delivery and evolution describe how results grow or change and can coexist with planning. Agile also plans, but it emphasizes adaptation rather than defining all activity commitments in advance as stated here.

evidence.quote: Classical waterfall separates planned phases with reviewed deliverables.

choices.label: A
choices.explanation: Agile uses planning but adapts content as feedback arrives rather than defining this fixed up-front emphasis.

choices.label: B
choices.explanation: Plan-driven explicitly organizes activities and progress measurement around an advance plan.

choices.label: C
choices.explanation: Incremental describes staged capability delivery and does not alone specify up-front planning commitments.

choices.label: D
choices.explanation: Evolutionary describes progressive change rather than necessarily advance planning of all activities.

reviews.answer_text: Requirements Specification.
reviews.hint: Read the SRS and agreed system obligations in SE08.
reviews.explanation: SE08 states that the Software Requirements Specification organizes agreed requirements. That is the artifact describing what the system should do for client/developer agreement. Analysis models support technical discussion, a use-case diagram captures only selected goals/relationships and a design document describes solution decisions. None replaces the overall agreed requirements specification.

evidence.quote: The Software Requirements Specification (SRS) organizes the agreed requirements.

choices.label: A
choices.explanation: Analysis models formalize selected aspects for discussion rather than replacing the full agreed requirements document.

choices.label: B
choices.explanation: A use-case diagram shows goals and roles but not the complete requirements specification.

choices.label: C
choices.explanation: The requirements specification organizes the agreed services and constraints the system must satisfy.

choices.label: D
choices.explanation: A design document describes how the solution is organized rather than the complete statement of required behavior.

reviews.answer_text: In the taught convention, natural-language client specification versus symbolic/diagrammatic analysis models.
reviews.hint: Read the module-specific representation convention in SE08.
reviews.explanation: SE08 explicitly describes natural-language specification for clients and analysis models that formalize it for technical discussion. B matches that teaching convention. This is not a universal ban on diagrams in an SRS: the note immediately allows them in real specifications. The other choices reverse the convention or impose unsupported exclusive audiences and purposes.

evidence.quote: In the module, a natural-language specification communicates with clients while analysis models formalize it for technical discussion; real specifications can also contain diagrams.

choices.label: A
choices.explanation: It reverses the natural-language specification versus formalized-model convention taught in the note.

choices.label: B
choices.explanation: This matches the taught convention, while real requirements specifications can also include diagrams.

choices.label: C
choices.explanation: The taught distinction does use different representation emphases rather than identical forms.

choices.label: D
choices.explanation: Neither artifact has the exclusive audience or testing-only purpose asserted here.

reviews.answer_text: External interacting roles played by people, devices or other systems.
reviews.hint: Read actor scope and system boundary in SE14.
reviews.explanation: SE14 explicitly permits a person, device or other system to play an external actor role. B is the only option including those categories. Actors are not restricted to primary users or humans, and internal components are inside the chosen system boundary rather than external roles. One person may play several actors, so actor instances should not be confused with individual people.

evidence.quote: An actor is an external role interacting with the system; it can be a person, device or another system.

choices.label: A
choices.explanation: Actors can be devices or external systems as well as human users.

choices.label: B
choices.explanation: People, devices and external systems can play roles interacting across the system boundary.

choices.label: C
choices.explanation: Supporting and administrative external roles can be actors, not only primary goal-seeking users.

choices.label: D
choices.explanation: Internal components are not external actor roles under the chosen system boundary.

reviews.answer_text: Nonfunctional performance requirement.
reviews.hint: Read response-time quality targets in SE10.
reviews.explanation: SE10 identifies response time as a performance quality. A one-second threshold constrains how well a service responds rather than naming the service itself, so C is the appropriate category. A complete measurable requirement should also define the operation, load and timing conditions. Those omissions affect test precision, not the underlying classification of the stated response-time target.

evidence.quote: Performance concerns response time, throughput and resource use

choices.label: A
choices.explanation: The statement constrains response speed rather than specifying which service is performed.

choices.label: B
choices.explanation: The specific quality is performance; this is not primarily a technology or implementation constraint.

choices.label: C
choices.explanation: The one-second limit is a nonfunctional response-time/performance target.

choices.label: D
choices.explanation: No domain-specific business rule is stated; the obligation concerns a general performance quality.

reviews.answer_text: System/technology constraint requirement.
reviews.hint: Read technology requirements separately from measurable qualities in SE10.
reviews.explanation: SE10 explicitly calls Use Java a technology/pseudo-requirement, often classified separately as a system constraint. C is therefore the most specific offered category. Some broad taxonomies put constraints under nonfunctional requirements, making B a broader possible description, but Quality Requirement would imply a measurable quality and Functional Requirement an observable service. The wording asks best classified, favoring C.

evidence.quote: “Use Java” is a technology/pseudo-requirement, often separately classified as a system constraint.

choices.label: A
choices.explanation: Choosing an implementation language does not itself specify an observable system service.

choices.label: B
choices.explanation: Some taxonomies include constraints under nonfunctional requirements, but C is the more specific category here.

choices.label: C
choices.explanation: Mandating Java constrains implementation technology rather than naming behavior or a measurable quality.

choices.label: D
choices.explanation: A programming-language choice is not itself a measured quality such as performance or usability.

reviews.answer_text: Compatibility.
reviews.hint: Read cooperating environments versus moving environments in SE10.
reviews.explanation: SE10 distinguishes compatibility, which concerns cooperating environments, from portability, which concerns moving environments. Supporting different browsers and devices in the question is the offered compatibility category. Reliability concerns failure-free service, scalability concerns growth and usability concerns task success/ease of learning. None of those names the stated cross-environment cooperation requirement as directly.

evidence.quote: compatibility concerns cooperating environments; portability concerns moving environments

choices.label: A
choices.explanation: Reliability concerns failure-free service rather than which browsers and devices can cooperate with the system.

choices.label: B
choices.explanation: Scalability concerns handling increased workload rather than cross-browser/device compatibility.

choices.label: C
choices.explanation: Usability concerns ease of learning and successful tasks, not the supported environment set itself.

choices.label: D
choices.explanation: Compatibility addresses operating/cooperating across the specified browsers and device environments.

reviews.answer_text: Portability is the exception to the usual central dependability categories.
reviews.hint: Read dependability versus platform movement in SE10.
reviews.explanation: SE10 explicitly includes reliability, safety and robustness in dependability and says portability is not its usual central category. Portability instead concerns moving environments. Thus D is the listed exception. The distinction does not imply portability never affects practical service outcomes, only that it is a different quality category from the taught dependability grouping.

evidence.quote: Dependability includes reliability, safety and robustness; portability is not its usual central category.

choices.label: A
choices.explanation: Reliability is explicitly included in the taught dependability grouping.

choices.label: B
choices.explanation: Robustness is explicitly included in the broader dependability concept.

choices.label: C
choices.explanation: Safety is explicitly included among dependability concerns.

choices.label: D
choices.explanation: Portability concerns moving environments rather than the usual central dependability categories.

reviews.answer_text: Identifying use cases by abstracting concrete scenarios.
reviews.hint: Read scenario instances versus use-case abstraction in SE13.
reviews.explanation: SE13 calls a scenario one concrete execution and a use case an abstraction of related success and alternative scenarios. Formalizing those interactions into the more general use-case description therefore identifies use cases. Identifying actors establishes external roles, identifying scenarios captures individual executions and later refinement adds detail to an already identified use case.

evidence.quote: A scenario is one concrete execution; a use case abstracts the related successful and alternative scenarios.

choices.label: A
choices.explanation: Actor identification establishes external roles rather than generalizing scenario executions into interaction descriptions.

choices.label: B
choices.explanation: Use cases abstract related concrete scenarios into structured goal-oriented interaction descriptions.

choices.label: C
choices.explanation: Scenario identification captures concrete executions rather than their use-case abstraction.

choices.label: D
choices.explanation: Refinement elaborates an existing use case; the scenario-to-use-case abstraction is the identification step asked here.

reviews.answer_text: Document exceptions separately from the main success flow.
reviews.hint: Read use-case writing at one abstraction level with explicit actors and alternatives.
reviews.explanation: SE15 instructs writers to use active subject–verb steps and separate errors from normal flow. C follows that rule directly. Passive voice hides responsibility, detailed UI design distracts from goal-level behavior, and combining unrelated tasks does not produce a clear use case. The distinction concerns organizing scenarios rather than omitting exception handling.

evidence.quote: Use active subject–verb steps at one abstraction level; separate errors from the normal flow.

choices.label: A
choices.explanation: Passive voice makes responsibility less clear, contrary to the active subject–verb guideline.

choices.label: B
choices.explanation: Detailed UI elements are not the goal-level behavior and flow structure emphasized by the guide.

choices.label: C
choices.explanation: Separating exception behavior keeps the main success flow clear while still documenting failures.

choices.label: D
choices.explanation: Combining multiple unrelated tasks sacrifices a coherent goal and consistent abstraction level.

reviews.answer_text: Technical risks and constraints are not one of the three initial FAST lists.
reviews.hint: Read the three categories in the taught FAST elicitation procedure.
reviews.explanation: SE12 explicitly lists environment elements, outputs and inputs as the initial participant categories. A, B and D match them. Technical risks and constraints can matter elsewhere in engineering, but they are not one of those three named initial FAST lists. The negative question asks about that procedure, not whether risk information is ever useful.

evidence.quote: In the taught FAST technique, participants list environment elements, outputs and inputs,

choices.label: A
choices.explanation: Environment elements are explicitly one of the initial FAST categories.

choices.label: B
choices.explanation: System outputs are explicitly included in the three initial lists.

choices.label: C
choices.explanation: Risks and constraints are not one of the specified environment/output/input categories.

choices.label: D
choices.explanation: Inputs and things the system uses are part of the stated initial categories.

reviews.answer_text: Exciting requirements.
reviews.hint: Read normal, expected and exciting customer needs in QFD.
reviews.explanation: SE12 distinguishes explicitly stated normal needs, assumed expected needs and exciting needs that bring unanticipated benefit. Features exceeding expectations and producing additional satisfaction match the exciting category. Calling them merely implicit would confuse customer assumptions with unexpected added value rather than identify the QFD term.

evidence.quote: QFD prioritizes customer value: normal needs are explicitly stated, expected needs are assumed, and exciting needs provide unanticipated benefit.

choices.label: A
choices.explanation: Normal requirements are explicitly stated needs rather than unexpected extra benefits.

choices.label: B
choices.explanation: Expected requirements are assumed by customers and do not denote surprising added satisfaction.

choices.label: C
choices.explanation: Exciting requirements deliver unanticipated benefit beyond the customer’s expectations.

choices.label: D
choices.explanation: Implicit describes assumed needs more generally, not the QFD category for unanticipated benefits.

reviews.answer_text: Consistency.
reviews.hint: Read the validation property that excludes contradictions.
reviews.explanation: SE11 directly defines consistency as excluding contradictions. Completeness covers agreed scope, clarity gives one intended interpretation, and correctness reflects stakeholder needs. A specification can be complete yet inconsistent, or clear yet wrong, so these properties cannot substitute for the precise no-contradictions condition.

evidence.quote: Consistency excludes contradictions.

choices.label: A
choices.explanation: Completeness concerns covering scope and behavior, not whether requirements contradict each other.

choices.label: B
choices.explanation: Consistency requires the specification’s statements to coexist without contradiction.

choices.label: C
choices.explanation: Clarity addresses interpretive ambiguity rather than logical compatibility between requirements.

choices.label: D
choices.explanation: Correctness concerns actual stakeholder needs, a different validation property.

reviews.answer_text: Stable requirements and familiar, stable technology.
reviews.hint: Read the fit between planned phases and low expected change.
reviews.explanation: SE03 says classical waterfall fits well-understood stable requirements and familiar technology, directly supporting C among these alternatives. Frequent change, evolving needs and early small deliveries call for feedback or incremental capability rather than waterfall’s late feedback. Short duration alone is not a proof, but C also supplies the decisive stability conditions stated in the note.

evidence.quote: It fits well-understood, stable requirements and familiar technology; late feedback makes changes costly.

choices.label: A
choices.explanation: Frequent requirement changes make late-feedback sequential planning a poor fit.

choices.label: B
choices.explanation: Large evolving needs do not establish the stable requirements that favor classical waterfall.

choices.label: C
choices.explanation: Constant requirements and stable technology match the note’s stated waterfall selection conditions.

choices.label: D
choices.explanation: Prioritized usable small deliveries are the rationale for incremental delivery rather than a single sequential release.

reviews.answer_text: Waterfall makes late change costly; none states that limitation accurately and uniquely.
reviews.hint: Distinguish expensive controlled rework from absolute inability to change.
reviews.explanation: SE03 explicitly rejects the claim that completed phases make change physically impossible; projects revisit work under control. B is therefore an overstatement of the intended disadvantage. Skilled developers are needed across approaches, waterfall provides milestone visibility, and it supports reviewed documentation. The supported drawback—costly late feedback and rework—is absent as an accurate offered option.

evidence.quote: It does not make change physically impossible: real projects revisit work under control, and modified waterfall explicitly includes feedback.

choices.label: A
choices.explanation: Developer skill is needed across approaches and is not a unique waterfall disadvantage.

choices.label: B
choices.explanation: Late changes can be costly, but cannot accommodate them at all contradicts SE03.

choices.label: C
choices.explanation: Waterfall’s reviewed phase deliverables provide clear milestone visibility rather than eliminate it.

choices.label: D
choices.explanation: Planned deliverables and documentation are supported, so this is not a waterfall limitation.

reviews.answer_text: Iteration refines a solution; increments add usable functionality. B is an overspecified conventional contrast.
reviews.hint: Read revisiting versus adding capability and how both can coexist.
reviews.explanation: SE04 distinguishes iteration from increments by refinement versus added usable capability. A reverses them, while C erases the distinction. B can describe a particular process but wrongly makes a complete development cycle and self-contained stacked pieces universal. The note says iteration need not rebuild the whole system and increments need not be perfectly independent, so the general correct distinction is not stated precisely.

evidence.quote: Iteration revisits and improves a solution; an increment adds usable functionality. A process may do both.

choices.label: A
choices.explanation: This reverses the refinement-versus-added-functionality distinction given in SE04.

choices.label: B
choices.explanation: This describes a conventional organization but overstates complete cycles and self-contained pieces as universal requirements.

choices.label: C
choices.explanation: The concepts differ even though one process can combine both.

choices.label: D
choices.explanation: Risk analysis is not the structural distinction between iteration and incremental delivery.

reviews.answer_text: Large size and future change do not uniquely distinguish iterative from incremental development.
reviews.hint: Read process selection using delivery needs, uncertainty and feedback.
reviews.explanation: SE04 permits processes to be both iterative and incremental, while SE02 requires more than one broad project characteristic to select a model. C addresses refinement after change; D supports adding capability with feedback. The stem supplies no early-delivery priorities, refinement objective or assurance constraints to rank them uniquely. Stable-phase models are not the natural change-focused contrast, but that does not isolate one alternative.

evidence.quote: Iteration revisits and improves a solution; an increment adds usable functionality. A process may do both.

choices.label: A
choices.explanation: Expected change does not supply the stable-requirement rationale normally favoring classical waterfall.

choices.label: B
choices.explanation: The V-model’s paired assurance structure is not uniquely selected by large size and future change.

choices.label: C
choices.explanation: Iteration supports revisiting and refining a changing solution.

choices.label: D
choices.explanation: Incremental delivery can add capability and incorporate feedback; it can also be iterative.

reviews.answer_text: User stories.
reviews.hint: Read small user needs versus timeboxes and broader work groupings.
reviews.explanation: SE05 defines a user story as a small user need and value supported by acceptance criteria. Sprints and iterations name cycles or timeboxes, not the need itself. An epic groups broader work. C therefore names the small functional work unit intended here, without claiming that Agile requirements consist only of story text.

evidence.quote: A user story states a small user need and value, supported by acceptance criteria; an epic groups broader work.

choices.label: A
choices.explanation: A Sprint is a timeboxed development interval rather than the individual user need.

choices.label: B
choices.explanation: An iteration is a cycle of work or refinement, not a small functional requirement.

choices.label: C
choices.explanation: A user story states a small user need and its value with acceptance criteria.

choices.label: D
choices.explanation: An epic groups broader work rather than naming the smaller story-sized need.

reviews.answer_text: Risk analysis and reduction in every spiral cycle.
reviews.hint: Read what drives spiral objectives, work and commitment.
reviews.explanation: SE06 defines spiral development as risk driven, with each cycle identifying objectives and alternatives, assessing and reducing risks, producing a result and planning commitment.
