That emphasis distinguishes it from merely repeating phases or delivering only at the end. It can adapt requirements and combine other activities rather than enforcing an unchangeable initial specification.

evidence.quote: Spiral development is risk driven. Each cycle identifies objectives and alternatives, assesses and reduces important risks,

choices.label: A
choices.explanation: A spiral can contain staged work, but sequential completion is not its defining driver.

choices.label: B
choices.explanation: Risk assessment and reduction guide each cycle’s work and further commitment.

choices.label: C
choices.explanation: Only delivering at the end is not the distinguishing spiral principle.

choices.label: D
choices.explanation: A risk-driven cycle can revise plans and requirements rather than rigidly freeze them.

reviews.answer_text: Coding/implementation.
reviews.hint: Read the V-model’s transition from specification/design to testing.
reviews.explanation: SE03 explicitly places coding at the bottom of the V while specification and design stages correspond to later testing levels. Requirements therefore begin the development side rather than occupy the bottom; deployment and maintenance are not that connecting implementation activity. This is a model-diagram convention, not a claim that all real work follows a perfect geometric sequence.

evidence.quote: Coding lies at the bottom. Test planning starts early.

choices.label: A
choices.explanation: Requirements occur on the specification side, not at the coding bottom of the V.

choices.label: B
choices.explanation: Deployment is not the implementation activity joining the V-model’s sides.

choices.label: C
choices.explanation: The note explicitly identifies coding as the bottom of the V.

choices.label: D
choices.explanation: Maintenance occurs in lifecycle evolution rather than at this implementation point.

reviews.answer_text: OMG is the standardizing/maintaining organization; the stem conflates that role with original development.
reviews.hint: Read what the note attributes to OMG and separate standards stewardship from invention.
reviews.explanation: SE17 explicitly attributes UML standardization and maintenance to OMG, making C the intended standards-body answer. It does not establish that an organization originally developed every part of the notation. The stem combines developed by with to standardize without fixing that historical scope. C is supported for stewardship, while the stronger origin claim cannot be certified from the stated note.

evidence.quote: UML is maintained and standardized by OMG; it is a modeling language, not a lifecycle process.

choices.label: A
choices.explanation: The note attributes UML standardization and maintenance to OMG rather than IEEE.

choices.label: B
choices.explanation: ISO is not the organization credited with UML stewardship in SE17.

choices.label: C
choices.explanation: OMG is explicitly the standardizing/maintaining body; original development is a different claim in the stem.

choices.label: D
choices.explanation: W3C is not the UML stewardship organization identified in the note.

reviews.answer_text: The system boundary box.
reviews.hint: Read which elements belong inside and outside a use-case diagram’s rectangle.
reviews.explanation: SE14 says actors are outside the system-boundary rectangle and use-case ovals are inside. The enclosing rectangle therefore marks the modeled system’s boundary. A context may be communicated by the diagram, but it is not the specific box name requested; packages and modules serve different grouping roles rather than defining this external actor boundary.

evidence.quote: Draw actors outside the system boundary rectangle and use-case ovals inside.

choices.label: A
choices.explanation: System context is broader information, not the specific name of this enclosing boundary rectangle.

choices.label: B
choices.explanation: The rectangle separates the modeled system’s use cases from external actor roles.

choices.label: C
choices.explanation: A package groups modeling elements but is not the stated system/actor boundary.

choices.label: D
choices.explanation: Module frame is not the use-case system-boundary term defined in SE14.

reviews.answer_text: Include incorporates required behavior when the inclusion is reached; every base execution need not reach it.
reviews.hint: Read required inclusion versus optional extension and conditional base branches.
reviews.explanation: SE16 defines include as factoring required reused behavior, but explicitly warns against inferring that every conditional branch in the base executes. B is correct if always means whenever that inclusion point is reached; it is too strong if it means every possible execution of the base. The other choices describe extension, generalization or timing rather than inclusion.

evidence.quote: Included behavior is incorporated where the inclusion is reached; do not infer every conditional branch in the base always executes.

choices.label: A
choices.explanation: Optional conditional added behavior describes extend rather than include.

choices.label: B
choices.explanation: Required at the reached inclusion point is correct; always for every base path overstates the relationship.

choices.label: C
choices.explanation: Inheritance or specialization is modeled by generalization rather than include.

choices.label: D
choices.explanation: Include specifies incorporated behavior, not an execution-time constraint.

reviews.answer_text: Protected visibility.
reviews.hint: Read UML class-member visibility symbols.
reviews.explanation: SE17 lists + public, - private, # protected and ~ package. The requested hash marker therefore means protected access. These symbols indicate visibility of a class member; they do not express object multiplicity, inheritance direction or class ownership, and the other choices correspond to different explicit markers.

evidence.quote: + public, - private, # protected and ~ package indicate visibility.

choices.label: A
choices.explanation: Public visibility is marked with + rather than #.

choices.label: B
choices.explanation: Private visibility is marked with - rather than #.

choices.label: C
choices.explanation: The note explicitly assigns # to protected visibility.

choices.label: D
choices.explanation: Package visibility uses ~ rather than the protected # marker.

reviews.answer_text: Shared aggregation.
reviews.hint: Read hollow versus filled whole-part diamonds.
reviews.explanation: SE18 defines shared aggregation with a hollow diamond at the whole end. Composition instead uses a filled diamond; dependency is a dashed arrow and generalization uses a hollow triangle. The question’s whole-end description is consistent with the notation, so the hollow shape uniquely identifies aggregation among these alternatives.

evidence.quote: Shared aggregation uses a hollow diamond at the whole end and weak whole-part meaning;

choices.label: A
choices.explanation: Composition uses a filled diamond, not the specified hollow diamond.

choices.label: B
choices.explanation: Dependency is represented by a dashed arrow rather than a whole-part diamond.

choices.label: C
choices.explanation: Shared aggregation uses a hollow diamond placed at the whole end.

choices.label: D
choices.explanation: Generalization uses a hollow triangle toward the general element rather than a diamond.

reviews.answer_text: Composition means strong exclusive ownership; parts may be detached or transferred.
reviews.hint: Read the lifecycle rule for parts that remain owned by a composite.
reviews.explanation: SE18 defines composition by a part being owned by at most one composite at a time and destruction of parts still owned when the composite is destroyed. It also permits detachment or transfer. B is the conventional shorthand only if independence refers to the continuing ownership context; a cannot-ever-exist-independently reading is too absolute. The other alternatives do not state the actual distinction.

evidence.quote: Parts may be detached/transferred under a defined model. Thus “cannot ever exist independently” is an oversimplification.

choices.label: A
choices.explanation: Both relationships concern whole-part modeling; composition is not limited to interfaces.

choices.label: B
choices.explanation: This is intended shorthand, but absolute independent-existence denial ignores permitted detachment or transfer.

choices.label: C
choices.explanation: Aggregation is not inheritance; generalization is the separate specialization relationship.

choices.label: D
choices.explanation: They have different ownership semantics and are not synonymous.

reviews.answer_text: A boundary object is second in the taught layout heuristic, not in a mandatory UML column order.
reviews.hint: Read the distinction between the module’s layout heuristic and UML semantics.
reviews.explanation: SE19 gives actor first, boundary second, control third and entities later as the module’s layout heuristic. C therefore answers under that convention. The note explicitly says this order is not required by UML, so the unrestricted should claim cannot establish a universal column rule. Lifeline placement alone does not determine participant semantics.

evidence.quote: The module’s layout heuristic puts initiating actor first, boundary second, control third, then entities. This is not a required UML column order.

choices.label: A
choices.explanation: The taught convention puts the control object third rather than second.

choices.label: B
choices.explanation: The taught convention puts the initiating actor first rather than second.

choices.label: C
choices.explanation: Boundary second is the documented layout heuristic, conditional on using that convention.

choices.label: D
choices.explanation: Entities follow the boundary/control participants under the taught convention, not necessarily second.

reviews.answer_text: A decision node, also usable as a merge node in the appropriate flow.
reviews.hint: Read activity-diagram node shapes and their flow roles.
reviews.explanation: SE20 names the guarded decision diamond and separately notes that the same shape can merge alternative flows. D is therefore a correct use of the shape, without claiming decision is its only role. Initial nodes are filled circles, actions are rounded, and final-state notation is not the diamond described.

evidence.quote: An activity diagram models workflow: filled circle start, rounded actions, guarded decision diamond,

choices.label: A
choices.explanation: The initial node is a filled circle rather than a diamond.

choices.label: B
choices.explanation: The diamond is not the standard final-state marker in the described notation.

choices.label: C
choices.explanation: Actions are rounded nodes rather than guarded-flow diamonds.

choices.label: D
choices.explanation: A diamond can represent a guarded decision; it can also merge alternative flows.

reviews.answer_text: The degree of dependency between subsystems.
reviews.hint: Read coupling between modules versus cohesion within one.
reviews.explanation: SE22 explicitly distinguishes cohesion within a module from coupling between modules. A describes cohesion; C describes coupling. Interface operation count can affect design complexity but is not the definition of dependence, and an architectural pattern may influence coupling without being the relationship measure itself. The goal is usually low coupling with high cohesion.

evidence.quote: coupling measures dependency between modules.

choices.label: A
choices.explanation: Related purpose inside a subsystem defines cohesion rather than between-subsystem coupling.

choices.label: B
choices.explanation: Operation count alone does not measure the actual dependencies between subsystems.

choices.label: C
choices.explanation: Coupling is the degree of dependency between modules or subsystems.

choices.label: D
choices.explanation: An architectural style can affect coupling but is not its definition.

reviews.answer_text: Calls are restricted to the immediately lower layer.
reviews.hint: Read closed versus open layered dependency rules.
reviews.explanation: SE23 defines a closed layered architecture as allowing calls only to the immediately lower layer. Open layering may permit approved skipping, so B describes a different policy. Closed does not mean no external access or a shared repository; it concerns permitted dependencies between layers rather than the system’s exposure or storage organization.

evidence.quote: A closed layered architecture permits calls only to the immediately lower layer; an open one permits approved skipping.

choices.label: A
choices.explanation: Closed layering restricts interlayer calls, not every form of external access.

choices.label: B
choices.explanation: Skipping freely to deeper layers contradicts the immediate-lower-layer restriction.

choices.label: C
choices.explanation: A layer calls only the immediately lower layer in the defined closed architecture.

choices.label: D
choices.explanation: A central repository is another architectural arrangement and does not define closed layering.

reviews.answer_text: Model–View–Controller.
reviews.hint: Read the separation of domain data, display and interaction control.
reviews.explanation: SE24 explicitly defines MVC as separating a domain model, display view and interaction controller. D names that exact style. Repository, client–server and peer-to-peer organize central data or interacting roles differently; any may be combined with MVC, but none is the name of this particular three-responsibility separation.

evidence.quote: MVC separates domain model, display view and interaction controller.

choices.label: A
choices.explanation: Repository style centers shared data rather than the specific model/view/controller separation.

choices.label: B
choices.explanation: Client–server separates requesters and service providers, not these three presentation-interaction responsibilities.

choices.label: C
choices.explanation: Peer-to-peer allows participants to play requester and provider roles rather than defining MVC components.

choices.label: D
choices.explanation: Model–View–Controller explicitly names the three responsibilities in the question.

reviews.answer_text: The storage layer/tier.
reviews.hint: Read presentation, application logic and persistent storage responsibilities.
reviews.explanation: SE24 separates three-tier presentation, application logic and storage. Persistent data storage and retrieval belong to the storage responsibility, whereas presentation handles interaction and application logic coordinates domain behavior. The question uses layer for a tier-style role; that terminology does not change which responsibility owns persistence.

evidence.quote: Three-tier separates presentation, application logic and storage;

choices.label: A
choices.explanation: The interface responsibility handles interaction rather than persistent storage and querying.

choices.label: B
choices.explanation: Application logic coordinates domain operations but delegates persistence to the storage responsibility.

choices.label: C
choices.explanation: The storage role handles persistent data, including retrieval and queries.

choices.label: D
choices.explanation: Presentation formats user interaction and output rather than owning persistent data storage.

reviews.answer_text: Boundary objects.
reviews.hint: Read entity, boundary and control roles in the analysis object model.
reviews.explanation: SE13 defines boundary objects as mediating interaction, with ReportForm as an example. That is the bridge between external actors and the system. Entity objects hold domain information, while controls coordinate use cases. Interface objects is a generic descriptive phrase, but boundary is the explicitly defined analysis-category name requested among these choices.

evidence.quote: boundary objects mediate interaction, such as ReportForm;

choices.label: A
choices.explanation: Entity objects represent domain information rather than the actor-facing interaction bridge.

choices.label: B
choices.explanation: Control objects coordinate use-case behavior rather than primarily mediate actor interaction.

choices.label: C
choices.explanation: Boundary objects are explicitly defined as mediating system–actor interaction.

choices.label: D
choices.explanation: Interface objects is not the named entity/boundary/control category specified by the note’s analysis model.

reviews.answer_text: The control-object identification heuristic.
reviews.hint: Read candidate control objects as a starting heuristic rather than a mandatory UML count.
reviews.explanation: SE13 permits one control per use case or participating actor as a useful starting point, while denying a mandatory UML rule. The stem already asks for a heuristic, so B correctly identifies the control-object selection guideline. CRC, boundary identification and column layout concern different tasks; none makes the count a required lifetime or architecture constraint.

evidence.quote: A control per use case or participating actor can be a useful starting point, not a mandatory UML rule or fixed object lifetime.

choices.label: A
choices.explanation: CRC records class responsibilities and collaborators rather than prescribing this candidate-control count.

choices.label: B
choices.explanation: This is the heuristic for identifying candidate use-case control objects, not a universal UML constraint.

choices.label: C
choices.explanation: Boundary heuristics identify interaction-facing objects rather than coordinating controls.

choices.label: D
choices.explanation: Sequence-column layout orders participants visually and does not define candidate control-object counts.

reviews.answer_text: Class, Responsibilities, Collaborators.
reviews.hint: Read the three fields represented by CRC cards.
reviews.explanation: SE13 expands CRC directly as Class, Responsibilities, Collaborators. The card identifies the class, what it must do or know, and which other objects help fulfill those responsibilities. The distractors replace these terms with requirements, components or unrelated design concepts and therefore do not preserve the stated expansion.

evidence.quote: CRC means Class, Responsibilities, Collaborators.

choices.label: A
choices.explanation: Requirements and Conditions are not the R and final C in the stated expansion.

choices.label: B
choices.explanation: Component, Relationship and Constraints do not match the class-card terminology.

choices.label: C
choices.explanation: This is the exact CRC expansion supplied in SE13.

choices.label: D
choices.explanation: Control, Reuse and Composition are different concepts rather than the CRC card fields.

reviews.answer_text: Zero or more instances.
reviews.hint: Read lower and upper bounds at an association end.
reviews.explanation: SE17 defines 0..* as any nonnegative number. Zero is allowed and the star places no finite upper bound, so C fits. The alternatives correspond to 1, 0..1 and 1..* respectively. Multiplicity at one end is interpreted relative to one object at the opposite end, not as a whole-system object count.

evidence.quote: 0..* any nonnegative number, 1..* at least one.

choices.label: A
choices.explanation: Exactly one corresponds to multiplicity 1 rather than 0..*.

choices.label: B
choices.explanation: Optional single-valued multiplicity is 0..1, not an unbounded star.

choices.label: C
choices.explanation: Zero is permitted and the upper star allows any number of related instances.

choices.label: D
choices.explanation: One or more requires lower bound 1, written 1..*.

reviews.answer_text: Verb phrases expressing relationships, such as manages or reports to.
reviews.hint: Read language heuristics for candidate objects, attributes and associations.
reviews.explanation: SE13 recommends nouns as candidate objects and verbs such as manages/reports-to as candidate associations. B is the relationship-phrase option. Adjectives generally describe properties, repeated nouns do not automatically imply an association, and UI terms suggest boundary concerns. These are candidate-identification heuristics rather than a proof that every verb must become a modeled link.

evidence.quote: Use nouns as candidate objects, possessive descriptions as candidate attributes, and verbs such as manages/reports-to as candidate associations.

choices.label: A
choices.explanation: Property descriptions suggest attributes rather than directly identifying links between classes.

choices.label: B
choices.explanation: Relationship verbs are the note’s direct heuristic for candidate associations.

choices.label: C
choices.explanation: Noun frequency is not the stated association-identification rule; nouns instead suggest candidate objects.

choices.label: D
choices.explanation: UI terminology may suggest boundaries but does not directly establish an association between domain classes.

reviews.answer_text: Black-box testing.
reviews.hint: Read specified behavior versus internal structure as the source of test cases.
reviews.explanation: SE36 contrasts black-box cases derived from required behavior with white-box cases derived from implementation structure. Grey-box uses partial internal knowledge. The question excludes internal-code knowledge, so black-box is the appropriate technique. Structural testing instead refers to the very internal paths or statements that this scenario does not inspect.

evidence.quote: Black-box techniques derive cases from specified behavior; white-box techniques derive them from internal structure; grey-box uses partial internal knowledge.

choices.label: A
choices.explanation: White-box testing explicitly uses internal implementation structure to derive cases.

choices.label: B
choices.explanation: Grey-box testing uses partial internal knowledge rather than excluding it.

choices.label: C
choices.explanation: Black-box testing derives cases from externally specified behavior without needing code structure.

choices.label: D
choices.explanation: Structural testing is based on internal control or code structure, contrary to the stem.

reviews.answer_text: Unit testing.
reviews.hint: Read isolation of a function, class or small component.
reviews.explanation: SE35 defines unit testing as isolating a function, class or small component, often replacing dependencies with stubs or mocks. Integration checks combined interactions and system testing evaluates the whole system. Regression describes testing after changes and can occur at different levels, so it is not the isolation level named by the question.

evidence.quote: Unit testing isolates a function, class or small component, often replacing dependencies with stubs/mocks;

choices.label: A
choices.explanation: System testing evaluates the complete integrated system rather than an isolated component.

choices.label: B
choices.explanation: Integration testing focuses on interactions among combined parts, not isolation.

choices.label: C
choices.explanation: Regression checks unintended effects after change and is not inherently a component-isolation level.

choices.label: D
choices.explanation: Unit testing evaluates a small component in isolation, with dependencies replaceable by test doubles.

reviews.answer_text: Performance testing, specifically load-oriented testing under expected demand.
reviews.hint: Read speed and resource measurements under a stated workload.
reviews.explanation: SE36 defines performance tests as assessing speed, throughput and resource use under a specified workload and distinguishes expected load from stress beyond normal limits. The stem explicitly adds workload and response speed, so it supports performance testing rather than merely a vague normal-condition test. Usability, reliability and compatibility target different quality questions.

evidence.quote: Performance tests assess speed, throughput and resources under a specified workload; load uses expected demands and stress exceeds normal limits.

choices.label: A
choices.explanation: Usability focuses on task success and ease of use rather than response-speed measurements under load.

choices.label: B
choices.explanation: Reliability concerns failure-free service, not primarily the stated response-time criterion.

choices.label: C
choices.explanation: Speed under an expected workload is performance/load testing as defined in SE36.

choices.label: D
choices.explanation: Compatibility examines cooperating environments rather than the specified speed-under-load behavior.

reviews.answer_text: The functional model.
reviews.hint: Read the functional, structural and dynamic parts of the analysis model.
reviews.explanation: SE13 explicitly associates use cases and scenarios with functional modeling, classes with structural/object modeling, and states/interactions with dynamic modeling. Thus C names the requested description of what the system should do. The alternatives describe state-dependent behavior or static object structure rather than this user-goal and scenario view.

evidence.quote: Analysis integrates functional (use cases/scenarios), structural/object (classes) and dynamic (states/interactions) models.

choices.label: A
choices.explanation: Dynamic models emphasize states and interactions rather than the named use-case/scenario category.

choices.label: B
choices.explanation: The analysis object model captures classes and relationships rather than the functional use-case view.

choices.label: C
choices.explanation: Use cases and scenarios are explicitly the functional analysis model.

choices.label: D
choices.explanation: Structural modeling describes static classes and links rather than required user-goal flows.

reviews.answer_text: State machines suit objects with significant event-dependent states; no universal most-common object category is established.
reviews.hint: Read behavioral significance rather than choosing by object stereotype alone.
reviews.explanation: SE20 says state machines are useful for objects with significant states, whether entity or control. That supports model selection by lifecycle behavior, not a universal frequency ranking across analysis categories. C may reflect a course control-object convention, but entities can have rich lifecycles too. The stem supplies neither the system’s behaviors nor a defined most-common convention.

evidence.quote: State machines are useful for objects with significant states, whether entity or control.

choices.label: A
choices.explanation: Entities with important lifecycle states can benefit from state machines; the note does not rank their frequency.

choices.label: B
choices.explanation: A boundary with meaningful event-driven modes may be modeled, but its stereotype alone does not establish need.

choices.label: C
choices.explanation: Control objects can have important states and are a plausible teaching convention, not universally most common.

choices.label: D
choices.explanation: Suitability depends on significant state behavior, not an equal need for every object.

reviews.answer_text: ReportEmergencyButton.
reviews.hint: Read the documented ReportEmergency interaction order.
reviews.explanation: SE19 explicitly says FieldOfficer activates ReportEmergencyButton, supplies details through EmergencyReportForm and later sees AcknowledgmentNotice. DispatcherStation belongs to the dispatcher side. Therefore the button initiates this particular scenario; the form handles later input and the notice reports completion. This is grounded in the named example rather than a generic rule that every use case starts with a button.

evidence.quote: In ReportEmergency, FieldOfficer activates ReportEmergencyButton, enters details through EmergencyReportForm, and later sees AcknowledgmentNotice;

choices.label: A
choices.explanation: The form receives incident details after initiation rather than starting the documented scenario.

choices.label: B
choices.explanation: The acknowledgment is seen later as feedback, not used to initiate reporting.

choices.label: C
choices.explanation: The note explicitly identifies this button as the FieldOfficer’s initiating boundary object.

choices.label: D
choices.explanation: DispatcherStation is on the dispatcher side rather than the FieldOfficer’s initiation interface.

reviews.answer_text: A general concept with more-specific specializations.
reviews.hint: Read UML generalization and its arrow toward the general element.
reviews.explanation: SE16 relates a specialized actor or use case to a more general one; SE18 gives the corresponding class generalization toward a superclass. B expresses that abstraction/specialization relationship. It does not merely package unrelated classes, create an external interface or split classes while denying shared general properties.

evidence.quote: Generalization relates a specialized actor/use case to a more general one, with a hollow triangle toward the general element.

choices.label: A
choices.explanation: Specialization is related through a general concept rather than requiring no shared properties.

choices.label: B
choices.explanation: Generalization identifies the common general element of which other concepts are more specific versions.

choices.label: C
choices.explanation: External communication interfaces do not by themselves define a generalization relationship.

choices.label: D
choices.explanation: Packaging unrelated classes is organizational grouping rather than specialization of a shared general concept.

reviews.answer_text: Related responsibilities within a subsystem, limited dependencies between subsystems.
reviews.hint: Read cohesion inside modules and coupling between them.
reviews.explanation: SE22 defines cohesion as related purpose within a module and coupling as dependency across modules, then recommends high cohesion and low coupling. B states both dimensions. It does not require minimal functionality, tight cross-connections or one shared repository; those choices can undermine coherent responsibilities or increase dependency rather than establish the principle.

evidence.quote: Cohesion measures how well elements inside a module serve a related purpose; coupling measures dependency between modules. Seek high cohesion and low coupling.

choices.label: A
choices.explanation: Tight interconnection increases coupling rather than meeting the low-coupling goal.

choices.label: B
choices.explanation: Closely related internal responsibilities and limited external dependencies express both parts of the principle.

choices.label: C
choices.explanation: Cohesion concerns related purpose, not simply having as little functionality as possible.

choices.label: D
choices.explanation: A shared repository is a style choice and can create dependencies; it does not define cohesion or coupling.

reviews.answer_text: Safety-critical government context does not universally make Agile least appropriate.
reviews.hint: Read process selection using explicit assurance obligations and allowed adaptations.
reviews.explanation: SE42 explicitly rejects the blanket Agile-least-suitable claim, and SE05 permits Agile combined with required documentation and assurance. Stable requirements can favor waterfall or the V-model, while spiral may manage risks, but these facts do not rank every allowed implementation. Selecting C uniquely requires a specified lightweight process that cannot meet the actual contractual assurance obligations, absent here.

evidence.quote: “Agile least suitable for safety-critical government work” assumes a particular lightweight process without required assurance; it is not universally true.

choices.label: A
choices.explanation: Stable requirements can favor waterfall, but suitability still depends on the stated assurance and feedback needs.

choices.label: B
choices.explanation: The V-model’s test planning can suit strong assurance, without proving a universal ranking of alternatives.

choices.label: C
choices.explanation: Agile can include required assurance and documentation; only a specified incompatible variant would justify exclusion.

choices.label: D
choices.explanation: Spiral’s risk focus may suit critical uncertainty, but overhead and risk profile are unspecified.

reviews.answer_text: Modeled destruction of the object at that point.
reviews.hint: Read the lifeline-destruction marker separately from runtime garbage collection.
reviews.explanation: SE19 explicitly identifies X as modeled destruction, so C is correct in UML diagram semantics. Temporary inactivity and waiting do not end an object’s modeled existence, and a recursive message is represented by an interaction rather than destruction. The marker does not guarantee the runtime moment at which a garbage collector reclaims memory.

evidence.quote: an X marks modeled destruction, not a guarantee about when a garbage collector runs.

choices.label: A
choices.explanation: Temporary inactivity does not terminate the object’s lifeline.

choices.label: B
choices.explanation: Waiting for a message does not mean the modeled object has been destroyed.

choices.label: C
choices.explanation: X marks the object’s modeled destruction at that point, not necessarily immediate memory reclamation.

choices.label: D
choices.explanation: A recursive call is an interaction message and does not use the destruction marker.

reviews.answer_text: SIZE controls approximate visible text-input width.
reviews.hint: Distinguish displayed width from an entered-character limit.
reviews.explanation: WEB09 distinguishes size from maxlength: size describes the approximate visible width of a text input, while maxlength limits how much text can be entered. That matches the stem’s focus on characters displayed without scrolling. VALUE provides initial content and TYPE selects the control kind; neither is the width-setting attribute requested here.

evidence.quote: For a text input, size indicates approximate visible width, whereas maxlength limits entered text length.

choices.label: A
choices.explanation: SIZE controls approximate visible width for a text input, matching the display-without-scrolling description.

choices.label: B
choices.explanation: MAXLENGTH limits entered text length rather than determining how wide the input appears.

choices.label: C
choices.explanation: VALUE supplies the control’s content, not its visible character-width setting.

choices.label: D
choices.explanation: TYPE selects the input-control kind rather than its approximate visible width.

reviews.answer_text: The benefits are conditional; the absolute wording does not establish one unique false claim.
reviews.hint: Read external CSS reuse, caching, and the limits of accessibility guarantees.
reviews.explanation: WEB11 supports reuse, consistent design, and caching, but explicitly denies guaranteed smaller pages or accessibility. D is false as an absolute denial of possible file savings; A is also too strong if read as a guarantee, because CSS alone does not establish accessibility. The stem does not distinguish possible benefits from universal effects, so its literal assertions lack a unique false option.

evidence.quote: External CSS promotes reuse, consistent design and caching; it does not guarantee that every page becomes smaller or accessible.

choices.label: A
choices.explanation: CSS can support accessibility, but styling alone does not guarantee it, making the unqualified assertion too broad.

choices.label: B
choices.explanation: Shared rules can create a consistent appearance, though consistency depends on the rules actually being applied.

choices.label: C
choices.explanation: Centralized reusable styles can ease maintenance, but this is a benefit rather than an unconditional guarantee.

choices.label: D
choices.explanation: An absolute denial of size savings is false when repeated markup is replaced or stylesheets are cached.

reviews.hint: Read absolute value as nonnegative magnitude.
reviews.explanation: WEB18 explicitly evaluates Math.abs(-9) as 9. Absolute value removes the negative sign from a negative numeric argument and leaves its magnitude, so the result is neither the original negative number nor a Boolean-like one or zero. This is an expression result; no rounding or text conversion is involved.

evidence.quote: Math.abs(-9)=9, Math.floor(5.9)=5, and Math.sqrt(36)=6.

choices.label: A
choices.explanation: The absolute value of negative nine is its nonnegative magnitude, nine.

choices.label: B
choices.explanation: Negative nine is the input; absolute value does not preserve its negative sign.

choices.label: C
choices.explanation: Math.abs returns numeric magnitude rather than a Boolean-like value of one.

choices.label: D
choices.explanation: The input is nonzero, so its absolute value is not zero.

reviews.answer_text: The broad capability claims depend on sandbox and API context.
reviews.hint: Separate language expressiveness from permission-based browser access.
reviews.explanation: WEB01 says JavaScript supports sophisticated applications and that browser scripts can access selected files or devices through permission-based APIs. Thus A’s lack-of-features claim is false as a general statement. B can be true for permitted hardware APIs but false if it means unrestricted access; C can mean sandbox restrictions or language limitations. Those unresolved meanings prevent a unique false literal claim.

evidence.quote: Browser scripts are sandboxed, but may access selected files/devices through permission-based APIs. They are not inherently limited to trivial programs, nor can they freely access arbitrary client hardware.

choices.label: A
choices.explanation: A blanket claim that scripting languages are not full-featured conflicts with the note’s sophisticated JavaScript applications.

choices.label: B
choices.explanation: Selected hardware access may be permitted; unrestricted hardware access is blocked by the browser sandbox.

choices.label: C
choices.explanation: Sandbox restrictions are real, but limited language expressiveness is not established; the intended meaning is unspecified.

choices.label: D
choices.explanation: Plain-text scripts can be run by applications, but this description does not settle the other broad capability claims.

reviews.answer_text: Extracted code errors (D); the inspected original prints 44 (A).

reviews.explanation: The current extracted x=4+"4"5 has no operator before 5, so it is a syntax error and fits D. I inspected the saved image: it instead shows x=4+"4"; and document.write(x), which prints 44 by string concatenation and fits A. WEB41 records this conflict. reviews.answer_text: CSS controls presentation rather than generating server-side pages.
reviews.hint: Compare presentation rules with server-response technologies.
reviews.explanation: WEB01 assigns CSS presentation and identifies PHP, JSP/Java, and ASP.NET applications as generating server responses. In this role distinction, CSS is the exclusion: it styles a representation rather than executing the server page-generation logic. CSS can affect displayed appearance, but that does not make it a server-side dynamic-page generator like the other offered technologies.

choices.explanation: JSP/Java applications are identified in WEB01 as server-side response generators.

choices.explanation: PHP applications can generate server responses and access databases, fitting dynamic-page generation.

choices.explanation: CSS supplies presentation rules rather than the server logic that generates dynamic page representations.

choices.label: D
choices.explanation: ASP.NET applications are identified as server-side response generators, so they are not the exclusion.

reviews.answer_text: None of the listed functions is a standard PHP MySQL TLS connection API.
reviews.hint: Read the MySQLi initialize, TLS-option, and real-connect sequence.
reviews.explanation: WEB31 specifies mysqli_init(), mysqli_ssl_set(), and mysqli_real_connect() with verification settings, or PDO driver TLS options. It explicitly says none of the four offered names is standard. Therefore no supplied function can be selected as the literal correct answer. This is an option-set defect, not missing SSL coverage in the new note.

evidence.quote: None of mysqli_ssl_connect(), pdo_connect_ssl(), mysql_ssl_connect() or secure_connect() is the standard offered function.

choices.explanation: mysqli_ssl_connect() is not the standard API; configure TLS options and call mysqli_real_connect instead.

choices.label: B
choices.explanation: PDO uses a driver DSN and options, not the invented pdo_connect_ssl() function.

choices.label: C
choices.explanation: mysql_ssl_connect() is not a standard offered function, and legacy mysql_* APIs are removed in PHP8.

choices.label: D

reviews.answer_text: file_exists()
reviews.hint: Distinguish existence of any filesystem entry from the regular-file-only check.
reviews.explanation: WEB30 directly distinguishes file_exists, which tests files or directories, from is_file, which narrows the test to regular files. The question explicitly includes either a file or directory, so file_exists matches. The other two named checks are not the provided APIs, while is_file is too restrictive for the requested test.

evidence.quote: file_exists tests files or directories; is_file narrows to regular files.

choices.label: A
choices.explanation: file_exists() checks existence for files or directories, exactly the two entry kinds in the stem.

choices.label: B
choices.explanation: file_exists_check() is not the filesystem existence API identified by the complete note.

choices.label: C
choices.explanation: is_file() tests regular files and would not report an existing directory as a regular file.

choices.label: D
choices.explanation: file_check() is not the filesystem existence API given in WEB30.

reviews.answer_text: The database API and a valid signature are missing; no bare offered function is established.
reviews.hint: Separate result-row counts from affected-row counts and identify MySQLi versus PDO.
reviews.explanation: WEB32 names mysqli_affected_rows($conn) for changed, inserted, or deleted rows and distinguishes result-row counts. WEB31 explicitly warns that affected_rows() alone is not a generic PHP function. No option supplies the actual procedural name or a defined object context, and row_count() is not PDOStatement::rowCount(). Thus the intended concept is clear, but none of the literal offered function calls is established.

evidence.quote: MySQLi procedural functions, object methods and PDO methods have distinct signatures; affected_rows() alone is not a generic PHP function.

choices.label: A
choices.explanation: num_rows concerns result rows rather than changed rows, and no valid procedural or object context is supplied.

choices.label: B

reviews.answer_text: Stored response delivery is supported; universal rendered-content claims are too broad.
reviews.hint: Separate static response bytes from browser-script changes.
reviews.explanation: WEB02 says a basic static server returns stored files but static pages can still run interactive browser scripts. Thus C describes stored response delivery, whereas A and D are too broad if content means the live rendered page. The note does not define the flat/stationary naming claim in B. Without identifying delivery versus rendered content, All cannot be established and the statements are not uniquely classifiable.

evidence.quote: A basic static server returns stored files; dynamic processing constructs a representation from logic, requests or data. Static pages can still run interactive browser scripts, and dynamic generation need not change visible text every time.

choices.label: A
choices.explanation: Stored file bytes require file changes, but a static page’s rendered content can change through browser scripts.

choices.label: B

choices.label: C
choices.explanation: A basic static server delivers stored representation bytes; this is supported when content means the served file.

choices.label: D
choices.explanation: The same stored file can produce viewer-dependent or interactive rendering, so the universal visible-content reading fails.

choices.label: E
choices.explanation: All requires every preceding claim under one meaning, which the delivery/rendering distinction and unsupported synonyms do not establish.

reviews.answer_text: PHP and Python are both server-side languages; ASP is a platform label.

reviews.explanation: WEB01 explicitly identifies PHP and Python applications as server-response generators, so both language choices satisfy the stem. ASP denotes server-page technology rather than naming a particular scripting language; the note discusses ASP.NET applications in the same role distinction. Treating the broad technology name as a language is what would make All appear plausible. At least PHP and Python independently fit the literal language question.

evidence.quote: PHP, Python, JSP/Java and ASP.NET applications generate server responses and access databases; C# is commonly used with ASP.NET.

choices.label: B

choices.label: C
choices.explanation: Python is explicitly identified as a language used for server-response applications.

choices.label: D
choices.explanation: All conflates the two clear language names with ASP’s platform or page-technology label.

reviews.answer_text: $_REQUEST can combine GET and POST input according to configuration.
reviews.hint: Read PHP request superglobals and their source distinctions.
reviews.explanation: WEB27 states that $_GET contains query parameters and $_POST supported form POST data, while $_REQUEST may combine GET, POST, and cookie data according to configuration. evidence.quote: $_REQUEST may combine GET/POST/cookie data according to configuration; it is not a database interface and has ambiguous precedence, so prefer the intended source.

choices.explanation: $_REQUEST can combine GET and POST values according to PHP configuration, matching the combined-source question.

choices.label: B
choices.explanation: $_POST holds supported form POST data and does not generally combine query GET values.

choices.label: C
choices.explanation: $_GET holds URL query parameters rather than combining both query and form POST sources.

choices.label: D
choices.explanation: Adding $_POST to the already combined $_REQUEST is redundant and is not the single combined mechanism requested.

reviews.answer_text: All listed connection inputs have signature defaults; database is not uniquely optional.

reviews.explanation: WEB31 gives the host, user, password, database, port, and socket signature and states that defaults make several arguments technically optional. choices.label: B

choices.label: C
choices.explanation: Username has a defaulted connection input; omission is permitted even though usable credentials are still required.

choices.label: D
choices.explanation: Password has a defaulted input; omitting it is syntactically possible without guaranteeing authentication success.

reviews.answer_text: The CSS removes bullets and default spacing, but the correct choice label is corrupted.

reviews.answer_text: Always serving the same prebuilt content is the static-generation description.

choices.label: D
choices.explanation: Server-side applications can access databases while constructing dynamic responses, as described in WEB01.

reviews.answer_text: An associated label gives the input an accessible name.

reviews.explanation: WEB09 connects a label’s for value to the control’s id. WEB07 requires programmatic labels for accessibility. That association does not store the form offline, encrypt data, or increase submission speed; its purpose here is accessible identification of the control.

evidence.quote: A label’s for matches the control’s id; name identifies its submitted field.

choices.label: A
choices.explanation: Label association identifies a control and does not create offline form storage.

choices.label: B

choices.label: C
choices.explanation: Linking a label to an input does not increase network or form-submission speed.

choices.label: D
choices.explanation: The associated label provides accessible control identification that screen readers can announce on focus.

reviews.answer_text: <pre> preserves program-listing whitespace.

A paragraph does not preserve the listing’s whitespace by itself, head is metadata, and sub marks a subscript. Therefore <pre> is the matching listed tag.

evidence.quote: <pre> preserves source whitespace; <code> marks code.

choices.label: D

reviews.answer_text: The stem conflates entered-length limits with visible width.

choices.label: D

reviews.answer_text: Float is not a separate JavaScript primitive type.

The broad wording therefore fails to identify one unique true claim; this is question ambiguity rather than an essential missing study-note rule.

evidence.quote: JavaScript originated at Netscape; it is distinct from Java and supports sophisticated applications through prototype-based objects and first-class functions.

choices.label: A
choices.explanation: Conventional Java class-based and JavaScript prototype-based object-oriented usage makes this another plausible true claim; WEB15 supplies the JavaScript part.

choices.label: B
choices.explanation: The exact compilation-and-interpretation phrase needs an execution-model definition absent from this course note.

choices.label: C
choices.explanation: The note explicitly states that JavaScript supports sophisticated applications.

choices.label: D
choices.explanation: No shared feature definition or counting metric is supplied for ranking JavaScript against Java.

reviews.hint: Read Math.floor as rounding downward.
reviews.explanation: WEB18 directly evaluates Math.floor(5.9)=5. The floor operation gives the greatest integer not exceeding the input, rather than rounding to the nearest integer or multiplying the input. Thus the fractional part does not push the result up to six; the expression value is five. No string or DOM behavior changes this math result.

evidence.quote: Math.abs(-9)=9, Math.floor(5.9)=5, and Math.sqrt(36)=6.

choices.label: A
choices.explanation: Nine is not the integer floor of 5.9; it is merely a digit appearing in the input.

choices.label: B
choices.explanation: 11.8 doubles the input and is unrelated to the floor operation.

choices.label: C
choices.explanation: Six would be upward or nearest-integer rounding here, not floor.

choices.label: D
choices.explanation: Five is the greatest integer no larger than 5.9, matching the explicit note example.

reviews.hint: Read the nonnegative square root.
reviews.explanation: WEB18 explicitly states Math.sqrt(36)=6. Six squared gives thirty-six, and this function returns the nonnegative square root rather than the original operand or an arithmetic difference. The expression is already a valid numeric function call and needs no parsing repair or context-dependent type coercion to obtain the stated result.

evidence.quote: Math.abs(-9)=9, Math.floor(5.9)=5, and Math.sqrt(36)=6.

choices.label: A
choices.explanation: Six is the nonnegative square root of thirty-six, exactly as WEB18 evaluates it.

choices.label: B
choices.explanation: Thirty is not a square root of thirty-six and does not match the defined function.

choices.label: C
choices.explanation: One squared is one, not thirty-six, so it cannot be the result.

choices.label: D
choices.explanation: Thirty-six is the input; sqrt does not simply return it unchanged.

reviews.answer_text: location.reload()
reviews.hint: Read the browser location reload method.
reviews.explanation: WEB22 explicitly says location.reload() reloads the current page. D names that method; it must be called with parentheses to perform the reload. The other alternatives invent relocate or refresh names not identified as the standard method in the note. This operation acts on the current browsing location rather than creating a new page context.

evidence.quote: location.reload() reloads the current page.

choices.label: A
choices.explanation: location.relocate is not the reload method identified in the browser API rule.

choices.label: B
choices.explanation: window.relocate is not the reload method given in WEB22.

choices.label: C
choices.explanation: window.refresh is not the standard reload method described by the supplied note.

choices.label: D
choices.explanation: Calling location.reload() reloads the current page; the option names that method.

reviews.answer_text: Use .className, but the option symbols are corrupted.
reviews.hint: Read the dot-prefixed CSS class selector.
reviews.explanation: WEB11 defines .notice as a class selector and #logo as an ID selector. The offered symbols contain damaged text Oca and Ne. rather than a recoverable .className option. A visible trailing dot cannot safely be reassigned as the entire correct choice. The missing original symbol mapping must be restored before a letter can be selected.

evidence.quote: Type p selects paragraph elements, .notice selects a class, #logo an ID

choices.label: A

choices.label: B

choices.label: D

reviews.answer_text: Request line plus headers fits HTTP/1.x; the word always needs a version.
reviews.hint: Read request-message structure and distinguish HTTP/1.x from HTTP2/3 framing.
reviews.explanation: The saved image confirms D says a request line and a header. WEB03 gives that structure for HTTP/1.1, with a blank line and optional body. It also says HTTP2/3 use different message encoding, so a textual request line is not universal. Thus D is the intended HTTP/1.x answer, but the literal always claim lacks a version qualifier.

evidence.quote: HTTP2/3 encode messages differently, so an “always contains a request line” question needs HTTP/1.x context.

choices.label: A
choices.explanation: An HTTP/1.x request also has a request line, so a header only omits its start line.

choices.label: B
choices.explanation: A request body is optional; even the supplied GET example can have none.

choices.label: C
choices.explanation: A status line belongs to a response, not a request, and a request body is not mandatory.

choices.label: D
choices.explanation: The inspected image supports this text for HTTP/1.x; it is not an always rule across HTTP2/3 encodings.

reviews.answer_text: itex
reviews.hint: Use zero-based start-inclusive, end-exclusive substring indices.
reviews.explanation: WEB18 explicitly gives exitexam.substring(2,6) as itex. Counting from zero yields index 2=i, 3=t, 4=e, and 5=x; index 6 is excluded. The saved image confirms the same source and options. The stray itex after the prompt is outside the script and does not change the code’s substring result.

evidence.quote: "exitexam".substring(2,6) is "itex".

choices.label: A
choices.explanation: xitex starts at index one and contains five characters, rather than the requested four-character interval.

choices.label: B

choices.label: C
choices.explanation: Indices two through five contain i, t, e, x, producing itex.

choices.label: D
choices.explanation: xite begins at index one rather than the specified zero-based start index two.

reviews.answer_text: GET
reviews.hint: Read the default HTML form submission method.
reviews.explanation: WEB09 explicitly says a form’s default method is GET. Therefore omitting the method attribute does not select POST or PUT. WEB04 further distinguishes GET query parameters from POST form bodies, but that difference does not change the default. Set is not the relevant form submission method named in the note.

evidence.quote: The default method is GET.

choices.label: A
choices.explanation: GET is the default method for an HTML form when its method attribute is omitted.

choices.label: B
choices.explanation: Set is not the default HTML form submission method defined by the note.

choices.label: D
choices.explanation: PUT is not the default method selected by an ordinary HTML form.

reviews.answer_text: Inside a function
reviews.hint: Read local bindings separately from global declarations.
reviews.explanation: WEB25 states that a function’s locals and by-value parameters are separate bindings from variables outside it. Thus a variable declared inside a function has ordinary local scope, unless a special explicit global binding is introduced. Outside function is the global-scope location, while outside program is not a meaningful declaration location in the script.

evidence.quote: A function’s locals and by-value parameters are separate bindings

choices.label: A
choices.explanation: Outside program does not describe a declaration location within the executing PHP script.

choices.label: B
choices.explanation: An ordinary declaration inside a function creates a local binding for that function.

choices.label: C
